en: The Five Lamps Compendium, Volume One:

The Seven Buddhas and Ancient Buddhas have appeared throughout the world in an endless succession; it is impossible to know them all or enumerate them completely. Therefore, I shall now discuss those who appeared in recent times.
In the Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Tathāgatas; yet, up to the time of Śākyamuni, only seven Buddhas have been recorded. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
"By the power of the diligence of the seven Buddhas, they emitted light to extinguish the darkness. Each sat beneath a tree and therein attained perfect enlightenment."

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of the seven Buddhas. When the Great Being Jinhuashanhuī ascended the summit of Mount Song to practice the Way, he was moved by a vision of the seven Buddhas leading before him and Vimalakīrti following behind. Thus, the present compilation begins from the seven Buddhas downward.
Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "The body arises from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is fundamentally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, having no place of abiding."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Kṣatriya caste, his clan name being Kauṛilya.
His father was Bandhu, and his mother was Bandhumatī. He resided in the city of Bandhumatī and sat beneath a Pāṭali tree.
He preached the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people. He possessed two disciples of supernatural power; the first was named Khaṇḍa.
Tea. His second name was Tiṣya. His attendant was Aśoka-putra Fangying.

Śikhin Buddha (the ninth of nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣita-kalpa*) spoke in verse: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the commission of all evil karma is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam, the mind is like the wind; they are illusory manifestations, rootless and devoid of real nature. (*Dīrgha Āgama*)
The *Saṃyuktāgama* states: When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Kauruṣya;

his father was Mingxiang (Vimalaprabha) and his mother was Guangyao (Prabhāvatī). He resided in the city of Guangxiang (Prabhāvatī), sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree, and preached the Dharma in three assemblies.
He delivered two hundred and fifty thousand people. He had two disciples with supernormal powers: the first was named Abhibhū and the second was named Vāsavagriva.
His attendant was the son of Kṣāntivādin, Ananta.

Vipaśyin Buddha (the first of the thousand Buddhas of the *Kṛtayuga*/*Tsan-yang-chieh*): The verse says: "By borrowing the four great elements, one forms a body; The mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects.
If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist; Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was named Good Lamp (Sudīpa) and his mother was named Renowned Precepts (Śīlaghoṣā). He resided in the city of Anupama and sat beneath a *bala* tree.

He held two assemblies for preaching the Dharma, through which he delivered one hundred and thirty thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Ayuvyuha and Uttara. His attendant was the son of Śānti, named Subuddhi.
Krakucchanda Buddha (the first of the Buddhas currently appearing in the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body;
To understand that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, How does such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brahmin caste and the Kāśyapa clan.
His father was named Li-de; his mother, Shan-zhi. He resided in the city of An-he, where he sat beneath a Śirīṣa tree and delivered a single assembly of teachings, delivering forty thousand people.
His two disciples with supernormal powers were Sa-ni and Pi-lou. His attendant was Shan-jue-zi, and his chief disciple was Shang-sheng.
The Buddha Kanakamuni (the second of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha;

If there were truly a knowing, there would be no Buddha apart from it. The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; Thus they remain composed and are not terrified by birth and death. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brahmin caste, and his clan name was Kāśyapa.
His father was Mahābhūti; his mother was Sujayā. He resided in the city of Śuddhavatī and sat beneath an Udumbara tree as a brahmin to preach the Dharma.
In a single assembly, he delivered the teaching and saved thirty thousand people. He had two disciples with supernormal powers: first, Śubhananda, and second, Uttara.
His attendant was the son of Anurādha, named Vinayaśikṣaka.
Kāśyapa Buddha (the third of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa) spoke in verse: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Brahmin caste, his clan name was Kāśyapa, and his father was Brahmā.

The Buddha, whose mother was the laywoman Dhanañjānī, resided in the city of Vārāṇasī. Seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, he delivered a single discourse on the Dharma, through which he liberated twenty thousand people.
He possessed two disciples with supernormal powers: first, Tiṣya, and second, Bhāradvāja. His attendant was the son of a good friend, Sañjayin.
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Śuddhodana; his mother was Queen Māyādevī.
Having attained the stage of the Bodhisattva destined for Buddhahood, he was born in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was named the Devaputra Viśeṣacintin, also known as the Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi.

There he delivered the celestial hosts, expounded the practices of the Bodhisattva destined for Buddhahood, manifested his body throughout the worlds of the ten directions to preach the Dharma, and universally illuminated all beings.
The Sūtra says: When the Buddha was first born into the family of the Kṣatriyas, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Golden lotuses sprang up from the earth, spontaneously supporting his two feet. He took seven steps each toward the east and west, as well as the north and south.
Pointing his fingers at heaven and earth, he uttered a lion’s roar: "In the zenith and nadir, and in the four intermediate directions, there is none who is my superior. Thus it is said.
It was the eighth day of the fourth month in the forty-second year of King Zhao of Zhou, the year of Jiayin (the twenty-fourth year of his reign).
At the age of nineteen, he desired to leave the household life and thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?
He then went out for excursions through the four gates and witnessed the four signs; with feelings of both sorrow and joy arising in his heart, he reflected: "This is old age... this is sickness..."
Death is ultimately something to be weary of and renounced. Then, at the hour of midnight, a deva named Śuddhāvāsa appeared at the window, joined his palms, and said:
"The time for your renunciation has arrived; you may depart. Upon hearing this, the Prince felt great joy in his heart and immediately leaped over the city wall and went away.
He practiced the Way on Mount Daṇḍaka, beginning his training under Ārāḍa Kālāma.

For three years, he studied under Ārāḍa Kālāma; when he realized that the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception was not the ultimate, he abandoned it. He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra for another three years, where he studied the sphere of nothingness;

realizing this too was not the way, he likewise abandoned it. He then went to Mount Elephant Head, where he joined the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) and subsisted on a daily diet of hemp and wheat for six years.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "By means of being without mind or intention and without the activity of sensation, he completely subdued them all."
The various non-Buddhists first undergo trials of heterodox methods; [the Buddha] demonstrates various skillful means and arouses diverse views in order to lead them to Bodhi.

Thus, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states: "On the eighth day of the second month, at the time when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva attained the Way and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
he was then thirty years of age. This was the year *Guiwei*, the third year of King Mu’s reign. Subsequently, at the Deer Park...
In the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya, whereby they realized the fruits of the Path.
He taught the Dharma while remaining in the world for forty-nine years. Later, he addressed his disciple Mahākāśyapa:
"I entrust to you my pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark of formlessness, and the subtle, sublime, Right Dharma. You must protect it."
"Maintain it, and command Ānanda to act as your deputy in transmitting this transformation so that it shall not be severed. Then he spoke in verse: "The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma;
The Dharma-less Dharma is also Dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting the Dharma-less, How has any dharma ever been a dharma?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed Kāśyapa: "I shall now transmit the saṃghāṭī robe of golden thread to you..."
"You must transmit this in turn to those in the position of succession, until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya, so that it shall not perish.
When Kāśyapa heard these verses, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and said, "Excellent! Excellent! I shall follow your instructions out of reverent obedience to the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly: "I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter parinirvāṇa. He then proceeded to the [Śāla Grove].
Proceeding along the riverbank to beneath the twin *śāla* trees, he lay with his right side down, feet叠疊 (one foot upon the other), in profound stillness and tranquility.
Then, rising from the coffin, he preached the Dharma for his mother. He specifically displayed his two feet to convert Vakkula and spoke this verse on impermanence:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. At that time, the disciples immediately [prepared] incense...

The attendants vied with one another to cremate [the Buddha] by means of firewood. After the embers were extinguished, the golden coffin remained as it had been before. At that time, the great assembly immediately praised the Buddha in his presence with a verse, saying:
"How could the fierce and blazing fires of common mortals Be able to cause the cremation of this body? We pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi May cremate this golden-hued body.
At that moment, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven *tāla* trees, moving back and forth through the air.
Through the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, ashes were produced in an instant, and eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra* were obtained.

This was on the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of *Renshen*, the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign. One thousand one hundred and seventeen years had passed since the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One when the teaching reached the Central Plains;
this was the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the year of *Wuchen*. Just as the World-Honored One...
Upon being born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, walked seven steps in every direction, and looked around the four quarters, saying:

"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored. One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:
"Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat. The World-Honored One.
One day, he ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly there are two bhikṣus who have violated the disciplinary rules; for this reason, I do not preach the Dharma.

Ānanda, using his supernormal power of reading others' minds, observed these bhikṣus and subsequently had them expelled. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda spoke again: "Just now..."
"Two bhikṣus have come who have violated the precepts; these two bhikṣus have already been expelled. Why does the World-Honored One not preach the Dharma?
The World-Honored One said, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles or for śrāvakas. He then descended from his seat.

One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat, and when the great assembly had gathered and settled, Kāśyapa struck the gavel and announced, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma. Thereupon, the World-Honored One...
The assembly descended from their seats. The World-Honored One had remained for ninety days in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother.

When he took his leave of the celestial realm and descended, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all went to the sky to welcome him. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā thought to herself, "I am a nun;
I will certainly be behind the great monks when seeing the Buddha. It would be better to use my supernormal powers to transform myself [into a male form]."
The Wheel-Turning Sage King, surrounded by a thousand sons, was the first to see the Buddha, thereby fulfilling his vow.
As soon as the World-Honored One saw him, he rebuked him, saying: "Utpalavarṇā Bhikṣuṇī, how could you bypass the great monks to see me?
Although you have seen my physical body (rūpakāya), you have not yet seen my Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Subhūti, sitting in meditative absorption within his cave, has instead seen my Dharma."
[The Buddha said: "Body. In the past, when Mañjuśrī arrived at the assembly place of the Buddhas, he encountered the various Buddhas each returning to their own abodes.
There was only one woman sitting near that Buddha, having entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Why is it that this person is permitted to sit near the Buddha while I am not? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: 'You need only awaken this woman and cause her to arise...'"
He arose from samādhi. "Ask her yourself," [the Buddha] said. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times, snapped his fingers once, and then lifted her up to the Brahma Heaven;
yet, even exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not bring her back down. The World-Honored One said, "Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs..."

Nor can this woman be made to emerge from her samādhi by anyone else. Forty-two Ganges-sands of worlds below, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā who is able to cause this woman to emerge from her samādhi.
In an instant, the Mahāsattva Vimalaprabhā surged forth from the earth.
He prostrated before the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One commanded Wangming to come forth. Wangming then went before the woman and snapped his fingers once;

the woman thereupon emerged from her meditative concentration. Thereupon, King Prasenajit asked the World-Honored One: "Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), is there conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
If one says there is not, then wisdom should not be dual. If one says there is, then wisdom should not be unitary."

"As for the meaning of 'one' and 'two,' what is that meaning? The Buddha said, "Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), you once asked about this same meaning.
Now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and absence of hearing—this is called the meaning of one and the meaning of two.
One day, the World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate and said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī..."
“Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter through the gate? Mañjuśrī replied, “I do not see a single dharma outside the gate. Why then do you instruct me to enter?
One day, while the World-Honored One was sitting, he saw two men carrying a pig past him.
He asked, “What is this? They replied, “The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; yet you do not even recognize a piglet. The World-Honored One said, “You should have asked me about it.”
Once, when a certain heterodox teacher questioned the Blessed One, asking, "Are all phenomena eternal? the Blessed One did not answer.
When the teacher asked again, "Are all phenomena impermanent? he likewise did not answer. The heterodox teacher said, "The Blessed One possesses all-encompassing knowledge; why do you not answer me?"

The World-Honored One said, "All that you have asked is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One day, the World-Honored One showed a *vaiḍūrya* gem that reflected the colors of its surroundings and asked the kings of the five directions, "What color is this gem?
At that time, the kings of the five directions each described it as having a different color.
The World-Honored One then hid the gem in his sleeve and raised his hand, asking, "What color is this gem? The kings replied: [that it was colorless].
There were no pearls in the Buddha’s hand; how could there be any color? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "How extreme is your delusion!
I presented you with worldly pearls, yet each of you insisted on saying they were blue, yellow, red, or white. When I presented you with genuine pearls, you knew nothing at all.
At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the five directions all attained awakening. It was because of the gandharvas that the World-Honored One [spoke thus].
The king presented music. At that moment, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all became the sound of a lute.
Kāśyapa rose and performed a dance. The king asked, "Is Kāśyapa not indeed an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? How can he still have residual habits?
The Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma. The king again stroked the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise danced three times.

The King said, "Kāśyapa performed a dance; was that not so? The Buddha said, "In truth, he never performed a dance. The King said, "World-Honored One, how could you speak falsely? The Buddha said, "I do not speak falsely.
When you plucked the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all wood and stone turned entirely into the sound of the lute;
was that not so? The King said, "It was. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa was just like this. Therefore, it is truly not..."

[The Buddha] once performed a dance, and the king then believed and accepted it. When the World-Honored One was questioned by a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), [the Buddha] asked: "What Dharma did you preach yesterday? The non-Buddhist replied: "I preached the Dharma of certainty. [The Buddha] asked: "What Dharma do you preach today? The non-Buddhist replied: "The Dharma of uncertainty.
