The World-Honored One, having been questioned by a rishi possessing the five supernormal powers, said: "The World-Honored One possesses six supernormal powers;
I possess five. What is that one power? The Buddha summoned the rishi of the five supernormal powers, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "That one power—ask me about it."
The World-Honored One, because the Bodhisattva Universal Eye desired to see Samantabhadra but could not find him—
even after entering meditative absorption three times and searching throughout the trichiliocosm— was unable to perceive Samantabhadra and thus came to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If you simply give rise to a single thought within the stillness of samādhi, you will immediately see Samantabhadra.
As soon as Puyan gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra riding upon a six-tusked white elephant in mid-air.

Furthermore, on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreat in three different places. When Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him, as soon as he raised the gavel, he beheld [him there].
There were hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs; although Kāśyapa exerted all his supernatural powers, he could not lift the mallet.

The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless. Subsequently, the World-Honored One encountered the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, who sought to debate with him.
They made a prior agreement, saying, "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head. The World-Honored One said, "As for your doctrine..."
"What is your thesis? The World-Honored One asked. Zhì replied, "My thesis is that I do not accept anything. The World-Honored One said, "Do you accept this [thesis]?

Zhì then brushed his sleeves and departed. Having traveled halfway, he suddenly realized the truth and said to his disciples, "I must go back to cut off my own head to apologize to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "Since you have fortunately achieved victory before the assembly of devas and humans, why would you cut off your head?"
The Master said: "I would rather have my head cut off before a person of wisdom than achieve victory before one who lacks wisdom.
He then sighed and said: "In both cases, my doctrine falls into defeat. If this view is accepted, the door of defeat is gross; if this view is not accepted, [the same applies]."

The point where his position was defeated was subtle; all humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles did not know where my meaning fell into error, but only the World-Honored One and the great bodhisattvas knew where my meaning had fallen.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said, "My doctrine has failed in two respects;
therefore, I shall cut off my head to offer an apology. The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing as this. You should turn back."
Their minds turned toward the Way; thereupon, together with their five hundred followers, they simultaneously threw themselves upon the Buddha to leave the household life and realized arhatship.

In the past, when the World-Honored One wished to lead the assembly of sages to the sixth heaven to preach the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, he commanded all the fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands and this land, from the human realm and the heavens, to assemble entirely and receive the Buddha’s entrustment, providing protection.
To protect the True Dharma, should there be any who do not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings shall fly hot iron wheels to pursue them and compel their assembly.
Once they have assembled, there shall be none who do not comply with the Buddha’s command; each shall make a great vow to uphold and protect the True Dharma.
Only one Māra King said to the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have become Buddhas. The multitude...
The realm of sentient beings is empty; there is no such thing as the name "sentient being. It was for this reason that I resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
Once, while the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, they came upon the stupa of an ancient Buddha. The World-Honored One paid his respects, whereupon Ānanda asked, "Whose stupa is this?
The World-Honored One replied, "This is the stupa of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked, "As for those Buddhas of the past..."
"Who is your disciple? the World-Honored One replied, "He is my disciple. Ānanda said, "It should be so.
At that time, a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One a question, but he did not ask whether there was speech or no speech. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while.

The non-Buddhist praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; he has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way]. Thereupon, he prostrated himself in worship.
He then departed. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what principle did the non-Buddhists praise [you] and then depart?

The World-Honored One said, "It is like a fine horse of the world that moves upon seeing the shadow of the whip. One day, the World-Honored One instructed Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching;
you should enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda responded, "As you command. The World-Honored One said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the example of the past."
Regarding the ritual of the Seven Buddhas: Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven past Buddhas?
The World-Honored One called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go. Subsequently, a bhikṣu asked the World-Honored One:
"Within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, there is that which is seen, yet there is no realization. What will the World-Honored One show me?"
The World-Honored One said, "Bhikṣu So-and-so, what should you show him? This is your question.
After the World-Honored One had attained enlightenment, he was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree in the Jeta Grove.
Two merchants were passing by the edge of the grove with five hundred wagons when two of the oxen refused to move forward. The merchants were astonished and saw that it was a mountain deity.
He replied, "In this forest there is a holy man who has attained the Way; forty-nine days have passed since he began his practice, yet he has not eaten.
You should offer him sustenance. The merchant entered the forest and indeed saw a man sitting upright and motionless.
He then asked, "Are you the Brahma King? Are you Śakra? Are you a mountain deity? Or are you a river deity? The World-Honored One smiled and raised a corner of his *kāṣāya* robe to show him.
The merchant prostrated and presented offerings. Because Jīvaka was skilled at discerning sounds, the World-Honored One went to a cemetery and saw five skulls.
He struck one skull and asked Jīvaka, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "This person was born into the human realm.
The World-Honored One struck another and asked, "Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, "This person was born into the heavenly realm. The World-Honored One [then] again...
He asked another question: "Where was this person born? Jīvaka did not know where he had been born.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, through the supernatural power of the brahmin Kāḷa, caused two stalks of *saṃyukta* and *śiṃśapā* flowers to be held up by his left and right hands, bringing them to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Buddha called to the rishi. The brahmin responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Let it go. The brahmin then let go of the flower on his left hand.
The Buddha called to the rishi again, "Let it go. The brahmin then let go of the flower on his right hand.
The Buddha called to the rishi once more, "Let it go. The brahmin said, "World-Honored One, both my hands are now empty."
"What more is there for you to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to discard those flowers;

rather, you should discard the six external objects (*viṣaya*), the six internal faculties (*indriya*), and the six intermediate consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Abandon them all at once. When there is nothing left to abandon, that is your place of liberation from birth and death.
At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This occurred because of [the teaching given by] the World-Honored One at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Five hundred bhikṣus had attained the four dhyānas and were endowed with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna-abhijñā*), each of them individually beheld their own past acts of killing fathers, harming mothers, and other grave offenses.
Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to penetrate the profound Dharma. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, proceeded—
Holding a sharp sword, he threatened the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī, "Stop!
Stop! You must not commit an act of parricide. Do not seek to harm me. Even if I am inevitably harmed, I shall be harmed for the sake of the good.
Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning there has been no self or person; it is only because of the internal mind that one perceives a self or person. When the internal mind arises, I..."
"Victim" is precisely what is meant by "harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized their own original mind to be like a dream and like an illusion;
within this dream and illusion, there is no self or person, nor even parents who give birth or are born from. Then the five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source and bottom of the Dharma. With his own hand he grasps the sharp [sword]..."
A sword—holding it to threaten the body of the Tathāgata—the sword and the Buddha are likewise thus: one mark, without duality; signless and unarisen.
Within this, how could there be killing? When the World-Honored One was on the path of practice, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara.
Seeing the place where the hair was spread, Dīpaṃkara then signaled for the assembly to withdraw and pointed to the ground, saying: "In this single plot of land, one [Buddha] should be established."

Regarding the construction of a Brahma-shrine (*brahmasthāna*): At that time, there was among the assembly a wise elder who held a marker and, inserting it into the spot where his finger had been, declared, "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is complete.
Thereupon, the various devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying, "This younger son possesses great wisdom!

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was wandering through the Śītavana cemetery with the Seven Virtuous Daughters, one daughter pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here; where has the person gone? One [of the others] said: [The text continues from this point].

The woman said, "How? How? The sisters observed her closely and each attained realization. Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray that you, Noble Sister, will let me know what you require; I shall provide for you for the rest of my life.
The woman replied, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided. I require only three things: first, a single rootless tree; second,"
"I require a place where there is no distinction between yin and yang; I require a mountain valley where three shouts would not cause an echo.
Śakra said, "I possess everything that is required, yet as for these three things, I truly have none.
The woman said, "If you do not have these, how can you save others? Śakra was at a loss for words, so he went together with her to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Kauśika, I..."
The great arhats among the disciples did not understand this meaning; only the great bodhisattvas understood it.
Because Devadatta had slandered the Buddha and entered hell in his physical body, the World-Honored One had Ānanda ask:
"Are you at peace within the hells? He replied: "Although I am in hell, it is as pleasant as the third dhyāna heaven. The Buddha then further instructed him to ask:
"Will you still come out? He replied, "I shall wait until the World-Honored One arrives before I come out. Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms;

how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads to entering hell? He replied, "Since the Buddha has no portion that leads to entering hell, how could I have any portion that leads to coming out of hell?
Because Mañjuśrī had suddenly given rise to the view of a Buddha and the view of the Dharma, he was subdued by the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One.
Facing the two Iron Ring Mountains, there was an old woman to the east of the city who had been born at the same time as the Buddha but did not wish to see him.
Whenever she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately avoid him; yet, even so, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha.
He then covered his face with his hand; within the palms of his ten fingers, there were likewise Buddhas everywhere.
When Aṅgulimāla went to the gate of a certain elder’s house carrying his alms bowl, the wife of that household was in the midst of a difficult labor, and mother and child had not yet been separated.
The elder said, "Disciple of Gautama, you are a most holy one; what dharma do you possess that can alleviate this difficulty of childbirth? Aṅgulimāla replied:
The elder said, "I have only recently entered the Path and do not yet know this Dharma. Wait for me to return and ask the World-Honored One; I shall come back and inform you.
Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla, "Go quickly and inform him, saying:
'Since I first came to the noble and holy Dharma, I have never killed a living being. Aṅgulimāla obeyed the Buddha’s words and went swiftly to tell her. When his wife heard this, she was relieved.
At that time, [the matter] was resolved. Once, while the World-Honored One was seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, two merchants asked him, "World-Honored One, did you see any carriages pass by?
He replied, "I did not see them. The merchants asked, "Did you hear them? He replied, "I did not hear them. The merchants asked, "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?
He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration. They asked, "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep. The merchants [were amazed].
The man then sighed and said, "Excellent! Excellent! The World-Honored One has awakened yet remains unseen. He then offered two pieces of white felt.

When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude; at that time, the entire assembly remained silent, and only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, which is truly..."
The Dharma-gate of form and formlessness is subtle and wondrous; it does not rely on written words and is transmitted separately outside the teachings. It was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
When the World-Honored One reached the Multi-Treasured Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit beside him, then wrapped him in his saṃghāṭī robe and said:
"I now secretly entrust to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. You must protect and uphold it."
To be transmitted to future generations. When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma once more.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, I have dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, yet I have never spoken a single word.
You ask me to turn the wheel of Dharma again; have I ever turned the wheel of Dharma before? At the assembly of the Nirvāṇa, the World-Honored One—
He rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the assembly, saying: "You should all observe well my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold.

Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied; do not let yourselves have cause for regret later. If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciples; if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa,"
"Nor are you my disciples. At that time, the assembly of hundreds of billions all attained realization.
The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. His clan was Brahmin; his father was [named] Yin... [text fragment].
Zé’s mother, Xiāngzhì, was formerly a goldsmith who was skilled in understanding the nature of gold and how to temper it until it became pliant and malleable.
The *Fǎfǔchuán* (Biographies of the Dharma Transmission) states that once, in the distant past, after the Parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa.

Within the stūpa, the golden face of the Buddha image had become damaged and disfigured. At that time, there was a poor woman who took a gold bead to the goldsmith’s workshop and requested [his assistance].
They adorned the Buddha’s face. Subsequently, they made a vow together, saying: "May we two become husband and wife without marriage.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were all golden in color. Later, they were born in the Brahma Heaven;

when their celestial lifespan ended, they were born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Madhyama-Magadha, named Kāśyapa—translated here as "Drinking Light" (Yǐn guāng) or "Victorious Honored One" (Shèng zūn). This was because...
He was named after his golden complexion. Consequently, he resolved to seek renunciation, hoping to cross over from the realms of existence (*bhava*). The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His hair and beard fell away naturally, and the *kāṣāya* robe appeared upon his body. The Buddha constantly praised him as the foremost among the assembly, further saying:
"I entrust this to you with my pure Dharma-eye; you must propagate it so that it does not perish. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Kāśyapa was not present among the assembly. The Buddha addressed the great disciples, saying:
'When Kāśyapa arrives, you should have him proclaim the Treasury of the True Dharma-eye. At that time, Kāśyapa was at the Śīrṣa..."
At the Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain, in the Piṇḍola Cave, he beheld a sublime radiance and immediately entered into samādhi.

With his purified divine eye, he saw that the World-Honored One was entering parinirvāṇa on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River. He then addressed his disciples, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa!
How swift it was! He then went to the space between the twin śāla trees and wailed in grief and longing. The Buddha emerged from the golden coffin.
He displayed his two feet. At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus: "The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; the diamond-like relics are not our concern.
We ought to assemble the Eye of the Dharma so that it does not perish. He then spoke this verse: "Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvāṇa!
Those who have attained supernatural powers (ṛddhi) should attend the assembly. Thereupon, those who had attained supernatural powers...
They all assembled at the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time, Ānanda was unable to enter the assembly because his outflows were not yet exhausted;
later, having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he was thus able to enter. Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying:
"This bhikṣu Ānanda is of great learning and possesses dhāraṇī; he has great wisdom and constantly follows the Tathāgata.

His pure conduct is immaculate, and the Buddha-dharma he has heard is like water being passed from one vessel to another, without any loss. He is praised by the Buddha as foremost in intelligence and quick-wittedness;
it would be fitting to request him to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka. The great assembly remained silent. Kāśyapa then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now proclaim the Eye of the Dharma. Hearing these words, Ānanda accepted them with faith. Observing the minds of the assembly, he spoke in verse:
"O monks and all followers, without the Buddha you lack adornment, Just as in the empty sky, the multitude of stars is without the moon."
Having spoken these verses, he prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, ascended the Dharma seat, and proclaimed these words: "Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in a certain place, preaching a certain sutra and teaching. ... [and so on] until the humans, devas, and others paid homage and practiced accordingly.
Then Kāśyapa asked the bhikṣus: "Is that which Ānanda has spoken free from error? They all replied: "It is no different from what the World-Honored One [taught]."
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying: "My life span is not long; I now entrust the True Dharma to you.
Guard it well. Listen to my verse: 'All dharmas are the original dharma; there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.'"
"How can there be both the Dharma and non-Dharma within a single dharma? Having spoken this verse, he took up his saṃghāṭī robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya;
this was the fifth year of King Zhou Xiaowang, the *bingchen* year.
When a non-Buddhist asked the Venerable One, "What is this 'self' of mine? he replied, "That which seeks the self is your self. The non-Buddhist said:
"This is my self," [the Master] said. "Where is your self, Teacher? He replied, "You seek me by asking about me.
One day, while the Venerable was treading mud, a novice saw him and asked, "Why do you do this yourself? The Venerable said, "If I do not do it myself, who will do it for me?"
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan was Kṣatriya; his father was King Droṇodana, who was indeed the younger brother of the Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Ānandā, which here means "Celebration of Joy" or "Rejoicing.

He was born on the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, and thus he was named accordingly. He was widely learned and profoundly erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom. The World-Honored One regarded him as...

He was foremost in dhāraṇīs and had always been praised for them. Furthermore, due to his great merit from past lives, he had received and upheld the Dharma-treasury like water being passed from one vessel to another.
The Buddha then appointed him as his attendant. One day, the Venerable addressed the Buddha, saying, "Today, upon entering the city, I witnessed a most extraordinary thing.
The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary thing did you see? He replied, "As I entered the city, I saw a—"
A troupe of musicians was performing a dance. Upon leaving the city, [the Buddha] saw that they were all gone.
The Buddha said, "Yesterday when I entered the city, I also witnessed a remarkable event. [The interlocutor] asked, "I do not know what remarkable event you saw.
The Buddha said, "When I entered the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, I also saw musicians performing a dance. One day, he questioned Kāśyapa.
He said, "Elder brother, apart from the golden-brocade *kāṣāya* robe transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.

Later, King Ajātaśatru addressed him, saying, "Virtuous one, both the Tathāgata and the venerable and supreme teacher Kāśyapa have already entered *nirvāṇa*, yet I remain burdened with many karmic obstacles."
[The assembly] was entirely unable to see him. When the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he wished to bid them farewell;
the Venerable One granted this. Later, he thought to himself: "My body is frail and brittle, like a mass of foam; how much more so now that I am aged and infirm—how could it endure for long?

King Ajātaśatru has made an appointment with me; I shall go to the royal palace and take my leave. He then went to the palace and said to the king: "I wish to enter parinirvāṇa; I have come to bid you farewell."
[The messenger] said, "The gatekeeper says that the King is sleeping and cannot be awakened. [The other] said, "Wait until the King awakens; I shall speak for you then.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw in a dream a precious parasol adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded and gazed upon by thousands of millions of beings.
Suddenly, a violent wind and rain arrived, blowing the handle off and causing the precious jewels and necklaces to fall all over the ground.
The king was deeply shocked and amazed. Upon waking, his gatekeeper reported the matter in detail. When the king heard this, he cried out in lamentation, his grief moving both heaven and earth.
He immediately proceeded to the city of Vaiśālī and saw the Venerable One sitting cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River.
The king prostrated himself and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms, who has abandoned me to come here. For a moment..."
Relying on the power of his compassionate vow, he did not yet enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, King Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank and spoke a verse, saying:
"O Venerable One, why so soon do you return to the field of quiescence? We pray that you remain for a brief moment and accept our offerings.
Seeing that both kings had come to entreat him, the Venerable One then spoke a verse, saying: "May the two kings dwell well and steadfastly."
"Do not grieve with sorrow; my nirvāṇa shall be pure, for I am free from all states of existence. The Venerable One then reflected:
"If I were to pass away in favor of one particular kingdom, the other kingdoms would contend; such a thing is not fitting. I should deliver all sentient beings with equanimity.
He then proceeded to enter parinirvāṇa in the middle of the Ganges River. At that moment, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.

At that moment, five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains beheld this auspicious omen and arrived by flying through the air. They prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and said:
"We shall realize the Buddha-dharma under the Elder; we pray that you will bestow great compassion upon us and deliver us."
The Venerable One accepted the invitation in silence. He immediately transformed the Ganges River entirely into golden ground and expounded the various Great Dharmas for that assembly of sages.
The Venerable One then thought, "My disciples whom I have previously delivered and liberated should now gather here.
In a brief moment, five hundred arhats descended from the sky; he granted them the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon them. Among that assembly of sages was...
There were two arhats: the first was named Śāṇakavāsin, and the second was named Madhyāntika. Knowing that they were vessels for the Dharma, the Venerable One said to them:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Great Eye of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; Kāśyapa entered into meditative concentration and entrusted it to me.
Now that I am about to pass away, I transmit it to you. Receive my teaching and listen to these verses."
"The Dharma originally possessed; having bestowed it, he spoke of the non-existence of the Dharma. Each must awaken for themselves; once awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence.

Having completed the transmission of the Eye-Treasury of the Dharma, the Venerable One leaped into the void, manifested the eighteen transformations, and entered the *vāyu-vega* (wind-swiftness) samādhi.
He divided his body into four parts: one part he offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; one part he offered to the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King; one...
One portion was presented to the King of Vaiśālī, and one portion was presented to King Ajātaśatru; each erected a precious stūpa to make offerings to them.
This was in the twelfth year of the reign of King Li, the year of Guisi (493 CE).
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā.
He was also named Śāṇavāsa; his family name was Viśākha, his father was Vanavāsin, and his mother was Kauśeya. He was born after remaining in the womb for six years.

In the Sanskrit language he is called Śāṇaka, which here means "naturally clothed"; this refers to the name of a nine-branched exquisite grass from the Western Regions. When a sage descends [into the world]...
As for its birth: this grass grows in a pure and clean place. When the Venerable Upasena was born, this auspicious grass appeared in response.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings and arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, he saw a grove of green trees with luxuriant branches and leaves, and said to Ānanda:
This forest is named Uruvelā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma here.
A century later, Gavāṃpati Śāṇakavāsin will be born; he will leave the household life, realize the Path, receive the Dharma-eye from the Venerable Ānanda, and guide sentient beings.
He shall dwell in this forest and subdue two fire-dragons, causing them to take refuge in the Buddha.
The Teacher [the Buddha] instructed that because the dragon had offered him the land, he should establish a Brahma-palace there.

After the Venerable One had long cultivated conditions for conversion and contemplated entrusting the True Dharma to another, he sought out Upagupta in the kingdom of Tāla and took him as his attendant. He then asked Upagupta, "How old are you?
He replied, "I am seventeen years old. The Venerable One said, "Is it only your body that is seventeen, or is your nature also seventeen? He replied:

He said, "Master, your hair has turned white. Is it that your hair has turned white, or is your mind white? The other replied, "I am merely one whose hair has turned white; it is not that my mind has turned white.
Guptaka said, "My body is seventeen years old, but my nature is not seventeen years old. Venerable sir, you know that I am a vessel for the Dharma."
Three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts. He then said: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the unsurpassed Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; do not let it be severed."
"Receive my instruction and listen to these verses of mine: 'Neither dharma nor mind; no mind and no dharma.
When speaking of this mind-dharma, this dharma is not a mind-dharma. Having spoken these verses, he immediately vanished into the White Elephant Mountain (Himavat) to the south of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he saw his disciple Guṇamati with a following of five hundred disciples who were frequently indolent.
[The Buddha said: "Māna! The Venerable One shall go there and subdue him by manifesting the Dragon’s Vigorous Samādhi. Then he shall speak this verse:
'Thoroughly penetrating that there is neither self nor other, the Most Holy One has neither long nor short. Cast away your mind of arrogance, and you shall swiftly attain Arhatship.'"
Having heard the verses, the five hundred bhikṣus followed the instructions and practiced accordingly; they all attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

The Venerable One then manifested eighteen transformations and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi) to cremate his own body. Kujūta collected the relics and interred them on Mount Vaṅkāla.
Each of the five hundred bhikṣus carried a banner to escort the remains there, where they erected a stūpa and made offerings. Thereupon, [he] informed the King.
The twenty-third year was the year of Yimwei (乙未).
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the country of Ṭhāḷi. He was also named Upagupta and alternatively called Upagupta.
His clan name was Śūdra; his father’s name was Kalyāṇamati. He left home at the age of seventeen and realized the fruit of arhatship at twenty. Following...
As he was traveling to convert others, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā, where those who attained liberation were exceedingly numerous.

Consequently, the palace of Māra shook, and Pāpīyān became sorrowful and terrified. He then exhausted all his demonic powers to harm the True Dharma. The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to observe its cause.
Pāpīyān again sought an opportunity and secretly took a necklace to bind it around [the Venerable’s] neck. When the Venerable emerged from *samādhi*, [he saw it].
He then took the three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands. He spoke with words of consolation to Pāpīyas, saying:
"The necklaces you gave me were truly exquisite; I have these flower garlands to offer in exchange. Pāpīyas was greatly delighted and stretched out his neck to receive them.
Immediately, they transformed into three kinds of putrid corpses, infested with maggots and rotting away. Pāpīyas felt loathing and was filled with great revulsion.
Distressed and troubled, he exerted all his supernatural power but was unable to move it. He then ascended to the six heavens of the desire realm and informed the various celestial lords;

he further went to the Brahma King to seek deliverance. They each replied, "The miraculous transformations performed by the disciples of the One of Ten Powers—how could we, who are ordinary and lowly, be able to remove them?
Pāpīyān asked, "If that is so, what shall we do? The Brahma King said, "You should return [to the Buddha]."
The Venerable One was immediately able to sever [the affliction]. He then spoke a verse to him, directing his merit toward awakening, saying:
"If one falls upon the ground, one rises from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.

Having received these instructions, Pāpīyān descended from the celestial palace, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable One, and offered a sincere confession. The Venerable One told him: "From this day forward, regarding the Tathāgata..."
“Will you no longer cause harm to the True Dharma? Māra said, “I vow to turn toward the Buddha-way and forever sever all unwholesome deeds.
The Venerable One said, “If that is so, you may yourself proclaim with your own mouth: ‘I take refuge in the Triple Gem. The King of Māras joined his palms and recited this three times;
his flower garlands were completely removed, and he was filled with joy and exultation. He prostrated before the Venerable One and spoke this verse:
I prostrate to the Honored One of Samādhi, the noble disciple endowed with the ten powers. I now dedicate my merit, praying that no one shall fall into weakness.

While the World-Honored One was in the world transforming and guiding beings, those who realized the fruits of the path were most numerous. For every person he delivered, he would place a tally-stick within a stone chamber.
That chamber was eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width; it became filled to capacity with them, until finally there remained but one long [tally].

"O son, one named Gandharvasena has come to pay homage to the Venerable One, seeking to go forth into homelessness. The Venerable One asked: 'Do you go forth with your body, or do you go forth with your mind?
He replied: 'I have come to go forth, not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One said: 'If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that goes forth? He replied:
'As for one who goes forth, because there is no self and no "mine," and because there is no self and no "mine," [there is no one who goes forth]. "
"The mind itself is neither born nor extinguished. That the mind is neither born nor extinguished is the eternal Way.
All Buddhas likewise possess an eternal mind that is formless; its essence is also thus. The Venerable One said, "You shall attain great enlightenment; the mind will naturally be realized by you.

You should take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and continue the lineage of the sages. He then performed his tonsure and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*), further instructing him, saying, "Your father once..."
"You were born on a day when gold appeared in a dream; you may be named Dīpamkara. He further said, "The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the great Dharma-eye in succession until it reached me.
Now I entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'The mind is itself the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma.
If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; if there is no mind, there is no original dharma. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, [he passed away]."
He then leaped into the air and manifested the eighteen transformations; subsequently returning to his original seat, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Dhitika used the tally-sticks from within the room to cremate the Master’s body and collected the relics, constructing a stupa to make offerings to them.
This was the year Gengzi, the thirty-first year of King Ping's reign.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Dīpaka, was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. In Sanskrit he is called Dīpaka, which here means "Measure of Penetrating Reality.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth;
before it stood a great mountain adorned with various jewels, from the summit of which a spring gushed forth, flowing in torrents in the four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Gupta.
To explain this: the "jeweled mountain" is my own body; the "gushing spring" is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma;
the "sun rising from the house" is the sign of your current entry into the Way; and the "illuminating heaven and earth" is the transcendence of your wisdom.
Having heard the teacher’s explanation, the Venerable One leaped for joy and uttered these verses: "Majestic is the mountain of the seven treasures,"
"Constantly flowing from the spring of wisdom, it turns back into the flavor of the True Dharma, able to deliver all those with whom there is a karmic connection.
Venerable Gupta also spoke a verse, saying: "I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom. Like the golden sun rising from the house, it shall illuminate heaven and earth.
Hearing his teacher’s sublime verse, Tiṭṭoka prostrated himself and received it. Later, he traveled to Central India. There...
In the kingdom there were eight thousand great ṛṣis, with Mīḍhika at their head. Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage.
They said to the Venerable One, "In the past, we were born together with you in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered the ṛṣi Asita, who bestowed the methods of the ṛṣis upon me."
The Master encountered a disciple of the Ten Powers who was practicing *dhyāna*. From that point, their karmic destinies diverged, and six kalpas have already passed.
The other said, "That you have been separated from me for so many kalpas is indeed not in vain. Now you may abandon heterodoxy and return to the orthodox, thereby entering the Buddha Vehicle."
Mecaka said, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me this prophecy: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall encounter a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness.
That we have now met—is this not due to past affinities? I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation.

Thereupon, he was ordained and left the household life; the holy ones conferred the precepts upon him. As for the other members of the assembly of seers, they were those who had been born at the same time as I.
Māna. The Venerable One displayed great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereupon they both gave rise to the bodhicitta and left the household life at the same time.
He then addressed Mucilinda, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-eye (*mahādharmanetra-kośa*) to Kāśyapa;
it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. Then he spoke this verse: "Thoroughly penetrating the fundamental..."
The Dharma-mind: there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and likewise no dharma.
Having spoken this verse, he leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations. Entering the Fire-Light Samādhi (*Tejorāśi-samādhi*), he spontaneously incinerated his own body.
Miśraka, together with eight thousand bhikṣus, collected the relics and erected a stūpa on Mount Paṇḍava to make offerings to them. This was the time of King Zhuang.
It was the year Jichou (609 CE), the seventh year [of the reign].
The Venerable Sixth Patriarch, Mijieqie, was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled for the sake of conversion until he reached the kingdom of Northern India.
There, seeing auspicious golden clouds above the city walls, he sighed and said, "This is the breath of a person of the Way."
"There must be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. In the midst of the marketplace, there was a man holding a wine vessel.
The Master went toward him and asked, "From where do you come, Master? Where do you wish to go? The man replied, "I come from my own mind; I wish to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize this object in my hand? The Master said, "This is a vessel for contact that carries purity."
He asked, "Does the Master recognize me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would not be my true self.
He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. He answered with a verse:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original surname was Bharadvāja, And my given name was Vāsukīta. The Patriarch said, "My teacher..."
Tidūka said: "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'Three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man in this country named Vasumitra, of the Bharadvāja clan. He shall be the seventh in the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs.
The World-Honored One predicted you; you ought to leave the household life. Thereupon, [Vasumitra] set down his bowl and paid homage to the Master. Beside...
Standing, he spoke, saying: "I recall a past kalpa when I served as a *dānapati* and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha bestowed a prediction upon me, saying:
'In the Śākya Dharma of this Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with the Master’s words; I pray that you grant me deliverance.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, then addressed him, saying: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye..."
"I now entrust this to you; do not allow it to be interrupted. He then spoke a verse, saying: "No mind can be apprehended; What is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.

If one realizes that mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas. Having spoken the verse, the Patriarch entered the Lion’s Boundless Agility Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).
His body leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed into fire to cremate himself.
Vasumitra collected the sacred relics and enshrined them in a casket made of the seven precious gems; he then erected a stupa and placed them on its upper level.
This was the year Jiashen, the seventeenth year of King Xiang’s reign.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. His surname was Bharadvāja.
He habitually wore pure garments and carried vessels for wine as he wandered through the streets and neighborhoods, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people regarded him as mad.

Upon meeting the Venerable Mithyaka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecy, he reflected upon his own prior karmic conditions. He cast aside his vessel, left the household life, received the Dharma, and traveled to transform others.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kāmarūpa, he extensively promoted Buddhist activities. Before the Dharma seat, a man of wisdom suddenly appeared and declared, "My name is Buddhānanda;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "O benevolent one, where there is debate, there is no true meaning; where there is true meaning, there is no debate.
If you intend to debate the meaning, it will ultimately not be a discourse on the meaning. Knowing that the Master’s principle was superior, Buddhānanda submitted with deep reverence in his heart.
He said, "I wish to seek the Way and be moistened by the flavor of the nectar. The Patriarch then granted him the tonsure and bestowed upon him the full precepts.
He further told him, "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
His mind is identical to the realm of empty space; he demonstrates dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, there is neither "is" nor "non-is.
He immediately enters the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came to pay their respects and spoke these verses:
"Ancestor of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position. O Venerable One, have compassion for us; we pray that you [will accept our request]."
He proclaimed the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not existent;
if one realizes the Buddha-ground, it is free from existence and non-existence. Having spoken, he re-entered samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa.
Nandi immediately erected a stupa of the seven precious gems upon his original seat to enshrine his entire body. This was the year *Xinwei*, the nineteenth year of the Reigning King.
This was the year [of his birth]. The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhānanda, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmala. His surname was Gautama.

He possessed a *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence. Initially, he encountered Vasumitra, from whom he left the household life and received instruction. Subsequently, he led a group of disciples as he traveled.

Huihua traveled to the country of Tiqia and arrived at the house of Viśāla. Seeing a white light ascending from the roof of the house, he said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this house who does not speak with his mouth;
he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk the four crossroads, for he knows that contact is defiling.
Having finished speaking, the elder came out and paid his respects, asking, "What do you require? The Master replied, "I seek an attendant. The elder...
The man said, "I have a son named Buddhamitra. He is already fifty years old; he has never spoken a word, nor has he ever set foot upon the ground.
The Patriarch said, "If it is as you say, he is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Buddhamitra rose immediately to prostrate himself and spoke a verse, saying:
"Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin? The Buddhas are not my path;"
"Who is the one most perfected in the Way? The Patriarch answered with a verse: "What you say is intimate with the mind; even parents cannot be compared to it. What you practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like what you have."
"I wish to recognize your original mind; it is neither joined nor separated. Having heard this verse, Votada (Bodhidharma) immediately took seven steps.

The Patriarch said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past; his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make him difficult to part with, he neither spoke nor stepped forward.
The elder then relinquished him to allow him to leave the household life. The Patriarch soon conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and further addressed him, saying:
"I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye. Do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one thoroughly understands space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Bodhidharma, receiving the Master’s entrustment, praised him in verse: "Among the patriarchs of Chan, I shall become the first."
8. He transformed immeasurable multitudes through the Dharma, and all attained the state of Arhat.

At that time, Buddhadatta manifested supernatural transformations and then returned to his original seat, remaining solemnly in parinirvāṇa. The assembly erected a precious stūpa and interred his entire body;
this was the year of Bingyin, the twelfth year of Emperor Jing’s reign.
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Tika. His secular surname was Viśāla.
Having received the entrustment of the Eighth Patriarch, he later traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma.

At that time, there was an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son to pay homage to the Patriarch and said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years; therefore, he is named Duṣprasaha (Difficult-to-Born). He once encountered an immortal."
"This child is no ordinary person; he shall become a vessel for the Dharma. Now that he has encountered the Venerable One, he may be permitted to leave the household life.
The Patriarch then shaved his head and conferred the precepts. At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven *śarīra* relics appeared before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Subsequently, the Patriarch said to him: "The Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata..."
"I now entrust this to you; you must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke a verse, saying: "Ultimate Truth is originally nameless; it is through names that Ultimate Truth is revealed.
Having received the True Dharma, it is neither true nor false. Having finished transmitting the Dharma, the Patriarch entered the Samādhi of Extinction and passed into Parinirvāṇa.
The assembly cremated his remains with fragrant oils and sandalwood, collected the relics, and erected a stupa.
Regarding Nālandā Monastery: it was in the thirty-fifth year of King Śrīharṣa, the year of Jiayin (the Year of the Tiger).
The tenth patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of Central India. His original name was Duḥprasaha.

When he was first about to be born, his father dreamed of a white elephant with a jeweled throne upon its back; atop this throne sat a bright pearl, which entered through the gate, its light illuminating the four directions.
Once the assembly had awakened, he was born. Later, he encountered the Ninth Patriarch and attended upon him at his side, never once sleeping;

it was said that his ribs did not even touch his mat, and thus he was called the Venerable Vakṣa. When he first arrived at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, telling the assembly, "When this ground turns golden in color, a sage shall enter this assembly. Having finished speaking, he immediately—
He transformed into the color of gold. At that time, there was a son of an elder named Pūrṇayaśas, who stood before him with palms joined.
The Patriarch asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "My mind does not go. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell?
He replied, "My mind does not stay. The Patriarch said, "Are you not settled? He replied, "The Buddhas are likewise. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. He replied, "The Buddhas..."
The Buddha was not [the one who did so]. The Patriarch, for that reason, spoke a verse, saying: "This ground turns the color of gold; it is known in advance that a Sage has arrived.

He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and having perfected himself through the flowers of awakening," Nayasena again spoke a verse: "The Master sits upon the golden ground and constantly proclaims the meaning of ultimate truth.
May he turn his light back to illuminate me, enabling me to enter samādhi. The Patriarch understood his intent and immediately ordained him.
He left the household life and further perfected the categories of the precepts. He then addressed him, saying: "The Great Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata is now entrusted to you.

You must protect and keep it in mind. He then spoke this verse: "The True Body is naturally true; Because it is true, there is reason in its explanation. Having realized the Dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation.
After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered nirvāṇa. Thus was the transformation.
The fire consumed itself. The fourfold assembly each took the relics in their robes and, at various locations, erected stupas to make offerings to them.
This was the year Jihai, the twenty-second year of King Jeong.
The eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Pūrṇāśa, was a native of the kingdom of Puṣpapura. His clan name was Gautama; his father was named Ratnagātra.
Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva, he subsequently traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

There, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa came forward to greet him with prostrations and asked, "I wish to recognize the Buddha. Which one is he? The Patriarch replied, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, do not..."

The Master said, "This is it. [Nanquan] said, "Since the Buddha does not recognize it, how can you know it is this? The Master said, "Since he does not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not?
[Nanquan] said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Master said, "That is the meaning of the wood. The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? [Nanquan] said:
He emerged from the retreat together with his teacher. Bodhidharma, however, asked him, "What is the meaning of 'wood'?

The Master replied, "You have been explained by me. Bodhiruci was suddenly enlightened; he prostrated himself in refuge and requested ordination. The Master said to the assembly, "This Great Being..."
In the past, he was the king of the country of Vaiśālī. In that land, there was a class of people who were as naked as horses.
The king exercised his supernatural power to divide his body into silkworms, whereby they obtained clothing. Later, the king was reborn in Central India;

the "horse-people" (the former subjects) were moved by longing and neighed piteously, and for this reason he was called Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh). The Tathāgata prophesied: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be..."
The worthy Aśvaghoṣa is in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; he has subdued the heterodox paths and delivered immeasurable people, continuing my transmission of the transformation.
Now is precisely the time. He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now entrusted to you.

He then spoke a verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; Light and darkness are not separate from one another. I now entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation; It is not merely one."
Nor did he pass away in a dual manner. After the Venerable One had entrusted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered profound parinirvāṇa.
The assembly erected a jeweled stupa to enshrine his entire remains; this was in the fourteenth year of Emperor An, the Wuxu year.
The twelfth patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
He was also named Saṅgharakṣita, as he was preeminent in all conditioned and unconditioned merits; thus he was so named.

Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Yaśas, he later turned the wonderful wheel of Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Suddenly, an old man prostrated himself on the ground before him. The Patriarch said:
The assembly said, "This is no ordinary person; there must be some extraordinary sign. As they finished speaking, he vanished.
Suddenly, a golden-colored man emerged from the earth and transformed into a woman. Pointing her right hand toward the Patriarch, she spoke this verse:
"I prostrate before the Venerable Elder; You shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this ground, You proclaim the Supreme Truth. Having spoken the verse, she vanished in an instant.

However, he did not see him. The Patriarch said, "A demon is about to come to compete with me for strength. After a short while, wind and rain arrived suddenly, and heaven and earth became dark and gloomy.
The Patriarch said, "The arrival of the demon is indeed true; I shall eliminate him.

He then pointed into the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power and shaking the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances subsided accordingly.
After seven days had passed, a small insect as large as a mayfly appeared, hiding beneath the seat.
The Master took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation produced by a māra, coming to eavesdrop upon my Dharma. He then released it, letting it go.
The Māra could not move him. The Patriarch said to him, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers.
Thereupon, he returned to his original form, prostrated himself, and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name?

How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Kambala. I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch asked, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what kind of transformations can you perform? He replied:

"I have transformed the vast ocean; that is but a minor matter. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the ocean of nature? He replied, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'? I have never known it.
The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature for him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth all depend upon it for their establishment."
The samādhis and six supernormal powers manifested from this. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāla conceived faith and, together with three thousand followers, sought ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon him. He further addressed him, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the very source.'"
The Dharma: light and darkness are fundamentally non-dual. Now, having entrusted you with the Dharma of realization, it is neither to be grasped nor abandoned.

Having thus given his final charge, he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi (*nāgavikrīḍita-samādhi*). His body rose into the air like the orb of the sun, and thereafter he manifested his passing.
The fourfold assembly enshrined his true remains in the Dragon Grotto; this was the year of the Jia-wu cycle, the thirty-seventh year of King [Jing]’s reign.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially, he was a follower of non-Buddhist paths with three thousand disciples, and he was well-versed in all heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers to Western India.
He had a crown prince named Meghasvāmin, who, hearing the Venerable One’s name, invited him to the palace to provide offerings.
The Elder said, “The Tathāgata has given this instruction: ‘A śramaṇa must not draw near to kings, ministers, or families of great power.
The Prince said, “To the north of our capital city there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave where you may practice meditative seclusion.”

"This is not so," the Patriarch said. "Yes," [the man] replied, and immediately entered that mountain. After traveling several li, he encountered a large python. The Patriarch walked straight ahead without looking back; the python coiled around his body. The Patriarch then conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and once the python had heard them, it departed. As the Patriarch was about to reach a stone cave, another old man dressed in plain white garments came out, joined his palms in greeting, and asked, "What do you seek? The Patriarch said, "I am seeking the Way. The old man said, "The Way is not something to be sought. If you seek it, you will lose it further. Turn back; do not go forward. The Patriarch then turned back. Upon reaching a village, he met a woman selling cakes. He gave her two coins and asked for a cake. The woman took one coin and gave him a cake; she took the second coin and gave him another. The Patriarch ate both cakes and felt satisfied. The woman said, "I have given you two cakes, yet you seem to be hungry as before. The Patriarch said, "My hunger is indeed not yet appeased. The woman said, "If you are still hungry, eat my head. The Patriarch said, "Even if I were to eat your head, how could it satisfy my hunger? The woman said, "How can you, a man of the Way, speak such words? The Patriarch said, "I am not speaking falsely. My hunger is truly not yet gone. The woman then cut off her head and offered it to him. The Patriarch ate her head and felt fully satiated. He then returned to the stone cave. The old man was still there. The Patriarch bowed and asked, "Just now I received your instruction, but I do not understand its meaning. The old man said, "I am Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. I have come here specifically to test you. You have now attained the Way. Having said this, he vanished. The Patriarch then ascended Mount Songshan. There, he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you going? The Patriarch said, "I am going to seek the Way. The monk said, "Seeking the Way is like chasing after a shadow; it will never end. Why do you trouble yourself thus? The Patriarch said, "I do not know where the Way is. I must go and ask someone. The monk said, "If you wish to know the Way, you must first abandon your mind. Once the mind is abandoned, you will naturally know the Way. The Patriarch said, "If I abandon my mind, who is it that knows the Way? The monk said, "This is precisely what is called 'knowing the Way. The Patriarch was greatly enlightened by these words. He then went to Mount Shaoshi, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Songshan. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Songshan? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Nanyue, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Shaoshi. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Shaoshi? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Heng, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Nanyue. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Nanyue? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Tiantai, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Heng. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Heng? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Lu, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Tiantai. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Tiantai? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Wudang, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Lu. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Lu? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Jing, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Wudang. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Wudang? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Jing? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Dongting? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Baizhang, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Huangmei. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Huangmei? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom.
