The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Baizhang? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Jingshan, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Nanping. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Nanping? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing, why do you say you saw something? The Patriarch said, "Although I saw nothing, I did not fail to see anything. The monk said, "You are a person of great wisdom. The Patriarch then went to Mount Shuangfeng, where he encountered a monk who asked, "Where are you coming from? The Patriarch said, "I am coming from Mount Jingshan. The monk said, "What did you see on Mount Jingshan? The Patriarch said, "I saw nothing. The monk said, "Since you saw nothing
Zhi replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in stillness and seclusion. There were several novice bhikṣus who frequently came to request instruction;
however, I grew weary of responding to them and conceived thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have resided in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to express my gratitude. The Patriarch asked:
He asked, "Who else dwells upon this mountain? He replied, "Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great dragons.
The king of trees is named Nāgārjuna, who constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of dragons; I too have listened to it and received its teachings."
The Patriarch then went with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is desolate and solitary, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
Most Virtuous One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am no 'Most Virtuous One'; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna thought to himself silently, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it with my mind. Simply prepare yourself for the renunciation of the household life; why worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination and, together with five hundred dragon followers, conferred upon them the full precepts.
He spoke to him again, saying: "I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury. Listen attentively to these verses: 'The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest;
this is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this Dharma of hiding and manifesting is neither ignorance nor wisdom.'"
Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and used fire to cremate his body. Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored śarīra relics and erected a stūpa there;
this was the year Renchen, the forty-first year of Emperor Nan’s reign.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India. He was also known as Nāgasena. He first received the Dharma from Venerable Māra.
Later, he traveled to South India, where the people there placed great faith in meritorious deeds (*puṇya-karma*).

The Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, but they said to one another, "If a person possesses meritorious deeds, they are foremost in the world. To speak in vain of Buddha-nature—who can [realize it]?"
He beheld them. The Patriarch said, "If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your pride. The men asked, "Is the Buddha-nature large or small?
The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; it is neither broad nor narrow. It has no merit and no retribution; it neither dies nor is born.
Hearing these superior principles, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a sovereign body from his seat, appearing like the full moon.
The entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma, but did not behold the Master’s physical form.

Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kāṇadeva, who said to the group, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never seen it with our own eyes; how could we possibly identify it?"
Deva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to demonstrate it to us. How do we know this?
It is because through the samādhi of formlessness, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous. Having finished speaking, [he prostrated].
The wheel-mark immediately vanished, and he returned to his original seat, whereupon he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the form of the full moon to symbolize the essence of all Buddhas;

The teaching of the Dharma has no fixed shape, employed to discern that which is neither sound nor form. When the assembly heard this verse, they suddenly attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
They all wished to leave the household life in order to seek liberation. The Patriarch immediately shaved their hair and commanded the various sages to confer the full precepts upon them.
Previously, there had been more than five thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths in that country who practiced great magical arts and were venerated by the masses;

the Patriarch transformed them all, leading them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. He further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, bequeathing them to the world.
Later, in this world, he addressed his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you.

Listen to my verse: 'To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, one speaks of the logic of liberation; yet regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it—there is neither anger nor joy.
Having completed the entrustment of the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*), extensively manifesting supernatural transformations, and then returned to...
The Master sat in profound meditative stillness. Kanadeva and the fourfold assembly together constructed a precious stupa to enshrine his remains;
this was the year Jichou, the thirty-fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds and also delighted in dialectical debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he approached the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [Kanadeva] immediately...

He cast a single needle into it and it moved forward; they joyfully reached a state of spiritual resonance. Nāgārjuna immediately preached the Dharma for him without rising from his seat, manifesting the form of a lunar disc;
they heard only his voice but did not see his physical form. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This auspicious omen now..."

The Master manifested the Buddha-nature, signifying that the teaching of the Dharma transcends both sound and form. Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch later traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was an elder there named Brahmanaviśuddhaguna; one day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden, and their flavor was most exquisite.
Only the elder and his second son, Rāhulabhadra, gathered and ate them, and as soon as they had taken them, the mushrooms grew back immediately.
When they had finished, they were born again; none of their other relatives could see them. The Patriarch, knowing the causes from their past lives, went to their home.
The elder then asked for the reason, and the Patriarch said, "In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu.

However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear, and because he had falsely partaken of the offerings of the faithful, his retribution was to become wooden fungi. Only you and your son [are able to see them]."
Only those who offer with sincere devotion may partake; all others are denied. He then asked the elder his age, and the elder replied, "Seventy-nine.
Thereupon, the Patriarch spoke this verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they shall return their body to the offerings of the faithful."
"You are eighty-one years old; this tree will not grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was even more deeply moved by admiration and submission.
He said, "I, your disciple, am aged and infirm, unable to serve my teacher. I pray that you accept my second son to follow you and leave the household life.
The Patriarch said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. That we have met now is surely..."

Fu, following his past karmic affinity, immediately shaved his head and attended upon him. Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.
After deliberating for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered among their assembly. They asked the Patriarch, "Why do you not come forward?
The Patriarch replied, "Why do you not stay behind? They said, "You appear to be a lowly person. The Patriarch replied, "You appear to be noble."
The man asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch said, "You do not understand anything. The man said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood.

The Patriarch said, "I have certainly attained Buddhahood. The man said, "It is not fitting for you to have attained it. The Patriarch said, "Originally I say that I have attained it, whereas you truly have not attained it.
The man said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Patriarch said, "Because you harbor a sense of self, therefore..."
"It cannot be obtained. Since I have no self, I shall naturally obtain it myself. When his arguments were thus exhausted, he asked the Patriarch, "What is your name?
The Patriarch replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Having previously heard of the Patriarch's reputation, he repented his errors and offered his thanks.

At that time, those in the assembly continued to raise various challenges and difficulties, but the Patriarch refuted them with unimpeded eloquence; consequently, they all submitted and took refuge in him.

He then addressed his senior disciple, Rāhulabhadra, and entrusted him with the Eye of the Dharma. He spoke this verse: "To those who have come to receive the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation.
Regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; it has neither end nor beginning. Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch entered the Samādhi of Agility (*vaiśāradya-samādhi*).
From his body, he emitted eight rays of light and returned to nirvāṇa. The assembly of disciples erected a stūpa to make offerings to him. This is the preceding account.
The nineteenth year of Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty was the *gengchen* year.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. While traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
There was a river there named Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine; in its midstream, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared. The Patriarch—
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away, where the holy one Saṃghanandin resides.
The Buddha prophesied that a thousand years hence, he shall succeed to the position of the Holy One. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream.
Upon reaching that place, they saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him for three...
After seven days, he finally arose from samādhi. The Patriarch asked him, "Was it your body that was in samādhi, or was it your mind? Daiten replied, "Both body and mind were in samādhi.

The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind were in samādhi, how could there be entering and exiting [the state]? Daiten replied, "Although there is entering and exiting, one does not lose the characteristic of samādhi;
it is like gold in a well—the essence of the gold remains eternally still. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or whether the gold has been taken out of the well,"
"Gold has neither motion nor stillness; what is it that enters and exits? Daiten replied, "If one speaks of gold’s motion and stillness, what is it that enters and exits?

If one speaks of gold entering and exiting, gold itself is neither motion nor stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold has come out of the well..."
"What is it that remains? Daiten said, "If the gold has come out of the well, what remains is not the gold; if the gold is still in the well, that which has come out is not the object.
The Patriarch said, "This principle is not so. Daiten said, "That principle is not attached [to the truth]. The Patriarch said, "This principle shall fall [into error]."
Dizang said, "Your thesis is not established. Nanyue said, "Your thesis is not established; my thesis is established.
Dizang said, "Although my thesis is established, the Dharma is not mine. Nanyue said, "My thesis is already established, for I have no self.
Dizang said, "Since you have no self, what thesis do you establish? Nanyue said, "Because I have no self, I establish your thesis. Dizang said, "Virtuous one..."
"Who is your teacher? Who has attained this non-self? The Patriarch said, "My teacher is Kanadeva;
he has realized this non-self. Nandī praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Deva, from whom you have emerged.
Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch replied with a verse: "Since I am already without self, you must see my 'self. You..."
"If you take me as your teacher, you shall know that what is 'I' is not 'I'. When Nandi heard this, his mind was suddenly enlightened;
he immediately sought liberation. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me.

Having spoken, he took a golden bowl in his right hand and lifted it up to the Brahma Palace to fetch fragrant food for the assembly. However, the members of the assembly suddenly felt a sense of revulsion. The Patriarch—
He said, "This is not my fault; it is the result of your own karma. He then commanded Nandi to share his seat and eat with him. The assembly again marveled at this.
The Patriarch said, "That you were unable to eat was entirely due to this reason. You should know that he who shared his seat with me is none other than the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifested his traces here. You all have also [attained realization] within the Bhadrakalpa."
He had reached the third fruit [of the path] but had not yet realized the untainted state (*anāsrava*). The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our teacher can indeed be trusted.
However, regarding his claim that there were Buddhas of the past, they harbored secret doubts. Nandika, perceiving the arrogance of the sentient beings, said:

"When the World-Honored One was in the world, the earth was level and even, without hills or mounds. There were no great rivers, streams, ditches, or canals; all water was sweet and delicious. The grasses and trees..."

The land flourished and was abundant; the eight sufferings were absent, and the ten wholesome deeds were practiced. Since his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin trees more than eight hundred years ago, the world has fallen into ruin and the trees have withered.
People lack profound faith, their right mindfulness is feeble, and they do not believe in *tathatā* (suchness), but only cherish supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the *vajra-maṇḍala*, and took hold [of it].

The Ambrosial Water. Holding it in a lapis lazuli vessel, he brought it to the assembly hall. When the great multitude saw it, they immediately felt deep admiration; repenting their transgressions, they prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch entrusted the Eye of the Dharma to Saṃghanandin, saying in verse: "In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned.
The Dharma has neither the mark of existence nor non-existence; How could it arise from within or without? The Patriarch thus transmitted the Dharma.

Having finished [his teaching], he sat peacefully and returned to stillness. The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for him; this was in the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, the Wuchen year (488 CE).
The seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the deeds of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents in verse, saying:
"I bow my head to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I pay homage to my Mother of flesh and blood. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me.

His parents tried to dissuade him firmly, but he subsequently refused to eat for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the home-life while remaining at home, and he was given the name Seng.
Kāṇḍinī further appointed the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He often thought to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light shone down upon him, revealing a level path.
Without realizing it, he walked slowly for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff, where there was a stone cave.
He then remained in tranquil seclusion within. When the father lost his son, he immediately banished Śrīlāta from the country and went abroad to search for him, but did not know where he was.
After ten years had passed, the Patriarch, having received the Dharma and the prediction of his attainment, traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to spread the teachings.
Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and comfort to both body and mind; yet they did not know its cause. The Patriarch said, "This is the Way..."
"This is the wind of virtue. Surely a sage shall appear in this world to continue the ancestral lamp.

Having spoken thus, he used his supernatural powers to lead the great assembly on a journey through the mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak.

He said to the assembly, "Upon the summit of this peak there is a purple cloud shaped like a canopy; a sage dwells here. He then wandered with the assembly for a long while until they beheld the mountain.
He set aside one boy and, holding a round mirror, went directly before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years.
The Patriarch said, "You are still quite young; why do you say you are a hundred years old? The boy said, "I do not understand the principle; I am truly a hundred years old."
The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in the kōan? The boy replied, "The Buddha said:

'If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the kōan of the Buddhas, it would be better to live for but a single day and attain decisive realization. The Patriarch asked, "What does that which is in your hand signify?"
The boy said, "The great perfect mirror of all Buddhas is without flaw or obscuration within or without; two people may see it together, for their eyes and minds are alike.
When his parents heard their son's words, they immediately relinquished him to allow him to leave the household life.

The Patriarch took him to his own dwelling, and after bestowing upon him full ordination, named him Gayāśata. Later, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, the Patriarch asked, "Are the bells ringing?"

"Is it the wind? "Is it the wind chimes? Śātavāhana replied, "It is neither the wind nor the chimes that sound; it is my own mind that sounds. The Patriarch asked, "And who is it that perceives this mind?
Śātavāhana replied, "Because all is utterly tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent! Excellent! He who shall succeed to my Way—if not you, then whom?
I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you. He then spoke a verse: "The ground of the mind is originally without birth; The ground arises from conditions. From conditions, seeds..."
They did not obstruct one another; the flowers and fruits were likewise so. After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he passed away while grasping the tree with his right hand.

The great assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; shall it provide shade for future generations? They intended to enshrine his entire body on a high plateau and erect a stūpa there, but the multitude's strength could not lift him.
Thus, they erected the stūpa directly beneath the tree during the tenth year of the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Former Han.
The third year was the year of Dingwei.
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the country of Mathura. His surname was Udrayana;
his father was Devavṛta and his mother was Bhadra. She once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. After exactly seven days, she gave birth. Her skin...

His body was as translucent as lapis lazuli; he never bathed, yet it remained naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and his speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
While traveling with a mirror in hand, he encountered the Venerable Nandī, through whom he received ordination. Subsequently, leading his disciples, he traveled to the kingdom of Mahācīna.
Seeing an unusual fragrance emanating from a Brahmin’s house, the Master led his disciples inside. The householder Kumāralata asked, "What kind of assembly are you?
The Master replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his mind and spirit were suddenly stirred with awe.
He immediately closed the door. After a long while, Sengzhu knocked on the door. Luoduo said, "There is no one in this house. Sengzhu asked, "Who is it that says there is no one?
Upon hearing these words, Luoduo realized he was an extraordinary person. He quickly opened the bolt to welcome him in. Sengzhu said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mozhì (Yuezhi) to propagate and uphold [the Dharma]...'"

The Mysterious Transformation: Now that you have encountered me, you should seize this auspicious opportunity. Thereupon, Kumārajīva awakened to the wisdom of his past lives and devotedly entered the monastic order.

Once he had been ordained and received the full precepts, [the Patriarch] bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma, saying: "When there is a seed and the ground of the mind, Through causes and conditions, a sprout can emerge.
If one does not obstruct the conditions, Then birth will give rise to non-birth. Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested...

Having displayed eighteen kinds of supernatural transformations, he entered the Samādhi of the Emanation of Fire and Incandescence and spontaneously cremated his own body. The multitude erected a stūpa for his relics;
this was in the twentieth year of Emperor Cheng of the Former Han, the Wushen year.
The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.

In a former life, he was a deva of sovereign power (the sixth heaven of the desire realm). Upon seeing the jeweled necklace of a bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (the second heaven of the desire realm).
There, he heard Kauśika preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*; because the Dharma was supreme, he ascended [to a higher realm].
In the Brahma Heaven (the Realm of Form), because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma; all the devas honored him as their teacher.
When the time came to succeed to the lineage, he descended to the country of the Yuezhi, and later arrived at the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Mahāsattva named Jayata.

A question was asked: "The parents of my household have long placed their faith in the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by illness, and whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish.
Meanwhile, the neighbors next door have long followed the occupation of *caṇḍālas*, yet their bodies are always vigorous and healthy, and everything they do succeeds.
How fortunate are they, and what crime have we committed? The Patriarch replied: "Why is there any need for such doubt? Furthermore, regarding the retribution of good and evil—"

There are three points [to be considered]. Ordinary people merely observe that the benevolent meet with early death while the violent enjoy longevity, or that those who act contrary to the Way meet with good fortune while those who follow righteousness suffer misfortune;

they then conclude that cause and effect do not exist and that merit and retribution are empty. Little do they realize that shadow and echo follow one another, never deviating by even a hair’s breadth.
Even if a hundred thousand million kalpas were to pass, this principle would never perish. When Śāṇakavāsa heard these words, his doubts were instantly dispelled. The Patriarch said: "You..."

Although one has already gained faith in the three types of karma, one has not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion (*kleśa*), delusion exists because of consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness depends upon non-awakening (*avidyā*), and non-awakening depends upon the mind (*citta*).
This mind is fundamentally pure; it is without arising or ceasing, without fabrication, without retribution, and without victory or defeat.
"Tranquil and still; numinous and alert. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas.
All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Jñānagupta (Shan-yeh-t'o) received these words and grasped their meaning;

he immediately awakened his latent wisdom and earnestly requested ordination. Once he had received full precepts, the Patriarch told him: "The time for my final nirvana has now arrived. You should succeed me."

Having completed his work of transformation, he then entrusted the Dharma-eye. He spoke in verse: "In the nature of reality, there is fundamentally no arising; it is spoken only to respond to those who seek.

Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts as to whether it is resolved or not? He further said, "These are the words of the Tathāgata Wonderful Sound regarding the purity of seeing one's nature.
You should propagate them for the sake of future students. Having finished speaking, he immediately scratched his face with his fingernails while sitting upon the seat.
Like a red lotus blooming forth, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the fourfold assembly before entering parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsa erected a stūpa for him during the fourteenth year of the Xinshi era, the *wuchen* (renwu) year.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Jayata, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep, and he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the teachings of the sudden school (*tun-jiao*). There, the assembly of students valued only dialectical debate;

their leader was named Vāsavadatta (translated here as *Biànxíng*, "Universal Practice"), who constantly ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day. Pure...

Jing was free from desire and was sought after by the multitude. When the Patriarch wished to deliver him, he first asked the assembly, "This ascetic Pien-hsing is able to cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*);
can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent; why should he not be capable?
The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice austerities for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would all be in vain."

"This is the fundamental principle. The assembly asked, "What virtues does the Venerable One possess that you can criticize our Master? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not deluded.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I am not disrespectful. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent."
"I do not eat but once a day, nor do I eat mixed foods. I am neither discontented nor greedy;
my mind has no expectations—this is what is called the Way. When Pūrvāśvaka heard this, he attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Patriarch then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It is because his resolve for the Way is so earnest. Now, as for the strings..."

He immediately cut it off. Therefore, I do not praise such acts; rather, I cause them to dwell in the ground of peace and happiness and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas. He further addressed Viśvāmitra, saying:
"I have just now, before this assembly, suppressed and humiliated you, my worthy friend. I trust that this has not caused distress within your heart? Viśvāmitra replied:
"I recall that seven kalpas ago, when I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss, my teacher and the wise Moon-Pure (Candraprabha) prophesied that I would [attain enlightenment] before long."
When I was realizing the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha appeared in the world. Because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.
The Master rebuked me, saying, "To honor a son while slighting a father—how can this be so base? At that time, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to point it out to me.
The Master said, "When you were paying respects to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, you leaned your staff against the wall where a painted Buddha was."

[He] said, "Because of this overweening pride (*abhimāna*), I have consequently lost two fruits [of the path]. Since I began to reproach myself and repent my errors, even when hearing various evil words, they have been like the wind or an echo.
How much more so now that I have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar (*amṛta*); would I instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that you, in your great compassion, will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage. Listen to me..."

The verse says: "In the moment of speech, they accord with non-arising; they are identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand it thus, one has fully penetrated both phenomena and principle.
After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he did not rise from his seat but suddenly returned to quiescence. His body was cremated, and his relics were collected to build a stupa.
This occurred in the seventeenth year of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the year of Jiashu (594 CE).
The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha; his father was named Prabhāvara, and his mother was named Śuddhā.
Although his family was wealthy, they had no son. Consequently, his parents prayed at a Buddhist stūpa in their quest for an heir.
One night, her mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark. Upon waking, she became pregnant. After seven days had passed, an arhat named Bhadrayaśas arrived at her home.
Guanggai (Guanggai) prepared offerings and performed a prostration; Bhadrayaśas sat upright and accepted them. When Yan (Yan) came out to pay his respects, he bowed down.
The assembly of worthy ones rose from their seats and said, "We return our salutations to the Great Being of the Dharma-body. Guanggai could not fathom the reason for this;
he then took a precious jewel and knelt to offer it, testing whether they were genuine or false. The assembly of worthy ones accepted it immediately without any sign of modesty or thanks.
Unable to restrain himself, Guanggai asked, "I am a man, yet when I offered my salutations you paid me no heed; what virtue does my wife possess that the Venerable One avoided her?"
The Venerable One said, "I have accepted your prostrations and the pearl; it is only for the sake of your noble merit.
Your wife is carrying a holy son who, upon birth, shall become a lamp and a sun of wisdom for the world; therefore, I avoided him, not out of any regard for women.
The Venerable One spoke again, "Your wife shall give birth to two sons: the first shall be named Vasiṣṭha, whom I shall honor; the second shall be named Kuṇi... (this means...)
The Wild Magpie: Formerly, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Snowy (Himavat), a female magpie nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the magpie received her karmic retribution by becoming the King of Nadi. The Buddha prophesied, saying:

"In the second five-hundred-year period [after my passing], you shall be born into the household of Viśākha in the city of Rājagṛha as a sibling to a noble one; now this has come to pass without fail. One month later, she indeed gave birth.
The two sons: when the Venerable Vasiṣṭha reached the age of fifteen, he paid homage to the Arhat Prabhāsa and left the household life.
Moved by this, the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣa conferred the precepts upon him. While traveling to propagate the teachings, he arrived at the country of Nadī.
Its king was named Nityeśvara and had two sons; the first was named Mahāla and the second was named Maṇḍala. The king asked his grandfather, "Rājagṛha..."
[The King asked: "How does the climate and customs of that land differ from this one? The Patriarch said: "In that land, three Buddhas have appeared in the world.
Now, in your kingdom, there are two masters who provide guidance and transformation. The King asked: "Who are these two masters? The Patriarch said:

"The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) of supernatural power who would leave the household life to succeed the Sages. One of them is your second son, Maṇḍara."
"Although my virtue is meager, I dare to accept one of them. The King said, "Truly as the Venerable One has spoken, I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa.
The Patriarch said, "Excellent! Your Majesty is able to follow the Buddha’s intent. He immediately conferred the full precepts upon him and transmitted the Dharma.
The verse says: "Like bubbles and illusions, they are equally unimpeded; why do you not awaken to this? To realize that all phenomena are contained therein is neither of this age nor of antiquity.

After the Patriarch had transmitted the Dharma, he leaped into the air to a height of half a yojana and remained suspended there. The fourfold assembly gazed up at him with reverence and made earnest entreaties for him to return.
He then sat down again in the lotus posture and passed away. His body was cremated, and his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa during the reign of Emperor Shang of the Later Han dynasty.
The twelfth year was the *ding-si* year.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇarava, was the son of King Nitya-vaśavartin of the country of Nādi.
At the age of thirty, he encountered the patriarch Vasu, left the household life, and transmitted the Dharma to Western India. The king of that country was named De... (or "De-").
Dudu was of the Gautama clan. Having turned toward the Buddha-vehicle, he practiced with diligent perseverance. One day, at the place where he walked in meditation, a small stupa appeared.

When he wished to take it up for worship, the multitude was unable to lift it. The King immediately convened a great assembly of the three groups: those of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), those engaged in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and those of incantations (*mantra*).
He intended to ask about his doubts. At that time, the Patriarch also attended this assembly; yet none of these three groups were able [to move the stupa].
Bennian said, "The Patriarch shall explain for the King the origins of the stupa (the stupa built by King Aśoka will not be recorded here at length).
Its appearance today is brought about by the power of the King’s merit. Upon hearing this, the King said, "A Supreme Sage is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.

He immediately passed the throne to his crown prince, entered the order under the Patriarch, and in seven days realized the fruit of Arhatship. The Patriarch [then] bestowed upon him profound [instruction].

He consoled and instructed him, saying: "You reside in this country; you must skillfully deliver people yourself. Now, there is a person of great Dharma-capacity in a foreign land to whom I must go to transform them.
Dedu replied: "The Master manifests traces throughout the ten directions; when you form a thought, you should arrive immediately. Why trouble yourself by going? The Patriarch said:

Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the bhikṣu Hakena of the country of Mozhī (Mūlasthāna), saying: "While you are in that country, teaching the flock of cranes, you are about to realize the fruit of the Path; you should know this for yourself. At that time, while Hakena was reciting sūtra verses for the king of that country, Ratnamudrā, he suddenly beheld a wondrous fragrance forming into tassels. The king asked: "What auspicious omen is this? He replied: [The following: "The fragrance of the Dharma is most rare; it is not something produced by worldly perfumes. It is because the crane-king has attained the Way that this fragrance has manifested. The king said: "Is this a sign of good fortune? He replied: "It is indeed so. The king further asked: "How can one attain such a state? He replied: "If one practices the Way with single-minded devotion, one will surely attain it. The king then had the bhikṣu preach the Dharma extensively. Afterward, the bhikṣu ascended into the air and vanished. The king subsequently built a stūpa at that site. Later, when the Trepitaka Master Xuanzang arrived at that location, he saw the stūpa, which was still standing today. He also saw the image of the bhikṣu, which was carved from sandalwood and remained as it had been made. Furthermore, he saw the image of the crane-king, which was carved from white jade. Its form was lifelike and its colors were brilliant. It was over ten feet tall. The Master prostrated himself before it and offered incense and flowers. He also saw the remains of the old stūpa, which had collapsed and been buried by the earth. He then had the local people excavate the ruins and restore it. The Master also visited the place where the bhikṣu had preached the Dharma for the crane-king. There, he saw a stone pillar over twenty feet high, upon which was inscribed a record of the event. The characters were clear and legible. The Master copied the inscription and then departed. It is said that the bhikṣu Hakena was originally a native of the country of Mozhī. He had long cultivated the Way and was deeply versed in the scriptures. At that time, he was preaching the Dharma for the crane-king. When the Master first arrived at the country of Mozhī, he encountered a great drought. The king issued a decree throughout the land, ordering everyone to pray for rain. The Master then went to the temple to offer incense and prayed for the people. That night, he dreamed of a deity who told him: "The crane-king is currently in the country of Mozhī, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the king. You should go there to seek his aid. The next day, the Master traveled to the country of Mozhī and sought out the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu said to the Master: "I have heard that the Great Tang Emperor has sent you to seek the Dharma. I am now going to the country of India to pay homage to the Buddha’s relics. If you wish to travel to the West, you may accompany me. The Master agreed. They traveled together for several thousand li. Later, they parted ways and proceeded separately. The bhikṣu eventually reached the country of India. The Master, however, continued on alone. Thus ends the account of the bhikṣu Hakena. It is said that the bhikṣu Hakena was originally a native of the country of Mozhī. He had long cultivated the Way and was deeply versed in the scriptures.
