At that time,

This was the transmission of the Buddha’s Mind-Seal from Western India; it was the time when the Patriarch Mañjuśrīmitra was about to arrive. First, he sent down a fragrant incense as a token of his arrival, saying:
"What is the spiritual power of this Master like? [The King] replied: "This Master has inherited the Buddha’s prophecy from afar; he shall widely proclaim the profound transformation in this land.
At that time, the King and Haklena both paid homage from a distance. The Patriarch, knowing this, immediately took leave and attained ordination.
The bhikṣu traveled to the country of the Yuezhi and received the offerings of King Huhelena.
Later, Huhelena asked the Master, "I have dwelt among the forests for nine *śveta* (the Indians reckon one year as one *śveta*). I have a disciple named Longzi, who was intelligent from his youth;
though I have investigated his origins through the three periods of time, I cannot know his root. The Master said, "This boy [is related to you] in the fifth..."
During that kalpa, he was born into a brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati).

Having once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist temple to serve as a mallet for striking the bell, he received the retribution of being exceptionally intelligent and wise, and was held in high esteem by the masses. He asked again: "By what conditions did I attract this flock of cranes?"
The Patriarch said: "In the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu. You were to attend an assembly at the Dragon Palace, and all your disciples wished to follow you.
You observed that among the five hundred members of the assembly, not a single person was worthy of receiving such exquisite offerings.
At that time, your disciples said: 'Master, you often preach the Dharma that those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma. Now, since this is not the case, why...'"

"Holy One, you must immediately summon him to the assembly. Since you passed from this life to the next and transformed various lands, your five hundred disciples—due to their meager merit and thin virtue—were born among the feathered tribes. Now, moved by your kindness, they follow you as a flock of cranes.
Harelana asked, "By what expedient means can you cause them to attain liberation? The Patriarch replied, "I have..."
"This unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, you should listen to and receive. To transform those of the future limit, he spoke these verses:
'The mind turns following the ten thousand objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. If, following the current, one recognizes one's nature, there will be neither joy nor sorrow.

At that time, the flock of cranes heard the verses, flew up with cries, and departed. The Patriarch sat in the *paryaṅka* posture and passed away peacefully and suddenly. Kṛṣṇa (He-le-na) and King Ratnamudrā (Bao-yin-wang) arose."
The stupa was erected in the nineteenth year of Emperor Huan of the Later Han dynasty, the year of Yisi (467 CE).

The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Holena (Holena is a Sanskrit term; "he" is the Chinese translation, so he was named thus because he constantly moved flocks of cranes to feel affection and longing for him), was a native of the country of Yuezhī.
His family name was Brahmin; his father was Qiansheng, and his mother was Jinguang. Because they had no son, [the parents] prayed to the Seven...
The Buddha’s Golden Banner. She then dreamed of a divine youth atop Mount Sumeru holding a golden ring and saying, "I have come.
Upon waking, she became pregnant. When she was seven years old, while wandering through a village, she saw the people performing vulgar sacrifices.

She entered the shrine and rebuked them, saying, "You recklessly invoke calamity and fortune to delude the people. You waste livestock and grain every year, causing immense harm. Having finished speaking, [she departed].
The temple structure suddenly collapsed. Consequently, his fellow villagers called him "The Holy Child. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life.

At thirty, he met the Venerable Maṇḍara, who transmitted to him the treasury of the Dharma-eye. While traveling to teach and transform others in Central India, he arrived at a kingdom ruled by a king named Abhayasāgara, who held deep faith in the Buddha-way.
After the Patriarch had expounded the True Dharma for the king, the king suddenly saw two men.
Wearing crimson robes, the Patriarch prostrated himself before the King. The King asked, "Who is this person? The Patriarch replied, "This is the Sun and Moon Deities.
I once preached the Dharma for them in the past; therefore, they have come to pay their respects. After a long while, they were no longer seen, and only a wondrous fragrance remained. The King said:
"How many suns, moons, and lands are there in total? The Patriarch replied, "In the worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, there are ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons each.
If I were to explain this extensively, I could not finish. When the King heard this, he was filled with joy.

At that time, the Patriarch expounded the Unsurpassed Way to deliver those with karmic affinity. Because his senior disciple, the Dragon Prince, had died young, he had an elder brother named Siṃha who was widely learned.
He possessed a powerful memory and served a Brahmin. When his teacher passed away and his younger brother also died, he took refuge with the Venerable One and asked:
"I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind? The Master said: "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply your mind. The student asked:
"If there is no application of the mind, who performs the work of a Buddha? The Master said: "If you have any application, it is not a meritorious deed."
"If you are without action, that is itself the work of a Buddha. As the Sūtra says: "The merit I have performed is without 'mine-ness' (*mamakāra*).
Upon hearing these words, Śiṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha. At that moment, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this?
Śiṃha replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth; furthermore, there are five black vapors."
A road runs straight across the center of it. The Patriarch asked, "What are its omens? He replied, "They cannot be known.
The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India. It shall befall you; I am about to pass away."
"Now I entrust the Dharma-eye to you. Guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse: "When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable.
When it is clearly understood, there is nothing to be attained; When it is attained, one does not speak of knowing.

Upon hearing this verse, the Bhikṣu Siṃha was filled with joy and satisfaction. However, he did not yet understand what kind of hardships he would encounter. The Patriarch then secretly indicated this to him. Having finished speaking, he manifested ten... [images].
After the eighth transformation, he returned to stillness. When the cremation was completed, his relics were distributed, and each group wished to erect a stūpa.

The Patriarch then appeared again in the air and spoke this verse: "One dharma is all dharmas; All dharmas are subsumed within one dharma. My body is neither existent nor non-existent; Why divide it among all these stūpas?
Upon hearing this verse, the assembly no longer divided the relics, but instead built the stūpa on the site of the cremation ground.
This was the year Jichou (the twenty-second year of Emperor Xian of the Later Han).
The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Bhikṣu Siṃha, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin.

Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was one named Parika who had originally practiced meditative contemplation; thus, he possessed dhyāna-concentration and [supernormal] knowledge.
The Master [Bodhidharma] saw five groups of people: those who perceived signs, those who clung to signs, those who abandoned signs, and those who remained silent.

He interrogated and transformed them; the four groups were all silent and submitted in their hearts. Only the meditation master Dharmadatta, hearing that the four groups had been rebuked, came forward in indignation.

The Master said, "Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*); why have you come here? Now that you have arrived here, how can you say you practice concentration? He replied: "I..."

"Although I have come here, my mind remains undisturbed. Concentration follows the person; how could it depend on the location? The Master said, "Since you, O virtuous one, have come, your practice has also arrived.
Since there is no fixed location, how could it depend on the person's practice? He replied, "Because concentration practices the person, the person does not practice concentration.
I came here, and my concentration was already habitually practiced. The Master said, "It is not that the person practices concentration; rather, concentration practices the person."
"Therefore, when you first arrived, what state of concentration (*samādhi*) were you practicing? He replied, "It was like a pure, bright pearl, with no obscurations inside or out;
if concentration is fully realized, it must necessarily be like this. The Patriarch said, "If concentration is fully realized, it is indeed like a bright pearl.
Yet, looking at you now, you do not seem to be of the pearl-like type. He replied, "That pearl is clear and penetrating, both inside and out; my mind is undisturbed, just as..."
"If this is pure," the Patriarch said, "that pearl has neither inside nor outside; how can you, O virtuous one, determine it? Impure things do not cause agitation;
this state of concentration is not purity. Having received the Patriarch’s awakening, Damodara’s mind became brilliantly clear.

Once the Patriarch had gathered the five groups of disciples and his fame spread far and wide, he began to seek a Dharma heir. He encountered an elder who led his son to the Patriarch and asked him about the boy. This...
The boy’s name was Sita. At birth, he had kept his left hand in a fist, and even now that he has grown up, he is still unable to open it.

"I pray that the Venerable One will reveal the karmic cause from his past life," [the father] requested. The Patriarch looked at him and immediately reached out his hand, saying, "Give me back my pearl.
The boy suddenly opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk, and there was a boy named Ba..."
"Give it up. I once went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea. You received a pearl as an offering (*dakṣiṇā*) and gave it to me;

now you must return my pearl. This is but natural. The elder then relinquished his son to leave the household life. The Master immediately conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*). Because of these prior conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha.
The Master then said to him, "My teacher had a secret prediction that you would encounter hardship before long. The Tathāgata’s True..."
"I now transmit the Treasury of the Dharma-Eye to you. You should protect it so that it may universally moisten all future ages. He spoke in verse:

"When the correct teaching of knowledge and vision occurs, Knowledge and vision are both the mind. When the mind is present, there is knowledge and vision; Knowledge and vision are right here and now.

Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Sengduo, sending him to another country to transform beings according to their capacities. Sengduo received [the robe].
The Teaching was transmitted directly to South India. The Patriarch, deeming that he could not evade his destiny, remained alone in Kaśmīra.
At that time, there were two non-Buddhist practitioners in that country named Māmukta and Durlabha, who studied various magical arts and plotted a rebellion.
They disguised themselves in the appearance of Śākyaputrīya monks and secretly entered the royal palace, saying, "If we do not succeed, it shall be our crime."

"O son of the Buddha, you have brought this calamity upon yourself; the disaster has followed immediately. The King was indeed enraged and said, "I have long since placed my heart's devotion in the Triple Gem.
Why have you contrived such harm as this? He immediately ordered the destruction of the monastery and the expulsion of the Śākya community.

Furthermore, he personally grasped a sword and went before the Venerable One, asking, "Have you realized the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have already realized the emptiness of the aggregates."

The king asked, "Have you transcended birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I have already transcended birth and death. The king said, "Since you have transcended birth and death, you may give me your head.
The Patriarch said, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The king then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable One's head.
White milk surged upward several feet high, and the king’s right arm likewise fell to the ground; he passed away after seven days.
Prince Prabhāśiras sighed, saying, "Why has my father brought this calamity upon himself? At that time, there was a seer named Śvetaśaila who lived on Mount Elephant.

Having deeply understood the principle of cause and effect, Guangshou then extensively proclaimed his past causes to resolve the web of doubts (the details of which are found in the *Shengzhou ji* and the *Baolin zhuan*).
He subsequently erected a stupa for the venerable Sīha based upon his physical remains; this was in the twenty-second year of Emperor Qi’s reign during the Wei dynasty, the year of Jīmáo.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (Póshè斯多), was a native of Kaśmīra. He was of Brahmin lineage; his father was named Śāntacaryā (Jìxíng) and his mother Nityasukhā (Cháng'ānlè).
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, he held his left hand in a fist.

He encountered the patriarch Siṃha (Shīzǐ), who revealed his past causes and conditions and secretly transmitted to him the Heart-Seal (Cittamudrā). Later, he traveled to Southern India and arrived in Central India.

In India, there was a king named Karṇa who offered him hospitality and support. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner known as Nirātma-guru (The Venerable Selfless One) who had previously been held in high esteem by the king.
Envious of Bodhidharma’s arrival, he wished to debate with him, hoping that by winning, he might consolidate his own standing.
Thus, before the king, he said to Bodhidharma, "I understand the art of silent debate; it requires no spoken words. Bodhidharma asked, "Who knows this?"
[They were about to] compete. The other said, "I do not contend for victory or defeat; I only seek the meaning.
The Patriarch asked, "What do you take to be the meaning? He replied, "Taking no-mind as the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you obtain the meaning?

He replied, "When I speak of no-mind, it is a designation, not the meaning itself. The Patriarch said, "When you speak of no-mind, it is a designation, not the meaning. When I speak of non-mind, it is..."
"Meaning is not name. He said, "When meaning is not name, who can discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your name is not meaning; what name is this name?

He said, "It is for the sake of discerning non-meaning; this name is a nameless name. The Patriarch said, "Since the name is already not a name, and the meaning is also not meaning, who is it that discerns?
And what is there to be discerned? Thus they exchanged questions and answers fifty-nine times. Outside [the hall],...

Dao Du remained silent in faith and submission. At that time, the Master suddenly turned his face northward, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, has encountered this calamity today;
how tragic! He then took leave of the king and traveled south, reaching Southern India. There he lived in seclusion among the mountain valleys.
At that time, the king of that land was named Devaśrī, who welcomed him and offered him sustenance. The king had two sons; the first was named...
Guṇabhadra was fierce and his physical strength was robust; his other name was Rāhula. He was gentle and mild, yet had long been afflicted by illness and suffering.
The Master then explained the principles of cause and effect to him, whereupon the King immediately resolved his doubts. Furthermore, there was a master of incantations who envied the Master’s Way;
he secretly placed poison in food and drink. The Master knew of it and ate it, while the other [the sorcerer] instead suffered the consequences.
Frightened, he then went to the Patriarch to leave the household life. The Patriarch immediately conferred the full precepts upon him. Sixty years later, Emperor De-sheng ascended the throne;

he again placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths and brought trouble upon the Patriarch. Unlike Upagupta, who was imprisoned for offering remonstrance, the King suddenly questioned the Patriarch, saying:
"In my kingdom, heterodox and deceptive doctrines have long been banned. What school is it that you, Master, profess? The Patriarch replied: "In your kingdom of old..."

"Come. In truth, there is no heterodox dharma. That which I have attained is precisely the lineage of the Buddha. The King asked, "One thousand two hundred years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
From whom did you receive it, Master? The Patriarch replied, "The Mahāsattva Kāśyapa personally received the seal of the Buddha.
It was transmitted successively down to the twenty-fourth generation, the Venerable Siṃha. I received it from him. The King said, "I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha..."

"Unable to escape execution, how could you transmit the Dharma to future generations? The Patriarch said, "When my Master’s time of peril had not yet arisen, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the Dharma verses to manifest the lineage of transmission. The King asked, "Where is that robe?

The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned; its five colors remained vivid, and even when the firewood was exhausted, it remained as it was. The King then—
He repented and paid his respects. Once it was clear that Shizi Zhen had truly succeeded him, he then pardoned Guṇamati. Guṇamati subsequently requested ordination.
The Patriarch asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so? Guṇamati replied, "If I leave the household life, I shall not engage in those things.
The Patriarch asked, "What things will you not engage in? Guṇamati said, "I shall not engage in worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "Then for what purpose will you engage in them?"
Guṇamati said, "This shall be performed as a Buddha-work. The Patriarch replied, "The Prince’s wisdom is divinely supreme;

surely it is the descent of various sages. He then granted permission for him to leave the household life. For six years he served [the Patriarch], and later received full ordination within the royal palace.

At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the earth shook violently, accompanied by many miraculous phenomena. The Patriarch then addressed him, saying, "I have already grown old and infirm; how could I remain much longer?"
"You must well protect the treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma and universally deliver all sentient beings. Listen to my verse: "The Sage speaks of knowledge and vision;
Within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong. I have now realized the true nature: There is neither Path nor Principle. Bodhidharma then recited this verse.
He addressed the Patriarch once more, saying, "The Dharma robe should be transmitted to you. The Patriarch said, "This robe is for the sake of what is difficult; it is a provisional..."
To prove this, he said, "Your body shall suffer no harm; why rely on his robe? His transformation will cover the ten directions, and people will naturally turn toward him with faith.
This was not as [the Master] had previously heard from Maudgalyāyana. He prostrated and withdrew. The Patriarch manifested supernatural transformations and, by means of samādhi-fire, self-immolated.

The śarīra on the ground was approximately one chi in height; King De-seung (Deokseong) first constructed a stūpa to enshrine it, during the third year of the Taíning era of Emperor Míng of the Eastern Jin, the year of Yǐyǒu.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was the second son of King Devaśrī of South India.
Having received ordination and attained the Dharma, he traveled to East India. There, the king was named Sthira; he followed the non-Buddhist teacher, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha.
When the Venerable One was about to arrive, the king and the Brahmin both beheld a white vapor piercing through from the zenith to the nadir. The king...
He asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Brahmin, having foreknowledge that the Elder [Upatiṣya] was entering the kingdom, feared that the King would convert to the good path;

he therefore said, "This is merely a portent of Māra’s arrival. What auspiciousness is there in it? He immediately gathered his disciples and deliberated, saying, "It would be better to keep him from entering the capital.
Who among us can defeat him? A disciple replied, "Each of us possesses incantations and arts by which we can move [him]."
"Entering fire and water, heaven and earth—what cause for concern? When the Patriarch arrived, he first saw black vapors over the palace walls and said, 'This is but a minor difficulty.
He went straight to the King's location. The King asked, 'Master, why have you come? The Patriarch replied, 'To deliver sentient beings. The King said:
"By what means do you deliver them? The Patriarch replied, "I deliver each according to their own kind.

When the Brahmin heard these words, he could not contain his anger and immediately used his illusory powers to conjure a great mountain atop the Patriarch's head. The Patriarch pointed at it, and suddenly it appeared above the heads of the entire assembly.

Terrified, the Brahmins and their followers threw themselves at the Patriarch's feet. The Patriarch, pitying their delusion and ignorance, pointed once more, and the conjured mountain vanished accordingly.
He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the king, leading him toward the True Vehicle (Saddharmayāna). He said to the king, "In this kingdom, there shall be a sage who will succeed me.
At that time, there was the son of a Brahmin, about twenty years of age, who had lost both parents in his youth and whose name and lineage were unknown.
He sometimes called himself "Mālākāra" (The Garlanded One), so people referred to him as the "Mālākāra Youth. He wandered through the streets and villages.
He begged for alms to sustain his daily life, much like the monk Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). When people asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly?
he would immediately reply, "Why do you walk so slowly? Or when they asked, "What is your surname? he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one knew the reason for this.
Later, the King was traveling in the same carriage as the Venerable One and saw the Mañjuśrī-kumāra-bhūta bowing his head before them. The Patriarch said, "Do you remember our past [encounter]?"
The Master asked, "Is this so? The boy replied, "I recall that in a distant eon, I lived together with you, Master.
You expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I turned the wheel of the profound *Sūtras*. Today’s events are surely in accord with our past causes.
The Patriarch further said to the King, "This boy is none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. After this holy one, two more shall appear."
One person transformed [beings] in South India; one person’s karmic conditions lay in China.
Within four or five years, he returned to this land. Thus, based on his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra (般若多羅). He was entrusted with the Dharma-eye Treasury. The verse says:

“The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither beginning nor end. Responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called ‘wisdom. Having thus transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch passed away.

He then took leave of the King, saying, "My transformative conditions have come to an end; I shall now return to nirvana. I pray that Your Majesty will not forget to provide external protection for the Supreme Vehicle.

He then returned to his original seat, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. A fire spontaneously emerged from within him to cremate his body, and his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa.
This occurred in the year Wuzi, the thirteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to South India to propagate the teachings.
There, the king was named Gandhāra; he venerated the Buddha Vehicle and offered him honor and sustenance beyond compare.
He also bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravyūha, Śrīcandra, and [the third son].
Tiduo (Devadatta) said, "Putiduo (Bodhidatta); he was the youngest of the bodhisattvas.

Their grandfather wished to test what they had attained, so he took the pearl he had bestowed upon them and asked the three princes, "This pearl is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it?
The first prince and the second prince both replied, "This pearl is the most honored among the seven treasures; certainly nothing surpasses it. It is not something for Your Honor [to possess]."
"As for the power of the Way, who is able to receive it? The third prince said: "This is a worldly treasure, yet it is not the supreme;
among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This is a worldly light, yet it is not the supreme; among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly clarity, yet it is not the supreme; among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. This...
The radiance of a jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely on the light of wisdom to discern it. Once it has been discerned, one knows it is a jewel;
once one knows it is a jewel, one understands its preciousness. If the jewel were precious by itself, it would not be a jewel;
if the jewel were discerned by itself, it would not be a jewel. That a jewel is not a jewel by itself means that it must rely on the "jewel of wisdom" to discern the worldly jewel.
"A jewel is not inherently a jewel; it must rely upon the jewel of wisdom to illuminate the jewel of the Dharma. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, his jewel manifests;
likewise, when sentient beings possess the Way, the jewel of their minds does the same. The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what is signless? He replied, "Among all things, non-arising is signless. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the highest?
He replied, "Among all things, the person-self (pudgala-ātman) is the highest. Again he asked, "Among all things, what is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. The Patriarch knew that he was his dharma heir.
Because the time had not yet arrived, he remained silent and mingled with the crowd. When the incense reached the king and he grew weary of the world, the assembly all wailed and fainted;
only the third son, Bodhidhara, entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days, whereupon he requested ordination.
Once he had received full precepts, his grandfather told him: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa."
This has been transmitted in succession down to me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: "The mind-ground gives rise to all seeds; From conditions, principles further arise.
When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; When the flower blooms, the world emerges. The Venerable One, having thus transmitted the Dharma, [passed away].
Immediately, he rose from his seat and extended his left and right hands, each emitting twenty-seven rays of light, brilliant with five colors.
He then leaped into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees and transformed himself into fire to consume his own body. Śarīras fell like rain from the sky;
they were collected and enshrined in a stupa. This occurred in the year Dingyou, the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty. Because of this, [the Master] Zu...
The King of East India invited the Patriarch for a meal. During the meal, the King asked, "Everyone here recites the sutras; why is it that you alone do not?
The Patriarch replied, "I, this poor monk, do not follow external conditions when breathing out, nor do I dwell within the aggregates or realms when breathing in.
I constantly turn such a sutra as this in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of volumes—not merely one or two."
The First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Gandharva of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitara. Later, he met the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra.

Upon arriving in his own country, he received the king’s offerings. Recognizing that his teacher was Guhyapada, the king tested him by having him distinguish the precious jewels bestowed upon his two elder brothers, thereby bringing forth the essential points of the mind.
Subsequently, the Venerable One said to him, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery."
Now, "Dharma" is the meaning of "penetrating the Great. It was thus appropriate to name him Dharma; consequently, he was renamed Bodhidharma.
The Patriarch then addressed the Venerable One, saying: "Since I have attained the Dharma, to which country should I go to perform the work of a Buddha?

I pray that you will grant me your instruction. The Venerable One replied: "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not yet travel far. Remain for now in Southern India and wait until after my passing."
"In sixty-seven years, you shall go to China to administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties.
Be careful not to travel too soon; you will suffer decline under the sun. The Patriarch asked again, "In that land, are there Great Beings capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma?
Will there be obstacles for a thousand years hence? The Master replied, "In the regions where you will transform others, those who attain Bodhi shall be beyond counting. As for me—"
More than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, that country will face a crisis. Wenbu will naturally subdue it from within the waters. When your time comes, do not remain in the south;
for there they value only conditioned achievements and do not perceive the principle of the Buddha. Even if you should go there, [you must proceed with caution].
"You must not remain here for long. Listen to my verse: Traveling along the road, crossing water, one encounters sheep again; All alone and weary, one crosses the river in the dark.
At the setting of the sun, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses; Two young cassia trees have long flourished in prosperity. He asked again:
"What further events will there be after this? The Master replied, "From now on, for one hundred and fifty years, there will be minor difficulties.

Listen to my prophecy: 'Though auspicious within the heart, it is inauspicious without; the monastery below the stream bears an ill-fated name. Because of encountering a venomous dragon, a martial son shall be born;
suddenly meeting a small mouse, there will be endless silence. He asked again, 'What will it be like after this? The Master said:"
He said: "Two hundred and twenty years hence, you shall see a person beneath these trees who will attain the fruit of the Way. Listen to my prophecy: 'Though Zhendan is vast, there is no other path;
one must rely on the feet of descendants to travel. A golden rooster knows how to hold a single grain of millet, providing sustenance for the Arhats of the ten directions.
He further recited various verses, all of which were premonitions regarding the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma."

(The details are found in the *Baolin zhuan* and the *Shengzhou ji*). The Master [Seng]zu reverently received the teachings and served at his side for nearly forty years without ever neglecting his duties.
When the Venerable One passed away, he subsequently propagated the Dharma in his own country. At that time there were two masters:
the first named Buddhajīva and the second named Buddhasānta. Originally, the Master had studied the Śrāvaka-vehicle meditation and contemplation of Buddhabhadra together with them.
After Buddhadasa encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, he abandoned the Hinayana for the Mahayana and worked together with the Patriarch to transform beings;
they were then known as the "Two Gateways to Ambrosia. Buddhadasa’s followers further divided into six schools:
first, the School of Characteristics; second, the School of Non-characteristics; third, the School of Samādhi and Wisdom; fourth, the School of Precept Practice; fifth...

The Wudeng school and the sixth, the Jijing school, each clung to their own interpretations and separately expanded the source of their teachings. Their monastic settlements flourished and their followers were exceedingly numerous.

The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so for these fragmented and proliferating groups that have divided into six schools?
If I do not eliminate them, they will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken, he subtly manifested his spiritual power.
[He] went to the place of the Sarvāstivādins and asked, "What is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas?
Among that assembly, there was an elder named Sarvaloka who replied, "That which does not mutually [confuse] the various marks among all marks is called the true mark."
The Patriarch said, "If all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) do not mutually interact, and if this is called the 'true reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), by what means would you establish it?
He replied, "Among all phenomena, there is truly no fixed establishment. If one were to fix phenomena, how could they be called real?
The Patriarch said, "That phenomena are not fixed is precisely what is called true reality. Since you yourself are not now fixed, how can you attain it? He replied, "I say that I am not fixed."

"One does not speak of the various marks; one should speak of the various marks. The meaning is likewise. The Patriarch said, "Your statement is not definitive. It should be the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because it is both definitive and non-definitive, it is not the true mark. He replied, "Since the definitive is itself non-definitive, it is not the true mark."

[The Master] said: "I know that you are not the same as before; you are neither fixed nor unchanging. The Patriarch said: "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
That which has already changed and passed away is likewise so [in its nature]. He replied: "Unchanging must exist; because it exists or does not exist, the true mark is change."

He sought to establish the meaning of this through meditative concentration. Zuzi said, "The true mark (*dharmatā*) is unchanging; that which changes is not the true mark. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, what can be called the true mark?
Sabara, perceiving in his heart that the holy master possessed profound and latent understanding, pointed his finger at space and said:
"This is a worldly phenomenon with marks; yet it can also be empty. Should this body of mine become like this? The Patriarch said:
"If you understand the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), you will see that there is no mark. If you realize that there is no mark, its form is likewise so. You should [seek it] within form."
"Not losing the physical form" means that within the absence of marks (*animitta*), one is not obstructed by existence. If one can understand it thus, this is called the "True Mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith. The Patriarch suddenly vanished from sight and went to the school of the Non-Form School (*animittavāda*).
He asked them, "You speak of non-form; how do you realize it? Among the assembly, there was one named Pratītya who replied:
He said, "I clarify formlessness because the mind does not manifest. The Patriarch said, "If your mind does not manifest, how can you clarify it?
He replied, "I clarify formlessness; the mind neither grasps nor rejects. At the very time of clarifying, there is also no one who clarifies.

The Patriarch said, "If, regarding all existence and non-existence, the mind neither grasps nor rejects, and furthermore there is no one who clarifies, then because all forms of clarity are absent," he replied, "I enter the Buddha's three..."

[The monk] said, "Even samādhi is unattainable; how much more so the signless (animitta), which one wishes to know? The Patriarch said, "If you do not know the sign, who can speak of existence or non-existence?
If even samādhi is unattainable, what is it called? He replied, "I say that I do not realize [it]. Since there is nothing to be realized in realization, it is not samādhi;
therefore, I speak of it as samādhi. The Patriarch said, "If it is not samādhi, how can it be named? You..."
"Since you have not realized it, what is there to realize if you have not realized it? When Boluotipo heard the Patriarch’s analysis, he immediately awakened to his original mind.
He prostrated in thanks to the Patriarch and repented for his past errors. The Patriarch prophesied, saying: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long.

There is a demon in this country who will be subdued by you in no time. Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished. Boluotipo then went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked: "What do you study?"
"Are concentration and wisdom one or two? A man named Bharanda among the assembly replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.
The Patriarch said, "If they are neither one nor two, why are they called concentration and wisdom? He replied, "In concentration, it is not concentration."
Abiding in wisdom is not wisdom; one is not one, and two are not two. The Patriarch said: "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two.
Since it is neither fixed wisdom nor insight, by what means can it be defined as wisdom or insight? He replied: "Neither one nor two—this is what wisdom and insight are able to know."
"It is the same for non-concentration and non-wisdom. The Patriarch said, "Because wisdom is not concentration, how then can one know it?
It is neither one nor two; who is concentrated and who is wise? When Parāntaka heard this, his doubts were cleared away like ice melting.

He then went to the fourth master, Śīlacaryāgupta, and asked, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? What is called 'practice' (caryā)? Regarding these precepts and practices, are they one or are they two?"
Among that assembly, there was a worthy man who replied: "One and two, two and one—these are all produced from them; by relying on the teaching, one remains unstained.
This is called the practice of precepts. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that 'one relies on the teaching' implies that there is still defilement.

Since both 'one' and 'two' are shattered, how can you say one relies on the teaching? These two are contradictory and do not reach the true practice. When what is internal and external is not clear, how can it be called the precepts? He [the worthy man]...

[The Master] said: "I have what is internal and what is external; he has already understood this to its conclusion. Having attained thorough penetration, this is itself the practice of the precepts (*śīla*).

If one speaks of contrariety, then both 'is' and 'is not' apply. When speech reaches purity, it is simultaneously the precept and the practice. The Patriarch asked: "If both 'is' and 'is not' apply, how can you speak of purity?
Since thorough penetration has been attained, why discuss 'internal' and 'external'? Upon hearing this, the worthy man felt ashamed and submitted. He then... [reached the point of realization].
Regarding the school of Non-Attainment (*wude*), a questioner asked: "You speak of non-attainment; how can there be attainment through non-attainment?

Since there is nothing attained, there is likewise no attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was Baojing, who replied: "When I speak of non-attainment, it is not the case that there is no attainment of non-attainment.

I shall explain the attainment of attainment: non-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said: "Since attainment is already non-attainment, attainment is also non-attainment. You have already spoken of 'attainment'..."
"Attainment. "What is attained by attainment? He replied, "Seeing attainment is non-attainment; non-attainment is attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called the attainment of attainment.
The Patriarch said, "Since attainment is non-attainment, the attainment of attainment is without attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, what is there to be attained by attainment?
Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt. He went to Jijing’s dwelling and asked, "What is meant by 'quiescence'?"
"Within this Dharma, what is stillness and what is tranquility? A venerable one among the assembly replied: "This mind being unmoving is called tranquility;
being unstained by phenomena is called stillness. The Patriarch said: "If the original mind were not already tranquil, it would require the cultivation of tranquility.
Since it is tranquil from the very beginning, what need is there for tranquility? The other said: "All phenomena are originally empty; they are empty because of emptiness."
Regarding that emptiness of emptiness, it is therefore called "quiescence. The Patriarch said: "Emptiness is already empty; all dharmas are likewise so.
Quiescent and signless—what is there to be quiescent, what is there to be still? Upon hearing the Master’s instruction, the Venerable One attained sudden enlightenment.

Subsequently, the six groups of disciples all vowed to take refuge. From this, his transformation spread throughout Southern India and his fame resounded across the five regions of Jambudvīpa. For sixty years, he delivered [beings].
There was a vast multitude of people. Later, they encountered King Heterodox-View (Vilomadarśana), who reviled and disparaged the Triple Gem.
He would say every time: "The ancestors of my lineage all believed in the Buddha-way, yet they fell into false views; consequently, their lifespans were not long and their reigns were short-lived.

Furthermore, I myself am the Buddha—why seek anything further outside? As for the retribution of good and evil, these are all fabrications concocted by those of great cleverness. This continued until his kingdom...

The elder officials within the court, who had been served by previous kings, were all dismissed from office. When Zu learned of this, he sighed, lamenting their meager virtue and wondering how he might save them.
He then recalled two leaders from the School of Non-Form (Wuxiangzong): the first was Boluoti, who shared a karmic affinity with the king and was on the verge of realizing the fruit of his practice;

He saw the Master carrying a single shoe, walking gracefully and alone toward the west. Songyun asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going to the West.
Upon his return, Songyun related these events in detail. When the disciples opened the tomb, they found only an empty coffin; a single leather shoe remained.
The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration. By imperial decree, his cast-off sandals were retrieved and enshrined for veneration at Shaolin Temple.

In the *dingmao* year, the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty (727 CE), they were stolen by a seeker of the Way at Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai; their current whereabouts are unknown.

Initially, when Emperor Wu of Liang met the Patriarch, their karmic conditions had not yet harmonized; however, upon hearing that the Master’s transformation of beings was flourishing in the Wei kingdom, he [sent envoys].
I intended to compose an inscription for my teacher’s stele but lacked the leisure; later, upon hearing the account of Song Yun, I finally completed it.

Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yuanjue (Perfect Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Kongguan (Empty Contemplation). (The reign titles follow the *Jinian tongpu*.)

(The General Discussion states: *The Transmission of the Lamp* records that Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty, admiring the Master’s extraordinary traces, issued three successive edicts inviting him; yet the Master ultimately did not descend from Shaolin. When the Master passed away, Song Yun was returning from the Western Regions and encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains.

Emperor Xiaozhuang issued an order to open the tomb. This was the eighth year of the Putong era of the Southern Dynasties History, which is the first year of the Datong era. Emperor Xiaoming had passed away on the day of Gui-chou, the fourth month of this year. The Master arrived in Liang in the tenth month. Thus, by the time the Master reached the Wei, Emperor Xiaoming had already died.

His son ascended the throne shortly thereafter but was assassinated by Er Zhu Rong, who then established Emperor Xiaozhuang. From this point, the Wei state fell into great chaos. Three years later, Emperor Xiaozhuang passed away; five years after that, the realm was divided into Eastern and Western Wei.)

Wei. Thus, when my ancestor was at Shaolin, it coincided precisely with that period of turmoil. By the time Song Yun returned, five or six years had already passed since the death of Emperor Xiaozhuang, and his kingdom had long been partitioned.

How could there be any truth to the claim that Emperor Xiaozhuang ordered the opening of the tomb? According to the *History of Tang*, at the end of the Later Wei, there was a monk named Bodhidharma who came by sea. After he passed away, the Wei envoy Song Yun encountered him while returning from the Pamir Mountains.
His disciples opened the grave, but there was nothing inside but a single shoe. This is indeed a factual record.
The Second Patriarch, Grand Master Huike, was a native of Wulao. His surname was Ji, and his father’s name was Ji.

Before he had a son, the father often thought to himself, "My family has long honored the good; how could we be without an heir? After he had prayed for a long time, one night a wondrous light appeared and illuminated the room.
Consequently, his mother became pregnant. When the child grew up, [the father] named him after this auspicious sign of the light illuminating the room.

Guang was from childhood possessed of an extraordinary spirit. He read widely in the *Shi* and *Shu* classics and was particularly proficient in the profound principles of the *Xuanxue* (Dark Learning) school;

yet he did not concern himself with family property and delighted in wandering among mountains and rivers. Later, upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a state of transcendent self-realization and immediately traveled to Mount Xiangshan at Longmen in Luoyang.
Relying on Master Baojing, he left the household life and received full ordination at Yongmu Temple. He traveled among lecture halls, studying the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
At the age of thirty-three, he returned to Xiangshan, where he sat in meditative seclusion all day long for another eight years.
While in a state of profound silence, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit of enlightenment; why do you linger here? The Great Way..."
"It is not far; you shall go south. Zu perceived that this was divine assistance and consequently changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).

The following day, he felt a pain in his head as if it were being pierced with needles. His master wished to treat him, but a voice from the air said, "This is the transformation of the bones; it is no ordinary pain."
The Patriarch then reported the matter of seeing the deity to his master. The master examined the bone of his crown and saw that it rose up like five peaks.

He then said, "Your marks are auspicious; you shall surely attain realization. As for the deity who directed you to the south, this must be the Great Being Bodhidharma of Shaolin who will surely be your teacher.
Having received these instructions, the Patriarch traveled to Shaoshi Mountain. There he received the Dharma and transmitted it.

The details of his life and deeds are fully recorded in the "Chapter on Bodhidharma. Since the Great Master entrusted his transformative manifestation at Shaolin and returned to the West, he successively propagated the profound wind of the Dharma and extensively sought a dharma-heir.
In the second year of the Tianping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, there came a layman over forty years of age who did not disclose his name or lineage.
He arrived to pay his respects and asked the Patriarch: "Your disciple’s body is entangled with a chronic ailment; I pray that you..."

The Master was performing a repentance for his transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgression, and I shall repent it for you. After a long while, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgression but cannot find it.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgression; you should now dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The layman said, "Now I see the Master."
"I already know what the Sangha is, but I do not yet understand what is called the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "This mind is the Buddha;

this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. The scholar said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma—they are non-dual. The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately—
When he was having his hair shaved, [Huike] said, "This is my treasure; you should be named Sengcan.

On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From then on, his illness gradually improved. After serving him for two years, the Patriarch told him:
"Bodhidharma came from afar from Central India to transmit the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, along with the robe of faith, secretly entrusting it to me."
"I now bestow it upon you; you should guard and protect it so that it is never severed. Listen to my verse: 'Originally there is the ground of conditions;
based on this ground, flowers grow from seeds. Originally there were no seeds; the flowers have likewise never been born. Having thus transmitted the robe and the Dharma, the Patriarch said:
He further said, "You have received my teaching; you should dwell in the deep mountains and must not yet go forth to transform others. There will surely be national calamities.

Huìcǎn said, "Since the Master already knows this in advance, I pray that you will deign to grant me instruction. The Patriarch replied, "It is not I who know this. This is what was recorded as a prophecy by Prajñātāra, whom Bodhidharma transmitted:
'Though auspicious within the mind, there is misfortune on the outside. I have calculated the years, and it is precisely [as he foretold]."
"It rests with you. You must carefully reflect upon my previous words so as not to encounter worldly hardships. However, I too have karmic debts from past lives that I must now repay.

Depart well and act virtuously; wait for the right time, and the transmission shall be made. Having thus given his final instructions, the Patriarch immediately departed for the capital city of Ye, where he preached the Dharma according to the needs of the occasion.
With a single voice, he expounded the teachings, and the fourfold assembly took refuge in him. In this manner, thirty-four years passed, after which he finally withdrew [into seclusion].
Guang mingled with the common crowd, altering his appearance and demeanor. At times he entered wine shops; at times he passed by butcher stalls;
at times he engaged in street chatter; and at times he followed after menial laborers. When people asked him, "Master, you are a man of the Way; why do you act in this manner?
the Patriarch replied, "I am merely disciplining my own mind; what does it concern you? Furthermore, beneath the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, he spoke of non-existence.
Regarding the Superior Way: The listeners gathered like a forest. At that time, there was a Dharma Master named Bianhe who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the monastery.

When the students heard their master expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away. Bianhe could not contain his indignation and instigated slander against Master Zu with the local magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan.
Zhai was deluded by those heterodox arguments and subjected Zu to unlawful treatment. Zu remained serene and submitted to fate with resignation; those who recognized him...

"True" refers to what is called "repaying a debt. At the age of one hundred and seven, on the sixteenth day of the third month in the guichou year, the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, he was buried seventy li northeast of Fuyang County in Cizhou.

Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dazuo (皓月). (Upon being questioned by the attendant Haoyue regarding the Venerable Master Chena of Changsha, an ancient worthy said: "When one has realized it, karmic obstructions are originally empty; when one has not yet realized it... [text fragment])

"One must repay former debts. [Daoyue asked: "As for Venerable Siṃha and the Great Master the Second Patriarch, why were they able to repay their debts? Sanda said, "Virtuous One, you do not recognize that the original nature is empty.

Daoyue asked, "What is the original emptiness? Sanda said, "Karmic obstacles are it. Daoyue asked, "What are karmic obstacles? Sanda said, "The original emptiness is it. Daoyue was speechless. Sanda then showed him with a verse: "Provisionally existent, yet originally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet also not non-existent. The meaning of Nirvana repaying debts— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, was a man of unknown origins. Initially, he approached the Second Patriarch as a layman (*avadāta-vasana*).
Having received ordination and the transmission of the Dharma, he lived in seclusion on Mount Wangong in Shuzhou.

During the period when Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddha-Dharma, the Patriarch traveled between Taihu County and Mount Sikong, dwelling in no fixed location for more than ten years. At that time...

No one was able to understand him. In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the year of Renzi, there was a novice monk named Daoxin, fourteen years of age, who came to pay respects to the Patriarch and said, "I pray that the Master will show compassion and grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Daoxin attained realization.

He attained great enlightenment. He served [Nanyue] with diligence for nine years. Later, he received the full precepts at Jizhou and attended upon his master with even greater reverence. Nanyue repeatedly tested him on the profound and subtle mysteries;
knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma. The verse said: "Though the seeds of flowers depend on the earth, From the earth the flowers grow.
If no one plants the seeds, Neither flowers nor earth will exist. The Master further said: "In the past, Great Master Huikong..."

"My Dharma," [he said], "will later travel to the capital of Ye to transform the people; it will not be until thirty years have passed that it shall come to an end. Now that I have found you, why do you linger here?
He then departed for Mount Luofu, where he stayed at leisure for two years before returning to his former site. Within a month, the local officials and commoners flocked there in haste.

A grand vegetarian feast was prepared. After the Master had extensively proclaimed the essentials of the mind to the fourfold assembly, he stood with palms joined beneath a great tree at the site of the Dharma assembly until his passing.
This occurred on the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Daye era (the Bingyin year) of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty.

Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jianzhi and erected a stupa named Jueji. The Master’s *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Believing in Mind) states: "The Supreme Way is not difficult."
Simply loathe discrimination; merely do not harbor hatred or love. Then all will be transparently clear. A difference of even a hair’s breadth makes heaven and earth apart.

If you wish for this to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of favorability or opposition. To contend with favorability and opposition is the sickness of the mind; it shows one does not recognize the profound principle.
To strive in vain for stillness is to be like the vast void—neither deficient nor redundant. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short.
Do not pursue conditioned objects; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of equanimity, all things subside of their own accord. Cease movement and return to stillness.

The more one attempts to still it, the more it moves; one merely stagnates at the two extremes. How can one know the single essence? If this single essence is not penetrated, effort is lost in both places.

To dispel existence is to follow emptiness and turn one's back on emptiness. Excessive words and excessive deliberations become increasingly discordant. Only by severing words and severing deliberations can one attain realization.

There is nowhere it does not penetrate. Return to the root and you will attain the essential meaning; follow after illumination and you will lose the source. If you reflect back for even a moment, this surpasses the previous emptiness.

That previous emptiness underwent transformation entirely due to deluded views. Do not seek the truth; simply require the cessation of views. When these two views do not abide, [the mind is liberated].
Be careful not to pursue them; as soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost. Two arise from the existence of one, yet even that one must not be clung to.

When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. When there is no fault, there are no dharmas; when there is no arising, there is no mind. Thus, the capacity [of the mind] ceases along with its objects.

The object sinks along with the subject; the object exists because of the subject-object relationship, and the subject exists because of the object-subject relationship. If you wish to know these two segments, they are fundamentally one emptiness.

This one emptiness is identical to the two, equally encompassing the myriad phenomena. When neither the refined nor the coarse is seen, how could there be partiality? The essence of the Great Way is vast.

There is neither ease nor difficulty. To perceive even the slightest doubt is to become increasingly frantic and ever more sluggish. To grasp it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path;

to let it go spontaneously, its essence is without coming or dwelling. To follow one's nature is to accord with the Way, moving at ease and free from affliction; to fixate the mind is to deviate from the Truth.

Laxity is not good; it is not good to weary the spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not revile the six sense-objects.
If you do not revile the six sense-objects, you will be identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise act without effort; the ignorant bind themselves. There is no dharma apart from the Dharma.
To falsely harbor self-attachment and to employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes.
All dualistic extremes arise from one's own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—what need is there to grasp at them? As for gain and loss, right and wrong...
At once let go. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves. If the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are as one.

The essence of this oneness is profound; in a state of stillness, one forgets external conditions. Observing all dharmas with equanimity, one returns to spontaneity. Thus, that which is the cause of perception is obliterated.
It cannot be compared or measured. Stillness and movement are without movement; movement and stillness are without stillness. Since both are not established, how could there be a "one"?
Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or patterns remain. The mind accords with equality, and all that is done ceases. All doubt is utterly purified.

With right faith, one becomes harmonious and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. The void and luminosity illuminate themselves spontaneously, without taxing the mind or strength.

This is not a realm of discursive thought, difficult for the intellect and emotions to fathom. Within the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. One must urgently seek resonance with this.

The word "only" signifies non-duality. In this non-duality, all things are identical; there is nothing that is not encompassed within it. All wise ones of the ten directions enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor expansive:
in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years. It is neither present nor absent; it is before one's eyes throughout the ten directions. The smallest is identical to the great.

Forget and sever all boundaries; the ultimate identity makes the great and the small indistinguishable, such that no limits or surfaces are perceived. Existence is itself non-existence, and non-existence is itself existence.
If it were not thus, there would be no need for guarding at all. The one is all, and all is the one. It is simply by being able to act in this way [that one attains liberation].
What concern is there that it would not be completed? The mind of faith is non-dual; this non-dual mind of faith cuts off the path of words and is neither past, future, nor present.

As for the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, his surname was Sima. His family had resided in Henei for generations, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou. From birth he was extraordinary and transcendent;
from childhood he admired the gates of liberation within the school of emptiness, as if they were the result of habitual practice from a previous life. Once—
Carrying on his patriarchal legacy, he restrained his mind and did not sleep; for nearly sixty years, his side never touched his mat.

In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Jizhou. At that time, a band of rebels had besieged the city for seventy days without lifting the siege, leaving the multitudes in a state of terror.
The Patriarch took pity on them and instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Then, from between the battlements, the rebels perceived as if there were...
The divine soldiers then said to one another, "There must be an extraordinary person within this city; we must not attack. They gradually withdrew.
In the Jia-shen year of the Tang Wude era, the master returned to Qichun and stayed at Mount Poutou. Disciples gathered there like clouds.
One day, he went to Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and superior to those of ordinary children. The Master questioned him.
The Master asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not an ordinary surname. The Master asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature.
The Master asked, "Do you have no surname at all? He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none.

The Master silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately ordered an attendant to go to his mother’s place to request that she allow him to leave the household life. Because of past affinities, the mother had no objection whatsoever.
Feeling a sense of reluctance, he nevertheless accepted him as a disciple. Upon the transmission of the Dharma and the entrustment of the robe, he spoke in verse:
"The nature of the lotus seed exists; Because of the ground, the lotus grows. When the great condition unites with this nature, That which was born is born as non-birth.
He then entrusted his students to him. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In the Wude era, while traveling on Mount Lu, I ascended its summit and gazed toward Mount Poutou."
He saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors spread horizontally into six paths. "Do you understand? he asked. The assembly remained silent.
Huineng said, "Could this not be the Dharma-branch that the Master will later extend crosswise? The Patriarch replied, "Excellent.

Later, in the year of Kaimao during the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, having heard of the Master’s flavor of the Way and desiring to behold his dignified bearing, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital. The Patriarch ascended [the throne].
He declined the honor three times in succession, finally declining on the grounds of illness. On the fourth occasion, the Emperor issued a command to a messenger, saying:

"If he does not rise from his refusal, then bring his head here. When the messenger arrived at the mountain to convey the imperial decree, the Master extended his neck toward the blade; his countenance remained solemn and composed.

He sent someone to report this extraordinary matter. When Hui reported the circumstances to the Emperor, the Emperor’s admiration increased further. He bestowed precious silks upon him so that he might fulfill his aspirations.
On the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month in the year of Xinhai during the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong, he suddenly offered these instructions to his disciples:
"All phenomena are entirely liberation. You must each protect and mind yourselves, spreading this transformation into the future. Having spoken, he passed away peacefully.

He passed away while seated. His age was seventy-two. He was interred in a stupa at his native mountain. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord without cause;
his physical features were as if he were alive. Thereafter, his disciples did not dare to close it again.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dayi and named his stupa Ciyun.
The Great Master Wuzu Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.

Formerly, while serving as a "pine-planting practitioner" at Mount Poutou, he once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You are already old."
"Perhaps I may hear from you. Will you be able to convert others extensively? If you should return again, I can still wait for you. He then departed.
Walking by the water's edge, he saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman replied, "I have father and brothers."
"You may go and seek him. She replied, "I dare to do so at once. The girl nodded her head in agreement and, turning her horse, departed.
This girl was the youngest daughter of the Zhou clan. Upon returning home, she immediately became pregnant. Her parents detested this greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere else to turn, she spent her days spinning for hire in the village and stayed at night beneath a public inn. Later, she gave birth to a son; because they considered it an ill omen, they...
He was cast into a turbid harbor. When he was seen the next day, swimming upstream with a bright and radiant countenance, everyone was greatly astonished.
They then lifted him up; he had become a young boy. He followed his mother to beg for food, and the villagers called him the "Child Without Surname. One wise man encountered him and sighed, saying:

This son lacked seven characteristics and had not yet attained the level of a Tathāgata. Later, he encountered the Great Master [Hongren] and became his dharma heir. He propagated the teachings on Mount Pótóu. During the Xiánhéng era, there was a layman surnamed Lú and named Huínéng who came from Xīnzhōu to pay his respects. The Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? Lú replied, "From south of the Ling Mountains. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? Lú replied: [The remainder of the text follows: "I have heard that the Great Master has the Dharma of the Buddha's seal; I wish to receive it and propagate it for the sake of all sentient beings. The Patriarch said, "The Dharma of the Buddha's seal is difficult to obtain; you must practice for three years before you may receive it. Lú said, "I have traveled from afar with great difficulty; I cannot wait for three years. The Patriarch said, "If you truly seek the Dharma, you must first undergo the tonsure and receive the precepts. Lú said, "I have already received the precepts in the past. The Patriarch said, "When did you receive them? Lú said, "I received them at the age of twenty-nine. The Patriarch said, "In what place did you receive them? Lú said, "At the temple of the Fifth Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "Did you receive the full precepts? Lú said, "Yes. The Patriarch said, "How many years have passed since then? Lú said, "Twenty-one years. The Patriarch said, "Since you have already received the full precepts, why do you still need to undergo the tonsure? Lú said, "Although I have received the precepts, I have not yet undergone the tonsure. The Patriarch said, "If you have already received the full precepts, you need not undergo the tonsure again. The Patriarch then said, "You have come from afar; you should stay here for a while. Lú said, "I have come from afar specifically to seek the Dharma; I cannot remain here for long. The Patriarch said, "If you truly seek the Dharma, you must practice diligently. Lú said, "I am willing to practice diligently. The Patriarch then taught him the Diamond Sūtra. Upon hearing it, Lú attained great awakening. He then prostrated himself and said, "I have attained the mind-ground. The Patriarch said, "You have attained the mind-ground; you shall be the Seventh Patriarch. Lú then departed. The Patriarch said, "You must go quickly; do not let others know. Lú then left and went to Caoqi. There, he propagated the teachings and established the monastery. He lived for seventy-six years and entered nirvana in the second year of the Tiānpíng era. His remains were enshrined in a stupa. His disciples built a temple at the site of his nirvana and named it Nánhuá. They erected a stele and inscribed it with the account of his life. This is the end of the record of the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Master Huínéng of Caoqi. It was written by the monk Zhìshēn, a disciple of the Great Master. The stele was erected in the third year of the Tiānpíng era. The inscription was composed by the scholar Wáng Shìzhōng. The calligraphy was by the calligrapher Yáo Shìyǐ. The stele stands at the Nánhuá Temple in Qīngyuán County, Shàndōng Circuit. It was carved in the spring of the third year of the Tiānpíng era. The date of the carving was the tenth day of the fourth month. The stele was erected by the local officials and the monastic community. It was intended to commemorate the virtue of the Great Master and to ensure that his legacy would endure for generations. The inscription concludes with a prayer that this merit may benefit all sentient beings and lead them to the path of enlightenment. The stele was completed on the aforementioned date. All those who see or hear of it shall plant the seeds of liberation. May all beings attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus ends the inscription. The stele was erected by the local authorities and the monastic community. It was intended to honor the memory of the Great Master and to serve as a testament to the flourishing of the Dharma.
