The inscription was composed by the scholar Wáng Shìzhōng. The calligraphy was by the calligrapher Yáo Shìyǐ. The stele stands at the Nánhuá Temple in Qīngyuán County, Shàndōng Circuit. It was carved in the spring of the third year of the Tiānpíng era. The date of the carving was the tenth day of the fourth month. The stele was erected by the local officials and the monastic community. It was intended to commemorate the virtue of the Great Master and to ensure that his legacy would endure for generations. The inscription concludes with a prayer that this merit may benefit all
“I seek only to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, “The people of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha?

Lu said, “People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be so? The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary person and rebuked him, saying, “Go and work in the fodder trough!
Lu prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling room to perform labor among the pestles and mortars, working day and night without ceasing. After some time had passed...
In the eighth month, the Patriarch knew that the time for the transmission had arrived. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma is difficult to understand;

it must not be left as a mere memorization of my words. You must take this as your own responsibility. Each of you should independently compose a verse according to your own inclination. If the meaning of your words accords with the profound essence, [I shall transmit the Dharma]."
Consequently, he entrusted all his robes and the Dharma to him. At that time, there were over seven hundred monks in the assembly.

Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all commended him, saying, "Were it not for the Venerable Shenxiu, who else would dare to receive this?
Hearing the public acclaim, Shenxiu no longer reflected further; he then inscribed a verse upon a wall in the corridor, which said: "The body is the Bodhi tree."
"The mind is like a bright mirror-stand; at all times diligently wipe it clean, lest dust and grime gather upon it.

When the Patriarch was walking about, he suddenly saw this verse and knew it had been composed by Shenxiu. He then praised it, saying, "If future generations practice according to this, they too shall attain the supreme fruit.
Originally, the wall was intended for the scholar Lu Zhen to paint the *Lengqie* transformation scenes; however, upon seeing this inscription...
The verse was written on the wall, whereupon [Huineng] stopped painting. He then instructed each of them to recite it. Lu was at the mill when he suddenly heard the recitation of the verse;

he asked his fellow student, "What are these lines? The fellow student replied, "You do not know that the Master is seeking a successor to the Dharma and has ordered each of us to compose a verse expressing our minds.
This is the one composed by Upādhyāya Xiu; the Master has praised it deeply and will certainly transmit the Dharma to him."
[This was] the transmission of the robe. Lu asked, "What is that verse? His fellow student recited it for him.
After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful, yet it is not yet fully realized. The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could a commoner like you know this?

Do not utter such mad words! Lu said, "Do you not believe me? I wish to harmonize it with a verse of my own. The fellow student did not answer, but they looked at each other and laughed. That night, Lu...

He secretly informed a young boy, who led him down to the corridor. Lu himself held a candle and requested Zhang Ruyong, the Vice Governor, to stand beside Xiu’s verse and write another one, which read: "Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is likewise not a stand.
Fundamentally there is not a single thing— Where, then, could dust and grime gather? Later, when the Patriarch saw this verse, he asked, "Who wrote this? It is not yet..."

[The Master] saw into [Huineng’s] nature. When the assembly heard the Master’s words, they paid him no further heed. By nightfall, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet?
Huineng replied, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted. The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff.
Huineng immediately beat the drum three times and entered the room. The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas appear in the world for one great matter; therefore, according to their capacities..."

He guided them by means of simplified [teachings], whereby there subsequently arose the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the principles of sudden and gradual [enlightenment] as the gateways of the teaching.
Nevertheless, he entrusted the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma—to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until Bodhidharma arrived in this land and attained it.
The Great Master has transmitted this lineage down to the present day. I now entrust to you the Dharma-treasure and the robe he transmitted;
protect them well yourself and do not allow them to be severed. Listen to my verse: "When sentient beings come to plant seeds, From the ground, the fruit is born again.
Since non-sentient things have no seeds, That which lacks nature is likewise without birth. The Layman Lu knelt and received the robe and the Dharma.
Dafu asked, "Now that you have received the Dharma, to whom shall the robe be entrusted? The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him;

therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention. It shall stop with your person and will no longer be transmitted.
Furthermore, you should remain hidden in seclusion for a time until the moment comes to travel and transform others. This is what is meant by 'the one who receives the robe receives the mandate.'"
"It is like a hanging thread," he said. Lu asked, "Where should you hide? The Patriarch replied, "When you meet Hui, stop; when you encounter Hui, conceal yourself.
After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed. That night he traveled south, and the assembly knew nothing of it.
Thereafter, the Fifth Patriarch no longer ascended the hall. The assembly, filled with suspicion and wonder, questioned him. The Patriarch said, "My Way has gone forth; why ask further?"
He asked again, "Who shall receive the dharma of the robe? The Patriarch replied, "He who is capable shall receive it. Thereupon, the assembly discussed that the name of Lu Xing was capable;

however, having lost his tracks during their search, they secretly learned that he had obtained it and immediately pursued him together. After the Fifth Patriarch had transmitted the dharma of the robe, another four years passed.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now finished; it is time for you to go."
He immediately entered his room and passed away while sitting in meditative composure. He was seventy-four years of age. A stupa was erected for him on East Mountain at Huangmei.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daman and the name of the stupa, Fayu.
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was of the secular surname Lu. His ancestors were originally from Fanyang.
His father, Xingtao, was transferred to serve in Nanhai’s Xinzhou during the Wude era and subsequently registered his residence there. He lost his father at the age of three;

his mother remained steadfast in her resolve to raise him until he reached adulthood. The family was exceedingly impoverished, and the Master provided for them by gathering firewood. One day, while carrying a load of wood, he arrived at—

In the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," he experienced a profound realization and asked the guest, "What teaching is this?
From whom did you receive it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*."
Having reached Master Ren at Huangmei, the Patriarch suddenly informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma and set out directly for Shaoyang Prefecture.
There he met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilüe, with whom he formed a friendship. A nun named Wujinzang was Liu Zhilüe’s aunt;
she was constantly reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Master listened to it briefly and immediately explained its meaning to her.
The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask for instruction on their meaning.

The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend the meaning? The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has no connection with written words. The nun was struck with wonder and marvel at this.

He announced to the elders of his village, "This man is one who possesses the Way; you should invite him to receive our offerings. Thereupon, the local residents vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
As there was a former site for the ancient Bao Lin Temple nearby, the community deliberated and decided to restore it so that he might reside there as its patriarch.

The fourfold assembly gathered like a mist, and in an instant, a jeweled monastery was formed. One day, the Patriarch suddenly thought to himself, "I have sought the Great Dharma; how could I stop halfway?
The next day, he set out and reached a stone grotto on the western mountains of Changle County, where he met Chan Master Zhiyuan.
The Patriarch then requested instruction. Zhiyuan said, "Observing your spiritual bearing, you are exceptionally outstanding; you are surely no ordinary man. The Patriarch...
Hearing that Bodhidharma of the Western Regions had transmitted the mind-seal at Huangmei, you should go there to seek his instruction and resolve your doubts.
The Patriarch took his leave and proceeded directly to Dongshan in Huangmei; this was the second year of the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty.
Upon seeing him, Master Ren recognized him silently. Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, instructing him to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihui until the Yi... period.
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Fengyuan era (the Bingzi year), [Huineng] arrived at Nanhai.

There he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Faxing Temple. The Patriarch took up residence in the corridors. One evening, as the wind blew the temple banner atop the pagoda, he heard two monks debating one another.
One said, "The banner moves. The other said, "The wind moves. They exchanged arguments back and forth, yet neither had grasped the underlying principle. The Patriarch said:
"Is it appropriate for those of the secular world to venture into such lofty discourse? It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind alone.

When Imprint Sect (Yinzong) privately heard these words, he was struck with awe and marveled at them. The following day, he invited the Patriarch into his chamber and questioned him regarding the meaning of the wind and the banner.
The Patriarch explained the matter to him in detail according to the truth. Without realizing it, Yinzong rose to his feet and said, "This practitioner is certainly no ordinary person.
Who is your teacher? The Patriarch, with nothing further to conceal, directly recounted the circumstances of how he had attained the Dharma.

Thereupon, Yinzong assumed the etiquette of a disciple and requested instruction in the essentials of Chan. He then addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "Yinzong was a complete ordinary person, yet now I have encountered a..."
The Bodhisattva Shen then pointed to the layman Lu beneath his seat and said, "This is the very person.

He then requested that the robe of transmission be brought forth so that everyone might gaze upon and pay homage to it. On the fifteenth day of the first month, he assembled various eminent and virtuous monks to shave [Lu's] head.
On the eighth day of the second month, I received the full ordination from Master Zhiguang at Faxing Temple.
This ordination platform was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty. The Tripiṭaka Master’s record states:

"In the future, there shall be an incarnate Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this platform. Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally [marked] the side of the platform with his hand...

He planted two Bodhi trees and addressed the assembly, saying: "One hundred and twenty years from now, a great Bodhisattva shall preach the Unsurpassed Vehicle beneath these trees, delivering immeasurable multitudes.
After the Patriarch had received full ordination, he opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan beneath these very trees, as if in accordance with a prior karmic agreement.
On the eighth day of the second month of the following year, he suddenly said to the assembly: "I shall no longer..."
He wished to reside here and intended to return to his former hermitage. Thereupon, Imprint Master Zong and over a thousand monastics and laypeople escorted the Patriarch back to Baolin Monastery.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, invited him to the Dafan Temple to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and receive the formless mind-ground precepts.
His disciples recorded these events, titling the work the *Platform Sutra*, which became widely circulated throughout the world. Later, he returned to Caoxi.

He rained down the great rain of the Dharma; those who studied under him numbered no fewer than a thousand. In the first year of the Shenlong era of the Zhongzong reign, an imperial edict was issued stating:
"I request that the two masters An and Xiu be provided with offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Both masters declined, saying: "In the south there is Master Neng, who secretly received the robe and dharma of Great Master Huineng. You may go to him to inquire."
I have now dispatched the Inner Attendant Xue Jian to ride with this decree to invite you. I pray that you, Master, will look upon me with compassion and proceed swiftly to the Capital.

The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining on the grounds of illness, wishing to spend his final years among the forest slopes. Xue Jian said, "The Chan masters of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi.
It has never happened before that anyone attained liberation without relying on dhyāna and samādhi. Unforeseen...
The Master asked, "How do you understand the Dharma taught by the Teacher? The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? The Sūtra says:
'If one perceives the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. That all dharmas are empty and quiescent—this is the purity of the Tathāgata."
"Seated, there is ultimately nothing to realize; how much less so when one is actually sitting? Jian said, "When your disciple returns, the Sovereign will surely question me.

I pray that you, Reverend, will out of compassion point out the essential core of the mind. The Patriarch said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of alternation."
Brightness and darkness are inexhaustible, yet they are also exhaustible; these names are established in mutual dependence. Thus, a sutra says:
"Dharmas have no counterpart, for they do not depend on one another. Jian said: "Brightness is a metaphor for wisdom, and darkness is an analogy for afflictions (*kleśa*).

If a practitioner of the Way does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means could they escape the cycle of birth and death that has no beginning? The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves..."
Bodhi is without duality and without distinction. To use wisdom to illuminate afflictions is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those such as the sheep and the deer.
Those of great wisdom and superior faculties do not act in this way. Jian asked: "What is the insight of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said:
"Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature. This non-dual nature is itself the true nature. The true...

As for its nature (*dhātu*): it does not diminish when dwelling among the ignorant and foolish; it does not increase when abiding with the worthy and holy. It is not disturbed while remaining amidst afflictions (*kleśa*);

it is not quiescent while residing in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes; it is neither within nor without, nor in between. It is neither born nor extinguished; its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and never shifting. This is called the Way (*mārga*). To summarize: The nature does not decrease among the ordinary and deluded, Nor does it increase among the worthy and holy. It is not disordered while abiding in afflictions, Nor is it silent while dwelling in meditative concentration. Neither severed nor permanent, neither coming nor going, Neither within nor without, nor in between. Neither arising nor ceasing, its nature and characteristics are suchness, Eternally abiding and unchanging—this is named the Way. A brief summary says:
The Master said, "Speaking of 'neither arising nor ceasing'—how does this differ from the non-Buddhists?

The Patriarch replied, "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither arising nor ceasing' involves using cessation to stop arising, and using arising to manifest cessation; thus, though they speak of cessation, it is not truly ceased, and though they speak of arising, it is said to be non-arising.
What I call 'neither arising nor ceasing' is that fundamentally there has been no arising, and now there is likewise no cessation. This is why it differs from the non-Buddhists. If you..."
If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever.

You will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet possesses wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Having been briefly instructed by him, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.

He paid his respects and took leave to return to the capital, where he submitted a memorial reporting the Master’s words. An imperial edict was issued to thank the Master, and he was further granted a *mohana* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, five hundred rolls of silk, and precious jewels.
One alms bowl. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, by imperial decree, the ancient Baolin Monastery was renamed Zhongxing Monastery.

On the eighteenth day of the eleventh month of the third year, there was again an imperial decree that the Prefect of Shaoyang Prefecture should further adorn and embellish it, granting it the name Fajian Monastery.
The former residence of the Patriarch in Xinzhou was designated as Guoen Monastery. One day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "All you virtuous ones..."
"Knowledgeable ones, each of you should purify your minds and listen to my preaching of the Dharma. You all, people of this assembly, your own minds are the Buddha;
do not harbor further doubt. There is not a single thing outside that can be established, for it is all the original mind that gives rise to the myriad kinds of dharmas.
As the sutra says: 'When the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, the myriad dharmas cease. If you wish to achieve [enlightenment]..."
Wisdom. The Samādhi of One Mark and the Samādhi of One Practice: if, in all places, one does not dwell upon marks;
if, amidst those marks, one gives rise to neither aversion nor attachment, and there is neither grasping nor rejecting;

if one does not think of matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure, but remains at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the Samādhi of One Mark. If, in all places, whether walking or standing...
Whether sitting or reclining, with a purely upright mind, one remains unmoving within the site of enlightenment; this is the true realization of the Pure Land, called the Samādhi of Single Practice.
If a person possesses two or three such samādhis, it is like the earth which, having seeds, can contain, nurture, and bring them to fruition.
A single characteristic and a single practice are likewise so. My preaching of the Dharma now is like seasonal rain that universally moistens the great earth; you all—
The Buddha-nature is like various seeds; when they encounter this moistening and nourishing rain, they all attain sprout and growth.

Those who receive my intent will certainly obtain Bodhi; those who follow my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit. In the first year of the Tianxian era, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:
"I have been honored to receive the robe and dharma of the Great Master Ren. Now I preach the Dharma for you, yet I do not transmit the robe to you, because you..."
The faculty of faith is matured; you are resolute and free from doubt, capable of undertaking this great task. Listen as I recite these verses: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds;
When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the essence of the blossoms is suddenly realized, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained.
Having spoken these verses, he said again: "That Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. That Way is pure and devoid of all marks. You must be cautious."
"Do not contemplate the mind as pure or empty; this mind is fundamentally pure. There is nothing to be grasped or rejected.
Each of you must exert yourselves; go forth according to conditions as best you can. Once, a monk recited the verse of Chan Master Wo Lun: "Wo Lun has skillful means; he can sever a hundred thoughts.
When facing objects, the mind does not arise; Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said, "This verse is not yet..."
"Clarifying the Mind-Ground: If one relies upon this and puts it into practice, it becomes an added fetter. To demonstrate this, he spoke a verse: "Wisdom can eliminate artifice;
It does not sever the hundred thoughts. When encountering objects, mental states arise; How could Bodhi grow? (Wolun’s "Non-Name" was his place of residence.
The Patriarch preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings for forty years. On the sixth day of the seventh month of that year, he commanded his disciples to go...
At Guoen Temple in Xinzhou, a Tower of Gratitude was being constructed; the Master further ordered that the craftsmanship be doubled.
There was also a monk from Shu named Fangbian who came to visit and said, "I am skilled at modeling clay. The Master looked at him with a stern expression and said, "Try modeling one for me to see.

Fangbian did not grasp the Master's intent, so he proceeded to model a portrait of the Master, seven feet in height, capturing every nuance with exquisite skill. Upon seeing it, the Master remarked, "You are skilled at modeling physical forms, but you are not skilled in [modeling the spirit]."
[The Master] bestowed his *foxing* (Buddha-nature) upon him and rewarded him with clothing and goods; [the recipient] performed the rites of gratitude and departed.

On the first day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he said to his disciples, "I wish to return to Xīnzhōu; you must quickly prepare the boats. At that time, the great assembly was filled with sorrowful longing and entreated the Master to remain.
The Patriarch said, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they still manifest *nirvāṇa*. That there must be a departure following a coming is a constant principle."
"This physical frame of mine must return to its source," he said. The assembly asked, "When you depart from here, Master, when will you return?
The Patriarch replied, "Leaves fall and return to the root; when one comes, there are no words. They asked again, "To whom will your Dharma-eye be transmitted? The Patriarch replied:
Those who possess the Way attain it; those who are without mind penetrate it. He asked again, "Will there be no difficulties after my passing?

The Patriarch said, "Five or six years after my death, there shall be a man who comes to take my head. Listen to my prediction: 'To support one's parents, one must nourish oneself with food from the mouth;
encountering the difficulty of Man, Yangliu shall become an official. Furthermore, he said, 'Seventy years after I depart, there shall be two..."

The Bodhisattva came from the East; one was a householder and the other a renunciant. Simultaneously they arose to transform the world, establishing our school, repairing monasteries, and causing the lineage of the Dharma to flourish.
Having finished speaking, he went to Guoen Temple in Xinzhou, bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
A wondrous fragrance pervaded the air, and a white rainbow stretched across the ground. This was on the third day of the eighth month of that year. At that time, Shao—

The two new prefectures each constructed a spirit-stupa, and neither the clergy nor the laity could decide where [the remains] should go. The Prefectural Governors of both prefectures together burned incense and prayed, saying:
"Wherever the smoke of the incense leads shall be the place where the Master wishes to return. At that time, the incense smoke rose and surged, piercing straight toward Caoxi.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he entered the stupa; his age was seventy-six. At that time, Wei, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou...

According to the inscription on the stele, the disciples recalled their master’s instructions regarding the preservation of his remains; they therefore first secured his neck with iron plates and lacquered cloth.
Within the stupa were the robe of faith transmitted by Bodhidharma (a *kucun* fabric from the Western Regions, woven with the fibers of the *mudua* flower;

later generations used blue silk as an inner lining), the *monastery robe* (*mo-na*) and precious alms bowl bestowed by Emperor Zhongzong, and the implements for fashioning the true likeness [of the Master]. The attendant in charge of the stupa was Shi... [text fragment].
On the third day of the eighth month in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era (the Renxu year), at midnight, there was suddenly heard from within the stupa a sound like that of dragging iron chains.
The monks rose in alarm and saw a filial son emerge from the stupa. Upon closer inspection, they found a wound upon the Master’s neck.
They reported the matter of the robbery in full to the local prefecture and county authorities. County Magistrate Yang Kan and Provincial Governor Liu Wutiàn received the official notification.
He was immediately arrested. In the fifth month, the thief was captured at Shijue Village and sent to Shaoyang Prefecture for interrogation.
He stated: "My surname is Zhang and my name is Jingman. I am a native of Liang County in Ruzhou.

At Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou, I received twenty thousand coins from the Silla monk Kim Daebi (Jin Dabeicheng) with instructions to take the head of the Sixth Patriarch Master and return it to the Eastern Sea for his veneration. Liu...
Upon hearing the circumstances, the Governor did not immediately impose punishment. He personally went to Caoxi and asked the Patriarch’s senior disciple, Lingtao, "How should he be dealt with?
Lingtao replied, "If judged by the laws of the state, he ought to be executed; however, according to the compassion of the Buddha's teaching—"
"Between enemies and kin, one should be impartial; how much more so when they seek to offer worship? Their offense may be forgiven.

Master Liu sighed in admiration, saying, "Only now do I realize the vastness of the Buddha-dharma," and he subsequently pardoned him (thereafter, there were many famous worthies who praised him, and offerings of rare treasures were made; these details are omitted for brevity).

In the first year of the Shangyuan era, Emperor Suzong sent an envoy to request the Master’s robes and alms bowl to be enshrined within the palace for veneration. This continued until the fifth month of the first year of the Yongtai era.
On the fifth day, Emperor Daizong dreamed that the Sixth Patriarch Master requested his robe and alms bowl. On the seventh day, he issued an edict to the Prefectural Governor Yang Jian, saying:
"I have been moved in a dream by the Chan Master’s request to return the Dharma-transmitting cassock to Caoxi.

I now dispatch Liu Chongjing, General of the State Guards, to carry it upon his head and deliver it. I consider this a national treasure; you may enshrine it in your temple according to the proper rites."

He was enshrined there, and those among the monastic community who had personally inherited his fundamental teachings were strictly charged with guarding them so that they would not be lost or allowed to fall into the hands of others.
Whenever such items were subsequently stolen, they were recovered from no great distance away; this occurred several times.

Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dajian, and his stupa was named Yuanhe Lingzhao. At the beginning of the Kaibao era of our present dynasty, the Imperial Army pacified the Liu clan of Nanhai.
The surviving soldiers caused obstruction; the ancestral pagoda was reduced to ashes and embers, yet the true body was protected by a monk guarding the stupa and remained entirely undamaged.
Soon thereafter, an imperial decree was issued for its restoration, but before the work was completed, Emperor Taizong ascended the throne.
He took a keen interest in the Chan school and greatly expanded its magnificent structures.
*Wudeng Huiyuan*, Volume One; *Wudeng Huiyuan*, Volume Two.
The first-generation Dharma heir who emerged from the side of the Fourth Patriarch, Chan Master Dayi, was Chan Master Farong of Mount Niutou.
He was a native of Yanling in Runzhou, surnamed Wei. At the age of nineteen, he...
His learning was thorough in the Classics and Histories. Upon examining the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtras, he attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

One day, he sighed and said, "The secular texts of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma; the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he entered the monastic order under a master and shaved his head.
Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou. There, hundreds of birds would bring him offerings.

Regarding the marvel of the flower: During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew that there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain.

He went in person to seek him out and asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way in this place? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, who is not a practitioner of the Way?
The Patriarch said, "Which one among them is the practitioner of the Way? The monks were speechless. Another monk said, "This..."
About ten *li* into the mountains, there was one named Lanrong. When he saw people, he would not rise, nor would he join his palms.
"Could this be a man of the Way? The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, showing no concern for anything. The Patriarch asked:
"What are you doing here? the Master asked. The Teacher replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch said, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind? The Teacher was speechless.
He then rose, prostrated himself, and asked, "Where does the Great Virtue dwell?
The Patriarch said, "This poor monk has no fixed abode; sometimes I go east, sometimes west. The Teacher asked, "Do you know Meditation Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him?"
The Master said, "I have long admired your virtue and hoped to pay my respects. The Patriarch said, "I am the Chan Master Daoxin.
The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. He then asked, "Is there any other place where we might rest?"
The Master pointed to the area behind him and said, "There is another small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the site of the hermitage;

as they circled it, they saw nothing but tigers, wolves, and other such beasts. The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this remaining. The Patriarch replied:
"What is this? The Master remained silent. After a short while, the Patriarch inscribed the character for "Buddha" (佛) upon a rock where the Master was sitting in formal meditation.
Upon seeing it, the Master stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining. The Master, not yet understanding, bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth.
The Patriarch said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all..."
Within the source of the mind, all gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as all supernatural powers and transformations, are inherently complete;
they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and quiescent. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions.
There is no triple world to escape, and there is no Bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics. Great!
The Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma you have now attained; there is nothing lacking.

How does this differ from that of the Buddha? There is no other separate Dharma. You need only allow the mind to be free and at ease. Do not perform contemplative practices; do not attempt to clarify the mind;
do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Be expansive and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions, and do not engage in various [conditioned] activities.
"Excellent! Not committing any evil—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whatever meets the eye or encounters the conditions—is all the wondrous functioning of the Buddha.
Joyful and free from sorrow, it is for this reason called 'Buddha'. The Master asked, "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha?

What is the mind? The Patriarch said, "If it is not the mind, do not ask about the Buddha; if you ask about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind. The Master said, "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation..."

"Regarding the arising of objects within the sphere of activity, how does the mind counteract them? The Patriarch said: "The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind.
If the mind does not apply forced designations, from where would deluded sentiments arise? Since deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind is free to exercise universal knowledge.
You need only follow the mind with ease and spontaneity, without further counteracting; this is what is called the eternally abiding Dharma-body. There is nothing more.
[The Master] said, "It has changed. I have received the Dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment from Great Master Huìcǎn; I now entrust it to you.
You must now receive my words with earnest attention and remain on this mountain. Hereafter, there shall be five men who attain realization and will carry forward your profound transformation.

Having finished transmitting the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng and spent the rest of his life there. From that time on, the master’s Dharma assembly flourished greatly. During the Yonghuī era of the Tang dynasty, his disciples...

Lacking grain, the Master traveled to Danyang to seek alms. Although it was eighty *li* from the mountain, he personally carried eighteen *dou* of rice, going in the morning and returning by evening, providing for three hundred monks without fail at the two meal times for three years.
The local magistrate, Xiao Yuanshan, invited him to the Jianchu Monastery to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Listeners gathered like clouds; when they reached the "Chapter on the Extinction of Stillness," the earth shook for this reason.

[The mountain] shook. Having finished his lecture, he returned to the mountains. Prince Boling asked the Master, "When an object-condition arises from form, you do not say that it arises because of the condition of form.
How can one know the condition, such that one wishes to still its arising? The Master said, "When the objective form first arises, the two natures of form and object are empty.
Fundamentally, there is no knower of the condition; the measure of the mind is identical to the knowing itself. When illuminating the source, there is neither arising nor non-arising."

At that time, arising occurs spontaneously from stillness. Embracing darkness gives rise to the conditions for awakening. When the mind does not pursue objects, it reaches the state prior to the birth [of phenomena].

At such a time, form and mind are not nurtured; they are fundamentally non-existent within emptiness. From this, thought, sensation, and speech arise through recollection. Their arousal has never truly arisen;

how could one employ the Buddha’s teachings to command them? Question: When the eyes are closed and forms are not seen, mental objects and deliberations nevertheless abound. Since form is no longer involved...
The mind asks: "From where do objects arise? The Master says: "When the eyes are closed, forms are not seen; yet the inner mind stirs with manifold deliberations.

Illusory consciousness falsely constitutes its functions; though names are given, they ultimately do not exceed [the nature of reality]. To know that form does not concern the mind, and that the mind likewise does not concern the person—yet as one acts, there is the turning of appearances.
When the bird has flown away, the sky remains true. He asks: "Since objects arise from no fixed location, through what conditions does awakening and knowledge arise?"
When the object ceases, the cognition returns and transforms; the cognition then becomes the object. If one uses the mind to drag the mind, it is once again what is perceived by cognition.

Following this, one goes along with it, never departing from the boundary of arising and ceasing. The Master said: "In the beginning, middle, and end of form and mind, there is truly no realm of dependent origination.
When a single thought forgets its own doubt, who can calculate movement and stillness? This knowing is itself without knowing; knowing and knowing are the conditions."

It will not. When you examine your own fundamental nature, why must you seek it beyond this realm? The preceding object does not change or pass away; the subsequent thought does not come into the present.
To seek the moon by grasping its dark reflection, or to track its traces by pursuing a flying bird—to wish to know the nature of the mind is just like looking at a dream.
It is likened to ice in the sixth month: everywhere it is the same. One cannot escape emptiness by avoiding it; yet to seek emptiness is likewise futile.

This is not established. Let me ask about the image in a mirror: from where does the mind arise? [The student] asks: "When one applies the mind with precision (*zhèzhè*), how can it be peaceful and secure?
The Master says: "When one applies the mind with precision, it is precisely the non-application of mind. To discuss names and characteristics in a roundabout way is wearisome;
to speak directly is free of redundancy. When there is no mind, there is precisely application; in constant application, there is precisely no [mind]. Now I speak of no-mind."
In its abiding, it is no different from the mind that possesses it. A questioner asks: "The wise cite sublime words; when these accord with the mind, they should be appropriate.

Yet if the words and the path of the mind diverge, then even if they coincide, they will be at odds ten thousandfold. The Master says: "Sublime words are spoken as skillful means to shatter the illnesses of sentient beings; this is the Mahāyāna path."

This does not concern a discourse on the fundamental nature; it arises from transformation within emptiness. Taking non-thought as the true permanence, one shall ultimately sever the path of the mind.
When detached from thought, the nature is immovable; birth and cessation are without contradiction or error. As the valley echo possesses sound, so the mirror-image can look back.

Question: When the practitioner’s substance [of mind] exists, the object exists; when, through awakening, one perceives it, the object perishes. Thus, there are three minds: the preceding awakening, the subsequent awakening, and the object itself.

The Master said: The function of the object is not its substance. Once awakening has ceased, one should not reflect upon it. Because the object perishes through the perception of awakening, the object does not arise at the time of awakening.
Thus, there are three delays: the preceding awakening, the subsequent awakening, and the object itself. Question: In abiding in meditative concentration, both are absent.
It turns; it shall become the true samādhi, such that no karmas can drag it away. Not knowing subtle ignorance, one slowly follows after its tracks. The Master said:
Furthermore, I have heard of others who falsely cling to the arising of mental constructs (*cittamātra*). The three matters do not hold together; they do not turn back from their delusions.
The mind is bound by what is correct, yet for this reason they create obstacles to pure karma. A mere ten-thousandth part of the dust of the mind remains uncomprehended.

I shall speak of ignorance: it arises from the subtle accumulation of causes; names and forms gradually emerge. Like waves surging when the wind blows, yet the water returns to stillness when the wind ceases.
I wish to speak further of the path ahead, yet I fear that later minds might be startled. The Great Beast of non-thought roars; the emptiness of nature lets fall frost and hail.
Stars scatter and foul weeds are crushed; birds fall from the sky in every direction. The five realms of existence are surely in turmoil; the four Māras...

It neither advances nor retreats; it is like a fierce fire blazing, and yet it is like a sharp sword cutting. A question was asked: "I rely on awakening to know the myriad dharmas, yet the myriad dharmas are thus from the beginning.
If one relies on illumination to employ the mind, one merely obtains the employment of the mind through illumination; this does not accord with the affairs within the mind."
The Master said: "One relies on the awareness of the myriad dharmas, yet the myriad dharmas ultimately have no need for reliance.

If you employ the mind through provisional illumination, it should not exist outside the mind. A questioner asked: "If one follows along with everything without making any discernment, the luminous mind will not manifest before one.

Furthermore, fearing that the mind may become dark and dull, one applies effort within the mind; yet even so, the obstacles of wisdom remain difficult to remove. The Master said: "That which exists should not be allowed to exist; seek that which cannot be found."
Investigation (*vicaya*). To discern without discrimination is true discernment; it is the mind that emerges from darkness into light. Those who harbor anxieties have minds that are obscure and dull;

they fix their minds upon relying on effort and practice. How could they discuss the difficulty of the obstacle of knowledge? Such things become a sickness only upon reaching Buddhahood. Question: In the midst of adjusting and communicating [the teachings], it is indeed difficult to find a stable footing.

Unless one is a practitioner who applies these methods, this difficulty will ultimately remain unseen. The Master said: "In wishing to adjust and communicate through 'breaking the middle' (*zhèzhōng*),..."
The transmission of the message is neither difficult nor easy. First, observe the mind within the locus of the mind; next, infer wisdom within wisdom. Third, illuminate that which infers;
fourth, penetrate the indeterminate. Fifth, it is called liberation; sixth, it equalizes the true and the false; seventh, it knows the root of all phenomena.

The eighth is the unconditioned of loving-kindness; the ninth is the pervasive emptiness of the aggregates. The tenth is that which is covered by clouds and rain; it is the ultimate exhaustion of that which is without sensation.

Fundamental wisdom arises from ignorance; the mirror-image manifests the three karmas. Like a phantom person appearing at the crossroads, one does not abide in the limit of emptiness nor in its exhaustion.

When one illuminates that which exists within [the realm of] existence, it does not emerge from within emptiness or existence; nor has one yet brought emptiness and existence together—this is termed "the Middle Way.

This Middle Way is beyond verbal expression; how can it be settled where there is no place to settle? How can its application and practice be determined? Question: There is another kind of person who skillfully understands emptiness and signlessness.
They claim verbally that stillness and distraction are one, and further say that there is nothing within existence. Is this the same as realizing the function [of the Middle Way]?
Ever quiescent, one knows that awakening is the constant function. Applying the mind to realize the True Principle, one further says that function is non-function.
Wisdom and skillful means are manifold; though words may seem chaotic, they accord with the Principle. Suchness and the Principle are as they are; they are not realized through the conscious mind.

Since one knows that mental realization is erroneous, mind after mind dissolves into one another. Such a dharma difficult to know cannot be known even throughout eternal kalpas; it functions in this very way.
"O person of mind, there are those whom the Dharma cannot transform. The Master said: "There are others who realize emptiness, yet it remains as discussed in the previous verse:

'Practicing emptiness while guarding at peace, the consciousness and views are momentarily overturned; though one may comprehend that this is the true measure of the mind, in the end, one knows not the original source.

Furthermore, regarding the function of quiescent mind: 'Though possessing much wisdom, one suspects what is similar; this is truly because the nature is not clear, and seeking emptiness merely exhausts oneself. Forever.
A kalpa-enduring, obscure consciousness embraces its forms yet knows nothing of them; when light is emitted, the earth immediately trembles—what could one possibly do with that? Question:
Regarding the aforementioned "observing the mind," there is again the difficulty of the "gauze curtain. Master: If observing the mind involves a gauze curtain, why wait to observe a delusory mind?
Moreover, for one who has no delusory mind, it is difficult to even open one's mouth with composure. Question: One has long possessed a great foundation and enterprise.
In the midst of the shifting and alternating paths of the mind, one may perceive subtle obstacles; yet, it is only by reaching the true limit that one realizes them.
Were it not for a skillful master, no one could resolve this principle. I look up to our Great Master, who shall surely open the essential gate to guide those who apply their minds.

"Do not allow them to lose the right path. The Master said: "The Dharma-nature is the fundamental basis; dream-realms give rise to confusion. The subtle body of true reality—matter and mind—are constantly unrecognized.
Suddenly encountering a man of primordial chaos, who pities all living beings with compassionate grief, he entrusts his doubts to pose broad questions.
Embracing the principle within, he is ever-luminous; having penetrated the dark paths of birth and death, his mind is undisturbed by praise or blame. Thus does the Wild Elder manifest."

He replied in sections. Feeling ashamed that his Dharma-characteristics had been brought forth, he was graced by the revelation of the medicine for all sentient beings; it was as if the nature of form itself were made manifest.
In the first year of the Xianqing era, the district magistrate Xiao Yuanshan requested that he establish a monastery at Jianchu. The Master declined, but could not avoid the request.

He then charged his foremost disciple, Zhiran, with the seal of the Dharma, commanding him to transmit it in succession. As he was about to descend the mountain, he said to the assembly: "I shall no longer..."
He once again ascended this mountain. At that time, the birds and beasts wailed in grief, continuing for more than a month without ceasing. Before his hermitage stood four large paulownia trees;
in the middle month of summer, they suddenly withered and fell. On the twenty-third day of the first month of the following year, he passed away without illness.
He was interred on Mount Jilong.
The Second Generation under the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral branch):
Chan Master Zhìyán of Niútóu Mountain, successor to Chan Master Róng of Niútóu Mountain in Jīnlíng.
Master Zhìyán was a native of Qū’ā. His surname was Huá. By the age of twenty, his wisdom and courage surpassed [those of others].
This man stood seven chi and six cun tall. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as a *langjiang* (colonel).
He habitually hung a water-strainer from his bow and used it for drawing water wherever he traveled. Having repeatedly followed generals on military expeditions, he frequently achieved martial merit.
In the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of forty, he requested permission to leave the household life and entered Mount Wangong in Shuzhou to study under Chan Master Baoyue.
He served as a disciple. One day, while sitting in meditation, he beheld a strange monk over ten feet tall, whose divine bearing was exceptionally refined and whose speech was clear and resonant.
The monk said to him, "You have entered the monastic life after eighty lifetimes; you ought to redouble your diligent practice. Having spoken, he vanished.
Once, while he was in meditative absorption within a valley, the mountain waters suddenly surged. The Master remained serene and unmoved, and the water receded of its own accord.
A hunter encountered him there and subsequently reformed his ways to cultivate goodness.

Furthermore, two men who had previously served with him in the army, hearing that the Master had retired into seclusion, entered the mountains together to seek him out. Upon seeing him, they said to the Master, "Was the General mad? Why did you do this?"

He stayed there. The Master said, "My madness is about to subside, but yours is now fully unleashed. As for those who indulge in lustful sights and lewd sounds, or who covet glory and seek favor, they wander through birth and death;
by what means can they emerge from this on their own? The two men were moved to realization and departed with a sigh.
Later, the Master went to visit Chan Master Rong to clarify the Great Matter. Rong said to him, "I have received the true instructions of Master Xinxin; that which I have attained—"
"All have perished. Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.

A single speck of dust flying can obscure the heavens; a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth. You have now transcended such views—what more need I say? The guidance of this mountain gate shall be entrusted to you.
The Master received the command and became the second patriarch; later, he transmitted the True Dharma [to his successor].
Master Fang resided at both Baima and Qixuan Monasteries, and later moved to Shitou City. On the tenth day of the first month in the second year of the Yifeng era, he manifested his passing.
His countenance did not change, and he could bend and stretch as if alive. A strange fragrance filled his chamber, which did not dissipate for ten days.
His final instruction was that he be buried in water.
The Chan Master Tanchui of Mount Zhong in Jinling was a native of Wu Commandery. His surname was Yan.
He first went to visit Master Rong, who looked at him and marveled at his extraordinary character, saying to him: "Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising;
sensation and perception are the pitfall of the ultimate person. Do you understand this? The Master pondered these words in silence and attained a great awakening to the profound essence. Thereupon—
He concealed his traces on Mount Zhong for many years, spending his final days in a thatched hut with earthenware vessels.
On the sixth day of the second month in the third year of the Tiānshòu era of the Tang dynasty, he entered meditative absorption with serene composure and passed away seven days later.
The Fourth Patriarch’s Third and Fourth Generations (collateral branches) (no chapter order listed);
The Fourth Patriarch’s Fifth Generation (collateral branches):
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Chi of Mount Niu-t’ou in Chin-ling.
Chan Master Zhìwéi of Niutou Mountain was a native of Jāngníng. His surname was Chén.

He left the household life under the Dharma Master Tǒng of Tiānbǎo Monastery and visited Chan Master Fǎchí, from whom he received the transmission of the True Dharma. Thereafter, students from the region east of the Yangtze River all flocked to his door.

One named Huìzhōng was regarded by him as a vessel for the Dharma. The Master once showed him a verse, saying: [Blank] [Blank] (Note: The original text contains two illegible characters marked with □□.)
"Do not fixate on thoughts. Thoughts form the river of birth and death; they cause one to circle through the ocean of the six realms, where there is no sight of the long waves from which to emerge.
Zhong replied: "Thoughts and perceptions have always been illusory; their nature is inherently without beginning or end. If one grasps this meaning within, the long waves shall naturally cease.

The Master further showed him a verse, saying: "My original nature is empty and non-existent; it is due to delusive conditions that 'self' and 'other' arise. How can one bring these delusions to rest?"
Feeling weary, he returned to sit in an empty place. Zhong replied, "Emptiness and non-being are the true substance; where do 'self' and 'other' exist?
There is no need to extinguish deluded feelings; simply board the boat of Prajñā. The Master knew that he had attained realization and thus entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery.
He traveled about to transform and guide others according to conditions, passing away at Yanzuo Temple.
The Sixth Generation after the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral branch):
Zen Master Wei of Mount Niutou in Jinling, successor to the Dharma of Zen Master Huizhong of Mount Niutou.
He was a native of Runzhou and surnamed Wang. At the age of twenty-three, he received [the precepts].
While at Zhuangyan Monastery, [Zhaozhou] heard that Chan Master Wei had appeared in the world, so he went to visit him. As soon as Wei saw him, he said, "The master of the mountain has arrived.
The Master was awakened to its subtle meaning and subsequently attended upon him. Later, he took his leave and traveled to various regions to pay homage to the sacred sites.
While at the Jiujie Monastery, he saw that the *lingxiao* vine had withered during the summer. When people wished to cut it down, he said to them, "Do not prune it.
When Huizhong returned, the vine grew back again; when the Master himself returned, it was indeed as he had said.

He then entrusted the mountain gate to his successor and departed to reside at Yanzuo Monastery. Throughout his life, the Master wore only a single robe which he never changed; his only utensils were—
There was once a single cauldron and two storehouses of grain provided for the monks. When thieves were watching for an opportunity to steal it, a tiger guarded it for them.
The district magistrate, Zhang Xun, went to the summit of the mountain to pay his respects and asked the Master, "How many disciples do you have? The Master replied, "Three or five. Zhang Xun said:
"How can I see them? The Master struck the meditation platform, and three tigers roared forth. Xun retreated in terror.
Later, the assembly requested him to enter the city, where he resided at the old Zangyan Monastery. The Master intended to construct a separate Dharma Hall to the east of the main hall.

There was an ancient tree there upon which a flock of magpies had built their nest. When the workmen were about to cut it down, the Master said to the magpies, "This site shall be used for construction..."
"Halls! Why do you not depart quickly? Having spoken these words, the flock of magpies moved their nests to another tree.
When the foundation was first laid, two divine beings fixed its four corners and secretly assisted with the night labor; thus, it was completed in no time.
Consequently, disciples from the four quarters gathered like clouds, and thirty-four who attained the Dharma each resided in a different region, converting many.
The Master had a verse on settling the mind that said: "When both person and dharmas are purified, good and evil are forgotten; with a straightforward and true mind, one is at the site of Bodhi.

In the third year of the Dali era, the tree before his stone chamber, upon which he hung his cooking pot, and the vine upon which he hung his robes, suddenly withered and died in the height of summer.
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month of the fourth year, after completing the *poṣadha* assembly for the monks, he ordered his attendant to shave his hair and bathe his body.
At night, auspicious clouds covered his vihāra, and the sound of celestial music was heard from the air. At dawn, he sat peacefully and passed away.
At that time, wind and rain broke out violently, shaking and breaking the trees; furthermore, a white rainbow pierced through the cliffs and valleys.
In the spring of the fifth year, his body was cremated, and śarīra relics were obtained in incalculable numbers.
When Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo Temple in Xuanzhou first visited Chan Master Wei, he stood in attendance.

At that time, a monk who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asked, "What is the meaning of the dependent origination of true nature? After Master Wei remained silent for a long while, Xuanting suddenly called out, "Virtuous One! (Dàdé).
At the very moment he raised a single thought and asked the question, this was the dependent origination within true nature. The monk attained great enlightenment upon these words. Someone asked:
"From what did the Southern School establish itself? He replied: "The Mind-School is neither north nor south."
Chan Master Chonghui of Mount Tiantu in Shuzhou was a native of Pengzhou. His secular surname was Chen.

At the beginning of the Qianyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he went to Mount Tiantu in Shuzhou and founded a monastery. In the first year of the Yongtai era, it was granted an official plaque. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Tiantu?
The Master said, "The heights of Mount Zhububu are so great that the sun is hard to see; before the Jade Mirror Peak, people are easily enlightened. [The monk] asked again.
[The student asked: "When Bodhidharma has not yet come to this land, does the Buddha-dharma still exist or not? The Master said: "Setting aside for a moment the future, what is the matter right now?
[The student] said: "I do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said: "Ten thousand ages, the eternal void."
"In a single morning breeze and moonlight. The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again, "Does the *ācārya* understand? He replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "How is it from the standpoint of your own self? What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma came or did not come? His coming here was much like a fortune-teller;
seeing that you did not understand, he broke open the lines of the divination for you. Once the auspicious and the inauspicious arise, they are all contained therein."

The Master said, "The moment you step out the door, you have already missed it. A monk asked, "What is the family style of Tianzhu? The monk asked, "What is the family style of Tianzhu? The Master said, "At times white clouds come to close the door; there is no more wind or moon, nor the flowing of the four mountains. [The monk] departs. The Master says: "The peaks of Mount Shiqian are high, ever accumulating emerald green; the bright moonlight of the River Shu shines with radiant splendor.
[The monk] asks: "What is the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? The Master says: "Throughout vast kalpas, there has never been any obstruction.
If it were not the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, what would it be? [The monk] asks: "Why do the Buddha-dharma and wisdom not manifest before me? The Master says: "Precisely because..."
“You do not understand. That is why it does not manifest before you. If you were to understand, there would likewise be no Buddha to be realized.

Question: “What is the Way? The Master said: “White clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies cling to the courtyard flowers. Question: “What have the sages of the past ever said? The Master said:
“Do you see anything I am saying right now? Question: “I ask about the matter of the Gate of the Patriarchs. The Master said: [Silence].

The Master raised his voice and sang: "The stone ox bellows beyond the void; when the wooden horse neighs, the moon hides behind the mountain. A monk asked, "What is the Master’s way of benefiting others?
The Master said, "A single rain nourishes all; the thousand peaks display their exquisite beauty. A monk asked, "What is it like to be among the people of Tianzhu Mountain?
The Master said, "Walking alone on the crest of a thousand peaks, strolling leisurely by the nine-fold spring. A monk asked, "... [The text ends here.]
"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master replied, "A white monkey carries its young to the green cliffs; bees and butterflies carry flowers amidst the green blossoms.
He entered nirvana in the fourteenth year of the Dali era and was interred in a stupa to the north of the mountain.
Chan Master Xuansu of Helin in Runzhou was a native of Yanling. His surname was Ma. Later, he studied under Chan Master Wei and attained enlightenment into the essence of the nature.
He subsequently resided at Helin Temple. One day, a butcher came to pay his respects and requested that the Master go to his dwelling to partake in a meal offering.
The Master went with joy, which caused the assembly to look on in astonishment. The Master said, "The Buddha-nature is equal; it is the same for the worthy and the foolish."
They are one and the same. However, as for those who can be saved, I save them immediately. What difference, then, could there be? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master said, "If you understand, it is not understanding; if you doubt, it is not doubting. He further said, "That which is not understood yet not doubted;
that which is not doubted yet not understood. A monk knocked on the door. The Master asked, "Who is there? The monk replied, "It is a monk. The Master said—

[The monk] said, "It is not only the Sangha; even if the Buddha were to come, he would not be attached [to it]. [The Master] asked, "Why would he not be attached? The Master said, "Because there is no place for you to dwell."
The seventh generation descendant of the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral line):
Zen Master Weize of Fuku Yan on Mount Tiantai, successor to Zen Master Zhong of Niu-tou Mountain in Jinling. He was a native of Jingzhao and surnamed Changsun. Initially...
He visited Chan Master Zhong and attained a great awakening to the profound principle. He then said: "Heaven and earth are without things; things and the self are without things.
Although there are no things, it has never been that there were not things. If this is so, then the sage is like a shadow and the common people are like a dream—who, then, undergoes birth and death?
The person of ultimate attainment is able to illuminate alone through this, and is able to be the lord of the myriad things. This I know."
Having done so, he traveled south to Mount Tiantai and lived in seclusion on the western cliff of the Waterfall.
During the Yuanhe era, seekers of the Way came daily. A disciple named Kesu built a dwelling for him, and it gradually became a center for the Dharma.
The title "Buddha Cave" originated with this master. A monk asked, "What is the Nārāyaṇa arrow? The Master said, "It hits the mark. One day, suddenly—
He addressed his disciples, saying, "You must all exert yourselves. After one day had passed, he sat in the lotus position and passed away.
Three years later, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the mountain monastery (the inscription composed by Han Yu of the Tang dynasty still exists today at Guoqing Temple).
The Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Su of Heilin, was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou. His surname was Zhu.
Having initially devoted himself to Confucian teachings, at the age of twenty-eight he encountered Master Su, who said to him, "I observe that your spirit and temperament are pure and refined."
"This is the true Dharma-treasure. The Master was moved by this realization and requested to become his disciple. Baizhang personally shaved his hair and then instructed him, saying:
"When you travel along the current, stop whenever you encounter a path. The Master then journeyed southward until he reached Lin’an.
There he saw a mountain to the northeast and asked a woodcutter about it. The woodcutter replied, "This is Mount Jing. He then settled there with his staff. A monk asked, "How [is it]?"
“This is the Way. The Master said, “There are carp on the mountain; there is dust on the seabed. Mazu sent someone to deliver a letter to him; in the letter, he had drawn a circle.
When the Master opened the seal, he placed a dot inside the circle and then sealed it back and returned it.

(When National Teacher Zhong heard of this, he remarked: “Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma. [Someone] asked, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, “I am asking you.”
"This is not appropriate," [Mazu] said. "How can it be made appropriate? The Master replied, "Wait until after I have passed away, and then I will tell you.
Mazu then sent Zhizang to inquire: "In the twelve hours of the day, what should be taken as the objective realm? The Master replied, "When you have returned, there will be news for you.
Zhizang said, "I am returning right now. The Master said, "As for delivering this message, you must go ask Caoxi. (Cui Zhao)
The Duke asked, "My disciple now wishes to leave the household life; may it be permitted? The Master replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. At this, the Duke attained a realization. In the third year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital, where he personally paid him homage.
One day, while sitting in the inner court together with National Teacher Huizhong, he saw the Emperor’s carriage approaching.
The Master rose to his feet. The Emperor asked, "Why have you risen? The Master replied, "How could a donor perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment?
The Emperor was pleased and said to the State Preceptor, "I wish to bestow a name upon the Venerable Master.

The State Preceptor joyfully accepted the imperial decree, and he was thus granted the title Guoyi (National One). Later, he took leave to return to his mountain home. In the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era...
Yue showed signs of illness; he preached the Dharma and passed away. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajue.
He was the eighth generation descendant under the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral line).
He was a dharma heir of Chan Master Fukuze.
Master Zhì of Yúnjū at Tiantái Mountain once had a Huáyán Cloister. The monk Jìzōng asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood'?
The Master said, "The nature of purity is fundamentally serene and without movement;

it does not belong to existence or non-existence, purity or impurity, long or short, nor to grasping or rejecting. Its essence is naturally free and easy. To see clearly in this manner is what is called 'seeing.'"
“Nature is itself Buddha; Buddha is itself nature. Therefore it is said: ‘seeing one’s nature is attaining Buddhahood. [The student] asked:
“If nature is already pure and does not belong to existence or non-existence, for what reason is there ‘seeing’? The Master said: “Seeing is seeing nothing. [The student] asked:

“If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing? The Master said: “Even the place of seeing is non-existent. [The student] asked: “When seeing occurs in this way, whose seeing is it? The Master said: “There is none.”
The questioner asked, "How is its principle ultimately realized? The Master said, "Do you know? To falsely reckon it as existing is to have subject and object;
this is what is called delusion. To give rise to understanding based on what is seen is to fall into birth and death.

It is not so for one who sees clearly: though seeing all day long, they have never seen. When seeking the name, location, essence, or characteristics, none can be found; both subject and object are utterly transcended."
[The student] said, "This is called 'seeing one's nature. Does this nature pervade all places? The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade.
[The student] asked, "Do ordinary beings possess it? The Master said, "I have just stated that there is nowhere it does not pervade; how could ordinary beings not possess it?
[The student] asked, "For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering? How has it ever been..."
[The student] said, "I have attained pervasiveness. The Master said, "Ordinary people, within the nature of purity, calculate the existence of subject and object; they thus fall into birth and death.
The Buddhas and Great Beings well know that within the nature of purity, one does not belong to existence or non-existence; thus, subject and object do not arise.

[The student] asked, "If it is explained in this way, then there must be people who understand and those who do not. The Master said, "Since even 'understanding' cannot be found, how could there be a person who understands?"
[The monk] asked, "Is there one who realizes [this]? The Master said, "As for the ultimate principle, how is it? I shall tell you the essential point:
within the nature of purity, there is neither ordinary person nor sage, nor is there anyone who realizes or fails to realize. Both 'ordinary' and 'sage' are merely names.
If you give rise to understanding based on these names, you will fall into birth and death; if you know that these are provisional names lacking reality, then there is nothing to attain."
As for "names," it is also said: this is the ultimate point of culmination. To say, "I can understand, but he cannot," is a great illness.

To perceive distinctions between pure and defiled, or ordinary and sage, is also a great illness. To interpret this as meaning there are no ordinary beings or sages belongs to the denial of cause and effect.
To perceive a pure nature in which one may dwell is also a great illness; to interpret this as meaning there is no place to dwell is likewise so.

This is also a great illness. Nevertheless, within the nature of purity, although there is no movement or agitation, one does not destroy the application of skillful means nor the arousal of compassion and mercy.
In such instances of arousal, the very place of that arousal is the entirety of the pure nature; this may be called "seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha.
Jizong leaped for joy, bowed in gratitude, and withdrew.
Chan Master Daolin of Niaoke, in Hangzhou, was a successor of Chan Master Guoyi Qin of Jingshan.
He was a native of Fuyang in his home prefecture. His surname was Pan, and his mother’s surname was Zhu.
She dreamed that the light of the sun entered her mouth, and consequently became pregnant. Upon her birth, an extraordinary fragrance filled the room; she was thus named Xiangguang (Fragrant Light).
At the age of nine, she left home to become a nun. At twenty-one, she received full ordination at Guoyuan Temple in Jingzhou.

Later, she went to Ximing Temple in Chang’an to study the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith* under Master Fuli, who instructed her with verses on truth and falsehood (*zhenwang*) and directed her in her cultivation.

Regarding Chan meditation: the Master asked, "How do you first observe? How do you apply the mind? Li performed prostrations for a long time without speaking; the Master performed three prostrations and withdrew.
Later, when Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree summoning National Teacher Guoyi to the capital, the Master went to pay his respects to him and thereby attained the True Dharma.
Upon returning south to Yongfu Temple on Mount Gushan, there was a Pratyekabuddha stupa where the clergy and laity together practiced the Dharma.
The assembly gathered. The Master entered, shaking his monk’s staff. Dharma Master Taoguang of Lingyin Temple asked, "Why do you make a sound at this dharma assembly?
The Master replied, "If there were no sound, who would know it is an assembly? Later, he saw a tall pine tree on Mount Qinwang.
Its branches and leaves were lush and dense, spreading out in a curve like a canopy. He consequently took up residence upon it; thus, people of the time called him Chan Master Niaoke (Nest of Birds).
Furthermore, a magpie had built its nest beside him, and the bird became naturally tame and familiar with him. People also referred to him as Master Qiaoke (Nest of Magpies).
He had an attendant named Huìtōng, who one day suddenly wished to take his leave. The Master asked him, "Where are you going now? He replied:

Tong said, "I have come here seeking the Dharma and have left the household life. My preceptor has not bestowed compassionate instruction upon me; I am now going to various regions to study the Buddha-Dharma.
The Master said, "If it is the Buddha-Dharma, I too have a small portion of it right here.

Tong asked, "What is the Preceptor’s Buddha-Dharma? The Master picked up a tuft of cloth from his body and blew upon it. Tong thereupon attained realization of the profound principle. The Yuanhe period.

[In the] middle [section]: When Minister Bai Juyi was sent to govern this prefecture, he entered the mountains to pay his respects to the Master. He asked, "The Chan Master’s dwelling is extremely perilous.
The Master replied, "Your Excellency’s peril is even greater. Bai said, "I, your disciple, hold a position that secures the rivers and mountains."
"What danger is there? the Master said, "When firewood and flame intersect, the nature of consciousness does not rest;
is this not a peril? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
Baizhang said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say this. The Master said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old..."

No one could approach him. He paid his respects and withdrew. On the tenth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Changqing era, the Master said to his attendants, "My life-force is now exhausted.
Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away (some say his name was Yuánxiū; this is likely a posthumous title).

Regarding the first generation of collateral dharma heirs of the Fifth Patriarch Daman Chan Master, Chan Master Shenxiu of the Northern School (as recorded in the inscription by Tripiṭaka Master Yashas: "The profound principle was born from the earth of Qian; both the honored and the lovely are likewise honored. He stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the three and nine clans; a single hair on his foot is a portion of the whole"): he was a native of Kaifeng. His surname was Li.
In his youth, he devoted himself to Confucian studies, becoming widely learned and well-versed in many fields. Suddenly, renouncing worldly attachments, he left the household life.

Seeking a teacher and inquiring after the Way, he arrived at the East Mountain Temple (Dongshan Si) on the Double Peaks (Shuangfeng) in Qizhou. There he encountered the Fifth Patriarch, who was dedicated to the practice of seated meditation.

He sighed in admiration and submission, saying, "This is truly my teacher. He vowed to undergo rigorous discipline, subjecting himself to the labor of gathering firewood and drawing water while seeking the Way.
The Patriarch silently recognized him and held him in high esteem. After the Patriarch passed away, Xiu subsequently resided at Jiangling Dang...
When Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty heard of Yangshan, she summoned him to the capital to provide offerings at the Inner Court Dharma Hall, where she treated him with exceptional reverence.

She ordered the establishment of Du-men Monastery on his former mountain to commemorate his virtue. At that time, princes, dukes, officials, and commoners alike prostrated themselves upon seeing his dust.
When Zhongzong ascended the throne, he honored him even more highly; the high minister Zhang Yue once inquired of him regarding the essentials of the Dharma.
He observed the rites of a disciple. His teacher had a verse for the assembly which said: "All Buddha-dharmas are inherently present within one's own mind;
to seek them elsewhere with the mind is to abandon one's father and flee. In the second year of the Shenlong era, he entered *nirvāṇa* at Tiangong Monastery in the Eastern Capital.

He was posthumously titled Chan Master Datong. With ceremonial insignia and ritual objects, his funeral procession was sent to Longmen. The Emperor escorted him as far as the bridge, followed by princes, dukes, officials, and commoners.
All attended the burial site. Zhang Yue and the retired scholar Lu Hongyi each composed a stele inscription and a eulogy.
His disciples, including Pujì and Yìfú, were both highly esteemed by the court and the common people alike.
