National Teacher Huian of Mount Song (recorded by Tripiṭaka Master Yashas: "Nine daughters left the human realm; eight daughters severed marriage ties. An old bed with six legs added—among the assembly of patriarchs, he is the most honored. was a native of Zhiyang in Jingzhou. His surname was Wei.
In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when the government conducted a census of all privately ordained monks and nuns, they sought out the Master.
The Master said, "I originally have no name," and subsequently fled into the mountain valleys. During the Daye era, the government mobilized a vast number of laborers.
When the Tongji Canal was opened, people perished from hunger and lay upon one another like pillows; the Master begged for food to rescue them, and many were saved.

Emperor Yang summoned him, but he did not go, instead entering Mount Dahu in secret. When the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu and the realm fell into turmoil, the Master took up his staff and ascended Mount Heng, where he practiced the dhūta austerities.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he went to Huangmei to visit the Patriarch Huineng, and subsequently attained [enlightenment].
The Essential Mind. In the first year of the Linde era, he traveled to the stone cliffs of Mount Zhongnan and settled there.

Emperor Gaozong once summoned him, but the Master did not comply with the imperial decree. Thereupon, he journeyed through various famous sites until he reached Mount Songxiao, where he declared, "This shall be the place of my final rest."

From that time on, practitioners flocked to him like spokes converging at the hub. Two monks, Tanran and Huairang, came to inquire, saying, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Why do you not ask about the meaning of your own self? They asked, "What is the meaning of one's own self?"
The Master said, "You should contemplate my secret function. [The monk] asked, "What is the secret function? The Master indicated it by opening and closing his eyes.
Thus, [Nanyue] understood where to turn upon hearing these words. Nanyue then went directly to visit Caoxi. Empress Wu summoned him to the capital and treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He was held in equal high esteem as Chan Master Xiu. The Empress once asked the Master, "How many years have you been ordained? The Master—
He replied, "I do not record them. The Master asked, "Why do you not record them? The teacher said, "The body of birth and death is like a revolving wheel;

the wheel has neither beginning nor end, so what use is there in recording? Furthermore, this flow of the mind is uninterrupted in its midst; those who perceive the rising and ceasing of bubbles are merely experiencing deluded thoughts.
From the first moment of consciousness until the cessation of the signs of movement, it is exactly like this. What need is there for years, months, [days, or hours]?"

Can this be recorded? Later, he heard [the news] and prostrated himself in worship, receiving it with faith. In the second year of the Shénlóng era, Zhōngzōng bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and ordained fourteen disciples.
He was subsequently invited into the imperial palace for offerings. In the third year, he was again granted a *monā* (patchwork robe). Taking his leave, he returned to Mount Sōng.
On the third day of the third month of that year, he addressed his disciples, saying: "After my death, take my corpse toward the forest."
In the midst of this, he waited for a wild fire to consume him. Suddenly, Master Wanhui arrived; seeing the Master acting in such a frantic manner, he took his hand and engaged him in conversation.

Those attending by his side strained their ears to listen, yet none could comprehend a word. On the eighth day, he closed his door, lay down, and passed away peacefully at the age of one hundred twenty-eight (born in the second year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Renyin;
died in the third year of the Jinglong era of the Tang dynasty, Jiyou; he was then known as National Teacher Lao’an). His disciples followed his instructions and carried [his body].
He was placed among the trees, where a wild fire spontaneously broke out. After cremation, eighty grains of *śarīra* were obtained;
five of these were purple in color and were kept within the palace. In the second year of the Xiāntián era, his disciples constructed a stupa for them.
Chan Master Daoming of Mount Meng in Yuanzhou was a native of Poyang. He was a descendant of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty. After the fall of his kingdom, he fell among the common people;
however, because he was a great-grandson of a king, he had once held an official appointment and thus bore the title of General. In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Yongchang Temple.
His aspiration for the Way was most earnest, and he went to rely upon the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch, where he investigated and sought the truth with all his heart. At first, there was...

Upon understanding this and hearing that the Fifth Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and Dharma to the Layman Lu, he immediately led several dozen companions to track his footsteps in pursuit.
They reached Mount Dayu, where the Master was the first to see him; the others had not yet arrived.
Seeing the Master rushing toward him, Lu immediately cast the robe and bowl onto a flat rock, saying, "This robe is a token of faith; can it be contested by force? It is yours to keep."

As he was about to leave, the Master [Nanquan] reached out and lifted him up; [Huangbo] remained as motionless as a mountain. Hesitating and trembling with awe, he said, "I have come to seek the Dharma, not for the sake of robes.
I pray that the Practitioner will grant me an instruction. Lu [Nanquan] said, "Do not think of good; do not think of evil.
At this very moment, which one is the Original Face of Master Ming? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Throughout...

His body broke into a sweat and he wept as he performed several prostrations. He asked, "Apart from these secret words and secret meanings you have provided thus far, is there still another underlying intent?
Lu said, "What I am telling you now is not a secret. If you turn back and reflect upon your own true face, the secret will reside within you.
The Master said, "Although I have been among the assembly at Huangmei, in truth I have not yet—"
"Examine your own true face. Now that you have received my instruction on the point of entry, it is like a person drinking water:
whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. From now on, this practitioner is your teacher. Lu said, "If it is so, then I and you share the same teacher at Huangmei.
Guard and uphold [the Dharma] well yourself. The Master asked again, "Where should I go in the future? Lu said, "When you encounter..."
Yuan Kezhi was at Mengji Ju. The Master paid his respects and took leave, then hurried back to the foot of the ridge.
He said to the group, "Just now we ascended the high peak, but looking out into the distance, there was no trace of him. We should seek him by another path. Everyone agreed.
Once the Master had returned, he went alone to Bushi Terrace on Mount Lu. After three years had passed, he finally went to Mount Meng in Yanzhou. Great...
He propagated the profound transformation. Originally named Huiming, he changed his name to Daoming to avoid the first character of the Sixth Patriarch’s name.
He sent all his disciples across the mountain pass to the south to pay their respects to the Sixth Patriarch.
The second generation under the Fifth Patriarch (a collateral line):
Chan Master Beizong Xiushou’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Jufang of Mount Wutai, was a native of Anlu. His surname was Cao. In his youth, he received his training at Mingfu Temple.

Chan Master Yuanlang initially lectured on the sutras and śāstras, but later joined a Chan assembly. When he arrived at the Northern School, Xiu asked him, "What is it like where the white clouds disperse?
The Master replied, "It is not obscured. Xiu asked again, "After reaching this state, what is it like? The Master replied:
"From the single branch of Right View, five leaves grow. Xiùmò approved of this. He entered the master’s chamber to serve him, responding to his teachings with unerring precision.
Subsequently, he went to reside at Hanling in Shangdang. Within a few years, his followers numbered in the thousands.
Later, he propagated the Dharma on Mount Wutai for over twenty years before passing away. His stupa was erected on that same mountain.

Chan Master Zhifen of Mount Zhongtiao in Hezhong Prefecture was surnamed Wu. Initially, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi lun), but he became mired in conceptual designations (*nāma-rūpa*).
When challenged by his fellow students, he grew indignant and ceased his lectures. He then traveled to visit Master Xiu, where his doubts were suddenly resolved.
He took his leave and resided at Anfeng on the Pujin River, not descending the mountain for ten years, subsisting on wild fruits and drinking from mountain streams.

The Provincial Governor, Wei Wensheng, established Jiananguan Monastery and resided there. Monastics and laypeople alike took refuge in him, their coming and going never ceasing. The Governor asked, "What will it be like for me from this day forward?
The Master replied, "The sun rises from the Mongsu [the western ocean]; it shines upon the trees, yet they cast no shadow.

At first, the Governor could not understand this; he bowed respectfully and withdrew. After a short while, he was enlightened, and his mind became clear and self-possessed. The Master— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "師" (the Master).*
He traveled back and forth through Mount Zhongtiao for over twenty years, and those who attained his Way were beyond counting.
After his passing, his disciples erected a stupa to the north of the city.
Chan Master Jiangmo Zang of Yanzhou was a native of Zhaojun. His surname was Wang, and his father served as a clerk in Bo. The Master entered the monastic order at the age of seven.

At that time, the countryside was infested with many malevolent spirits who deluded and bewitched people; the Master, however, subdued them alone through his physical presence, never showing even the slightest fear.
Thus, he acquired the name "Jiangmo" (Subduer of Demons). He received the tonsure under Chan Master Mingzan of Guangfu Monastery. Later...
Encountering the flourishing propagation of the Northern School, he vowed to follow them as a disciple. Xiu asked him, "Your name is 'Subduer of Demons' (Jiangmo).

Here there are no mountain spirits or forest monsters; why do you instead act as a demon? The Master replied, "There are Buddhas and there are demons. Xiu said, "If you are a demon, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm.
The Master said, "Even a Buddha is empty; what realm could there be? Xiu then made a prediction of his future attainment.
He said, "You have a karmic affinity with the ruins of Shao Hao. The Master then entered Mount Tai, where he remained for several years. Students gathered there like clouds.
One day, he addressed his disciples, saying, "I am now old and decrepit; when things reach their limit, they must return to their source. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou was a native of Tangzhou. His surname was Wen. In his youth, he explored the classics and scriptures.

When he was nearly fifty years old, he encountered an eminent monk who exhorted and instructed him; he subsequently vowed to leave the household life. He paid homage to Huiwen of Mount Mingyue in his own region as his teacher.

The master felt ashamed that Daoshu’s age was advanced and that his pursuit of the Dharma had been so delayed. Consequently, Daoshu resolved to travel abroad, visiting every place without exception. Later, he returned...
In Eastern Luoyang, he met Zen Master Xiu and, upon hearing his words, realized the subtle truth. He then chose Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou to build a thatched hut and dwell there.

There was often a rustic man of simple appearance and plain dress whose speech was strange and unconventional; beyond ordinary conversation and laughter, he would manifest the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and celestial immortals.
At times he emitted divine light, and at other times produced sounds and voices. [The Master]— (Note: The source text ends abruptly with "師之" (the Master's...), indicating an incomplete passage.)
The disciples observed this, yet none could fathom it. This continued for ten years, after which he suddenly vanished without a trace. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The rustic has employed many-colored arts and wiles to dazzle and delude people; it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them.
His wiles are finite, while my non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible. In the first year of the Baoli era of the Tang dynasty, he manifested illness.
He passed away.

Chan Master Renjian of Fuxian Monastery in Luoyang was a successor of National Teacher An of Mount Song. Having ceased his inquiries on Mount Song, he lived in leisure and ease amidst the suburban markets; thus he was known as...

The monk Teng Teng was summoned before the palace by Empress Wu during the Tiance Wansui era of the Tang dynasty. Looking up at the Empress, he gazed at her for a long while and asked, "Do you understand?
The Empress replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This old monk observes the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed.
The following day, he presented nineteen short songs. When the Empress read them, she praised him and bestowed upon him generous gifts and rewards.
The Master declined to accept them all. He further ordered that the lyrics be transcribed and circulated throughout the world;
these verses all expounded the ultimate truth to admonish the customs of the age. Only one song by Liao Yuan became widely popular in the world.

The Monk Pòzào Duò of Mount Song did not disclose his name or lineage; his words and deeds were unfathomable. He lived in seclusion on Mount Song, where there was a shrine in a mountain valley that was exceedingly efficacious.
Within the hall stood only a single hearth, upon which offerings were made by people from near and far without ceasing, and many living beings were slaughtered for cooking.
One day, the Master led an attendant monk into the shrine and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying: "Tut! This—"
"A stove is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the sacred come? From where does the numinous arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings.
He struck three more blows, and the stove immediately collapsed and fell apart. A moment later, a man appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap.
He prostrated himself before the Master. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am originally the stove deity of this temple.

Having long endured the retribution of karma, today I have been fortunate enough to hear the Master preach the Dharma of non-arising and have attained liberation from this place to be reborn among the devas. I have come specifically to express my gratitude.
The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it was not my words that forced it upon you. The spirit bowed once more and vanished. A short while later—
An attendant monk asked, "We have long served the Master, yet we have not received any instruction. What essential principle did the hearth-god obtain that he was able to be reborn in heaven?
The Master said, "I simply told him that he was composed of clay and tiles; there was no other principle to impart to him.
The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is originally present."
"What is the nature of this? Why does it not function? The attendant monks then prostrated themselves. The Master said, "Falling! Falling! Broken! Broken!
Later, Zen Master Yifeng recounted this to National Teacher An, who sighed and said, "This man has realized it completely."
The identity of things and self is one; it may be said to be like the bright moon dwelling in the sky—there is no one who does not see it. It is difficult to grasp the pulse of his speech.
Feng asked, "I do not yet understand what kind of person can grasp his pulse of speech? An said, "One who does not know. At that time, he was known as "Puo-zao-duo" (The One Who Broke the Oven).
A monk asked, "When every thing is formless, how is it? The Master said, "As for 'reverence,' it belongs only to you, not to me."
"I do not prostrate; it is simply I, not you. The monk then bowed in apology. The Master said, "That which is inherently present is neither a thing nor a non-thing.
Therefore it is said that when the mind can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. A monk came from the place of Niutou;
the Master asked him, "From whose Dharma assembly have you come? The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and circumambulated the Master once.
[The monk] went out. The Master said, "There should not be such a person under Niutou’s assembly. The monk then returned to stand with his hands clasped at the Master's shoulder.
The Master said, "As expected. As expected. The monk then asked, "When responding to things without depending on another, how is it?"

The Master said, "How could it not be due to him? The monk said, "If that is so, then one follows the correct path and returns to the source. The Master said, "What 'returning to the source' is there to follow?
The monk said, "Had it not been for you, Master, I would have nearly incurred a transgression. The Master said, "That is still the principle before you have seen the Fourth Patriarch.
Try saying it after you have seen him. The monk then circumambulated the Master once and departed. The Master said, "Following the correct path."

This is the Way. It has been thus from antiquity to the present. The monk prostrated. After the monk had stood in attendance for a long time, the Master said, "From patriarch to patriarch and Buddha to Buddha, it has only been taught that there is nothing other than the original nature and original mind of man; there is no other principle. Understand this! Understand this! The monk bowed in thanks.
The Master then struck him with his whisk and said, "If it is thus in one place, it is likewise in a thousand places.
The monk then joined his palms, stepped forward, and gave a single response of assent. The Master said, "You do not believe further; you do not believe further.
The monk asked, "What is a person of great *icchantika*? The Master said, "To pay respect and prostrate. [The monk] asked, "What is a person of great diligence? The Master said, "To revile..."
He was humiliated by anger and resentment. Afterward, nothing was known of his final destination.

Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was a native of Yique. His surname was Li. He entered the monastic life in his youth and received full ordination in the second year of the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty.
He was registered at Xianju Monastery and studied the Vinaya without slackening. Later, he went to pay respects to National Teacher An. Suddenly—
Having realized the profound essence of the Way, he subsequently chose a site at Pangwu on the mountain to build his hermitage.

One day, a strange man arrived, wearing a tall cap and *kuxi* trousers (the "xi" pronounced as *jie*), accompanied by a vast retinue. He walked with light steps and composed ease, announcing that he came to pay his respects to the Great Master.

Upon seeing the man’s appearance, which was exceptionally grand and extraordinary, the Master addressed him, saying: "Welcome, benevolent one; for what purpose have you come? The man replied: "Master..."
"Do you perhaps recognize me? The Master said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions?
The spirit replied, "I am the mountain deity of this peak, capable of bringing life and death to others. How can you, Master, view me with a single eye?"
The Master said: "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you cause me to die? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy space or yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished.
Since you cannot even do this, how could you possibly bring about my birth or death? The Spirit bowed his head and said: "I, too—"
"Since you are wise, sagacious, and upright beyond other deities, how could you not know that your Master possesses vast wisdom and eloquence?
I pray that he may bestow upon you the true precepts, so that you may cross over the world. The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them. Why is this?"
"Outside of precepts there are no precepts; what, then, would a precept be? The spirit said, "This principle is vast and obscure as I have heard it;

I merely seek for my teacher to ordain me so that I may become a disciple. The teacher immediately prepared a seat, held the incense burner, and straightened the table, saying, "I shall confer the five precepts upon you.
If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'No'. [The spirit] said, "I respectfully receive these instructions. The teacher said:
"Are you able to refrain from sexual misconduct? He replied, "I am married. The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean the absence of lustful desire. He replied, "I can.
The Master said, "Are you able to refrain from stealing? He replied, "What would I lack that I should steal? How could I ever take anything by theft?"
The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that one brings blessings upon the licentious by making offerings, and brings calamity upon the virtuous by failing to offer them.

[The Official] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from killing? [The Official] said, "I truly hold the handle of authority; how could I say I do not kill? The Master said, "I do not mean this.

I mean that there may be errors, oversights, doubts, or confusions [in the execution]. [The Official] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from falsehood? [The Official] said, "I am upright."
"Is it not straightforward? How could there be any delusion? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that the preceding and succeeding [actions] do not accord with the Will of Heaven.
[The student] said, "I can. The Master said, "Would you not be ruined by wine? [The student] said, "I can. The Master said, "As described above, this constitutes the Buddha-precepts."
It is further said: "To maintain with a mind yet lack a mind of clinging; to act for the sake of others with a mind yet lack a mind that conceives of a self.
One who can do so is not considered a 'vital essence' when born before heaven and earth, nor is one considered 'old' when dying after heaven and earth."
Throughout the day one undergoes transformations yet does not move; throughout the night one remains in profound stillness yet does not rest.

To believe this is to realize that though one marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though one feasts, it is not for the sake of taking; though one holds office, it is not for the sake of power; though one acts, it is not for the sake of habit; though one is intoxicated, it is not for the sake of delusion.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then even if one is ensnared by desires, it does not constitute lust. [As for] rewarding the licentious and bringing calamity to... [the text here is incomplete].
Not stealing out of goodness; not killing through negligence, error, suspicion, or confusion; not lying by contradicting the Way of Heaven in one's prior or subsequent actions;
and not being intoxicated through delusion, negligence, or perversion—this is called "no-mind. Where there is no mind, there is no precept; where there is no precept, there is no mind.
"There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor me. Who, then, would observe the precepts? The spirit said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.
The Master said, "Of your ten supernatural powers, five are effective and five are not. Of the Buddha’s ten powers, seven are effective and three are not.
The spirit was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat. Kneeling, he asked, "May I hear these explained? The Master said, "You can fly upward..."
The Emperor said, "Can one travel east through the heavens while the seven luminaries move west? He replied, "No.
The Master said, "Can you seize the Earth Deity, melt the Five Sacred Peaks, and bind the Four Seas? He replied, "No. The Master said, "These are called the five impossibilities.
The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha can know all that exists..."

Nature exhausts the events of billions of kalpas, yet it cannot transform or guide those who lack the conditions for connection. A Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings.
These are the three "incapacities. Even fixed karma is not eternal; even the absence of conditions is but a single period.
The realm of sentient beings fundamentally neither increases nor decreases; throughout all time, not a single person can master its laws. There is...
“Dharmas have no master; this is called the absence of dharmas. When there are no dharmas and no master, this is called the absence of mind.
As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through the absence of mind.

The deity said, “I am indeed shallow and ignorant, having not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). I shall faithfully observe the precepts you have bestowed upon me. Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue; please allow me to offer my service.”
The Master said, "I contemplate the body as having no substance and contemplate all phenomena as impermanent; being but a lump of flesh, what further desire could I have?

The spirit said, "The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly deed to display my minor divine powers, so that five types of people—those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment], those who have first resolved, those who have not yet resolved, those who lack faith, and those who will certainly gain faith—may behold my divine traces and know that [the Way] exists."

"The Buddha possesses spiritual power (*śakti*). There are things he can do and things he cannot; there are things that are spontaneous and things that are not. The Master said, "Non-action (*wuwei*) is it. Non-action is it.
The Spirit said, "The Buddha also commands spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, ever rebel against the Buddha?
I pray that you will deign to instruct me as you please. Reluctantly, the Master spoke: "The grounds of Dongyan Temple are vast and treeless. To the north..."
"The mountain clefts possess them, yet their backs are not shielded by barriers. Can you move the northern trees to the eastern ridge? The spirit replied, "I have received your command.
However, there will surely be clamor and commotion during the dark night; I pray that the Master does not be startled. He then performed a prostration and took his leave.
The Master saw him off at the gate, watching him as he went. His ceremonial retinue was long and winding, like the appearance of a sovereign, amidst mists, vapors, smoke, and clouds.

Amidst a swirling profusion, banners and streamers, and tinkling ornaments, vanished into the air. That evening, as expected, there was a violent wind and thundering peals, with rushing clouds and flashing lightning;
the buildings shook and swayed, and the nesting birds cried out in a tumultuous clamor. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not fear, do not fear! The deity has entered into a covenant with me.
At dawn the next day, when the weather had cleared and become bright, all the pine and cypress trees from the northern cliff had been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense array.
However, Xingzhi’s master said to his disciples, "After my death, do not let outsiders know; if they have something to talk about, people will treat me as a sorcerer.
On the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of Bingchen, he entrusted his followers, saying, "I originally resided on the eastern ridge of the temple.
When I pass away, you must place my remains there. Having finished speaking, he was like one casting off a discarded shell.
The Third Generation under the Fifth Patriarch (a collateral branch):

Chan Master Jì of Mount Sōng, whose Dharma successor was Chan Master Wéizhèng of Zhōngnán Mountain. He was a native of Píngyuán and surnamed Zhōu. He received his monastic training at Yán... in his home prefecture.
The Dharma Master Shuandeng of Heshi Temple received the Dharma from Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song. He subsequently entered Mount Taiyī, where his disciples filled his chambers.
During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Wenzong was fond of eating clams; officials along the coast had previously been required to present them to him in succession.
The people were also weary from their labors. One day, among the imperial offerings, there was a lotus that had been split open but would not close.

The Emperor, finding it extraordinary, immediately burned incense and prayed to it; it then opened, revealing the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of a Brahma-like appearance.

The Emperor subsequently placed it in a casket made of gold-dusted sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and bestowed it upon Xingshan Temple, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and pay homage to it. He then questioned his ministers.
"What auspicious omen is this? Someone memorialized that Chan Master Weizheng of Mount Taiyi had a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma and was widely learned with a powerful memory;
they requested that an imperial edict be issued to question him. The Emperor immediately issued the edict. When the Master arrived, the Emperor asked about the matter.
The Master replied, "Your servant has heard that nothing occurs in vain. This is merely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, a sūtra says: 'One should [regard] this body...'"

"To those who attain deliverance, he immediately manifests this body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has already appeared, yet we have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.
The Master said, "Does Your Majesty perceive this as permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it or do you not believe it?"
The Emperor said, "This is a most extraordinary matter; I believe it deeply. The Master replied, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma to its conclusion.

The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy and satisfaction, such as he had never experienced before. He issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the empire to establish an image of Avalokiteśvara in order to express gratitude for this extraordinary grace.

He invited the Master to remain at the Inner Sanctuary (Neidaochang), but the Master repeatedly declined and requested to return to the mountains. By imperial decree, he was instead appointed to reside at Shengshou Monastery. This continued until the reign of Emperor Wuzong.
Upon his accession to the position, the Master suddenly retired to live in seclusion in Mount Zhongnan. When people asked him the reason for this, the Master said, "I am avoiding my enemies.
After his death, he was cremated; forty-nine śarīras were collected, and a stupa was erected over them.
The monk asked Master Po-zao-duo, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Junji of Mount Song: "What is one who practices good? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue and wearing shackles.
The monk asked, "What is one who commits evil? The Master said, "Cultivating dhyāna and entering samādhi. The monk said, "My faculties are shallow."
"Please, Master, point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good. If you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had been silent for a long while, the Master said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness."
"A good person has no evil mind. Thus it is said that "good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing.
Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, when Puzuo heard this being cited, he remarked, "This man has realized that all phenomena are unborn."
The Fourth Generation under the Fifth Patriarch:
Chan Master Wuxiang of Yizhou and his Dharma heir, Chan Master Wuzhu of Baotang Temple in Yizhou. Having first received the Dharma from Great Master Wuxiang, he then resided in the South.

Yang Bai was at Yaishan, where he devoted himself exclusively to tranquil seclusion for many years. As students gradually arrived and their earnest requests never ceased, he began to bestow his instructions from that time on.
Although he extensively expounded upon the verbal teachings, he took "non-thought" as his sole principle.

When Du Hongjian, the State Councilor of the Tang Dynasty, went to govern the region of Kunwei, he heard of the Master’s reputation and longed to pay him homage. He dispatched an envoy to the mountain to extend an invitation. At that time, the season...
The Regional Inspector Cui Ning also ordered the monks of various temples to come forth from afar to welcome and escort him to Konghui Temple.
At that time, Lord Du and the military commander summoned eminent masters of the Three Studies to assemble within the temple.

After the formal greetings were concluded, the Lord asked, "I, your disciple, have heard that the Master now teaches the Dharma-gate of the three phrases: 'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not be deluded. Is this so? The Master replied:

The Duke said, "Are these three phrases one or three? The Master replied, "'No recollection' is named precept; 'no thought' is named concentration; 'do not delude' is named wisdom. When the single mind does not arise, it possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; thus it is neither one nor three. The Duke asked, "In the last phrase, is the character for 'delusion' (妄) the same as the 'forgetting' (忘) that is written with the radical for 'heart' (心)? The Master said, "It is the one written with the radical for 'woman' (女). The Duke said, "Is there a textual basis for this? The Master replied, "There is. The Duke said, "I have heard that the characters for 'forgetting' and 'delusion' are interchangeable. The Master said, "That is so. However, the character for 'delusion' (妄) is composed of 'woman' and 'speech' (言); it means that when a woman speaks, she causes delusion. The character for 'forgetting' (忘) is composed of 'heart' and 'my' (我); it means that when the heart forgets the self, it attains liberation. Therefore, they are not the same. The Duke was greatly enlightened. He bowed and withdrew. The Master then composed the following verse: "Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom— These three are not separate. When the single mind does not arise, One naturally possesses them all. If you wish to know the Buddha, Do not seek outside yourself. The Buddha is right within you; Why go elsewhere to find him? If you seek him elsewhere, You will never meet him. If you do not seek him, He is already present before you.

The Duke read the verse and attained great realization. He subsequently composed a poem to express his gratitude: "The Great Master’s teaching is truly wondrous; His words are like a bright mirror. My former ignorance was deep and vast; Today, I have finally seen through it. From now on, I shall follow the Way; I shall never again turn back. The Duke then took leave and departed. The Master remained seated, smiling. The assembly was moved to tears. This event became widely known throughout the world. It is recorded in the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (*Jingde Chuandeng Lu*). The Duke was the renowned scholar and statesman Li Ao (李翱). The Master was Mazu Daoyi (馬祖道一). The dialogue between them is preserved as a classic example of the encounter-dialogue style of Chan Buddhism. It illustrates how the Master used the very terminology of the Duke’s own Confucian learning to point directly to the nature of mind, thereby leading him to awakening. The distinction he made between the two characters for "forgetting" and "delusion" serves as a profound metaphor for the difference between the deluded state of the ordinary mind and the liberated state of the enlightened mind. The final verse encapsulates the core of his teaching: that the Buddha-nature is inherent and requires no external seeking. The Duke’s subsequent poem reflects his transformation from a seeker of external truth to one who has realized the truth within himself. This exchange remains a celebrated testament to the power of direct pointing in the Chan tradition.
"No," the Master said. "The *Dharmapada* states: 'If one gives rise to a mind of striving, this is delusion, not true striving. If the mind can remain free from delusion, striving will be boundless.
Upon hearing this, the official’s doubts were completely dispelled. The official asked again, 'Does the Master still instruct people by means of the three phrases?

The Master replied, 'For a beginner practitioner, one must first cause them to cease their discursive thoughts and settle the waves of consciousness; only when the water is clear [can the moon be seen]...'"
Manifesting as reflections, one awakens to the essence of non-thought; with quiescence manifest before one, even "non-thought" does not stand. At that time, a crow cawed in a tree in the courtyard.
The Master asked, "Did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it. After the crow had gone, he asked again, "Did you hear it? The Master replied:
[The Master] said, "When the crow flies away, there is no sound. How can you say you hear? The Master then addressed the assembly at large:
"A Buddha appears in the world but rarely; the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively. To 'hear' is to have no hearing;

it does not concern the nature of hearing itself. It is fundamentally unarisen—how could it ever cease? When there is sound, that is merely the sense-object of sound arising of its own accord. When there is no sound..."
The auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) perishes of its own accord, yet this nature of hearing does not arise with the sound, nor does it perish with the sound.
To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape being turned by the auditory object. You should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing; hearing is without coming or going.

The Duke, together with his officials and the great assembly, prostrated themselves and asked again: "What is called the 'Ultimate Truth' (paramārtha)? From what sequence does the Ultimate Truth proceed?"
[The monk] entered. The Master said, "The primary truth (paramārtha-satya) has no sequence; it neither enters nor exits. In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), everything exists;
in the primary truth, there is nothing. That all phenomena (dharmas) have no intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) is what is called the primary truth.

The Buddha said that the existence of phenomena is named the conventional truth, while the absence of intrinsic nature is the primary truth. The Official said, "As the Master has explained, this is truly inconceivable. The Official spoke again.
The disciple said, "My nature and understanding are shallow. Previously, during my leisure time, I composed two fascicles of commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*.
May these be called the Buddha-dharma? The Master replied, "In composing commentaries, one invariably employs the conscious mind to engage in deliberation and discrimination."
That which is conditioned and constructed arises from the movement of the mind and the stirring of thought; thus it can be brought into being.

According to the treatise, one should know that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects.

They are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and consist solely of the One Mind; therefore, they are called True Suchness (*tathatā*). Now, you, Excellency, are clinging to the characteristics of verbal expression.

[He] clings to the characteristics of names and words; he clings to the characteristics of mental objects. Since he clings to such various characteristics, how can this be the Buddha-dharma? The Master rose and paid homage, saying:
"Your disciple has also once questioned the various venerable masters in attendance, and they all praised your disciple as inconceivable.

One should know that they were merely following worldly sentiment. You, Master, now explain from the standpoint of understanding; this accords with the Dharma of the mind-ground and is truly [the truth]."
"This True Principle is inconceivable. The Master was asked again: "What is meant by 'non-arising'?

What is meant by 'non-extinction'? How does one attain liberation? The Master replied: "When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called non-arising. Non-arising is itself non-extinction.
Since there is neither arising nor extinction, one is not bound by external sensory realms; one is liberated right where one is. Non-arising is called non-thought. Non-thought..."
This is precisely non-extinction. Where there is no thought, there is no bondage; where there is no thought, there is no liberation.

To state the essential point: to recognize the mind is to be free from thought; to see one's nature is to attain liberation. Apart from recognizing the mind and seeing one's nature, it is impossible for there to be any other dharma-gate by which one may realize unsurpassed bodhi.
The Master asked, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing one's nature'? The Teacher replied, "All [phenomena]..."
The practitioner of the Way wanders along with their thoughts because they do not recognize the true mind. As for the true mind: when thoughts arise, it does not follow their arising;
when thoughts cease, it does not rely on stillness. It neither comes nor goes; it is neither fixed nor chaotic;
it neither grasps nor abandons; it neither sinks nor floats. Unconditioned and signless, it is lively and agile—ordinary and sovereign. This essence of mind is ultimately...
It can be attained; there is nothing to be known or perceived. Everything met by the eyes is thus; there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the Buddha-nature.
The official and the great assembly prostrated themselves in worship and offered praise, then departed with great joy. Later, the Master resided at Baotang Temple until his passing.
The First Generation of the Dharma Heirs Branching from the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Chan Master:
The Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta (Jueduo) of the Western Regions was a native of India. Under the words of the Sixth Patriarch, he attained realization.

Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he saw a monk sitting in meditation within a thatched hut. The Master asked him, "For what purpose do you sit alone? The monk replied, "I am practicing *guan-jing* (contemplating stillness). The Master—
[The Master] said, "Who is the observer? What is that which is still? The monk bowed and asked, "What is the principle of this?
The Master said, "Why do you not observe yourself and bring yourself to stillness? The monk was at a loss. The Master asked, "From whose lineage do you come? The monk replied:
Master Xiu said, "Among the heterodox paths of the Western Regions, even those of the lowest standing do not fall into such views as these.
To sit blankly and vacantly—what benefit does this bring to the Way? The monk then asked, "Who is the master of your master? Master Xiu replied, "My master is the Sixth Patriarch.
Why do you not go quickly to Caoxi to resolve the essential truth? Thereupon, the monk went at once to visit the Sixth Patriarch.
The Sixth Patriarch’s instructions accorded perfectly with the Master’s [realization], and the monk immediately attained awakening. The Master’s final whereabouts were unknown.

As for Chan Master Fahai of Shaoshan, he was a native of Qujiang. When he first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked, “‘This very mind is Buddha’—I pray you will grant me an instruction and illustration.
The Patriarch said, “When the preceding thought does not arise, that is the mind; when the succeeding thought does not cease, that is the Buddha. Thus it was accomplished.
All phenomena are identical with the mind; to be free from all phenomena is to be the Buddha. If I were to explain this in full detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.

Listen to my verse: "That which is the mind is called wisdom; that which is the Buddha is concentration. When concentration and wisdom are held in equal balance, the mind becomes pure. To awaken to this Dharma-gate is due to your habitual nature;
by employing that which is fundamentally unborn, these two are cultivated together as the correct path. The Master accepted this with faith and [responded] with a verse.

The eulogy says: The mind itself is originally the Buddha; failing to realize this, one remains self-abased. I know that the causes of concentration and wisdom must be cultivated together, free from all external things.
Master Zhicheng of Jizhou was a native of Tahe County in that same province. Initially, he studied under Master Xiu, and later, because...
As the two schools flourished, the disciples of Xiu often derided the Southern School, saying, "Master Neng does not recognize a single character;
what excellence does he possess? Xiu replied, "He has attained teacherless wisdom and deeply realized the Supreme Vehicle; in this, I am not his equal.
Furthermore, my master, the Fifth Patriarch, personally entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma—how could that have been for nothing? What I regret is that I cannot travel far [to follow him]."
"Go and draw near [to him]. You have received the bounty of the state in vain. All of you should not remain stagnant here; you may go to Caoxi to resolve your doubts.
When you return one day, you must speak of it for me. Upon hearing these words, the Master (Nanyue) paid his respects and took his leave, traveling to Shaoyang.

There he joined the assembly for formal inquiry, yet he did not mention where he had come from. At that time, the Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "There is now a thief of the Dharma who is secretly staying among us."
Huike emerged from the assembly and prostrated himself, recounting the matter in detail. The Patriarch said, "How did your teacher instruct the assembly?

Huike replied, "He used to exhort the great multitude, commanding them to settle the mind and contemplate stillness, sitting for long periods without lying down. The Patriarch said, "To settle the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not dhyāna;
to sit for long periods and constrain the body—what benefit is there in this according to principle? Listen to my verse: 'Since birth, he sits and does not lie down.'"
"Dead and lying down, not sitting; a single set of stinking bones. Why establish merit and fault? The Master asked, "I do not yet understand by what Dharma the Venerable One instructs people.
The Patriarch said, "If I were to say that I have a Dharma to give to others, I would be deceiving you.
It is merely following the circumstances to untie the bonds, provisionally named 'samādhi. Listen to my verse: 'When the mind-ground is free from transgression, it is the precept of self-nature.'"
"The ground of mind is free from delusion, its self-nature is wisdom; the ground of mind is free from distraction, its self-nature is concentration.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the natural vajra-body; going and coming, it is fundamentally samādhi. Upon hearing this verse, the Master repented and apologized, immediately vowing to take refuge.
He then presented his own verse, saying: "The illusory body of the five aggregates—how can illusion reach its ultimate end? Turning toward True Suchness, the dharmas are still not pure."
Regarding the biography of Chan Master Xiaoliao of Biandan Mountain, it is not recorded in [standard] annals;

only the stupa inscription composed by Chan Master Hulei Cheng, a disciple of the Northern School, is widely circulated in the world. Its brief account states: "The Master resided at Biandan Mountain and was styled Xiaoliao."
He was the direct successor of the Sixth Patriarch. The Master attained the mind that is no-mind and realized the appearance that is no-appearance.
As for "no-appearance," the myriad phenomena dazzle the eyes; as for "no-mind," discrimination blazes forth. Transcending every word and every sound, no resonance can be transmitted.

The transmission has been passed on; words cannot be exhausted. To exhaust them would be an error. You, Master, have attained the "non-existence" of non-existence, yet you do not remain non-existent within that non-existence.
I, for my part, employ the "existence" of existence, yet I do not remain existent within that existence. This existence that is not existent means that coming and going do not increase [reality].
This non-existence that is not non-existent means that *nirvāṇa* is not annihilation. Alas! While you, Master, dwell in this world, Caoxi is illuminated.
The Master has entered nirvana; the Dharma-boat has capsized. The Master’s discourse on non-discourse fills the universe. He revealed the vehicle of definitive meaning to deluded disciples.
The mountain colors of Bian Shan hang over this very place; the name "Xiaoliao" remains in the empty valley.
Chan Master Fada of Hongzhou was a native of Fengcheng in Hongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
After receiving full ordination, he went to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch, yet his head did not touch the ground. The Patriarch rebuked him, saying, "Your prostration does not reach the earth."
"How is it that you do not pay homage? Within your mind there must be some object; what have you been habitually practicing?

The Master replied, "I have recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times. The Patriarch said, "If you were to recite it ten thousand times and, upon grasping the meaning of the sūtra, did not regard this as a superior achievement, then you might walk with me.
But now you are burdened by this undertaking and do not recognize your own fault. Listen to me..."
The verse says: "Prostration fundamentally breaks the banner of pride; why would one's head not touch the ground? When the notion of 'self' arises, transgression is born;
when it perishes, merit is beyond compare. The Master asked again, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Fada. The Master said, "Your name is Fada."
"How could you have ever attained the Dharma? He then spoke a verse, saying: "You are now named Fada (Dharma-Attained), Yet you recite with diligence without ceasing.
You recite in vain, merely following the sounds; To clarify the mind is what is called a Bodhisattva. Because you now possess the necessary conditions, I shall now speak for your sake.
Simply believe that the Buddha is wordless, And the lotus will blossom from his mouth. Upon hearing the verse, the Master repented and said: "From this day forward, I shall be humble..."
He paid his respects to all. "I pray that the Upādhyāya, in your great compassion, will briefly explain the principles within this sutra.

The Patriarch asked, "As you recite this sutra, what do you take as its essential tenet? The Master replied, "I am a dull-witted student; from the beginning, I have merely relied on the text for my recitation. How could I know its fundamental purport?
The Patriarch said, "Try reciting it once for me, and I shall explain it to you. The Master then [began to] recite aloud—

While reciting the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, they reached the "Chapter on Expedient Means. The Patriarch said, "Stop! This sūtra fundamentally takes the appearance of the world through causes and conditions as its primary tenet.
Even though it expounds many kinds of parables, none exceed this principle. Why? Because causes and conditions constitute the single Great Matter."
The "one great matter" is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra.

If you were to see it as others do—that "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong solely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision while we have no share in it—then such an interpretation would be to slander the sutra and revile the Buddha.
Since he is already a Buddha, he has already fully possessed knowledge and vision; what need would there be for him to further "open" them? You should now believe that the Buddha...
As for this "knowing and seeing," it is simply your own mind; there is no other substance apart from it.

It is because all sentient beings obscure their own luminosity, greedily craving sensory objects, and being disturbed internally by external conditions that they willingly submit to being driven about. Thus, you must labor to rouse him from samādhi.
With various bitter words, he exhorted him to rest and cease, telling him not to seek outwardly, for he is no different from the Buddha. Thus it is said: "He opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If you merely exhaust yourself in clinging to mental recitations, claiming them to be your spiritual practice, how is this any different from a yak that loves its own tail?

The Master said, "If that is so, then one need only understand the meaning; is there no need for the labor of reciting the sutra? The Patriarch said, "What fault is there in the sutra? How could it obstruct your mindfulness?
It is simply because delusion and awakening depend on the person, while loss and benefit depend on you. Listen to my verse: When the mind is deluded, the Lotus Sutra revolves [around it];
When the mind is awakened, it revolves the Lotus Sutra. To recite for long without clarifying oneself Is to become an enemy to the meaning. Non-thought..."

"Mindfulness is itself correct; yet there are instances where mindfulness becomes perverse, and others where one does not reckon with either existence or non-existence. Thus one forever drives the white ox-cart.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master replied again, saying: "The Sūtra states that even the great Śrāvakas, up to and including the Bodhisattvas, cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom despite exhausting their thoughts and measurements.
Yet now you claim that an ordinary person, merely by awakening to their own mind, is said to possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

Unless one possesses the highest faculties, one cannot avoid doubt and slander. Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of three vehicles; how are the "great ox-cart" and the "white ox-cart" to be distinguished?
I pray that the Venerable Master will deign to explain this further. The Patriarch said: "The intent of the Sūtra is clear, yet you yourself are deluded and turn away from it.
That those of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom lies in their habit of measuring it with their own limited intellects. Even if they were to exhaust..."
As we reflect together, the matter becomes increasingly remote. The Buddha originally taught for the sake of ordinary beings, not for the sake of Buddhas.

If you are unwilling to believe this principle, you may withdraw from the assembly as you please; yet you do not realize that you have already boarded the white ox cart, only to seek the three carts outside the gate once more.
Moreover, the scriptural text clearly says to you: "There are neither two nor three. Why do you fail to understand these three?
The carriage is provisional, as it pertains to the past; the One Vehicle is real, as it pertains to the present. I am merely teaching you to abandon the provisional and return to the real.
Once you have returned to the real, even "the real" has no name. You should know that all precious wealth belongs entirely to you.

"Because you have received and utilized [this teaching], you no longer conceive the thought of him as a father, nor do you conceive the thought of him as a son, nor do you conceive the thought of utility.
This is called upholding the Lotus Sutra. From kalpa to kalpa, your hand shall not let go of the scroll; from day to night, there shall be no time when you do not keep it in mind.
Having received this inspiration, the Master leaped for joy and praised him with a verse: "I have recited three thousand volumes of sutras... Cao...
A single phrase from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* was lost; I had not yet clarified the intent of the world-transcending truth, so how could I have ceased my lifelong delusions?

The provisional teachings of the sheep, deer, and ox were established, and the excellence of the beginning, middle, and end was proclaimed. Who would have known that within the burning house there originally dwells the King of the Dharma?

The Patriarch said, "From this day forward, you may truly be considered a monk who recites the scriptures. From then on, the Master understood the intent and continued his recitation and upholding without ceasing.

Chan Master Zhītōng of Shòuzhōu was a native of Ānfēng. Initially, he studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* approximately one thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
He paid obeisance to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies..."
The pure Dharma-body is your nature. The perfect Reward-body is your wisdom. The thousand billion Transformation-bodies are your practice.
If you were to separate from your original nature and speak of the three bodies as distinct, they would be called "having bodies but lacking wisdom.
If you realize that the three bodies have no self-nature, they are called the four wisdoms of Bodhi. Listen to my verse: "The original nature is inherently endowed..."
The three bodies manifest and give rise to the four wisdoms; without departing from seeing and hearing, one transcends to the stage of Buddhahood.

I shall now explain this for you: believe it with earnest faith so that you will never again be deluded. Do not follow those who run about in pursuit, for they spend their whole days merely talking about Bodhi.
The Master asked, "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Patriarch replied, "Since you have already understood the three bodies, you naturally understand the four wisdoms. Why ask further?"
This is incorrect. If one were to speak of the four wisdoms separately from the three bodies, this would imply having wisdom without a body;
such "having wisdom" would, in turn, result in having no wisdom at all. Furthermore, a verse is spoken: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure;

The Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in its mind; The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done is identical to the Perfect Mirror. Five, eight, six, and seven...

The transformation of cause and fruit consists merely of conventional designations and lacks any intrinsic nature. If one does not harbor attachment toward this process of transformation, then amidst all that arises in profusion, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*.

(Regarding the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, the scriptures state: the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done; the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Although the sixth and seventh are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed at the stage of fruition, it is only their names that are transformed, not their substance. The Master bowed in gratitude.
He praised it with these verses: "The three bodies are originally my own essence; The four wisdoms are fundamentally the luminosity of the mind.

Body and wisdom are fused without obstruction, Responding to things as they take on various forms. To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; To cling to maintenance is not true refinement. Through the teacher, the wondrous principle is understood;
At last, even the name of defilement perishes."
Chan Master Zhiche of Jiangxi was surnamed Zhang and named Xingchang. In his youth, he was a man of chivalry.
Since the division into Northern and Southern schools, although the two patriarchs had ceased their mutual favoritism and animosity, their disciples vied with one another in love and hate.

At that time, the followers of the Northern school established Chan Master Huixiu as the Sixth Patriarch, yet they resented the fact that the transmission of the robe to Dajian (Huineng) was widely known throughout the world. However—
The Patriarch had foreknowledge of this matter and immediately placed ten taels of gold in the abbot’s quarters.

At that time, Xingchang, having been instigated by a follower of the Northern School, entered the Patriarch’s room with a blade hidden about him, intending to do him harm. The Patriarch extended his neck toward him;

Xingchang struck three times with the blade, yet it did not cause the slightest injury. The Patriarch said, "A true sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not true. You have merely brought [this] upon yourself."

"Jin, I shall not take your life. Startled, Xingchang fell prostrate; after a long time he regained consciousness. He begged for mercy and repented his transgressions, immediately vowing to leave the household life.
The Master then gave him gold, saying, "Go for now; I fear that the assembly might instead harm you. You may come back another day under a different guise, and I shall accept you.
Having received these instructions, Xingchang fled by night and entered the monastic order, receiving full ordination.
With great diligence, he recalled the Patriarch’s words one day and traveled a long distance to pay his respects. The Patriarch said, "I have long been mindful of you; why have you come so late?

He replied, "Yesterday, I was graced by the Master’s absolution of my transgressions. Although I have now left the household life and practice asceticism, it will be difficult to repay your profound kindness.

Is it not only through the transmission of the Dharma and the salvation of sentient beings that one may do so? Your disciple has often perused the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I have not yet understood the meaning of 'permanence' and 'impermanence.'"

[The monk] said, "I constantly seek the meaning [of permanence]. I beg the Venerable Master’s compassion to explain this briefly for me. The Patriarch said, "'Impermanence' is precisely the Buddha-nature.
'Permanence' is precisely the discriminating mind regarding all dharmas, both good and evil. [The monk] said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts.
The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how would I dare to contradict the Buddha's sutras? [The monk] said, "The sutras state that the Buddha..."

"Nature is permanent, yet you, Preceptor, say it is impermanent. All dharmas, whether good or evil, up to and including the bodhicitta, are all impermanent, yet you, Preceptor, say they are permanent.
This is contradictory and causes the student to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch said:
"In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, I once heard the nun Wu-jin-tsang recite it once through; I then gave an exposition upon it."
"There is not a single word or a single meaning that does not accord with the scriptural texts; even for you, I have never given two different teachings.

[The student] said, "My understanding and capacity are shallow and dull; I pray that the Master will explain this to me in detail. The Patriarch said, "Do you know? If buddha-nature were permanent..."
What need is there to speak further of various dharmas of good and evil? Even until the exhaustion of kalpas, not a single person would have given rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, what I call impermanence is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the Way of True Permanence.
Furthermore, if all dharmas were merely impermanent, then every object would possess its own self-nature that accommodates birth and death; yet, the nature of True Permanence exists.
Because it is not present in all places, what I describe as "permanent" is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.

The Buddha [taught this] because ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles who cling to false permanence, or who conceive of the permanent as impermanent, together constitute the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on *nirvāṇa*, he refutes those biased views and explicitly proclaims true permanence and true...
Bliss, true self, and true purity—now you rely on the words while turning your back on their meaning.

By taking the impermanence of cessation and the permanence of death as definitive, you have misinterpreted the Buddha’s final, subtle, and perfect words. Even if you were to read them a thousand times, what benefit would there be?
Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor. He then spoke this verse: "Because one guards the mind of impermanence, the Buddha expounds the nature of permanence.
Those who do not know the skillful means are like those picking pebbles from a spring pond. Now, without exerting effort, the Buddha-nature appears before me."
"It was not transmitted by a teacher, nor did I have anything to obtain. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhiche (Voluntarily Penetrating).
The Master bowed in thanks and departed.
Chan Master Zhichang of Xinzhou was originally from Guixi in that province. Having entered the monastic life at the age of seven, he was determined to realize the nature of his own being.
One day, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? What do you seek?

The Master replied, "I recently paid my respects to Chan Master Datong, who instructed me on the principle of attaining Buddhahood by seeing one's own nature. However, I have not yet resolved my doubts. Upon arriving in Ji...

On the way, he encountered a man who pointed out his confusion and directed him to seek out the Abbot. He prostrated himself with the wish: "I pray that you will bestow your compassion and take me under your care.

The Patriarch asked, "What did he say? Try reciting it for me; I shall provide you with verification. The Master replied, "When I first arrived there, three months had passed without receiving any instruction.

Because my desire for the Dharma was so urgent, I entered the Abbot’s quarters alone during the middle of the night, prostrating and entreating him with grief. At that time, he said, 'Great Penetration (Dàtōng)..."* *Note: The text ends abruptly here.*
He then said, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. The Master asked, "Do you see any form or characteristics in empty space?
He replied, "Empty space has no shape; what form or characteristic could it have? The Master said, "Your own fundamental nature is just like empty space."
Turning back to contemplate one's own nature, one realizes that not a single thing can be seen; this is called right view. Not a single thing can be known; this is called true knowledge.
There is no blue, yellow, long, or short—only the original source, pure and pristine, the essence of awakening, perfect and luminous.
This is what is called seeing one’s nature and attaining Buddhahood; it is also called the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and it is also called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Although the student...
Having heard these words, he was still not fully resolved and requested the Master’s further instruction so that he might no longer be hindered by lingering doubts.
The Patriarch said, "The teacher you followed still maintained views and intellectual knowledge; this is why you have not yet attained understanding. I shall now show you a verse, which says:

'Not seeing a single dharma, yet maintaining the view of non-existence— This is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun. Not knowing a single dharma, yet clinging to the knowledge of emptiness—'"
Like a flash of lightning arising in the vast void, this cognition and view arise in an instant. How could such a mistaken recognition ever understand the skillful means?
You should, in a single thought, recognize it as wrong yourself; then your own spiritual radiance will be constantly manifest.

Upon hearing this verse, the Master’s mind was suddenly enlightened. He then composed a verse of his own, saying: "Groundlessly giving rise to conceptual understanding, One clings to appearances while seeking Bodhi. If one harbors even a single..."

Reflecting on this awakening, how could I have remained deluded as in the past? The self-nature is the source and essence of enlightenment; yet by following appearances, I have wandered through the flux of samsara.
Failing to enter the chamber of the Patriarchs, I was lost in confusion, pursuing the two extremes.

Zen Master Zhidao of Guangzhou was a native of Nanhai. Initially, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch and asked, "I, a student, have been a monk for over ten years and have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I have not yet clarified its great meaning. I pray that the Honored Monk will grant me instruction.
The Patriarch said, "What is it that you do not understand? He replied, "'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased...'"
"Quiescent extinction is bliss. Regarding this, he harbored doubts. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it?
He replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the physical body and the dharma-body. The physical body is impermanent; it has birth and death. The dharma-body is permanent;
it is without cognition or awareness. As the sutra says, 'When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. I do not yet understand this."
By what body is there quiescence? By what body is there the experience of bliss? If it is the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its extinction, the four great elements disperse;
this is entirely suffering. What is suffering cannot be called bliss. If it is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that is quiescent, then it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones.

Who, then, would experience pleasure? Furthermore, the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is the substance of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing.

With one substance and five functions, arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the substance; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the substance.
If further rebirth were permitted, the class of sentient beings would neither be interrupted nor extinguished; if further rebirth were not permitted, they would forever return [to extinction].
"Quiescent extinction is identical to insentient things. If this were so, then all dharmas would be suppressed and constrained by nirvana;
they would not even be able to arise—what joy could there be in that? The Patriarch said, "You are a son of the Śākyas.
Why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism, and discuss the Supreme Vehicle? According to your understanding, apart from the physical body, there exists..."

The Dharma-body is free from arising and ceasing; one seeks quiescence therein. Furthermore, when one infers the permanence and bliss of Nirvana and yet claims there is a body that experiences it, this is merely clinging to birth and death and being addicted to worldly pleasures. You should now know that the Buddha [speaks thus] for the sake of all who are deluded.
They recognize the aggregation of the five aggregates as their own self-nature and discriminate all phenomena as external objects.
They take birth as good and death as evil; they flow and shift from moment to moment, unaware that all is like a dream or an illusion and devoid of reality, thus needlessly undergoing saṃsāra.
They perceive the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as a state of suffering and spend their days in frantic pursuit. Out of compassion for them, the Buddha reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa. Kṣetra.
That which has no characteristic of arising does not have the characteristic of ceasing in each moment; there is nothing further to be extinguished through arising and ceasing.
This is quiescent extinction manifest before one. At the time it is manifest before one, there is also no measure of its being manifest before one;

this is called "eternal bliss. This bliss has no experiencer, nor is there anyone who does not experience it. How could there be such designations as "one substance" or "five functions," let alone anything more?
To say that *nirvāṇa* restrains and subdues all phenomena so that they never arise again is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
The unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa* is perfectly luminous, eternally quiescent, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation.
Those who seek the two vehicles regard it as non-action (*akṛtaka*). All these belong to the conceptualizations of the mind—the sixty-two views.

Fundamentally, one falsely establishes empty and provisional names; what, then, could be their true meaning? Only those of transcendent capacity thoroughly penetrate this state of neither grasping nor rejecting.

By knowing that the phenomena of the five aggregates, as well as the "self" within the aggregates, and all external manifestations of forms and individual sounds and appearances, are equal to dreams and illusions, they do not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages, nor do they form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. [They transcend] the two extremes and the three temporal limits.
Severance. Constantly employing the functions of the sense faculties, yet not giving rise to the thought of such employment; discerning all dharmas, yet not giving rise to the thought of discernment.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds strike mountains together, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—such is the mark of Nirvana.
I now speak these words by force, so that you may abandon false views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you only a slight understanding.
Upon hearing the verse, the Master was filled with joy; he prostrated himself and withdrew.

The Chan Master Zhenjue of Yongjia, whose name was Xuánjué, was the son of the Dài family from his native commandery. He entered the monastic order at the age of eight and extensively investigated the Tripiṭaka.

He mastered the perfect and subtle dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and constantly practiced meditative contemplation in accordance with the four postures of daily life.
Later, inspired by the Zen Master Zuo Xi Lang, he traveled together with the Zen Master Dong Yang Ce to Caoxi.

Upon first arriving, he shook his staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood there upright. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa should possess the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From what region have you come, Great Virtue, that you display such great arrogance? The Master replied, "I was born [in this way]."
"The matter of death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising and understand that there is no swiftness?
The Master said, "Realizing is itself non-arising; understanding is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is. So it is.

At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment. The Master then assumed his full dignified demeanor and paid his respects. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Your return is very swift, is it not?"

The Master said, "Fundamentally, there is no movement; how then could there be swiftness? The Patriarch asked, "Who knows that there is no movement? The Master said, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising. The Master said, "In non-arising, how could there be any meaning?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? The Master said, "Discrimination itself is not a matter of meaning. The Patriarch sighed in admiration and said, "Excellent!"

"Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night. Thus he was called "The One-Night Awakened One" (*Ekāṃśa-buddha*). The Master descended the mountain the following day and returned to Wenzhou, where students gathered like spokes converging at the hub.

He composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) in one chapter, as well as the *Essential Meaning of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School* (*Chanzong wuxiu yuanzhi*), which proceeds from the shallow to the profound.
Wei Jing, the Prefect of Qingzhou, compiled these works and wrote a preface, forming ten chapters, which were titled the *Yongjia*.

Collected and circulated in the world. Part One: The Aspiration for the Way and the Rituals for Attending a Teacher. Now, one who wishes to cultivate the Way must first establish their resolve and observe the ritual protocols for serving a teacher;

these are clearly manifested in the rules of training. Therefore, this is designated as the first part, clarifying the rituals for aspiring to the Way. Part Two: Guarding Against Arrogance and Indulgence.

Although one has initially established the resolve to cultivate the Way and correctly understands the rules and rituals, if the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] are characterized by arrogance and indulgence, [the practice will fail].

When the mind is agitated, how can one attain meditative concentration? Therefore, secondly, the pride and indulgence regarding the precepts are clarified. Thirdly, the three modes of action (*trikarma*) are purified through cultivation.
While the previous section on the precepts briefly indicated the essential framework, this section involves a detailed examination and reproof so that coarse transgressions do not arise;
thus, thirdly, the purification of the three modes of action is clarified. The precepts pertain to body, speech, and mind. *Śamatha-gāthā*.
Fourth: Having already examined and restrained body and speech so that coarse transgressions do not arise, one must next enter the gate of the path of cultivation through its gradual stages.
This does not go beyond the five ways of giving rise to the mind and the six kinds of discernment within *samādhi* and *prajñā*.
