When the Great Being had finished preaching the sutra, on another day during his lecture, the Emperor arrived. The entire assembly rose, yet the Master alone remained seated upright without moving.
An attendant reported, "The Imperial carriage is here; why do you not rise? The Master replied, "If the ground of the Dharma were to move, [then I would move]."
All were uneasy. One day, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) appeared for an audience wearing a patched robe (*kaṣāya*), a crown upon his head, and sandals on his feet.
The Emperor asked, "Is this a monk? The Great Being pointed to his crown. The Emperor said, "Is this the Way (*mārga*)? The Great Being pointed to his sandals. The Emperor said, "Is this a layman?
The Great Being pointed to his patched robe. The Great Being’s *Mind-King Inscription* (*Cittarāja-mudrā*) says: "Contemplate the Mind, the Sovereign of Emptiness; it is profound and wondrous."
It is unfathomable. Formless and signless, it possesses great spiritual power capable of extinguishing a thousand calamities and accomplishing ten thousand virtues.

Although its essential nature is empty, it can bestow the Dharma rules. When observed, it has no form; when called upon, it has a voice. It serves as the Great General of the Dharma, transmitting the scriptures through the mind-precepts.
Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of lacquer-blue within color, it certainly exists, yet its form is not seen. This is the Mind-King.
It is likewise so. Dwelling within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face, it responds to objects and follows conditions with sovereign freedom and without obstruction;
all that it does is accomplished. One realizes the fundamental consciousness-mind (*ālayavijñāna-citta*); the consciousness-mind sees the Buddha. This mind is the Buddha, and this Buddha is the mind.

In every thought-moment, there is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha. If you wish to achieve realization early, let the mind of precepts govern yourself; purify the precepts and purify the mind. The mind is...
This is the Buddha. Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Upon entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way observes their own mind; knowing that the Buddha is within, they do not seek him outwardly. This very mind...

This is precisely the Buddha; this is precisely the Buddha, which is the mind. When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, it thoroughly understands the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind.
That which is not the Buddha cannot be fathomed; it is incapable of being grasped. Clinging to emptiness and lingering in stillness, one drifts and sinks within this state.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind in this. The Great Being who clarifies the mind awakens to this profound resonance. The nature of body and mind is wondrous; its functioning is without limit.
It undergoes change. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in its natural freedom. Do not say that the "King of the Mind" is empty and devoid of essence;
it is that which enables the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly. It is neither existent nor non-existent, appearing and disappearing without fixed certainty.

The nature of the mind transcends emptiness; it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely. For this reason, I urge you: guard yourself well. Every momentary action leads once again to drifting and sinking. [Only through] purity...

The mind and intellect are like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind. This treasure of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is neither shallow nor deep.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this original mind; those who encounter it through the proper conditions do so beyond past, future, or present.

As a verse says: "Night after night, one sleeps embracing the Buddha; Morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, they are always in each other's company; In speech or silence, they dwell together."
"Cease! Not even a hair's breadth apart; they are like a shadow and its form. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech.
He also said: "Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; walking, one rides a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge;

the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. And he also said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally still and vast. It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena."
It does not wither along with the four seasons. The Verse on the Four Marks says: Birth, aging, illness, and death.
Consciousness rests upon the rising of floating bubbles; birth comes from craving and desire. In former times one was once grown, yet today one is again an infant.

Star-like eyes follow others as they turn; red lips open toward the breast. Out of pity for those who delude their enlightened nature, one returns once more to undergo saṃsāra. Beholding one’s own countenance in a mirror...
Alas! My strength for ascending the steps has declined. How lamentable that I am now old; my bowing and prostrations have grown deficient.
My body is like a tree on a precipice; my mind is like a tortoise brooding over water. Yet I still indulge in outflows (*sāsrava*), refusing to study the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Suddenly afflicted by a deep-seated illness, I have thus become one who lies bedridden. My wife and children grieve in silence; friends weary of my presence. A thousand piercing pains tear at me.
The pulse falters; moans resound through the four neighboring houses. Unaware of the perils ahead, one still indulges in greed and anger.
The vital spirit follows the path of birth, while the wandering soul enters the barrier of death. One hears only of millions departing, yet sees not a single person returning.
The fine steed stands neighing in vain; the courtyard flowers can never again be plucked. Seek the Unsurpassed Way early, and you shall surely escape the mountains of the four quarters.

Sitting always in majestic stillness, his billions of transformation bodies are beyond measure. Even if they were to fill the entirety of empty space, when one looks, not even a particle of form can be seen.
How laughable this thing is—beyond all comparison! From his mouth he spits forth bright pearls, their light shimmering and dazzling.
What is commonly seen and spoken of as inconceivable, with a single word he marks and names it as it truly is. It is further said: "Heaven cannot cover it; Earth cannot contain it."
It is not recorded; there is no going and no coming, no obstruction. It is neither long nor short, neither blue nor yellow. It is not in the middle, nor within, nor without.
Transcending all and surpassing the multitude, it is the great void and mystery. Pointing to things to transmit the mind, people do not understand.

Mount [Zhao] asked, "What are you doing, going to travel to Mount Wutai? The Master replied, "To pay homage to Mañjuśrī. Mount Zhao said, "You are not of my kind.
The Master then entered Mount Wutai alone. There he encountered an old man and asked, "Are you Mañjuśrī?"

[The Master] said, "How could there be two Mañjuśrīs? Before the teacher had finished his prostration and risen, [Mañjuśrī] suddenly vanished. Zhaozhou spoke on his behalf, saying, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī."
While the monks at Mount Tiantai were roasting eggplants, Hanshanzi took an eggplant skewer and struck one monk on the back.
When the monk turned his head, Hanshan held up the skewer and asked, "What is this? The monk replied, "This madman.
Hanshan then said to a nearby monk, "Tell me, how much salt and vinegar did this monk cost me? This was because of Zhaozhou.
While traveling to Mount Tiantai, they met along the way. On the mountain, Xuefeng saw the tracks of an ox and asked Baizhang Zongzhi, "Upādhyāya, do you recognize this ox?
Zongzhi replied, "I do not. Xuefeng pointed to the ox tracks and said, "These are the tracks of five hundred arhats wandering the mountain.
Zongzhi asked, "If they are arhats, why did they turn into oxen? Xuefeng cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! Zongzhi then laughed heartily.
Xiao laughed. Shanshan asked, "What are you doing? Zhou said, "Heaven! Heaven! Shanshan remarked, "This fellow truly possesses the bearing of a great man."
One day, Shide was sweeping the ground at Mount Tiantai. The Abbot asked him, "Your name is Shide;
it was Fenggan who picked you up and brought you here. Ultimately, what is your surname? Shide set down his broom and stood with his hands folded.
The Abbot asked again, and Shide picked up his broom, swept the ground, and departed. Hanshan beat his breast and cried out, "Heaven!"
"O Blue Heaven! Shide said, "What are you doing? The Mountain Master replied, "Have you not heard it said that when a member of one family dies, the members of another family offer their condolences?
The two men performed a dance, laughing and weeping as they departed from Guoqing Temple. Half a month later, the assembly gathered for the recitation of the precepts.
Shide clapped his hands and said, "Gathering your heads together to dwell on thoughts—what of that matter? The *vina* (chant leader) rebuked him, to which Shide replied, "Great Virtue!"
Stop for a moment. Absence of anger is itself the precepts; a pure mind is itself the renunciation of home. My nature is in harmony with yours; all dharmas are without distinction.
The monk Pùdàng of Fènghuà County in Míngzhōu called himself Qìchǐ. His physical form was stout and fleshy... (wēi-nèi).
With a furrowed brow and a protruding belly, his speech was inconsistent and he slept wherever he happened to be. He constantly carried a cloth bag and a tattered mat upon a staff.
All his personal belongings were stored within that bag. When he entered markets or villages, he would beg for whatever he saw;
even when he received pickles, sauces, fish, or pickled vegetables, he would take only a small portion to eat and cast the rest into his bag. At that time, he was known as Changting.
One day, as a monk was walking ahead of the Master, the Master patted him on the back. The monk turned his head, and the Master said, "I beg of you one *wen* of copper.
The monk replied, "If you can speak, I will give you one *wen. The Master dropped his cloth bag and stood with his hands folded.
When Monk Bailu asked, "What is this cloth bag? the Master immediately dropped his cloth bag and asked, "What is it?"
This was a matter of the "cloth bag. The Master took it upon his back and departed. Previously, when Master Baofu asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
the Master dropped the cloth bag, stood with his hands clasped, and remained silent. Baofu said, "Is it only this, or is there something further beyond this?
The Master took the bag upon his back and departed. While the Master was standing on the street, a monk asked, "Master, why are you here?"
"What are you doing? The Master said, "I am waiting for someone. [The monk] said, "He has come! He has come! (Master Niu-tou Huo-er added: "Go back! Go back! The Master said:
"You are not this person. [The monk] asked, "What is this person? The Master said, "Beg me for one coin.
The Master had a song which said: "This very mind—mind is Buddha. It is the most wondrous thing in the ten directions. Its transverse and vertical wondrous functions are truly pitiable;
nothing compares to the reality of this mind. It is carefree and self-sovereign, with nothing to do. At ease.
Tranquil is the ultimate state of one who has left the household life. If you behold the true Great Way before you, not seeing even a hair’s breadth of it is truly marvelous.
How can the myriad dharmas differ from the mind? How could they be different? Why labor further to seek the meaning of the scriptures? The Mind-King is fundamentally beyond manifold knowledge;
the wise simply clarify the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Being neither sage nor ordinary person—how could it be otherwise? Do not forcibly discriminate between sages.

Lonely in spirit. The priceless jewel of the mind is fundamentally perfect and pure; all else is but the deluded emptiness of divergent forms. If a person can propagate the Way, the Way becomes manifest;

its immeasurable purity and loftiness accord with the nature of the Way. Should you carry your staff and ascend the roads of your former kingdom, do not lament that the sound will not be heard in every place.
Furthermore, there is a verse which says: "In this world, likes and dislikes, right and wrong, are exceedingly prevalent. Reflect upon them carefully, for what can be done?"
What can I do? I shall broaden my belly and practice patience; I shall open my mind and let things take their course.
When meeting those who understand me, I shall act according to the occasion; even when encountering enemies, I shall remain in harmony.

If one can resolve these matters of the heart, one will naturally realize the six *pāramitās*. I have a cloth bag, empty and unobstructed like space; when spread out, it pervades the ten directions. Enter!
At that time, Avalokiteśvara, I have a Hall of the Three Jewels. Within it is empty and devoid of form or appearance; it is neither high nor low, neither obstructed nor hindered.
Those who study it find no likeness within themselves; those who come find it difficult to grasp its model. Only one in a thousand craftsmen possesses the wisdom to arrange it.
From its four gates arise the four fruits [of the path], and all throughout the ten directions offer worship. I have a single image of the Buddha... the world...
No one recognizes it. It is neither molded nor adorned; neither carved nor engraved. There is not a single drop of plaster, nor a speck of color.
No man can paint it, and no thief can steal it. Its form and characteristics are naturally so; its purity requires no wiping away.
Though it is but a single body, it manifests in hundreds of thousands of millions of forms. Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "A single bowl..."
"Meals from a thousand households; a solitary body wandering ten thousand *li*. With azure eyes, I see few people; I ask for the way at the head of white clouds.
In the third month of the year Bingzi, the third year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty (916 CE), the Master was about to manifest his passing.

At the eastern corridor of Yue-lin Temple, he sat upright upon a flat rock and spoke this verse: "Maitreya, the true Maitreya, Manifests a thousand, ten thousand, and ten million bodies. From time to time, he reveals himself."

People of the time did not recognize him. When the verses were finished, he passed away peacefully through transformation. Thereafter, he reappeared in another province, likewise walking while carrying a cloth bag on his back.
The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his likeness.
Fahua Zhi was the son of Xu of Shouchun. In his early twenties, he traveled to the Eastern Capital, where he subsequently received full ordination at Qijuzhi Monastery.
He remained in the lecture halls for a long time. One day, while reading the *Record of Yunmen*, he suddenly attained awakening. Not long after, he...
His knowledge of past lives was subsequently realized; he would speak and laugh to himself alone, his lips murmuring incessantly throughout the day.

It was said that he had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in his previous life, and thus he was named accordingly. When Minister Lü Xǔgōng asked about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma, the Master replied:
"Originally there is not a single thing; a single flavor, however, becomes the truth. When Jíxiān Wángzhèn questioned him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? the Master—
He said: "Within the shadows of the green mountains, the azure sky surges forth; from the lofty pagoda, a chant shakes the morning breeze. He also said: "Please invite Fahu to burn incense.

The Master replied: "Do not seek it through fasting and precepts; do not seek it from the Buddha. Xu Yue, Assistant Instructor at the National Academy, asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.

The Master replied: "At the bottom of the eastern side of the street. Xu said: "I do not yet understand. The Master [replied]: "... (The text here implies the Master's response was unyielding or direct).
He said, "Three types of people cannot understand this. A monk asked, "Does the Buddha exist in the world? The Master replied, "Mañjuśrī in the temple.
Someone asked the Master, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? He then raised his hand and said, "I do not dwell here.

On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the Wuzi year of the Qingli era (1048), as he was about to pass away, he said to those around him, "Since immeasurable kalpas ago, I have accomplished the passing away [of birth and death]."
He has manifested his body to propagate the teaching across many lands; now he returns to the South. Having finished speaking, he passed away lying on his right side.
Kōu-ŭng, who washed [the Buddha’s] feet at the ice [of the *Kauṣṭhila* story], was the son of the Weng family of Jianxing and Xinfeng.

His mother dreamed of a bhikṣu with a radiant and majestic spirit, carrying a mendicant’s staff and seeking lodging. People pointed to him and said, "This is a Pratyekabuddha. Subsequently, she became pregnant and gave birth during the Wuzong era.
In the fourth year of the Huichang era, fragrant mists filled the room and did not disperse for days on end. At the age of thirteen, he sought to leave the household life;
his parents granted him permission. He took Xingquan of Usan Xingfu Temple as his preceptor. In the year of Yiyou during the Xiantong era, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
Initially, he was sought after by the assembly for his lectures. He then went to visit Xuefeng, carrying a bundle of *fu-ci* (water chestnuts) and a jar of sauce in his hands to present to him.
Xuefeng asked, "What is in that bundle? The Master replied, "Water chestnuts. Xuefeng asked, "Where did you get these?"
The Master said, "Found in the mud. Feng asked, "How deep is the mud? The Master said, "It is several zhang deep. Feng asked, "Is there anything else besides this?
He replied, "The more one goes, the deeper it becomes. Feng then asked, "What is in the vessel? He replied, "Soy sauce. Feng asked, "Where did you get it from?
He replied, "I made it myself. Feng asked, "Is it cooked yet? He replied, "It is not far from being done. Feng marveled at him and said, "You—"

"In the future, he will surely become a teacher to a king. Later, returning from Ehu, he established a hermitage at Wenling (which is now Yongfeng Temple) and subsequently resided at General’s Rock (*Jiangjunyan*).
Two tigers attended him by his side, and a divine being offered the land for Ruiyan Monastery. Students flocked there in great numbers.

He once said to the assembly, "The ancient sages practiced their cultivation by relying on rigorous austerity. In summer I now wear paper clothing, and in winter I bathe by striking the ice with my fists.
For this reason, people of the world called him the "Ancient Buddha Who Strikes the Ice. Later, while residing at Lingyao, he ascended the hall; the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds.
He asked, "What can this old monk say? and immediately descended from his seat. There was a monk who was burning charcoal, piling it up into a fire.
Kān said, "I invite the Master to enter here to practice. [The Master] said, "True jade does not change by following flowing water;

lapis lazuli vies with the multitude of stars for its brilliance. [Kān] said, "Is it not simply this very thing? [The Master] said, "Do not mistake the servant for the lord. [Kān] asked, "Ultimately, how is it?
[The Master] said, "The plum blossoms bloom in the twelfth month, formed by Heaven. In the year Wuzi, he responded to the summons of the ruler of Min and was invited to reside within the palace.
In the hall, he paid his respects, saying, "Thank you for descending from afar. During the serving of tea, the Master lifted up his bag and asked, "Does the Great King understand?
The King replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The King of Men and the King of Dharma each illuminate one another. He remained for ten days, after which he declined on account of illness.

On the second day of the twelfth month, he bathed, ascended the hall, and passed away while addressing the assembly. The King, along with the clergy and laity, prepared the fragrant wood for the cremation.
He was cremated using *sūtra* oil, and an auspicious radiance filled the mountains. Five-colored śarīra were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at Ruiyan Zhengqin.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Miaoying Fawei Ciji.

The Venerable Master Baoguang, who lived for a thousand years, was a native of Central India. In the twelfth year of the reign of Emperor Weile of the Zhou dynasty, the year Dingmao, he descended as an incarnation and received his physical form.

He held his left hand in a fist at birth, which only opened when he was seven years old; consequently, he was named Baoguang (Precious Hand). During the Wei and Jin periods, he traveled east to this land.
He entered Shu to pay homage to Samantabhadra and remained at Daci Monastery. He never ate food, reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras daily.
His collected works comprise over one thousand scrolls. One who praised him said: "The weary jade teeth are cold; they seem like rushing rock springs.
Sometimes sitting at midnight, the gods and ghosts weep before his steps. One day, he said to the assembly: "I have a vow to remain in this world for a thousand years.
This year marks six hundred and twenty-six; therefore, I am called 'the Thousand-Year One'. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Wutai and moved [to another location].
He resided at Huayan on Mount Zhurong, at Shuangfeng in Huangmei, and at Donglin on Mount Lu. Eventually, he traveled to Jianye, where he encountered Bodhidharma’s arrival in the Liang dynasty.

The Master approached him to inquire about the essential meaning of the Dharma and attained awakening. Emperor Wu, highly regarding his years of practice and realization, invited him into the inner court.
Not long after, he went to Wu, where he composed a verse: "In the city of Liang I met the Teacher; through Zen meditation, I realized the ground of the mind."
Wandering through the two provinces of Zhejiang, I have fully exhausted their finest mountains and waters. Following the current downstream, I traveled from Qianqing to Tiantong and Tianzhu;
I went to Maofeng, ascended Taibai, and passed through Yanfang. I stayed at leisure among the seventy-two hermitages of Cuifeng.
Returning to Chicheng, I rested at Yunmen, Fahua, Zhujia, Yupu, Chifu, Dayan, and other locations. Finally, I returned to Feilai and took up residence there.
He stayed at Shiqudou. There was a verse circulating throughout the four hundred prefectures of China that praised him as a wandering man of the Way.
This was during the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Later, he resided at Baoyan Monastery in Pujiang, where he formed a close friendship with Chan Master Lang.
Whenever he sent a message, he would dispatch a white dog to gallop there; Hui-lang likewise employed a green monkey as his messenger.

Thus, he inscribed upon Lang’s wall: "The white dog arrives with a letter; the green monkey returns with the bowl washed. All the places where the Master passed became monasteries (bǎofāng) in later times.

On the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Xianqing era, he fashioned a statue with his own hands. By the ninth day, the statue was completed. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble?
Yun replied, "It is no different from the Master himself. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus posture.
Addressing Yun, he said, "I have remained in this world for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years; now I am about to pass away. Listen to my verse: The Essence..."
"In coming, there is no birth-and-death; now I likewise manifest birth-and-death. I have attained the mind that comes and goes; having been born elsewhere, I shall return here again.
After a short while, he gave this instruction: "Sixty years after my passing, there will be a monk who comes to take my bones; do not refuse him. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Fifty-four years after his entry into *parinirvāṇa*, the Elder Dafu came from Yunmen to the site of the stupa and paid his respects, saying:
He hoped that the stupa would open of its own accord. After a short while, the door of the stupa indeed opened; his bones were linked together like golden rings.
He immediately took them to Mount Qinwang and erected a *stūpa* to enshrine them.

Calculating from the *dingmao* year of the reign of King Weile of the Zhou dynasty to the *dingyi* year of the Xianqing era of the Tang Emperor Gaozong, it was exactly one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years. Since arriving in this land, four hundred years have passed.
The rest have been lost from the monastic histories. During the Kaiyuan era, Zongyi, a disciple of Huiyun, once had this recorded by carving it into stone.
*Wudeng huiyuan*, fascicle 2.
*The Five Lamps Meeting Their Source*, Scroll Three:
Zen Master Nanyue Huairang, Dharma Heir of the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Mirror Zen Master, was surnamed Du and was a native of Jinzhou. In the second year of the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty...
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he was born. A white vapor appeared as an auspicious sign in the celestial phenomena over the region of Anqiang.

The Grand Astrologer observed this and reported it to Emperor Gaozong. The Emperor then asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "A Dharma-vessel of the state who shall remain unstained by worldly glory.
The Emperor then issued an imperial decree for Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, to go in person to offer his condolences and comfort.
In his family, there were three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest. He was radiant and exceptionally extraordinary; by nature, he was solely devoted to kindness and yielding.
His father therefore gave him the name Huairang. When he was ten years old, he took pleasure only in Buddhist scriptures. At that time, the Tripiṭaka master Xuanjing passed by their house.
He said to his parents, "If this son leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings.

In the third year of the Chuigong era, when he was fifteen years old, he took leave of his kin and went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu, where he followed the Vinaya Master Hóngjǐng to receive the tonsure.
In the second year of the Tōngtiān era, after receiving full ordination, he studied the Piṇī-piṭaka. One day, he sighed to himself, saying, "Now, as for leaving..."
"The 'House' (Jia) is the unconditioned dharma; among gods and humans, there is none superior to it.
At that time, his fellow student Tanran, knowing that his teacher’s resolve was lofty and transcendent, urged him to visit Master An of Mount Song.
An enlightened him, whereupon he went directly to Caoxi to study with the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What..."
When the matter was presented in this way, the Master remained silent. Thus eight years passed until he suddenly attained realization.
He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so? The Master replied, "To describe it as a thing is not to hit the mark.
The Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization? The Master replied, "There is no lack of cultivation and realization, yet it cannot be defiled. The Patriarch said:
"Simply this is non-defilement; it is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus.
The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied that from beneath your feet would emerge a colt that would trample the people of the world to death.
The illness lies within your own mind; there is no need to speak of it hastily. The Master attended him at his side for fifteen years. In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he departed.
Mount Heng was home to the Prajñā Monastery. During the Kaiyuan era, there was a śramaṇa named Daoyi (who was Mazu) who resided at Mount Heng constantly practicing seated meditation.
The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation?
Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Master then took a brick and began polishing it on a stone slab in front of the hermitage. Daoyi said, "What are you polishing this for?"
"What? the Master asked. He replied, "Grind it into a mirror. The monk said, "How can grinding a brick produce a mirror?

The Master said, "If grinding a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha? The monk asked, "What then is the way? The Master said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart.
If the cart does not move, do you strike the cart or do you strike the ox? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again:
"You practice seated meditation; are you practicing by sitting as a Buddha? If you practice seated meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down.

If you practice sitting as a Buddha, the Buddha is not a fixed form. Within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is precisely killing the Buddha."
If you cling to the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle. Upon hearing my instruction but once, it will be like drinking *amṛta* (clarified butter).

He asked while prostrating, "How should I apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi? The Master said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is like sowing seeds in the earth;
my teaching of the essential Dharma is like the rain from heaven. Because the conditions meet, you shall see the Way. He asked again:
"The Way is not a form or appearance; how can it be seen? The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way;

the same is true for the signless samādhi. The student asked, "Is there arising and ceasing? The Master said, "If one sees the Way through arising and ceasing, gathering and dispersing, that is not seeing the Way.
Listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground contains all seeds; when meeting with moisture, they all..."* *(Note: The source text ends abruptly here.)*
All things sprout forth; the flower of samādhi is signless—what is there to destroy, and what is there to establish? Once he was graced with awakening, his mind became transcendent.

He attended [the Master] for ten years, and day by day the teachings grew more profound and mysterious. There were six disciples in total who entered the inner chamber, each of whom the Master certified through the seal of approval.
He said, "You six have together realized my person; each has accorded with one aspect of it. One has attained my eyebrows and excels in dignified demeanor (Chang Hao);
one has attained my eyes and excels in looking about (Zhida); one has attained my ears and excels in listening to principles (Tantan);
one has attained my nose and excels in perceiving the vital breath (Shenzhao); one has attained my tongue and excels in discourse (Yanjun); and one..."

He has grasped my mind. Dao-yi, who was skilled in both ancient and modern [learning], further said: "All dharmas arise from the mind; the mind has no place of arising, and dharmas have no place of abiding.
If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be unimpeded. Unless one meets a person of superior capacity, one should be cautious with words."
A certain great virtuous one asked, "When a mirror casts an image, once the image has been formed, I do not know where the light has gone.
The Master said, "When you were a young child, where was your appearance? (Fayan remarked alternatively: "Which one is the image that you, Great Virtue, have cast?")
[The monk] asked, "Once the image has been completed, why does it not reflect? The Master said, "Although it does not reflect, it cannot deceive him by even a single point.
Later, when Mazu was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi, the Master asked the assembly, "Does Daoyi preach the Dharma for the assembly?
The assembly replied, "He has already preached the Dharma for the assembly. The Master said, "No one has yet brought me a single [verse]."
News arrived, but the assembly had no reply. Thereupon, he sent a monk away, instructing him:
"When he ascends the hall, simply ask him, 'What is it? and remember the words he speaks. The monk went and acted exactly according to the Master's instructions.
Upon his return, he said to the Master, "Master Ma said, 'Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. The Master approved of this.

On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tiānbǎo era, he entered parinirvāṇa at Mount Héng. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dàhuì, and his stupa was named Zuìshènglún (Wheel of Supreme Victory).
He was the dharma successor of Chan Master Nányuè Ràng (the first generation).
Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi was a native of Shifang County in Hanzhou. His surname was Ma. He left the household life at Luohan Temple in his home district.
His appearance was extraordinary: he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger; his tongue could extend past his nose, and the soles of his feet were marked with two wheels.
In his youth, he received the tonsure under Venerable Tang of Zizhou and received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou. Tang...

During the Kaiyuan era, he practiced *dhyāna* concentration on Mount Heng. There he met Master Rang, with whom six others studied together; however, the Master alone received the seal of the mind (*citta-mudrā*).

(Rang was one of Huineng’s disciples, just as Si was a disciple of Shenhui; though they shared the same source, they formed different lineages. Thus, the flourishing of the Chan method began with these two masters. Liu Ke said: "In Jiangxi, Mazu Daichi is the master.")

In Hunan, the Master presided over Shitou. People came and went in great numbers, yet they did not see the two Great Beings; this was because they lacked true understanding. As Prajñātāra of the Western Heaven had prophesied of Bodhidharma: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; one must rely on the feet of the descendants to travel."

The golden rooster unclenched a single grain of millet to offer as sustenance to the arhat-monks of the ten directions. Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch said to Master Rang, "In the future, the Buddha-dharma shall proceed from you; a horse colt will trample the people of the world.

Subsequently, his lineage flourished in Jiangxi and spread throughout the land (he was then known as Mazu). He first moved from Mount Foji in Jianyang to Linchuan, and later to Gonggong Mountain in Nankang.
During the Dali era, he registered his name at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling, where the regional commander Lu Sigong [served as patron].
Having heard of his reputation and admired him, they personally received his fundamental teachings. Consequently, scholars from the four quarters gathered at his seat like clouds.
One day he said to the assembly, "All of you, each believe that your own mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha-mind.
Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, the single mind."
You have attained awakening. Furthermore, I cite the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the minds of sentient beings.

Fearing that you might fall into delusion and lack self-confidence regarding this Dharma of the One Mind—which each and every one of you possesses—the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its essence and "no-gate" as its Dharma-gate.
Now, those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek; outside of the mind, there is no separate Buddha.

Outside the Buddha, there is no separate mind. It does not grasp at good, nor does it reject evil. Regarding both extremes of purity and defilement, it relies on neither. It realizes that the nature of offenses is empty;
in every thought-moment, they are ungraspable because they lack intrinsic nature. Therefore, the triple world is mind-only.

The myriad phenomena of the forest and the mountains are all sealed by this single Dharma. Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not a mind in itself; it exists in dependence upon form.
Therefore, it exists. You merely speak according to the occasion; whether in terms of phenomena or principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever. It is the same with the fruit of the path to Bodhi:
that which arises within the mind is called "form" (rūpa). Because one knows that form is empty, arising is itself non-arising.
If you understand this meaning, then you may, according to the occasion, put on your robes and eat your meals, nurturing the holy embryo and passing the time with effortless spontaneity.
What further matter could there be? You have received my instruction; listen to my verse: "The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion;
Awakening is likewise only thus. When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, That which arises is, in truth, non-arising. A monk asked: "Why did the Master speak thus?"
"This very mind is Buddha. The Master said, "This was to stop a small child from crying. [The monk] asked, "When the crying has stopped, what then? The Master said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
[The monk] asked, "Setting aside these two types of people, how would you instruct them? The Master said, "I would tell them, 'It is not a thing.
[The monk] asked, "If someone who has already realized this were to come, what then? The Master said, "For the time being, I would have him realize the Great [Function]."
The Master asked, "What is the meaning of [the Patriarch’s] coming from the West? The Master said, "What is the meaning right now?

The cook replied, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter such as this. He asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak.
The monk bowed, and the Master struck him. Ascending the hall, he said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending..."
The faculties and their objects reveal the true permanence of the essence; they are not bound by words and letters. The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally perfected from the beginning.
Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Who are you? He replied: "I am so-and-so."
The Master asked, "Do you recognize this person? He replied, "I see him clearly. The Master then raised his whisk and asked, "Do you see it?
He replied, "I see it. The Master remained silent. Later, while they were working together digging the earth, a monk suddenly heard the drum sounding.
Raising his hoe, he laughed loudly and returned. The Master said, "How brilliant! This is the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters the principle.
Upon returning to the monastery, the Master called the monk and asked, "What principle did you perceive just now that you acted in such a manner? The monk replied, "Just now I was hungry;
hearing the sound of the drum, I went back to eat my meal. The Master then smiled and asked, "To interpret the meaning according to the sutras, the Buddhas of the three periods..."
"A grievance! To depart from a single word of the Sūtra is like the teaching of a demon. When asked, "How is it at such a time?
the Master said, "To stubbornly cling to movement and stillness is a grievance against the Buddhas of the three periods. To seek anything else besides this is to speak like a demon.

Because a monk asked Xitang, "Setting aside for a moment the case where there is a question and an answer, how is it when there is neither question nor answer? Tang said, "I am afraid it will rot away! When the Master heard this being cited, he said:
"I have always suspected this old brother. [The monk] said, "Please, Master, speak. The Master said, "A unified totality (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended.
The Master said to the assembly, "There is one person who has never eaten a meal and yet does not say he is hungry; there is another person who eats all day long and yet does not say he is full.
The assembly was speechless. Yunyan asked, "For whom do you, Master, labor so diligently every day? The Master—
A man said, "I have a request. Yunyan said, "Why do you not let him act for himself? The Master said, "He has no livelihood.
A monk asked, "What is the essential teaching for sudden enlightenment in the Mahayana? The Master said, "First, you must bring all conditions to rest;
let all matters cease. Whether good or not good, mundane or supramundane—regard all dharmas as things not to be remembered and not to be conditioned by."
Contemplate: relinquish body and mind, allowing them to be free and at ease. Let the mind be like wood or stone, devoid of discrimination;
let the mind have no activity, and the ground of the mind will become like empty space. The sun of wisdom will manifest of itself, like the sun appearing when the clouds disperse.

Simply cease all攀缘 (pān-yuan, mental clinging/seeking), greed, anger, craving, and grasping. When the sentiments of defilement and purity are exhausted, one remains unmoved by the five desires and the eight winds, and is not caught by views.
Bound by hearing, sensation, and cognition, yet not deluded by external objects, one naturally possesses the wondrous functions of the supernormal powers;
such a person is liberated. Facing all sensory realms, the mind is neither still nor disturbed, neither concentrated nor scattered.
Transcending all sounds and forms without obstruction, they are called a "person of the Way. They do not employ good or evil, right or wrong, nor do they harbor attachment.
Not grasping at a single dharma and not abandoning a single dharma is called being a person of the Mahāyāna.
Being unrestrained by anything—good or evil, emptiness or existence, defilement or purity, conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, merit or wisdom—is called the Buddha-wisdom.

When all sentiments regarding right and wrong, beauty and ugliness, what is rational and what is irrational, and all such views and attachments are exhausted, one cannot be bound; thus one dwells [in liberation].
Mastery over the spheres of existence is called the Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment; he then ascends directly to the stage of Buddhahood. Question:

Facing all objects of perception, how can one cause the mind to become like wood or stone? Master: All dharmas fundamentally do not say of themselves that they are empty, nor do they say of themselves that they are form.
They do not speak of right or wrong, nor of defilement or purity. Furthermore, there is no mind that binds people; it is only that people themselves are deluded and false.
They become attached and form various interpretations, giving rise to various cognitions and views, and producing various forms of craving and fear.
They merely fail to realize that all phenomena do not arise of themselves, but exist only through one's own single thought of deluded, inverted grasping at signs.
Mind and objects fundamentally do not reach one another; they are liberated in their very place. Each and every phenomenon is quiescent in its own place.
It is extinguished. It is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) right where it is. Furthermore, this originally existing nature cannot be named or designated.

From the beginning, it is neither ordinary nor holy; it is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither empty nor existent; and it is neither good nor evil. Yet, it is associated with all defiled phenomena.
Beyond the realms of humans, devas, and the two vehicles, when both defiled and pure minds are exhausted, one dwells neither in bondage nor in liberation.
There is no sphere of mental measurement (*cittamātra*) involving any conditioned or unconditioned states of bondage or liberation; thus, the mind attains mastery over birth and death.
Ultimately, it does not conjoin with any delusions, illusions, afflictions, aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of birth and death, remaining utterly detached and without dependence.
Nothing binds them; they are unimpeded in going or staying. Their coming and going within birth and death is like a door opening.
Indeed, a practitioner of the Way, when encountering various forms of suffering or pleasure, or matters that are agreeable or disagreeable, remains without mental retreat or dejection.
They do not dwell on fame, profit, gain, food, or clothing; they do not crave merit or benefit; and they are not obstructed by any worldly dharmas.

Obstructed. Without kin or affection, with equanimity toward suffering and joy, wearing coarse clothing to ward off the cold and eating plain food to sustain life, remaining steadfast like one who is dull-witted or deaf, one may have some degree of resonance with the practice.
However, if within the mind one extensively pursues learning and intellectual understanding, seeking merit and seeking wisdom—[this is not the way].

All of these belong to birth and death and offer no benefit to the ultimate principle (*li*). Instead, one is drifted and drowned by the winds of the realm of intellectual understanding, returning once more to the ocean of birth and death.
The Buddha is one who seeks nothing; to seek him is to deviate from him. The principle is a principle that seeks nothing; to seek it is to lose it.
If one clings to "seeking nothing," this is the same as having a seeking mind. If one clings to "non-action" (*wuwei*), this is the same as being engaged in action (*youwei*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Do not grasp at dharmas; do not grasp at non-dharmas; do not grasp at what is neither dharma nor non-dharma. It further says:

"The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. If one can for a lifetime maintain a mind like wood or stone, remaining unswayed and unsunken by the aggregates, the elements, the five desires, and the eight winds, then the cause of birth and death will be severed, and one will attain freedom in going and staying.

One is not bound by the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), nor is one constrained by outflows (*āsrava*). At another time, one takes that which was previously considered a causeless bond as a cause;
through common purpose, one benefits others. With a mind free from attachment, one responds to all things; with unimpeded wisdom, one releases all bonds.
This is also called "prescribing medicine according to the illness. Question: If, as now, one receives the precepts and the body and speech are pure...

"Having already perfected all virtues, has one attained liberation? The Master replied, "One has attained a partial liberation, but has not yet attained liberation of mind, nor has one attained liberation in all places.
[The student] asked, "What is liberation of mind and what is liberation in all places?"
The Master said: "Do not seek the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; do not even seek merit, wisdom, knowledge, or understanding.
When both defiled and pure sentiments are exhausted, do not cling to this state of non-seeking as being 'right,' nor dwell in the place of exhaustion. Do not rejoice in heaven or fear hell.
When bondage and liberation are without obstruction, then body and mind, as well as all places, are called liberation. Do not say that it exists."

To consider a mere fraction of precepts—the purity of body, speech, and mind—to be sufficient is to remain ignorant of the gates of the river-sands of discipline, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the untainted liberation;
you have not yet traversed even a hair’s breadth of them. You must strive forward and investigate with fierce resolve;

do not wait until your ears are deaf, your eyes dim, your face is wrinkled, and your hair is white, when the suffering of old age has overtaken your body and you are entangled by the grief of attachment, with tears flowing from your eyes and your heart...
Internally terrified and panicked, with nothing whatsoever to rely upon and no knowledge of where one is going—at such a moment as this, one cannot even manage one’s own limbs.
Even if one possesses fortune, wisdom, fame, and gain, none of these can provide salvation, for the eye of the mind has not yet opened.
They merely contemplate various objects without knowing how to reflect back upon themselves, nor do they perceive the Buddha-way.
All the karmic conditions of good and evil from their entire lives appear before them; they experience either joy or fear as the six realms and the five aggregates manifest simultaneously.
Fully arrayed and magnificent dwellings, boats, ships, carriages, and litters appear with brilliant radiance—all of which are manifested from the greed and attachment of one’s own mind. I.
All evil objects are transformed into sublime realms. However, wherever one’s craving is most intense, there one is led by the karmic consciousness and takes birth accordingly;
in this state, there is no freedom whatsoever. Whether as a dragon or a beast, whether noble or lowly—none of these are yet determined.

Question: How can one obtain freedom? The Master said: "If you were to obtain it now, you would obtain it. Or, when confronted with the five desires and the eight winds, let your mind have no grasping."

He abandons stinginess, envy, greed, and attachment; his sense of "mine" is exhausted, and both defilement and purity have vanished. Like the sun and moon in the sky, he illuminates without depending on external conditions.
His mind is as firm as wood or stone, yet every thought is like one rushing to extinguish a fire on one's head. Furthermore, it is like a fragrant elephant crossing a river:
having cut through the current, he passes over without further hesitation or obstruction. Such a person cannot be encompassed by either heaven or hell. Now, as for reading...
When studying the scriptures and teachings, all words and phrases must be turned back and brought into alignment with one's own self.

However, all verbal instructions merely clarify the nature of one's present discerning awareness. It is simply that you must not be swayed by any objects of existence or non-existence; this is your guide.
That which can penetrate and shatter all objects of existence and non-existence is adamantine wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*); it is this very state that possesses freedom and independence.
[This is] a section. If you cannot understand it in this way, then even if you can recite the twelve Vedas, it will only result in arrogant conceit;

it is actually slandering the Buddha and not practicing cultivation. Simply leave behind all sounds and forms, yet do not dwell in that state of leaving them behind, nor dwell in intellectual understanding.
This is true practice—reading scriptures and studying the teachings. If judged by worldly standards, this may be considered good.
As for this matter: if one counts oneself among those who understand the principle, one is actually a person who is obstructed;
even a person of the Ten Stages cannot escape, as they flow into the river of birth and death. All teachings of the Three Vehicles treat the illnesses of greed, anger, and so forth.

Therefore, if at this very moment, in every thought-moment, there are illnesses such as greed and anger, you must first treat them. There is no need to seek out meanings, phrases, or intellectual understanding. Know this.

Understanding belongs to craving; craving turns into illness. Simply by now remaining detached from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and even detaching from that detachment itself, one passes beyond the three propositions.
Naturally, one is no different from the Buddha. Since you are yourself the Buddha, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your words?
One only fears not being the Buddha, being bound by the dharmas of existence and non-existence so as to lack freedom. By means of this principle...
If one has not yet established [the foundation], although one possesses merit and wisdom beforehand, one will be carried away by that merit and wisdom—like a lowly servant being elevated to nobility.

This is not as good as first establishing the principle and subsequently possessing merit and wisdom; for if one requires merit and wisdom, they can be produced at the moment of need, turning a handful of earth into gold or a handful of gold into earth.
He transforms the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd; he shatters Mount Sumeru into fine dust; he gathers the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore.
He renders a single meaning into immeasurable meanings, and renders immeasurable meanings into a single meaning. I humbly entreat you to take care of yourself.
Once, when the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called out to them. The assembly turned their heads, and the Master asked, "What is this?"

(Mo—Yaoshan referred to this as "Baizhang’s sentence after descending from the hall"). When the Master was a child, he accompanied his mother to a temple to pay homage to the Buddha. Pointing to the Buddha image, he asked his mother:
"What is this? His mother replied, "It is the Buddha. The Master said, "His appearance is no different from that of a human being; I too shall become like him in the future.

Whenever the Master performed manual labor or took up strenuous tasks, he invariably preceded the assembly. The head of the community could not bear it and secretly collected his tools to ask him to rest.
The Master said, "I have no virtue; why should I strive to avoid laboring alongside others? Having searched everywhere for his tools, [he found them not].
He attained such realization that he even forgot to eat; thus, the saying "if one day you do not work, on that day you shall not eat" spread throughout the world.

On the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he entered nirvana. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dazhi, and his stupa was named Dabaoshenglun.
Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of Chizhou was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou. His surname was Wang. From his youth, he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In the second year of the Zhide era of the Tang dynasty, he followed Chan Master Dahui on Mount Dawai to receive formal training.

He then traveled to Mount Song to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Initially, he studied the ancient regulations of the Xiangbu school and investigated the *vinaya* rules and categories. Subsequently, he traveled among various lecture halls.
He extensively studied the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Avataṃsaka*, entered the contemplations of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*, and refined his understanding of profound meanings.
Later, he sought out Mazu Daoci; upon entering his room, he suddenly forgot the fish-trap [the means] and attained the Samādhi of Līlā (Playful Mastery).
One day, while serving rice gruel to the assembly of monks, Mazu asked, "What is inside this bucket? The Master replied, "Old man, shut your mouth and talk like that! Mazu—
He then ceased speaking. Among his fellow practitioners, none dared to question him further. In the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he stayed at Chiyang, where he established a meditation hall.
For more than thirty years, he did not descend from Nanquan. At the beginning of the Dazhao era, Lu Gong Heng, the Intendant of Xuancheng, was drawn to the Master’s reputation for the Way;
he subsequently requested, together with the Military Supervisor, that the Master descend from the mountain to fulfill the duties of a disciple.
The Rites: The profound principles were greatly revitalized. From this time forth, his disciples numbered no fewer than several hundred, and his reputation filled every quarter;

he was acclaimed as a "Master of Ying. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is exhausted here. If one gives rise to various phenomena through the conceptualizations of the mind's characteristics, they are empty and unreal.
Why is this? Since the mind itself does not exist, how could it give rise to various phenomena? They are like forms and shadows, distinct yet inseparable."
It is distinct from space. It is like a person taking sound and placing it inside a casket; or like blowing into a net, wishing to make it full of air.
Therefore, the elder masters said: "It is not the mind, not the Buddha, and not a thing. This is merely to instruct you brothers in your practice.
According to the teachings, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, which is spontaneous.

They attain the wondrous functions of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Reaching all worlds, they universally manifest form-bodies (*rūpakāya*);
they may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, turn the great wheel of Dharma, or enter *nirvāṇa*, causing immeasurable beings to enter their pores.
To expound a single phrase of a sutra for immeasurable kalpas, its meaning remains inexhaustible;

yet, though one may teach and transform immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), this is still termed "ignorance regarding the knowable" (jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha)—an extremely subtle ignorance regarding the knowable. This is entirely at odds with the Way.
"A great difficulty! A great difficulty! Take care! He ascended the hall and said: "Master Wáng has raised a water buffalo since childhood.

If he intends to pasture it east of the stream, he cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass; if he intends to pasture it west of the stream, he likewise cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass.
It is better to simply accept things as they are—yet even this is not seen. The Master then asked:
The monk said, "A fine wind last night. The Master said, "A fine wind last night. The monk said, "It blew down the pine tree in front of the gate.
The Master said, "It blew down the pine tree in front of the gate. Next, he asked another monk, "A fine wind last night. The monk said, "What kind of wind was it?
The Master said, "It blew down the pine tree in front of the gate. The monk said, "What kind of pine tree was it? The Master said, "One who has attained."

The first failure: The Master sent a letter to Zhuyou, saying: "Principle follows the transformation of phenomena; its vastness is not external. Phenomena attain the harmony of principle; their stillness is not internal.
When Sengda finished reading the letter, he asked Zhuyou, "What is meant by 'its vastness is not external'?
Zhuyou said, "It does no harm to ask one and receive a hundred answers. He asked again, "What is meant by 'their stillness is not internal'? Zhuyou said, "To perceive and face [the world]."
"Sound and form are not the mark of a skilled hand. The monk asked Changsha again; Changsha stared at him with wide-open eyes.
When the monk uttered the subsequent phrase, Changsha closed his eyes to show him. The monk then asked Zhaozhou; Zhaozhou made the gesture of eating a meal.
When the monk uttered the subsequent phrase, Zhaozhou made the gesture of wiping his mouth with his hand. Later, the monk related these instances to the Master (Linji), who said, "These three men..."

He mistakenly became my disciple. Beneath Nanquan Mountain there was a hermitage master. Someone said to him, "Recently, Master Nanquan has appeared in the world; why do you not go to pay him a visit?
The master replied, "It is not merely that Nanquan has appeared in the world; even if the thousand Buddhas were to arise, I would still not go.
When the Master (Linji) heard this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go and investigate him. Upon arriving, Zhaozhou immediately prostrated himself.
The Master did not look back. As the Governor moved from west to east and again from east to west, the Master still did not look back.
The Governor said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," whereupon he drew the curtain down and returned to report this to the Master. The Master said, "I have always suspected this man.
The following day, the Master took a novice monk and carried a bottle of tea and three cups; they went to the hermitage and threw them to the ground.
The Master said, "That of yesterday. That of yesterday. The Head asked, "What is that of yesterday?
The Master struck the novice on the back once and said, "You have deceived me! You have deceived me! Then he shook out his sleeves and departed. Upon ascending the hall for discourse, he said:
"To speak of 'suchness' (tathatā) is already a transformation. These days, monks must walk among the heterodox."—Guizong.
[The monk] said, "Even if one performs the deeds of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The Master said, "Mencius, you fellow fellow, have you gone off like that again?
He ascended the hall and said, "Last night at the third watch, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fought each other; I gave each of them twenty blows with my staff."
Taking advantage of his discharge from the hospital, he departed. Zhaozhou asked, "Whom did the Master intend for the staff to strike? The Master said, "Tell me, where was Old Teacher Wang’s fault?
Zhaozhou bowed and withdrew. The Master then went to a manor estate. The master of the estate had prepared a reception in advance.
The Master said, "I usually enter and leave this place without letting anyone know. Why have you made such elaborate preparations? The master of the estate...
The Master said, "Last night the Local Deity (Tudishen) reported that the Abbot would come today. The Teacher said, "Old Wang lacks the power of cultivation;
he was spotted by ghosts and spirits. The attendant then asked, "Since you, Master, are a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), why were you spotted by ghosts and spirits?
The Teacher said, "Serve another portion of rice before the Local Deity. (Xuanjue said: "Where is the Local Deity?")
Before the earth, he further set down a portion of rice. Yunju Xi said, "This is both rewarding him and punishing him. As for what was seen before the earth—is it Nanquan or is it not Nanquan?
The Master once said, "In Jiangxi, Mazu taught 'this very mind is Buddha. Old Wang does not speak thus; I say, 'It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
If one speaks in this way, is there any fault? Zhaozhou bowed and departed. At that time, there was one...
A monk followed [the Master] and asked Zhaozhou, "When the Senior Monk (Upādhyāya) bowed and immediately left, what was his intention? Zhaozhou said, "You should ask the Abbot instead.
The monk then asked, "What was the intention of the Senior Monk Shen just now? Zhaozhou said, "He, however, understood the old monk's meaning.
Once, when Huangbo was serving as the Head Seat (Prathama-śrāvaka) for the Master, he took up his alms bowl and headed toward the Master’s seat.
The Master entered the hall and saw the Senior Monk (Shangzuo). He asked, "In what year did you begin practicing the Way? Huangbo replied, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.
The Master said, "You are still the descendants of Old Wang; get down from there! Huangbo then moved to the second seat and sat. The Master then desisted.
One day, the Master asked Huangbo, "If the world were made of gold and the earth of white silver..."
[The Master] pointed to the wall and said, "What kind of person lives here? Huangbo replied, "A sage lives here. The Master said, "There is yet another person; in what land does he dwell?
Huangbo then stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. The Master said, "You cannot say it. Why not ask Old Teacher Wuzhuo?
Huangbo then asked, "In what land does that other person dwell? The Master said, "What a pity! The Master then questioned [Huangbo].
Huangbo said, "The equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom leads to clearly seeing the Buddha-nature. What is the principle of this?

Huangbo replied, "In the twelve periods of the day, one does not rely upon or depend on a single thing. The Master asked, "Is this your own realization, Elder? Huangbo replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "..."
"Let us set aside the money for the gruel; to whom shall you have the money for the straw sandals returned? The Master saw a monk chopping wood and struck the wood three times.
The monk set down his axe and returned to the monks' hall. The Master returned to the Dharma Hall.

After a long while, he entered the monks' hall again and saw the monk sitting beneath his robes and bowl. The Master said, "You will ruin people! [Question: "The Master returned to his quarters. Taking [the staff]..."
"What is the guiding principle? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost my fire.
Once, when the monks of the East and West Halls were disputing over a cat, the Master encountered them. He addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak [the truth], I shall save the cat;
if you cannot, I shall kill it. The assembly was speechless. The Master then killed it. Zhaozhou returned from outside.
The Master brought up the previous words and showed them to him. Daizhou then took off his sandals, placed them on his head, and went out.

The Master said, "If you had been here, you would have saved the cat. While the Master was in the abbot’s quarters warming himself by the fire with Xiangshan, he said, "Without pointing east or west, speak directly of the matter of your own fundamental share.
Xiangshan stuck his fire tongs upright and stood with his hands clasped. The Master said, "Although..."
It was indeed so; yet it still fell short of the Master Wang’s "single thread of the Way. A monk came to pay his respects and stood with hands folded.
The Master said, "Too worldly. The monk then pressed his palms together in prayer. The Master said, "Too monastic. The monk had no reply.
While another monk was washing his bowl, the Master snatched the bowl away from him. The monk stood there empty-handed. The Master said, "The bowl is in my hand."
"What are you mumbling about? The monk had no reply. The Master then entered the vegetable garden and saw a monk there;
he struck him with a tile. The monk turned back to look, and the Master stood on one foot. The monk remained speechless, and the Master returned to his quarters.
A monk followed him in and asked in greeting, "Master, you just now threw a tile and struck me; was that not to alert me?
The Master said, "What about when I stood on my tiptoes? The monk had no reply. (Later, a monk asked Shishuang, "What was the meaning of Nanquan standing on his tiptoes?
Shishuang raised his hand and said, "Is it like this? He ascended the hall and said, "Old Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?"
"Ma. A monk stepped forward and said, "I will buy it. The Master said, "Neither as something expensive nor as something cheap—how will you buy it?

The monk was speechless. (Wolong [Dongshan Liangjie] spoke on his behalf: "It belongs to me. Heshan [Shouchu] spoke on his behalf: "What kind of principle is this? Zhaozhou [Congshen] spoke on his behalf: "Next year, I shall sew a robe for the Master.")
The Master went with Guizong and Magu to pay their respects to National Teacher Nanyang.
On the road, the Master drew a circle and said, "If you can speak, then we shall go. Guizong immediately sat within the circle; Magu performed a woman’s bow.
The Master said, "In that case, we shall not go. Guizong asked, "What kind of mental activity is this? The Master then called them by name and they returned together.

He did not go further to pay respects to the National Teacher. (Xuánjué said: "As for Nánquán speaking thus, was it an expression of approval or disapproval? Yúnjū Xī said: "Previously, he went to pay his respects to the National Teacher.")

Why did Nanquan nevertheless call him back? Tell me, what was the meaning of the ancient? While the Master was performing manual labor on the mountain, a monk asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead?
The Master picked up his sickle and said, "This thatch-sickle of mine was bought for thirty coins.
The monk said, "I am not asking about the thatch-sickle; where does the road to Nanquan lead? The Master said, "I use it."
It was just as it should be. A monastery head was taking his leave of the Master. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "Down to the mountains.
The Master said, "Above all, do not slander Old Wang. He replied, "How would I dare slander the Abbot?

The Master then sneezed and said, "How much? The head immediately departed. (Yunju Ying said, "This was not the Master’s original intention. Caoshan Xuanzong said, "Fortunately. Shishuang Qingyuan said, "He did not deliberate on behalf of others. Changqing Huilang said, "Please.")
[The Master] acknowledged the remark. Yungju Xi said, "When the Dharma Master went out at that time, was he enlightened or not?

One day, the Master closed the gate of the abbot’s quarters and surrounded the outside of the gate with ashes, saying, "If anyone can speak a word [of realization], I shall open it. Many who offered responses failed to satisfy the Master's intent.
Zhaozhou said, "Heaven! The Master then opened the gate. While the Master was enjoying the moon, a monk asked, "When will I become like this?"
The Master said, "In my youth, twenty years ago, I also came in this very same way. Gao asked, "How is it now? The Master then returned to his quarters.
Dagu Lu Xun asked, "I have come from the Six Realms; do they still possess bodies there?
The Master said, "Keep this clearly in mind and present it to a master of the Way. Lu Xun said, "The Master is inconceivable. [Upon hearing this, Lu Xun] arrived.
When he was dwelling in the world, he achieved [realization]. The Master said, "What you have just said is entirely the business of a high official.
Later, Lu said to the Master, "I too have a slight understanding of the Buddha-dharma. The Master then asked, "How do you conduct yourself throughout the twelve periods of the day?

He replied, "Not a thread of silk hangs upon me. The Master said, "You are still but a man standing at the foot of the steps. The Master spoke again, saying, "Have you not heard it said: 'There is...'"?

Where there is thought, it returns to no-thought; where there is dwelling, it returns to non-dwelling. They come for the sake of sentient beings; they go for the sake of sentient beings.
