The student said, “Does the Master have no way of receiving people? The Master said, “I will receive you when you come seeking to be received.
The student said, “Please receive me right now, Master. The Master said, “What is it that you lack? A student asked, “How can one become mindless? The Master said:
Mountains collapsed and oceans were overturned, yet all remained calm and still; the earth shook while he slept peacefully—how could anyone have grasped this?

On the twenty-third day of the third month in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, having bathed and burned incense, he sat upright and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma-body is perfect stillness; it manifests coming and going as a skillful means.
The thousand sages share one source; the myriad spirits return to the One. Now that I am like a bubble dispersing, why should you feign grief? Do not do so."
"Exert your spirit; you must maintain right mindfulness. If you follow this instruction, you will truly repay my kindness. Should you stubbornly disobey these words, you are not my disciple.
At that time, a monk asked, "Where is the Master going? The Master said, "Nowhere. The monk said, "Why do I not see you?
The Master said, "It is not something seen by the eyes" (Dongshan remarked, "A true adept"). Having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away peacefully.
While Master Baoji of Panshan in Youzhou was walking through a marketplace, he saw a guest buying pork.
He said to the butcher, "Cut me a pound of the finest meat. The butcher set down his knife, joined his palms, and said, "District Magistrate, which of these is not the finest?
At this, the Master attained realization. On another day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw people carrying a funeral procession and sang:
Lang Zhenling said: "The crimson wheel will surely sink to the west; I do not know where the soul and spirit have gone. Beneath the curtain, a filial son wept, crying, "Alas! Alas!
The Master suddenly felt his body and mind leap with joy. Upon returning, he recounted this to Mazu, who gave him his seal of approval.
Later, while residing there, a monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master simply snapped his fingers. The monk said, "I, your student, have not yet grasped the meaning. The Master—

He said: "Go. He ascended the hall and said: "If the mind is free from affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise. When the intellect is cut off from the subtle mechanism, how could even a speck of dust be established?
The Way has no substance; it is because of substance that a name is established. The Way has no name; it is because of a name that a title is obtained.
If one says 'this very mind is Buddha,' at present one has not yet entered the profound mystery. If one says 'neither mind nor Buddha,' this is still merely pointing to the tracks."
The ultimate limit. The path that leads upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies in vain, like monkeys grasping at reflections.

[Ascending the hall: Now, the Great Way has no center; who, then, can speak of before or after? The vast sky reaches its limits—what need is there for measurement? Since emptiness is thus, what more can be said of the Way?
[Ascending the hall: Now, the moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. This light does not illuminate objects.
The objective realm does not exist either; when both light and the realm have vanished, what thing remains? Zen Master, it is like brandishing a sword through the air:
do not concern yourself with whether one reaches it or not. This is the traceless whirling of emptiness, where the blade’s edge remains unimpaired. If you can act thus, [you will realize this].
Mind after mind is without cognition. The entire mind is the Buddha; the entire Buddha is the person. When there is no distinction between person and Buddha, one has finally entered the Way.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Virtuous Chan practitioners, you may study the Way within this. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. If you can act in this manner, it is called 'leaving home. Therefore, the Teacher said:"
Phenomena are fundamentally non-obstructive; the three periods of time are likewise so. Even for one who is unconditioned and without affairs, it remains difficult like a golden chain.
Thus, the numinous source shines alone; the Way is absolute and birthless. Great wisdom is not "bright," and true emptiness leaves no trace.
True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and *nirvāṇa* are both merely figurative designations. Chan practitioners must simply look within yourselves.
There is no one to replace me. Entering the hall: In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The Four Elements are fundamentally empty; upon what does the Buddha dwell?
The celestial sphere is unmoving; it is silent and wordless. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more. Be careful!

As the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Is there anyone who has captured my true likeness? The assembly presented the portraits they had painted, but none accorded with the Master’s intention.
Puhua stepped forward and said, "I have captured it. The Master asked, "Why do you not present it to this old monk? Puhua then performed a somersault and left.
The Master remarked, "This fellow will go on to act like one driven by madness in the future. The Master... [passed away].
He then passed away suddenly; he was posthumously titled the Great Master Ningji.
While Chan Master Baoche of Mazugu Mountain in Puzhou was attending Mazu while traveling, he asked, "What is great nirvāṇa?
Mazu said, "Hurry! The Master said, "Hurry for what? Mazu said, "Look at the water. While the Master was fanning himself, a monk asked him:
"The nature of wind is eternally abiding; there is nowhere it does not pervade. Why, then, does the Master wave a fan?
The Master said, "You know only that the nature of wind is eternally abiding, but you do not yet know that it pervades everywhere.
The monk asked, "What is the principle of its pervading everywhere? The Master again waved his fan. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Useless, monk! You have applied it where it belongs."
"What is the benefit of a thousand [people]? He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I am not sure.

The Master asked again, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "Take care. The Master stepped down from his seat, seized him, and said, "This monk, when questioned, immediately answers with the Dharma.
The monk said, "It is very much like a blind master. The Master let go of him and said, "I spare your life; I allow you to breathe. The monk bowed.
The Master wished to seize him, but the monk brushed out his sleeves and walked away. The Master said, "Do not take a three-year-old bamboo and attempt to compare it to a ten-thousand-year-old pine.
Later, the Master went with Nanquan and two or three others to visit Jingshan. On the road, they encountered an old woman, and the Master asked, "Which way does the path to Jingshan go?
The woman replied, "Go straight ahead. The Master asked, "Is the water deep ahead? Can one cross it? The woman—
[The Master] said, "Your feet are not wet. The Master asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so fine; why is the rice on the lower bank so poor?
The woman said, "It has all been eaten by crabs. The Master said, "The grain is so fragrant. The woman said, "It has no scent."
The Master asked again, "Where does the old woman reside? The old woman replied, "She resides right here.
When the three men arrived at the shop, the old woman brought a pot of tea and three cups and said, "If you monks possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), then drink the tea.
While the three were looking at one another, the old woman said, "Watch as this decrepit old woman displays her own supernatural powers," and she picked up a cup and poured [the tea].
Changsha went out to attend to his duties. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master remained silent. The monk then asked Shishuang about this matter.
Shishuang said, "The master raises his fists and brings trouble upon himself; you, O *dārala*, drag through mud and wade through water."
Chan Master Ruhui of Dongsi Temple in Hunan was a native of Qujiang in Shixing. He first visited Mount Jing and later studied under Daji.
As his disciples grew numerous, the beds and benches in the Sangha Hall were worn down and broken by their weight; thus, he was popularly known as "Zhechuang Hui" (Hui of the Broken Beds).
Since the Great Śānta [Mañjuśrī] passed away, the Master often lamented that his disciples incessantly recited and memorized the discourse on "the mind itself is Buddha.
He remarked, "Where does the Buddha abide, such that you say 'the mind itself'? The mind is like a painter; how can you say it is 'Buddha'?
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since departed, yet you are still marking the boat. At that time...
He gave Dongsi the name "The Zen Cave. When Prime Minister Cui Gongqun was appointed as the Inspector of Hunan, he visited the Master and asked, "By what means did you attain realization?

The Master replied, "I attained it by seeing my nature. At that time, the Master was suffering from an eye ailment, so the official ridiculed him, saying, "If you say you have 'seen your nature,' what can you do about your eyes?
The Master said, "Seeing one's nature is not the function of the eyes; what harm does an eye ailment do to that? The official bowed his head in reverence.

Xie (Fayan’s alternative commentary says: "This is the Eye of the Duke") saw birds and sparrows dropping dung on the Buddha’s head and asked, "Do these birds and sparrows possess Buddha-nature or not?
The Master said, "They do. The Duke said, "Why then do they drop dung on the Buddha’s head?"
The Master said, "Why does this fellow not let it loose upon the hawk? Yangshan went to visit him. The Master asked, "Where are you from?
Yangshan replied, "I am a man from Guangnan. The Master said, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Bright Pearl that Subdues the Sea'."
“Is it so? Yang replied, “It is. The Master said, “What is this pearl like? Yang replied, “In the dark moon it is hidden; in the bright moon it appears.
The Master said, “Have you brought it back with you or not? Yang replied, “I have brought it back. The Master said, “Why do you not present it to me, old monk?
Yang joined his palms, stepped forward, and said, “Yesterday I arrived at Mount Gui, and there too I was asked for this pearl; it left me with nothing to say.”
Yangshan said, "There is something that can be discussed; there is a principle that can be set forth. Yangshan replied, "A true lion cub indeed knows how to roar.
Having bowed and paid his respects, Yangshan withdrew to the guest quarters. There, he assumed the full dignified demeanor and went up again to pay his respects to the Master.

As soon as the Master saw him, he said, "We have already met. Yangshan asked, "Meeting in this manner—is it not appropriate? The Master returned to his quarters and shut the door. Yangshan [stood outside].
He returned and related this to Guishan. Guishan asked, "What kind of mental activity is this, Jizang? Yangshan replied, "If it were not so, how could one recognize him?
Later, someone asked the Master, "May I request the Master to open the hall [for formal teaching]?
The Master said, "Wait until you can wrap a stone in cloth and warm it; then you may. The man was speechless. (Yaoshan spoke on his behalf: "The stone is warm. Tang.
He entered nirvana in the *gui-mao* year of the Changqing era. His posthumous title was Great Master Chuánmíng.
Chan Master Xītáng Zhìzàng of Qiānzhōu was the son of the Liào family of Qiànhuà. He followed a teacher at the age of eight and received full ordination at twenty-five.
A physiognomist, observing his extraordinary features, said to him, "Your bone and spirit are not ordinary; you shall become a Dharma King."

As his attendant, the Master subsequently went to pay his respects to Daji (Mazu Daoyi). Together with Chan Master Baizhang Hai, he entered the inner sanctum and both received the seal of transmission.
One day, Daji sent the Master to Chang’an to deliver a letter to National Teacher Zhong.
The National Teacher asked, "What dharma does your teacher preach? The Master walked from east to west and stood there. The National Teacher said, "Only..."
"There is something else besides this. The Master then moved from the west to stand on the eastern side.
The National Teacher said, "This is Master Ma's way; what about yours, worthy one? The Master replied, "I have already presented it to you, Venerable Sir.

He then sent a letter to Mount Jing (the details of which are recorded in the chapter concerning the National Teacher). Subsequently, the regional commander Lu Sīgōng invited Dàjì to reside at his headquarters. He accepted.

The period of flourishing transformation arrived. When the Master returned to the commandery, he received the robe and *kaṣāya* transmitted by Daji (Nanyue Huairang) and instructed his students to draw near to him.
A monk asked Mazu, "Leaving behind the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I pray that you, Master, will directly point out the meaning of the Westward Transmission.
Mazu said, "I am weary today and cannot explain it for you; go ask Zhizang. That monk then came to ask the Master. The Master—
The monk said, "Why do you not ask your own teacher? The monk replied, "My teacher sent me here specifically to ask the Venerable.
Baizhang said, "I have a headache today and cannot explain it for you. Go and ask my elder brother Hai.
The monk went again to ask Baizhang Hai, who said, "When I arrived here, I did not understand either. The monk then reported this to Mazu.
The Patriarch said, "The head of the storehouse is white; the head of the sea is black. One day Mazu asked the Master, "Why do you not read the sutras?
The Master replied, "How could the sutras be different [from this]? Mazu said, "Even so, when you act as a teacher for others in the future, you must ensure they understand."
[The Master] said, "Zhizang is ill and is thinking only of nourishing himself; how would he dare speak for others? Mazu said, "In the final years of your life, you will surely flourish in the world.
The Master then paid his respects. After Mazu passed away, in the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the assembly requested that the Master open the hall [for formal teaching].
Once, Minister Li asked a monk, "What kind of verbal instructions did the Great Master Mazu have? The monk replied, "The Great Master sometimes spoke of 'this very mind'..."
"This is precisely the Buddha. Or he said, "It is neither mind nor Buddha. Li said, "In general, you have gone too far. Li then asked the Master, "What teachings does Master Mazu have?
The Master called out, "Li Ao! Li responded, "Yes. The Master said, "The drums and horns are sounding.

While the Master was leading the community in labor, he said, "Cause and effect are clearly evident; what can be done about it? What can be done about it? At that time, a monk stepped forward and, with his hand—
He prostrated himself on the ground. The Master asked, "What are you doing? He replied, "Save me! Save me! The Master said, "O assembly, this monk is still somewhat better than others.
The monk brushed out his sleeves and walked away. The Master said, "A worm within the body of a lion eats the lion's own flesh.
A monk asked, "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined; but what about when there is neither question nor answer? The Master said:

Fearing that [the teaching] might rot away (later, a monk raised this question to Changqing. Changqing said: "Everyone who meets them says they have retired from office; but since when has anyone been seen beneath the forest trees?").
Chan Master Zikong said to the Master, "The sun has risen too early. The Master said, "It is precisely the right time.

Later, while the Master was residing at Xitang, a layman asked, "Are there heavens and hells? The Master said, "There are. [The man] asked, "Are there the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? The Master—
[The monk] said, “Yes. He was asked further questions, and he answered them all, saying, “Yes. [The Master] said, “Does the Venerable Master not speak erroneously?
The Master replied, “Have you ever met any venerable elders? [The monk] said, “I have previously attended upon the Venerable Master of Mount Jing. The Master said:
“Jingshan, how would you answer him? he asked. The layman replied, “He says that everything is entirely non-existent. The Master said, “Do you have a wife? “He does,” the layman replied.
The Master said, “Does Master Jingshan have a wife? “He does not,” the layman replied. The Master said, “In that case, it is appropriate for Master Jingshan to say he has none.
The layman bowed in thanks and departed. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era, the Master returned [to his monastery].

Ji. Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Great Propagation of Teaching (Daxuanjiao Chanshi). Emperor Muzong further conferred the title Chan Master Great Enlightenment (Dajue Chanshi).

Chan Master Huahui of Zhangjing Temple in Jingzhao Prefecture was the son of the Xie family of Quanzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate principle transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it.
They strenuously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual efficacy, unaware that their own nature is fundamentally not a mundane object."
The objective realm is this subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation. All its discerning awareness is unstained and unimpeded; such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned.
From past kalpas until now, it remains eternally without change. It is like the solar disc, which shines upon both the distant and the near;
though it reaches all forms, it does not become fused with anything. This spiritual torch and wondrous clarity do not depend on refinement or cultivation. For...

Because of this lack of understanding, one grasps at objective phenomena; it is merely like pressing on the eyes and falsely perceiving flowers in the sky—exhausting oneself in vain and needlessly passing through kalpas.
If one can turn the light back upon itself, there is no second person; every movement and action will not fall short of the true mark (*dharmatā*). A monk asked:

"When both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, where does one point toward? The Master said: "The man of Ying has no grime on his face; he need only laboriously wield his adze. The monk said: "..."

[The monk] requested the Master’s words on not returning. The Master said, "There are no words for returning. (Later, a monk raised this question with Dongshan. Dongshan said, "As for speaking, there is much to speak; it is rare to encounter a true adept.")
Baizhang Huashang sent a monk to wait upon him. When the Master ascended the hall, the monk spread out his sitting mat, performed prostrations, and then stood up.
He took one of the Master’s sandals, brushed off the dust with the sleeve of his robe, and turned it upside down toward the ground. The Master said, "I, this old monk, am at fault. Someone asked:
"The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground; is this the mind of True Suchness or the mind of deluded thought?"
"It is neither true nor false mind; it is the mind established separately outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
The Master asked, "Do you see the empty space before you? He replied, "I know with certainty that it is always before me, yet people simply do not see it.
The Master said, "Do not mistake this for a reflected image. He asked, "How about you, Preceptor? The Master struck the air three times with his hand. He asked, "What is it, then?"
The Master said, "You will understand this later. A monk came, circumambulated the Master three times, shook his staff, and stood there.

The Master said, "It is so! It is so! (Changqing spoke on his behalf: "Where are the body and mind of the Master's Buddha-dharma? That same monk went to Nanquan and likewise circumambulated him three times, shook his staff, and stood there.
Nanquan said, "It is not so! It is not so! This is merely turned by the force of the wind; in the end, it will come to ruin."
Nanquan said, "Wrong. The monks asked, "Zhangjing said it was right; why does the Master say it is wrong? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is indeed right, but you are wrong.

(Changqing spoke on his behalf, saying: "What kind of mental state is the Master's? Yunju Xi said: "Zhangjing did not necessarily say it was right, and Nanquan did not necessarily say it was wrong. He further said:
When this monk first departed, he simply took his staff and went out. It happened that a junior attendant was returning from a pilgrimage.
The Master asked him, "How many years has it been since you left here? He replied, "It has been nearly eight years since I left your presence, Master.

The Master asked, "What have you accomplished? The junior attendant drew a circle on the ground. The Master said, "Is this all? Is there anything else? Thereupon, the junior attendant drew a line through the circle.
[The monk] drew a circle and then prostrated. The Master said, "Not so. Not so. The monk asked, "Within this body of the four elements and five aggregates, which one is the original Buddha-nature?
The Master then called the monk’s name. The monk responded, "Yes. After a long silence, the Master said, "You have no Buddha-nature.
He entered nirvana in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajue.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou was the son of the Zhu family of Jianzhou. He received his training under Master Zhi of Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou.
When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou.
Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "In my place, there is..."
"Things do not exist. Why seek the Buddha-dharma? You neglect your own precious treasury; why do you abandon your home and wander about?
He asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Haima? The Patriarch said, "That which is asking me right now is your precious treasury."

Everything was fully complete; there was nothing lacking. Its function was sovereign—why rely on seeking it elsewhere? Under these words, the Master spontaneously recognized his own original mind, not through intellectual cognition.
He leaped for joy and prostrated in gratitude. After serving the Master for six years, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him.
Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hid his capacities, outwardly appearing dull and slow of speech. He himself composed the *Wuwei Ru* (Entering Sudden Enlightenment).
The *Treatise on the Essential Gate of the Way* (Dàoyào mén lùn), one fascicle. His Dharma-nephew Xuanyan secretly took it outside the Yangtze River and presented it to Mazu.

After Mazu had finished reading it, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a Great Pearl; it is perfectly bright, its radiance penetrating through, free and at ease, with no place of obstruction.
Among the assembly was one who knew the Master’s surname was Zhu; they recommended him to go to Yuezhou to seek him out and rely upon him (at that time he was called Master Dazhu). The Master said:
He said, "O Zen guests, I do not understand Zen; there is not a single dharma that can be shown to others. Do not trouble yourselves by standing here so long; please rest for now.
At that time, the number of students gradually increased, and they pressed him with questions day and night. Having no other choice, he answered them as each question was asked.
His speech was unimpeded. At that time, several Dharma masters came to visit him and said, "We intend to pose a question;

will you respond to us? The Master replied, "The moon’s reflection in a deep pool may be grasped at will. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "In this clear conversation face-to-face, who else could it be but the Buddha?
The assembly was all at a loss (Fayan said: "This is precisely where there is no connection"). After a long silence, the monk asked again, "Master..."
"What Dharma do you teach to save people? The Master said, "I, this poor monk, have never had a single dharma by which to save people. [The other] said, "The houses of Chan masters are all like this.
The Master then asked in return, "Virtuous One, what Dharma do you teach to save people? He replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master said:
[The Master] asked, "How many lectures have you given? He replied, "More than twenty. The Master said, "Who preached this sutra?

The monk raised his voice and said, "Master, you are mocking me! Do you not know that it was preached by the Buddha? The Master said, "If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they slander the Buddha;
such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. If one says this sutra is not [the Buddha's teaching]..."

The Master said, "To say that the Buddha spoke this would be to slander the sutra. Please, Venerable Sir, speak upon it. The monk had no reply. After a short while, the Master asked again, "The sutra says:
'If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Venerable Sir, tell me: which one is the Tathāgata? The monk replied, "When I reach this point, I am lost. The Master said, "So be it."
[The monk] said, "I have never awakened from the beginning; why speak of being deluded? [The Master] said, "Please, Zen Master, explain this for me.

The Master said, "Great Virtue, you have lectured on the sutras more than twenty times, yet you do not recognize the Tathāgata. The monk prostrated and said, "I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Master said:
"Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. How could you forget this? He replied, "This is the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena.
The Master said, "Virtuous One, even this is not yet it. He asked, "The scriptural text is clear; how can it be 'not yet'? The Master said, "Virtuous One, are you such?
He replied, "I am such. The Master said, "Are wood and stone such? He replied, "They are such. The Master said, "Virtuous One, are you such as wood and stone are such?"

"No," he said. "There are none. The Master asked, "What distinguishes you, Venerable One, from wood or stone? The monk had no reply. After a long silence, the monk asked again, "How does one attain Great Nirvana?
The Master replied, "By not creating the karma of birth and death. The monk asked, "What is the karma of birth and death?"

The Master said: "Seeking great nirvāṇa is the karma of birth and death. Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death. Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death.
Not transcending the gate of counteractive measures is the karma of birth and death. [The student] asked: "How then can one attain liberation? The Master said:
"Fundamentally there has been no bondage; there is no need to seek liberation. To proceed directly and act directly—this is the peerless equality."
He said, "A Chan Master such as you, Reverend, is truly rare indeed. Having paid his respects and departed, a practitioner asked, "'The very mind is Buddha.
Which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "Which one do you doubt is not the Buddha? Point it out to me. The practitioner had no reply. The Master said, "To penetrate it, the entire realm is it;

if you do not awaken to it, you will remain forever estranged. The Vinaya Master Faming addressed the Master: [Note: The provided text ends with the mention of Vinaya Master Faming addressing the Master. The full dialogue would typically follow.]

[The Master] said, "In the houses of Chan masters, there is much falling into emptiness. The Master [Baizhang] replied, "On the contrary, it is the house of the Dharma Masters (*zhuzu*) who fall into emptiness.

Ming was greatly startled and asked, "How can they fall into emptiness? The Master said, "The sutras and treatises are but paper and ink characters. Paper, ink, and characters are all established as empty constructs.
The names, phrases, and other dharmas established upon sounds are none other than emptiness. Yet the Dharma Masters cling to and stagnate in the teachings."
"Does your essence not fall into emptiness? Ming asked. The Master said, "It does not fall into emptiness. Ming asked, "How is it that it does not fall into emptiness?
The Master said, "Texts and such all arise from wisdom; when the great function manifests before one,"
"Then you have fallen into emptiness," the Master said. Ming replied, "Therefore, I know that if one does not master even a single dharma, one cannot be called Siddhārtha.
The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not only fallen into emptiness; he has furthermore misunderstood the terminology. Ming flushed with anger and asked, "Where is the point of error?
The Master said, "Without discerning the sounds of China and India, how can one lecture and explain? Ming said, "I beg the Chan Master to point out the specific point of error."
The Master said, “Do you not know that *Siddhārtha* is a Sanskrit term? (In full, it is *Vighnāntasiddha*;

in the Central Kingdom [China], it is translated as ‘All Meanings Accomplished. The old rendering ‘Siddhārtha’ is itself a corrupted abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Although Ming acknowledged his error, his mind remained indignant.

[The student] asked again, “Since the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the words of the Buddha, and one recites them and practices according to their teachings, why is it that one does not see one’s nature? The Master said, “It is like a mad dog.”
"Seizing a clod of earth. "A lion biting a man. "The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the function of the nature; reading and reciting them are the phenomena of the nature.
Ming asked, "Does Amitābha Buddha have parents and a clan? The Master said, "Amitābha’s clan is Kauśika;
his father’s name is Candrottarā, and his mother’s name is Viśeṣacāritra. Ming asked, "In which scriptural text does this appear? The Master said, "It appears in the *Dundubhisvara* [Sūtra]."

After the King had finished his recitation of the sutra, Fahong paid his respects, withdrew after offering words of praise, and departed. A Tripitaka Master asked him, "Does True Suchness undergo change?

Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person; they do not reside in whether the teachings are the same or different.
The Chan Master Weizheng of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou once saw an old practitioner observing sunlight streaming through a window.

The master asked him, "Is it the window that moves toward the sun, or is it the sun that moves toward the window? The practitioner replied, "Venerable sir, there is a guest in your room; you had better go back.

[The monk] asked, "How is it? The Master said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. The monk said, "If that is so, then you have already explained it to people.

The Master said, "I have already told you quite enough. A monk asked, "What is the state where the Buddhas and the Way are equal? The Master said, "Equilibrium.

The Master suddenly attained realization and said, "I thank the Great Assembly for their testimony. He then circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.
When Chan Master Zhijian of Shanshan in Chizhou was first traveling as a pilgrimage monk with Guizong and Nanquan, they encountered a tiger on the road.
Each passed by the tiger’s side. Nanquan asked Guizong, "What did that tiger just now look like?
Guizong replied, "It looked like a cat. Guizong then asked the Master (Zhijian), who said, "It looked like a dog. He then asked Nanquan. Nanquan—
He said, "I see this as a great tiger. While the Master was eating his meal, Nanquan gathered some raw rice and said, "Is it raw?
The Master replied, "It is not raw. Nanquan said, "'Not raw' is still the secondary. After Nanquan had walked a few paces, the Master called out, "Elder!"
Nanquan turned his head and asked, "What is it? The Master said, "Do not say that this is merely the secondary.

While they were all being asked to gather and select bracken shoots, Nanquan picked up a single stalk and said, "This is excellent for making offerings. The Master said, "Not only this; even the hundred flavors of exquisite delicacies [are likewise so]."
He also did not heed it. Quan said, "Even so, each and every one must taste it before they can attain it" (Xuánjué said:
"Are these words of mutual recognition, or are they not?"). A monk asked, "What is the primordial body? The Master said, "In all the world, there is nothing like it."
One day, Chan Master Ledu Weijian of Hongzhou was sitting in meditation behind the Dharma Hall.
Mazu saw him and blew into his ear; he blew twice, and the master rose. Seeing it was Mazu, he returned to his meditative absorption.
Mazu went back to his quarters and ordered an attendant to bring a bowl of tea for the master. The master paid no heed and simply returned to his hall.
Chan Master Daoheng of Mingxi in Lizhou once said, "I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world.

Later, a monk asked Caoshan, "The ancients said, 'I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world. I wonder what kind of illness this is? Caoshan replied, "It is an illness that cannot be gathered or concentrated. The monk asked, "Do all sentient beings also have this illness? Caoshan said, "Everyone has it. The monk asked, "Does the Master also have this illness?

Caoshan said, "I am searching for its point of origin, but I cannot find it. The monk asked, "Why then do all sentient beings not fall ill? Caoshan said, "If all sentient beings were to fall ill, they would no longer be sentient beings. [The monk asked], "Before..."

The monk examined whether the Buddhas themselves were subject to this illness. Deshan said, "They are. The monk asked, "Since they have it, why do they not fall ill? Deshan said, "Because they are alert and aware (*xingxing*). A monk asked, "How does one practice cultivation? The Master said, "What a fine master you are!
Do not act like a hired laborer. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "To try to settle it would be inadequate."
Question: "What is the path of correct practice? The Master said: "It exists after nirvāṇa. Question:

Chan Master Huizang of Shigong in Fuzhou originally made his living as a hunter and held monks in contempt.
Once, while chasing a deer, he passed by Mazu’s hermitage. Mazu went out to meet him, whereupon the Master asked, "Did you see the deer pass by?

"Do you, Master, know how to shoot? he asked. "I do," the Patriarch replied. "Then with one arrow, how many do you shoot? "With one arrow, I shoot a whole flock," the Patriarch replied.
"The lives of both are precious; why shoot a whole flock? "Since you know this to be so, why do you not shoot yourself? the Patriarch asked.
[The Master] said, "If you were to teach me how to shoot myself, there would simply be no place to begin. The Patriarch said, "This fellow’s ignorance and afflictions have persisted through kalpas;
today they are suddenly stilled. The Master cast down his bow and arrows and entered the Patriarch’s service to leave the household life.
One day, while he was performing labor in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing? He replied, "Tending the ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you tend it? He replied, "Once..."
[The master] went into the grass. [The monk] pulled him back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You truly know how to herd an ox. The Master then desisted.
After the Master took up residence, he constantly used the bow and arrow to test his disciples (as recorded in the *Sanping Zhang*). The Master asked Xitang, "Do you understand how to capture space?"
Xitang said, "I have caught him. The Master asked, "How did you catch him? Xitang reached his hand into empty space. The Master said, "You do not know how to catch him.
Xitang then asked, "How does my elder brother catch him? The Master grabbed Xitang’s nostrils and pulled them. Xitang made a cry of pain and said, "That is too much!
You are pulling on a person's nostrils until they are about to tear off! The Master said, "You must indeed act in this way."
Only by grasping empty space can it be attained. During the next session of formal inquiry, the Master said, "Where has that which was just now gone?
A monk replied, "It is here. The Master asked, "Where is it? The monk snapped his fingers once. [The Master] asked, "How can one escape birth and death?"
The Master said, "What would you avoid by doing so? [The monk] asked, "How can one avoid it? The Master said, "This very thing is neither birth nor death.
Later, Elder Liang of Hutang asked Chan Master Lanrang of Jiangxi Beilan, "I have heard that you, Elder Brother, painted a portrait of our late Master;

Chan Master Daoming of Nanyuan in Yuanzhou ascended the hall and said: "A swift horse requires but one whip; a quick-witted man needs but one word.

The Master stuck out his tongue and said, "Wait until I possess the mark of a broad and long tongue, and then I shall tell you. Dongshan went to visit him. Just as he was about to ascend the hall...

Xianshan said, "How could I have let this slip away? Then Xianshan took his leave of the Master.
The monk said, "Study the Buddha-dharma extensively and bring great benefit to others. Dashi said, "I do not ask about studying the Buddha-dharma extensively;

Chan Master Lifu of Xinzhou ascended the hall and said: "The present is no different from the past; the Dharma is naturally so. What more is there to say?

The Master said, "I knew well that you would be at a loss. As the monk was about to offer further words, the Master said, "I thought..."

its scales make flight difficult. The monk asked, “How can one avoid this fault? The Master said, “If one has the form of a dragon, who would discuss high or low?
The monk bowed. The Master said, “Alas! What a pity! Who is like me? He ascended the hall and said: “Setting aside the brightness of day and the darkness of night, furthermore...”

Whenever Zen Master Hong'en of Zhongyi in Langzhou saw a monk arrive, he would snap his fingers and make a "he-he" sound. Yangshan...
Xie Jie clapped his mouth, making a "he-he" sound, and bowed as he passed from west to east.
The Master again clapped his mouth, making a "he-he" sound, and bowed as he passed from east to west. The Master again clapped his mouth, making a "he-he" sound, and stood bowing in the center.

When Shangzuo came to visit, the Master said, "Tell me, for what kind of person did Caoxi employ this samādhi?
Yangshan said, "To receive Yixiu Jue. Yangshan asked, "From where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? The Master said, "I obtained this samādhi from Great Master Ma.
Yangshan asked, "How does one realize the meaning of seeing the Buddha-nature? The Master said, "I shall explain it to you."
I shall provide an analogy. Suppose there is a room with six windows, and inside there is a monkey.
Outside, a monkey calls out from the eastern side, "O ape! and the monkey inside responds. In this manner, it is called out from all six windows and responds to each.
Yangshan prostrated in thanks and, rising, said: "I have just received the Master’s analogy; there is nothing I do not understand. However, there is one further matter: as for the one inside..."
The monkey fell asleep. An outside monkey wished to meet him; how did he do so?
The Master descended from his rope-corded seat, took Yangshan’s hand, and danced, saying: "The *xingxing* has met you.
It is like a tiny gnat making a nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, shouting at the crossroads: "The land is vast and people are few; those who meet here..."
Shao (Yunju Xi said: "If at that time Zhongyi had not received this single phrase from Yangshan, where would Zhongyi have been? Choushou Chou said: 'Is there anyone who can settle this principle?

If it cannot be settled, it is merely the maneuvering of a restless spirit; where then would the meaning of Buddha-nature lie? Xuangjue said: 'If it were not for Yangshan, how could Zhongyi have been seen? But tell me, in what place did Yangshan see Zhongyi?')"
A monk asked Chan Master Ledu Changxing of Hongzhou, "What is it like to be a guest under the gate of Caoxi?

The Master said, "A swallow coming from the south. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Nurturing its wings, waiting for the autumn wind. Another monk asked, "What is the ultimate matter of the ancestral vehicle?
The Master said, "Autumn rains, the grasses fall in disarray. When Nanquan arrived, he saw the Master sitting with his face against the wall and patted him.
The Master turned his back. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Puyuan. The Master said, "How so? He replied, "It is just as usual.
The Master said, "Why do you make such a fuss?"
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou was the son of the Du family of Shangluo in Shangzhou. His mother, Lady Li, heard a voice from the air asking, "May I take up residence here?
and she then became aware that she was pregnant. On the evening of his birth, a divine light filled the room. When he had just reached the age of seven, he was already [of keen intellect].

When walking, he always kept his gaze straight ahead; when sitting, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). At the age of nine, he studied the Mahāyāna sūtras under Chan Master Zhiben of Kaiyuan Temple;

he could read five lines at once and recited them from memory without omission. At twelve, he shaved his head. At twenty, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master You of Xiangzhou and studied the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*).
As soon as he finished his studies, he was able to expound upon it for the assembly of monks. Every time he taught for the community...

He lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* without ceasing during either winter or summer. Later, hearing that the Chan school under Master Ma was flourishing, he went specifically to pay his respects.
Upon seeing that the Master’s appearance was extraordinary and grand, and that his voice resonated like a bell, he remarked, "Aloft is the Buddha-hall, yet within it there is no Buddha.
The Master prostrated himself and knelt, asking, "I have roughly exhausted the essential meanings of the literature of the Three Vehicles; I have often heard of Chan..."

"The gate is precisely the mind that is Buddha. [The Master] truly did not yet understand this. The Patriarch said, "It is precisely this very mind that you do not understand; there is nothing else besides it.

The nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing coexists with the Great Void; it is neither born nor extinguished.

All objective realms are fundamentally empty and still from the beginning, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended. Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus confused by objects. Once they are confused by objects, [they are bound].
The cycle of transmigration is inexhaustible. You should know that the nature of the mind exists inherently from the beginning; it is not produced through artificial construction.
It is like a diamond, indestructible. All phenomena are like shadows and echoes; they possess no substantial reality. As the Sūtra says:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Constantly realizing that all is empty, there is not a single thing that accords with the mind.
This is the place where all Buddhas apply their minds; you all should practice it with diligence. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

On the day of his cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors appeared and a wondrous fragrance permeated the four quarters. The *śarīra* relics obtained were as brilliant as pearls and jade. His disciples...
He was enshrined in a golden jar and interred within a stone stupa. In the third year of the Changqing era, he was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada.

The Master said, "A wheeling sword cast into the air does not harm anything. The monk asked, "What is the person of original nature? The Master said, "Sitting together, we do not [see one another]."
The student said, "If that is so, then I, this student, take my leave with gratitude. The Master said, "In secret, one writes of a grieving heart; to whom can it be sent?
Chan Master Dayi of Gehu in Xingzhou was a native of the Xu clan from Xujiang in Quzhou.

During the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang Dynasty, he was once summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace, where he debated the principles of the Dharma at Linqide Hall. A Dharma Master asked, "What are the Four Noble Truths? The Master replied, "The Holy..."
[The Emperor] said, "I have ascended to the previous throne. Where are the three previous emperors? He asked again, "The realm of desire has no dhyāna; dhyāna resides in the realm of form.

Upon what does this land rely for its establishment? The Chan Master replied, "Dharma Master, you only know that the realm of desire has no dhyāna; you do not know that the realm of dhyāna has no desire."
The Emperor asked, "What is Chan? The Master pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master was speechless.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has lectured on infinite sutras and śāstras, yet he cannot account for this single point.

The Master then asked the eminent scholars, "In walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, what ultimately constitutes the Way? One replied, "That which knows is the Way. The Master said, "It cannot be grasped by cognition."

[The student] said: "It is known. Since it cannot be known by consciousness, how can there be one who knows it? [The Master] replied: "There is. It is the one who is without discrimination. [The student] said:

"One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena, yet remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (paramārtha). How can there be one who is without discrimination? [The Master] replied: "There is.
It is the four dhyānas and eight samādhis. [The student] said: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and does not fall into any numerical categories. How can..."

When [the Master] raised the question, "In the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, how can the myriad beings see their nature and attain Buddhahood? the entire assembly remained silent. The Master then cited Emperor Shunzong’s question to Chan Master Śrī:
"How can the sentient beings of the great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śrī replied, "Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water."
"It can be seen, yet it cannot be grasped. He said to the Emperor, "The Buddha-nature is not something that is seen by means of seeing;

The Emperor silently realized the True Principle and treated him with even greater reverence. A monk requested permission to erect a stupa. Minister Li Ao asked:

"He has attained great icchantika-hood. He passed away in peace in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era and was posthumously titled Chan Master Huijue.
Chan Master Zizai of Mount Funiu at Ique was the son of the Li family of Wuxing. Initially, he relied upon National Teacher Guoyi to receive full ordination;
thereafter, he attended Mazu Daoyi to realize the mind-ground. Mazu ordered him to deliver a letter to National Teacher Huizhong.
The National Teacher asked, "By what Dharma does Master Mazu instruct his disciples? He replied, "It is 'this very mind is Buddha. The National Teacher asked, "What is that?"
After conversing for a long while, [Nanyue] asked again, "Beyond this, what further words of instruction do you have? The Master said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
Someone remarked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. The National Teacher said, "That is still somewhat better. The Master said:

the curve is like a sickle for reaping grain. Later, when the Master resided at Mount Funiu, he ascended the hall and said, "This very mind is Buddha."
This is the phrase for one who is without illness seeking medicine; it is neither mind nor Buddha. This is the phrase for the remediation of medicine and illness.
A monk asked, "What is the phrase for being free and unencumbered? The Master said, "It has been transmitted from ancient times beneath Mount Funiu. He passed away at Kaiyuan Temple in Suizhou.
Chan Master Weikuan of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao was the son of the Zhu family of Xin’an, Quzhou.

At the age of thirteen, upon seeing those who were slaughtering living beings, he was struck with such compassion that he could not bear to eat meat; he therefore sought to leave the household life. Initially, he studied the *vinaya* and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Later, he visited Daji (Huairang) and attained the essential point of the mind. In the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang Dynasty, he began to propagate his teachings throughout the regions of Wu and Yue. Eight...
When he reached Poyang, a mountain deity requested to receive the eight precepts. In the thirteenth year [of his monastic life], he stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "A truly fine mountain. The monk said, "I am asking about the Way; why do you speak of a fine mountain?"
The Master said, "You only recognize fine mountains; when did you ever attain the Way? A monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
The Master said, "It has. The monk asked, "Does the Master have it? The Master said, "I do not. The monk asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
why alone do you lack it? The Master said, "I am not a sentient being. The monk asked, "If you are not a sentient being..."

"Are you not the Buddha? The Master said, "I am not the Buddha. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what thing are you? The Master said, "I am also not a thing. [The monk] asked, "Can you be seen or can you be conceived?
The Master said, "They cannot be reached by thought; they cannot be grasped by deliberation. Therefore, it is called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*).

In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital. The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Bai Juyi, once questioned him: [The text continues with the dialogue between Bai Juyi and the Master.]
[The questioner] said, "Since you are called a Chan Master, why do you preach the Dharma? The Master replied, "As for supreme Bodhi: when it is applied to the body, it is the Vinaya;
when spoken from the mouth, it is the Dharma; when practiced by the mind, it is Chan. These three are its applications, yet their ultimate aim is one.

It is like the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Han rivers, which each receive different names according to their location; though the names are not the same, the nature of the water is no different. The Vinaya is precisely this."

The Master said, “The mind is fundamentally without injury; why must it be repaired? Whether defiled or pure, do not give rise to any thoughts at all.
He asked, “If the defiled is not to be thought of, may the pure be thought of without thought? The Master said, “It is like a person’s eye...”
"A single thing cannot remain upon the eye. Though gold dust is a precious treasure, in the eye it becomes a disease.

[The student] asked, "If there is neither cultivation nor thought, how does this differ from that of an ordinary person? The Master said, "Ordinary persons possess ignorance (*avidyā*), while those of the Two Vehicles harbor attachment.
To be free from these two maladies is called true cultivation. One who truly cultivates must neither strive nor forget. To strive is to draw near to attachment."
To forget [this] is to fall into ignorance; this is the essential point of the mind, so it is said. A monk asked, "Where does the Way reside?
The Master said, "It is right before your eyes. The monk said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have the notion of 'I,' you do not see it.

The monk said, "If I have the notion of 'I,' then I do not see it; but does the Master see it? The Master said, "As long as there is 'you' and there is 'I,' we shall circle around each other without end."
[The Master] looked and said, "There is no self and no you; can you still see? The teacher replied, "With neither you nor me, who is there to seek to see?
On the final day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, having finished preaching the Dharma from the hall, he passed away. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dache.
Chan Master Wudeng of Ezhou was a native of Wei County. He left the household life at Mount Gonggong and received the essential points of the mind in secret.

Later, he went to reside at Tumen in Suizhou. One day, he visited the local governor, Attendant-in-Ordinary Wang. As the Master was about to depart and was leaving the gate, the Governor called out, "Ho-shang!

Chan Master Taiyu of Fuyong Mountain in Changzhou was the son of the Fan family of Jinling. Once, while serving food, he arrived before Layman Pang.
As the Layman reached out to receive it, the Master withdrew his hand and said, "To receive a gift with a conceptual mind was already rebuked by Vimalakīrti. Depart from this.
"One turn of the key. Layman, do you find this sweet? The layman said, "At that time, was Subhūti not a master of his craft? The Master said, "That has nothing to do with him.
The layman said, "When the food reached the edge of his mouth, it was snatched away by another. The Master then set down his food. The layman said, "One phrase would have sufficed.
The layman asked again, "As for the place where Master Madao truly benefited people—did he transmit it to our Master?"
The Master said, "I have not yet seen him; how can you know his point of ultimate reality? The Layman said, "As for this very seeing and knowing, there is nowhere to seek it.
The Master said, "Layman, you must not speak with one-sidedness. The Layman said, "If you speak with one-sidedness, you, Master, lose the essence.
If you speak from two sides or three sides, would you still be able to open your mouth, Master? The Master [remained silent].

He said, "It is simply that one cannot open one's mouth; this may be called 'reality' (shí). When the scholar clapped his hands and departed, [Zhi] returned to Qiyun during the Baoli era and entered nirvana.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dàbǎo.
Chan Master Daotong of Ziyu Mountain in Tangzhou was the son of the He family of Lujiang. Following his father while serving as an official in Quannan, he left home to become a monk.
He traveled to Jianyang to visit Mazu; when Mazu subsequently moved to Gonggong Mountain, the Master followed him there as well.
As the Patriarch was about to enter nirvana, he said to the Master, "There is a mountain where jade and stone are lush and the scenery is magnificent;

it will further your spiritual practice. When you encounter it, you may dwell there. The Master did not understand his words at the time. That autumn, while traveling through Luo, he returned to Tangzhou and saw a mountain to the west.

Its slopes were precipitous on all sides, and its peaks and ridges were exceptionally beautiful. He inquired of the local people, who told him it was Mount Ziyu. Thereupon, the Master ascended to the summit of the mountain.
Seeing a stone that was square and brilliant purple, he sighed and said, "This is indeed purple jade; it is the prophetic prediction of my former master.
He then trimmed the thatch to construct a hut and dwelt there. Later, disciples gathered from the four directions. A monk asked, "How can one escape the three realms?
The Master replied, "How long have you been inside them? The monk asked, "How does one achieve liberation?"

The Master said, "Green mountains do not obstruct the flight of white clouds. When Prime Minister Yu Di asked, "What is it like when black winds blow their ship and they drift down into the realm of rākṣasa demons? the Master said, "Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a thing?
Prime Minister Yu turned pale with fear. The Master then pointed and said, "This very thing is drifting down into the realm of rākṣasa demons."
The Duke asked again, "What is the Buddha? The Master called out, "Lord! The Duke responded. The Master said, "Do not seek anything else. When Yaoshan heard of this, he remarked, "Alas!

A man of the Yu clan has been buried alive within Mount Ziyu. Upon hearing this, the Duke went to visit Yaoshan. Yaoshan asked, "I have heard that you, Lord, are performing great Buddhist rites at Mount Ziyu; is this true?

The Duke replied, "I dare not say so," and then added, "I have heard that you have words to save me, so I have come here specifically today. Yaoshan said, "If you have any doubts, ask away. The Duke asked, "What is the Buddha? Yaoshan called out, "Yu Di! The Duke responded. Yaoshan said, "What is it? At these words, the Duke attained realization.
[There was a brief visit]. In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, when his disciple Jincang returned from visiting Baizhang, the Master said, "You have finally arrived;
this mountain now has its master. Having thus completed the formal entrustment (*parīndanā*), he took up his staff and departed directly for Xiangzhou.
The clergy and laity welcomed him there, and on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he passed away without illness.
Chan Master Yingfeng of Mount Wutai was the son of the Deng family from Shaowu Commandery (commonly known as Deng Yingfeng).

In his youth, he appeared to lack intelligence; consequently, his parents permitted him to leave the household life. He first traveled to the gate of Mazu, yet he was unable to perceive its profound depths. He subsequently went back and forth to Shitou;
although he did not achieve success on two occasions (as recorded in the section on Mazu), he later attained resonance with Mazu’s words. Thus it was with the Master.
He asked Shitou, "How can one attain accord with the Way? Shitou said, "I, too, do not accord with the Way. The Master said, "Ultimately, how is it?
Shitou said, "How long has it been since you were caught by this? While Shitou was weeding grass, the Master stood to his left with his hands folded.
Shitou threw his weeding tool toward the Master and weeded a blade of grass before him. The Master said, "And..."
Dongshan said, "You have only managed to weed this one; you have not managed to weed that one. Holding up his weeding tool, Dongshan presented it to the Master.
The Master took it and immediately made a gesture of weeding grass. Dongshan said, "You have only managed to weed that one;

you do not understand how to weed this one. The Master was speechless. (Dongshan remarked, "Is there still any mound left? One day, while the Master was pushing a cart, Mazu sat on the road with his legs outstretched. The Master...
The Master said, "I request that you withdraw your feet. The Patriarch replied, "What has been extended shall not be retracted. The Master said, "What has been advanced shall not be withdrawn.
Thereupon, he pushed the cart, which crushed the Patriarch's foot. The Patriarch returned to the Dharma Hall, grasped an axe, and said, "Come out, you who just now crushed the old monk's foot!
The Master then stepped forth before the Patriarch and held out his neck. The Patriarch then set down the axe. The Master went to Nanquan and beheld the assembly.
During a formal visit by the assembly, Xuanquan pointed to a water pitcher and said, "The copper pitcher is an object. There is water within it;
do not disturb the object, but bring me some water, old monk. The Master picked up the pitcher and poured the water directly onto Xuanquan’s face. At that, Xuanquan ceased his questioning.
Later, the Master arrived at Mt. Gui. He entered the hall and, at the head of the upper platform, unfastened his robes and bowl.
Hearing that his "uncle" had arrived, Guishan first assumed a dignified demeanor and descended from the hall to meet him. Upon seeing him coming, the Master made a gesture of lying down.
Guishan then returned to his quarters. The Master departed. A short while later, Guishan asked his attendant, "Is my uncle still here? The attendant replied, "He has already left."
Miaoyan asked, "What words did you have when you left? The Master said, "I had no words. Miaoyan said, "Do not say there were no words; that sound was like thunder.
The Master resided at Mount Heng during the winter and stayed at Qingliang during the summer. During the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled repeatedly to Mount Wutai.

On his way, he passed through Huaisi, where Wu Yuanji was obstructing the military path and defying the imperial mandate. The government troops and the rebel forces were engaged in combat. Before long—
The two sides were engaged in combat. The Master said, "I shall go and resolve this calamity. He then cast his *śikya* staff into the air and flew over it.
The generals and soldiers of both armies looked up in awe; the event corresponded exactly with their prior dreams, and their hearts to fight instantly subsided.

Having manifested such supernatural wonders, the Master feared they would delude the masses, so he entered Mount Wutai. Before entering the Vajra Cave to demonstrate his passing, he first asked the assembly: "All of you..."

Regarding the manner of passing away—whether sitting, lying down, or standing—I have personally witnessed it. "Is there also such a thing as passing away while standing? he asked. "There is," they replied.
"Is there anyone who passes away while standing on their head? he asked. "I have never seen such a thing," they replied. The Master then stood on his head and passed away;

he remained perfectly upright, his robes falling naturally over his body. At that time, the assembly discussed carrying him to the cremation ground, but he remained motionless. People from near and far came to gaze upon him.
They marveled at this beyond measure. The Master had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also there at that time.

She patted him and rebuked him, saying, "Old brother, you did not follow the laws and precepts in life, yet after death you continue to delude people. She then pushed him with her hand, and he fell down dead.
Thereupon, his body was cremated, and his relics were collected to build a stupa.
A monk asked Chan Master Dashan (also written as Longshan) of Tanzhou, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, “The rooster crowing on a spring day. The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “The dog barking on the Mid-Autumn festival.
He ascended the hall and said, “Come forth, come forth! I have a vital teaching; after my passing, it shall not trouble you. The assembly said, “We pray you, grant it to us.”
The Master said, "It will not take more than a single pile of fire.
Chan Master Wuliao of Guiyang in Quanzhou was the son of the Shen family of that prefecture. At the age of seven, his father took him to Baizhang Monastery;
he regarded it as his own home and consequently renounced worldly attachments. When he reached eighteen, he received the tonsure and the full precepts at Lingyan Monastery.

Later, he visited Daji (Mazu Daoyi) and attained a thorough understanding of the ancestral vehicle. He then returned to the north of his original monastery, where the paths for gathering firewood had long been abandoned.
One day, the Master set out with his staff, pushing through the thickets, when he encountered a giant six-eyed tortoise;

in an instant, it vanished. He subsequently built a hermitage on this peak, which was consequently named Guiyang (Tortoise Pond). One day, a tiger chasing a deer entered the hermitage; the Master warded off the tiger with his staff, and thus [the deer] was saved.
Luk-ming (Ruru-jīva), as he was about to manifest his passing into nirvana, composed a verse, saying: "For eighty years I have distinguished east from west;
Now I need no more this white-haired old man. Neither long nor short, neither large nor small— It is identical to the nature of all beings.
Without coming, without going, and without abiding, I have realized that the original self-nature is empty. Having finished the verse, he passed away peacefully. He was interred at...
The main hall had stood for nearly twenty years when it was submerged by mountain waters. A disciple opened the stupa and saw the entire body floating in the water.
Upon hearing of this, the King of Min sent an envoy to carry the remains into the palace courtyard for veneration. Suddenly, a foul odor wafted from afar.

The King burned incense and prayed, saying, "May you return to your former site at Guiyang to have a stupa built. As soon as he finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance permeated everywhere. The entire [assembly]...
He went to the capital to pay his respects. The local governor memorialized the court, and he was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Zhenji (True Quiescence).

His stupa was named Lingjue (Numinous Awakening). Later, his disciple Huizhong was buried to the left of the stupa. Today, the two *dharmakāya* relics remain at Guiyang. Huizhong received the Dharma from Master Yiyuan of Ca’ān.
Chan Master Tanzang of the West Garden Hermitage on Mount Nanyue received the mind-seal from Daji. Later, he visited Shitou, where his realization became brilliantly clear and penetrating.

He subsequently went to reside at the West Garden, and his circle of dharma companions flourished daily. One day, while the Master was bathing by himself, a monk asked, "Why do you not have a novice attend to this?

The Master clapped his hands three times. (The monk reported this to Caoshan, who said, "In one sense, it is equally clapping and patting the hands; however, among them, the West Garden [is supreme]. )

How strange! Zhizhigui’s "one-finger Zen" was likely due to his failure to grasp the matter with complete clarity. Later, a monk asked Caoshan, "When Xiyuan clapped his hands, was that not the business of slaves and servants? Caoshan said, "Yes. The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this?

Caoshan said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the matter above this? Caoshan shouted, "You slave and servant! The Master kept a dog. Whenever he practiced walking meditation at night, [the dog would follow him].
The dog bit the Master’s robe, whereupon the Master immediately returned to his quarters. Furthermore, it would often crouch and guard by the side of the gate.
Suddenly one night, it barked repeatedly, leaping up and assuming the posture of a fierce bite. At dawn the following day, there was a large python in the eastern kitchen, several *zhang* in length.
The serpent opened its mouth and hissed; its poisonous flames blazed fiercely. An attendant requested that he move away from it, but the Master said, "Can death be escaped?
It comes with poison, but I receive it with compassion. Poison has no inherent nature; it becomes potent only when provoked.

If compassion is truly unconditional, then enemies and kin are of one essence. Having spoken these words, the python lowered its head and moved slowly away, suddenly vanishing from sight. Again, one night, a group of...
The thief arrived, and the dog likewise bit at his clothes. The Master said to the thief, "In this thatched hut there is whatever you find pleasing; feel free to take it all away.
I shall never begrudge you anything. Touched by these words, the thief bowed his head in reverence and departed.
Chan Master Zhentou of Yangqi Mountain in Yuanzhou ascended the hall and said: "The myriad spirits share a single source; they are provisionally named 'Buddha.

Though their substance is exhausted and their forms dissolve, they do not perish; though the metal melts and the raw ore disperses, they always remain. In the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, the golden waves surge of themselves;

in the spiritual mind, where all distinctions cease, the ten thousand phenomena are simultaneously illumined. One who realizes this principle does not need to speak to traverse the sands of the world-systems."
Without being employed, its function further deepens the mysterious transformation. How can one turn one's back on awakening and instead unite with worldly toil?
Within the aggregates and realms, one falsely imprisons and clings to oneself. Chan Yue asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master held up his rosary. Chan Yue was at a loss. The Master said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "I have studied under Shitou. [Chan Yue] said, "I see."
"What meaning has Shitou attained? The Master pointed to the deer in the courtyard and said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "It has attained freedom.
He passed away in the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty. Upon cremation, seven hundred grains of *śarīra* were obtained.
A stupa was built at the foot of East Peak.
Zen Master Shenzang of Maitou Peak in Cizhou ascended the hall and said: "To know while being without knowing—this is not a state of non-knowing;

yet it is called 'non-knowing. He then descended from his seat. (Nanquan said: "If one follows the Master's path in this way, one has only spoken half the truth. Huangbo said: "It is not that Nanquan refutes him; he wishes to complete the previous statement.")
Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin in Tanzhou constantly carried a mendicant’s staff. At night, he would go out among the forest thickets;

every seven steps he would shake his staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once. Jia Shan asked him, "I have heard from afar that you, Master, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara—is this true?"
The Master said, “Indeed. Xiangshan asked, “What is it like when one is already mounted upon the head? The Master said, “If you put your head out, I will let you mount it;
if you do not put your head out, what is there to mount? Xiangshan was speechless. A monk came to attend upon him; as he was unfolding his sitting cloth, the Master said, “Slowly, slowly!
The monk asked, “What do you see, Preceptor? The Master said, “It is a pity! You have smashed the bell tower. From this, the monk attained awakening. (Observation)
The Provincial Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Do you have any attendants?
The Master replied, "There are one or two, but they cannot see guests. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng!
At that moment, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage. Pei was struck with terror upon seeing them. The Master said to the two tigers, "A guest is here; depart now."
The two tigers roared and departed. Pei asked, "What kind of practice did you master, Master, that you were moved to such an extent?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara."
The monk Shuitang of Tingzhou asked Guizong, "What kind of person are you? Guizong replied, "A man from Chenzhou. The master asked, "How old are you? Guizong said, "Twenty-two.
The master asked, "Before you were born, where did this old monk go and come from? Guizong said, "[I was already here]."
"When was the Master born? The Master held up his whisk. Zong said, "How could this have a birth?
The Master said, "If you understand it, there is no birth. Zong said, "I do not yet understand. The Master remained silent.
A monk asked Master Mengxi, "What is it like when not a single thought arises? The Master remained silent for a long while. The monk then bowed. The Master said, "How do you understand this?
The monk replied, "I truly cannot bear to be without a sense of shame. The Master said, "You have indeed gained sufficient faith.
Another asked, "How does one realize the fundamental matter? The Master said, "Why do you not ask me? The monk said, "Please, Master, [explain it]."
The Master replied, "You have asked well. The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master said, "Only this monk is truly sharp-witted.
Another monk came from outside; the Master immediately shouted at him. The monk said, "What a fine occasion! The Master said, "He still requires a blow of the staff.
The monk said, "Take care," and departed. The Master said, "He has attained true mastery."
Whenever Master Fozha of Wenzhou saw someone coming, he would strike the ground with his staff and say, "The Buddhas of the past were like this;
the Buddhas of the future will be like this. A monk asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The Master drew a circle.
A monk performed a woman’s bow. The Master struck him. The monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Thief! Thief!
The monk asked, "What is the 'different kind' (heterogeneous)? The Master struck the bowl and said, "Huanu, Huanu, come eat your rice!"
The two senior monks, Xuán and Shào, visited Master Wujou. The Master asked, "Where have you two Zen travelers set out from?
Xuán replied, "Jiangxi. The Master struck him. Xuán said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a vital pivot. The Master said:

Since you do not understand, that monk behind you is merely looking on. As Shao was about to step forward, the Master struck him and said, "I know for certain there is no difference in the soil within the same pit.
Go to the hall. He then asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Dingzhou. The Master said, "How is the Dharma-way of Dingzhou compared to here?
The monk replied, "It is no different. The Master said, "If it is no different, then go back there."
[The Master] struck him. The monk said, "There are eyes at the tip of the staff; one must not strike people so recklessly.
The Master said, "Today I have hit one indeed," and struck him three more times. The monk then went out. The Master said, "It turns out there was someone to eat this 'bent' staff.
[The monk] said, "But the handle of the ladle is still in the hands of the Master. The Master said, "If you want it, I, the mountain monk—"
[The monk] returned it to him. The monk stepped forward, snatched the staff, and struck the Master three times. The Master said, "A wasted blow! A wasted blow!

The monk said, "There is someone here who has eaten [of the Dharma]. The Master said, "In a flurry, I have struck this fellow. The monk bowed and departed. The Master said, "He can take it! He can take it!
The monk laughed loudly and went out. The Master said, "He can take it! He can take it!"
