The Master remained silent. A monk asked, "What is Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles. The monk asked, "What is Avalokiteśvara?
The Master said, "Sounds and speech. The monk asked, "What is Samantabhadra? The Master said, "The minds of sentient beings."

[The student] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "It is the physical body of sentient beings. [The student] asked, "Since the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical, why are there various names?
The Master said, "Returning to the source through the faculty of the eye is named Mañjuśrī; returning to the source through the faculty of the ear is named Avalokiteśvara;
returning to the source through the mind is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Avalokiteśvara...
Sound is the Buddha’s unconditioned great compassion; Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous, unconditioned practice;
the Three Sages are the Buddha’s wondrous function; and the Buddha is the true essence of the Three Sages. In terms of function, there are as many provisional names as there are sands in the Ganges;
in terms of essence, they are collectively named the One Bhagavān. Question: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. How is this principle to be understood? The Master said: "Listen."

The Old Monk’s Verse: Where there is obstruction, it is not the wall; where there is penetration, it is not empty space. If one understands in this way, mind and form are fundamentally the same. It is also said:
Buddha-nature is majestically manifest, yet sentient beings dwelling within its nature find it difficult to see.
If you awaken to the selflessness of sentient beings, how does my face differ from the Buddha’s face? Question: Regarding the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses...
In the end, there is no substantial entity. How, then, can it be said that the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom?

The Master shows a verse: "The seven arise dependent on the one; the one ceases while sustaining the seven. When the one ceases, they too cease; the six and the seventh never again undergo transition. Question:
An earthworm was cut into two segments; both ends moved. [The student] asked, "I do not know in which end the Buddha-nature resides.

The Master said, "Why do you engage in such deluded thinking? He replied, "What can be done about its movement? The Master said, "Do you not know that the elements of fire and wind have not yet dispersed? [The student] asked.
"How can one transform mountains, rivers, and the land so that they return to oneself? The Master said, "How can one transform oneself so that it becomes mountains, rivers, and the land?
[The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Under the city walls of Hunan, the people are well-nourished;

rice is cheap and firewood is plentiful, sufficient for all neighbors. The monk was speechless. The Master then presented this verse: "Who asks how mountains and rivers are transformed? Mountains and rivers are transformed."
"To whom? "Perfect penetration has no two sides; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) fundamentally has no place of return.

The Master of the Avataṃsaka asked: "Is space definitively existent, or is it definitively non-existent? The Master said: "To say it exists is permissible; to say it does not exist is also permissible.

When space exists, it is merely a provisional existence; when space does not exist, it is merely the absence of provisional existence. [The Master of the Avataṃsaka] said: "According to what the Master has said, it exists..."
"What are the scriptural passages? The Master said: "Virtuous One, have you not heard what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says?

'The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky. Is this not to say that when empty space arises, it merely gives rise to a provisional name? Furthermore, it says:
'If even one person among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away. Is this not so?"
"It is not that when empty space is extinguished, only conventional designations are extinguished. This is why the Old Monk says: 'Existence is conventional existence;
non-existence is conventional non-existence. He asked again: "The Sūtra says, 'As if within pure lapis lazuli, the image of true gold appears. What is the meaning of this? The Master said:
"Take pure lapis lazuli as the substance of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and take the image of true gold as the substance of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna)."
It can give rise to wisdom. Wisdom can penetrate the essence; therefore, it is said that within pure lapis lazuli, the image of true gold appears.
Question: What is the sphere of activity for those of the highest rank? The Master said: It is like the eyes of a dead man. Question: When those of the highest rank meet one another, what is it like?
The Master said: It is like the hands of a dead man. Question: Why did Sudhana travel through the universe for immeasurable kalpas?
“Does the body of Samantabhadra not pervade the worlds? The Master said, “From immeasurable kalpas past, have you ever traveled everywhere?
He replied, “What is the body of Samantabhadra? The Master said, “Seeking Chang’an while inside the Han-yuan Hall. He asked, “What is the mind of a student?
The Master said, “The entire world of the ten directions is your mind. He said, “If that is so, then for me as a student...”
“Is this where you place your body? The Master said, “This is where you place your body. [The monk] asked, “What is the place where one places the body?

The Master said, “The waters of the great ocean—deep and ever deeper. [The monk] said, “I do not understand, Teacher. The Master said, “Fish and dragons come and go; they rise and sink as they please.
[Another] asked, “When someone asks the Master, you answer according to the causes and conditions. But when no one asks the Master, what then?”
The Master said, "When weary, one sleeps; when vigorous, one rises. A monk asked, "How should a student understand this?
The Master said, "In summer, one is bare-boned; in winter, one must have a robe. A monk asked, "Where does a deceased monk go after passing away? The Master showed him a verse, saying:
"Unaware of the diamond body, Yet calling it dependently arisen. The ten directions are truly quiescent; Who is there, and who departs?"
"Who is practicing? The Master praised Nanquan Zhen, saying: "Majestic is Nanquan, the source of the three periods. The Vajra is eternally abiding; throughout the ten directions it is boundless.
Birth and Buddhahood are inexhaustible; having manifested, they return once more. Having long relied upon Nanquan, there is a verse of seizing the opportunity which says:
'Today I return home and enter the great gate; Nanquan’s direct path pervades heaven and earth. Every dharma is distinct and clear.'"
The Patriarch turned his head and said with shame, "What fine descendants! Nanquan replied, "Today’s opportune matter need not be discussed.
Nanquan does not say it pervades the entire universe; returning home is entirely the business of descendants, for the patriarch has never gone out the door."
The Verse on Encouraging Study says: "Even atop a ten-thousand-fathom pole, one must not rest; Majestic is the path, yet few travel it. May you, O Chan Master, reach Nanquan;
Before your eyes, ten thousand autumns of green mountains. Linji said: "Upon this lump of red flesh, there is a true person of no rank.
The Master [Zhaozhou] then composed a verse: "The myriad dharmas are as one; there is no need for selection. If they are as one, who..."
Whether one discriminates or does not discriminate, this very life-and-death is fundamentally bodhi; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time share this same eye.
A verse on the admonition against cutting pines and bamboos says: "A thousand-year bamboo, a ten-thousand-year pine— Branch by branch, leaf by leaf, they are all the same.
I inform you, seekers of the profound from the four quarters: To raise your hand is nothing other than touching the Patriarch."

When the Monk of Caishan Mountain at Ezhou first resided at Huguo Monastery in Suizhou, he ascended the hall and held up a piece of bamboo, saying, "Is there anyone who can drive a wedge into empty space?
At that time, the Senior Seat-holder Lingxu stepped forward from the assembly and said:
"Empty space is the stake. The Master threw down a bamboo staff and descended from his seat. Zhaozhou went to Yunju, who said, "You are old and decrepit;
why do you not seek a place to stay? Zhaozhou replied, "Where could I possibly stay? Yunju said, "In front of the mountain there is the site of an old temple.
Zhaozhou said, "Venerable Sir, you may take it for yourself. Later, he arrived at the Master’s [Baizhang’s] place. The Master said, "You are old and decrepit."
"Why do you not seek a place to stay? Zhaozhou asked. "Where would you stay? the Master said. "Old as you are," Zhaozhou remarked, "you do not even know where to stay.
Zhaozhou said, "For thirty years I have been riding horses, but today I have been thrown by a donkey" (Yunju Xi said:
"Where is the place where Zhaozhou was thrown by a donkey?"). While the assembly of monks stood in attendance, the Master said, "Just standing here like this, there is no place to speak."
A fit of frustration. As the monk prepared to ask a question, the Master struck him and said, "Exerting one's utmost for the sake of the assembly," and then entered the abbot’s quarters.
A novice attendant came to visit; the Master asked, "Have you been to see Zhaozhou? The attendant replied, "Does the Master dare to say so?
The Master said, "Not only Zuyuyu, but no one at all can say it. The attendant said, "May the Master let me pass? The Master said, "Here..."

[The Master] said, "In the past, you were not attuned to human feelings. [The monk] replied, "Nevertheless, compassion still remains. The Master then struck him and said, "I shall act for your sake once you have awakened.
Chan Master Lizong of Zihu Rock in Quzhou was a native of Dancheng; his secular surname was Zhou, and he was from Kaiyuan Temple in Youzhou.

He left home to become a monk at a temple and received full ordination according to his age. Later, he entered the quarters of Nanquan. Subsequently, he traveled to Matishan in Quzhou, where he settled in a thatched hut for his residence.
In the second year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, a local resident named Weng Qiangui offered the Zihu (Son’s Lake) area below the mountain and established a monastery there.
The Master hung a signboard at the entrance that read: "At Zihu there is a dog; it seizes people's heads."
He seizes people by their hearts; he seizes people by their feet. To hesitate for even a moment is to lose one’s body and life. Two monks from Linji’s assembly came to visit;
as they were just lifting the curtain, the Master shouted, “Look out for the dog! The monks looked back, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.

While plowing the garden with Master Shengguang, the Master suddenly pressed down on his hoe; looking back at Guang, he said, “The matter is not non-existent, but as soon as you conceive a thought, it is already gone.”
"Go. Guang then asked, "What is the matter? The Master stepped forward, caught him by the chest, and kicked him down. From this, he attained realization.
When the nun arrived for an audience, the Master said, "Are you not Liu Tiemo? She replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Turn left? Turn right? She replied, "..."
"Preceptor, do not be so confused. The Master then struck him. That night, the Master cried out in front of the Sangha Hall, "Thief!
Thief! The assembly was all startled. A monk came out from within the hall; the Master seized him and said, "Vina, you have caught him!
You have caught him! The monk replied, "It is not I. The Master said, "It is indeed I, but it is simply that you are unwilling to take responsibility for it."
He addressed the assembly in verse, saying: "For thirty years I have dwelt at Zihu; The strength of my coarse gruel and rice at the two meals is sufficient.

When there is nothing to do, I go up the mountain for a stroll; I ask you, people of this age, do you understand? During the Guangming era, he returned to his final resting place without illness. He was interred in a stupa on the mountain where he resided.
Chan Master Tanzhao of Baima in Jingnan used to say constantly, "How happy! How happy!
When the time of his death arrived, he cried out, "Suffering! Suffering! He further said, "King Yama has come to take me away.
The head monk asked, "When you were thrown into the water by the Regional Commander, your countenance remained unmoved; why now are you acting like this? The Master raised his pillow.
The Master said, "You say that it was so at that time; is it so now? The head of the monastery had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf: "At such a time, simply cover your ears and leave.")
When National Teacher Yunji of Zhongnan Mountain first visited Nanquan, he asked, "The *maṇi* jewel is not recognized by people;
it is personally held within the *tathāgatagarbha*. What is this *garbha*? Nanquan said, "That which comes and goes with you is it. The Master said, "What about that which does not come and go?
Nanquan said, "That too is it. [The Master] asked, "What is the jewel? Nanquan called out, "National Teacher! The Master immediately realized his meaning.
The Master assented. Quan said, "Go. You do not understand my words. From this, the Master entered into faith.

Later, when Chan Master Yidu of Xiangyan in Dengzhou ascended the hall, he said, "Brothers, since we have not yet reached full realization ourselves, what business is there for us to discuss together?
In three or five days, I shall depart. Those who study now must reach realization."
Set aside the present moment. Do not merely crave the "nothingness" of those superior men.
Brothers, even if you manage to learn all manner of diverse paths of meaning, it will never substitute for your own personal realization; you must ultimately exert effort to attain it.
Merely memorizing others' clever phrases will only cause you to become increasingly confused. If you wish to achieve accord with the Way, simply be as humble and respectful as possible.
"Do not linger for even a hair’s breadth; be directly like empty space, and only then will you have a small measure of it.
For empty space has no locks or bolts, no walls or barriers, no form or segments, and no eyes or mind. At that time, a monk asked, "When the ancients met one another, how was it?
The Master said, "I have never seen the ancients. The monk asked, "How can we look up to and admire the place where the life-lineage remains unbroken in the present day?"
The Master said, "What is there to admire? The monk asked, "I am not asking about idle matters;
I ask the Master to provide an answer. The Master said, "What more do you seek from me? The monk said, "It is not for idle matters. The Master said, "Then you are instructing me to speak.
He then continued, "Brothers, the Buddha is dust; the Dharma is dust. You spend your whole days racing and seeking; what rest can there be? Simply at this moment—"
In the midst [of practice], do not allow sentiment to hang upon you; let sentiment not hang upon things. There is no good to be grasped, and no evil to be discarded.

Do not let yourself be caged or shrouded by them—this is the true place of study. A question was asked: "I once took leave of an elder master, who said to me, 'Go and associate with virtuous companions and attach yourself to good friends.
Now I take leave of the Master; I do not know what instructions he may have for me. The Master said: "Pay your respects."
[The Master] prostrated. The monk bowed. The Master said, "As for bowing, feel free to bow; you must not mistake a servant for a lord.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the direct source? The Master then cast down his staff and immediately returned to his quarters.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence, there is a path. This old monk’s mouth is too narrow;
I cannot explain it to you. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, a monk asked: "For what reason is there nothing at all?

The Master replied: "I have never paused. He then continued: "Even if one were to strip away layer after layer until everything is exhausted and nothing remains to linger upon, [this is merely] provisional..."
"Provisioning at the time" is also a skillful means for guiding people; it is impossible that it could be a matter of "that side.
Chan Master Xian of Lingjiu in Chi Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "This is the fundamental task of you all.
If I were to instruct you on it myself, it would be like drawing legs on a snake. At that time, a monk asked: "I do not ask about 'drawing legs on a snake'; how [is it]?"
"This is the fundamental matter," the Master said. "Venerable, try to speak on it. When the monk was about to ask again, the Master said, "Why do you paint the feet?
Master Mingshui asked, "What is the sudden attainment of the Dharmakāya? The Master replied, "Once you have passed through the Dragon Gate, look toward the clouds beyond;
do not be a fish that strikes its forehead against the Yellow River. Yangshan asked, "In the state of profound stillness and wordlessness, how can there be seeing and hearing?"
The Master said, "Before the seamless stupa, there is much rainwater. A monk asked, "What is it like when both of them remain silent? The Master said, "It is the constant.
The monk asked, "Is there anything that transcends the constant? The Master said, "There is. The monk said, "Please, Master, proclaim it for us.
The Master said, "The mysterious pearl shines of itself; why need one seek light from outside the wall? A monk asked, "Today we offer sustenance to the Great Master Wuran of West River."
“Is it not yet certain whether he will return? The Master said, “Originally there was nowhere to go; how could he now be turned by the wind?
[The monk] asked, “If that is so, what is the use of making offerings? The Master said, “Exertion and conditioned effort do not interfere with the nature of ultimate meaning.”
A monk asked the Venerable Master of Mount Song at Luojing, “When the ancient path is level and open, what then? The Master said, “It does not proceed forward.
The monk asked, “Why does it not proceed forward? The Master said, “Because there is no place of obstruction. [The monk] asked, “What is the realm of Mount Song? The Master said:
“The sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west. The student said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “I do not understand ‘east’ or ‘west’ either.
A question was asked: “What is it like when the six consciousnesses arise together? The Master said, “Different. The student asked, “Why is it so? The Master said, “The same.”
When Master Rizi was visited by Yaxi for an audience, the Master made a gesture as if rising. Yaxi said, "This old mountain ghost still sees me here.
The Master said, "My fault, my fault; just now I failed to respond properly. As Yaxi was about to offer a word, the Master gave a shout.
Yaxi said, "Facing a great battle array, it is indeed difficult to withstand. The Master said, "It is so, it is so. Yaxi said, "It is not so."
"Not so" (Zhaozhou said: "Pitiful, these two fellows; they do not know the phrase for turning back"). A monk asked West Chan Abbot of Suzhou:
"I do not ask about the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. What is the very intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master raised his whisk and showed it to him. The monk did not prostrate and departed. He went on to study further.
Xuefeng asked him, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Zhejiang. Xuefeng said, "Where were you this summer?
The monk replied, "At Xichan. Xuefeng asked, "Is the Master there well? The monk replied, "When I arrived, he was in full health. Xuefeng said, "Why did you not stay there at your leisure?
The monk replied, "I have not yet clarified the Buddha-dharma. Xuefeng asked, "What is the matter? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Xuefeng said, "You..."
"How is it that you do not accept him? [The monk] said, "He is an object. Feng said, "Do you see the men and women in the houses within the city of Suzhou?
[The monk] said, "I see them. Feng said, "Do you see the trees, groves, ponds, and marshes along the road? [The monk] said, "I see them.
Feng said, "In seeing all these people in the houses, as well as the vast earth, forests, and marshes—is this entirely an 'object'? Do you accept this? [The monk] said, "I accept it. Feng said:
"As for raising the whisk—why do you not accept it? The monk bowed and said, "I, your disciple, have spoken thoughtlessly;
I beg the Master’s compassion. Feng said, "The entire universe is this single eye.
Where will you sit and squat? The monk was speechless.
The Grand Master Lu Xing, the Prefectural Governor of Xuancheng, asked Nanquan: "An ancient once raised a gander in a bottle.
As the gander grew larger, it could no longer get out of the bottle. Now, one must not break the bottle, nor may one harm the gander.
How would you have it come out, Master? Nanquan called out, "Grand Master! Lu responded, "Yes. Nanquan said, "It has come out. From this, Lu attained awakening. Immediately—
He paid his respects with a formal expression of gratitude. When Nanquan passed away, the Abbot of the monastery asked, "Why does the Great Official not weep for the late Master?
Lu said, "If the Abbot can speak, then I shall weep. The Abbot was unable to respond. (Changqing spoke on his behalf, saying: "Should one weep, or should one not weep?")

One day, the lay practitioner Gan-zhi of Chizhou entered Nanquan’s hall to provide a vegetarian feast. Huangbo was serving as the head seat (shouzuo). The practitioner requested that alms be distributed.
The head seat said, "The two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are equal and without distinction.

Gan-zhi said, "If you speak thus, how can you deserve my offering? He then took [the offering] and went out. A short while later, he re-entered and said, "Please distribute the material wealth. The head seat said, "Material wealth and the Dharma..."

The two patrons were equal and made no distinction between them; Gan then distributed the alms-food. On another day, Gan entered the monastery to provide a gruel offering and invited Nanquan to recite the scriptures.
Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the sake of the wildcat and the white ox.
Gan then brushed out his sleeves and departed. After the gruel meal, Nanquan asked the head cook, "Where has the practitioner gone?"
Zuo said, "He would have gone right then and there. Quan immediately smashed the cooking pot. Gan Chang received visitors and travelers;
once, a monk asked him, "It is no easy matter for you, practitioner, to receive guests. Gan replied, "It is like feeding donkeys and horses. The monk then desisted.
There was a monk living in a hermitage who was soliciting alms for household goods. Gan said, "I have a question. If you can answer it, I shall give you the gift.

He then wrote the character for "mind" (心) and asked, "What word is this? The monk replied, "The character for 'mind'. Gan then asked his wife, "What word is this? His wife replied, "The character for 'mind'."
Gan said, "My wife should also live in this hermitage. The monk remained silent, and Gan likewise offered nothing.
He then asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Mount Gui. Gan said, "Once a monk asked Mount Gui, 'What is the meaning of the West?
Mount Gui raised his whisk. How do you understand Mount Gui's meaning? The monk said:

"Using events to clarify the mind; attaching to objects to manifest the principle. Gan said, "It would be better to return to Mount Miao for now. (Upon hearing this, Baofu raised his hands and then covered them with his palms.)
Master An of Yanguan was a successor of Chan Master Chang of Guannan in Xiangzhou. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the West? The Master raised his staff.

He asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. The Master then struck him. Whenever he saw a monk come to pay his respects, he would mostly drive him away with his staff, sometimes saying, "You are one moment late," or "This strikes the drum of Guannan. Yet among his contemporaries, few were able to respond in kind.

When Chan Master Xuanzhen of Shuangling in Hongzhou first asked Wuduo, "Why is it that the footprints of the Bodhisattva Without Supernatural Powers are difficult to find? Wuduo said, "Only those who walk the same path know. The Master said, "Does the Master know them? Wuduo said: [He does not. The Master said: [I do not know either. Wuduo said: [If you do not know, how can you say you walk the same path? The Master said: [I do not say so. Wuduo said: [Then why did you ask me just now? The Master said: [Because I have no other way. Wuduo said: [If you had no other way, why would you have come here? The Master said: [I did not come for the sake of this question. Wuduo said: [If you did not come for the sake of this question, then what did you come for? The Master said: [I came to see the Master. Wuduo said: [If you came to see me, why did you ask about the Bodhisattva Without Supernatural Powers? The Master said: [I asked because I wished to see the Master's true face. Wuduo said: [If you wish to see my true face, you must look at your own face. The Master said: [I have looked at my own face, but I do not see it. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that asks the question? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I ask. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that answers? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I answer. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that knows? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I know. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that does not know? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I do not know. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is neither knowing nor not knowing? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am neither knowing nor not knowing. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is beyond both knowing and not knowing? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am beyond both knowing and not knowing. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the ultimate reality? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the ultimate reality. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the Buddha-nature? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the Buddha-nature. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the Way? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the Way. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the Patriarch? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the Patriarch. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the disciple? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the disciple. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the teacher? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the teacher. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the master? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the master. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the student? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the student. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who has attained the Way? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the one who has attained the Way. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who has not yet attained the Way? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the one who has not yet attained the Way. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is neither attaining nor not attaining the Way? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the one who is neither attaining nor not attaining the Way. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who transcends all attainment and non-attainment? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the one who transcends all attainment and non-attainment. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the Dharma? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the Dharma. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the person? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the person. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the mind? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the mind. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the nature? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the nature. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the body? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the body. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the world? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the world. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the universe? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the universe. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of all phenomena? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of all phenomena. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the absolute? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the absolute. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the relative? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the relative. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of both the absolute and the relative? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of both the absolute and the relative. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of neither the absolute nor the relative? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of neither the absolute nor the relative. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the unconditioned? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the unconditioned. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of the conditioned? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of the conditioned. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of both the conditioned and the unconditioned? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of both the conditioned and the unconditioned. Wuduo said: [If you do not see it, then who is it that is the one who is the very essence of neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned? The Master said: [It is precisely because I do not see it that I am the very essence of neither the
[The monk] did not understand. The Master said, "Why do you not understand? [The monk] replied, "Go away! You do not recognize my words.
Later, [the monk] realized the essential meaning under Master Yanguan.
Chan Master Jiǎnzōng of Jìngshān in Hángzhōu was the son of the Qián clan of Húzōu. He left home life under the Venerable Gāoxián of Kāiyuán Monastery in his native prefecture;
he mastered the *Sīyì jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) and the Pure Land teachings. Later, he went to Yànhuán to resolve his lingering doubts and obscurities.

In the third year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, he resided at Mount Jing. He had a junior disciple named Hongxin (Hongxin was Master Fajie), who took pride in his skill in lecturing and debate.

The Master said to him: "The true Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is direct and beyond verbal expression. Your calculation of grains of sand in the ocean—what benefit does this have for the ultimate principle?
If you can simply refrain from clinging to knowledge and views, extinguish all external conditions, and detach from every state of mind, that is your own true nature. Hongxin [was thus enlightened].

At a loss for words, he then paid his respects and took his leave. Traveling to various regions, he eventually reached Mount Wei, where he finally awakened to the profound essence [of the Dharma]. He subsequently became a successor to the Master of Mount Wei.
In the seventh year of the Xiantong era, he passed away; he was posthumously titled the Great Master Wushang (Supreme).
Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Furong in Fuzhou was a successor of Chan Master Guizong Chang. When he first visited Guizong, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Guizong replied:
"I have spoken to you; will you believe me? He replied, "If it is the Honored One’s sincere word, how would I dare not believe?
Zhong said, "It is you yourself. The Master asked, "How do you maintain this? Zhong said, "A single speck of film in the eye causes empty flowers to fall in confusion" (Fayan said:

"If there were no subsequent words, how could there be a 'returning to the source'?"). The Master took his leave. Zhong asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going back to the Lingnan mountains."
Zhong said, "You have been here for many years; now that you have finished your preparations, come and let me explain the Buddha-dharma to you.
The Master (Huichao) packed his belongings and ascended the mountain. Zhong said, "Come closer. The Master approached him. Zhong said, "The weather is cold; take care on your journey.
Upon hearing these words, the Master suddenly forgot his former understanding and entered *nirvāṇa*. He was posthumously titled Great Master Hongzhao.

A monk came from Jia Shan to pay his respects to National Teacher Gaoting of Hanning. The Master struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects; why do you strike me?
The monk bowed again, and the Master struck him once more and drove him away. When the monk returned, he related this to Jia Shan.
Jia Shan asked, "Did you understand? The monk replied, "I did not. Jia Shan said, "It is fortunate that you do not understand. Had you understood, then..."
At the mouth of the mountain pass, the Mute One.
Master Daemao of Silla ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to know the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance.
If you wish to know the eternally abiding, undecaying nature, recognize it in the midst of the shifting and changing of all things. A monk asked: "What is..."
At Dameao Jing, the Master said, "The blade is not revealed. [A monk] asked, "Why is the blade not revealed? The Master said, "Because there is no one who can meet it.
Chan Master Zhītōng of Wǔtái Mountain (who called himself Dàchánfó) was formerly in the assembly of Guīzōng. One night, he suddenly cried out repeatedly, saying, "I have attained great enlightenment!
The community was startled by this. The next day, when the assembly had gathered for the hall discourse, Guīzōng said, "Last night, [Zhītōng]..."
The monk who had attained realization came forward. Master [Zhao]zhou stepped out and said, "I am here. Yunmen Zong said, "What principle have you seen that you speak of 'great enlightenment'?
Try to explain it to me. The master replied, "A nun was originally made by a woman. Zong was struck with wonder. The master then took his leave.
As Zong saw him off at the monastery gate, he offered him his straw hat. The master took the hat, placed it on his head, and walked away without another word.
Looking back, he later resided at Fahua Temple on Mount Tai. At the time of his death, he composed a verse which said: "Raising my hand, I grasp the Southern Dipper;
Turning my body, I lean against the Northern Star. I peer out beyond the heavens to see: Who else is there like me?"
A monk asked National Teacher Kajin of Silla, successor to Chan Master Dame Chang: "What is the meaning of [the Patriarch’s] coming from the West?
The Master said, "I will tell you when you come from within. The monk asked, "What is the essential purport of Dame? The Master said, "Curdled milk is originally all at once."
"Discard!
Thus spoke Master Tianlong of Hangzhou while ascending the hall. "The assembly, do not wait for this old monk to come up before you come up, or for him to go down before you go down.
Each of you possesses the ocean of the nature of the Flower Treasury (Huazang Xinghai), complete with merit and unimpeded radiance. Each and every one...
Take this up. Be careful. A monk asked, "How can one escape from the three realms? The Master said, "Where are you right now?
[This was] the Dharma successor of Chan Master Foguangman.

Bai Juyi, styled Ledan, was the Prefectural Governor of Hangzhou. For a long time he had attended upon Foguang, through whom he attained the Dharma-method (*dharmaparyāya*), and he also received the Mahāyāna Vajra-precious precepts.
During the Yuanhe era, he visited the Dharma Hall of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao and posed four questions (the words of which appear in the "Xingshan" chapter).
In the fifteenth year [of Yuanhe], while serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, he sought out Master Niaokuo, and their exchange of questions and answers is recorded (as seen in the "Niaokuo" chapter).

He once sent a letter to Dharma Master Ji, arguing that since the Buddha’s unsurpassed great wisdom expounds the principles of the teachings, how could there be a yielding to the high or low capacities of beings, or different responses to their various ailments?
He contended that such views contradict the doctrine of the single, equal flavor (*ekarasa*).
Citing six scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Vajrasamādhi*, he refuted these two positions. Furthermore, regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the twelve...

Regarding the explanation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) based on conditions, the preceding and succeeding parts are not analogous. Establishing principles to investigate them, [the text] probes the profound and seeks out the hidden, penetrating the obscure and illuminating the subtle.
Yet, I have not seen the Dharma Master’s response, nor has there been anyone among those who came later to provide an answer in his stead.

Furthermore, I have received the eight stages of gradual cultivation from Master Ning of the Eastern Capital; for each stage, I have expanded upon a single word into a verse to explain its essential meaning.
From the shallow to the profound, his works are like pearls strung together. Whenever he held office, he frequently sought out the ancestral teachings; in his studies, he took no fixed teacher.

Later, serving as a Palace Attendant (*Binkè*) stationed in the Eastern Capital, he exhausted his own salary to restore Longmen Xiangshan Temple. Upon its completion, he composed a record for it himself.
All his writings were invariably concerned with edification, and there was not one that did not praise the Buddha Vehicle, as seen in his collected works. His...
The sequence of his official appointments and his final return to the state of completeness for the purpose of ancestral sacrifices are recorded in the historical annals.

Chan Master Mo of Wuxi was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Zhengyuan of Guishan in Fuzhou; he was the son of the Cai family of Xuancheng. He once composed a verse to instruct his disciples, the first of which says:
How many times has the vast ocean turned to mulberry fields? Only empty space remains solitary and serene. Those who have reached the shore need no longer cling to their rafts;
those who have not yet crossed must surely rely on a boat. Second: Having sought a teacher and recognized the source of one’s own mind, both banks are profound while the center is not fixed.
If you are already a Buddha, there is no need to seek another Buddha; it is simply because of this that you forget all conditions. Xiantong.
He spent the final ten years of his life at the home mountain. He was posthumously titled Great Master Xingkong (Nature-Emptiness).
A monk asked Master Suxi, "What is the Buddha Dingguang? The Master said, "A duck swallows a snail.
The monk asked, "Does this allow the student to turn about? The Master said, "The eyes protrude."
The Master Puhua of Zhenzhou, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Panshan, was a man of unknown origins. He served Panshan as his master and secretly received the true instructions;
however, he feigned madness and spoke without restraint. Following the passing of Panshan, he went to the northern regions to propagate the teachings. At times—

In a city, or among the graves, he shook a single bell and said: "If it comes from the side of light, strike it on the side of light; if it comes from the side of darkness, strike it on the side of darkness;
if it comes from the four quarters and eight directions, strike it with a whirlwind; if it comes from empty space, strike it with a continuous blow.
One day, Linji ordered a monk to seize him and asked, "What if it does not come in any of these ways? The Master pushed him away and said, "Come tomorrow, Great Compassionate One."
There was a vegetarian feast in the monastery. When the monk returned, he related this to Jie. Jie said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Whenever he saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would ring his bell once; he was thus known at the time as Master Puhua.
Sometimes he would ring the bell right by a person's ear or against their back. If someone turned around, he would immediately open his hands and say, "Give me a coin."
He would eat even at improper times. Once, at dusk, he entered Linji’s monastery to eat raw vegetables.
Linji said, "This fellow looks very much like a donkey. The Master then brayed like a donkey. Linji said to the steward, "Prepare a fine supply of fodder for him.
The Master said, "The people of Shaoshi did not recognize me; now I have come again to Jinling. Linji’s single eye sees through everyone everywhere."
He opened [the door]. When the Magistrate of Mounted Troops saw him, he shouted, "Clear the way! The Master also shouted, "Clear the way! and assumed a wrestling stance.

The Magistrate ordered his men to strike the Master with five blows of the staff. The Master said, "It is similar, but it is not the same. The Master once wandered through the marketplace shaking a bell and singing:
"I search for a place to go, but it cannot be found. At that time, Daowu encountered him, seized him by the collar, and asked:
"Where do you intend to go? The Master said, "From where have you come? I was speechless. The Master pulled me by the hand and departed.
One day, Linji was sitting in the monks' hall together with the Elder Mudata of Heyang.

They were discussing how the Master daily behaves in the streets and markets, acting like one driven by wind and madness, and whether he was an ordinary man or a sage. Just as they were speaking, the Master suddenly entered.
Linji approached. Jishi asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? The Master said, "Now tell me, are you an ordinary person or a sage?
Linji gave a shout. The Master pointed his finger and said, "The bride of Heyang; the old woman’s Zen of the wooden pagoda; Linji, that little fellow—yet he possesses a single eye.
Linji said, "This thief! The Master said, "Thief! Thief! and then went out. (Recorded by Tang Xian)
Tongchu was about to enter extinction. He went into the marketplace and said to the people, "Give me a *zhidu* (a monk’s robe).
Some people gave him a padded jacket; others gave him a cloth cloak. He accepted neither, shaking his staff as he departed. Linji sent someone to deliver him a coffin.
The Master laughed and said, "Linji, that fellow with the long tongue," and then accepted it. He then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Puhua is clear."
"Today we leave through the East Gate; it is death. The people of the commandery followed one another to escort him out of the city.

The Master said in a stern voice, "A burial today does not accord with the principles of the *qīngwū* (the auspicious bird). Therefore, tomorrow we shall pass away through the South Gate," and the people followed accordingly.

He spoke again, "Tomorrow we shall exit through the West Gate; that alone will be auspicious. As he left, the people gradually thinned out, and once they had departed, they returned. The people's resolve grew somewhat slack. On the fourth day—
He personally lifted the coffin out beyond the north gate, shook his rattle-drum, entered the coffin, and passed away. The people of the commandery rushed out of the city;
when they lifted the coffin to look, he was already gone. They heard only the sound of the rattle-drum fading gradually into the air, its origin unfathomable.
Chan Master Liaosu of Shouzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Magu Chang, went to visit Magu. Upon seeing him approach, Magu took up a hoe and went out to weed.

When the Master arrived at the spot where Magu was weeding, Magu paid him no attention at all and simply returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him. The next day, the Master went there again.
Dagu again closed his door. The Master knocked on the door. Dagu asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "Liangsui.

As soon as he uttered his name, he attained sudden enlightenment and said, "Master, do not deceive Liangsui. Had I not come to pay my respects to you, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life.
Dagu then opened the door and they met. Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly:
What all people know, Liangsui knows entirely; what Liangsui knows, all people do not know.
When Chan Master Huichao of Shushan in Jizhou, a successor of Chan Master Hui of Dongsi, came to pay his respects, the Master said, "You have already occupied one [position]."
“Where have you come from? Fang replied, “I am Liang-jia; unable to resolve my doubts, I have come specifically to see the Master.
The Master called out, “Liang-jia! Liang-jia responded. The Master said, “What is it? Liang-jia was speechless. The Master said, “A fine Buddha indeed, yet he simply lacks radiance.”

A monk asked Chan Master Chuwai of Qianzhou, successor to Chan Master Xitang Zang: "The three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings have attained the wondrousness of their underlying principle;

are they the same as or different from the meaning of the Patriarchs? The Master said: "One must discern beyond the six propositions; one must not be turned by sounds and forms. The monk said: [The Master continued: "..."
“What are the six phrases? The Master said, “Speaking, silence, neither speaking nor silent, both together, neither together, and how would you do it?
The monk had no reply. He asked Yangshan, “What is your name? Yangshan said, “Huiji.
The Master said, “Which one is Hui (wisdom) and which one is Ji (stillness)? Yangshan said, “It is right here before my eyes. The Master said, “There is still that which precedes it.”
Later, while at the mountain, [Changqing] said, "Setting aside for a moment what came before and after, what did the Master see? The Master replied, "Go drink tea.

Chan Master Huiyun of Zhangjing was the dharma successor of Chan Master Hongbian of Da Jianfu Monastery in Jingzhao. Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty asked him, "Why is there the division of North and South in the Chan school?"
He was asked for his name. He replied: "The Chan school originally has no North or South.

In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and it was transmitted from one to another until it reached the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma. He came to this land and became the First Patriarch.
When the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, was expounding the Dharma at Mount Dongshan in Qizhou, there were two disciples..."
One was named Huineng; he received the robe and the Dharma and resided south of the Ling Mountains as the Sixth Patriarch. The other was named Shenxiu; he propagated the teachings in the north.
Later, Shenxiu’s disciple Pujì established Shenxiu as the Sixth Patriarch and claimed himself to be the Seventh Patriarch.

Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, there was a difference between them in their methods of guidance and the awakening they inspired—namely, the sudden and the gradual. Therefore it is said:
The designations "Southern Sudden" and "Northern Gradual" were not originally part of the Chan school’s nomenclature.

The Emperor asked, "What is called precept (*śīla*)? He replied, "To guard against what is improper and to cease from evil is called precept. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by concentration (*samādhi*)?

He replied, "When the six sense faculties encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions; this is called concentration. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by wisdom (*prajñā*)? He replied, "When both mind and objects are empty, [wisdom] illuminates..."

"To discern without delusion is called wisdom. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes skillful means (upāya)? He replied, "Skillful means is the gateway of provisional expediency that conceals the ultimate reality and covers the true marks.
To provide guidance for those of middling and inferior capacities through indirect application and instruction is called skillful means.
Even to speak of abandoning skillful means and teaching only the Unsurpassed Way for those of superior faculties is itself a discourse of skillful means," and so on, up to the Patriarch.

The Master spoke of the profound mystery: "He forgets his achievements and severs all designations; yet there is likewise no trace of expedient means. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the Buddha-mind?

He replied, "Buddha is a term from the Western Heaven; in the language of Tang it means 'Awakening. It refers to the fact that when a person possesses wisdom and illuminating insight, this is the Buddha-mind.
'Mind' is another name for the Buddha, which has hundreds of thousands of different appellations, yet its essence is but one. It has no form or shape, and is not—"

The characteristics of blue, yellow, red, and white; male and female; whether among devas or non-devas, humans or non-humans—they manifest as devas and manifest as humans, capable of being male and capable of being female.
Having neither beginning nor end, and being without birth or cessation, it is therefore called the nature of numinous awakening.
Just as Your Majesty responds to the myriad affairs of state every day, this is precisely Your Majesty’s Buddha-mind. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, it could not...
[The monk] thought that there must be something else to be gained. The Emperor asked, "Suppose there were someone today who practices the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti);
how would it be? He replied, "The Tathāgata appeared in the world as the Teacher of Gods and Humans. As a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he preached the Dharma according to their capacities.

For those of superior faculties, he opened the way to the Supreme Vehicle (agrayāna) for the sudden realization of the ultimate principle. Those of middling or inferior faculties could not yet understand it suddenly; therefore, the Buddha [taught] for Vaidehī..."
He wished to open the gate of the sixteen contemplations so that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha would be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Thus the sutra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor asked:

"If there are people who recite the sutras and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, or who maintain mantras and seek the Buddha, what of them? He replied: "The Tathāgata’s various teachings and praises are all for the sake of the Supreme Vehicle."

"Vehicle. Just as the myriad streams and currents of the hundred rivers do not fail to flow toward the sea as their ultimate destination, so too do all these various numerical distinctions return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

The Emperor asked, "Since the Patriarch has already attained the seal of the mind (*citta-mudrā*), and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of the 'Dharma of non-attainment,' how is this so?
He replied, "In the Buddha’s entire ministry, he truly did not bestow a single dharma upon others; he merely showed everyone that each [person]..."

Each possesses its own nature; they are one within the same Dharma-treasury. At that time, when the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara merely certified Śākyamuni’s original dharma, there was nothing to be attained, and only then did he accord with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent. Thus the Sūtra says: "There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
This dharma is equal. Cultivate all wholesome dharmas, yet do not dwell upon their marks. The Emperor said: "Since the Chan Master..."

[The Emperor] asked, "Do you understand the meaning of the Patriarchs? Do you still prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sutras? He replied, "The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya family prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sutras;
this is indeed the constant practice for those who maintain the Dharma. There are four types of retribution [for such actions].

Nevertheless, they cultivate their persons according to the Buddha’s precepts, seek out wise teachers, gradually practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and tread upon the path traversed by the Tathāgata. The Emperor said, "What is 'sudden realization' (dunjian)? What is 'gradual cultivation' (jianxiu)?"

Xiu replied, "I have suddenly realized my own nature and am the equal of the Buddhas; however, because of beginningless defiled habits, I rely on gradual cultivation as an antidote to allow the functioning of that nature to arise accordingly.
It is like a person eating rice: one is not satiated by a single mouthful.

On this day, Xiu debated for seven *ke* (approximately three hours), whereupon he was granted a purple robe and the title Chan Master Yuanzhi. Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued to repair the ancestral stupas throughout the empire.
Each was commanded to guard [the teaching].
Chan Master Zhiju of Guishan in Fuzhou was the son of the Liu family of Yangzhou. Initially, he visited Zhangjing, who asked, "From where have you come?
The Master said, "I have come from nowhere; I have arrived at nowhere. Although Zhangjing remained silent, the Master likewise...
Wu (Wuzhu) said: "After I attained realization, I ascended the hall. A movement of expression or a blink of an eye—nothing emerges apart from one's own single thought of pure mind.
This is fundamentally the Buddha. He then spoke a verse: "The mind is originally free from dust; what need is there to wash it? The body is without illness; why seek a physician?

If you wish to know the place where the Buddha is not the body, Look at the bright mirror when it has not yet reflected anything. Later, he encountered the suppression of Buddhism under Emperor Wuzong. There was...

The verse was presented to the assembly as follows: An imperial decree falls like thunder upon the emerald peaks; Before the wind, he sheds tears and casts off his dhyāna robe. Amidst the clouds lies a temple where he may no longer stay;
In the midst of dust there is no home—where shall he return? The bright moon divides its form, ever new in every place;

How could a layperson (baiyi) fail to fall [to the ground] before one who has realized emptiness? Who says that being in the secular world hinders the cultivation of the Way? Kanakamuni once took the body of a lay devotee (gṛhapati).
"When the Rishi Kṣānti sat in meditation beneath a forest tree, he was once maimed by the King of Singers. How much less could such a thing occur in our sagely dynasty?
To merely command him to cease his practice of the Way—what cause for sorrow is there? Subsequently, during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he no longer donned the monastic robes.
He passed away at his mountain monastery in the sixth year of the Xiantong era; he was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Guiji.
Chan Master Cao of Jinzhou invited Master Mi for a meal. He did not arrange any seating positions. When Master Mi arrived, he spread his sitting cloth and prostrated.
Master Cao descended from his meditation seat. Master Mi then sat upon the master’s seat, while Master Cao sat on the floor instead.
When the meal was finished, Master Mi departed. An attendant said, "The Master is revered by all people; today your seat has been usurped by another."

The Master said, "If he comes after three days, I shall accept him; his salvation lies therein. After three days, the man indeed came and said, "The other day I encountered bandits" (a monk asked Jingqing about this:

"What was the meaning of the ancients saying, 'The other day I encountered bandits'? Jingqing replied, 'I see only the sharpness of the awl's point, but I do not see the squareness of the chisel's head").
Whenever Master Gudī of Langzhou saw a monk coming, he would simply say, "Go! You have no Buddha-nature. The monks had no response;
those who did respond failed to grasp his intent. When Yangshan arrived to pay his respects, the Master said, "Go! You have no Buddha-nature."
Dongshan joined his palms, stepped forward three paces, and responded with an assent. Master [Baizhang] smiled and said, "From where did you obtain this samādhi?
Dongshan said, "I received my name from Danyuan; I obtained my ground from Guishan. The Master said, "Are you not then Guishan’s son?
Dongshan said, "In terms of worldly truth, it is not that I am not; in terms of the Buddha-dharma, I do not dare. Dongshan then asked, "Master..."
"From where did you obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Zhangjing.
Mount Shandao sighed and said, "It is inconceivable; it is difficult for those who come here to find a place of rest."
A monk asked Master Gaoji of Hezhong Prefecture, "What is the Way? What is Chan? The Master showed him with a verse, saying:
"The named is not the Great Way; right and wrong are both not Chan. If you wish to know the meaning within this, it is like the 'yellow leaf' used to stop a child's crying."
Chan Master Shanglin Jieling of Hunan was a successor of Chan Master Yongtai Tuan.
When he first visited Mount Gui (Weishan), the Master asked, "Virtuous One, what have you come here for?"
The Master said, "Your armor and helmet are fully equipped. Dajue said, "Strip them all off before you can meet with the Venerable One. The Master said, "I have stripped them off.
Dajue scolded him, saying, "The thief has not yet been beaten; why are you stripping yourself? The Master had no reply. Yangshan spoke on his behalf, saying:

"Please, Preceptor, clear the space of those around us. Guishan made a gesture with his hand and said, "Yes. Yes. It was only later, when the Master visited Yongtai, that Yongtai explained its meaning to him.
The Master of Bimoksha Rock on Mount Wutai constantly carried a wooden fork. Whenever he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would immediately thrust the fork through the monk's neck and say:
"Which demon-spirit taught you to leave the household life? Which demon-spirit taught you to travel as a pilgrim?"
"If you can speak, you die under the crossbar. If you cannot speak, you die under the crossbar. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Few among the disciples were able to respond.
(Fayan spoke on their behalf: "Beg for your life. Fadeng spoke on their behalf: "He simply extended his neck to show him. Xuanjue spoke on their behalf: "Old man, you may set down the crossbar.
When Master Tong of Huoshan visited the Master, as soon as he saw him, he did not bow but instead leaped into the Master’s embrace. The Master patted Tong’s back three times.
Tong rose, clapped his hands, and said, "Brother Teacher, you have enticed me here from three thousand li away! You have enticed me here from three thousand li away! He then returned.
Master Zhilin of Hunan used to scold Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them both malevolent spirits; he held a wooden sword in his hand.
He claimed to have subdued demons. As soon as he saw a monk come to visit him, he would say, "The demon comes! The demon comes! and brandish his sword wildly before returning to his quarters.
This continued for twelve years, after which he set aside his sword and remained silent. A monk asked, "Why did you subdue demons twelve years ago?
The Master replied, "A thief does not strike the home of a poor man. The monk asked, "And why [did you stop] twelve years later?"
"Ma! Does one not subdue demons? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
Chan Master Huiyanzang’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Qi’an of Huangzhou, ascended the hall and said:
"When words do not fall into fixed phrases, Buddhas and Patriarchs have nothing left to bestow; when the profound resonance does not decline..."
"Who can know this? A monk asked, "How does one recognize one's own Buddha? The Master said, "When a single leaf is revealed, it cannot be exhausted;
when the melody of the pines and wind ceases, there is no one to lament. The monk asked, "What is one's own Buddha?

The Master said, "The swift horse before the grass is truly difficult to fathom; to reach the ultimate subtlety, one must walk as a beast. Someone asked, "How old are you, Master? The Master [replied].
It is said: "Five, six, four, and three cannot be categorized; how could one and two be the same? Truly, they are difficult to fathom. The Master has a verse that says:
"Within fiercely blazing flames, there is a path for people; atop the whirling wind, one dwells steadfastly. Constantly thus throughout kalpas, who could ever deviate?"
The radiant sun shines silently upon all equally.
Fourth generation descendant of the lineage under Nanyue,
Chan Master Huangbo Yun, successor to the Dharma.
The Venerable Master of Muzhou was named Daoming. He was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. At the time of his birth, a crimson light filled the room and auspicious clouds covered the sky;

they did not disperse for ten days. His eyes possessed double pupils (*chongtong*), and his face displayed the seven stars. His physical features were extraordinary, setting him apart from the common crowd.
Once, while going to Kaiyuan Temple to pay respects to the Buddha, he recognized a monk as an old acquaintance. Upon returning home, he informed his father.
His mother wished for him to seek ordination as a monk, and his parents gave their permission. Later, he maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and mastered the Tripitaka.

While traveling, he attained realization of the essential meaning under Huangbo. Subsequently, at the request of the fourfold assembly, he resided at Guanyin Monastery, where he was constantly attended by more than a hundred followers.
After several decades, students would come to question and challenge him; he would respond immediately to whatever was asked, his words being steep and profound.

As this did not follow conventional paths, those of shallow capacity often ridiculed him; however, only those of the Mysterious Learning (*xuánxué*) who were naturally gifted in their acumen revered and submitted to him.

Consequently, seekers from all quarters flocked to him, and everyone addressed him as a "Venerable Elder" (*zūnsù*). Later, he returned to Kaiyuan (now changed to Doushuai), where he lived in a room weaving *púxié* sandals.
Because he was raised by his mother, he was known as "Pu-xie (Sandals) of Chen. When the Khitan rebels entered the territory, the Master displayed a large straw sandal at the city gate.
The Khitans wished to discard it, but though they exerted all their strength, they could not lift it. They sighed, saying, "There is a great sage in Muzhou," and they abandoned the city and departed;
thus, the area was spared from turmoil. One evening during the *wanchan* (evening assembly), he said to the assembly, "Have you all attained anything?"
"You have not even entered the gate. If you have not yet found a point of entry, you must seek one.

If you do find a point of entry, you must never again betray this old monk. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed, saying, "I shall certainly never dare to betray the Master. The Master said, "Already you have betrayed me. He added, "It is clear."
"I have explained it clearly to you, yet you still do not understand; how much less could you grasp it when it is covered over?
He continued, "Since I have been the abbot residing here, I have never seen a person who is truly 'without affairs' come before me. Why do you not step forward?
At that moment, a monk stepped forward, and the Master said, "The Rector is not here. Take him yourself outside the main gate and give him twenty blows."
[The Master] struck him with his staff and said, "Where does your fault lie? The monk replied, "It is like adding shackles to a collar.

The Master usually closed his door whenever he saw a *nanseng* (monk in patched robes) arrive; however, when he saw a lecturer-monk, he would call out, "Lecturer! When the lecturer responded, the Master would say:

"A man carrying a wooden board. Someone said, "There is a bucket here; give me some water. One day, while standing on the corridor steps, a monk asked, "Where is the room of the Venerable Master Chen?
The Master took off his straw sandals and struck him over the head. The monk immediately ran away. The Master called out, "Virtuous One!
The monk turned his head back. The Master pointed and said, "Go back that way! A celestial messenger asked, "The three gates are all..."

[The Master] opened the door. As the official entered through that gate, the Master called out, “Minister! The official responded with an assent. The Master said, “You have entered through the Gate of Faith.

Again, seeing the painted murals on the wall, the official asked, “What were those two venerable ones discussing as they sat face-to-face? The Master struck the pillar and said, “Among the three bodies [of the Buddha], which one does not preach the Dharma?
A lecturer-monk came to visit. The Master asked, “Are you not the one who lectures on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only)? The monk replied, “I dare not say so.”

The Master said, "Leaving for India in the morning and returning to the land of Tang in the evening—do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Ho! Ho! You do not even observe the five precepts!
The Master asked an elder, "When one is enlightened, a single hair-tip swallows the vast ocean; only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust.
Elder, what do you say to this? He replied, "To whom are you asking? The Master said, "I am asking you, Elder. He replied, "Why do you not acknowledge it?"

[The Master] spoke. The Master said, "You do not understand my words; I do not understand your words. He asked, "Seat Master, what sutra are you lecturing on? [The Seat Master] replied, "I am lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Master said, "May I ask about a certain passage of meaning? [He] replied, "Yes. The Master kicked at the air and blew upon it once, then said, "What is the meaning of this?
[The Seat Master] replied, "This meaning is not found in the sutra. The Master said, "You are a man of empty talk and deceitful speech! (5)
Regarding the meaning of the *Hālāhala* (Baili) lifting the rock, [the master] instead said, "There is none. When the Master saw a monk, he said, "This is a settled case;
I grant you thirty blows. The monk said, "I am like this. The Master said, "Why does the *Vajrapāṇi* at the entrance of the three gates raise his fist?"
[The monk] said, "Even a Vajra [weapon] is like this. The Master then struck him. [The monk] asked, "What is the path that leads upward?
The Master said, "If you want to speak, what is difficult about it? [The monk] said, "Please, Master, speak. The Master said, "The first and third, the eleventh; the middle ninth, the seventh below."
Question: “If one layer does not remove another layer, I do not ask about that. But when one layer does not remove another layer, how is it?
The Master said: “Yesterday morning we planted eggplants; today we plant winter melons. Question: “What is the true meaning of Caoxi? The Master said:
“This old monk loves anger and does not love joy. [The student] asked: “Why is it so? The Master said: “When you meet someone on the road...”
A swordsman must present his sword; one who is not a poet should not speak of poetry. He questioned a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Liuyang.
The Master asked, "When the senior master there was questioned on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, what did he say? The monk said, "Everywhere there is no path to walk upon.
The Master asked, "Did that senior master truly say this? The monk replied, "He truly did. The Master took up his staff and struck him, saying, "This..."
Mindful of the man of Han, the Master asked an elder, "If a brother were to come, how would you receive him?

He replied, "I will wait for him to arrive. The Master said, "Why do you not speak? He replied, "What is lacking in the Master? The Master said, "Please, do not trouble yourself with such complications.
A monk came to visit. The Master said, "Are you not a wandering monk? He replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Have you yet paid homage to the Buddha?"

[The monk] asked, "What is the ritual for a mound of earth? The Master said, "Go out and take it upon yourself. Another asked, "I have studied the teachings and traveled as a pilgrim, yet I do not understand the meaning of the doctrine.
What then? The Master said, "Truly, you must confess this as a sincere statement. The monk said, "I beg the Master for instruction.

"How was it then? The Master said, "Yesterday someone asked this; I chased him out. [The monk] said, "Master, were you perhaps afraid that I was not sincere?
The Master said, "My staff is not here; I will give you thirty blows with the handle of a broom instead. He then ascended the hall and said, "I saw Baizhang not knowing good from bad.
As soon as the assembly had gathered, he struck them all down at once with his staff, and then called out, 'Great..."

[The Master] addressed the assembly. As the assembly turned their heads, he said, "What is it? What common ground is there for conversation? Huangbo Zen Master did the same. He again called to the assembly;
as the assembly turned their heads, he said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind—it is still somewhat better than that.
He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "I, this old monk, have been shouted at by you. The monk—
Again he shouted. The Master said, "After three shouts and four shouts, what then? The monk was speechless. The Master struck him and said, "This fellow who flouts emptiness!
A scholar visited the Master and claimed he understood twenty-four styles of calligraphy.

The Master pointed a single dot in the air with his staff and asked, "Do you understand? The scholar was at a loss. The Master said, "And yet you say you understand twenty-four styles of calligraphy?"
[The Master] said, "I do not even recognize the 'Eight Strokes of the Character 'Ever' (永). When ascending the hall, [he continued: 'To split them apart is up to me;
to gather them together is also up to me. At that time, a monk asked, "What is it to split them apart? The Master said, "'Three times nine is twenty-seven.
Bodhi and Nirvana, True Suchness and Liberation, 'this very mind is Buddha. I speak thus for now; what about you? The monk said, "I..."
"Not so," [the student] said. The Master said, "The cup falls to the ground; the dish shatters into seven pieces. [The student] asked, "What is 'gathering together'?
The Master then sat with his hands folded. [The student] asked, "Are the meaning of the teachings and the meaning of the patriarchs the same or different?

The Master said, "The green mountains are themselves green mountains; the white clouds are themselves white clouds. [The student] asked, "What are the green mountains? The Master said, "Give me back my..."
Diyu came and said, "I cannot say it; I beg the Master to say it. The Master said, "The battle array before the blade of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
the withdrawal after the phrase of *Nirvāṇa*. He asked a monk, "Where have you been this summer? The monk replied, "I will tell you when the Master has a place to stay.
The Master said, "A fox is not of the lion’s kind; a lamp is not as bright as the sun and moon. He asked another monk, "Where have you come from? The monk stared back at him with wide eyes.
The Master said, "Donkey in front, horse behind, Han. The monk said, "I ask the Master to examine it. The Master said, "Donkey in front, horse behind, Han.
Bring me a phrase, monk! The monk had no reply. While the Master was reading a sutra, Chancellor Chen Cao asked, "What sutra is the Master reading?
The Master said, "The Diamond Sutra. The Chancellor said, "Translated during the Six Dynasties; which volume is this? The Master raised [the sutra] up.
The Sūtra says: "All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow. Following this passage in the scripture, a monk asked, "Master, what sūtra are you reading?
The Master replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The 'Chapter on the Cremation' is at the very end. He then asked the monk, "Where have you been this summer?

The monk replied, "At Mount Jing. The Master said, "You eater of evening meals! The monk asked, "Venerable elder, why do you say I am an eater of evening meals when I am in a monastic community (*saṅghārāma*）?"
The Master chased him out with his staff. Hearing that an elderly master was difficult to approach, he went to visit him in person.
As soon as he entered the abbot’s quarters, the elder gave a shout. The Master slapped him on the side and said, "A double case. The elder asked, "Where does the fault lie?
The Master replied, "This wild fox spirit," and then withdrew. He then asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Jiangxi. The Master said, "You have worn it through."
"How many straw sandals? The monk had no reply. While the Master was drinking tea with a lecturer-monk, he said, "I cannot save you.
The monk said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master to grant me an instruction. The Master picked up an oil cake and asked, "What is this?"
[The Master] said, "The dharma of form. The Master said, "This fellow who has entered the boiling cauldron! When the Great Virtue in Purple Robes arrived, he prostrated.

The Master picked up his hat and its band and asked, "What is this called? He replied, "A 'Heaven-Pointing Cap' (*chao tian mao*). The Master said, "If that is so, then I shall not take it off either.
He asked again, "What is your field of study? He replied, "Consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). The Master said, "How do you explain it? He replied:
"The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. The Master pointed to the door panel and asked, "What is this? [The monk] replied, "It is a dharma of form (*rūpa*).
The Master said, "When you were granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and lectured on the sutras before the Emperor, how could you have failed to observe the five precepts?

De was speechless. [Another monk] asked, "I have only recently entered the monastic community; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "You do not know how to ask. [The monk] said, "Master..."
“Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, “I grant you thirty blows; take them and depart on your own.

A monk asked, “I request the Master to provide the essential framework for the intent of the Teachings. The Master said, “Just ask, and I will tell you. The monk said, “I request the Venerable One to speak.

The Master said, “Burn incense in the Buddha Hall; join your palms at the Main Gate. The monk asked, “What are the words for unfolding and rolling up [the teachings]? The Master said, “Appraise the talent.”
Supplementing the office duties, [the Master] asked: "What are words that do not unfold or display? The Master said: "I humbly pray you may enjoy [this offering].

While borrowing an axe at Jiaoshan, the Master called to the attendant boy, saying, "Bring the axe. When the boy brought the axe, the Master said, "Since there are no measuring lines yet, first chop the coarse parts.
He then gave a shout. Again he asked the boy, "How about your axe? The boy then made a chopping motion.
