If the stream were sound and the mountain were form, Then without mountain or water, one would be a person of great sorrow. He specifically told this hermitage master, who said, "I told you before that you are a man from outside the gate. The Master bowed in thanks. Not long after, there was one who was soliciting contributions to
He said, "Send word to the old adept of Jiangxi: let him be scorched by the sun and fanned by the wind. It is not that his descendants lack the means to manage it;

they simply wish to see the moment it melts away like ice and crumbles like tiles. When Chan Master Ciana saw this, he laughed and said, "One must indeed be this very *śramaṇera* to achieve such a thing."
The Vinaya Master Ben-sōng, in response to the inquiry of the layman Yang Jie regarding the essential nature of the *vinaya* as expounded by Master Xuán, replied with this verse:
"How could emotion and wisdom ever be different? A dog barks while a snake slithers on its own.
The true meaning of Zhōngnán— At midday, it strikes the third watch."
Once there was an elderly master who did not speak with his disciples for an entire summer retreat. A monk sighed and said, "I have spent this summer in vain;
I do not dare hope that the Master will preach the Buddha-dharma, but even to hear two characters of the True Cause would be enough.
When the elderly master heard this, he said, "Disciple, do not speak so hastily. As for the True Cause, there is not even a single character. Thus he spoke.
He struck his teeth and said, "Just now, without cause, it was improper to speak in such a manner.

An old master living in the neighboring wall heard this and remarked, "What a fine pot of soup that has been defiled by a single mouse dropping! (Xuedou’s substitute says: "Whose kitchen does not have one or two in its pot?")
Once there was a monk who did not read the sutras while in the scripture hall, but sat in meditation every day.
The Librarian asked, "Why do you not read the sutras? The monk replied, "I am illiterate. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask others?
The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, bowed, and asked, "What character is this? The Librarian had no reply. (The Dàtōng edition reads: "The Great Way does not recognize [characters].")

Long ago, there was an elderly master who lived in a hermitage. He wrote the character for "mind" (心) above his door, he wrote the character for "mind" on his window, and he wrote the character for "mind" on his wall.
(Fayan said: "Above the door he should have written the character for 'door,' above the window the character for 'window,' and on the wall the character for 'wall. Xuangjue said:

'There is no need to write the character for 'door' above the door, no need to write the character for 'window' above the window, and no need to write the character for 'wall' on the wall. Why? Because the meaning of the characters is already manifest.")
In the past, there were two *amaju* (hermit abbots) living in separate huts. They did not see one another for ten days, and when they suddenly met, the senior *amaju* asked the junior *amaju*:
"I have not seen you for a long time; where have you been? The junior *amaju* replied:
"I have been in my hut building a seamless pagoda. The senior *amaju* said: "I also wish to build one. May I borrow your pagoda from you?"
[The Master] looked at the model. The attendant said, "Why did you not say so sooner? It has just been borrowed by someone else. (Fayan said:
"Now tell me, was it the model itself that was borrowed, or was it not the model itself?")
Once there was a hermitage master. Seeing a monk approach, he held up a fire-tube and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not.
The master said, "This is something that has been used for thirty years without being exhausted. The monk then asked, "What did you use before those thirty years?
The master had no reply. (Gui-zong Rou offered this on his behalf: "One must also know.")
Once there was an elder who, when asked by the Ruler of the State of Jiangnan, replied: "I have a water buffalo that has not a single blade of grass for ten thousand *li*.
I do not know where to let it loose. The elder had no answer. (Gui-zong Rou spoke on his behalf, saying: "Let it loose in a good place.")
Once there was an elder who asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from Niu-tou Mountain to pay respects to the Patriarch.
The elder asked, "Did you see the Patriarch? The monk had no reply. (Gui-zong Ruo spoke on his behalf, saying: "It is very much like not believing him.")
Once there was an elder who spoke in verse: "A single void atop the mountain of the five aggregates; Entering and exiting through the same gate, we do not meet.
For immeasurable kalpas we have lived in rented rooms; In the end, we do not know the true host. [Another elder said: "If you do not know him, [what then?]"
[This refers to] who it was that he originally asked for the lease.
A monk asked an old master, "What is it like to be among those within the secret chamber? The old master said, "When there is a guest, one does not converse.
(Xuan Sha said, "When has it ever been secret? Niu Gui-zong said to the old master, "Why did you allow him to see [the truth]? [The old master replied,] "Because I am his guest.")
Once there was an elderly master. A monk asked him: "The soul returns home; eat the mulberries of my family garden.
What are the mulberries of the family garden? (Xuanguo replied on his behalf: "Even these cannot be eaten. Fadeng said: "They would soil your mouth.")
Once there was an elder who said, "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years in search of one who could understand him.
If you understand it in this way, the day will come when you will eat iron rods. Another elder said, "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years;
how can he not feel ashamed? If you understand it in this way, you must buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty more years. (Langye Huijue said: Since it is not so, then...)
"What was the meaning of the Patriarch facing the wall? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata."
Once there was an elder master. When a monk asked him, "A lion exerts its full strength when seizing a rabbit, and it exerts its full strength when seizing an elephant.
I wonder, what kind of strength does it exert fully? The elder replied, "The strength of non-deception" (Fayan commented separately: "He did not understand the words of the ancients").
Once there was an old master who said: "This plot of land has been entrusted to you for a long time now.

I shall stand here waiting for you to grasp it. (Fayan said: "I, this mountain monk, shall sit here now and wait for you to grasp it. Is there any principle in this? Which is intimate and which is distant? Try to judge and decide.")

In the past, there was an elderly master who kept a young attendant, yet neither of them knew the proper rules of conduct. One day, a wandering monk arrived and instructed the boy in the rituals of etiquette.
Later that evening, seeing the elderly master returning from outside, the boy went forward to offer his greetings. The master was astonished and suspicious.
He then asked the boy, "Who taught you this? The boy replied, "A certain senior monk (shangzuo) in the hall.
The old master summoned that monk and asked, "Senior monk, you travel about visiting teachers like a common householder; what kind of mental conduct is this?
This boy has been raised by me for two or three years and is naturally quite pitiable. Who taught you to corrupt him? Pack your things quickly and leave at once!"

At twilight, it rained heavily. [The Master] was driven out [of the hall]. (The Eye Commentary says: "The ancients were so forthright in revealing even a fragment of their family style; how strange! But tell me, what was their intent?")
Formerly, there was a monk who arrived at Caoxi. At that time, the monk in charge of the robes and bowl held up the robe and said, "This is what could not be lifted at the head of Dayu Ridge.
The visiting monk asked, "Why is it in your hands, Venerable? The monk in charge had no reply.
(Yunmen said, "Neither of them understood," and he also said, "I thought you were a lion cub.")
In the past, there was a monk who, while studying the *Lotus Sūtra*, reached the passage: "All dharmas from their very origin are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction.
Suddenly, he was gripped by doubt that he could not resolve. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he constantly investigated this within himself, yet found nothing at all.

One spring day, hearing the song of a warbler, he attained sudden enlightenment. He then completed the preceding verse, saying: "All dharmas from their very origin are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction."
When spring arrives, the hundred flowers bloom; the yellow oriole sings atop the willows.
Long ago, an old master asked a presiding abbot, "Regarding the commentaries (*śāstra*) that explain the meaning of the commentaries (*vṛtti*): which is more extensive, and which is more concise?
The abbot replied, "The commentaries explain the commentaries; the commentaries explain the sutras. The old master asked, "What do the sutras explain? The abbot was speechless.
Formerly, from the kingdom of Goryeo, they came to Qiantang to carve a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara.

When it was time to lift it onto the ship, it could not be moved at all. Consequently, they invited it into Kaiyuan Temple in Mingzhou to offer it worship. Later, someone posed a question: "It is said that there is no land where he does not manifest his body;

why then did the sacred image not go to the kingdom of Goryeo? Changqing Ling said, "Though his manifestations are universal, the forms perceived by beings are partial. Fayan Ze said, "If you can recognize Avalokiteśvara... (The text ends here).
Before the pagoda at Sizhou, a monk was prostrating. Someone asked him, "Venerable sir, you prostrate every day; do you actually see the Great Sage?
(Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "Tell me, what is the meaning of this prostration?")
The attendant at the Sishou Pagoda locked the door at the appointed time. Someone asked, "Since you are the Great Master of the Three Realms, why are you locked up by your disciple?
The attendant had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf: "The disciple locks [him], and the Great Master locks [the disciple]. Fadeng spoke on his behalf: "Give me back my key!
An old master also spoke on his behalf: "Jizhou locks it; Qianzhou locks it.")
A statue of a holy monk was being dripped upon by leaking roof water. Someone asked the monk, "Since you are a holy monk, why do you have leaks?
The monk had no reply. (National Teacher Shao spoke on his behalf, saying: "Being leakless does not constitute being a holy monk.")
Someone asked, "What kind of lamp does the monk light? The monk replied, "A perpetually burning lamp. [The questioner] asked, "When was it lit? [The monk] said, "It was lit last year.

[The questioner] asked, "Where is the perpetual light now? The monk was speechless. (Changqing Ling, speaking on his behalf, said: "If it were not so, I would know that you do not allow yourself to be deceived. Fayan spoke differently, saying: "Profit moves the gentleman.")
There was a presiding master (zuozhu) who was reciting the name of Amitābha. A junior monk called out, "Preceptor!
When the master looked back, the junior monk did not respond. This happened three or four times. The preceptor scolded him, saying, "I have called you three or four times; what is the matter?

The junior monk replied, "For how many years have you been calling him [Amitābha] and yet succeeded? As soon as I call you, you immediately give rise to karmic obstruction" (Fadeng added: "Shoo! Scold him!")
There was a monk who, having finished reciting the sutra with a young boy, told him to place the sutra inside the case.
The boy said, "That which I have recited—where shall I put it? (Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying: "What sutra did you recite?")
A monk was annotating the *Daode jing*. Someone asked him, "I have long heard that the Great Virtuous One has annotated the *Daode jing*.
The monk replied, "I dare not say so. The man asked, "How is it then? [Fadeng said on behalf of the monk: "It is the disciple."]

There was a monk who entered the underworld and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Kṣitigarbha asked him, "What practice have you cultivated throughout your life? The monk replied, "I recite the Lotus Sūtra.
[Kṣitigarbha] said, "'Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Is this speaking, or is it not speaking?"
The monk had no reply. (Nianzong Rou’s substitute said: "This one returns; I dare to circulate it.
Under the assembly of Master Yanguan, there was an administrative monk who suddenly saw a ghost messenger come to pursue him.
The monk said to him, "I am currently serving as an administrator and have not yet had the leisure to practice. May I request seven days’ grace? The messenger said, "Wait while I report this."
"O King, if you permit it, I shall come back after seven days; otherwise, I will arrive in an instant. Having spoken, he vanished.
When the seven days had passed, he returned again and sought out the monk, but could not find him at all. Later, someone questioned another monk:
"If you were to be sought out and found, how would you deal with them? (Dongshan spoke on his behalf: "He has already been found.")
A monk from Liutong Monastery in Taizhou wished to cross the river by boat. Someone asked him, "Since you possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why do you rely on a boat?
The monk was speechless. (National Teacher Shao of Tiantai spoke on his behalf, saying: "I did not wish to startle the assembly.")
One day, the Prefect of Hongzhou, Lord Song, requested that a monk from Dajian Temple be invited to open the hall as the second seat.
The Lord asked, "Why not invite the first seat? The assembly was speechless. (Fayan spoke on their behalf, saying: "There is no need for such trouble.")
The Chancellor of Jiangnan, Feng Yanshi, was traveling with several monks on Mount Zhong. Upon reaching the "One-Person Spring," he asked, "The spring is for one person;
how can so many people share it? A monk replied, "We do not allow it to be deficient. Feng Yanshi did not approve of this answer and instead said, "Who is it that is deficient?
(Fayan added a different version: "Who is it that is insufficient?")
The official asked, "What is your name, monk? He replied, "No selection. The official said, "If someone were suddenly to give you a bowl of sand, what then?
He replied, "I thank the official for his offering. (Fayan commented separately: "This is still a case of making a selection.")
There was a monk living in a hermitage in Guangnan. When the ruler of the country went out hunting, his attendants informed the master of the hermitage: "The Great King is coming; please rise.
The master said, "Not only would I not rise for the Great King, I would not rise even if the Buddha were to come. The king asked, "Is the Buddha not your teacher?"
The official said, "Is that so? The King asked, "Seeing the Master, why do you not rise? (Fayan spoke on his behalf: "Not yet sufficient to repay your kindness.
On Hongtang Bridge in Fuzhou, there were monks sitting in a row. An official asked, "Is there a Buddha among these people?
The monks had no reply. (Fayan spoke on their behalf: "Who are you?")
Once, an official entered the Tianwang Temple in Zhenzhou and, beholding the divine image, asked the temple master, "What merit does this represent?
The master replied, "It is the Guardian King of the State. The official asked, "Does he protect only this country, or does he protect all other countries as well?

The master replied, "In Qin he is for Qin; in Chu he is for Chu. The official said, "On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month, you shall break down the city walls of Zhenzhou! The deity replied, "Heaven..."
"Where has the King gone? The Master had no reply.
Formerly, there was an official who composed a "Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. One night, while he was wielding his brush, he suddenly saw a ghost appear and say:

"You claim there is no self; what about this? (Wuzu Yan said: "If I, the old monk, had seen him at that time, I would have simply made my hand into a hoopoe's beak and said to him: 'Gu-gua! [a cry of alarm].)
Once there was a practitioner of the Way who sat with his back to the Buddha in front of the Buddha Hall. A monk said, "Practitioner of the Way, do not sit with your back to the Buddha.
The practitioner replied, "Great Virtue, according to your own fundamental teaching, the Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm. In what place could one possibly sit?
The monk had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "I recognize you.")

There was a practitioner who followed a Dharma Master into the Buddha Hall. As the practitioner spat toward the Buddha, the Master said, "Practitioner, you lack propriety; why do you spit at the Buddha?
The practitioner replied, "I have come from where there is no Buddha, so I am free to spit here. The Master had no response. [Master Guishan] said:

"The benevolent one is actually not benevolent, while the non-benevolent one is actually benevolent. [Yangshan] spoke on behalf of the Dharma Master, saying: "Simply spit back at the practitioner. He added: "If the practitioner has anything to say, then tell him: 'Return it to me!'"
[He came from a place where there are no practitioners].
A dead fish was floating on the surface of the water. Someone asked a monk, "Is it not the case that this fish takes water as its life? The monk said:
[The Master] said, "It is so. [The monk] asked, "Why, then, did he die in the water? The monk had no reply. (Master Tianlong Ji of Hangzhou spoke on his behalf, saying:
"It is so; why did he not go to die on the bank?")
A hawk pursues a pigeon, which flies onto the railing of the Buddha Hall and trembles.
Someone asks a monk, "All sentient beings dwell in constant peace and joy within the shadow of the Buddha. Why does this pigeon tremble upon seeing the Buddha?
The monk is unable to answer. (Fadeng speaks on his behalf: "He is afraid of the Buddha.")
Once, there was a monk traveling toward Fushan. On the road, he encountered an old man selling salt.
The monk asked, "Which way does the road to Fushan go? The old man remained silent for a long while. The monk asked again. The old man said, "Are you deaf?
The monk replied, "What did you say to me? The old man said, "I told you the way to Fushan. The monk asked, "Do you understand Chan? The old man said, [and remained silent].
"Do not say you understand Chan; even the Buddha-dharma will eventually come to an end. The monk said, "Try to explain it to me.
The old man lifted up his salt basket. The monk said, "Difficult. The old man asked, "What do you call this? The monk said, "Salt. The old man said, "What connection does that have [to the Dharma]?
The monk asked, "And what do you call it? The old man replied, "I cannot tell you again that it is salt."
In the past, there was a householder who supported a hermit for twenty years. He constantly sent a young girl of eighteen to serve him by bringing his meals.
One day, he ordered the girl to embrace him firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The master replied:
"A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff; for three winters there has been no warmth.
When the woman reported this to the old woman, the old woman said, "For twenty years I have supported nothing but a common layman. She then sent her away and burned down the hut.
Once, there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hermitage.
The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, the great earth, whether grass or trees—all these are my kinsmen.
The monk said, "Are you not perhaps a nun (śramaṇī)? She replied, "What do you see in me? The monk said, [nothing].
The laywoman said, "You cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Lady, do not cause confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma.

The laywoman said, "I am not causing confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act like this, is that not causing confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma? The laywoman said:
"You are a man; I am a woman. How could we ever have been confused?

Laywoman Pang entered Lukmen Temple to offer a vegetarian feast. When the *vina* requested her instructions, the laywoman took a comb, tucked it behind her hair-knot, and said, "I have dedicated my merit. She then departed.

The nun Chen Dao from Wenzhou once traveled extensively to consult renowned masters throughout the various regions. Later, she attained enlightenment under the guidance of Master Jing at Changlao Mountain.
She composed a verse which says: Upon the level summit of the high hill, There are but woodcutters everywhere.
Everyone harbors the intent of axe and hatchet, Yet they do not see the mountain flowers reflecting red upon the water.
Once, there was a laywoman who entered the monastery to distribute money to the assembly of monks according to their seniority. A monk said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monk (*āryasaṃgha*).
The woman asked, "How old is the Holy Monk? The monk had no reply. (Fayan [Dahui Zonggao] spoke on his behalf: "One knows it when the heart’s intention is fulfilled.")
For years, he had been making offerings only to an ordinary layman, so he finally sent him away and burned down the hermitage.
Long ago, there was a monk who went to visit Mihu; on the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hut. The monk asked her, "Do you have any family?"
He said, "There is. The monk asked, "Where is it? He replied, "The mountains, rivers, and great earth; whether grass or trees, all are my kinsmen.
The monk said, "Are you not coming as a nun? He replied, "What do you see me as? The monk said:
The layman said, "Old woman, you cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Old woman, do not cause confusion and defilement within the Buddha-dharma.
The old woman said, "You are a man and I am a woman; how could we ever be confused or defiled?"

The laywoman Pangxing entered Lukmen Temple to offer a vegetarian feast. When the rector requested her intention for the dedication of merit, the laywoman took up a comb, stuck it behind her hair-knot, and said, "I have already dedicated it. She then departed.

The laywoman Chen Dao from Wenzhou once traveled extensively, seeking instruction from renowned masters throughout the various regions. Later, she attained enlightenment under the guidance of Master Jing at Changlao Mountain.
She composed a verse which says: Upon the level summit of the high hill, There are but woodcutters everywhere.
Everyone harbors the intent of axe and hatchet, Yet they do not see the mountain flowers reflecting red upon the water.

Once, a laywoman who was a patron entered the monastery to distribute "money according to seniority" (*sui-nian qian*) to the assembly of monks. A monk said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monk (*sheng-seng*).
The woman asked, "How old is the Holy Monk? The monk had no reply. (Fayan [Dahui Zonggao] spoke on his behalf, saying: "One knows it when the heart’s intention reaches its fullness.")
The Five Lamps Compiled (Wǔdēng Huìyuán), Scroll Six;
The Five Lamps Compiled (Wǔdēng Huìyuán), Scroll Seven:
The Second Generation under Qingyuan.
Chan Master Tianwang Daowu of Jingzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Shitou Xiqian.
He was a native of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou. His physical presence was exceptionally distinguished, and he possessed innate wisdom from childhood.
At the age of fourteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it; he consequently reduced his intake of food and drink day by day.

After eating only once a day, his physical form became emaciated and haggard; his parents, having no other choice, granted him permission. He followed a Great Virtue from Mingzhou to receive the tonsure.
At twenty-five, he went to Zhulin Monastery in Hangzhou to receive full ordination. He cultivated the holy life with great diligence and was esteemed for his courage and vigor.
Whether in wind, rain, or the darkness of night, he would sit in meditation among burial mounds; his body and mind remained tranquil, free from all fear. One day...
While traveling through Yuhang, he first visited Mount Jing to pay his respects to Guoyi, from whom he received the mind-dharma. He served him diligently for five years.

Later, he went to study under Mazu, who reaffirmed his previous understanding; the Dharma was not different. He remained in attendance for two summers, after which he visited Shitou and posed this question:
[The monk] asked, "Setting aside concentration and wisdom, by what dharma do you instruct people? Baizhang said, "In my place here, there are no servants.
What is there to set aside? The monk asked, "How can one attain clarity? Baizhang said, "Can you grasp empty space? The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall not follow you today.
Baizhang said, "I wonder, at what time and from which direction have you come? The monk said, "Daowu does not..."
The Master said, "That person over there. Wuzu said, "I already knew where you came from. Wuzu asked, "Why do you falsely accuse another of a crime?
The Master said, "Your body is right here before me. Wuzu said, "Even though it is so, how ultimately will you show this to people in the future?"

Tou asked, "Tell me, who is the successor? At this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment; he completely exhausted all traces of the "attainment of mind" he had previously held under the guidance of those two former masters.
Later, he settled at Mount Ziling in Dangyang, Jingzhou, where disciples followed one after another in such numbers that their shoulders brushed against each other.
The men and women of the capital flocked there, drawn by his reputation. At that time, the head monk of Chongye Monastery reported the matter to Master Lian, who welcomed him into the city.
To the left of the district was Tiantai Monastery, a renowned temple that had been destroyed by fire.
Its presiding monk, Lingjian, intended to restore it and said, "If we can secure Master Wuzhu as the spiritual leader for this transformation, he will surely bring us blessings."
Thereupon, he went secretly in the middle of the night to offer his sorrowful plea. [The Master] arrived being carried on a shoulder-litter.

At that time, the Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, Lord Pei, the Governor of Jiangling, bowed his head and inquired about the Dharma, paying him the utmost respect. The Master was by nature neither welcoming nor seeing off guests;

regardless of their rank, whether noble or humble, he would always have them sit and then bow to them. Lord Pei’s devotion increased all the more. From this, the Dharma path of Shitou flourished. Because of Longtan, the Master...
A monk asked, "How is it with the matter handed down from the masters above? The Master said, "It is not that I do not recognize where you have come from.
Dan said, "How many people possess such an eye as this? The Master said, "In shallow grass, even a reed grows easily.
A monk asked, "What is the discourse on the profound mystery? The Master said, "Do not say that I understand the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "But what can be done about this student?"
"What is your doubt? the Master asked. The monk said, "Why do you not ask the old monk [for it]? The Master said, "I have already answered you. The Master said, "Go; this is not where you may stay.
On the fourth month of the Dinghai year of the Yuanhe era, he manifested illness and instructed his disciples to announce his passing in advance.

On the final day of the month, the assembly came to inquire after his health. The Master suddenly called out to the head cook. As the cook approached, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The cook replied, "I do not understand.
The Master picked up his pillow, threw it to the ground, and immediately passed away. He was sixty years old, with thirty-five years of monastic seniority.
On the fifth day of the eighth month of that year, he was interred in a stupa to the east of the prefecture. (According to the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Shitou Xiqian emerged from under Qingyuan.)

From Qiānxià came Tiānhuáng Wù; from Wù came Lóngtán Xìn; from Xìn came Dèishānjiàn; from Jiàn came Xuěfēng Cún; from Cún came Yúnmén Yǎn and Xuánshā Bèi; Bèi’s second-generation successor was Fǎyǎn Yì.

It has been universally asserted that the two schools of Yunmen and Fayan originated from Qingyuan and Shitou; even their respective descendants have likewise claimed to be the direct lineages of Qingyuan and Shitou. It has long been unknown how this error came about. At the time of Daowu, there were two individuals with that name:

one resided at Tiangwang Temple west of the city of Jingnan and succeeded Mazu; the other resided at Tianhuang Temple east of the city of Jingnan and succeeded Shitou. The one from whom Longtan Xian emerged was Daowu of Tiangwang Temple under Mazu, not Daowu of Tianhuang Temple under Shitou. How is this known?

According to the record by Qiu Xuansu, Grand Master for Regular Discussion, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, and Chancellor, who served as the Regional Inspector of Jingnan: [The text continues with the historical account.]

The *Epitaph for Chan Master Daowu of Tianwang* states: Daowu was a native of Zhugong. His surname was Cui, and he was a descendant of Ziyu. At the age of fifteen, he left home to become a monk under Vinaya Master Tanzhu of Changsha Temple. At twenty-three, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.

At thirty, he visited Shitou and frequently received his instructions, yet for some time he failed to grasp the essential point. He subsequently called upon National Teacher Huizhong. At thirty-four, accompanied by National Teacher Huizhong’s attendant Yingzhen, he returned south to visit Mazu.

Mazu said: "Recognize your own mind; it is fundamentally Buddha. It does not belong to gradual stages, nor does it require cultivation. Its essence is naturally such-like (*tathatā*), and its myriad virtues are complete. Upon hearing these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Mazu instructed him, saying: "If you take up the leadership of a monastery, do not leave your current location."

Having received these instructions, the Master returned to Jingmen. Not far from the city wall, he constructed a thatched hut. Later, when the Regional Inspector questioned his attendants about the matter, they explained the circumstances to him. The Inspector personally visited to seek the Way;

Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun of Fuzhou was the son of the Zeng family of Nanan County, Quanzhou. His family had served the Buddha for generations.

As he was about to pass away, he ascended the hall to assemble the congregation. After a long silence, he extended his left hand;

the attendants did not understand its meaning, so he ordered the monks on the eastern side to step back. He then extended his right hand and ordered the monks on the western side to step back as well.
He then said, "To repay the Buddha's kindness, nothing surpasses the circulation of the Great Teaching. Go back! Go back! Take care! Having spoken, he smiled gently and passed away.
Ji. Chan Master Congfan of Xiangxi in Fuzhou arrived for an audience. The Master said, "Are you not a monk from Gushan? The monk replied, "I am.
The Master said, "Why is the pearl on your forehead not visible? The monk had no reply. When the monk took his leave, the Master saw him off at the gate.
He called again, "Elder! The monks turned their heads. The Master said, "Your bellies are full of Zen. They asked, "What kind of mental activity is this, Preceptor? The Master simply laughed loudly.
As the Master put on his patched robe (*kāṣāya*), he spoke this verse: "The upper robe of Kāśyapa— To don it requires swift wit.
The moment the beckoning arrow is distinguished, The hidden tortoise is revealed without concealment."
While Chan Master Yan of Shengshou Monastery in Fuzhou was mending his robes, a monk came for an audience. The Master held up the robe to show him, saying:
"This mountain monk has but a single robe; I spread it out for all to see. The two strips of cloud-patterned cloth are divided—do not let the needle and thread be exposed. Speak quickly!"
"Quickly! Quickly! The monk had no reply. The Master said, "What have you been doing for all this time?
Chan Master Lingyan Huizong of Jizhou was the son of the Chen family of Fuzhou. He received his monastic training at Guishan. A monk asked him:
"What is the realm of Lingyan? The Master said, "The pines and cypresses stand in dense, thick rows. [The monk] asked, "What is the person within the realm?
The Master said, "Every night there is the cry of a monkey. [The monk] asked, "What is the student’s own fundamental matter?"
The Master said, "Why do you cast away true gold to pick up shards and rubble?

Chan Master Xuan Sha Shi Bei Zong Yi of Fuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuefeng Cun. He was the son of the Xie family of Min. From his youth, he was fond of fishing. Once, while drifting...

On a small boat on the Nantai River, he associated with fishermen. At the beginning of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, when he was only thirty years old, he suddenly developed a longing to transcend the mundane world.
He abandoned his boat and went to receive the tonsure under Master Xun of Furuang Temple. He then traveled to Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang to receive full ordination.

Wearing a coarse cotton robe and straw sandals, he took only enough food to sustain his breath; he often sat in meditation throughout the entire day. Everyone marveled at him. Together with Xue... [text continues]
Feng was originally a fellow practitioner of the Dharma-gate with Baizhang, yet they were as close as teacher and disciple.
Because of his ascetic practices, Feng called him "Dhūta. One day, Feng asked, "Which one is Dhūta Bei? The Master replied, "I would never dare to deceive anyone."
On another day, Feng summoned him and said, "Head-tato Bei, why do you not go on a pilgrimage to study everywhere?

The Master replied, "Dharma did not come to the Eastern Land; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Feng approved of this. When they ascended Mount Xianggu, he and the Master joined forces in constructing the monastery.

Disciples from afar arrived in great numbers. The Master entered the inner quarters to seek resolution of his doubts, never flagging from morning until evening. Furthermore, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained awakening.
He clarified the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*). Consequently, his responses were swift and nimble, in perfect resonance with the *sūtras*.

Whenever scholars from various regions encountered points they could not resolve, they invariably sought instruction from him. Even when debating with Xuefeng, he did not shrink from the role of the benevolent one.
Xuefeng remarked, "Tuduo Bei is a man who has returned for a second time. When Xuefeng ascended the hall [to teach], he said: "To understand this matter, it is like an ancient mirror."

At the dais, [Master Fengxue] said, "When a Hu comes, he appears as a Hu; when a Han comes, he appears as a Han. A monk stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "What if a bright mirror were to suddenly arrive?
Fengxue said, "Both Hu and Han are hidden. The monk said, "The old monk’s heels have not yet touched the ground."

After residing [there], he ascended the hall and said: "The Way of the Buddha is leisurely and vast; it has no fixed path. It is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intent of the Way-man that has no intent.
It does not abide within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking. To establish it is to deviate from the Truth; it does not belong to the realm of creation.
Movement gives rise to the root of birth and death; stillness leads to intoxication in the land of dullness. When both movement and stillness are simultaneously extinguished—"
Falling into emptiness and loss. Gathering both movement and stillness, the Buddha-nature remains vast and boundless; yet one must necessarily face the dust and encounter the sensory objects.

Like withered wood or cold ashes, when applied according to the occasion, its suitability is never lost. A mirror reflects all forms without its radiance being disturbed; a bird flies through the sky without mixing with the space or color.
Therefore, throughout the ten directions there are no images, and within the three realms there is no trace of movement. One does not fall [into error].
The mechanism of coming and going does not abide in the intermediate state of mind. Within the bell there is no sound of the drum; within the drum there is no sound of the bell.

Bell and drum do not intersect one another; in every phrase there is no before or after. Like a strong man extending his arm, he relies on no external power; like a lion roaming, how could he seek a companion?
The nine heavens are free from obscuration—where is there any need for piercing through? This single segment of luminosity has never been darkened.
Obscure! If you reach this point, the essence is tranquil and still, eternally lucid, blazing like the sun with no boundaries. Within the empty space of perfect enlightenment, it does not waver;
it devours and incinerates heaven and earth, shining forth in total transcendence. Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world, fundamentally there is no coming or going.
Names and forms have no substance; the Way is fundamentally suchness. The Dharma is naturally so by its own nature; it is not a matter of cultivation or realization.

It simply requires that one remain empty and at ease, yet unconfused in one's functioning, without being mired in the dust and mud of the world. Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully expressed; to do so would be to become a follower of the Mara-king.
Whether before or after a phrase is the difficult point for the student. Therefore, when a single phrase accords with the Way, the eighty thousand gates are forever [sealed].

To sever birth and death: even if one attains a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—unimpaired by being struck and undispersed by touching the waves—it remains, nonetheless, a matter belonging to the shore of birth and death.
Where the Path-walker moves, it is like fire melting ice; the ice will never become ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return. Therefore, it cannot be caged.

Willingly abiding, they do not turn their heads when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements; to this day, there is no fixed location. If you reach this point, you ascend the profound with every step;

it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it. To move is to lose the source; to awaken is to be deluded regarding the essential meaning.
The followers of the Two Vehicles tremble with fear, and those of the Ten Stages are startled in spirit. The path of speech is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity—
Extinction. Thus, Śākyamuni closed his room in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed non-speaking to manifest the Way;
and Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening as flowers rained down. If you see it in this way before you, what further matter could you doubt? Where would there be a place to dwell?
Transcending the past, present, and future, it cannot be delimited or constrained; the paths of mind and thought are cut off, not because of...
Adorned from the beginning, it is truly pure; in every movement, word, and smile, it is clearly manifest wherever one is, lacking nothing at all.

People of the present age do not awaken to this underlying principle, but instead recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached everywhere and bound by every circumstance.

Even if they should attain some awakening, the realms of sense-objects remain chaotic and names and forms are seen as unreal; they then attempt to settle the mind and withdraw their thoughts, seeking to constrain all phenomena.
To return to emptiness, closing the eyes and hiding the pupils, yet for thoughts to eventually arise— gradually breaking them down,
and as soon as subtle conceptions are born, immediately suppressing them— with such a view, one is a non-Buddhist who has fallen into nihilism, a walking corpse whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Dark and vast, without sensation or cognition, one plugs the ears and steals the bell, merely deceiving oneself. Here, however, discernment is not so;
it is neither hiding behind doors nor lurking by windows. Every phrase is manifest before one, beyond deliberation and untouched by literary artifice.
Fundamentally severed from the realm of dust, fundamentally devoid of rank or position, we provisionally name such a person a "renunciant," yet in the end, they leave no trace.
The traces of True Suchness—ordinary beings and sages, hell-dwellers and devas—are merely expedient means for healing the madness of a son. Even empty space undergoes no change;
how could the Great Way have rising or sinking? To awaken is to move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit. If you reach this point:
For both the ordinary and the sage, there is no place to stand. If you direct your attention toward the words, you will be drowned and destroyed by them.

If you run outward in pursuit, you fall once more into the realm of Māra. As for the state of suchness, it admits of no contrivance; it is just like a blazing furnace that harbors not even a mosquito.
This principle is fundamentally level—what need is there to clear away anything? Whether moving or still, whether raising an eyebrow or not, this is true liberation.

The Way does not consist in forcibly forming mental conceptions; to establish such views is to deviate from the Truth. If you arrive at this point, you must not admit even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization].
To point toward it with the mind is already an error; even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not place a single character here.
Long standing, take care. [Ascending the hall: I now ask you all: what matter can you actually take responsibility for? In what world do you dwell?

To establish one's life upon the Way—can you still discern this? If you cannot discern it, it is just like pressing on the eyes and seeing flowers; as soon as you perceive things in this way, you are mistaken. Do you understand?
What you see before you now—the mountains, rivers, the great earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness, and all such various things—are all but the phantom flowers of a weary delusion;
they are called inverted views. As for those who have left the household life, they must recognize the mind and attain realization...

This is the source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. Now that you have already shaved your head and donned the robes, assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, you possess the capacity to benefit both yourself and others.
Yet, as I observe you now, you are entirely black, like a vast expanse of ink.
If you cannot even save yourself, how can you claim to have attained realization? O Benevolent One, the matters of the Buddha-dharma involve profound causes and conditions;

do not treat them with indifference or engage in superficiality. Do not gather together to chatter aimlessly, indulging in idle talk for the sake of profit, allowing time to pass. Time is difficult to obtain; it is truly a pity for such great men.
Why do you not examine and reflect upon what this matter truly is? As for the ancestral tradition from of old...
This is the lineage of the crowns of all Buddhas. Since you are unable to uphold it, I have used skillful means to urge you:
simply follow the gate of Kāśyapa to achieve immediate transcendence. This single gate transcends the cause and effect of ordinary beings and sages;
it transcends the wondrously adorned world-ocean of Vairocana; and it transcends the expedient gates of Śākyamuni. From this very moment, for all eternity, do not allow [delusion] to exist.
A single thing is presented to you as an object of visual perception; why do you not urgently investigate and grasp it for yourself?

It is not necessarily the case that one says, "I shall wait for three or two lifetimes to accumulate pure karma over a long period. O worthy one, what is this matter of the *zongcheng* (the essential vehicle)?
It cannot be attained merely by applying effort and adornment; nor can it be attained through the knowledge of others' minds or past lives. Do you understand? Just as...

Śākyamuni has emerged from his place and performed all manner of transformations; he preached the twelve divisions of the teachings like pouring water from a jar, creating a grand display of Buddhist ritual.
Yet, within this very gate, not a single point can be applied, nor can even a hair’s breadth of artifice be used.
Do you understand? It is like a dream, or like the prattle of one asleep. A śramaṇa should not emerge from his place. Not.
The matter of the shared dream is simply that it was recognized. Do you understand? To recognize it is to be one who has attained great liberation and great penetration.

Therefore, one transcends the ordinary and surpasses the sages; one is born beyond birth and departs from death; one leaves behind cause and effect; and one transcends Vairocana and surpasses Śākyamuni.
You will not be deceived by the causes and effects of ordinary beings or sages; no one anywhere can recognize you. Do you understand?
Do not remain forever entangled in the net of love for birth and death, where you will be bound and carried away by good and evil karma, leaving you with no freedom.

Even if you were to refine your body and mind until they were as empty as space, or even if you reached the state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness, it would still not transcend the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).
The ancients called this "like a rapid torrent. Because the flow is so swift, one is unaware of it and falsely deems it stillness.
Practicing in such a manner, one will never be able to transcend the bounds of saṃsāra; as before, one will continue to be driven by the cycle of rebirth.

Therefore it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Even the fruits and attainments of the Three Vehicles are thus to be feared. Without the eye of the Way, they too are not ultimate. Why?
Is it not as if an ordinary person of this world, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, could suddenly transcend and understand, thus saving their mental and physical strength?
Would you not wish for this? I exhort you: I shall stand here now and wait for you to grasp it;
I will not require you to add further effort or refine your practice. If you do not act like this now, when will you? Will you consent? Then he descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "All of you are like those sitting within the great ocean; submerged up to your heads and drenched, you still stretch out your hands to ask others for water to drink.
Now, a bodhisattva who studies Prajñā must possess great capacity and great wisdom before they can succeed.
If one possesses wisdom, one may escape at this very moment. But if one’s faculties are dull, one must simply..."
Exert yourself with diligence and endurance; day and night, forget your fatigue. Be without sleep and lose your appetite, as if you had lost your parents.

If you are this urgent, and spend your entire life in this way, further receiving the support and guidance of others, then you will be able to penetrate to the very bone and investigate the reality until it is easily realized.
Moreover, considering the present age, who is there capable of receiving and studying [the Dharma]? O worthy one, do not merely memorize words.
This is a record of his words. It was as if he were reciting a dharani; he stepped forward with a "tō-tō hō-hō" sound in his mouth.
When someone seized him and questioned him, finding no way out, he immediately grew angry and said, "The Master will not answer for me!
Learning the Way like this is truly bitter. Do you understand? There are some masters who sit upon the meditation seat and call themselves "virtuous."
Regarding "knowledge": when questioned, they merely shake their bodies and move their hands; they blink their eyes, stick out their tongues, and stare blankly.

Furthermore, there is another class who speak of a "luminous clarity," a "spiritual intelligence" (*lingtai zhixing*), which is said to be capable of seeing and hearing, acting as a sovereign within the field of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
To act as a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) in such a manner greatly deceives people. Do you understand? I now ask you: if you identify this luminous clarity...
This "bright and lucid" state is your true reality. Why, then, does it not remain bright and lucid when you are drowsy?
If it were not present during drowsiness, why would there be this brightness at other times? Do you understand? This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son";
it is the root of birth and death, a deluded thought and a condition of karmic energy. Do you wish to know its origin?
I tell you: this "bright and lucid" awareness exists only because of the dharmas of external objects—forms, sounds, scents, and so forth—which give rise to discrimination.
It is then that one says, "This is the bright and lucid. If there were no external objects, this bright and lucid awareness of yours would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Benevolent one, where does true reality actually reside? If you now wish to escape these five [aggregates]...
The sovereign of the field of the aggregates and the body merely perceives your secret vajra-body. An ancient said to you:
"Perfectly complete and pervasive, it extends throughout the realms of the sands. I shall now briefly explain this for you; the wise may attain understanding through analogy.
Do you still see the sun over Jambudvīpa? It is that which people of the world employ in their activities, sustenance, and livelihood.

All activities of the various mental formations and karmic deeds are established by relying upon the light of the sun. As for the substance of the sun itself, does it possess many kinds of mental formations?
Does it have any place where it is not all-pervasive? If you wish to recognize the adamantine essence (*vajra-dhātu*), you must likewise view it in this way:
right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness; light and darkness—and so forth.
Your body and mind are entirely sustained by the manifestation of your perfected majestic light.

Indeed, the karmic succession of actions performed by all classes of beings—gods, humans, and the multitudes—as well as the retributive fruits of their births, whether sentient or insentient, are all sustained by your majestic light.

Even the Buddhas’ attainment of the Way and the realization of the fruit, their reception of beings and benefitting of living things, are all entirely sustained by your majestic light. It is just like this...
The Vajra-body. Furthermore, are there ordinary beings and Buddhas? Is there the activity of your own mind? You must not say it does not exist and thereby pass away;
do you understand? Since you possess such a wondrous place of manifesting yourself in the presence of reality, why do you not investigate and realize it?
For what reason, instead, do you follow others and make your living within the ghost-realm of the field of the five aggregates?
You are simply deceiving yourself right now. Suddenly, when the demon of impermanence arrives, your eyes will roll back and your body will see only itself and its own life.
At such a time, it will be difficult indeed to sustain yourself; it will be like a living turtle struggling to free itself from its shell—a great suffering.
O worthy one, do not take this drowsy understanding and pass it off as sufficient. You have not yet been able to cover even a hair’s breadth [of reality]. Do you still understand?
Ho! There is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house. Furthermore, you have not yet attained a state of true peace and happiness.
You merely form large groups to interfere with the affairs of others, flying and running here and there like wild deer, seeking only food and clothing.
If you act in this way, how can you practice the Way of the King? Do you know that kings and great ministers do not constrain you? Nor does your father...
Your mother has permitted you to leave the household life. The donors of the ten directions provide you with food and clothing; the local spirits and dragon deities protect you.
Yet, you must possess a sense of shame and know how to repay kindness before you may succeed. Do not fail these people. You have spent your time on long rows of beds, wasting your days away.
To say that this is true peace and happiness is premature; it is all merely the nourishment provided by rice gruel and meals. [It will eventually] rot.
A winter melon is transformed and carried away; buried within the earth, the karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (vastly bewildered), with no foundation to rely upon.
Why does a śramaṇa come to such a state? As for all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth, I call them "dwelling in hell for kalpas.
If you do not resolve this now, tomorrow or the day after, you will enter the wombs of donkeys and horses and be dragged along.

Dragging plows and pulling harrows; bitting iron and bearing saddles; being pounded by pestles and ground by millstones; burned and boiled in water and fire—it is not at all easy to undergo such things.

You must feel great dread! It is entirely your own doing. Do you understand? If you were to realize it, from this very moment down through eternal kalpas, I would never have let you receive such news as this.
If you do not realize it, there will be the causes and conditions of afflictions and evil karma.
"It is not that you shall find rest after one or two kalpas; I grant you a lifespan equal to that of a *vajra*. Do you understand?

While the Master was in the midst of his formal session, he heard the sound of a swallow and said, "Profoundly expounding the true reality (*dharmatā*), skillfully preaching the essential teachings. He then descended from his seat.
At that time, a monk requested instruction, saying, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go away! Who would believe you? When Gushan arrived, the Master made a gesture.

[Zhaozhou] showed him a circular diagram. Xuefeng said, "Everyone fails to get out of this. Zhaozhou said, "I knew you would be making your living in the womb of a donkey or a horse. National Teacher Shenyuan of Gushan in Fuzhou, whose posthumous name was Xingsheng, was the son of the Li clan of the Great Liang. From childhood, he loathed the smell of meat and delighted in hearing the sounds of bells and sutras.

He fell gravely ill. In a dream, a divine being gave him medicine; upon waking, he was instantly cured. The following year, he again dreamed that a Buddhist monk told him, "The time for you to leave the household life has arrived.
He subsequently shaved his head under Master Gui of Bailu Mountain in Wei Prefecture and received full ordination at Mount Song.

The Master said, "I have not yet drunk tea today. [The monk] said, "Please give me some instruction, Master. The Master said, "It is already past.

The Master then pushed him out and closed the door; the monk was speechless. [The Master] asked: "When meeting a man who has attained the Way on the road, one does not respond with speech or silence;

He said, "Please, Master, examine this. The Master said, "If you speak thus, does it accord with the truth? He replied, "It would be improper to do so intentionally.
The Master said, "That is another matter entirely. A question was asked: "What is the single path of the spiritual source?

The Master said, "Why try to step across it? The Head Monk of Xuefeng sent a letter inviting him, saying: "The Abbot at the mountain head is advanced in years; why does the Elder not return there once more?"
When he had crossed the ridge once, the Master sent a letter back, saying: "Wait until the Monk of the Mountain Head has some further insight;
only then shall you enter the ridge again. A monk asked, "What is Xuefeng’s insight? The Master said, "I am also startled."
Chan Master Xuantong of Dapu Mountain in Fuzhou was a native of that same prefecture. A monk asked, "How can one obtain the pearl from beneath the chin of a black dragon?
The Master clapped his hands and winked at him. The monk asked, "What is the state prior to the application of skillful means? The Master then pushed him out.
Another monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "A fellow who bites on a bone comes forth."

[The monk] departs. [The Master] asks: "When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? The Master says: "Come discuss this after you have removed your shackles. [The monk] asks: "We seek refuge in you with great urgency;
we pray that the Master will receive us. The Master says: "Dull-witted fellow!"
Chan Master Jiaoran of Changsheng Mountain in Fuzhou was a native of that province.
Having long relied upon Xuefeng, one day while he was cutting down a tree with a monk, Xuefeng said, "Stop when you reach the heartwood. The Master said, "Cut it away!
Xuefeng said, "The ancients transmitted mind-to-mind; why do you say 'cut it away'? The Master threw down his axe and said, "Transmitted. Xuefeng struck him with his staff.
He took his staff and departed. A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the first phrase? Xuefeng remained silent for a long while.
The monk reported this to the Master (Linji), who said, "This is the second phrase. Xuefeng then sent the same monk back to ask again, "What is the first phrase?"
The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! During a communal work period (*pǔqǐng*), Xuefeng asked, "An ancient said, 'Who knows that beneath this scholar’s cap is originally a man of old sorrow'?
What was the intent of the ancients? The Master tilted his bamboo hat askew and said, "What kind of person speaks such words?
Xuefeng asked the Master, "One who upholds the sutras is able to shoulder the Tathāgata. What is it to shoulder him?"

Xuefeng was carrying the Tathāgata when his teacher took the Xuefeng statue and placed it upon the meditation seat. During a communal work session (*pingsheng*), Xuefeng was carrying a bundle of rattan.
On the road, he encountered a monk and threw it down. As the monk reached out to pick it up, Xuefeng kicked him over.
Upon returning, Xuefeng said to his teacher, "I felt quite swift kicking that monk today. The teacher replied, "The Master should instead have carried that monk into the Nirvana Hall."
Feng then stopped. Xuefeng asked, "When both light and object have vanished, what is it?
The Master said, "Let me pass through where there is the Way. Xuefeng said, "How do you speak when I let you pass? He replied, "I also let the Master pass.
Xuefeng said, "I grant you twenty blows. The Master then bowed. Later, while staying there, a monk asked, "An ancient had a saying..."
“Ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; there is no need to eliminate afflictions. “How is it that ignorance is itself Buddha-nature? The Master’s expression turned stern with indignation;
raising his fist, he rebuked him, saying, “Today I shall strike this monk! “How is it that there is no need to eliminate afflictions?
The Master seized the man by the head with his hand and said, “This monk creates such karmic obstacles for others! [The monk] asked.
On the road, he encountered a man who had attained the Way. [The Master] did not respond with speech or silence. [The man asked: "I do not understand what you will use to respond.
The Master said: "What can ink and paper on a sheet of paper possibly do? The Military Governor of Min appointed him as the Zen Master Dashi; his final whereabouts are unknown.
Chan Master Zhifu of Ehu in Xinzhou was a native of Fuzhou. A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?
The Master said, "It is not only you, Dharma brother, who are busy. The monk asked, "When space preaches the sutras, what does it take as its fundamental principle?"
The Master said, "You are not among the audience; get out. A monk asked, "Does the son of one who has committed the five heinous crimes still receive his father's legacy?
The Master said, "Though he may have his own way of acting, he cannot avoid injuring himself. A monk asked, "Who is the person above the Buddha?
The Master said, "I knew well that you, Venerable, would be at a loss. The monk asked, "Why are you at a loss? The Master said, "It is certainly not a small matter."

"A person attains the vision of the Noble One. [The monk] asked: "This was in the previous sentence; please, Master, speak upon it. The Master said: "What are you searching for beneath your own heels?
[The monk] said: "I am asking right now. The Master said: "Look, but you cannot transform your body. [The monk] asked:
"What was the meaning of Xuefeng throwing down his staff? The Master threw the incense spoon to the ground. The monk said: "I do not yet understand this meaning."

"What matters are we discussing? The Master said, "There is only the Mirror Lake before my gate; its clear breeze does not alter the waves of old.
Chan Master Shaokuo Xingfa of Longshou in Zhangzhou was the son of the Chen family of Quanzhou.

[The Master] said, "This is what is within your own house. Why do you fear it? At these words, the Master attained realization. He subsequently resided at Longxi.
A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'The Maṇi Hall has four corners; one corner is always exposed. What is this corner that is always exposed? The Master raised his whisk.
The monk asked, "If not a single grain of rice is stored, how can the hunger of ten thousand people be relieved? The Master said:
"Before a knight-errant, it is like snatching a sword away. I see that you are no clever fellow. The monk asked, "What is it like when the ears and eyes have nowhere to reach?
The Master said, "You do not act in such a way. The monk said, "If so, then I hear. The Master said, "A truly deaf man!"

Chan Master Xingrenhui of Quanzhou, a native of the Wang family, resided at Qianzong Monastery in Fuzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "I have studied together with Śākyamuni. Tell me, whom have you studied with?
