The Master then burned all the texts he had studied throughout his life and said, "In this life, I shall not study the Buddha-dharma. I will instead become a simple monk who prepares rice gruel, so as to spare my mind from toil.
He then wept as he took leave of Mount Guishan and traveled directly to Nanyang, where he visited the remains of National Teacher Duzhong.
He then settled there to rest. One day, while clearing away grass and trees, he happened to toss aside some tiles and rubble, which struck a bamboo stalk and produced a sound.

Suddenly, he attained awakening. He immediately returned to bathe and burn incense, prostrating from afar toward Mount Miao. He praised him, saying: "The Master’s great compassion exceeds that of my own parents.

The Master said: "If you had heard of him, you would have been the same as those who have heard. (Fadeng commented: "He has already finished his studies. The old man said: "I have heard of the seven Buddhas of the past, but I have never heard of a 'Qishishe'. The Master said: "If you had heard of him, you would have been the same as those who have heard. (Fadeng commented: "He has already finished his studies. The old man said: "I have heard of the
Xiu said, "A peach pit from a thousand years ago. The Master then sent a monk to ask Yangshan, "In these times, is awakening still necessary?
Yangshan replied, "Awakening is not absent; however, it would fall into the second rank. The Master deeply approved of this.
He then sent another monk to ask Dongshan, "What is the ultimate state? Dongshan said, "You must ask him yourself before you can know."
The Master also agreed with him. A monk asked, "Since ancient times, have the supreme sages attained the true principle or not? The Master said, "They have.
The monk asked, "As for this true principle itself, how is it attained? The Master said, "At that time, Huo Guang sold a counterfeit silver city to the Xiongnu.
Who wrote the contract? The monk said, "I am at a loss for words. The Master said, "That is so."
[The Master] said: "On level ground, I teach people to act as guarantors. [A monk] asked: "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? The Master said: "Let your ugliness be as you will loathe it;
it does not bear the colors of clouds or mists."

A monk from Mount Heng in Jinzhou once arrived at the monastery of National Teacher Heoshan. He announced himself, saying, "I am a great Chan Buddha from beneath Jiyun Peak who has come to receive four blows of the staff.
The Master then called for the *weina* to strike the bell. The "Great Chan Buddha" immediately turned and strode away.
When Master Yuankang went to visit Shilou, as soon as Shilou saw him, he drew up his feet and sat down.
The Master said, "How complete your dignified bearing is! Shilou asked, "What did you just see? The Master said, "I have been led astray by someone without cause.
Shilou said, "It must be like this before it can be called true seeing. The Master said, "How tragic! How many people have been deceived!"
Liu then rose from his seat. The Master said, "You have seen it, but you have not moved. Liu replied, "I exerted all my strength, yet I could not emerge from samādhi.

The Master clapped his hands three times. Later, a monk recounted this to Nanquan, who said, "No one in the world can settle the right and wrong of this fellow. If they could, they would be his fellow student."
During a period of turmoil, the Master Fayu of Sanjiaoshan in Qizhou was visited by a military commander who entered the mountain wielding a blade.
The commander asked, "Monk, what treasures do you possess? The Master replied, "The treasures of a monk are not suitable for you. The commander asked, "What kind of treasure is it?
The Master let out a thunderous shout; the commander did not understand and struck him with his blade.
While Wang Jingchu, an attendant official of Xiangzhou, was presiding over his duties, Master Mi arrived. The official then raised his brush and showed it to him.
Master Mi asked, "Can you judge the void? The official threw the brush away, went into his residence, and did not come out again. Master Mi was filled with doubt.
The next day, he relied upon the Master of Offerings at Gushan to enter and probe his intentions. The rice also arrived with him.
He hid himself behind a screen to observe. As soon as the Master of Offerings was seated, he asked, "Yesterday, what words did Master Mi speak?"
They no longer saw each other. The Official said, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. When Huimi heard these words, he immediately realized his former error.
He suddenly came out and laughed heartily, saying, "I understand! I understand! The Official said, "Understanding is not non-existent;
try to explain it to me. Huimi said, "Please, Attendant, demonstrate it. The Official then held up a single chopstick. Huimi said, "This wild..."
A fox-spirit. The Duke said, "This fellow is thorough. He asked a monk, "Do all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature? The monk replied, "They do.
The Duke pointed to a painting of a dog on the wall and said, "Does this one have it too? The monk was speechless. The Duke spoke on his behalf, saying, "Watch out! It’s going to bite you!"

The Dharma successor of Chan Master Yangshan Ji of the fifth generation under Nanyue was Chan Master Xitai Guangmu of Yangshan, Yuanzhou. A monk asked, "What is true hearing? The Master said, "Not..."
[The monk] entered through the ear and asked, "How is it? The Master said, "Do you hear? [The monk] asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment whether they are the same or different, tell me: what thing comes out and enters into the spout of a jar? [The monk] asked.
"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "You have no Buddha-nature. Question: "What is the Sudden?
The Master drew a perfect circle and showed it to him. Question: "What is the Gradual? The Master made three strokes in the air with his hand.
Chan Master Guangyong of the Southern Pagoda at Yangshan in Yuanzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Fengcheng in Yuzhang.

On the night his mother nursed him, a divine light illuminated the courtyard, startling all the horses in the stable; he was therefore named Guangyong. As a youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and quick-witted.
He went to Yangshan to receive the tonsure and left for the north to visit Linji. Upon returning, he again attended Yangshan. Yangshan asked him, "Why have you come?"
The Master said, "I come to pay my respects to the Abbot. Sanshan said, "Have you seen the Abbot? The Master said, "I have.
Sanshan said, "How is the Abbot like a donkey? The Master said, "In my view, the Abbot is not even like a Buddha. Sanshan said, "If he is not like a Buddha..."
"What is it like? The Master said, "If there were anything it resembled, how would it differ from a donkey? Daowu was greatly startled and said, "Both ordinary and sage are forgotten;
emotions exhausted, the essence is revealed. I have used this to test people for twenty years, yet none have reached a definitive realization.
You must maintain this. Daowu often pointed to him and told others, "This man is a Buddha in a physical body. A monk asked, "Mañjuśrī is the seventh..."
"The Buddha has a teacher. Does Mañjuśrī also have a teacher? The Master said, "He has one whenever he encounters conditions.
The monk asked, "Who is Mañjuśrī's teacher? The Master held up his whisk. The monk said, "Is it not simply this? The Master lowered the whisk.
He joined his palms and asked, "What is the single phrase of wondrous function? The Master said, "When the water arrives, the channel is complete.
He asked, "Where does the true Buddha dwell? The Master said, "Without form beneath a word; he is not elsewhere."
When Chan Master Jingtong of Mount Huo in Jinzhou first visited Yangshan, Yangshan sat with his eyes closed.
The Master then raised his right foot and said, "Thus it is! Thus it is! The twenty-eight patriarchs of India were thus; the six patriarchs of China were thus;
the Master was thus; and Jingtong is also thus. Yangshan rose and struck him four times with his staff.

[The Master] struck [the monk] four times with his staff. From this, the Master referred to himself as "The Great Zen Master of the Four Staff-Blows under Mount Jiyun" (also known as Dazenbutsu, who possessed supernatural powers).
After he took up residence there, an attendant asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master then bowed. The attendant said, "Why does the Master bow to an ordinary person? The Master replied, "Do you not see that it says: 'Reverence your elders and younger brothers'?"
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk held up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master said, "A dragon's head and a snake's tail.
He asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master struck him. The monk also struck him. The Master said, "It is reasonable that you strike me;
it is unreasonable that I strike you. The monk was speechless. The Master struck him again and drove him out. As the Master’s fundraising was nearing its end, he first prepared firewood.
In the countryside, he took his leave of all his donors. Having finished his meal, he went to the place where the funeral pyre was prepared and said to his disciples, "Come to report to me at noon.
When noon arrived, the Master himself took up a torch and ascended the stacked wood. Placing his alms bowl on the crown of his head, he manifested the sign of a halo;
holding his staff in his hand, he assumed the posture of the *vajra* (thunderbolt) used to subdue Māra. He remained standing until his end amidst the crimson flames.

Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi of Hangzhou was a native of Yuxi in Jiahe. His surname was Zhu. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order at Changle Temple (now known as Chongfu) in his home district;

he received the tonsure and the precepts at Guoqing Temple. Thereafter, he studied the Vinaya and listened to the teachings. During the Huichang era, when the Buddhist clergy were suppressed and purged, he returned to lay dress and lived in obscurity.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, he followed the general regulations for re-ordination and received the full precepts at Qifeng Temple in Yan’an.
Later, he visited Chan Master Xingkong of Mount Daci. Xingkong asked, "Why do you not travel extensively to seek instruction?
The Master went directly to Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai, where he arrived at the Vajra Cave to pay his respects. There he encountered an old man leading an ox along the path.
He invited the Master into the temple. The old man called for "Kuntī," and a young boy responded by coming out to welcome them.

The old man released his oxen and led the Master up into the hall; the entire building was radiant with a golden light. The old man sat upon his couch, pointed to an embroidered cushion, and commanded him to sit.

The old man asked, "Where have you come from recently? The Master replied, "From the South. The old man asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South? The Master replied, "It is the age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*)."
The bhikṣu had observed the precepts for only a short time. The old man asked, "How large is your assembly? The master replied, "It is either three hundred or five hundred.
The master then asked in return, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here? The old man said, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together."

The Master asked, "How many people are in the assembly? The Old Man replied, "Three times three before, three times three after. The Old Man called to his attendant boy to serve tea, along with some whey and curd.
The Master partook of the flavors, and his mind was suddenly enlightened. The Old Man picked up a crystal cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South?
The Master said, "No. The Old Man asked, "What do you usually use to drink your tea? The Master was speechless.
"Yes. As the color of the sun grew somewhat late, the Master asked the old man, "May I stay for one night?
The old man said, "You still have a mind of attachment; you may not stay. The Master said, "I have no mind of attachment. The old man asked, "Have you ever received the precepts?"
The Master said, "I have received the precepts for a long time. The old man said, "If you have no mind of attachment, what need is there to receive the precepts?
The Master took his leave; the old man ordered a youth to see him out. The Master asked the youth, "Three times three before, and three times three after—how many is that?
The youth called out, "Virtuous One! The Master responded. The youth said, "How many is that? The Master asked again, "What place is this? The youth...
He said, "This is the Vajra Cave Prajñā Monastery. The Master was moved to grief and realized that the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī, who could not be seen again.
He immediately prostrated before the youth and requested a single word as a parting gift. The youth spoke this verse: "A face without anger is an offering;
A mouth without anger emits a wondrous fragrance; A mind without anger is a precious treasure."
"Stainless and undefiled is the truly eternal. Having spoken these words, Junti and the temple both vanished.
Only within five-colored clouds was Mañjuśrī seen riding a golden-maned lion, coming and going. Suddenly, white clouds arose from the east and covered them so they were no longer visible.
At that time, monks such as Xiuzheng from Pútí Temple in Cangzhou arrived; they still heard the mountain rocks shaking and roaring.

...the sound. The Master consequently stayed his staff at Mount Wutai. In the third year of the Xiantong era, he went to Guanyin in Hongzhou to visit Yangshan, where he suddenly attained realization and their minds were in accord.
Yangshan appointed him as the steward (*dianzuo*). Once, Mañjuśrī appeared atop the rice-pot;
the Master struck him with his rice-stirring paddle and said, "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī, and Wenxi is Wenxi. Mañjuśrī then spoke this verse: "Suffering..."
"The bitter melon is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to end. Having practiced for three great kalpas, you have nevertheless been disparaged by this old monk.
One day, a strange monk came to seek alms-food. The Master reduced his own portion and gave it to him. Yangshan, having foreseen this in advance, asked:
"A person from the stage of fruition has just arrived. Will you provide him with food? The Master said, "I shall set aside my own portion and give it to him in return.

Yang said, "You will bring great benefit. Later, he returned to Zhejiang and resided at Longquan Temple. A monk asked, "What is the mark of nirvana? The Master said, "It is verified where the incense smoke ends.
[The monk] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Call the temple steward here. This master—
A monk was suffering from epilepsy. He asked, "What is one's own true self? The Master remained silent. The monk was at a loss for words and asked again.

The Master said, "The azure sky is shrouded in obscurity; it does not fly toward the moon. The King of Qian petitioned the throne to grant him purple robes and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Wuzhuo (Non-Attachment).

As he was about to pass into *parinirvāṇa*, at the hour of midnight, he addressed the assembly, saying, "When the mind within the three realms is exhausted, that is *nirvāṇa*. Having spoken, he sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away, and a white light illuminated his chamber, such that the bamboo and trees took on the same color. His stupa was erected in the western valley of Lingyin Mountain.

In the second year of the Tianfu era, Tian Jun, the regional commander of Xuancheng, joined the rebellion of the Hangzhou general Xu Si; he unleashed his troops to plunder extensively and opened the stupa.
There, he beheld the flesh body, which had not decayed, with both nails and hair having grown long. Qian Wang, known as Wuku, marveled at this and dispatched his subordinate general Shao...

His remains were subsequently reinterred with an additional posthumous title. In the *jiachen* year of the Jiading era of our Imperial Dynasty, they were moved to the left of the stupa of Chan Master Zhijue Shou at Jingci Mountain.
A monk asked Chan Master Sunzhi Liaowu of Wuguan Mountain in Silla: "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?"

The Master held up his whisk. A monk said, "Is it not this very thing? The Master lowered the whisk and asked, "It is not formed by the character 'yi' (以), nor is it the character 'ba' (八). What character is it? The Master drew a circle to show him.
Another monk drew a five-petaled circle before the Master; the Master struck through it and drew a single circle.
A monk asked the Master of Yangshan Dongta in Yuanzhou, "What is the King’s sword? The Master said, "The mooring rope is cast off; no merit is claimed. The monk asked, "How is it when it is used?
The Master said, "It does not fall into human hands. The monk asked, "When the Dharma King and the secular King meet, how is it?
The Master said, "Both palms are impartial. The monk asked, "After they have met, how is it? The Master said, "In between."
An extraordinary likeness.
A monk asked Master Zhi Guan of Jizhou, a successor of Chan Master Xiangyan Xian, "What is the Vairocana Teacher? The Master grabbed him by the chest and gave him a shove.
Question: "What is sudden? The Master said: "Neither Liang nor Chen.
Chan Master Shaoshong of Shouzhou was asked by a monk: "What is the meaning of the West? The Master said: "Good news does not leave the door;
bad news travels a thousand miles. An official said to the Master: "I have heard it said that in Jiangxi they do not establish a school. The Master...

[The monk] asked, "When meeting conditions, one establishes [the teaching]. [The monk] asked, "What is it that you establish when meeting conditions? The Master said, "In Jiangxi, we do not establish a school.
Chan Master Wuran of Nanchan in Yizhou was asked by a monk, "Regarding the phrase that has no phrase, will you, Master, give an answer?
The Master said, "From the beginning, I have only clarified such matters as these. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "Just ask and see."
A monk asked the Master of Changping Mountain in Yizhou, "What is it like at the point where even a blink of an eye cannot reach?

The Master said, "I do not even have the leisure to blink. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s intent? The Master said, "Coming from the Western Heaven; going to the land of Tang."
A monk asked Chan Master Chengfu Yanjiao of Yizhou, “What is the speech that is vast and expansive? The Master said, “Attaining the Way without a mouth.
The monk asked, “What is the meaning of the coming from the West? The Master said, “Today and tomorrow.”
A monk asked Zen Master Qinggan of Dajian Mountain in Anzhou, "How did all the sages of antiquity realize [enlightenment]?
The Master merely raised his brow. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "A sheep-headed cart pushes the bright moon."
A monk asked the Abbot of Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan, “What is the house style of the Master?
The Master said, “I am wall-faced in every matter. The monk asked, “What is the matter of original nature? The Master said, “I would never ask another person again.”
A monk asked Zen Master Fuyan Yan of Mount Wudang in Junzhou, "I have been ill for some years and was recently poisoned;
I beg the Master to act as my physician. The Master said, "One bowl of 'double-appropriate' broth. The monk asked, "What is the matter that lies beyond the Buddha?"
[The monk] said, "What about the matter of the Buddha’s descent? The Master said, "The lotus seat.
A monk from Shuangxi of Tian, a practitioner from Mount Lu in Jiangzhou, asked, "What is the mechanism of the 'cracking' and the 'pecking'?
The Master made a pecking gesture with his hand. [Another monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the West? The Master said, "Where did you get that question?"

"Come," said Master Hongzhou Miling Heshang, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Yin of Mount Jing. His constant teaching was: "There is nothing that surpasses this. A monk asked: "I do not yet know what it is."
"There is nothing beyond this. The Master said, "It does not go beyond this. Later, a monk asked Changqing, "Why does it not go beyond this?
Changqing replied, "What do you intend to call it?"
The Dharma heir of Master Shuangfeng was Chan Master Gu of Shuangfeng in Fuzhou. His original vocation was lecturing on the sutras, but he subsequently went to visit the former Shuangfeng.
Shuangfeng asked, "Virtuous One, where do you reside? He replied, "In the city. Shuangfeng said, "Do you ever think of me, the old monk? He replied, "I always think of the Master."
"Furthermore, there is no way for me to pay my respects and have an audience. Feng said, "This very state of thinking is you, Great Virtue. From this, the Master understood the essential meaning;
he immediately ceased his lecturing and attended upon him for several years. Later, he went to Shishuang, where he merely followed the assembly and did not seek formal instruction.
The community remarked that the former attendant had once received the seal of transmission from Shuangfeng, and this was often heard by Shishuang. Shishuang [intended]—
He pressed him for an account of his realization, yet he could find no opening. The Master then took his leave.

As he was about to depart, Xuefeng brushed away the whisk and called out from the doorway, "Attendant Gu! The Master turned his head. Xuefeng said, "To conceive of it is already an error; to grasp it is already a deviation.
Not to conceive of it is not it either, so do not try to form a conceptual understanding. Unless one knows that there is [something], one cannot know it. Go well, go well."
The Master responded, "Yes, yes," and immediately set forth. Shortly thereafter, Shuangfeng entered nirvana, and the Master succeeded him as the abbot.
A monk asked, "When you took your leave of Shishuang at that time, what was the meaning behind Shishuang’s words?
The Master said, "He simply told me not to cling to right and wrong. (Xuange said: Now tell me, did he understand Shishuang’s meaning or not?)

Chan Master Ruyao of Zifu in Jizhou, successor to Chan Master Xita Mu of the sixth generation under Nanyue, was asked by a monk: "What is the phrase that responds to the occasion? The Master remained silent.
Question: "What is the profound purport? The Master said: "Close the door for me. Question: "What was the meaning of Lu Zu facing the wall?
The Master said: "There is no connection. Question: "What is the true eye from of old? The Master struck his breast and said:
"Heaven! Heaven! [The questioner] said: "Is there any harm in asking? The Master said: "I am weary. Question: "Does this accept instruction?"

"No. The Master said, "I have never dug into the earth to plant empty space. He asked, "What is the urgent matter for a patch-robed monk? The Master said, "It does not go beyond this. He asked, "Before I have even asked, I request the Master to speak. The Master said, "Alas! He asked again. The Master said, "Alas! He asked once more. The Master said, "Alas! He asked, "Why do you say 'alas' three times? The Master said, "Because you have asked three times. He asked, "What is the meaning of the three 'alas'? The Master said, "The first 'alas' is because you have no eyes; the second 'alas' is because you have no ears; the third 'alas' is because you have no mouth. He asked, "What is the meaning of having no mouth? The Master said, "If you had a mouth, you would surely be unable to ask. He asked, "How can one attain liberation? The Master said, "If you wish to attain liberation, you must first abandon your own body. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own body? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own body, you must first abandon your own mind. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own mind? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own mind, you must first abandon your own views. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own views? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own views, you must first abandon your own self. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own self? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own self, you must first abandon your own consciousness. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own consciousness? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own consciousness, you must first abandon your own thoughts. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own thoughts? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own thoughts, you must first abandon your own perceptions. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own perceptions? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own perceptions, you must first abandon your own attachments. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own attachments? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own attachments, you must first abandon your own desires. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own desires? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own desires, you must first abandon your own delusions. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own delusions? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own delusions, you must first abandon your own ignorance. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own ignorance? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own ignorance, you must first abandon your own grasping. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own grasping? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own grasping, you must first abandon your own clinging. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own clinging? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own clinging, you must first abandon your own craving. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own craving? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own craving, you must first abandon your own thirst. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own thirst? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own thirst, you must first abandon your own heat. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own heat? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own heat, you must first abandon your own fire. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own fire? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own fire, you must first abandon your own fuel. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own fuel? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own fuel, you must first abandon your own wood. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own wood? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own wood, you must first abandon your own axe. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own axe? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own axe, you must first abandon your own hands. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own hands? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own hands, you must first abandon your own arms. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own arms? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own arms, you must first abandon your own shoulders. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own shoulders? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own shoulders, you must first abandon your own back. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own back? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own back, you must first abandon your own chest. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own chest? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own chest, you must first abandon your own belly. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own belly? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own belly, you must first abandon your own heart. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own heart? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own heart, you must first abandon your own liver. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own liver? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own liver, you must first abandon your own lungs. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own lungs? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own lungs, you must first abandon your own kidneys. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own kidneys? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own kidneys, you must first abandon your own spleen. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own spleen? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own spleen, you must first abandon your own gallbladder. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own gallbladder? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own gallbladder, you must first abandon your own intestines. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own intestines? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own intestines, you must first abandon your own stomach. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own stomach? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own stomach, you must first abandon your own blood. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own blood? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own blood, you must first abandon your own flesh. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own flesh? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own flesh, you must first abandon your own skin. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own skin? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own skin, you must first abandon your own bones. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own bones? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own bones, you must first abandon your own marrow. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own marrow? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own marrow, you must first abandon your own brain. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own brain? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own brain, you must first abandon your own head. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own head? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own head, you must first abandon your own face. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own face? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own face, you must first abandon your own eyes. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own eyes? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own eyes, you must first abandon your own nose. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own nose? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own nose, you must first abandon your own mouth. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own mouth? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own mouth, you must first abandon your own tongue. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own tongue? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own tongue, you must first abandon your own teeth. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own teeth? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own teeth, you must first abandon your own lips. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own lips? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own lips, you must first abandon your own chin. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own chin? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own chin, you must first abandon your own neck. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own neck? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own neck, you must first abandon your own throat. He asked, "How can one abandon one's own throat? The Master said, "If you wish to abandon your own throat, you must first abandon your own windpipe. He asked,
"How is it that 'a single mote of dust enters right concentration'? The Master assumed the posture of entering meditative absorption and said, "How is it that 'all motes of dust arise from samādhi'?
The Master said, "Whom are you asking? [The student] asked, "What is the one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa?
The Master snapped his fingers once and then opened both hands wide. [The student] asked, "How should I understand this? The Master said, "It is not the brightness of the autumn moon, my son."
[The Master] acted recklessly for eight or nine years. A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Three bowls of tea after the meal.
One day, the Master picked up his meditation cushion (*pútán*) and showed it to the assembly, saying, "All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sages who have entered into principle all emerge from here.

Having entered the monastery, as the end of the summer retreat approached, he said, "I have not yet received instruction from the Master; I pray you will grant me your guidance.

One day, the Master placed a meditation cushion upon his head and said, "At such a time as this, it is difficult for me to converse with you all. The assembly had no reply.
As the Master was about to sit down, he then said, "It is still somewhat better than that."

Chan Master Huiqing of Bajiao Mountain in Yingzhou was a successor of Chan Master Nanta Yong; he was a native of the kingdom of Silla. Once, while ascending the hall, he held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying:

"Unfortunate; it will not be auspicious hereafter. Question: "The Northern Dipper conceals its body—what is the meaning of this? The Master said: "Nine times nine is eighty-one.
He then asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said: "One, two, three, four, five. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"When I was twenty-eight years old, I went to Yangshan to visit Nanta. I saw him ascend the hall and say: 'All of you here, if you are...'"
This fellow, as soon as he emerged from his mother’s womb, let out a lion’s roar—was it not so?
Under these words, I found rest for my body and mind, and I remained there for five years. A monk asked, “How was it before the Ancient Buddha appeared in the world?
The Master said, “The root of a thousand-year-old eggplant. [The monk] asked, “And after he appeared? The Master said, “Vajrapāṇi opens his eyes. [One day] he ascended the hall. Good!
Jiuzhi said, "I am deeply honored by your visit. Take care. A question was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s intent? The Master said, "Which Patriarch’s intent are you asking about?
He replied, "The meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West. The Master said, "Alone and weary, he crossed the river in the dark. A question was asked: "Master, what is this?"
[The monk asked: "Before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch, how was it? The Master said, "Known. [The monk] asked, "After he saw him, how was it?
The Master said, "Known. [The monk] asked, "What thing has no two heads? What thing has no front or back? The Master said, "My body has no two heads."
"My words have no front or back. [The student] asked, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya? The Master said, "First, you must not ask;
second, you must not rest. [The student] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Come for a third time, and I shall meet with you."
Chan Master Quanfu of Qinghua in Yuezhou was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery. He first visited Nanta, who asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Ezhou. Nanta asked, "What is the name of the Prefect of Ezhou? The Master said, "Being under his jurisdiction, I dare not offend him.

The Master laughed with a broad, open smile and thereby granted his seal of approval. At that time, the Magistrate of Anfu County in Luling established Yingguo Chan Garden and invited the Master to gather disciples there.

The Master said, "In the morning look to the southeast; in the evening look to the northwest. The monk said, "No..."
[The assembly] gathered. The Master said, "You merely boast of the traveler from Dongyang; you do not recognize the treasure of Xiyang. A monk asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye?

Later, when the Master returned to his native country, the Prince Wenmu of the Qian family treated him with special honor and respect. [Recorded in] the Jin [Dynasty].
In the second year of the Tiānfú era, the year of Dīngyǒu (977), a garrison commander of the Qián clan cleared Yunfēng Mountain to establish a monastery, also naming it Qinghuá.

[The monk] said nothing in response. The Master said, "The pupils in the eyes are blowing whistles. [The monk] asked, "How old are you, Preceptor?
The Master said, "I first saw last year on the ninth day of the ninth month; now I see again the autumn leaves turning yellow. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then you are countless."
The Master said, "Go ask for the yellow leaves. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is the matter? The Master said, "Six dice, the entire basin is red.
[Another monk] asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master said, "The long river flows without interruption;
gathered foam drifts at the mercy of the wind. [The monk] asked, "Does he still receive offerings? The Master said, "Offerings are not lacking. [The monk] asked, "How so?"

During a sacrificial rite, the Master said, "The sound of a fisherman’s song as he raises his oar is heard within the valley. The King, Zhongxian, presented him with a purple cassock, which the Master would not accept.

He feared that later generations would emulate him and indulge their desires. In the autumn of the fourth year of the Kaiun era, he manifested parinirvāṇa. At that time, a great wind arose, shattering and toppling the bamboo and trees.

Chan Master Jiche of Bajiao Mountain in Yingzhou was a successor of Chan Master Bazhao Qing. When he first visited Fengxue, Fengxue asked him, "What is the True Dharma Eye?

"The Way: two mouths and no tongue—this is my school's fundamental principle. Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. Later, while residing there, a monk asked, "What is the scenery of Línxī?

The Master said, "In front of the main gate; behind the Buddha hall. The monk asked, "What is the place of deepest depth? The Master said, "The stone man opens the stone [gate]."
The door: the stone lock wobbles at both ends. Entering the hall: In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the Brahma King requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.

With our eyes beholding Your Honored Countenance, we pray that You will proclaim the Prajñā. The Master says: "Take note clearly. The monk says:

"As the Master proclaims the wondrous Dharma, may the King live ten thousand years, and may the people be at peace and happy. The Master says: "Who told you this? The monk says: "It is so by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*)."
The Master said, "But you are indeed quick-witted. [The student] asked, "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is; the 'tawny cat' and the 'white ox' do know that there is.
Since they are the Buddhas of the three periods, why do they not know that there is? The Master said, "It is actually you who know that there is.
[The student] asked, "Why do the tawny cat and the white ox, however, know that there is? The Master said, "Where have you seen them?"
Question: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught that 'the eye does not see form-objects and the mind does not know dharmas.

What does it mean for the eye not to see form-objects? The Master said: "It is actually the ear that sees. Question: "What does it mean for the mind not to know dharmas? The Master said: "It is the eye that knows. Question:
"If that is so, then while the paths of seeing and hearing are cut off, sounds and forms remain clamorous. The Master said: "..."
"Who told you that? He replied: "As for all questions and answers, they are like the meeting of needle points;
there is not the slightest discrepancy. There is no matter that is not penetrated, and no principle that is not complete.

This is truly because all speech, all samādhis—whether horizontal or vertical, deep or shallow, hidden or manifest, coming or going—are the gate of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas. It is simply to be verified right now, at this very moment."
Take this up. Be careful. Entering the hall: An ancient said, "What is Chan? The three realms are continuous.
What is the Way? The ten directions are vast. Why does he say the three realms are continuous? Where is the principle that the ten directions are vast?
Do you wish to understand? Block the eyes; block the ears; block the tongue, body, and mind. Leave no space for deficiency.
There is no place for movement. Elder, how do you understand this? It cannot be grasped horizontally; it cannot be grasped vertically; it cannot be grasped lengthwise; it cannot be seized away.
There is no place for the application of mind, nor is there any place for its establishment. If you can understand it in this way, [you have attained it].
From the very beginning, the Dharma-gate of assembly is free from selection; all speech is free from leakage.
Once there was a monk who asked, "What is the speech that is free from leakage? I told him, "The mouth is like the nostrils. "Excellent! said the Elder.
If you understand it in this way, naturally no wind will pass through. If you realize it completely, the ten directions of the world are the adamantine eye.
There is nothing more to say. Take care. [The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "The world is at peace;
may Your Majesty live long. What is the King? The Master says, "The sun rises and the moon is bright. The monk asks, "How should one understand this? The Master says, "Who is the student?
He then says, "The world is at peace; may the Great King live long. The land is abundant and joyful, free from all calamities. These are the words of the Buddha. Ancient..."
The present is not altered; a single word does not shift. With this, one can settle both the ancient and the present. All you venerable elders, please grasp this well.
Furthermore, a monk asked: "I have heard an ancient saying: 'There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally desolate.

What is meant by 'there is a thing prior to heaven and earth'? The Master said: "Neither identical nor conjoined. [The monk] asked: "What is meant by 'formless, it is fundamentally desolate'? The Master—
[The monk] asked, "Who asks about that which precedes heaven and earth? [The Master] said, "If that is so, then you shall go alone to roam the quiet forests.
The Master said, "Why do you speak such nonsense? He then said, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of this sort. Do you wish to understand? When words are uttered, they are not sound;
when form appears, it is not an object. Only then will you understand: 'All under heaven is at peace; may the Great King live long. [The monk] stood for a long time. Take care."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddha-dharma is already perfected; all is fully complete. Have you not heard it said: 'Perfectly identical to the great void, lacking nothing and having no excess'?
If this is so, then who is deficient and who is redundant? Who is right and who is wrong?
Who is one who understands and who is one who does not understand? Therefore it is said: 'Going east is also the Seat-Holder (Upādhyāya); going west is also the Seat-Holder'; south..."
Going west is also the Elder; going north is also the Elder. For what reason do east, west, south, and north come to be established?
If you can understand this, the paths of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will naturally be cut off, and all dharmas will manifest before you. Why is this so?
Because the Dharmakāya is formless, yet forms appear before every eye; Prajñā is without cognition, yet it reflects in response to conditions. All at once.
"Understand this thoroughly, all you elders. For one who has left the household life, what is there to do?
This is the principle that has existed from the beginning; it is not something extraordinary. To recognize the mind and reach the source—therefore, one is called a śramaṇa.

If you recognize the mind, it is bright and clear, truly without even a hair’s breadth of obstruction. You have stood here for a long time, elders; take care. [He] ascended the hall. A monk asked: "I wish to enter the non-..."
[The Master said: "It is the ocean. First, one must board the boat of *prajñā*. What is the boat of *prajñā*? The Master said: "Always abiding nowhere. [The student] asked:

"What is the ocean of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? The Master said: "First, understand the boat of *prajñā*. [The student] asked: "An ancient worthy said: 'To ascend to heaven, one does not borrow a ladder;
throughout the earth, there is no path to walk. What is 'ascending to heaven without borrowing a ladder'? The Master said: "Not leaving behind even a single thread."
Fadi asked, "What is it like to have no path anywhere on the ground? The Master said, "What did I just tell you?

He then continued, "The hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi, the hundreds of thousands of gates of supernormal powers, and the hundreds of thousands of gates of wondrous function—all do not transcend the ocean of prajñā.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are established upon the foundation of non-abiding. Therefore it is said:"

Arising and ceasing, going and coming, wrong and right, movement and stillness—the thousand transformations and myriad changes: these are the gate of the great samādhi of all Buddhas; nothing surpasses this.
All you venerable elders, investigate and grasp this thoroughly, so as to increase the life-span of the Buddha-dharma. Be careful! Ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"The World-Honored One entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa. Now, as for Kāśyapa being at Piṇḍava..."
Luo Ku asked, "I do not know to whom you have entrusted [the Dharma]. The Master said, "Who would you have me teach it to?
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then the entrustment at Vulture Peak is no different from today. The Master said, "Where have you seen Vulture Peak?

[The monk] asked, "The Precious Seal of the Dharma Eye was personally transmitted by the Master; I wonder to whom it should now be entrusted? The Master said, "The drum beats, *dong dong*; one end [is struck]."
[The Master] struck [the gong]. It rang twice. He said, "If that is so, then the thousand sages are of one kindred, and past and present are no different.
The Master said, "The waves of the Zen river are stilled; you seek the water but lose the source. The monk Qingyu asked, "The Emperor has requested your presence to receive the King’s grace.
At the Prajñā assembly, we request that you proclaim the Dharma. The Master said, "Take this clearly to heart. [Qingyu] said, "If that is so, then the jeweled nets of the Cloud Terrace..."
They all performed the wondrous sound together. The Master asked, "Where is Qingyu? They replied, "The Dharma King’s Dharma is thus. The Master asked, "Who can testify to this?
He then said, "The entrustment at Vulture Peak was clear; let all you venerable elders verify it at once.

If you verify it, there will be no other principle—there is simply 'now,' like the great void. When the sun is bright or the clouds are dark, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth [are all present]."
The entire world of conditioned phenomena appears clearly and manifestly; even the unconditioned is likewise so.
From the time the World-Honored One entrusted [the Dharma] until the present day, there has not been the slightest difference. To whom else could it be entrusted? Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"The mind is itself the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma. If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; but it is neither mind nor original mind."
Dharma. This is the model for the entrustment at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. All you venerable elders, grasp this thoroughly; do not let your time pass in vain. The kindness of kings is difficult to repay;
the kindness of the Buddhas is difficult to repay; the kindness of parents and teachers is difficult to repay; the kindness of donors from the ten directions is difficult to repay.
Moreover, the establishment of such a sequence and the flourishing of the Buddha-Dharma would not have been possible were it not for the [support of] the state.
"O King, by the power of your grace, how could it be otherwise? If you wish to repay this kindness, you must clarify the eye of the Way and enter the ocean-nature of Prajñā;
only then will it be attained. I shall take my leave for now. Adieu. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "An ancient worthy said: 'The person is empty, and phenomena are also empty.'"

"The two marks are fundamentally identical. The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. The student said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, "Where is it not a skillful means?

The student asked, "Regarding the provisional nature of names and the provisional nature of dharmas, and the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas—having set aside all external conditions, I ask the Master to point directly.
The Master said, "Thank you for this question. The student said, "If one does not behold the magnificence of the royal palace, how can one know [its splendor]?"
The Heavenly Son was honored. The Master said, "In greedily gazing at the moon in the heavens, you have lost the oar in your hand.
He asked, "Regarding the Middle Way: because the mind is pure, the Dharma-realm is pure. What is this pure mind? The Master said, "The kalaviṅka bird; the saṃjīva bird.
He asked, "Is it one with the Dharma-realm, or is it two? The Master said, "You should ask someone else yourself," and then he spoke further.
The Great Way is vast and open; how could it be confined by past or present? Nameless and formless, this is the Dharma and this is cultivation.
This is truly because the Dharma-realm is boundless and the mind is likewise limitless. There is no phenomenon that does not manifest, and no word that does not reveal it.

To realize this in such a way is called the manifestation of Prajñā. Its principle is identical to the True Limit (bhūtakoṭi); all mountains, rivers, the great earth, the myriad phenomena of the cosmos, and even walls—[are all thus].
"Bricks and rubble—there is not the slightest thing lacking or deficient here. I shall not stand for long; take care.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I have heard the Master say: 'The nine heavens uphold the jade seal; the seven Buddhas manifest the prior mind. What is this seal? The Master said:

Buluo Wen asked, "What is the mind? The Master said, "Your name is An-si. He then said, "The nature-ocean of the Dharma-realm is like a box and its lid, like a hook and its shackle, like gold and gold;
in every position they are perfectly equal, without the slightest discrepancy, never becoming confused or intermingled.
They are neither one nor different, neither the same nor distinct. If you return to the ground of reality, then every dharma..."
All of these reach the bottom [of the truth]. It is not that it is "so" simply because one comes up and asks, "How is it? What is it? Nor is it "not so" when one does not ask.
It exists when sitting on the long benches; it does not exist when not sitting. It is just like the venerable elders of all quarters.

The verbal teachings remain in the world like the sands of the Ganges River. In the Tathāgata’s great treasury of scriptures, every scroll expounds the Buddha’s principle, and every phrase speaks entirely of the Buddha’s mind.
Why is it that you fail to understand? If you merely continue to weave together these verbal teachings, [you will never realize it].
The conscious mind attempts to understand and interpret; yet even a venerable elder who has passed through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could never attain thorough penetration.

This is called inverted knowledge and views, the active calculations of the discriminating consciousness—there is no place here where any power can be gained. This is because the foundation of one's roots is not clear.

If one exhaustively investigates the source of all Buddha-dharmas, the great treasuries as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will manifest all at once, lacking not even a hair’s breadth and exceeding not even a hair’s breadth.
The Buddhas constantly appear in the world and constantly preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings without ever ceasing;
even the cries of monkeys and birds, and the grasses, trees, and forests, always assist this Elder in triggering his realization. There has never been a single moment when this was not so.
As the Elder, there is such a marvelous state of affairs here that it is truly to be cherished.

May all you Elders investigate this thoroughly so that the Dharma may long abide in the world, increasing the lifespan of humans and devas, and bringing peace, security, and prosperity to the kingdom. Be careful.
[He] ascends the hall and cites the ancients: "I have a single word; whether in heaven or among men, if people do not understand it, the green waters and blue..."
"Mountain. Furthermore, what is the principle of this single word? The words of the ancients must be understood through deep penetration before they can be grasped.

If you merely employ words as names, you will have no realization regarding those words. It is only by thoroughly investigating the very root of all phenomena that one begins to understand this single word.
This single word is not something to be conceptualized or intellectually grasped through mere thoughts; it is called "the single word" only in that sense. If...
When the path of speech is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, one finally arrives at the realm of the ancients.

This is not merely closing one's eyes and hiding one's sight, seeing nothing in the dark, which is then called "the cutting off of the path of speech. Do not misunderstand this! The Buddha-dharma is not such a principle.
Do you wish to understand? Even if one were to speak for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there would never have been even half [of it].
These words have reached the various elders; though they have passed through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not even a single phrase has ever been omitted.

You must understand them thoroughly from the very depths before you can attain realization. If you merely deliberate upon these names and phrases in this manner, you will only exhaust your mind and strength to no avail.
May the elders bear witness to this together. Those of later generations and beginners must investigate this with urgency. I shall now take my leave. Adieu.
[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "The skull is constantly interacting with the world; the nostrils touch upon the family style. What is 'the skull constantly interacting with the world'?
The Master says, "Wait until I have finished answering you. [The monk] asks, "What is 'the nostrils touching upon the family style'?
The Master says, "I will repeat it once more at the appropriate time. [The monk] asks, "One person holds a torch and burns his own body; another..."
A man was carrying ice while another lay dead across the road. "Which of these two can distinguish the Way? the Master asked. The man replied, "Neither.

He said, "I do not understand. I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Your name is Jingxin (Respectful New). The man asked, "I wonder if there is anyone else who can bear witness to this?
The Master said, "There is. The man asked, "Who is it that bears witness? The Master said, "Jingxin. [The man] asked, "Before Niu-tou saw [the First Patriarch]..."
"How was it during the time of the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said, "A wondrous site and a sacred trace; all who behold it admire it.
[The student] asked, "What is it like after one has seen it? The Master said, "What did I just tell you? [The student] asked, "An ancient said: 'Striking the void, the hollow resounds.'"
The stone man and the wooden man respond in unison. Snow falls thick and fast in the sixth month.
This is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. "What is it that strikes at empty space? The Master said, "A servant from Mount Kunlun wearing iron trousers;
for every blow he receives, he takes a step forward. [The student] said, "If so, then the stone man and the wooden man respond in unison. The Master said, "Do you hear it yet?"

Mo then said: "The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas are always thus. They are like the great ocean, with its thousands of waves and myriad billows, which never for a moment remain still, never for a moment exist, and never for a moment do not exist. In this vast expanse, luminosity is sovereign;

it encompasses the three periods of time within the tip of a hair and perfects past and present within a single thought. You must achieve thorough and fundamental penetration before you can attain it; it is not otherwise."

I ask a single word and you record a turning phrase; you skillfully construct rationalizations, comparing wind and clouds to water and moon, or matching four-character and six-character couplets as if they were the Buddha-dharma.
Do not deceive yourselves; such things, O venerable elders, ultimately provide no benefit. If you understand thoroughly to the very bottom, there is truly nothing to hide.
There is not a single land where it is not manifest, nor a single speck of dust where it does not appear. Even a common person here and now stands on the same level as all Buddhas.
"Do not use even a hair’s breadth of effort; grasp it all at once. It is well. No need for further concern. Take care.
The Master was then asked by Master Ming of Xingjiao: "Kāśyapa held Śākyamuni’s six-foot robe while waiting on Mount Kukkuṭapāda for Maitreya’s descent.
When he draped the six-foot robe upon Maitreya’s thousand-foot body, it fit perfectly according to measure. But as for Śākya..."
“Kāśyapa’s body was sixteen feet tall; Maitreya’s body is one thousand feet tall. Is it that his body understands shortness, or is it that his robe understands length?
The Master said, “You understand it backward. Ming shook out his sleeves and went out. The Master said, “Little fellow, if I had answered you as ‘not so,’ there would have been cause and effect.
If you were not [right], I would have seen it through. Ming returned home. Seven days later—
One day, Ming vomited blood. Master Fuguang urged him, saying, "You must go quickly to repent.

Ming went to the master’s quarters and said with tears of grief, "I pray that the Master will show me compassion and grant me permission to repent. The Master replied, "It is like a person who has fallen to the ground;
they rise from the ground. I have never taught you how to rise while still on the ground. Ming spoke again, "If you grant me permission to repent, I shall serve you for the rest of my life."

The attendant asked, "Master, please provide a verse for this. The Master spoke: "The Way of Buddha after Buddha is equal; yet, how distinct are high and low! Śākyamuni and Maitreya are like a seal impressing upon clay.
In the fourth year of the Kaibao era (the *xinwei* year), the western peak of Mount Kōfuku suddenly collapsed, its sound shaking the entire mountain. The Master said:
"It will not be long. In the sixth month of next year, a great star shall fall upon the peak, and the forest trees shall turn white.

Thereupon, the Master manifested illness at Lotus Peak; he received visitors and inquiries as usual. On the twenty-eighth day, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.
Chan Master Taichin Fading of Qingliang in Jinling was a native of Weifu. From birth, he knew the Way; his eloquence was unimpeded.
Having entered the chamber of Fayen, the assembly of disciples turned to him in devotion, and all acclaimed him as a skillful master. He first resided at Shuanglin Monastery in Hongzhou.
On the day he ascended the Dharma seat, he pointed to it and said: "In former times, venerable masters of this mountain have preached the Dharma here."
The seat is high and vast; how could one of no talent ascend it? There is an ancient saying: "One must pay homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja before one may take a seat.
But tell me, where is the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja now? Does the great assembly wish to see him?
At one time, after performing a single prostration, he ascended the seat. After a long silence, he said, "The assembly is just like this;
is there anyone who understands? A monk asked, "What is the realm of the Twin Trees? The Master said, "Even a painting cannot capture it.
The monk asked, "What is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Go away! You have not even recognized the realm; first find that! Another monk asked, "When a Buddha appears..."
[The Master said: "The world shakes heaven and earth. When a Master appears in the world, in what direction does it shake?
The Master said: "Where do you see shaking? [The monk] said: "What can be done about the present moment? The Master said: "What business is there today? A monk came forward and bowed.
The Master said, "As for 'the Way,' you thanked me for my previous visit; what would I have given you?

As the monk was about to ask a question, the Master said, "I thought we were in accord, yet it turns out you do not understand. A monk asked, "What is the hidden, profound meaning of the West [coming from India]?
The Master said, "Suffering. A monk asked, "When a Buddha appears in the world, he universally moistens all living beings. When the Master appears in the world, for whom are you intended? The Master—
[The Master] said, "It is not for nothing. [A monk] asked, "If that is so, then the assembly has something to rely upon. The Master said, "Why bother? Then he said, "For now, you may stay.

[He remained standing] for a long time. To the high official and the great assembly: Today your invitation was most diligent and earnest. This extraordinary merit—how can it be compared to anything else?
Therefore it is said: "Let those who have not yet attained listen to one word. Who is this very person right now?
He moved his mouth and immediately descended from the seat. Standing leaning on his staff, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Do you understand?
The Heavenly Dragon listened in silence while the flowers rained down; do not treat this as a mere painted image of Subhūti. Just believe and practice accordingly."
Question: "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. The Master picked up the incense box and said, "Is there such a thing as this on Mount Lu?
The monk had no reply. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying, "I have come seeking the fragrance to pay my respects to the Master. Question.
"The hundred skeletal parts all crumble away, yet one thing remains eternally spiritual. I do not know how much distance there is between the hundred skeletal parts and this one thing.
The Master said, "The hundred skeletal parts are the one thing; the one thing is the hundred skeletal parts. Next, he resided at the Huguo Cloister of Shanglan.
A monk asked, "When drums are struck in the ten directions, they are heard simultaneously in the ten places. What is 'hearing'? The Master said, "From which direction have you come?"

Question: “One practices the Bodhisattva path without being stained by the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). What is this Bodhisattva path? The Master said: “The characteristics of all phenomena. [The questioner] asked:
“How can one avoid being stained? The Master said: “Where would you be stained? Question: “Before long, the selection field will open.
Will you allow students to select [the candidates] or not? The Master said: “You are one whose forehead is marked with a dot. He said again: “You are...”
"What subject matter? he asked. "What is the expounding of the Great Dharma? The Master said, "How could my expounding be like yours?

Later, while residing at Longguang Monastery in Jinling, he ascended the hall. The *vinaya* master struck the gavel and said, "O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
The Master said, "The *vinaya* master has already provided the secondary meaning (*dvitīyārtha*). Elder, as for you right now, what rank does it occupy?"
Yi raised his sleeve and said, "Do you understand? O assembly, this is dancing with hands and feet.
Do not say that he was once a master of music five hundred lifetimes ago. If anyone has doubts, please ask for instruction.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the orthodox lineage of all Buddhas? The Master said, "What lineage are you? The monk asked, "How so? The Master said, "How?"
[The monk] did not understand. He asked, "Master Shanglan sang this 'one tune' (*yiqu*) himself; what is the matter with Longguang today? The Master said, "When did you ever come to Shanglan?
[The monk] said, "What about the matter of being 'thoroughly correct' (*didang*)? The Master said, "If it is not thoroughly correct, then seek it elsewhere.
He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "First ask about the small meaning; then come back and I will give [the answer]."
"Great Intention," the Master later resided at the Great Practice Site of Qingliang.

He ascended the hall, and as a monk came forward to prostrate, the Master said, "This monk comes forth first to repay the profound kindness of the State Ruler on behalf of the great assembly. The monk then asked, "The State Ruler has issued an invitation."
The patriarchal seat was opened once more. A student came forward and requested, "I ask the Master to point directly to the source of the mind. The Master said, "Come up, then go back down.
The student asked, "The single lamp of Fayan illuminates the whole world; as for the Master’s single lamp, whom does it illuminate? The Master said:
"From where does the Dharma-eye shine forth? The Master replied, "I originally intended to dwell in the mountains to hide my ineptitude and spend my time tending to my illness.
However, because my late teacher left behind an unresolved case, I have come out to settle it for him.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is this unresolved case of the late teacher? The Master struck him and said, "The grandfather did not [finish it]."

[The Master] said, "It is finished. The calamity will extend to your descendants. [The other] asked, "Where does the fault lie? The Master said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity will fall upon you.
When the Prince of Jiangnan was still the Duke of Zheng, he received the mind-dharma in the hall of Fayen. Subsequently, when Fayen entered nirvana...
He once asked the Master, "Does the former master have any unresolved kōan? The Master said, "I am currently analyzing it.
On another day, he asked again, "I have heard that you, Elder, have some extraordinary teachings regarding the former master.

The Master made a gesture as if rising from his seat. The Ruler said, "Please sit down. The Master addressed the assembly, "The former master’s Dharma assembly consisted of five hundred people; now..."
There are only a dozen or so people who act as leaders in various quarters. Do you think there might not be anyone among them who points the way to others incorrectly?
If they were to point the way wrongly, it would cause those people to enter water and fire, or fall into pits and ditches. Yet the ancients also said:
"If I head toward the mountain of blades, the mountain of blades shall naturally crumble; if I head toward the cauldron of boiling oil, the cauldron of boiling oil shall naturally vanish. Now then—
How do you deliberate upon this? Your words are fluent, yet when questioned, you become hesitant.
Why is that? It is simply because it has been a long time since we last met. Elder, you merely understand where I cannot go;

yet there is that which cannot be gone to—namely, the eyes and other sense organs, as well as forms and other phenomena. Setting those phenomena aside for a moment, Elder, when you open your eyes, what do you see?
Therefore it is said: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara. Take care.

In the sixth month of the eighth year of the Kaibao era, the Master manifested illness. He addressed the assembly, saying: "This old monk lies ill; I have forced myself to drag my body here to see you.
Now, every place is a site of practice (*dojō*), yet it is like a conjured city (*keijō*). But tell me, what is this conjured city?"
The ancient Master did not say that the place of treasure is not far away; one must simply press forward.

Upon reaching the city, he further said, "That which I have manifested through transformation—now you all, try to explain its principle and see if you can definitively determine whether it is Tathāgata-dhyāna or Patriarchal-dhyāna.
Although you are of later birth, you must know that you are by good fortune the subjects of our national sovereign. In all matters...

A single site of practice has been established at this sacred ground; all necessities are provided without lack. It requires only that you open your mouth. Yet, now you do not know which one is your mouth.
How can you respond and repay the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence? Do you wish to understand? Simply recognize the mouth and there will surely be no fault.
Even if there were a fault, it would arise because of you. Now, as fire and wind press upon me, going and staying are the eternal Way.

I, this old monk, have served as abbot for nearly twelve years. Throughout this time, I have constantly received the support and encouragement of the sovereign, as well as from donors, fellow practitioners from the ten directions, administrative officials, and junior disciples;
all have served me with sincere hearts. This remains a silent matter difficult to express, yet some have even gone so far as to wear hempen robes and headbands of coarse cloth.
This is merely to conform with worldly convention; my Way contradicts the conventional truth. Now, tell me: is it better to conform or to contradict?
However, if one simply conforms to my Way, there will be no delusion. As for my remains, I must request a burial plot from the side of National Teacher Dazhizang on South Mountain.
Thus, my ascent and descent shall be clear and manifest, and I shall not sink into oblivion. Strive on! Take care! On the twenty-fourth day, I sat peacefully.
He passed away.

Chan Master Qingsong of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a native of Fuzhou. Initially, he visited Fayen, who pointed to the falling rain and said to him, "Every drop falls into the eyes of the Venerable.
At first, the Master did not understand the meaning; later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he finally realized it.
