As a young śrāmaṇera, he witnessed a monk enter the master’s room to inquire about the karmic conditions regarding the courtyard cypress at Zhaozhou.

When the master interrogated that monk, Yuanjian attained a realization by his side. After receiving full ordination, he visited Fenyang and Yexian, both of whom granted him their seal of approval. Once, while with...
Daguan Ying, Xue Datou, and several others like them were traveling through Shu when they nearly met with disaster. The Master liberated them through his wisdom.

Because the group recognized that the Master was well-versed in administrative affairs, they titled him "Master Yuanlu" (the Record-Keeper). When he ascended the hall to offer incense, he said: "You are flowers blooming upon a withered tree by the sea;
you welcome the spring colors in a unique way. A monk asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind do you succeed? The Master—
[The Master] said: "An eighty-year-old man rolls a brocade ball. [The questioner] said: "If that is so, then a single phrase suddenly opens the ancestral lineage;
the weapons of the three mysteries shake the monastic forests. The Master said: "Li Ling was originally a subject of the Han dynasty. [The questioner] asked: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said, "The elder is like an elder brother; the younger is like a younger brother. A question was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "A pile of bones rising from level ground. A question was asked: "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, it stands as steep as a thousand fathoms;

the true command is being exercised, cutting off the ten directions. With what will you, the Master, express this? The Master said, "A cold cat does not catch mice. [The questioner] said, "Is this not it?"

[The monk] asked, "When acting as a human being, where does one dwell? The Master said, "A Persian does not tie a sash. [The monk] asked, "As the New Year has already arrived, where has the Old Year gone?
The Master said, "There is nothing strange before one's eyes; there is no need to paste up a Zhong Kui. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said:
"I thought there was nothing before my eyes. The monk drew a circle with his hand and said, "What can be done about this? The Master then struck him.

While discussing the Way with Imperial Consultant Wang Zhi, the Master drew a circle and asked: "First, one must not have a single horse and a lone spear; second, one must not return home wearing brocade.
The magpie must not be joyful, and the crow must not suffer misfortune. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Wang was at a loss.
"Enough," the Master said. "I have seen through you. He ascended the hall and said, "Do not further discuss the past or talk of the present;
I shall, based solely on the matter before us, settle and distinguish it for all of you. A monk then asked, "What is the matter before us? The Master replied, "The nostrils.
The monk asked, "What is the matter that transcends this? The Master replied, "The eyes. When the Duke Ouyang Wenzhong heard of the Master’s extraordinary character, he was deeply impressed.

Yi went to his room, but the Master did nothing out of the ordinary. He was playing *qi* (go) with a guest, and the Master sat beside them. Wenzhong suddenly gathered up the board and requested that the Master expound the Dharma by means of the game.
The Master immediately ordered the drum to be beaten and ascended the seat, saying: "If one discusses this matter, it is like two families playing *qi*. Why is this so?
When opponents are of equal skill and understand one another, they do not yield when the moment arises. If one is to connect five..."
There are three [points]. Furthermore, one must first penetrate a single path before attaining it. There is a certain class of people who only know how to close the door to make a living;

they do not understand how to seize the corner and break through the barrier. Their stubborn knots and tiger-mouths manifest simultaneously, yet once the enclosure is broken, their efforts at maneuvering are in vain.
Therefore it is said: "The fat edges are easy to find; the thin belly is hard to seek. If one thinks and acts, one often loses the connection; because the mind is coarse, at times—
At that moment, he struck his head. Cease boasting of being a national master; do not vainly speak of being an immortal. Let us not ask about winning the game or losing the counters;
tell me, before black and white have been distinguished, where does that first move fall? After a long silence, he said: "From of old, the nineteen paths."

"How many people have there been who have wandered in delusion and attained awakening? Wen Zhong sighed with admiration and said calmly to his colleagues, "When I first began, I suspected that Chan discourse was merely empty and exaggerated.
Today, seeing this old man’s karmic conditions and attainments, I realize that what he has gained and realized is nothing less than awakening and clarity within the mind-ground."
"How could one possibly possess such a wondrous principle? He ascended the hall and said: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear;

Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and brings order to the world. When a patch-robed monk attains the One, calamity descends upon his person. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they establish gates of transformation that do not depart from the wisdom-eye of the three bodies (trikāya).
This is like the three eyes of Maheśvara. Why is this? One eye is so tightly sealed that no water can leak through; it is difficult for the ordained and the laity to discern.

One eye is fully open across the great earth; it penetrates freely throughout the ten directions. One eye casts a single glance over high and low, and all myriad beings gaze together. Nevertheless, even though this is so..."
When Zen monks of the fundamental school meet on a crossroads, they must possess the extraordinary, heaven-penetrating true eye to succeed.

Thus it is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is; the cat and the white ox, however, do know that there is. But tell me, what is it that the cat and the white ox know? Do you wish to understand?
Deep autumn rain falls across a thousand homes through the curtains; the setting sun rests upon the towers of a hundred pavilions.

Difeng. In his later years, the Master retired at Huishengyan and expounded upon the profound meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He composed the Nine Banners (*jiu dai*), which are: the Banner of the Buddha’s True Dharma Eye;

the Banner of the Buddha-Dharma Treasury; the Banner of the Pervasion of Principle; the Banner of the Pervasion of Phenomena; the Banner of the Vertical and Horizontal Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena;

the Banner of the Crookedly Hanging [Teaching]; the Banner of the Subtle Accordance and Simultaneous Integration; the Banner of the Golden Needle and Twin Locks; and the Banner of the Constant Reality of Impartiality. Once the students had...
[The assembly] had already recited [the preceding nine sections]. The Master said: "If one relies on the Dharma-gate of Perfect Ultimate Reality, there are originally ten sections.
Now, these nine sections have already been explained for you all. Is there yet another section that you can perceive?

If you can perceive it intimately and clearly, then please come forward and explain it for the assembly. If you can explain it clearly, I shall grant you the perfection of the previous nine sections."

"To clarify the eye of the Way: if one's vision is not intimate and one's explanations are inconsistent, yet one relies solely on my words as their own understanding, this is called slandering the Dharma.
When you people reach this point, what do you say? The assembly was silent. The Master rebuked them and departed.
A monk asked Chan Master Fashao Yanchiao of Baoying Monastery in汝州 (Ruzhou): "When a single word accords with the Way, what then?
The Master said: "Seven topsy-turvy, eight upside-down. The monk said: "I, this student, prostrate myself. The Master said: "He tells him to stop, yet he refuses to stop;

he simply waits until his head is soaked by the rain. [The monk] asked: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him. Why was this?"
"One attains the Buddha-way. Why is it that one cannot attain the Buddha-way? The Master said, "Barefoot, riding an iron donkey, one goes straight to dwell in South China.
Entering the hall, he said: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, if you allow yourself one moment of 'cessation of study,' that is precisely studying the Buddha-dharma.
Have you not seen how Ānanda, though foremost in much-hearing, was nonetheless expelled by Kāśyapa and was not permitted to participate in the compilation [of the scriptures]? Only then...
Knowing one’s own intelligence and extensive learning, one relies on memory, retention, and conceptualization, racing outward in pursuit. This is in no way connected to the awakened, numinous mind;
it fails to penetrate beyond the shell of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). When circumstances accord with one's desires, joy arises; when they oppose them, anger arises.

Thus, the coverings become deep and thick, entangling and binding oneself so that there is no liberation. One wanders through birth and death, with the six sense faculties becoming a source of affliction and suffering.
Pressed by circumstances, one lacks any freedom, yet the deluded mind presides over it as its master. A true man of great character should seize this opportunity early on!
(He lets out a shout) and says: "Investigate! Ascending the hall, he said: "The gate of Baoying is a place of peril;
those who enter lose their entire bodies. What is the phrase for emerging from it? If you cannot speak it, thirty years from now—"
A monk asked Chan Master Huiguo of Dasheng Mountain in Tangzhou, “What is the meaning transmitted from of old?

The Master said, “The golden platter is spread out for all to see. The monk asked, “When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? The Master said, “To brush away the dust is already a deviation;
to see the Buddha is an error. The monk said, “If it is not like this at all, then what? The Master said, “An error. The monk asked, “As for...”
"What is the Way? The Master said, "It is wide where it is wide; it is narrow where it is narrow. The student asked, "What is one who is on the Way?

The Master said, "He suffers where there is suffering; he rejoices where there is joy. The student asked, "How far apart are the Way and the one on the Way? The Master said, "One hundred and eight thousand [miles].
The student asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "When the sky is clear, the sun shines. The student said, "As for me..."
"No," the Master said. "When it rains, mud grows.
Zen Master Yundi Yin of Shending was succeeded by the Abbot Baoqing of Kaisheng in Jingnan Prefecture. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Kaisheng? The Master said, "Three."
Wulu led the way and asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "Two tigers patrol the mountain.
A monk asked Zen Master Guangyun of Miaozhi Temple on Mount Tiantai, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The Master said, "Yellow chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "The Double Ninth Festival.
Chan Master Daguang Tan-ying of Jinshan in Runzhou, a successor of Chan Master Cong of Guyin, first visited Chan Master Xuan of Dayang and asked: "The Cave..."
Shanshan specially established the categories of "partial and correct" and "ruler and subject. What did he intend to clarify? Yang said, "The state of affairs before one's parents were born.
The Master asked, "How do you realize this? Yang said, "At midnight it is perfectly bright; at dawn, nothing is revealed. The Master was perplexed.
He then went to visit Guyin and recounted the previous conversation. Guyin said, "Daiyang did not say it was wrong; it is simply that his mouth is too narrow. It fills his entire mouth..."
[The Master] had not yet finished speaking when the Old Monk [Yaoshan] said, "It is not so. The Master asked, "What is the matter before one's parents were born?
Yinyuan said, "A dung-brick. The Master asked, "What is 'midnight, perfectly bright; at dawn, it is not revealed'? Yinyuan said, "A cat sleeping beneath a peony flower.
The Master became even more perplexed and startled. One day, during a communal work assignment (*pǔqǐng*), Yinyuan asked, "Today we are transporting firewood."
"Is it so? the Master asked. Yunyan said, "Yunmen once asked: 'When a monk carries firewood, the firewood carries the monk; how do you understand this? The Master had no reply.

Yunyan said, 'This matter is like a person learning to write: that which can imitate the dots and strokes is skillful; that which cannot is clumsy. This is because they have not yet forgotten the method.
One must reach the point where the brush forgets the hand, and the hand forgets the mind—only then will it be possible. At this, the Master attained silent realization."
After a long silence, he said, "As Shitou said: 'The grasping at phenomena is fundamentally delusion; even to accord with principle is not awakening.
Yunyan asked, "Do you consider these words to be medicine or a disease? The Master replied, "They are words of medicine. Yunyan rebuked him, saying, "You take the disease for the medicine!"

"Furthermore, how could this be acceptable? The Master said, "The fact is like a box finding its lid; the principle is like an arrow with a straight shaft and a wondrous point—how could there be anything added?

Yet you still regard it as a defect; truly, you have not yet grasped the essential meaning. Yinyue said, "Even when the wondrous reaches such a state, it is still merely called 'principle and fact' (li-shi)."
The intent of the Patriarchs cannot be reached by intellectual consciousness; how much less can it be exhausted through phenomena and principles?

Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "Principles obstruct right view; phenomena obstruct the continuity of birth and death. At these words, the Master was as if awakened from a dream and asked, "How does one make use of this?
Yunyan replied, "If speech does not leave the nest, how can one escape the entanglements? The Master sighed and said, "As soon as it touches the lips..."

"Once you engage in verbal expression, you fall into conceptual thought; this is entirely the gate of death and is by no means the path of life. After his realization, he addressed the assembly, saying:

'As soon as one involves the lips and tongue, one falls into conceptual thought; this is entirely the gate of death and is not the path of life. Even if one manages to break through, one still remains mired in delusion.
Do not let your lifelong efforts go to waste, nor spend this life in vain. If you wish not to let your life be in vain, [you must act accordingly].'"
Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said, "You must not be deceived by this staff;
look, this staff pierces through the skulls of you all and leaps right into your nostrils! He struck it again.
A monk asked, "What are the first two characters of the sutra? The Master said, "The character 'yi' (以). The monk asked, "What does that mean?"

"What kind of engagement is this? The Master said, "The eight characters. [The monk] said, "What a trick for people! The Master said, "Because you slandered this sutra, you have incurred such retribution.
[The monk] asked, "Who is to carry the one hundred and twenty-jin iron cangue? The Master said, "I, the old monk. [The monk] said, "One reaps what one sows.
The Master said, "Suffering! Suffering! [The monk] asked, "Have you, Reverend, ever recited the Buddha’s name? The Master said, "I have never recited it."
The Buddha said, "Why do you not recite the Buddha's name? The Master replied, "I fear it will defile people's mouths. He ascended the hall.

When the assembly had gathered, the Head Seat came forward to prostrate. The Master said, "Ask well. The Head Seat bowed his head. As he was about to ask a question, the Master said, "Today I shall not answer questions," and immediately returned to the Abbot’s quarters.
He ascended the hall again. "The gate of this mountain monk is unique; I have already altered the tracks of all other quarters. For..."
Mañjuśrī pulls out the wedge from the eye; he instructs Samantabhadra to cease chewing the iron in his mouth. He exhorts people to loosen the hand that grips the coiled snake;
he cuts away for you the hitching post for the donkey. As someone pauses to contemplate this, [the Master] shouts: "Squeeze! Squeeze! Investigate! Ascending the hall, he said:
"In my life, I have always been fond of wrestling, yet there has been no one to match me. Today, let us first engage."
The seat was set in opposition; he rolled up his *kāṣāya* and descended from the seat, calling for the head seat to engage in a "sumo match.

Just as the head seat stepped out, the Master said, "A fall on level ground," and immediately returned to the abbot’s quarters. He ascended the hall for formal discourse. "The Buddhas of the three periods are my servants," he said.
"The entire Great Canon of teachings is my spittle. After a long pause, he asked, "Tell me, whose servants are the Buddhas of the three periods? Thereupon, he took up his whisk.
The Master drew a single line and said, "The Buddhas of the three periods have passed over this side.
Now tell me, who is it that spat out the entire Great Canon? He then spat himself once. Ascending the hall, he said: "The scale-weight suddenly floats from the bottom of the well;

the old rat has been transformed into an ox for many years. When Hui-kong saw this, he clapped his hands and laughed: 'A three-legged monkey is different from an ordinary ape. Ascending the hall again, he said: [He spoke as before.]
The five thousand scriptures are the constant discourse of all Buddhas; the eighty thousand afflictions are the wondrous functioning of sentient beings. Yet, even these are not yet the Vajra Eye.
What is the Vajra Eye? After a long silence, he said: "Blind. One day, when the assembly had gathered and settled, a monk just as he stepped forward to prostrate, the Master said:
"If you wish to recognize the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and circumstance."
A monk then asked, "What is the causal condition of the season? The Master immediately descended from his seat. The monk asked, "Who is the person who goes forth?
The Master said, "Once returned to the green peaks, one does not emerge from the white clouds. He asked, "Who is the person who returns?
The Master said, "Since wandering the purple thoroughfares, who would be willing to hide in the green mountains? He asked, "What is 'seizing the person'?"
"Not robbing the realm. The Master said, "At home there is no longer any news of returning; by the roadside stands empty the signpost for longing for one's hometown.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'robbing the realm but not robbing the person'? The Master said, "The vast ocean is made to dry up to its very bottom;
the green mountains are ground down until they become dust. [The monk] asked, "What is 'robbing both person and realm'? The Master said, "Heaven and earth are yet empty; Qin..."

[The Master] said, "The sun and moon, the mountains and rivers—none see the Han sovereign or his ministers. [The student] asked, "What is it like when both the person and the environment are not taken away?

The Master said, "The oriole sings through the thousand forests; flowers cover the ground. A traveler wanders for three months; the grasses encroach upon the heavens. [The student] asked, "What is the house style of the Master?
The Master said, "Stretching out one's hand, one cannot even see one's own palm. [The student] said, "If a guest who has attained the Way (a *siddha*) should suddenly arrive, what then?"
The Master said, "Facing each other across a thousand li. [The monk] asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose lineage of the patriarchal wind do you succeed? The Master said, "Linji.
[The monk] said, "In that case, you are the son of Guyin. The Master said, "Deshan. [The monk] asked, "What is the long Dharmakāya?
The Master said, "A six-foot staff. [The monk] asked, "What is the short Dharmakāya? The Master said, "Three-inch counting sticks."
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then the Dharma-body has two [aspects]. The Master said, "There is still more—squareness and roundness. He ascended the hall and said:
"In other quarters, the hook is crooked and the bait is fragrant; they swarm together like bees around their queen. Here at this monastery, the hook is straight."

"There is no bait either; it is like pressing a gourd down to the bottom of the water. He raised his staff, assumed the posture of fishing, and said, "To catch fish in deep waters, one must have long confidence in their fate;
I have never used wine to sacrifice to the River God. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Huìyuè of Cùfēng on Mount Dōngtíng in Sūzhōu: "When 'one flower opens and five petals emerge,' and the fruit is naturally formed—what then?
The Master said: "Cast off the head-stall; unburden the yoke. The monk said: "Having squeezed out the void, everywhere one hears its fragrance.
The Master said: "Clouds grieve as they hear the ghosts wail; snow presses down as the skulls chant. [The monk] asked: "And..."
"Before you have even seen Guyin, how would you express it in a single phrase? The Master said, "With every step, the mountain grows further.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like after you have seen him? The Master said, "Hurrying along, following the horse's hooves."
Chan Master Xiujǐ of Zhàngxī Mountain in Míngzhōu traveled with Fúshān Yuǎn. He once established a hermitage at Fóshǒu Yán on Mount Lúshān.
Later, he went to Shànxīn on Mount Sìmíng, where he lived alone for over ten years with tigers and leopards as his neighbors. He once said:
A goat’s gut path and a bird’s trail—no one reaches them. In the silence of the clouds, there is but a single person. Thereafter, monastics and laypeople heard of his reputation and came to him;
thus, a Zen monastery was established. A monk asked, "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said, "Its four corners touch the ground."
[The monk] asked, "What is it like to be the person within the stupa? The Master said, "High on one's pillow, free from worry. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "A merchant ship crosses the sea; barefoot, he returns to his hometown."
Chan Master Dezun of Dashengshan in Tangzhou asked Guyin, “When the ancients asked for fire, what was their underlying meaning?
Guyin replied, “Let it go out. The Master asked, “What is it like after it has gone out? Guyin said, “The first of the third month; the eleventh.
The Master said, “In that case, it is a fine occasion. Guyin asked, “What principle have you perceived? The Master said, “Today I am utterly exhausted. Guyin [nodded].

He struck him. The Master then spoke in verse: "The mechanism for seeking fire is truly swift; The subtle function of concealing the point is rarely guessed. If you wish to understand my Master’s direct intent, When the furnace fire is spent, do not add more wood. A monk asked, "Please, Master, speak one phrase regarding the perfect integration of the world. The Master said, "A full seven feet or so. The monk asked, "What is the Patriarch from the West? The Master said, [struck him]. The monk then asked, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma coming from the West? The Master said, "I am not a merchant who trades in goods. The monk asked, "How is it when there is no longer anything to sell? The Master said, "Then you will see me for what I am. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the mind-ground is originally complete'? The Master said, "I have already told you. The monk asked, "Why did you tell me? The Master said, "Because you asked. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the mind-ground is originally complete'? The Master said, "It is like a mirror reflecting a face. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the mirror is broken and the face is lost'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in water. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the water is dried up and the reflection is gone'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in the sky. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the sky is overcast and the reflection is obscured'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in a dark room. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the room is lit and the reflection appears'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in a bright hall. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the hall is destroyed and the reflection vanishes'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in the wind. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the wind is still and the reflection is silent'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in a still pond. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the pond freezes and the reflection is hidden'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in ice. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the ice melts and the reflection flows away'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in a river. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the river dries up and the reflection is lost'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in the earth. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the earth is overturned and the reflection is scattered'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in the void. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the void is empty and the reflection is non-existent'? The Master said, "It is like a person looking at their reflection in a dream. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the dream awakens and the reflection is gone'? The Master said, "It is like a person waking from sleep. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'waking from sleep'? The Master said, "It is like a person rising from their bed. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'rising from bed'? The Master said, "It is like a person walking outside. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'walking outside'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the sun rise. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the sun rise'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the moon set. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the moon set'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the stars appear. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the stars appear'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the clouds disperse. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the clouds disperse'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the rain fall. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the rain fall'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the wind blow. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the wind blow'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the mountains. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the mountains'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the rivers. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the rivers'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the forests. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the forests'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the people. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the people'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing themselves. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing oneself'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Buddha. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Buddha'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Dharma. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Dharma'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Sangha. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Sangha'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the world. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the world'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the self. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the self'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing emptiness. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing emptiness'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing form. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing form'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing sound. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing sound'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing smell. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing smell'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing taste. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing taste'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing touch. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing touch'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing phenomena. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing phenomena'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the mind. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the mind'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the nature. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the nature'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Way. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Way'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Truth. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Truth'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Reality. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Reality'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Source. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Source'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Beginningless. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Beginningless'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Endless. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Endless'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Unborn. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Unborn'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Undying. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Undying'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Eternal. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Eternal'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Immutable. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Immutable'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Unchanging. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'seeing the Unchanging'? The Master said, "It is like a person seeing the Non-dual. The monk asked,
Regarding the intent of his arrival, the Master said: "A large nose and deep-set eyes. He then ascended the hall and said: "Those who come above do not question;
those who go below do not doubt. I know not whether this is so or not. If it is so, then it is truly marvelous! Thereupon, he descended from his seat.

At the beginning of the Zhihe era, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Jingde Temple. He would frequently spend the day sightseeing in the city and return home at the second watch.
One night, unable to enter, he lay down beneath the gate. Emperor Renzong dreamed that he arrived at the temple gate and saw a dragon coiled upon the ground.
Startled, the Emperor dispatched a central messenger during the middle of the night to observe him. Seeing that the Master was sleeping soundly with snoring, the messenger shook him awake in alarm.

Upon being asked his name, he returned to report it. When the Emperor heard the name Daolong, he said joyfully, "This is an auspicious omen. The next day, he summoned the Master to the private palace.

When asked about the fundamental tenets [of his school], the Master responded with detailed and appropriate explanations. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Thereafter, they exchanged verses and rhymes back and forth, which circulated extensively along the roads.

On some occasions, he was summoned for an audience and stayed overnight within the imperial palace; the honors accorded to him were exceptionally generous. He was granted the title Chan Master Mingwu (Enlightened Wisdom) by Imperial Decree.
During the Huángyù era, when Chan Master Dàjué Lián was invited to expound the Dharma in the Huìchéng Hall, the Emperor summoned the Master to engage in formal dialogue.

His spiritual pivot was swift and incisive, and the Emperor was greatly pleased. The attendants all raised their voices in mountain-like acclamation. The Master immediately submitted a memorial requesting that Liǎn be appointed in his stead.

He remained in the imperial forest awaiting summons and discoursed on Chan in the secret palace; however, he requested to return to Mount Lúshān. Upon reading the petition, the Emperor did not grant permission.

An imperial decree was issued to construct a vihāra outside the Cáo Gate to welcome the Master, which was granted the name Huáyán Chányuàn. When he opened the hall for formal discourse, a monk asked: "How is it..."
"This is the Way. The Master said, "High and low. [The monk] asked, "What is it like to be one who is on the Way? The Master said, "The feet are thin, but the straw sandals are wide.
When the Master was over eighty years old, he passed away during the height of summer. He sat upright for seven days; his hands and feet remained supple and soft.
His entire-body stupa is located to the east of the monastery.

The Layman Yang Yi of Wén-gōng, courtesy name Dànián, was designated as a "divine infant" when he was young. Upon reaching maturity, he possessed great talent and fame, yet he was unaware of the existence of the Buddha.
One day, while visiting a colleague, he saw him reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Laughing, he criticized it; however, the other continued to read as if nothing had happened.

At first, he was bewildered and possessed only a slight degree of respectful faith. Later, he met with Lord Li Wei of the Hanlin Academy, who urged him to pose questions.

He spun around and chopped some fresh firewood, burning it while the leaves were still attached. Entering the hall, he said: "The ancients said, 'If you recognize it, it is as before—not it.
This is truly difficult to understand. The barbarian from the East has a thick beard under his chin; the Persian has deep-set eyes and large nostrils. How extraordinary!
In an instant, he has passed through the borders of Silla. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From the hall. The Master said, "What did the Holy Monk say?"
"What is it? A monk stepped forward and said, "I do not presume to ask. The Master said, "If you become a donkey for the eastern neighbor, you will become a horse for the western neighbor.
The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? The Master said, "Ten thousand miles away in Yuzhou. The Master was unwell. A monk asked, "How is your venerable state these days, Master?
The Master said, "The head cook cannot manage his affairs. The monk was speechless. The Master snapped his fingers once. He then ascended the hall.
Puhua struck both openly and secretly;布袋 (Baidai) scattered [his bag] horizontally and vertically; the Stone Chamber Practitioner trod upon the pestle—why did he forget to set his foot down?
Question: "What is the first mystery? The Master said: "The light of Śākyamuni Buddha shone upon Ānanda’s shoulder."
[The student] asked, "What is the second mystery? The Master said, "A solitary wheel surrounded by a throng of elephants. [The student] asked, "What is the third mystery?

The Master said, "Weeping toward a withered mulberry tree, tears flow in endless streams. [The student] asked, "What is the first essential? The Master said, "The finest clarity illuminates both the subtle and the coarse.
[The student] asked, "What is the second essential? The Master said, "A flash of lightning; heaven and earth are filled with dazzling radiance."
[The student] asked, "What is the third essential? The Master said, "The road is flanked by aged green pines. Ascending the hall, he raised an anecdote: A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the Buddha?
Shoushan said, "The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it. The Master said, "Hand in the nose-ring, foot on the tail;
looking up at the sky, listening to the flowing stream; at daybreak she is sent out to the roadside, and when night falls, she returns."
He returned to his thatched cottage.
A monk asked Chan Master Baoxin of Jiangshan, "How is it when the moon is not yet full? The Master said, "Count forward.
The monk asked, "And after it is full? The Master said, "Count backward. [The monk] asked, "What is the 'blow-off-hair' sword? The Master said:
A black-lacquered pillar. A question was asked: "How can one penetrate the two characters 'sound' and 'form'? The Master said: "With one hand blowing, and with the other hand clapping.
Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng of Hongzhou ascended the hall. The Venerable Yantou obtained it for three copper coins.
This wife of his only knew how to dredge for shrimp and gather clams; she simply did not know how to give birth to sons or raise daughters.
Thus, until this very day, the lineage of his family line has been severed. Do you all wish to recognize the wife of Master Huo? Today, Baizhang will not spare his lips.
I have annotated this for you all: "Tangled hair and thorn-leaf hairpins are rare in the world; the cloth skirt is still the dress from her wedding day.
A monk asked, "When Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring flowers in their beaks to offer him?

The Master said, "With money, one can communicate across a thousand li. [The monk] asked, "After he saw him, why did they no longer bring flowers? The Master said, "Without money, one is deaf even next door."
Question: "How is it when Bodhidharma has not yet arrived? The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. Question: "How is it after he has arrived?
The Master said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. Question: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Mushrooms grow on the tops of trees. Question: "All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas; what is the intent of this? The Master said, "Beneath a mountain range."

One monk asked, "The saying that 'the superior leads and the inferior follows' is not yet the talk of a master. Only by turning one's back on Chu and heading for Wu can one be considered a man of true attainment.
Is this not the Master’s own words? The Master said, "It is. The monk said, "This is like a father’s wealth being used by his son. The Master said, "Try using it then.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him. Ascending the hall, he said: "Tiantai’s communal labor is known to all; Nanyue’s wandering..."
"Mountain. Again, how do you understand this? If you understand, the lantern laughs at you; if you do not understand, having eyes is like being blind.
A monk asked Zen Master Yunliang of Mount Xiangshan in Mingzhou, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya?

The Master said, "Dancing the *Santai* on the tip of the banner pole. The monk asked, "What is the phrase for receiving beginners? The Master said, "The *Shang Daren* (The Great Man Above). The monk asked again.
"What is the final phrase? The Master said, "Under the twin śāla trees. [The monk] asked, "What is the place where the student turns over?
The Master said, "In the mill. Ascending the hall, after a long silence, he laughed loudly and said, "Laughing at what?
Laughing at the swans and cranes flying up to the heavens, while the tortoise chases fish at the bottom of the water. Three old women with six breasts."
The back of the vajra is as rotten as mud. A-he-he! Do you know? Or do you not? "The old fellow Chen from East Village" enters. Master Chan Master Weiguang of Nanfeng in Suzhou ascends the hall.
One question and one answer are like a bell containing its resonance, or a valley responding to a sound.
This is because he has no choice in the matter; for the time being, within the gate of transformation and edification, he lets down a single thread of the Way. As for the reality—
Within the school of the patch-robed monks, there is a vast difference from the world at large. But tell me, what excellence do these patch-robed monks possess? After a long silence, he said:
"Searching all day long, one cannot find it; yet sometimes it comes of its own accord. *Du!* (A shout)
A monk asked Chan Master Da Miao Deqian of Tanzhou, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, “Water flows down from the mountain. The monk asked, “What is the intent of this? The Master said, “How could a mountain stream or a ravine retain it?
He then continued, “Mountain flowers like brocade—Mañjuśrī strikes right in the eye. Deep birds warbling—Avalokiteśvara blocks the ears. All [phenomena].
"Virtuous ones, what more is there for you to contemplate? Last night at the third watch, unable to sleep, I turned over and seized Samantabhadra, banishing him to the Realm of Non-arising.
A single awakening lasted until dawn; this morning, I have met with all of you again to recount my dream.
Alas! What kind of talk is this? He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Insan Benyan of全州 (Chonju), "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Who taught you to ask such a question?
The monk said, "Today I have stirred the Master from his rest. The Master said, "Thank you for visiting."
A monk asked Chan Master Fayan of Guangfu Temple in Anji Prefecture, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, “Bricks and tiles. The monk asked, “How is it when seeking stillness amidst bustle? The Master said, “One must not harbor resentment. The monk asked, “...? The Master said, “...”.
"What is the Eye of the True Dharma? The Master said, "Below the eyebrows. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when one understands it just so?
The Master said, "The pupils smile and nod their heads. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter that transcends [the world]? The Master said, "The sun, moon, and stars. [The monk] asked, "..."
"What is the matter of going downward? The Master said, "The boiling cauldrons of hell. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when there are no clouds for ten thousand miles?
The Master said, "A monkey starving. [The monk] said, "I beg the Master for deliverance. The Master said, "What color is the fire?

[The monk] asked, "When the ancients raised their mallets or brandished their fly-whisks, what was their intent? The Master said, "In broad daylight, there are no idle people. [The monk] asked, "How does one take this up?"
The Master said, "Like the wind passing by the ear. A monk asked, "What is it like when one holds a sword across the chest?

The Master said, "Crows in a flock. The monk said, "That is exactly where you, Master, see it. The Master said, "A snake piercing through the nostrils. The monk brushed out his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "..."
The assembly met one another. A monk asked, "Where do the sages of the past go about their practice? The Master said, "At the crossroads. The monk said, "If that is so, then there is deficiency.
The Master said, "I knew you had not yet reached this state. The monk asked, "Once one has reached it, what then? The Master said, "Everyday tea and rice.
A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said, "Dry..."
[The Master] said, "Ginger and *vatsanābha* [aconite]. [A monk] asked, "In that case, they are not the same. The Master said, "Camphor and balls of snow. Ascending the hall, he said:

"The spring rain falls gently; water drips from the eaves. Failing to awaken upon hearing this sound, one returns to the hall and faces the wall. Ascending the hall, he said: "If we discuss the Great Way..."
This would leave Zhushan with no opening for speech. You all, try and open your mouths! A monk then asked, “What is the Great Way?
The Master said, “It cannot be carried. The monk asked, “Why can it not be carried? The Master said, “The Great Way. Ascending the hall, the Master said:
“If one discusses this matter, do not speak of it at all. To speak of it is to give rise to horns. A monk stepped forward and said, “Horns...”
A horn grew on his head. The Master said, "This is a calamity. [The monk] said, "It is my own transgression. The Master said, "A dragon’s head with a snake’s tail. "I pray you, take care.
On the evening of the twelfth day of the tenth month in the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era, the Master suddenly wrote this verse:

"With snow-white hair and frosty beard for ninety-nine years, With a shawl over one shoulder, all conditions are exhausted. Suddenly laughing, he points to the clouds dispersing; The jade hare flows [in the sky]."
His light illuminated the great trichiliocosm; he cast aside his brush and entered stillness.
Chan Master Dezhang of Lingyin first resided at the Western Sūtra Repository Hall of the Great Xiangguo Monastery.

On the first day of the ninth month in the eighth year of the Qingli era, Emperor Renzong summoned the Master to the Yanchun Pavilion for a meal and proclaimed the *Puzhao Dajie* (Great Precepts of Universal Illumination).
The Master asked, "What is the single phrase that meets the occasion? The Master said, "A single word transcends the azure heavens; one walks on the precipice before a ten-thousand-fathom peak.
[The Emperor] asked, "How is it to walk on the precipice? The Master then gave a shout. [The Emperor] said, "In the presence of the Emperor, how can you act like this?
The Master replied, "I cannot let this pass either. The following year, he was again summoned to the inner palace for a vegetarian feast. Once more...
Xuān Pùzhào asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'? The Master said, "Thunder startles the fine grass and its sprouts emerge;
advance upon the high mountain, do not delay. He asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not taking away the person'?
The Master said, "Wearing horns and shrouded in fur, yet coming and going with total freedom. He asked, "What is 'taking away both person and environment'? The Master said:
"Stepping out the gate, one is far beyond the heavens; flowing light and shadows are not real. The Emperor asked, "What is it like when both the person and the environment cannot be taken away?
The Master said, "In the cold forest there are no overnight guests; in the great ocean, one listens to the dragon's roar. Later, he was again summoned to the Huacheng Hall for a vegetarian feast.
Xuanchen Shouxian asked, "Now that the banquet has been grandly opened, how do you repay the Sage Ruler? The Master said, "Seeking bird tracks in the void."

[The student] asked, "What is the meaning? The Master said, "Seeking the tracks of a fish within the water. The Master then offered the *Song of the Heart-Jewel*: "The heart is as one wishes; the heart is as one wishes.
Spontaneously following conditions, it is never apart from them. Know this, and do not seek outwardly. To seek outwardly is ultimately not the way;
It is a waste of effort to obscure the True Principle. Recognize the Heart-Jewel: its radiance shines daily, A secret treasury of profound depth."
Secret and formless, brought forth within the palm, it startles all who behold it. How could those of the Two Vehicles, despite their diligence, ever fathom it?

The blue-eyed barbarian points it out with his finger; how could its wondrous application ever fail when the occasion arises? One must take care never to show it to others in ordinary circumstances, lest the mountains and rivers of the great earth tremble and quake.
In the second year of the Huángyòu era, the Master requested to return to the mountain forests to spend his final years. An imperial decree was issued for him to reside in Hángzhōu.
The Abbot of Lingyin Temple, who was granted the title Mingjue (Enlightened Awareness), was Chan Master Chaoxin Haiyin, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Jue of Langye.
While at Dinghui Monastery in Suzhou, a monk asked: "What is the very essence of the Buddha-dharma?"
The general meaning: The Master said, "A bamboo staff from Xiangyuan. [The monk] asked, "What is the underlying intent? The Master said, "Every branch bears traces of tears.
[The monk] asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Narāyaṇa in a fit of rage.
[The monk] asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "The patch-robed monk is at a loss. [The monk] asked, "What is the third phrase? The Master said, "Western Heaven and this land."
Ascending the hall: A clay snake bites a stone turtle; the pillar chirps and squeaks. Mount Sumeru receives a blow from the staff;
Old Yama laughs aloud. *Chan.* Ascending the hall: If you recognize Prajñā, you are bound by Prajñā. If you do not recognize Prajñā, you are likewise bound by Prajñā.
Setting aside both recognition and non-recognition, I ask you all: what is Prajñā?
If it is the essence: go to the hall; ascend the hall. The song of the orioles has ceased, the sound of the cicadas grows urgent. A tortoise entering the water does not get its head wet;
a heron flies into the reeds. The combined brilliance of snow and moon cannot compare to this. HŪṂ.
A monk asked Chan Master Letan Xiaoyue of Hongzhou, "The teachings of the *Sūtras* are like a finger pointing at the moon;
I wonder what it is that the finger points to? The Master said, "Please raise your eyes high. The monk said, "When the dawn light has not yet parted, all gaze upward;
once daybreak comes, it is as usual. The Master said, "In old age, ghosts play with people."
A monk asked Chan Master Fang of Jiangshan in Yuezhou, “What is the Venerable One Who Is Immovable?
The Master said, “Wearing only his cotton robe, he passes through the marketplace. The monk said, “I do not yet understand. The Master said, “Riding a donkey, he tramples the waves of Lake Dongting.

The monk said, “Having passed through the three-tiered waves, he waits attentively for a single clap of thunder. The Master said, “Reaching out his hand, he cannot see his own palm. The monk said, “Do you permit me, your student, [to ask further]?”
The man stepped forward, and the Master said, "Treading upon the earth, you address the void. The man said, "Beneath the Gate of Thunder, a cloth drum is difficult to sound.
The Master said, "Upon the eight-flowered ball, there is no need to embroider a red banner. The man said, "Thirty years from now, these words will spread far and wide. The Master then struck him.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water? The Master said, "One who tries to thread a needle complains of having eyes too large."
Xiaoyou asked, "What is it like after emerging from the water? The Master said, "Throughout the day, one spreads a frowning brow.
He asked, "What is 'one mote of dust entering right concentration'? The Master said, "A snake biting the tail of a rat. He asked, "What is 'the samādhi arising from all motes of dust'?
The Master said, "A turtle gnawing on a fishing rod. He said, "In that case, east and west are not distinguished, and north and south are not discerned."

The Master said: "A single bowl of night-bright lamp before the hall; several stalks of green, slender bamboo outside the curtain. [The monk] asked: "How was it before all Buddhas appeared in the world?
The Master said: "I do not recognize the wine-scoop. [The monk] asked: "How was it after they appeared in the world? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
On a fishing boat, he presented three blows to the staff. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Leaving a beard to manifest one's manhood.
Another asked, "The rushing torrent passes through the blade; the swift flame exceeds the wind. I wonder, under the gate of Jiangshan, is it permitted to borrow [this teaching] or not?"

The Master said, "The sky is cold, the days are short, and the nights are even longer. The monk said, "An embroidered phoenix and mandarin duck in a brocade curtain; travelers find it difficult to behold.
The Master said, "From within the skull, the vital breath surges toward heaven. The monk called out, "Master! The Master said, "The head of a rooster and the tail of a phoenix. The monk said, "..."
Washing in the mud in all directions; Jiangshan has brought it here on paper. The Master said, "Jiangshan is acting as a guest today, so I hope you, Ācārya, will transmit this well.
Even so, I cannot let this pass," and he struck him. Ascending the hall, he said: "To pierce the clouds but not cross the water;
to cross the water but not pierce the clouds. Heaven and earth are held fast, yet not held fast; empty space is let go, yet not let go."
Three horizontal and four vertical; parting and joining, using the long to compensate for the short.

Setting aside for a moment whether you all can say, "Rice is made from grain"—a single phrase that is indeed difficult to speak—after a long silence, he said: "Private matters shall not be rewarded by official decree. He ascended the hall and said:
"It is not a matter of being able to speak or unable to speak; everywhere people take this to be extraordinary. Hanshan burns fire, his head covered in ash."
"Laughing and scolding Fenggan as this old thief!
Chan Master Xian-yan of Mount Bailu in Fuzhou was asked by a monk, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The nine provinces and the hundred Yue regions.
[The monk] asked, "What is one who walks the Way? The Master said, "Riding in fatness and wearing brocade. [The monk] asked, "What is great goodness?"
Zhishi asked, "Master, why do you hold a knife and press a sword? The Master said, "To prevent the gentleman from being overly formal. He asked, "What is meant by 'different species'?
The Master said, "A phoenix hatches from a crow's nest. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Kāśyapa Mātanga entering the Han was like carving a sore upon flesh;
Saṃghavarman coming to Wu was like adding grit to the eyes. Bodhidharma sitting against the wall for nine years was the origin of a demonic apparition."
The Second Patriarch stood in the snow seeking his heart, yet he ended up becoming unworthy. When you people reach this point, how will you express it?
If you can speak it, you shall roam freely across the sea; if you cannot speak it, you shall lie alone among the forest trees.
(He struck the meditation seat once with his staff. He asked: "What is the formless Buddha? The Master said: "A stone lion at the riverbank. He asked again.
"What is the meaning? The Master said, "With a mind dwelling upon the river, one does not fear the waves washing away the sand.
A questioner asked, "What is it like when one is stilled and profoundly tranquil? The Master said, "This is not where you, Venerable Sir, establish your body and life.

The questioner asked, "Then what is the place where this student establishes his body and life? The Master said, "The clouds have the momentum to leave the mountains; the water has no sound as it plunges into the ravine. A questioner asked, "As for such..."
"What is the meaning of the teachings? The Master said, "At the assembly on Mount Laṅkā. "What is the meaning of the Patriarchs? The Master said, "Before Bear Ear Mountain.
"How far apart are the meaning of the teachings and the meaning of the Patriarchs? The Master said, "Cold pines join with green bamboo;
autumn waters face red lotuses."
A monk asked Zen Master Zhiyou of Langya Mountain in Chuzhou, "What is the realm of Langya?
The Master said, "The pines, being finite, grow thin with age; the flowers, being insentient, bloom at random. The monk asked, "What is the person within the realm?"
The Master said, "Your hair is long and your monastic appearance is ugly. [The monk] asked, "What is the Master’s phrase for guiding people?
The Master said, "Three feet of snow before one's eyes. [The monk] said, "Is it not this very thing? The Master said, "A flower on the back of the head."
A monk asked Chan Master Yuan of Liangfeng Cave in Quanzhou, “What is nirvana? The Master said, “Cut with a blade; split with an axe. The monk asked, “What is liberation?
The Master said, “The shirt is long; the trousers are short. A monk asked, “Do you know the place where all the sages do not reach?
The Master said, “In my old age, I have no strength to descend from the meditation seat. A monk asked, “Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations—”
“How is it now? The Master said, “The thatched gate is overgrown with weeds. He asked, “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?
The Master said, “Pines are straight and thorns are crooked. He asked, “What is the Buddha? The Master said, “A reflection in the golden sand. He asked, “What is the Way?
The Master said, “A jade maiden casting her shuttle. He asked, “How far apart are the Buddha and the Way? The Master said, “Turtle hair is long.”
The rabbit's horn is two *zhang* long; it is eight *chi* long.
Zen Master Fang of Zhennu Temple in Zhenzhou went to visit Langye and looked only at the "pine tree" koan. Every time he entered the room for instruction, [he was asked about this].
He set forth what he had seen, finding no words sufficient to express it; he was repeatedly shouted out of the hall.

One day, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and went straight into the abbot’s quarters, saying, "I understand! Langye asked, "How do you understand? The Master replied, "Last night the bedding on the bed was warm."
He remained awake until dawn. Langye approved of him.
Chan Master Tan of Xingjiao Monastery in Xuanchuan was the son of the Niu family of Yongjia. He had worked as a silversmith;

while sharpening and polishing a vessel, he attained realization and immediately left the household life. He went to visit Langye, whose words and meaning he suddenly grasped. Later, he relied upon Chan Master Tianyi Huai.
At that time, [Yuan]yi was residing at Xingjiao Monastery and had been promoted to the position of First Seat.

When he received an invitation from another temple and wished to go to Wenzhou to request Master [Tian]tan to succeed him, the scholar Diao Jingchun was serving as the governor of Wanling. Fearing that Diao might raise external objections, Yi made a vow before Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"If the Head Seat Tan possesses clear insight into the Way and is fit to serve as abbot, I pray that you will manifest a dream to the scholar Diao."

The official Diáo had a dream at night that an ox was on the seat where the Dharma was being taught. The next morning, when Fenyang was about to take his leave of the Prefect, Diáo recounted his dream.
Fenyang laughed heartily. Diáo asked for the reason, and Fenyang said, "The Head Seat Tan is surnamed Ox (Niú) and was also born in the year of the Ox.
Diáo then went to the seat and issued an invitation. The Master accepted the invitation and ascended the platform. Xuedou’s attendant, Shengzong, stepped forward and asked, "All Buddhas..."
"Before he appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens. After he appeared in the world, why was there no news at all?
The Master said, "Before Mount Jizu, the wind is still. Zhaozhou said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "Great snow fills Chang'an.
Zhaozhou said, "Who understands this meaning? It makes me remember Nanquan. He then shook his sleeves, returned to the assembly, and did not pay his respects.
He bowed. The Master said, "The New Teaching has lost ground today. He then returned to his quarters and sent someone to invite Zong to see him.
The Master said, "Just now I gave a wrong response to a turning phrase. Why did you not bow before the assembly of gods and men to cover it over?"
Zhong said, "A man of great character has gold beneath his knees; how could he be willing to prostrate before an eyeless elder?
The Master said, "I have another saying. Zhong then attempted to justify his previous words, reaching the point where he had said, "Wait until tomorrow night, and then I will speak further.
The Master said, "I have thirty blows to spare; I entrust them to you to strike Xuedou. Zhong then prostrated himself.
Chan Master Guizong Ke Xuan of Jiangzhou was a native of Hanzhou. He became a monk in his prime and left the gorges to rely upon Langya [Huijue].
A single word suddenly struck home, and his many doubts were instantly extinguished; Langya approved of him. Before long, he was ordered to share the teaching seat.
When the layman Jingkong Guo Gongfu visited his door to inquire about the Way, they became close friends. Later, when the Master took charge of Guizong, at that time Gongfu was serving as...

He was appointed as the Commandant of Nanchang. Shortly thereafter, the Prefect became resentful that the Master did not pay him due courtesy and began to persecute him severely. He then wrote a letter to Gongfu, saying:
"My karmic ties to this world remain for six more years; however, as the Governor oppresses me, I shall cast off my remaining breaths and take rebirth into your family."
"I hope there will be no obstacles. Gongfu was just reading a book when he was startled and delighted; he nodded his head in agreement.

In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream. She cried out in alarm, "This is not the place where the Monk comes from! Gongfu shook her awake and questioned her.

His wife related the matter in detail. She called for a lamp, took out the letter, and showed it to him; they laughed together without ceasing. Consequently, she became pregnant. When the child was born, he was named Xuānlǎo (Proclaimed Old Man).
At one year of age, his memory and questioning were as they had been before. When he reached three years old, Chan Master Băizhūn Wéndān arrived at their home and saw him for the first time.
He said, "My nephew has come! Wén asked, "How many years have passed since we parted from you, Master? Xuān counted back on his fingers and replied: [The number of years].
"It has been four years now" (it appears he died exactly one year after parting from him). Yun asked, "Where did you part? He replied, "At Bailian Zhuang. Yun said:
"What will serve as proof? he asked. [Baizhang] replied, "Father and mother, tomorrow we shall invite the Master for a vegetarian meal.
Suddenly, the sound of a cart being pushed was heard. Yunman asked, "What is that sound outside the gate? Xuan made a gesture with his hand as if pushing a cart.
Yunman said, "What happens after it passes? He replied, "Two ditches across level ground. Indeed, six weeks later, he passed away without illness.
The lecturer Zixuan of Changshui in Xiu Prefecture was a native of Jiaxing in the commandery. From the time he shaved his head, he recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* without ceasing.
When following Master Hongmin’s lectures, he reached the passage: "The two characteristics of movement and stillness are clearly seen as not arising. He had an awakening and said to Min:

"Even 'knocking on empty space' or 'striking wood' (where 'wood' is alternatively read as 'bamboo') still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare; even 'raising one's eyes' or 'lifting one's eyebrows' has already become a matter of deliberate deliberation."

Only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this essential principle. Min Fu realized this through his own experience; yet, wishing to explore the source of Chan, he was at a loss as to where to turn.
Hearing that Langya Huijue’s Way was esteemed in his time, he immediately went to attend his lectures. Coinciding with the Master’s ascent to the high seat, Min stepped forward and asked:
"The fundamental nature is pure and still; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Langya responded with a haughty air: "The fundamental nature is pure and still..."

"However, how did these mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly come to be? The Master attained realization and, bowing in gratitude, said, "I wish to serve you with the ritual cloth and water jar.

Langye said to him, "The tradition of your school has not flourished for a long time. You should rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha's kindness; do not let differences in lineage be an obstacle.
The Master then followed these instructions, prostrating twice to take his leave. Later, he resided at Changshui, where he received daily instruction from Langye.

The assembly said: "The Way is not attained through words or symbols; Chan is not known through conjecture or deliberation. To realize the meaning and penetrate the source, there is never anything extraordinary.
Consequently, the two schools looked up to him. He once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and other scriptures, which became widely circulated in the world.

Chan Master Yunfeng Wenyue of Nanyue was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dayu Zhi. He was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. Initially, he went to visit Dayu, where he heard the master address the assembly, saying:
"Everyone gathers here to eat a spoonful of vegetable soup. If you call it 'a spoonful of vegetable soup,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow."
He then descended from his seat. Master Daguang was greatly startled. That night he went to the abbot’s quarters. Yunwu asked him, "What do you seek by coming here?
The master replied, "I seek the Dharma of the mind. Yunwu said, "The wheel of the Dharma has not yet turned; the wheel of food must turn first. You are a young man with strong physical vigor;
why do you not go out for alms for the sake of the community? I am too busy enduring hunger to have the leisure to explain Zen to you. The master did not dare disobey. Not long after—
After some time, Yuyi moved to Cuiyan. Once the Master had finished submitting his memorial of resignation, he went back to Cuiyan to request further instruction.

Cuiyan said, "The Buddha-dharma has not yet reached the point of being overcooked; since the snow is cold, you should go and beg for charcoal for the assembly. The Master obeyed this command. When his duties were completed, he returned to the abbot’s quarters.

Cuiyan said, "There is a vacancy in the Hall Administration; I shall now trouble you with that task. The Master accepted it with displeasure, resenting that Cuiyan had not [given him further instruction].
He was removing the floorboards from the meditation hall. After he had finished his work, the hoops of a wooden bucket suddenly came loose, and it fell from the scaffolding.

At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and clearly perceived the essential point of Yanguan’s teaching. He hurriedly adjusted his *kāṣāya* robe and ascended to the dormitory. Yanguan met him with a smile and said, "Venerable Karmadāna, congratulations;

you have successfully accomplished the great matter. The Master bowed twice and departed without uttering a single word. He served under Yanguan diligently for eight years before later entering the world as a teacher.
At Cuiyan, the head seat led the assembly out to welcome him. He asked, "I do not ask about the lineage of Deshan;
what is the great function of Linji? The Master said, "Where have you come from? As the head seat hesitated, the Master struck him.
As the head seat was about to respond, the Master shouted, "Lead the assembly back! From then on, the entire assembly was awed and submissive. A monk asked, "What is the Way?"
The Master said, "On this road, nothing is left behind. The monk asked, "What is it like for one on the Way? The Master said, "The grass bandits have been utterly defeated.
The monk bowed; the Master let out a long sigh. The monk asked, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return?
The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends. The monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "His hands hang down below his knees. The monk asked, "What is the second?"
[The Master] said: "Ten thousand miles to Yuzhou. [The monk] asked: "What is the third phrase? The Master said: "A dustpan and a broom. [The monk] asked:
"What is the Buddha-dharma of the deep mountains and rocky cliffs? The Master said: "A monkey climbing a tree upside down.

[The monk] asked: "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? The Master said: "Skin and bone. [The monk] asked: "Without being entangled in trivialities, I pray the Master will speak quickly. The Master—
[The Master] said, "Mount Sumeru. [A monk] asked, "What is the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Firewood and reeds at the marketplace. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If speech does not depart from its conceptual nest, how can one transcend the entanglements? A single cloud hangs across the valley mouth, causing many people to lose their way to the source."
Therefore it is said: "Words do not unfold the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who cling to phrases are deluded.
You people here—relying on what do you discuss and understand? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish to avoid incurring karma of the Avīci Hell..."
"Do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the past have already passed into extinction; the Buddhas of the future have not yet been born.
Right now, at this very day, the Buddha-Dharma rests entirely with Cuiyan. If I let it go, it benefits beings according to their capacities;
if I hold it fast, it dissolves like ice and crumbles like tiles. Now tell me: is holding it fast better, or is letting it go better? After a long silence, he said: "Tsk! You wild fox!"
[The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it. He ascended the hall and said: "All of you who come up here in this manner are very much like poking your heads into a vat of glue.
To go down in this manner is likewise to stumble on level ground. Even if you neither come nor go, I shall strike you three thousand times in the morning and eight hundred times in the evening.
He ascended the hall and said: "How distant is the Way? It is true in every encounter. How distant are the sages?"
Ah! To embody this is the divine. Thus, in the Sahā world, the Buddha-work is performed through sound; in the Gandhavatī world, the Buddha-work is performed through fragrant food.

Here at Cuoyan, one simply makes offerings and serves within the cycle of inhalation and exhalation, so that not a single one among the dust-like Buddhas of the past, present, and future passes by empty-handed. The dust-like [Buddhas] of the past, present, and future...
"All Buddhas—this attendant of Cuiyan has reached every one of them. If there were even one who had not reached them, he would receive thirty blows of the staff.
Do you all understand, venerable elders? 'To offer this profound mind to the dust-motes and lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
[He ascended the hall: "The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source. The stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as its totality."
The essence is simply that when emotions arise, wisdom is obstructed; when perceptions shift, the essence becomes distinct. When one realizes the source, emotions vanish;
when one knows the mind, the essence merges. Do you all, practitioners of Zen, understand? The ancient Buddhas intersect with the pillar; the Buddha hall vies for the forehead-mark with the lantern.
If you do not understand, you will suffer a single, heavy defeat. Entering the hall: Staff and wooden pole follow me wherever I go; I perform my play as the occasion demands. Even so, it is thus.
"A single hand cannot clap alone. Is there among you any masterly Chan guest or a monk of true standing who will come forth to join in this mutual chanting?
Is there anyone? At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated. The Master said: "Vague and indistinct, like a melody just barely worth hearing."

Then, being blown by the wind into another tune, he descended from his seat. He ascended the hall. At dawn, when all affairs were settled, there was long-grained rice from the continent of Uttarakuru.
He descended from his seat. He ascended the hall. "Where a Buddha is, one must not dwell; where no Buddha is, one must pass quickly.
You people, carrying your staffs slung across your shoulders—where will you go on pilgrimage? After a long silence...
He said: "In Pūrvavideha on the eastern continent, he holds the bowl; in Aparagoyānī on the western continent, he eats his rice. He ascended the hall and said:

"Even if the mind were to penetrate across immeasurable times, throughout kalpas, how could it ever have been different from today? But tell me, what is the matter of today like? After a long silence, he said:
The turtle breaks through the wall. Entering the hall [he said]: "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction;
sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch are always in samādhi. The monk said: "I understand! Mountains are mountains; waters are waters. When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps."
"Suddenly Mount Sumeru leaps into your nostrils; the makara fish pierces through your eyes. How will you deliberate upon this?
After a long silence, he said, "Go to the hall. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "To cut it in two with a single stroke is not yet to be called a master.
To level the high by following the low is certainly not the work of a true adept. When I, Cuoyan, reach this point, my mouth is like a flat carrying-pole. You all—"
"How do you all deliberate upon this? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you see that all marks are non-marks, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely without fault.
All you venerable seniors spend your days wearing robes and eating rice, yet you have never bitten into a single grain of rice, nor have you ever hung [a robe]..."
By applying a single strand of silk, one can transform the great earth into gold and churn the long river into cream and curd.
Although this is so, eating and wearing clothes are not lacking; yet, even the stench of sweat from the gate of the patch-robed monks has not been dreamed of.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The conduct of Samantabhadra, the wisdom of Mañjuśrī—on Mount Potalaka a pure breeze rises; the blind donkey chases after the herd."
Passing through Shilla, he reached Jiliao Sheitou, three thousand *li* away. He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said:
"Holding the alms bowl toward the world of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*), why is there no way to emerge? Carrying the sun and moon upon the tip of my staff."

Why is it that having eyes is like being blind? When one reaches the point where the wind blows and the grass bows, where echoes follow sounds and harmonize, such that not even a speck of dust remains—this is still a dharma of mutual contention. What is the dharma that does not involve contention?
[He] planted his staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Linji’s vanguard lets one move pass; Deshan’s subsequent command sets aside for a moment."
"How do you express the single phrase that is uniquely revealed and free from partiality? After a long silence, he said, "It is truly lamentable that Zhongli under Chu was ignorant [of this].

He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall for the discourse, he said: "The teachings of the scriptures state: 'All manner of grasping and rejecting are but saṃsāra.

To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) without having escaped saṃsāra is for that nature of Perfect Enlightenment to likewise undergo the cycle of transmigration. If one would avoid..."
“Samsara? There is no such place. You people here—how will you discern Perfect Enlightenment? After a long silence, he said: “The lotus leaf is round and round, as round as a mirror;
the water chestnut horn is sharp and sharp, as sharp as an awl. He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and ascended the hall.
The ancients said, “Mountains, rivers, and stone walls do not obstruct the eye of wisdom. The Master asked, “How so?”
"This is the eye. [The Master] took up his staff, struck the meditation seat once, and said: "I need not ask about Mount Sumeru being shattered into a hundred fragments;
tell me, how old is the Dragon King Sāgara? A layman asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: [He struck him.]

[The Master] said, "When putting on clothes and eating rice, one must measure the capacity of the household. [The student] said, "If that is so, then I shall step back three paces and place my hands together at my chest.

The Master said, "Adding a cup after one is already drunk is better than having none at all. In the *Small Assembly* (Xiaocan), he cited Baizhang’s address to the assembly during the New Year's Eve vigil: "He who knows the meaning of the Buddha-dharma is called a 'Buddha'... [text continues]."
"You lot, this generation of youths—you certainly do not know the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras; you enter the assembly to practice Chan, yet you do not understand Chan either.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month [the day of death], how will you resolve it? The Master said, "Truly so, all you Chan practitioners."

The time since the Sages passed away is remote, and the hearts of men have grown indifferent. Looking at the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) of today, it is even more difficult to find a place that truly exists as such.
Some gather three hundred or five hundred disciples; they boast of great success merely because their meals are plentiful and rich, and their quarters are comfortable and convenient.
Among them, not a single person is diligently devoted to the Way, even if there were ten or five.
A person. Running up and running down; half green, half yellow. If they understand, everyone says, "I understand.

Each one claims to hold the jewel of the spiritual serpent, yet who is willing to admit their error? When pressed and prodded with the whip of inquiry, there is not even one in ten thousand who can do so.
Alas! Alas! As it is said: "The groves of Prajñā wither year by year; the wild weeds of ignorance grow more thick each spring."

Among those of advanced age, there are especially those of the present day who, as soon as they enter the monastic community, sit upright with hands folded in a gesture of reverence and accept the offerings of others.
Everywhere they go, they do not select even a single stalk of vegetables nor carry away a single bundle of firewood;

their ten fingers never touch water, and they concern themselves with nothing at all. While this may bring them temporary gratification, how can it avoid burdening them with the three realms of suffering? Is this not so?
Seeing the Middle Way in the teachings, one would rather wrap one's body in glowing red-hot iron than accept the robes of a person of faith;
one would rather pour molten copper down one's throat than accept the food of a person of faith.
