Do you understand? It is precisely when the autumn wind enters the door; at one stroke, whose house is the sound of the mortar and pestle?

A monk asked, "What is it like when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished? The Master said, "The spirit frowns. The monk asked, "What is it like after it has been polished? The Master said, "The Persian."
He snapped his fingers and said, "Why is it so? The Master replied, "Good news does not leave the door.

On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month in the Dingchou year of the Xiangshu era, he passed away while seated. After the cremation, his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa on Mount Xueshe.
Chan Master Zizhao of Jingyin in Tokyo was the son of the Wang family of Qingzhou. In his youth, he gained recognition for his Confucian studies through Sima Guang (the Duke Wen).

However, he pursued noble ideals and had no interest in fame or official rank. One day, he shaved his head and followed Fuyong. His practice was precise and thorough, and his realization was transcendent.
He left the secular world to reside at Dacheng Monastery; during the Chongning era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Jingyin.
The Cause. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing this matter. Since then, people have been unwilling to comprehend it thoroughly;
instead, they have sought it outwardly, like casting oneself into clear water to search for pearls or visiting the mountains of Jing to seek jade.

Little do they realize that what enters through the gate is not one's own family treasure. To mistake the dust for the head—is this not a great error? Only when the school of our lineage is thus upheld..."

The essence is quiescent and without dependence; divergent thoughts do not arise. From antiquity to the present, there is no interval. The myriad phenomena of the universe are the family style encountered at every turn.
The avian path stretches across the vast void, yet it does not hinder one’s stride. The golden rooster announces the dawn; the vermilion phoenix soars aloft; the flowers bloom upon the jade trees.
Withered branches bear fruit. Only beneath the Gate of the Sun does every day mark the third autumn; before the Hall of the Bright Moon, every moment is the ninth summer.
Do you wish to understand? A shadowless tree hangs over the moon in the cold stream; the ocean tide flows east while the Dipper shifts west.
Chan Master Tianning Xipu of the Western Capital was the son of the Song family from Caizhou. He first resided at Shaoshan, and subsequently visited Tianning and Danxia.
Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Lately, Shaoshan has been without a trace; his eyes hear sounds and his nose tastes flavors.
Sometimes he sleeps until dawn, neither on the bed nor upon the ground. Tell me, Great Assembly, where is he?"
At this point, if people can produce a single turning word, they will not only have saved Shao Shan, but will also have made their journey of pilgrimage meaningful.
If you have not yet reached this level, then "When the three-tiered waves are high, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the fool still uses a bailer to drain the water from the night pond."
Question: "What is the Sovereign? The Master said: "In the universe there is no second sun; in heaven and earth there is but one person.

Question: "What is the Minister? The Master said: "Virtue clearly manifests the transformation of the ruler; the Way accords with the mechanisms of things' nature. Question: "What is the minister facing the sovereign?
The Master said: "With a sincere heart returning to the sun of Shun; exhausting one's integrity to repay the sky of Yao. Question: "What is the sovereign looking upon the minister?"
The Master said: "The dark pupils are fixed and do not blink; the wondrous body reflects what comes from the side. [A monk] asked: "What is the union of the ruler and the minister?

The Master said: "The curtains and talismans separate the noble and the humble; the secret correspondence passes through and is communicated. On the fourth day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Zhenghe era.

Suddenly, he summoned the administrator and ordered him to divide a paper bag into four parts—one for the assembly of monks, one for the novices, one for the monastic estate, and one for the funeral transport.
After a moment, he spoke again: "Danxia has a public case (gong'an) that from of old has been toppled and then raised up;
today it is shown universally to all people. Tell me, what is it? He looked to his left and right and asked, "Do you understand? They replied, "We do not."
The Master said, "How magnificent is this great man! He did not understand the final word," and then he went to sleep and passed away while lying on his right side.
Later, Zen Master Dayong Qilian of Tianting in Chang’an ascended the hall and said: "The principle of pure emptiness is where the Buddhas and Patriarchs alike return."
Ultimately there is no body; the holy and the mundane are of one essence. Such is the principle. But as for the myriad phenomena arrayed before one’s eyes—how are they?

Not even a speck of dust exists at their limit; those beings possess their own eyes, so why look on from the side? Officially, not even a needle may pass; privately, carts and horses find their way through.

If you reach such a state, only then can you respond to circumstances as they arise and employ them at hand; wondrously responding without fixed direction, you walk the mysterious path against the wind.
You will truly attain the golden needle and brocade seams where the stitching is not apparent, and the jade palace and jeweled steps where the pearl curtain has not yet been drawn.
At this very moment, tell me: whose realm is this? The autumn wind blows cold across the ancient ferry.
*Sā*. Red reeds and white *lúhuā* fill the river bends.
A monk asked Master Jǐ of Mēishān in Tóngchuān Prefecture, "What is the matter of the Dharma-body?
The Master said, "A withered tree blossoms without violating the spring. [The monk] asked, "What is the matter beyond the Dharma-body? The Master said, "The stone woman..."
Applying makeup to the eyebrows.
A monk asked Chan Master Shanshou of Puxian in Fuzhou, "What is 'deviation within the center'?

The Master said, "The dragon’s cry after the first watch of night; the tiger’s roar before the fifth watch. [The monk] asked, "What is 'the center within deviation'? The Master said, "Light mist envelops..."
A bright moon; thin mist locks the cold crags. [The student] asks: "What is 'coming from the center'? The Master says: "How could the withered pine ever grow old?
The flowers bloom though they have not yet sprouted. [The student] asks: "What is 'arriving through the integration'? The Master says: "The sound of the monkey’s cry cannot be distinguished."
The cry of the crane resounds, yet its meaning is difficult to clarify. [A monk] asked, "What is 'reaching within the integration'? The Master said, "Clearing the path beyond the clouds;
shedding oneself before the moonlight."
Chan Master Faden of Lumeng in Xiangzhou was the son of the Liu family of Chengdu.
He took the tonsure under Daci Baofan and was instructed to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, through which he grasped its essential meaning. Later, he abandoned his studies to visit Furong.

Furong asked him, "What is one's own true self prior to the empty kalpa? At these words, the Master’s mind and traces vanished into stillness. With composure, he stepped forward and said, "A single phrase that transcends..."
The Herd of Elephants: Transcending the Three Vehicles without relying on cultivation. [Zhao] Rong caressed him and sealed him, opening the Dharma at Mude Gate.
A monk asked, "When the void and the profound are not transgressed, and the light of the precious mirror is cold, what then? The Master said, "Dig a hole and bury it deep.
A monk asked, "What is one who dwells in carefree seclusion beyond the mundane world? The Master said, "His entire body is red and raw; he cannot be supported."
On the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday, National Teacher Nanchan of Jianchang Commandery ascended the hall and, looking around at those present, said:

"Do you all understand? The Lord outside the curtain of night-brightness never alters through the myriad transformations; the Honored One atop the crystal palace is not obscured by the four ministers.

He governs with effortless composure, and his commands are carried out without being issued. His longevity exceeds that of a hundred billion Sumeru mountains, and his transformative influence permeates the great trichiliocosm."
Throughout the sands of worlds. Now tell me: at such a time as this, how does one conduct oneself? "The rustic elder knows not the nobility of the imperial palace;
he is too weary to listen to the sound of the silent whip in the six streets."
Chan Master Weizhou Dongshan Wei ascended the hall and said: "The sun is warm and the wind is gentle; the willow buds turn green. The ice melts and the fish leap; ripples form upon the water.
One who attains the wondrous seal of the Sovereign of Emptiness at the front line walks through the night with Mount Kunlun upon his head, covered in snow.
A monk asked, "What is the matter of silent resonance? The Master replied, "A mute man eating bitter melon."

The Grand Tutor Gao Shize was a lay practitioner (upāsaka) whose courtesy name was Zhongyi and whose sobriquet was Wugong. Initially, he attended upon Master Fuyong to seek instruction on the essential point of the mind.
Fuyong instructed him to set aside all that he valued and to investigate by turning inward. One day, he suddenly attained the subtle and profound; he presented a verse, saying: [Verse omitted]
Letting go at the edge of the precipice, one moves freely in all directions; the great earth and empty space are naturally level and plain.
Illuminating the ravines and shining upon the cliffs without borrowing from the moon, there is another screen of light within the hermitage.
Chan Master Shousui of Da Hong in Suizhou, a successor of Chan Master Da Hong’en, was the son of the Zhang family of Suining. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
"With one punch, he knocks down Huanghe Lou; with one kick, he overturns Yingwu Zhou. He is accustomed to galloping his jade horse atop high towers. He had once...
One strikes a golden ball in swift-flowing water. Although it is thus, what can be done? There are five-colored silk cords binding one’s hands and feet, and three gold locks fastening one’s throat.

Even if you were to smash the gold locks to pieces and cut through the silk cords, you must know that there is yet another layer obstructing you. Tell me, what is this one layer? Do you understand? Śāriputra.
Mó tán was unable to reach him; Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra looked upon him as if they were blind. He ascended the hall and raised this case:

A Prefect Li asked Yàoshān, "What is your surname? Shān said, "It is precisely now. Li could not fathom this, so he asked the temple attendant, "Just now I asked the Elder what his surname was, and he replied, 'It is precisely now.
What exactly is his surname? The attendant said, "He simply has the surname Hàn."

Shanwen said, "If you were to meet him in the sixth month, you would simply say his surname is 'Heat' (Re). Furthermore, Yantou asked a lecturer-monk, "I hear it is said that you understand the teachings;
is this true? He replied, "I dare not [claim such]. Yantou raised his fist and said, "What teaching is this? The monk replied, "[It is this]."
"This is a provisional teaching. The Head said, "How bitter! Had I extended my leg and questioned you, you could not have said it was the 'teaching of the leg.
The Master said, "Remarkable! These two elders possess the blade that kills and the sword that gives life. One turn of phrase is like planting flowers upon a rock;
another turn of phrase is like hanging a sword in mid-air. Had there not been the subsequent words at that time, [the lineage of] Bodhidharma would have perished."
The school has been swept from the ground and utterly destroyed. Do you people wish to see these two old masters? It would be better to cut out one’s tongue than to violate the national taboo.
[This concludes] the thirteenth generation under Qingyuan.

Chan Master Zhenxie Qingliao of Changlu in Zhenzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Danxia Chun. He was the son of the Lady Yong of Yongzhou in Zuomin. From infancy, he entered a temple where he saw a Buddha statue;

his joy moved his brows and lashes, and everyone marveled at this. At the age of eighteen, he underwent the *dharmapada* examination on the *Lotus Sūtra* and received full ordination. He then went to Chengdu.
Cizhi studied the sutras and śāstras and grasped their general meaning. He left Shu and traveled to Mian and Han, where he sought out Danxia’s quarters.
Danxia asked, "What is your original self prior to the empty kalpa? As Cizhi was about to respond, Danxia said, "You are making a fuss; go for now.
One day, while ascending Potu Peak, Cizhi attained sudden and complete enlightenment. He returned directly to stand in attendance. Danxia struck him with his palm and said, "I thought you knew."
The Master bowed joyfully. The following day, Yunxia ascended the hall and said, "The sun shines upon the solitary peak’s emerald hue; the moon descends upon the mountain stream’s chill.
The profound and wondrous secret of the Patriarchs—do not seek it within the space of a single inch. He then descended from his seat.
The Master stepped directly forward and said, "Today you have ascended the hall; you can no longer deceive me. Yunxia said, "Try to cite my words from today's ascent of the hall and see. The Master—
After a long silence, Yu Xia said, "I thought you had already seen through it. The Master then departed. Later, he traveled to Mount Wutai and then to the capital.

Crossing the Bian River, he went directly to Changlu to pay his respects to Zu Zhao. They reached a state of mutual accord in a single word, and Zu Zhao appointed him as his attendant. After more than a year, he was assigned a seat alongside the master.
Before long, Zhao retired on the grounds of illness, and the Emperor commanded the Master to succeed him on the seat. Students flocked to him as if returning home.

At the end of the Jianyan era, he traveled to Siming, presiding over Putuo, Tianfeng in Tiantai, and Xuefeng in Min. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Yuyang, then moved to Longxiang in Wenzhou and Jingshan in Hangzhou.
Empress Dowager Cining commissioned him to open the monastery of Gaoning Chongxian. Entering the hall, he said: "I..."
Under the single palm-strike of my former teacher, all my skills were exhausted; I could find no opening through which to speak. Is there anyone today who is so swift yet not thorough?
If there is none, then wear the iron bit and carry the saddle—each must take his own ease.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "I have long kept this essential matter in silence, not seeking to speak of it hastily. The Old Śākyamuni waited, wishing to sell it with full detail."

"Playing! Alas, even before emerging from the mother’s womb, one has already been seen through by others. But tell me, what was it that was seen through? One cannot deceive Xuefeng. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Climbing to the peak of a solitary mountain, crossing a single-plank bridge, and walking straight ahead in this manner—this is still where people's feet are high or low.
If you see through it thoroughly, without leaving your door, your body pervades the ten directions. Unfinished.
When entering the gate, one is always inside the house. If this is not yet so, take advantage of the cool breeze to go fetch some firewood.
[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "If you can utter the first phrase, you will not be deceived by the staff. Even recognizing the staff is still a matter of being on the road.
What is the phrase for reaching the destination? [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "It cannot be found anywhere; there is only one..."
Seeking it not in any place, one finds it spontaneously. Tell me, in which place is it? After a long silence, he said: "The thief’s own body has already been revealed. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Only when the white mold from the mouth is gone does one begin to enter the gate. Only when the entire body is scorched and raw does one know there is a matter within the gate."
Furthermore, you must know that there is that which does not go out the gate. He then said, "What do you call the 'gate'?
A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel within a mass of flames; is this truly so? The Master laughed heartily and said, "I, however, have my doubts.
The monk asked, "Why, Reverend Sir, do you have doubts? The Master replied, "Wildflower fragrance fills the path; the secluded birds..."
"I do not know spring. [A monk] asked, "If one does not fall into the traces of wind and color, is it permitted to turn back?
The Master said, "Where the stone man walks, his merit is not the same as others. [The monk] asked, "What of the matter that transcends this? The Master said, "The marvel lies before a single bubble;

how could it admit the eyes of a thousand sages? The monk bowed. The Master said, "I only fear you will not understand it thus. One day, the Master entered the kitchen to watch the noodles being boiled.
Next, suddenly the bottom of a bucket fell out. The assembly all cried out in alarm, saying, "What a pity! The Master said, "When the bottom of a bucket falls out, one ought to rejoice;
why then do you grieve? A monk said, "The Master may find it acceptable. The Master said, "Indeed, it is truly a pity—a whole bucket of flour!
He then asked a monk, "After you die and are burned to ashes, once they have been scattered away, where will you go?"
The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout! But you must not turn back on your own words. The monk shouted again.

The Master said, "The public case is not yet complete; you must shout once more before it is finished. The monk was speechless. The Master struck him, saying, "You dead man! He ascended the hall and said:

"Moss seals the ancient path, yet it does not fall into empty stillness. Fog locks the cold forest, yet it willingly reveals the essential wind. The hook and needle are steady and subtle—who would dare say otherwise?"
The fisherman dwells in his nest; he simply accepts things as they are. This is naturally ordinary and joyful.

Is there anyone here who possesses the eye that penetrates the barrier? After a long silence, he said: "Even if one hears of it early and returns at once, how can this compare to never having left the door at all?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes raining, sometimes clearing; sometimes cold, sometimes hot. As for my own state, I alone know it; as for yours, you yourselves must know."
"An individual," he said. "Everyone speaks for themselves; tell me, what else did Xuefeng intend to do with his mouth besides eating rice?

He asked a monk, "When a jade maiden throws her shuttle upon the crystal palace, what matter on the side of clarity does she illuminate? The monk replied, "She avoids the immediate occasion through mutual interpenetration.

The Master said, "Is there still continuity or interruption? The monk said, "From ancient times to the present, there has never been an interval. The Master said, "Precisely at that moment, there is no interval."
"How is it now? "Monks, take care. He then went out. Upon ascending the hall, he shook his staff and said, "Look!
Look! The trichiliocosm shakes all at once. Master Yunmen attained this; Xuefeng was not so.
He struck the ground with his staff and said, "Where has the trichiliocosm gone? Do you understand? One must not encounter heavy plum rains twice."
The seedlings vie to show their green. [He] ascends the hall and says: "The illusory, transformed empty body is itself the Dharma-body. He then performs a dance and asks: "Do you see? Do you see?
If you see in this way, the village wine by the bridge is delicious. Again he performs a dance and asks: "Do you see? Do you see?
If you do not see in this way, the wild flowers on the opposite bank are fragrant. [He] ascends the hall and asks: "Is there anyone who is not defiled by the profound and the subtle?"
After a long silence, he said, "This single drop would overturn the waters of the four seas; it is already too much for one to wash away.
A monk asked, "What is the self prior to the empty kalpa? The Master said, "A white horse enters the reeds. He ascended the hall and said, "To exhaust the subtle is to lose the root."
The essence is subtle, yet its primary principle is lost; a single phrase cuts off the flow, reaching the ultimate depth of the profound mystery.

Therefore, where the golden needle is hidden, its brilliance and edge are not revealed; when the jade thread passes through, it silently displays extraordinary colors. Even so, this is still a case of mutual illumination between two.

Furthermore, tell me: when neither skill nor clumsiness reaches the mark, how can one be entrusted with the matter? After a long silence, he said: "Where the cloud-vines are exquisite, the green shadows close together;
on the crags, trees high and low are locked in deep emerald. Ascending the hall, he said: "To turn the function and settle in the position is for one who moves forward.
A jade gem hidden in the mountains of Jing is precious. To turn the position and accord with the function is for one who returns. A flake of snow in a red furnace is spring. Function and position—"

They turn together; throughout the body there is no obstruction. Letting go of the hand, one is free from reliance. The stone woman ascends the loom at night; the secret chamber has no one to sweep it.
At such a time, how can you entrust yourself to a single word that cuts off the breath? After a long silence, he said: "Returning to the root, the wind falls the leaves;
the moon shines to its end, and the pond is empty. The Master passed away at Gaoning Chongxian Temple and was interred in a pagoda to the west of the temple in Huatong.
His posthumous title was Chan Master Wukong.
Chan Master Hongzhi Zhengjue of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Li family of Xi Prefecture. His mother dreamed that a monk from Mount Wutai untied a ring and fastened it upon her right arm;
she then became pregnant and observed the precepts of fasting and purification. Upon his birth, his right arm rose prominently as if...
He was of a round face and seven years of age when he could recite several thousand words daily. His grandfather was Ji and his father was Zongdao, who had long studied under Chan Master Fotuo Xun.
The master once pointed to him and said to his father, "This boy’s spiritual resonance is most excellent; he is no one of the mundane dust.
If he leaves the household life, he will surely become a vessel for the Dharma. At eleven, he received the tonsure from Jingming Benzong; at fourteen, he received full ordination. Ten...
Eighth, while traveling abroad, he took leave of his master, saying, "If I do not realize the Great Matter, I vow never to return.

Upon reaching Mount Xiangshan in Ruzhou, he met Cheng Kumu, who immediately held him in high esteem. One day, while hearing a monk reciting the Lotus Sutra, when he reached the passage, "The eyes born of one's parents can see the three thousandfold world-system," he had a sudden realization. He immediately went to the master’s quarters to explain what he had understood.
Wu pointed to the incense casket on the altar and asked, "What is inside there? The Master said, "What kind of mental activity is that?
Wu asked, "And how is it at your place of awakening? The Master drew a circle with his hand and presented it; he then threw it behind him.
Wu said, "You fellow who plays with mud balls—what limits do you have? The Master said, "Wrong. Wu said, "I see it differently."
When the man first arrived, the Master responded, "Yes, yes. He then went to see Danxia. Danxia asked, "What is one's own self prior to the empty kalpa?
The Master said, "A frog at the bottom of the well swallows the moon; at the third watch, one does not borrow the night-bright curtain. Danxia said:
"I have not yet spoken further. As the Master hesitated, Xiang struck him with a whisk and said, "And you say it is 'not borrowed'?

At these words, the Master was suddenly enlightened and prostrated himself. Xiang said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase? The Master replied, "Today I have lost my money and incurred this punishment.
Xiang said, "I have no time to beat you; go for now. Xiang took charge of Dahong, and the Master served as the director of correspondence.

Later, he was appointed as the head of the assembly. Those who had attained the Dharma already numbered several people. In the fourth year, after [Dongshan] Yuan-tong had passed away, Zhenxie was newly residing at Changlu and sent a monk to invite him there.
When the assembly came out to welcome him, they saw that his robes and sandals were worn and tattered, so they offered to change them for him.

Zhenxie ordered an attendant to provide him with new shoes, but the Master declined, saying, "Did I come here for the sake of shoes? Upon hearing this, the assembly was filled with admiration and submission, and they earnestly [pressed him to accept].

He requested the Dharma and occupied the foremost seat. After six years, he went to reside at Puzhao Temple in Sizhou. He subsequently filled the positions of Yuantong at Taiping, Nengren, and Changlu.
The dwellings at Tiantong were cramped and dilapidated; upon the Master’s arrival, he renovated them entirely. Disciples vied with one another to gather there.
He ascended the hall and said: "The curtains hang down in the imperial palace; who transmits the family message? The purple silk screen is closed; in the dark, true pearls are scattered."
At such a time, there is that which hearing and sight cannot reach, and that which words and explanations cannot attain. How can one penetrate this message?
"The night returns from a dream, the colors of the sky are faintly bright; laughing, he points to the family style—a spring in full bloom. He ascended the hall.
The mind cannot perceive it; the mouth cannot discuss it. Even if you retreat and take it upon your shoulders, you must strictly avoid hitting upon its tabooed name.
"Wind and moon, cold and clear at the ancient ferry; the night boat turns upon the crystal ground. [He] ascended the hall and said: "In the empty kalpa there is a true source;
before sound, one asks of one's own person. A brand-new livelihood in utter poverty; the old family style of purity and clarity. This is the very essence of the Three Vehicles."
Outside. Within this vast, solitary seal, one nevertheless proceeds through the manifold categories; ten thousand streams naturally flow toward the east.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Today is the anniversary of Śākyamuni’s birth. Changlu does not know how to preach Chan, so I shall draw a likeness for you all.
Suppose he were in Māyā’s womb—what would it be like? With his whisk, he drew this circle (○) and said:
If one uses pure water to bathe the golden body, how then does it fare? Again, he draws this symbol of water [a circle with a drop].

He says: "As for taking seven steps, gazing in the four directions, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, attaining enlightenment and preaching the Dharma, manifesting supernatural powers and transformations, and possessing wisdom and eloquence—throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, he spoke of green and explained of yellow, pointing..."
"Painting west from the east. "When entering *parinirvāṇa*, how then? Thereupon he painted this ⊕ symbol and further said:
"If you are a monk with eyes, you will surely grant me your assent; if not, you must pass through each and every stage before you may attain it.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "What is one who is heading toward the future? The Master said: "The white clouds have vanished into the ravines; the green peaks lean against the sky."
Konggao asked, "What is the person who returns? The Master said, "With a head full of white hair, he leaves the mountain valleys;

at midnight, he pierces the clouds to enter the marketplace. [The monk] asked, "What is the person who neither comes nor goes? The Master said, "The stone woman calls back the dream of the three realms;
the wooden man sits and cuts off the mechanism of the six gates. He then said, "It is easy to clarify the essence within a phrase."
It is difficult to discern the essential point within the school. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? The frozen rooster has not yet crowed, yet the dawn breaks in the home-grove;
silently, a traveler passes over the Snowy Mountains. A monk asked: "What is it like when not a single thread of attachment remains?
The Master said: "He travels side-by-side with the boatman. The monk asked: "What is the matter therein? The Master said: "A swift blade or a sharp axe cannot cut through it."
Question: "What is it like when the mouth of the cloth bag is opened? The Master said: "Let it fill the ditches and block the ravines as it pleases. Question:
"When the principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body, what then? The Master said: "Before a trace of pattern appears, the message is difficult to transmit at its limit."
[The student] said: "With a single step, one secretly shifts; the profound path turns. When the whole body is cast down, the kalpa-jar is empty. The Master said:

"At the moment of birth, as one approaches the father, the entire being is present without a trace of omission. [The student] asked: "If the principle is thus, what of the phenomenon? The Master said:

"As each distinct instance returns, the affairs of differentiation unfold; what hindrance could there be to the responsive functioning throughout the ten directions? [The student] said: "In that case, every particle of dust manifests [the truth]."

"Your original body has departed," the Master said. [The monk] asked, "It penetrates all forms and transcends all mind. The Master said, "How about 'as it is in principle' and 'as it is in fact'? [The monk] asked, "And how about that?
The Master said, "When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; carry it home in a bottomless basket."
[The Master] said: "Entering the marketplace, one can let out a long whistle; returning home, one puts on a short shirt. The Teacher said: "The wooden man sings atop the ridge;
the stone woman dances by the stream. He ascended the hall and said: "O Zen practitioners: why is it that the person who has swallowed all Buddhas of the three periods cannot open their mouth?
Why is it that the person who has illuminated the four worlds cannot close their eyes? Such are these many ailments."
"I have already removed it for you all at once. But how can you attain complete and thorough mastery? Do you understand?
It splits apart Mount Hua so it reaches the color of the sky; it releases the Yellow River so its roar reaches the sea. Since the Master took up residence [at this monastery],...

Accepting offerings without covetousness, he practiced giving without weariness. During a year of food shortages, he exhausted his own possessions as well as the surplus from supporting the community, thereby saving tens of thousands of lives.
He regularly observed the practice of not eating after noon. In the ninth month of the Dingchou year of the Xiangshu era, he called upon his local officials and donors;
subsequently, he visited Zhao Gong Lingcong, the Governor of Yue, with whom he took leave. On the seventh day of the tenth month, he returned to the mountain.

Later, he left that study to visit Nányáng Jǐn, and subsequently attended Dàhóng Zhì; for over ten years, he attained nothing.

He attained realization later upon hearing the words of Hongzhi. He went to reside at Shanquan, and subsequently moved to Jinsu. There, he ascended the hall and said: "The bright moon hangs high, yet has not yet shone before;

Chuchi emerged from [seclusion]. From that time on, his question-and-answer sessions were unhindered, and Zhi recognized him as a true son within the hall.

In the *ding-si* year of the Xiangshu era, he began teaching the Dharma at Putuo; he subsequently moved to Wanshou, Jixiang, and Xuedou. In the third year of the Chunxi era, by imperial decree, he was appointed to Jingci.

He ascended the hall and said: "The cold wind blows fiercely, sweeping through the withered forest; Leaves fall and return to their root, revealing the bare heartwood. The myriad streams flow toward the source; the boat [is ready]."

Reaching the shore: the six windows reflect emptily; a mustard seed meets a needle. It is fundamentally manifest—do not seek it elsewhere. The nature-ground is vast and tranquil, shining through ancient and modern times.
Outside the door, the frost melts and the spring colors stir; the four mountains all become the chanting of wooden dragons. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"Śākyamuni, the Old Man, exhausted principle and perfected nature; his golden mouth proclaimed the teachings for a lifetime. Pearls turn and jade revolves, yet he was betrayed by people..."
They call it "wiping away the filth of impure paper. The Patriarch Bodhidharma directly pointed to the One Vehicle for single transmission;
he sat facing the wall for nine years, establishing no reliance on words or letters, yet people called him the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin.
Tell me, how should one conduct oneself so as to avoid being pointed out and criticized by bystanders? "The patched robe covers the head, and all affairs cease; at this time, the mountain..."
The monks did not understand. He ascended the hall and said: "The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. What is sweet is sweet; what is bitter is bitter.

"This is a phrase for those who have fully trained in the monastic groves. Do you all understand it thoroughly? The village elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun;

To investigate from the side within this realm, one returns to the path and attains the wondrous. Though the clouds move, they are ever tranquil; though the moon is obscured, it shines all the more clearly. Guest and host intersect and merge. Right...

"Reaching both the partial and the comprehensive: when spring ends on the Ten Continents, the flowers wither; the coral forests are bright under the blazing sun. A monk asked, "What is 'partial within the central'?
The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, the stars filled the sky. The monk asked, "What is 'central within the partial'?
The Master said, "White clouds shroud the mountain peak; its towering majesty is never revealed. The monk asked, "What is 'coming from the center'?"
The Master said: "Do not say that the Kun and Jing lack wings; today I have come directly by way of the birds' path. [The student] asked: "What is 'reaching within the partial'?

The stone man’s robe is torn; there is no one on earth to sew it. Entering the hall: When skin and flesh have fallen away, all boundaries are severed;
when body and mind are clearly understood, not a single thing remains. Wondrously entering the profound and still realm of the Way, the jade person uprightly drives the white ox cart.
The ground of wondrous clarity is rarely reached by those who merely understand; it lies beyond the reach of conscious intellect, known only through direct realization.

The child of white clouds shines with self-illumination; the father of green mountains stands forth in eternal presence. The pivot of function is the light behind the crown; wisdom accords with the eye before kalpas.
Thus it is said: "The road to Xinfeng is steep and rugged; the caves of Xinfeng are deep and lush.

Those who ascend do so without wavering; those who roam do so without haste. Though there are pavilions and halls, few people visit them; though groves and springs abound, they do not grow ordinary trees.
O virtuous practitioners of Zen: the one supreme step beyond is noble and difficult to clarify. Within the crystal palace..."
"Not titled as noble. Before the emerald curtains, they still join their companions. At this very moment, the needle and thread are threaded through;

Ascending the hall, he cited the Verse on the Dharmakāya by Master Fu: "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe; Walking, I ride a water buffalo."
Water buffalo. A person passes over a bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Master Yunmen said:
"People come from the east, come from the west, come from the south, and come from the north—each and every one comes riding upon a water buffalo. Although it is thus:
"A thousand heads, ten thousand heads—simply recognize this one head. The Master said, "Yunmen is usually dry and parched;
no awl can penetrate him. Yet here he is, able to drag through mud and water. Do you all wish to see this one head right now?
The weather is somewhat cold; each of you return to your hall. He ascended the hall and raised the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner, saying:

To gain an eye at the very moment the wind moves the banner—this is the Venerable One’s achievement. To lose that eye at the very moment the wind moves the banner—is this not the wind and the banner themselves?
If you have not yet reached this realization: it is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind; it is merely the patch-robed monk persisting in his own efforts like a needle and awl.
After the rain has passed through the mountain retreat, the murky smoke clears; lying down, one listens as the cool breeze arises from the bamboo grove. Autumn of the seventh year. Retired.

His entire body was interred to the right of the Mingjue Pagoda.
Chan Master Fagong of Shichuang at Ruiyan in Mingzhou was the son of the Lin family of Fenghua in the commandery. At Qizhen...

He received the tonsure and full ordination at the Monastery (Yuan). He went to the lecture hall of Yanqing, where one night, while reciting the Lotus Sūtra up to the passage, "The eyes born of one's parents see the three thousandfold world-system," he heard the sound of wind striking the leaves of a *tāla* tree. Suddenly, he attained a profound realization.

He left Tian Tong and began to clarify the Great Meaning. He visited all the masters of the Dharma of his time to consult them and resolve his doubts. Eventually, he emerged to reside at Nengren Temple.
Guangxiao Ruiyan addressed the assembly in the Hall: "The spring breeze and willow brows; The spring birds warble their hundred-tongued songs.
A single mind of the Patriarch— In both places, it is fully revealed. Without moving a step, one returns home; Habitual outflows are instantly extinguished.
Darkly cast is the jade thread’s gleam; At dawn, it pierces the golden needle’s eye. Profound, firm, and truly remote— Who can discern it, if no one is there? How pitiable!"
Life. Every single instance accords with the Way. If you do not contemplate Amitābha, then "Namu to the dry dung-club. Do not speak of this before those who lack wisdom and are deluded;
it must never be told to them. Ascending the hall, he said: "When you see through to the bottom, you are intimate when it is time for action.

Those we meet are all people of this very kind. To rain down jewels from the sky is no reason to boast of wealth; to have no place to stick a锥 (a small awl) is not yet poverty. Treading upon a scale-weight is hard."

Chan Master Fazhen of Qingliang at Shimen in Xiangzhou was a native of Jianmen. He ascended the hall and said: "The willow colors hold mist;
the spring light is brilliantly exquisite. A single peak rises solitary and steep; ten thousand plants vie for their fragrance. The white clouds are limpid and already heartless;

Chan Master Fahui of Dahuang in Suizhou was the son of the Bao family of Tiantai. He ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-body is formless; it cannot be sought through sound or voice.

The monk said, "This man indeed has a point of view, yet he does not recognize the fundamental principle. During the next period of entering the room, Yunmen had five attendants stand in a formal sequence.
When the Master arrived, they all called out, "Venerable Shishang! Thereupon, the Master secretly realized the profound essence and uttered this verse:
"The single rank is just revealed, and the five ranks are distinguished; Where ruler and subject harmonize, purple clouds gather thick."
The night-bright curtain is rolled up, illuminating all without partiality; the layered golden halls reveal the Supreme Honored One. His robes were well-suited to him. Later, he resided at Jixiang.
Chan Master Daoyuan of Touzi in Shuzhou had long served Tiānyī, yet he attained no realization. Tiānyī rebuked him, and the Master forgot [his former self].
He remained in seclusion for over a month. One night, hearing the sound of the watchman’s bell, he was suddenly struck with a profound realization and exclaimed:
"Stop! Stop! One sound penetrates straight to the path of the azure heavens; who knows of the bright moon in the cold pond? The mud ox bumps and breaks the coral tree.
Later, when appointed to the post of Librarian, whenever he was questioned, he would gesture with his whisk as if shaking a bell.
Chan Master Xuedou Zhijian of Mingzhou, a descendant of the fifteenth generation under Qingyuan and a successor of Chan Master Tiantong Ju,
was born into the Wu family of Chuzhou. In his childhood, his mother washed a sore on his hand.
The Master asked, "What is this? He replied, "My hand is like the Buddha’s hand. Having long lost his parents, he relied upon Zhenxie at Changlu.
Da Xiu took charge of the assembly and immediately recognized his potential as a vessel. Later, he withdrew to Mount Xiangshan, where no manner of strange phenomenon could distract him.

In the deep of night, he attained awakening and sought certification from Yanshou. Subsequently, he went to see Da Xiu again. After taking up residence there, Da Xiu ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One has a secret..."
[The Master] spoke: "Kāśyapa does not conceal [the truth]. One night, falling flowers rain down; the entire city is filled with the fragrance of flowing water.
Chan Master Zao of Chao-hua in Yue State, successor to Chan Master Shanjian Zhi, ascended the hall for the opening of the furnace: "Snow fills the cold window; the wood of Danxia is burned away."
The Buddha crossed the frozen fields at the ford; he froze the iron ox of Shanzhou to death. Thus, cold ashes burst into flame, and not a flake of snow remains.
Moving freely and spontaneously, it is the realization of ready-made enjoyment. Do you all Zen practitioners wish to understand? Sitting with one’s patched robe covering the head.
Cold and warmth are utterly unknown.

Chan Master Weigan Daqin of Guangfu Monastery in Taizhou was a successor of Chan Master Zongxue of Xuedou and a native of the Yu clan of that prefecture. He ascended the hall and, citing a case, said: A monk asked...
Tongan. "What is the house style of the Master? Tongan said, "The golden rooster carries its chicks back to the Milky Way;
the jade hare conceives her fetus and enters the Purple Microcosm. [The monk] asked, "If a guest should suddenly arrive, with what will you entertain them?
Tongan said, "The golden fruit was plucked by the monkey early at dawn; the jade blossom was brought back by the phoenix late in the evening. The Master said, "Guangfu does not think so. Thereupon...
Question: "What is the house style of the Master? He replied to him: "Singing 'ai-nai' amidst clusters of green bamboos;
lying down in misty vines deep within the blue crags. "Should a guest suddenly arrive, what will you use to receive them?
"A bottomless basket to hold the bright moon; a mindless bowl to store the pure wind."

The Yunmen School.

Chan Master Wenyuan of Guangfeng Monastery on Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Xuefeng Cun of the sixth generation under Qingyuan. He was a native of Jiaxing and surnamed Zhang. In his youth...
He entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Zhicheng at Kongwang Temple. Of keen character and innate wisdom, his eloquence was divinely bestowed.
Upon reaching adulthood, he shaved his head and received full ordination at the platform in Pilin. He attended Zhicheng for several years, exhaustively investigating the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Because his own realization remained unclear, he went to visit Master Muzhou. As soon as Muzhou saw him approaching, he closed the door. The Master then knocked on the door, and Muzhou asked, "Who is it?"
The Master said, "I am such-and-such. The Governor asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction.
The Governor opened the door, looked at him once, and then closed it again. The Master did this, knocking on the door for three consecutive days.

On the third day, the Governor opened the door; the Master then pushed his way inside. The Governor immediately seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! As the Master hesitated, the Governor pushed him out.
He said, "During the Qin dynasty, a carriage ran over and pierced me, so I closed my door; this damaged one of my legs. From this, the Master attained awakening.
He was directed by the Prefect to visit Xuefeng. Upon arriving at Xuefeng’s estate, he saw a monk and asked, "Are you going up the mountain today?
The monk replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Please deliver a koan to the Abbot for me, but you must not say anything."
"This is the speech of another person," the monk said. "Yes," the Master replied.

"When you go into the mountains and see the Abbot ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly has gathered, you must step forward, clasp his neck, stand on the ground, and say: 'Why does this old fellow not cast off the iron cangue upon his neck?
That monk followed the Master's instructions exactly. When Xuefeng saw the monk speak in such a manner, he descended from his seat and seized him by the chest."
Holding him back, Feng said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The monk had no reply. Feng pushed him away and said, "These are not your words.
The monk said, "They are my words. Feng said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff! The monk said, "It is not my words;
it was an elder from Zhejiang on the manor who instructed me to come and speak this. Feng said, "Let the assembly go to the manor to welcome him back."
Five hundred spiritual friends came to him. On the following day, the Master ascended Xuefeng Peak. As soon as the Master saw him, the Peak asked, "For what reason have you reached such a state?
The Master then bowed his head. From that point on, they were in accord. Having refined their understanding together for many years, the Master was secretly entrusted with the seal of the school.

After leaving the mountain ridges, the Master traveled everywhere to visit various quarters, investigating and exhausting the diverse paths; his sharp eloquence was formidable and peerless in the world.
What he heard was fulfilled later when he arrived at Lingshu Temple. This accorded with the mysterious sign that Master Zhisheng would receive him as his head seat (*śrāmaṇera*).

Initially, Zhisheng had resided at Lingshu for twenty years without appointing a head seat, often saying, "My head seat is born," "My head seat is tending the ox," and "My head seat is traveling on pilgrimage.
One day, he ordered the bell to be struck at the outer gate of the three gates to welcome the head seat.

The assembly came out to welcome him. When the Master arrived, they invited him directly into the Head Seat’s Quarters to unpack his belongings (as seen in the *Lingshu* chapter of the *Rendiantiyanmu*).

Later, the Lord of Guangzhou commissioned the Master to take charge of Lingshu Temple. On the day he opened the hall, the Lord personally attended and said, "I, your disciple, request your instruction.

The Master replied, "Before one's eyes, there is no other path" (Fayan added a different commentary: "It must not fail to benefit people"). The Master then said, "Do not say that today I am deceiving you all."
People are fond of such things; otherwise, I would not have had to make such a mess before you all.
Should a person of clear eyes encounter this, they would see it as a source of laughter. Now, there is no avoiding it. Let me ask you all:
from the very beginning, what business has there been? What has ever been lacking? To tell you that "there is nothing" is already to bury you in oblivion. Nevertheless...
It is thus. You must reach this stage before you can succeed. Furthermore, do not ask haphazardly just for the sake of a quick retort;
your own mind will remain in darkness. Great matters lie ahead tomorrow and the day after.

If your faculties and understanding are hesitant, then for now look toward the gateways of the ancient masters' transformative teachings—gazing east and west—to see what kind of principle this is. You desire...
Do you understand? It is entirely because your own delusive thoughts have been thick and heavy since immeasurable kalpas past.
As soon as you hear someone speak, doubt arises; you question the Buddha and the Dharma, inquire about the "upward" and "downward" paths, and seek a conceptual understanding.

It turns into a matter of conceptual engagement; the moment you direct your mind toward it, you have already missed the mark. How much more so when there are words and phrases? Is it perhaps that not directing the mind is the way?
Do not misunderstand! What else is there? Take care. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "I have no choice but to speak to you all:
'There is nothing directly here'—this already constitutes a mutual obscuration. Yet you still wish to take steps toward it..."
Previously, you followed words and pursued phrases, seeking understanding through myriad distinctions and raising countless objections;
you have merely gained a slippery tongue, moving further and further away from the Way. When will there ever be a time of rest? If this matter were found within words, [it would be as you have done].
How could the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings be devoid of words? For what reason, then, do you speak of a "separate transmission outside the teachings"?

If [enlightenment] were obtained through scholarly understanding or intellectual acuity, then even a sage of the tenth stage—who preaches the Dharma like clouds and rain—is still rebuked for seeing his nature as if through a fine gauze screen. From this, one knows that all who possess a mind are worlds apart from the truth.
Shu. Nevertheless, for one who has attained it, the fire of words cannot burn the mouth;
though speaking of matters all day long, it never touches the lips or teeth, nor is a single character ever uttered.

Though putting on clothes and eating meals all day long, one never touches a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk. Even so, this is still merely talk concerning the gateway to the teaching.

One must truly attain such realization; only then is it possible. If one speaks from the standpoint of the Zen monk’s school, presenting one's capacity within the words is merely a vain exertion of thought.
Even if one can take responsibility for a single phrase, one is still but a dozing fellow. At that time, a monk asked: "What is this one phrase?

The Master said: "Lift it up! [Later,] while ascending the hall, he said: "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of scripture—whether explained horizontally or vertically—are like the heavens..."
The Junior Abbot has spoken with纵横 (zōnghéng) [horizontal and vertical] freedom. Bring me the principle you have spoken of, even if it were as small as the point of a needle.
Look at how he speaks—it is already like trying to save a dead horse with medicine. Nevertheless, how many people have actually reached such a realm?

I do not dare hope that you will have resonance within your words or conceal the blade’s edge within your phrases; yet, in a single blink of an eye, there are a thousand differences, while the wind remains calm.
The waves have stilled. I humbly pray that you will partake of this offering. A monk came to visit;
the Master then picked up his *kāṣāya* and said, "If you can speak, you fall within the circle of my *kāṣāya*. If you cannot speak, you remain sitting in a ghost cave. How about it?
He spoke on the monk's behalf, saying, "I have no strength. One day, the Master struck the wooden mallet and said, "In the world of Wondrous Joy..."
Miscellaneous fragments. He took his bowl and went into the city of Hunan to eat porridge and rice. Upon ascending the hall, he said:

"Brothers, you have all come from various quarters seeking out masters of knowledge to resolve the matter of birth and death. In every place you have visited, surely there were no venerable elders who offered compassionate and expedient words?
Is there any phrase that you have not yet penetrated? Come forward and cite it; I shall wait for you so that this old man may [explain it] to you."
"Everyone, let us deliberate. Is there anyone? Is there anyone? At that time, a monk stepped forward, intending to pose a question. The Master said, "Go, go!

The road to the Western Heaven is long, more than one hundred thousand miles," and he then descended from his seat. He then cited: When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed with one hand to heaven and with the other to earth;
he walked seven steps, gazing in the four directions, and declared: "Above heaven and below heaven, only I..."
[The Master] said alone and with authority: "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
While the Master was attending a vegetarian feast at Wende Hall, Attendant Ju asked, "Is the fruit on Lingshu mature yet?
The Master replied, "In what year did you come to believe that the Way is born? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?"

The student asked, "What is the mind? The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. The student asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "There is. The student asked, "What is this further matter?
The Master said, "Śākyamuni Buddha is in the Western Heaven; Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells in this Eastern Land.
The student asked, "What is Yunmen Mountain? The Master said, "The fixed site of Mount Geng. The student asked, "What is the Great Cultivation? The Master said, [as above].
A practitioner asked, "Master, a single cup is held in your hand. Ascending the hall, the Master heard the sound of the bell and said, "The world is so vast;
why does the sound of the bell wear the sevenfold robe? A monk asked, "One lifetime accumulates evil without knowing good;
one lifetime accumulates good without knowing evil. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A candle. A monk asked, "What is the Master’s 'untimely' [time]? The Master said, "A candle."
Regarding a single phrase for people, the Master said: "In the early morning one plows with the ox; in the evening one drags the harrow. He cited Xuefeng, who said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the flames. The Master said:

"The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods, and the Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and listen. Entering the hall, he cited a saying and instructed you to directly accept it as such.
It was already too late; you had already been struck on the head by my excrement.

Even if you were to pick up a single hair-tip and perceive the entire universe all at once, it would still be like gouging out flesh to create a sore. Nevertheless, you must truly reach this state before you can succeed.
If you have not yet attained this intimacy, do not engage in empty verbiage; you must instead take a step back and return to your own fundamental root.

Push down and investigate further: look into what kind of principle this is. In reality, there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything to provide you with an intellectual understanding or to cause you doubt.
Furthermore, each of you possesses within yourself a segment of reality where the great function is manifest.
It does not require even a hair’s breadth of effort from you, and you would be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

It is simply that your roots of faith are shallow and your evil karma is thick; thus, you suddenly sprout all these horns, carry your alms-bags, and undergo such indignities traveling thousands of miles through a myriad villages. Furthermore, what is lacking for you, you great men?
In this land of Han, who is without their share? Only one can truly take it up; yet even so, they find no advantage. One must not allow oneself to be deceived or to accept the instructions of others.
As soon as you see the old monk open his mouth, you should immediately take a stone and shove it into his mouth.
It is like flies on excrement, vying with one another to swarm over it; three or five of them gather their heads together to deliberate upon it in bitter earnest.
I yield to my brothers. The ancient masters, for all their efforts, could do nothing for you people;
therefore, they used skillful means to leave behind a word or a phrase to open a path for your entry.
If you set aside such matters and apply some effort of your own, would that not be a point of mutual affinity? Hurry, hurry! Time does not wait for man. As the breath goes out...
I cannot guarantee that you will even manage your inhalation; what other use have you for your body and mind elsewhere?
You must pay close attention. Take care. Ascending the hall [the Master said]: "The entire universe is brought at once and placed upon the lashes of your eyes.
Hearing this being said, I do not dare hope that any of you will come forward and, in your impatience, give this old fellow a slap. For now, proceed slowly and with careful discernment."

Look! Is it existence? Is it non-existence? What kind of principle is this? Even if you were to understand it clearly at this point, should you encounter the gate of a Zen monk (nanseng), your legs would be well worth breaking with a staff. If you are such a person, upon hearing it said, "Where is there an old master appearing in the world?
you should spit right in his face, thinking, "He defiles my ears and eyes! If you do not possess such capability, [you will not understand].
As soon as one hears someone mention it, to immediately take it upon oneself already falls into the secondary level of function.
Do you not see how Master Deshan, as soon as he saw a monk enter the gate, would drag his staff and drive him away?
Or how Master Muzhou, as soon as he saw a monk enter the gate, would say, "This is a settled case; I grant you thirty blows. As for those of lesser caliber, what should they do?
If one were a mere hollow talker, feeding on the spittle and saliva of others,
who memorizes a heap or a load of antiquated trifles and roams everywhere with the lips of a donkey and the mouth of a horse, boasting that he understands questions involving ten or five turns—
then even if you were to question him from morning until night, for kalpas like this, have you ever seen him in a dream? Where is there any real exertion of power for others?
As for such people as these, even when someone offers a meal to a monk, they can say, "I have eaten. What is there worth conversing with?
On the day you stand before King Yama, he will not accept your verbal explanations.
Brothers, if you are people who have attained realization, you may spend your days living among the community. But if you have not yet attained it, do not easily let the time pass. Great!
You must be meticulous. The ancients had many instances of "entanglements" (ge-teng) in their mutual dealings. For example, Xuefeng said, "The entire earth is your own self.
Jia Shan said, "Realize the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses; recognize the Son of Heaven in the bustling marketplace.
Luopu said, "As soon as a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained within it; the lion’s whole body is present in a single hair."
Always take this up yourself and reflect upon it from every angle. If you look at it for a long time and many years, a path of entry will naturally appear.
This matter admits of no substitute; it must reside within each person’s own sphere. This is why the Old Monk has appeared in the world.
I shall simply act as your witness. If you have even the slightest grounds for your claim, I cannot fail to perceive it.

If, in truth, you have not yet attained the skillful means, it would be improper for me to dismiss you. Brothers, we are all equally those who have worn out our straw sandals and cast aside our teachers and parents to travel on foot;
you must truly exert some measure of spirit before you can succeed. If you have not yet found a point of entry...
In this situation, you must encounter your own kind—those who will bite the pigs and dogs for you—and, disregarding your own life, enter the mud and the water to assist one another.
When there is something to be chewed upon, raise your eyebrows; hang up your alms-bag, break your staff, and for ten or twenty years, strive until you reach the end.
Do not worry that you will not succeed; even if you do not reach the end in this life, you shall in the next.
Furthermore, you will not lose your human form. Entering through this gate will also save you effort;
you will not have lived your life in vain, nor will you have failed your teachers, parents, or the donors of the ten directions. You must simply take heed.
Do not wander aimlessly from prefecture to county, carrying your staff across a thousand or two thousand *li*, spending the winter here and the summer there.
Fine mountains and fine waters are suitable for taking up one's nature; there is much vegetarian offering, and robes and bowls are easily obtained. How bitter, how bitter!
To scheme for another’s single grain of rice, one loses half a year’s provisions. What benefit is there in such a pilgrimage?
When a faithful donor offers a vegetable or a grain of rice, how can you possibly digest it? You must look within yourself; no one can take your place. Time does not wait.
In dealing with others, one day suddenly the light of the eyes will fall to the ground. When you arrive before that point, what will you have to offer as a defense?
Do not be like a crab falling into boiling water—your hands and feet will be in a frantic scramble, and there will be no room for you to engage in empty talk or boastful exaggerations.
Do not let this time pass in vain; once a human body is lost, it is not regained for ten thousand kalpas. This is no small matter. Do not rely merely on what meets the eye.
Formerly, even laypeople valued the Way, thinking, "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening. How much more so for us śramaṇas—what matters must we practice?
You must exert yourselves with great diligence. Take care. A monk asked Master Lingshu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Lingshu remained silent.
After he passed away, his disciples were drafting an inscription for his memorial stele and wished to include this dialogue. They asked the Master [Xuefeng]: [How should we record this?]
"How shall we write upon the stele for our late master who remained silent? The Master replied, "When the Master ascended the hall, he said, 'The Buddha-dharma is indeed abundant;
it is only that my tongue is too short. After a long pause, he added, 'Now it is long.

Later, while they were working together carrying firewood, the Master picked up a piece and threw it down, saying, "The entire Tripitaka speaks only of this. Seeing a monk measuring rice, he asked, "The rice basket..."

"How many Dharma-eyes are there within? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf: "Measured by pecks, they would not be exhausted. Ascending the hall, he said: "Each person possesses their own radiance;
yet when one looks for it, it is dark and obscured. What is this radiance of your own? [On behalf of himself,] he said:
'The kitchen, the storehouse, and the main gate. He further said: "'A good thing is not as good as having none at all. He addressed the assembly:
An ancient worthy said: "Medicine and disease treat one another; the entire earth is medicine. Which of these is your own self? He then said:
"When encountering the base, it is immediately noble. A monk asked: "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master clapped his hands once, took up his staff, and said: "Take this staff!
When the monk took it, he snapped it into two pieces. The Master said: "Even if you were capable of such a thing, I would still give you—"
"Thirty blows! [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The moment a single word is raised, a thousand carts follow the same ruts.
To encompass even a mote of dust is still but the discourse of the gate of transformation. If you are a monk, what should you do?

If you attempt to deliberate here using the intent of the Buddhas and the patriarchs, the single path of Caoxi will sink into oblivion. Is there anyone who can speak? Come forward and speak! A monk asked:"
"What is the discourse that transcends the Buddhas and surpasses the Patriarchs? The Master said, "Steamed buns. [The monk] asked, "What connection is there here?
The Master said, "Truly, what connection is there? He then said, "All of you have reached a point where there is nothing more to be done."
Seeing that people were attached to the "meaning of the Patriarchs," he asked about talk that transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs:
"What do you call 'Buddha'? What do you call 'Patriarch'? First, explain the principle of transcending Buddhas and Patriarchs.
He asked about "exiting the three realms": "Bring forth the three realms for me; see what sights, sounds, sensations, or cognitions are obstructing you? There was none.
What sensory objects of sound or dharmas of form can you possibly comprehend? What kind of bowl are you trying to understand?

To take that as a basis for the view of differentiation—ancient sages could do nothing about it; they threw themselves across the path for the sake of beings, saying, "The entire body is the absolute truth.
Yet, in every single thing, the essence itself cannot be grasped. I tell you: right now, what business is there? You have already begun to bury yourself.
It is gone. If you truly have no point of entry, then for now, investigate and contemplate it alone.
Aside from dressing, eating, defecating, urinating, and such, what other matter is there? Why do you give rise to all these various delusive thoughts out of nowhere?
Furthermore, there is another class who seem to take it quite casually, gathering together to learn some ancient...
People talk about the Way; they recognize their own natures and employ memory to hold onto things, using deluded thoughts to speculate and calculate, saying, "I have understood the Buddha-dharma.
They do nothing but speak of tangled vines, passing their time according to their whims, yet still resent it if things do not suit them.

Abandoning their parents and teachers to travel thousands of miles and tens of thousands of leagues, making such a departure—what kind of urgency drives these fellows who wander like gathering firewood? Why must you go on pilgrimage?
He drove them out with his staff and ascended the hall, saying: "One must know that the times are degenerate and we live in the age of decline.
Lately, monks go north claiming to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, or go south claiming to travel to Mount Heng. To practice pilgrimage in such a manner is merely to be a monk in name;
they vainly consume the offerings of the faithful. Alas! Alas! When questioned, they appear as if made of black lacquer, doing nothing but following their own whims."
At that time, there may be three or two who are recklessly learned and possess much erudition;

they memorize the paths of discourse and travel everywhere seeking similar phrases to gain the seal of approval from elder masters. They treat those of superior standing with contempt and perform deeds of meager merit.
When the King Yama nails them down on the day of reckoning, do not say that no one told you so. If you are beginners or junior students, you must truly exert yourselves.

Be alert! Do not vainly remember what others have said; much emptiness is not as good as a little reality. Otherwise, you will only deceive yourself in the future. What is there to do? Come forward. The Master ascended the hall.

When the assembly had gathered, he pointed with his staff toward those before him and said: "The great earth of heaven and earth, and all the buddhas as numerous as motes of dust—all are contained within this very space.
They contend over the Buddha-dharma and seek victory or defeat. Is there anyone here who can offer a word of admonition?"
"Is that so? If no one dares to admonish you, wait until this old man admonishes you. The monk said, "I beg the Master to admonish me.
The Master said, "You wild fox spirit! Entering the hall, he took up his staff and said, "The Bodhisattva Maitreya (Tiānqīn) has, for no reason, transformed himself into a single *zhílì* staff.
He then drew a line and said, "All the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are entirely caught within this tangle."
He then descended from his seat and ascended the hall, saying: "I look at you all; even within two or three turns of the teaching, you cannot yet grasp it.
What benefit is there in vainly donning the patched robe? Do you understand? I shall provide you with a commentary to break through this.
In the future, when you travel to various places, if you see an elder raise a finger or hold up a whisk and say, 'This is Chan, this is the Way,' pull out your staff and smash it to pieces!"
Go straight ahead! If you do not act thus, you will all fall into the retinue of the celestial Māras and destroy my school.
If you truly do not understand, then for now look within the thicket of entanglements. I have always told you: "Within every atom of lands and worlds..."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven, and the six patriarchs of the Tang land—all of them preach the Dharma upon the tip of this staff.
Their spiritual powers and transformations resound throughout the ten directions; they act with total freedom as they please. Do you understand?
If you do not, do not merely pretend to know. Even so, have you yet seen it with true, authentic clarity? Even if you reach this point—
"In this field, I have not even dreamed of meeting a monk or a novice; in this village of three families, I do not encounter a single person.
He suddenly took up his staff, drew a line, and said, "All are here. He drew another line and said, "All are departing from here as well.

There are two kinds of illnesses regarding the Dharmakāya. First, although one has attained the Dharmakāya, because one has not yet forgotten the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), one's own views still persist; thus, one remains seated within the Dharmakāya. This is also a case where the light has not been fully penetrated and released.

Furthermore, there is a state where all things are not clearly understood; while there is something directly before one’s face, it is "one" [undifferentiated]. Even if one has penetrated the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), yet there is a lingering sense that something exists indistinctly—this too is a failure of the light to be fully penetrated and released.

Moreover, the Dharmakāya itself has two kinds of illnesses. Upon reaching the Dharmakāya, if one does not forget the attachment to dharmas and one's own views still remain, one sits within the Dharmakāya.
The extreme is one. Even if you manage to penetrate through to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is still not permissible to let it go.

If you examine it closely, what trace of it remains? That too is a sickness. A monk asked: "Is it not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo that 'radiant, silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges'?
