it cannot be pried out with a needle, nor can it be lifted up with a spoon. Upon whom does the fault rest? Though there be a thousand kinds of green grass..."
A single stalk of orchid from Xiangji. Entering the hall: neither square nor round, neither above nor below; the braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs—priceless throughout the ten directions.
[He] strikes the meditation seat and descends.
Chan Master Tanzhou Lianquan Yuan Tanshu asked a monk: "When you cannot speak even with your mouth full, what then?
The Master said, "The talk has fallen. A monk asked: "When you do not act as a companion to the myriad dharmas, what then?
The Master said, "One draws on one's own belly. A monk asked: "What is the place where the student turns? The Master said, "Sweeping the floor and watering the flowers. The monk said, "It is like..."
"What is the intimate point for a student? The Master said, "Highly propped upon one's pillow. [The student] asked, "What is it when it is not like this at all?
The Master said, "The oriole sings on the ridge; flowers bloom before the crag. [The student] asked, "What is the mouth of a patch-robed monk? The Master said:
"Killing people without using a blade.
A monk asked Chan Master Xuanming Foyin of Gaotai Temple on Mount Nanyue, "The treasury of the true Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of nirvana—please bring them forth.

The Master looked directly upward. The monk said, "In that case, humans and devas have someone to rely upon. The Master said: [The text provided ends here; the Master’s subsequent response is not included in the source.]
"Though gold dust is precious...
A monk asked Chan Master Huize of Sanjiaoshan in Qizhou: "When the Master ascends the jeweled seat and the great assembly listens intently, the Master strikes his staff once.
The monk said, 'If you were to answer, you would have answered; why strike it again? The Master said, 'A hundred kinds of confusion.'"
*Suì*. Master Chánshī Wényù of Fǎlún on Nányuè ascended the hall, struck the ground once with his staff, gave a shout, and said:
"Adding frost to snow; adding grit to the eyes. If you do not understand this, you will end up in Uttarakuru."

Chan Master Huijue of Lingjiu in Xinzhou ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Great assembly, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings are all beneath the feet of each of you.
Please, each of you, go back and forth [to examine them] for yourselves. Do you understand?
Whether you go back and forth or do not go back and forth, recognize the path home. Let wisdom serve as the bridge and gentleness as your refuge. When dwelling in peace, one must contemplate."
Danger! While in pleasure, one must know suffering. Have you not seen how Layman Pang cast away gold as if it were mere dross?
Father and son sat together in a circle, speaking words of non-arising. Remember these words of non-arising: throughout the nine months of summer, snowflakes fly.
Three winters, my sweat has been like rain.
Huangbo Jicui Yong Anzhu addressed the assembly: "Since I have resided in this hermitage, there is no Chan to be preached and no Dharma to be transmitted.
I possess no rare or precious treasures; I have only secured a single ember from a continuing firebrand to leave for those who come after."
The Master caused the smoke and flames to continue without ceasing and the firelight to remain bright for a long time. He then threw down his whisk-broom.

At that moment, a monk picked it up from the ground, blew upon it once, and the Master immediately shouted, "Who would have known that the continuation of the ember would vanish like smoke and die out like fire from this fellow?
Thereupon, he shook out his sleeves and returned to his hut. The monk stuck out his tongue in dismay and departed.
The Abbot Zhi of Guizong on Mount Lu was a native of Linjiang. In his prime, he became a bhikṣu and relied upon Huanglong at Guizong, whereupon he grasped the profound essence [of the teachings].
He had a verse that said: "If one has not yet arrived, one must arrive; Once arrived, it makes people laugh.
Eyebrows originally have no use; They possess no cleverness at all. Not long after, Huanglong retired, and Zhi sank into obscurity among the assembly. One day—
After finishing the communal labor for the day, he wrote a verse: "The tea buds, rustling, have just left the kiln; The bamboo shoots, in haste, again emerge from the mud.
In this mountain cottage, the spring tasks of the year are complete; If one has leisure, who cares that the board at the head of the bed is low? Because of this, the monastics grew close to him.
The Master was displeased and retired to a thatched hut on a mountain peak, where he composed another verse: "A single room atop a thousand peaks; An old monk..."
Half a cloud, half a space. Last night the clouds followed the wind and rain away; in the end, they were not as idle as this old monk.
Disciple of Chan Master Huanglong Xin of the Thirteenth Generation under Nan Yue.
Chan Master Wuxin Wushin of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Huang family of Shaoyu.
At birth, he had a purple flesh-mat covering his left shoulder, which, when exposed on the right side, resembled the shape of a *saṃghāṭī* robe. In his youth, he relied upon De-xiu of Fotuo Temple.
After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he traveled to Huanglong to visit Huichang. There, Huichang held up a fist and asked, "If you call this a fist, then..."
"Touching it—do not call it a fist, then you are at fault. What do you call it? The Master was at a loss. After two years, he finally attained realization;

yet his eloquence remained such that there was nothing it could not penetrate. Guishan was troubled by this. Once, as they were conversing and the Master reached the height of his sharpness, Guishan suddenly said, "Stop!
Stop! Talking about food can never satisfy one's hunger. The Master was cornered and said, "I have come to this point where my bow has broken and my arrows are spent."

[The Master] said, "It is exhausted. I hope the Venerable One will, out of compassion, point out a place of peace and bliss. The Hall Master said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens;
a single mustard seed falls and covers the earth. As for a place of peace and bliss, I strictly forbid you, Reverend, from possessing such a multitude of 'treasures' (conceptual baggage).
You must simply die the mind that has existed since immeasurable kalpas, and only then will it be possible. The Master hurried out. One day, he heard the administrative official beating a novice.
Suddenly, a clap of thunder shook the air, and he attained great enlightenment. He hurried to see Huìtáng, forgetting to remove his shoes as he entered.

He immediately proclaimed, "All people under heaven merely practice Zen; I am one who has attained enlightenment. Huìtáng laughed and said, "To have been ranked first in the examination for the selection of Buddhas—how could you possibly be contained by such a title?
Consequently, he was given the sobriquet "Old Man Sīxīn" (Dead Heart). A monk asked, "What is it like when Huánglóng receives people?"
The Master said, "Opening one's mouth is intended to scold people. [The monk] asked, "That which scolds is a phrase for receiving people;
what about that single phrase for testing people? The Master said, "Simply recognize the one who scolds. [The monk] asked, "With bow and arrow in hand, the blade of wisdom meets the fray.

The ranks of dragon and tiger are complete; I pray you, Master, appear before me. The Master said, "A defeated general is not executed. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then the Bronze Pillar is near."
[The monk] pointed to the side of the water and said, "The iron gate is locked high upon Fenghuang Peak. The Master said, "If one has not reached the Wu River, one will not yet be willing to rest.
The monk said, "If that is so, then the 'seven captures and seven releases' is the full exertion of the correct command. The Master said, "Staring with eyes wide open inside a coffin.
The monk bowed; the Master said, "Suffering! Suffering! A monk asked, "I have heard the Master’s words: 'This old monk this summer was within the Yellow Dragon Pond.'"
He lowered three hundred and sixty fishing baskets, yet never once encountered a fish with scales like brocade and a tail like vermilion.
Was it that the hook was not skillful? Or was it that the fragrant bait was difficult to find? The Master said: "When the rain has passed, the bamboo breeze is clear;

when the clouds part, the mountains and peaks are revealed. [The student] said: "If this is so, then I have already received the good news from the True Man; throughout the human world and the heavens above, there is nothing more."

A doubt arose. The Master said, "The hook-tip is not subtle; the fragrant bait is difficult to find. [The monk] said, "To manifest one's person may still be easy; to shed the entire body to realize the Way should be difficult.
The Master said, "Disciples of Chan who follow a confused lineage are as numerous as hemp and millet. He ascended the hall and said: "Profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching."
"No one can reach it. Has Śākyamuni reached it or not? If he has reached it, why is there no one there?
If he has not reached it, who says it is profound and remote? Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs resembles the mechanism of an iron ox:
if you go toward it, it seals you; if you stay still, it breaks you. But as for neither going nor staying—does it seal you, or does it not seal you? [He then recited: "The golden fruit..."
At dawn, the monkeys plucked them away; at evening, the phoenix carried the Jade Flowers back. Entering the hall:
The eminent traveler unties his cloth bag, sets down his alms bowl, and discards all taboos. One must reach the place where a single person is; one must reach the place where half a person is;
one must personally reach even the place where no person is. Entering the hall: He snaps his staff in two. With what will he ascend?
Crossing mountains and traversing waters—set aside the bowl and the chopsticks; with what will you eat your gruel and rice?
It would be better to go to the crossroads and cast your divination sticks east and west. If you suddenly hit upon the truth, it will be a credit to all of you;
if you do not hit upon it, you cannot blame Yunyan. [He] ascended the hall and said: "Mañjuśrī rides a lion; Samantabhadra rides an elephant king. Śākyamuni...
Kālacandra treads upon red lotuses; tell me, what does Huanglong ride? After a long silence, he said:
"Lately I am old; every step is a true step. He ascended the hall and said: "When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear.

When the recitation of the Buddha's name is directed toward a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become the Buddha. Since the Buddha is not distracted, the turbid water naturally clears itself."
"Clear. When turbid water has become clear, where does the merit reside? After a long silence, he said: "How many times have black winds overturned the great ocean?
Yet I have never heard of a fishing boat capsizing. He ascended the hall and said: "At times I break two into three; at times I bring three back to one."
Sometimes the three and one are blended; sometimes they do not fall into numerical categories. Tell me, where is Huanglong’s point of acting for others?
After a long silence, he said, "Take care. A monk asked, "What are the four great poisonous snakes? The Master said, "Earth, water, fire, and wind.
The monk asked, "What are earth, water, fire, and wind? The Master said, "The four great poisonous snakes. The monk said, "I, your disciple..."
[The monk] did not understand and requested the Master’s expedient means. The Master said: "If it is so for the one great element, it is the same for the four great elements.
He then asked a monk in the hall: "Suppose the darkness of the final day of the month were colored with the five hues;

if a hundred thousand million people were to look at those colors in the night, would any among them be able to distinguish blue, yellow, red, or white? The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf: "Every single one of them is [it]."

The Blind Man: Because the Master was questioned by King Zhengyan, [the king] said: "I have heard that birth occurs through the conjunction of three conditions. I have also heard that one dies and is immediately reborn.
Why is it that there are those who are 'snatched from the womb' and born? I find this deeply puzzling. The Master said: "Suppose you, Zhengyan, were appointed as a Commissioner of Transport (Zaoshi).
Wherever you reside, you would immediately occupy that position. Would you still harbor doubts about this? The King said: "I would not doubt it. The Master said: "Furthermore..."

"What doubt is there? At these words, the King attained realization. When the Master was approaching his passing, he presented this verse: "When speaking, there are seven perversions and eight inversions;
When silent, two fall away and three fall away. To report to the Chan travelers of the Five Lakes: The Mind-King is sovereign—cease your inquiry. His cremation yielded relics of five colors.
Later, those who passed by his site obtained them in great abundance. He was enshrined in a stupa at Huìtáng.
To the north of the Master’s chamber was Chan Master Huanglong Lingyuan Weiqing of Longxing Prefecture, a native of the Chen family of that same prefecture.
Having had his mind sealed by Huaitang, he would often say to people: "The reason students of today have not yet escaped birth and death—where does their illness lie? Their illness lies..."
The thieving mind has not yet died; however, this is not the fault of the student, but the fault of the teacher. It is like Emperor Gaozu of Han, who deceived and killed Han Xin.
Although Xin was dead, was his mind truly dead? As for the students of antiquity, they attained liberation from birth and death beneath a single word.
Where is the proof of this? It lies in the fact that the thieving mind has already died. Yet, this is not something the student can achieve by themselves; it is truly [the work of the teacher].
For one who acts as a teacher, the tongs and hammer must be subtle and precise. It was like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty when he saw Hou Jing from the Great Hall;
without shifting his voice or expression, the heart of Jing was already withered and drained of all remainder. What is taught by various quarters is not without its beauty.

In short, it is like Zhao Chang’s painting of flowers: though the flowers are lifelike, they are not real flowers. When he ascended the hall and the drum sound had just begun to vibrate, the great assembly gathered like clouds;
infinite celestial mechanisms were revealed all at once. To not fail the true eye, one should have returned to the hall immediately;
to wait for further elaborate words would only bury the essential principle. Even if one were to say that Śākyamuni did not appear in this world, [his forty-nine years...]
Nian said: "Dharma did not come from the West; Shaolin possesses a wondrous secret. Master Xiu was like one gazing ten thousand *li* toward his hometown. He also said:
"If a person recognizes the Patriarchs and Buddhas, they transcend at that very spot. Even if one attains such an intimate realization and entry, there is still another path for turning around.
"Pass the test, then strike! [With this, he] struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended.

Taking his seat, he ascended the hall and said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Through the eternal night, in this clear evening, who else is there? Mist, dew, clouds, and mists cannot obscure it.
Within this very state, one still says, 'It would be better to return. But to what does one return? The lotus leaf is round and round, as perfect as a mirror."
The water chestnuts are sharp as awls. Entering the hall: The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is grace for which no heavy requital exists;
the cats and white oxen, however, know that merit is never bestowed in vain. They clarify the great function and understand the complete mechanism, leaving no trace behind.
Inconceivable! It is best to go back; no one knows. Piercing through the azure void, a thousand-foot pine; cutting off the red dust, a single stream of water.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will see clearly and brightly.
The Patriarch speaking thus blinds the eyes of all people in the world—those who recognize right from wrong and distinguish the black from the white.
How can a patch-robed monk discern the truth upon reaching this point? "If one has not yet reached the place where the water ends, it is difficult to understand sitting and watching the clouds arise.
Chan Master Shànqīng of Cǎotáng at Lètán in Lóngxīng Prefecture was a native of the Hé family in Nánxióng Prefecture. Initially, he visited Dà...
Chan Master Shouzhe of Guiyang attained nothing for some time. Later, he visited Huanglong, who showed him the "wind and banner" koan. For a long while, he failed to reach a realization.
One day, Huanglong asked, "How do you understand the 'wind and banner' koan? The Master replied, "I have no way of entry; I beg the Master for a skillful means.
Huanglong said, "Have you seen a cat catching a mouse? Its eyes do not blink, and its four paws are planted firmly on the ground."
The faculties are directed toward their objects; from beginning to end, they are straight, so that where there is no aiming, there is no missing the mark.

If you, my son, can truly act thus—without other conditions in the mind, the six sense-faculties will naturally become still. If you investigate in silence, it is ten thousand to one that you shall not miss a single thing.

From then on, the Master withdrew from worldly distractions. After more than a year, he attained sudden and clear realization. He addressed Long with this verse: "Following, following, following. In the past, in the past, in the past. Following, following."
Thereafter, no one recognized him. At night, the bright moon rose over the high peak. It was originally just this very thief. Longling took hold of him and further told him:
"Attaining the Way is not difficult; propagating the Way is difficult. Propagating the Way depends on oneself; teaching the Dharma for others is difficult.
Once you have attained clarity, it lies in your diligent practice. Generally speaking, when a master teaches the Dharma, a single phrase—

Within this [teaching] are contained the Three Mysteries; within each Mystery are contained the Three Essentials. When the disciple enters the place of reality, he attains the seat and puts on the robe.

Looking back from there, he proceeds naturally with the seven openings and eight thoroughfares unobstructed. The Master remained in attendance for another seven years before taking his leave to travel extensively through the monastic communities.
Later, he appeared in the world at Huanglong and passed away at Letan. A monk asked: "Before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch..."
"How is it? The Master said, "Three in the capital, four in Bian. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after seeing it? The Master said, "Ash on the head, dust on the face.

[The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "A scene of utter embarrassment. He ascended the hall for the opening of the teaching session. He raised the case of Master Fushan Yuan, who said:
"If you wish to obtain an outstanding talent, you must still have the four matters fully prepared; only then will the path of the ancestral teacher be revealed. What are they?"
Furthermore: first, one must possess the patriarchs' true nose; second, one must have the adamantine eyes; third, one must have the claws and fangs of a lion;

fourth, one must obtain the monk’s staff of killing and giving life. Only when these four things are attained can one act with sovereign ease, manifesting transformations at will, rolling up or unfolding as circumstances demand, towering above devas and humans, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. If it is not so, then those who "preserve the good path until death" are but defeated soldiers.

This is the omen. Why? Striking a stone man with a staff values the reality of things. Therefore, arriving here, one attains a state where the Yangtze River flows brilliantly and the vast plains hold gathered clouds;
green bamboos embrace the mist, and the green mountains lock in their azure hues. Wind and clouds are of one essence; water and moon are viewed as equal.
A single phrase encompasses all—this has already been revealed by this decaying old man. The Master said: "Today, Huanglong has appeared in the world. At that time...

In these final ages, when the Buddha-dharma has become diluted and corrupt, there is no use for the patriarchs’ essential core, no use for the adamantine eye, no use for the lion’s claws and fangs, and no use for the staff that kills and gives life. There is only this single fly-whisk used as a path;

it can manifest in all manner of transformations at will, rolling up and unfolding according to its natural course, and it can tower high above gods and men, standing like a cliff ten thousand feet tall.

At times, when encountering the strong, one becomes weak; at times, when meeting the noble, one becomes lowly. When lifted up, the hosts of demons vanish and the Buddhas and Patriarchs hide their tracks.
When set down, it blends with water and mud, such that the holy and the ordinary share the same path. Now tell me: is it better to lift it up? Or is it better to set it down?
"Let it go—how good! The line on the tip of the pole is for you to handle as you please; without disturbing the clear waves, your intent is naturally distinct.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Form and mind are not different; self and other are without distinction. He raised his whisk and said:
"If you call this a whisk, you will enter hell like an arrow. If you do not call it a whisk, you have eyes but are as if blind. Even if you manage to escape both extremes, it is still black."
A cow lies dead in the water.
Chan Master Qingyuan Weixin of Jizhou ascended the hall and said:
"When I was thirty years ago, before I had studied Chan, I saw mountains as mountains and saw waters as waters. Later, when I personally met a teacher and attained a point of entry..."
Seeing mountains as not mountains; seeing water as not water. Now, having attained a place of rest, one sees mountains as simply mountains again, and sees water as simply water.
O Great Assembly, are these three kinds of understanding the same or different?
If there is someone, whether monastic or lay, who can discern this, I grant that you have personally seen the old monk.
Chan Master Xiaochun of Lingquan Monastery in Jia Mountain, Liuzhou, once had a creature carved from wood with the head of a lion, the hooves of an ox, and the body of a horse.
Every time he ascended the hall, he would hold it up and show it to the assembly, saying: "If you call this a lion, it is also..."
A horse’s body; it is called a horse’s body. Yet it has ox feet. Tell me, ultimately what would you call it?
[The Master] had the monk offer a response, but none were in accord. The Master then presented this verse: “A lion’s head, majestic and proud; Ox feet and a horse’s body.”

The three paths are as if they could be entered; the profound gates open one after another. [Ascending the hall: There is a man who, since the vast kalpas of antiquity, has neither dwelling nor reliance.
Above, there is not a single tile to cover his head; below, there is not an inch of earth for him to stand upon.
Tell me, throughout the twelve hours of the day, where does he establish his body and maintain his life? If you can know this, then morning you go to the Western Heaven, and evening you return.
In the eastern lands, there was Chan Master Jichang of Sansheng in Hanzhou, a native of the Li family of Pengzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "The wooden Buddha does not pass through fire;
before the Terrace of Ambrosia, he meets Bodhidharma. Regrettably, the people of Luoyang have not yet arrived; for nine years he sat facing the wall in empty stillness."
Sitting. A golden Buddha does not pass through the incense burner. Sitting, he sighs over the toil of life as one rushes along the path.

Had he not looked at the painting on Mount Hua, how would he have known Pan Lang riding backward on his donkey? A clay Buddha does not cross water. A single ray of numinous light illuminates heaven and earth.
One can admire the old, ancient master Xuan Sha; he did not want the South Mountain, he wanted the turtle-nosed snake. Entering the hall, he raised the case of Zhaozhou visiting the two...

He then raised his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? Even if you recognize it, as before, it is still not it. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
A monk asked Chan Master Xiaozhin of Guishan Shuilu Monastery in Sizhou, “What is a guest among guests?
The Master said, “Chao Fu feeding his ox. The monk asked, “What is a host among guests? The Master said, “Xu You washing his ears.
The monk asked, “What is a guest among hosts? The Master gave a shout. The monk asked, “What is a host among hosts? The Master said, “Having finished prostrating.”

[The Master] withdrew. He ascended the hall and said: "The ground is secure and firm, yet transgressions fill the heavens. Clearly, one lifts the foot; yet there is no manifesting of spiritual powers or playful mastery.
To wound oneself where there is no wound, one specifically cannot set the foot down. Tell me, where does the fault lie?

Let those who possess the eye of a seeker of the Way come forth and discuss this together. If you wish to see the mountain of your own true nature, do not take the forked path. Do not... [the text ends].
They simply continue to nod their heads, letting the years slip by. At some future time, when the blow falls upon the crown of your head, do not say that I did not warn you.

At Huitang’s place where he raised his fist, [Dongshan] thoroughly realized the source. His wit and eloquence emerged with swift brilliance.

Chan Master Jingqi of Shuangfeng on Mount Wuyue in Tanzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said:

"Held crosswise or used upside down, throughout all quarters they stride like tigers and walk like dragons; beating dogs and propping up the gate, Shuangfeng remains cast within the armor of non-action.

Dharma. Where shall one seek the mind? If you wish to know the "phrase facing the sun" for protecting the nation, look at the grove of bamboo before the gate.

One day, when the assembly had just gathered, Zen Master Huanglong Zhiming of Ezhou ascended the hall and said, "I cannot allow you to continue opening your eyes and speaking dreams," and he immediately descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall again, he said: "A single secret of the north and south—cutting through nails and severing iron."
Be careful not to engage in intellectual deliberation; it will only turn into a habitual track. The Master, together with Inspector Hu, arrived at the Two Sages Temple in Gong’an.
Inspector Hu asked, “Dharma Bodhidharma told Emperor Wu of Liang that ‘it is vast and empty, there is no sage. Why is it that there are now two sages here in Gong’an?”
The Master said: "A single drop of ink forms two dragons.

When the ancients spoke thus, it was like looking at a leopard through a tube; one sees only a single spot. Even if one enters the forest, one does not stir."
Grass. Entering the water without stirring a wave; it is also like riding a horse across jagged ice.
If one were a master archer capable of shooting down a vulture, why not rub an itch on the head of a snake? Let those who possess the true eye try to discern this. After a long pause, he said:
"The embroidery of mandarin ducks originates from the golden needle."

The Grand Historian and Layman of Shanyu Valley, Huang Tingjian, styled Lüzhi, possessed the karmic predispositions of past practice in Prajñā; thus, despite holding high office, he remained detached.
Although he entered the Zen school, he had not yet found his direction and was fond of composing flowery verses. He once visited Chan Master Yuantong Xiu, who rebuked him, saying:
"A great man with such mastery of calligraphy—how can you willingly apply it to this? It was then that Xiu began to instruct him.
Regarding the matter of Li Bashi’s painting of horses, the Master (Dahui) rebuked him, saying, "Are you not placing me once again within the belly of a horse?

Xiu replied, "You stir up the lustful hearts of all people under heaven with your flowery words; it is not merely that they will end up in the belly of a horse—I fear they will actually be born in the *niraya* hells.
The Master was struck with awe and repented, apologizing profusely. Thereupon, he ceased his brushwork and devoted himself solely to the Way, composing the *Pranidhāna* (Vows).

The text states: He strictly observed the precepts against alcohol and sexual indulgence, taking only morning congee and midday meals. He went to rely upon Huìtáng, requesting that he be shown the direct and swift path.
Huìtáng said, "As for what Zhòngní said, 'Do you think the disciples think I am hiding something from them?
I hide nothing from you,' how would you, the Grand Historian, ordinarily explain this theory? When Wén was about to offer a reply, Huìtáng said, "Not so! Not so! Wén...

He remained in a state of confusion and distress for some time. One day, while attending Master Tang as they were walking in the mountains, it was the season when the rock-olibanum (mugichika) was in full bloom.

Master Tang asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the mugicha flowers? The official replied, "I do. Master Tang said, "Is there anything I have hidden from you? At this, the official was suddenly enlightened and immediately prostrated himself before him.
The Master said, "My teacher possesses such a compassionate and earnest heart. Xuedou laughed and said, "I only wish for you to reach home.
After some time, he went to visit Chan Master Xin of Yunyan at Sishi. Following the assembly, he entered the room for private instruction.
Upon seeing him, Xin opened his eyes wide and asked, "When Elder Xin dies and the Scholar dies, they will be burned into two heaps of ash. In what place will you meet them? The Master was speechless.

Xin Yuochu remarked, "What you have attained through your studies under Huitang has not yet reached its full realization. Later, while serving as an official in Qian-nan, his spiritual power grew even more profound.
Amidst a state of non-conceptualization, he suddenly clarified the meaning of the question posed by Sishi. He sent a letter in reply, saying:

"In years past, I was repeatedly exhorted by your persistent guidance, yet for a long time I remained as if in a drunken dream, with things appearing only vaguely within a realm of light and shadow. This was because my doubts had not been resolved."
My life-force was not yet severed; therefore, I merely retreated out of respect for the precipice.
While traveling on the road through Qian-nan during my exile, I woke from a nap and suddenly reflected: "How much have I been deceived by the old monks throughout the land?
Only the monk Siji refused to accept me, and that was truly the greatest act of kindness. This was nothing short of a thousandfold blessing. Later, he composed the inscription for Huītáng’s stupa.

The Inscription reads: "I, [Name], have long since received the transmission of the seal of enlightenment and am capable of upholding the Great Dharma. Yet, as my eye of the Way has not yet reached full perfection, I come now to gaze upon this stūpa.
Truly, I am moved by a profound sense of veneration and admiration; thus I carve these words upon this enduring stone to reverently praise his remaining virtues.

The Master further prepared an offering of simple greens and water lilies, sacrificing with a prose text and consoling him with a verse, which says: "The wind of the sea blows down Mount Laṅkā; The Chan of the four seas..."
Look directly with your eyes. A single tangle of willow filaments cannot be grasped; it is draped with mist upon the jade balustrade.
When Wenwang Shao, the lay practitioner Zichun, was serving as the Prefect of Hongzhou, he invited Huìtáng to inquire about the Way.
Having attained silent realization, he composed a verse on seizing the vital point, which says: "By day I forgot to eat, by night I forgot to sleep; I have taken up the pearl from the dragon's jaws."

Desiring to ascend to heaven, he instead casts everything down within his own body; the four corners collapse to the ground, yet it is perfectly round. He presented this to the Hall Master (Huitang), who deeply approved.
Layman Wu Xun, courtesy name Defu, resided at Huítáng. During a session for entering the room, Huitang said to him: "Throughout your life..."
"Your learning, understanding, memory, and extensive erudition are irrelevant. Before your parents were even born, bring me a single word.
As the official hesitated, the Abbot struck him with his whisk, whereupon he immediately grasped the profound meaning and presented three successive verses.

Beholding this, one cannot help but harbor doubts. From of old, there have been no masters and disciples; yet now, it is permitted that the Old Barbarian knows.

Chan Master Letan Yingqian of Longxing Prefecture was a native of the Peng family in Yuanzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "The numinous light shines through with penetrating clarity, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
Its essence reveals the true permanence, unbound by written words. The nature of mind is undefiled; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected."

"Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. When the ancients spoke thus, they did not realize it was a pitfall—a flesh-bound undershirt that cannot be removed nor passed through.

Only then can one utterly eradicate it. Nevertheless, even so, this is still an old crow in a cloth bag. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Chan Master Guangjian Kaixian Xingying of Mount Lu was a native of the Mao clan in Guizhou. A monk asked: "What is..."

The Master said, "White waves surround it on all four sides; from where could the red dust come? He ascended the hall and spoke of the profound and explained the mysterious.
"Exquisite! It is like a painted cake used to satisfy hunger; to enter the holy and transcend the mundane is much like a moth flying into a flame.

"All those previous views and understandings have been swept away. What is the one phrase by which you all may penetrate and be liberated? Liang [asked].
Jiur said: "The iron ox does not eat the grass by the fence; he goes straight to sleep atop the summit of Mount Sumeru.

"Bending the bow of Shigong, mounting the arrow of Xinghua, exerting the strength of Nārāyaṇa, and fixing the gaze of Śakra—yet he does not shoot the great tiger of Daxiong, nor the deer of Yaoshan, nor the lion of Yunyan. He did not shoot...
"An elephant’s bone and a monkey—tell me, what is it that he shoots? After a long silence, he said, "I let this one pass. Ascending the hall, he said: "Climbing a mountain, one must reach the summit;
entering the sea, one must reach the bottom. Studying the Way, one must reach the place where even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot speak.
If it is not like this, you are all merely spirits clinging to grass and trees, ghost-children who feed on the spittle of wild foxes."
When Huayan speaks thus, it is like a potent medicine; though it may be bitter to the taste, it is intended to cure the illness. A-ye, a-ye!
Chan Master Fajing (Dharma-Mirror) Ciyuan Kechian of Mount Lu was the son of the Chen family of Yanzhou.

A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "An inch nail and an ox’s strength. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go and study that which you do not understand."

Chan Master Xiangtian Fanqing of Shaoxing Prefecture was a native of Jiaxing. His secular surname was Qian. A monk asked, "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion employ so many hands and eyes?
The Master said, "The wealthy feel that even a thousand mouths are too few. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the True Eye?

The Master said, "When Zhang Gong drinks wine, Li Gong gets drunk. [The attendant] asked, "Is this because he yields to strength when encountering it, or is it the exercise of wondrous spiritual power?"
The Master said, "The Holy Monk in the hall understands this matter well. A monk asked, "Xiangtian possesses the sword for slaying dragons;
how would it be to borrow it for a look? The Master held his staff crosswise. The monk then shouted. The Master threw down the staff.
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "This dead shrimp! He ascended the hall and said: "Spring is already at its end; falling blossoms shower down like crimson rain."
Whether travelers from north and south return or not, thousands upon thousands of forests resound with the cries of the cuckoo.
I have no home—where shall I go? Among the lands of the ten directions, what can I rely upon? This old man has a true message: last night at the third watch, the moon was reflected in the pond.

[He ascended the hall. "The Buddha-dharma has reached this point; life is as precarious as a thread hanging from a string. To transcend one's lineage through a different eye is likewise difficult to inherit and uphold."
He held up his whisk and said: "Fortunately there is this very thing; it is fit for circulation.

If you can perceive it here, you will see that the Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel within the lanterns and the pillars. The sentient beings of the six realms hear the essentials of the Dharma within the Iron Ring Mountains.
Whether sound or non-sound, sight or non-sight, they follow accordingly; the four types of birth among diverse species each attain liberation."
"Deliverance! To proclaim such a thing is not only to bury the ancestral style, but it is also to sink oneself into oblivion.

At Hōshin Shōtokuin in Tokyo was Zen Master Raibutsu Kaishin, a native of the Chen family from Xinghua Prefecture. He first visited Zen Master Nanyuan of Huanglong.
Huanglong asked him, "Have you come for the sake of human affairs, or have you come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma? The Master replied, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
Huanglong said, "If you have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, I shall entrust it to you right now," and he struck him with his whisk.
The Master said, "Even a monk must not trouble others. Long immediately took this to heart. Later, he followed Zhaojue and deeply awakened to the profound mysteries.

He ascended the hall and said: "In the Buddha-world, even a single speck of dust or a single hair performs the work of a Buddha, causing those who perceive a single dharma to be fully endowed with all dharmas.
Therefore, it is provisionally called a 'pallet' (a temporary structure). Within the transformative realm of the Buddha, words are forgotten."
Silent stillness constitutes a great Buddhist service (*buddhakārya*). It causes those who study it to depart from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*); this is precisely what is called "the Buddhas.

Therefore, [this land] favors the three types of fire and the bamboo shoots. In certain Buddha-fields, yellow flowers and green bamboos constitute the Buddhist service, causing those who behold these marks to see that form is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
thus, they are entrusted to Maitreya. In certain precious Buddha-lands, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) serves as the service.
Sitting, he manifests Buddha-activities. This assists practitioners so that they do not seek the Buddha externally.

Thus, having thoroughly investigated and penetrated this, there is a Buddha-field where Buddha-activities are accomplished through offerings of the four requisites, causing those who know contentment to sever divergent thoughts;
therefore, it may be transmitted to those of lower capacity. There is a wondrous realm of the Buddha where Buddha-activities are performed through the samādhi of all speech, enabling—
One who enters spontaneously does not abandon movement or stillness; thus, they serve as a conduit to carry the great assembly. Now tell me:
within this, is there any distinction of superior or inferior? After a long silence, he said: "Those who arrive must know this to be the work of a master. *Chan*.
A monk asked Chan Master Kechang of Huili Monastery in Linjiang Commandery, "I do not ask about the power of the Buddha or the power of the Dharma;
what is the power of wisdom? The Master said, "To kick over the mountain of self and others, and to raise up the Bodhi tree.

The monk said, "Since Bodhi is fundamentally no tree, where does one apply effort? The Master said, "Where there is no place to apply effort, that is precisely where one should exert effort. The monk said, "Now..."
Today I have heard what I had not heard before. The Master said: "Do not mistake pure gold for brass. He ascended the hall and said:

"The source of the Buddha-dharma cannot be realized and entered through anything other than right faith and wondrous wisdom. The pivotal gate of the Patriarchs cannot be opened by anything other than great compassion and profound vows.
When one possesses both faith and wisdom, the provisional and the real are practiced together, like gold remaining within its ore. When one fully possesses compassion and vows, [one’s goodness...]"
Evil can be discerned; it is like the moon emerging from the clouds. "Great assembly, consider this: when your parents had not yet been born, where could all these many metaphors have been expressed?
After a long silence, he said: "Nine out of ten words may hit the mark, yet they are not equal to a single moment of silence."
Chan Master Desong of Qizhen Monastery on Mount Bazhi in Huangzhou ascended the hall and said: "Heaven and earth are but one finger—there is no heart of contention.
The myriad things are but one horse—there is no discourse of right and wrong. Thus, the Māras hide their traces and the Buddhas and Patriarchs flourish.
Hanshan claps his hands in joy; Shide laughs out loud. O assembly, these two ancient sages laugh!"
"What is this? After a long silence, he laughed heartily and said, "A single *tánhuā* flower meets spring once again.
Chan Master Shao Ci of Wanshan Monastery on Mount Lu was a native of the Zhao clan from Guizhou. He studied under Chan Master Zhaojue.
Shao Ci asked, "Aside from the golden robe bestowed by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted? Zhaojue raised his whisk. The Master said, "In the end, what is it?"
Jue struck him across the mouth with his whisk. As the Master prepared to open his mouth, Jue struck him again.

At this, the Master attained realization; he then seized the whisk and prostrated himself. Jue said, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself? The Master replied, "The whisk now belongs to me.
Jue said, "A veteran general of thirty years has today been defeated by a mere recruit. From then on, [he was known as] Baizhang.

This profound style of teaching flourished greatly; he was esteemed as the preeminent leader of Donglin. When ascending the hall, [he taught that] "the initial step has not yet reached its goal," like Mount Sumeru standing amidst a vast river;
"the final step goes too far," like a fierce warrior loosing a wild arrow. Sometimes high, sometimes low, there is no fixed standard.
Because of this, what is affirmed is subsequently negated, leading him to be scrutinized by others. Tell me, how can one attain resonance? Truly.
Jiur said: "In the flames of the red furnace, more fire is added; the blazing vajra-eye opens of itself. *Duḥ*! Entering the hall: My ancestors possessed the supreme, distinct function;
their纵横 (zōnghéng) [transverse and vertical] life-giving and death-dealing is free from suspicion. Although they have blocked the path of the foxes,"
"One who returns a thrown ball must be a lion cub. Is there anyone among this assembly with golden fur blazing and fangs and claws fierce?
Try to let out a single roar! After a long silence, he said: "Even if you were such a one, you could not escape the hook and the snare of Master Liáo of Yùxī. *Cán* (Enter)."
A monk asked Chan Master Daobian of Nanyue Hengyue Temple, "Setting aside for a moment the raising of the mallet and the brandishing of the whisk, how does the Master act for the sake of others?
The Master said, "When a guest arrives, one must receive them. The monk said, "Is this not the very point of acting for others?
The Master said, "Coarse tea and plain rice. The monk bowed. The Master said, "You must know its flavor before you have attained it."
In the lineage of Chan Master Zhizhuan of Mount He, Ganlu, in Jizhou, a monk asked: "This is a single-stringed lute; I ask the Master to play a melody.
The Master said, "This mountain monk is deaf. The monk said, "I have come to seek instruction. The Master said, "Begone! The monk said, "Where is your compassion?
The Master said, "There are eyes everywhere in all directions."
The Zen Master Yulu of Tokyo Hōshin Shōtoku-ji ascends the hall: "New Korea beats the drum; Great Song enters the hall.
The cypress tree in the courtyard poses its question; the lanterns and the pillars are in a flurry. The incense stand and the staff rise to perform a dance;
the sick Vimalakīrti still remains upon his bed. I know this old fellow well—do not be surprised by his disheveled illness. *Du!* (A shout)"
When the assembly had gathered, Master Kūi of Longquan on the Western Mountains of Lǒngxìng Prefecture ascended the hall and said:
"To disperse just as you are would be quite exquisite. Nevertheless, even this is already raising waves where there is no wind and driving a stake into empty space;

how much more so to drag in branches and extend vines, discoursing on the marvelous and discussing the profound? This is truly like gold dust acting as a film over the eyes, while the pearl remains within one's own garment."
"The dust upon the Dharma. Now tell me, who is it that brushes away the dust and removes the dross? [He] planted his staff and descended from the seat.
Chan Master Zhien of Doushuai in Nankang Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Languid and listless, dwelling in villages or in city wards;
sprawling and muddled—what is now and what is ancient? Do not value your own spiritual essence; cease speaking of Buddhas and patriarchs. [I] seize Śākyamuni by the nose!"
A hole! He has pulled off the ears of Avalokiteśvara. Let him roll his ball on the snowy peaks; let him not mind Heshan beating the drum.
If one is a monk of true substance, one will never sit and wait for a rabbit at a tree stump. *Chan*.
Chan Master Kangyuan of Xingfu Monastery in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "I, this mountain monk, have a secret method that I have never leaked in the past, nor shall I conceal today;
I shall explain it clearly for you. After a long silence, he said: "When it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot."
The Venerable Huìyuán was the son of Mr. Suānzǔ of Kānfēng. His family occupation had been farming since antiquity.

In his youth, he relied upon Déguāng of Jiànfú Monastery in the district as his teacher. By nature he was blunt and simple, yet he was diligent in the ancestral Way, sitting steadfastly without lying down.

After several years, he received full ordination and traveled to Mount Lú, arriving at Dōnglín, where he frequently inquired about his own spiritual progress. When his peers observed his appearance...
He was considered vulgar; his deportment was coarse and unconventional, so everyone mocked him. One day, while walking through the palace courtyard, he suddenly tripped and fell.

At that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse and had an attendant write it on the wall, saying: "This one blow! This one blow! Even ten thousand taels of gold would not have sufficed for this.
A hat upon my head, a bundle at my waist— I carry the clear breeze and the bright moon upon the tip of my staff. Thus it was.
Ri left Donglin, and the news spread to Zhi Zhaojue. Zhaojue was greatly delighted and said, "If a monk’s investigation is such as this, nothing could be better.
He had people track down Ri’s destination, but in the end, no one knew where he had gone. (The *Dahui Wuku* claims this was the speech of Zhengwu Yong, but that is incorrect.)

The Inner Secretary, Layman Dongpo Su Shi, style name Zizhan, while staying overnight at Donglin Temple, engaged in a discussion on the "discourse of the insentient" with Zhaojue and attained a realization.
At dawn, he offered this verse: "The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is surely the pure and serene body.
Last night, eighty-four thousand gāthās were born; How shall I explain them to others in days to come? Not long after, he arrived at...

In Jingnan, it was heard that Chan Master Yuquan Hao’s spiritual sharpness (jīfēng) was unassailable. The official intended to subdue him and, immediately dressing in humble attire, sought an audience with him.
Yuquan asked, “What is your honorable surname? The official replied, “My surname is Chéng. [Yuquan said,] “That is the scale used to weigh the elders of the world.”
Jianquan shouted, “Now tell me, how much does this one shout weigh? Gong had no reply, whereupon Jianquan paid him the highest respect.

Later, while passing through Mount Jin, there was someone who wished to have Gong’s portrait painted. Gong playfully inscribed it with these words: “The mind is like wood whose fire has long been extinguished;
The body is like an unmoored boat. If you ask about my life’s achievements: Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Qiongzhou.”
Chan Master Doushuai Congyue of Longxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Baofeng Wen; he was the son of the Xiong family of Ganzhou.

Initially, while serving as the head of the assembly at Daowu, he led several monks to visit Master Yun’gai Zhi. As Zhi spoke with him, he fully understood the depth of Congyue’s inner realization within fewer than a few sentences. Thereupon—

The verse says: "Once Lingyun saw it, he did not see it again; On every branch, red and white, no flowers cling.

Addressing the assembly, he cited the words of the Tathāgata from the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* to Ānanda: "You should smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If even one *xiu* of this incense were burned..."
Within forty *li* of Rājagṛha, people simultaneously smelled the fragrance. What do you think?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, or does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?

Ānanda, if this fragrance were to arise from your nose, then being designated as produced by the nose, it would have to emerge from the nose. Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be sandalwood within the nose?
Regarding "odor": you claim that you perceive odor when it enters through the nose. Yet, if the odor issues from within the nose, your statement that you "perceive" it is illogical.
If it were produced in space, then since the nature of space is eternal, the odor should be eternally present; why then rely on burning this dry wood in the incense burner?

If it were produced in the wood, then this material substance of the odor would become smoke due to the burning. If the nose perceives it, it ought to be enveloped by the scent of that smoke; yet the smoke rises [and does not reach the nose].
[The air] is empty. Since it has not yet traveled a great distance—being within only forty *li*—how is it that [the fragrance] is already perceived?

Therefore, one should know that the nose and the act of smelling, as well as the fragrance and the act of smelling, are both devoid of a fixed location; they are both illusory in nature. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor do they possess an inherent nature.
The Master said: "By entering this contemplation of the nose, one personally realizes the unborn (*anutpāda*). Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is the hearer?"

How is it? Is it heard by means of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), or is it heard by means of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), or is it heard by means of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)?

If it were heard by the ear-faculty, the ear-faculty lacks discernment and cognition, and therefore cannot hear. If it were heard by the ear-consciousness, the ear-consciousness lasts for only a single moment.
Therefore, it cannot distinguish [them] and should not hear [them]. If the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) were to hear, the mental consciousness likewise could not hear.

Having realized non-arising (*anutpāda*), it again accords with the original wondrousness. Ultimately, what kind of realm is this? After a long silence, he said:

He spreads the great cloud of compassion and widely opens the sun of wisdom. The teachings are divided into the Three Piṭakas, yet they directly point to the One Mind.

Sometimes he fully upholds the tradition, applying both the staff and the shout; sometimes he employs granting and taking away, establishing the roles of host and guest in alternation. At times he is like a Vajra pressing his sword, or a lion turning its body;

at times his illumination and function roar like thunder, or his spiritual pivot flashes like lightning. All these are nothing other than methods for cutting away delusion and error, opening up and expanding the mind.

Profound and subtle! Directly below, the fundamental principle is clarified; one arrives at the ground of reality. O worthy ones, only upon reaching this point may I allow you a single thread of the path with which to deliberate.
If it is otherwise, all is merely following a teacher to form intellectual interpretations—this is simply not the case.
Chan Master Zuquan of Daomiao in Tanzhou was a successor of Chan Master Daomiao Xiu. He was a native of the Wu clan of Fuzhou. A monk asked, "What is the house style of Daomiao?
The Master said, "The bamboo has joints above and below; the pine is green now and forever. The monk asked, "I do not understand what is consumed therein."
"What do you eat? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat the jade-grained rice of the Excellency; when thirsty, I drink the tea from before the Shen-yun Granary.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Way has no fixed disorder; the Dharma is free from seeing and knowing. When words and phrases coincide, there is no fixed definition at all.

From of old, there have been no overnight guests at the Dragon Gate; to this day, the Bird Path is cut off of all tracks. If you wish to understand the essential meaning within this, [it is like] in the midst of fire..."
The grasshopper swallows the large insect. *Duḥ!* [He] ascends the hall. Rain falls and the steps are damp; when the sun shines and it is dry, the water does not flow.
Bird nests are at the bottom of the vast ocean; fish leap from the tops of rocky mountains. Among the assembly there is much deliberation:
"The first two lines are words of plain reality; the latter two lines are talk beyond the ordinary. If you understand it thus, you see only the jagged rocks. No.
Seeing the jade scattered and fallen; if one sees the jade scattered and fallen, only then will one know the path is vast and expansive.
Heh! When a monk asked Chan Master Wenyuan of Nanyue Fuyan, "What is the Buddha? the Master spat directly in his face.
On the day Chan Master Yungong of Nantai at Mount Nanyue opened the hall for formal discourse, he ascended the seat and said: "Rarely encountered and difficult to meet—this is precisely the time.
Why say that Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya is not yet born? [He] took up his whisk and said:
'Right now, at this very moment, the Buddha-dharma is entirely upon the tip of this whisk. Letting go or holding fast is all determined by the occasion. He let go."
As the wind blows, the grass bows; even shards of tile and rubble give off luster. Shide and Hanshan nod their heads and clap their hands.
Held fast, there is no leakage of water; even refined gold loses its brilliance. Deshan and Linji swallow their breath and silence their voices.
At such a time, is it letting go? Is it holding fast? After a long pause, he said: "Look after five days."
Chan Master Chengdu Fu Zhaoguo Chunbai Shaojue, a successor of Chan Master Huangbo Sheng, ascended the hall and said: "When cold, one turns toward the fire; when hot, one fans oneself.
When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Thus, Zhaozhou’s cypress in front of the courtyard and Xiangyan’s ridge behind."
Pine trees: planted for no other purpose than to draw in the pure breeze. But tell me, what is the ultimate reality?
Jiazi and Yichou: gold in the sea. Bingyin and Dingmao: fire in the furnace.
Chan Master Daoying of Jianfu in Raozhou, a successor of Chan Master Kaiyuan Qi, was asked by a monk: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master said:
"A lapis lazuli vase holding flowers. The monk asked: "How was it after he appeared in the world? The Master said: "An agate bowl filled with fruit. The monk asked: "I do not yet understand..."
"Is today the same as before, Master, or is it different? The Master said, "He kicks over the jar; he drags down the bowl. Entering the hall for formal instruction, he said:
"Speaking from the standpoint of the Way, speech is not permitted, nor is silence permitted. Even if one were to forget both speech and silence, there would still be no connection [to the Way]."
Why is this? There is no path within the phrase; the meaning resides within the phrase. It is neither intention nor non-intention, and it is beyond the reach of calculation.
If one is struck directly on the crown of the head and the eyes suddenly open wide, there is indeed a sense of swift realization here.
If, however, one lowers the head and seeks it within the roots of intention, one will ultimately fail to grasp it. Thus one knows that all phenomena...

It has no root. Those who seek to exhaust it err; its single source leaves no trace. Those who seek to return are lost. Behold the radiance of the ancient Buddhas and the majestic bearing of the former masters:
each and every one was manifested from within the state of desirelessness and non-reliance. At times, they were solitary, lofty, and steeply transcendent.
Ultimately, it cannot be grasped. At times, it is harmoniously fused and blended together, such that nothing at all can be perceived.
It never fixes itself upon a single point, nor does it bind itself to two extremes. There is neither "is" nor "is not"; there is neither "wrong" nor "not wrong.
To gain is to gain nothing; to lose is to lose nothing. It has never been separated by even a hair’s breadth, nor has it ever shifted by even a thread’s width. It is luminously clear.

The ancient road does not belong to the subtle and mysterious. Brought forth face-to-face, it passes away in a mere flash. It does not abide in the position of correctness; how could it fall into the path of deviation?

It does not tread upon the Great Way; how could it hasten along a narrow track? Drifting and unshaken, where does it dwell, and what does it do? Turning back, nothing is encountered; looking around, there is no counterpart.
When one contemplates universally with a single thought, all is vast, empty, and still. This is the essential core of the teaching, [transmitted by] the thousand sages.
It is not transmitted; it is directly and thoroughly understood. One transcends at that very place. Thus, it is easy in the state of bare, unadorned clarity.
Yet, it is difficult in the state of vivid, distinct awareness. Without any clinging or defilement, one must simply strip away and eliminate [all obscurations].
If it is one's own fundamental portion, let go of hands and feet; there is nothing that does not come back when released. Each and every thing emits light and manifests auspicious omens;

each and every thing eliminates traces and severs footprints. In the functioning of the pivot, there is no lingering; in speech, there is nothing to be revealed. Thoroughly stirred to the bottom, it does not become turbid.
The entire body strikes it, yet it does not shatter. Tell me, after all, what is this? How can it be so penetratingly intelligent? How can it be so extraordinary?
How can it be so firm and certain? O virtuous ones! Do not seek to recognize its face; there is no need to assign it a name;
nor should you search for its location. Why? Because it has no location; it has no name; it...
It has no face. As soon as a single thought of seeking arises, even for as much as a speck of dust, one is already separated by ten or five lifetimes.
If you further attempt to manage it with discursive thought, you will only see increasing confusion and clutter. It is better to let it go for a long time, allowing it to be free and at ease.
When you wish to arise, it arises; when you wish to abide, it abides. This is both the natural and the non-natural; this is both suchness and the non-such.
Suchness is both profound stillness and not profound stillness; it is both decay and not decay. It has no attachment to birth and no fear of death;
it seeks no Buddha and fears no Māra. It does not meet with Bodhi, nor does it coexist with afflictions (*kleśa*). It accepts no dharma and rejects no dharma;
it neither exists nor does not exist, neither being apart from nor not apart from [phenomena]. If one can be thus, one attains liberation.
"Kāśyapa is Kāśyapa; Dharma is Dharma. What does this have to do with me?

To speak in such a manner—when subjected to scrutiny within the school of the patch-robed monks, even one wearing a coarse skirt and straw sandals cannot avoid getting his feet somewhat splattered in the mud and water.
How much less can you people say that 'this is a statement of plain reality' or 'this is a distinct teaching tradition'?"

This is the pivotal point; this is the root of the Way and its sensory objects. They are taught and practiced to one another like the passing of a secret word from house to house in a village of seven families. What connection is there? There is nothing to do; take care.
Lecturer Zunseng Youpeng of Quanzhou was the son of the Jiang family of that prefecture. At the age of seven, he passed the scriptural examination and received the tonsure.
He spent many years studying at various monastic academies and once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and other texts; scholars held him in high esteem.

However, he often harbored doubts regarding the path of direct pointing by the Patriarchs and thus frequently associated with Chan monks. One day, he went to visit Kaiyuan; before his foot had even crossed the threshold—
His mind was suddenly enlightened. Yuanchu then asked, "Master, what have you come for? The Master replied, "I do not dare to hold my ears in high esteem while treating my eyes with contempt.
Yuanchu said, "Though you are old and venerable, why must you be like this? The Master said, "He who considers himself self-sufficient does not grow.
Yuanchu said, "I shall not ask about your morning study of the *Avataṃsaka* and your night reading of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. But what is the single phrase for the present moment? The Master—
[The Master] said, "The sun is exactly at noon. Yuan said, "Idle talk—say something more. The Master said, "Throughout my life I have relied on loyalty and trust;
today I leave myself to the winds and waves. Although it is so, what connection is there between this and the Master saying such things?
One must have the new precept-holder’s straw sandals worn through. Yuan said, "I will let you pass for now. But if you suddenly encounter Bodhidharma..."
The questioner asked, "How would you say it? The Master then gave a shout. Yuan said, "This lecturer, today you have seen the old monk’s spirit charging toward the ox and the dipper.
The Master said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. Yuan clapped his hands and laughed loudly.
A monk asked Chan Master Shansui of Longwang Mountain in Tanzhou, a successor of Chan Master Weiyang Wei: "What is the realm of the Dragon King? The Master said, "The crystal palace.
The monk asked, "What is the Dragon King’s wish-fulfilling jewel? The Master said, "Within the topknot upon his head. The monk— [remained silent].
[The monk] prostrated. The Master said, "Do not say it is not as you wish.
A monk asked Chan Master Yongtai of Zhiyuan on Huangbo Mountain in Ruizhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Cast in iron. The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Do you understand? The monk prostrated. The Master said, "Why [do you hesitate]?"
It has always been thus.
Zen Master Huiri of Mount Lu ascended the hall and said: "There is no need to seek the mind; one must only cease [dualistic] views.
Although the Great Master of the Third Patriarch avoided the golden hook, he was unaware that he had already swallowed the red line. But Huiri is not like that.
There is no need to seek the Truth nor to cease all views; riding a cow backward, one enters the Buddha Hall. With a single blast of the herdsman’s flute, heaven and earth are vast and wide.
I bow my head to Gautama—the true Yellow-Faced One.
Chan Master Fayuan Ganshi’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Fada Baopian of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture, was a native of the Yu clan of Raoyou.

A monk asked, "Please, Master, speak of that place where there are no stages or ranks. The Master said, "A wax figure facing the fire. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "Thin."
At Chuchu, he first attained penetration.

Chan Master Yungai Zhi was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dafaru of Daochang Monastery in Anji Prefecture. He was the son of the Xu family of Quzhou. Having studied under Yungai, he attained enlightenment through the teachings of Fenyang.
The "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality" (Shi-zhi tong-zhen). It is commonly said that the Ten Wisdoms are identical with reality;
thus, the monastic communities refer to it as the "Ten Identicals. Both Shui-an and Yuanji followed this teaching. Yuanji once praised it, saying: "A face of raw iron is difficult to approach;
in an ordinary step, he moves heaven and earth. Playfully grasping the talk of the 'Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality,' he does not fail Huanglong."
The Legitimate Bone-Descendant. Entering the Hall: "When knowledge and views establish further knowing, this is the root of ignorance.
When knowledge and views are without seeing, this is nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could anything else be admitted within this? The Old Śākyamuni has laid himself down completely;
how shall his descendants of later generations continue the lineage? Do you wish to understand? The Way that penetrates the profound is not of the human world. Full.
Where can one seek the green mountains?
Chan Master Baoshou Zuile of Fuzhou was a native of Gutian. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas are not real; they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
Bodhisattvas possess wisdom, yet their vision of nature is not clear. White clouds have no intentionality; they scatter [the rain]."
It rains for the world; though the great earth has no sentient beings, it can cause all grasses and trees to grow. If you understand this, you still remain within the realm of conceptual cognition;
if you do not understand it, you fall into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). How can one be identical with reality by departing from these two paths?
The sea is so vast that the moon cannot be hidden; the mountains are so deep that they are exceptionally cold.
A monk asked Chan Master Huiming Jiekong of Shifosi in Xiangzhou, “What is the realm of the precious marks?
The Master said, “Carved out over three lifetimes. The monk asked, “Who is within that realm? The Master said, “One Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.”
Chan Master Guanghui Daga of Fuzhou, successor to Chan Master Wenzhu of Xuansha, ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha awakens through mindlessness; the mind becomes deluded because of the Buddha."
In the place where the Buddha-mind is pure, a wild monkey cries beyond the clouds.
One day, Chan Master Yongyuan of Sizhou in Pingjiang Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Jianlong, asked Jianlong: "When Linji was at Huangbo..."
Three times he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times he was struck. What was the intent? Before his words were even finished, he was struck with a whisk.
The Master suddenly realized the fundamental principle. On the day he opened the hall for teaching, a monk asked: "The fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds;
we pray that the Master will preach the Dharma. The Master said: "Having eyes but no ears, sitting by the fire in the sixth month. [The monk] said: "A single phrase cuts off the flow; ten thousand—"

The student’s mental activity suddenly ceased. The Master said, “When you do not listen properly, you call a bell a water jar. The student asked, “From morning attendance to evening requests, what kind of business have you accomplished?
The Master said, “I only want you to come to rest. The student said, “Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago.
The Master said, “Why is it that your nostrils are pierced by this staff? The student said, “To straighten the crooked.”
"Even so, what can be done? The Master said, "Let him first let out his breath. He ascended the hall and said: "One, two, three, four, five— A cricket swallows a tiger in the fire.
Six, seven, eight, nine, ten— An earthen ox stands upon waves in the water.
Day and night, the rain falls in torrents; A seamless iron hammer cannot be drenched. It cannot be drenched; those who cling to it are in haste. The hundred rivers surge and roar."
"Sumeru is towering high! The eight-armed Nātha comes crashing out, prostrating and praising it as something beyond reach. Heh!
[The Master] ascends the hall, holding his staff horizontally across his chest, looks at the assembly, and says: 'Today, we have met with a fall on level ground! Then he descends from the seat."

Chan Master Yuanzheng Chuandeng of Chengtian Yong’an Temple in Pingjiang Prefecture, a dharma heir of Chan Master Baoben Yuan, was the son of the Zheng family of Yanzhou. He ascended the hall and said:
"All beings among gods and humans receive this power of grace. Great assembly, suppose there were a person who said, 'I do not receive the Buddha’s grace.'"
The power of grace. It does not abide within the three realms; it does not belong to the five elements. The Patriarchs dare not define it, and the Buddhas of the past dare not assign it a name.
Tell me, who is this person? After a long silence, he said: "Leaning against the stone cliff, he burns his iron bowl."
A copper pitcher was hung upon a pine branch.
Chan Master Wen Yi of Qineng, Anhua, Tanzhou, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Longqing Xian, ascended the hall and said: "Picking up the flower and smiling was a vain exertion of effort. He stood.
"Snow reaching the waist is a labor spent in vain. How does it compare to Old Lu, who had no use for such things? Yet he transmitted the robe and bowl to stir up the true wind.
"Great assembly, tell me: which one is the robe and bowl transmitted by Old Lu? Is it that which could not be lifted at the head of Mount Dayu?
Do not mistakenly fixate on the zero point of the scale. [He strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and descends from the seat.]

Chan Master Weishuang of Kuangxiao Monastery in Ningguo Prefecture, a dharma heir of Chan Master Zongzong, ascended the hall and said: "Today is the first day of the sixth month; already half the year has passed.
I announce this to those who seek the mystery: recognize your mother’s birth-face! As for this mother’s birth-face—whether you realize it or not—the egret flies away."
Entering the azure waves, he shook out a ball of silver embroidery thread.
Zen Master Qitian, a successor of Zen Master Ying of Lestam, was asked by a monk: "I, a student, have come before you; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said:
"Did you just hear the sound of the drum? The monk replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "Give me back the head of this talk.
The monk bowed. The Master said, "This will leave people with doubt. He ascended the hall, let out a shout, and said, "The lion’s roar! Then he let out another shout and said:
The Elephant King let out a yawn and then gave a shout, saying, "A mad dog chasing a clod of earth. He gave another shout, saying, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its basket.
Then he said, "Of these four shouts, there is one shout capable of serving as a teacher for the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Let those monks with clear eyes try to discern it. If you cannot discern it, you are much like one who has lost their way in broad daylight. He then ascended the hall and, after a long silence, spoke.

His nature was tranquil and his disposition leisurely. He then let out a shout, saying, "The mind stirs and the spirit grows weary. He then looked to those on his left and right and said, "Guarding the truth, one’s will is fulfilled.

Picking up his staff, he said, "Following after things, the intention shifts. Suddenly calling to the assembly, he said, "If you do not find strange what is strange, the strangeness will dissolve of itself.
Leaning on his staff, he descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Yun of Huiming in Quanzhou, "Within the ocean of Prajñā, how do you act for the sake of others?
The Master said, "The clouds part; the Milky Way stretches far. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "Seeing blood at the tip of the staff.
Another asked, "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind on this long ago, yet until now he has not attained the wondrous. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Ugly and clumsy; it is unbearable."
Dharma successor of Chan Master Baoning Ji was Chan Master Wujie Jingtan of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture; he was a native of Jiahe. In his later years, he returned to Qiantang.
Fahui once ascended the hall and said: "Originally I lay among the white clouds in the deep mountains; by chance, I have come here to lodge this idle body.

Do not come to ask me about Chan or the Way; I am but a man who eats rice and defecates. In the summer of the Bingyin year of the Xiangshi era, he took leave of the court nobility to return and hand over the affairs of the monastery.
The fourfold assembly crowded around to watch him as he fanned himself for a long time, then wrote this verse: "This fellow..."
Coming and going, there is no seam or fissure. For fifty-six years he has established his reputation as a master.

Today he dies and meets King Yama; the Sword-Trees and Knife-Mountains strike fear into people. He then drew a circle and said, "Aha! Let the various quarters do as they please—drilling tortoises and beating tiles."
He passed away with his legs drawn up. After the cremation, his *śarīra* were like fine sleet. His disciples took the bones and returned to Mount Aśoka to erect a stupa.
Chan Master Jiexiang of Zhenru Temple in Taizhou, a native of the Lin family of Xinghua, ascended the hall and said: "At the break of dawn in early winter..."
The weather is cold; leaves fall and return to their roots, revealing the distant mountains. This is not the dharma of seeing, hearing, arising, and ceasing.
Do not look upon it as seeing or hearing.
—A Dharma Heir of Chan Master Wuzu Chang.
A monk asked Chan Master Chuching of Nanyuya Shousheng in Qizhou, "Where does a deceased monk go after his transformation?
The Master said, "The waters at Lingfeng are swift. The monk said, "In that case, he is not reborn? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!"

Zen Master Weigu of Baizhang in Ruizhou, successor to Zen Master Huanglong Su, ascended the hall. Once the assembly had gathered and settled, he held up his staff and showed it to the congregation, saying:
"Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.
*He struck once and immediately rose.* Chan Master Yuezhuzujian of Jiading Prefecture requested the Master’s essential words for the assembly. The Master said:

"When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the mind-seal alone. The Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi did not recognize a single character. Today, when those throughout the various quarters emerge into the world, their speech..."
The phrase is like a mountain; add further ropes to it. Then, striking the meditation seat, he said: "If you can realize it here, you are still of dull faculties.
If you have not yet done so, sleep as you please in the depths of the white clouds, but by all means avoid the howling of the cold monkeys in the middle of the night."
A monk asked Master Shi, the Abbot of Jingzhao Hermitage, a dharma successor of Chan Master Shilang Lin: "What is the master of this hermitage? The Master said:
"I have never granted permission from the beginning. When the monk hesitated, the Master said, "If you understand, then understand that which is original;

do not attempt to establish names or characters for it. As the monk prepared to open his mouth, the Master struck him out. In his quarters, the Master would constantly hold up his whisk to the assembly, saying:
"If you call this a whisk, it remains as before—not it. If you do not call it a whisk, you are particularly ignorant of it. So, what do you call it?"
"What are you doing? he asked. Because a monk requested further instruction, the Master replied with this verse: "I have a single fly-whisk;
in its use, there is no other contrivance. Sometimes it hangs from a pine branch, letting its head droop and its horn be revealed."
Chan Master Nian of Wanshou Monastery in Chenzhou, successor to Chan Master Huaguang Gong, was asked by a monk: "The peerless assembly of the Dragon Flower has commenced this morning;
I wonder, Venerable Maitreya, where does he currently reside? The Master replied, "At the head of the pork counter. The monk said, "If it is indeed Venerable Maitreya..."
"Why are you at the pork stall? The Master said, "If you are not one who plays in the tide, do not enter the surging waves.
[The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what about the matter? The Master said, "The barbarian does not tie his sash. On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall.
Coming and going are boundless; movement and stillness share a single source. It contains virtue yet returns to emptiness; it transcends selflessness and stands apart.
The sun of yesterday and the sun of today shine with no duality of light; the wind of yesterday and the wind of today blow with no duality of motion.
It rained yesterday; it rains today. The moisture provides no double wetting. Within this interval, one seeks the marks of coming and going, yet they cannot be found.
Why? When the minds of self and other arise, there is no trace at the place of their arising. When the mind of self is forgotten, there is no mark of extinction in that forgetting.
"Great assembly, if you can understand it here, you will share the same root as heaven and earth and be one body with the myriad things.
