If you have not yet attained clarity, I, this mountain monk, shall chant it out for you verse by verse. First Verse of the New Year: The ancient Buddha’s style emerges from here;
No need to labor further upward. Throughout kalpas, how has it ever been different from today? Second Verse of the New Year: Silence..."
"Desolate and cold, devoid of flavor. Zhaozhou calls out, 'Come, let us drink tea. Raising your eyebrows, you must have a sudden flash of insight.
On the third day of the New Year, he bowed his head and offered greetings to those assembled. "If you ask about the affairs within Mount Xiangshan, the stream of Lingyuan flows clear as indigo.
He then gave a shout and descended from the seat.

The layman Su Che, courtesy name Ziyou, was a descendant of Chan Master Shun of Shanglan. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, while serving as an official in Suiyang, he was demoted to the position of salt and liquor tax collector in Ruizhou.
At that time, Chan Master Shun of Shanglan in Hongzhou and his father, Wen’an...

The Master had a mutual affinity with him, so he went to visit him. They found great joy in their meeting. The Master consulted him regarding the Dharma of the Mind, and Shun showed him the karmic conditions of "pinching the nose.
Thereupon, he attained realization and presented a verse, saying: "In middle age I heard the Way and realized my former errors; By chance we have met, O Master Shun.
Pinching the nose, I directly entered upon the true countenance; Shaking my head, I will not accept any other tongs or hammers. Kū... [text fragment]
What business has the venerable Fǎpò Nà? White wine and green salt—who am I? With shame before the waning moon over the eastern eaves, I drink a cup of nectar as smooth as molasses.

The Dharma successor of Chan Master Huanglong Xin of the fourteenth generation under Nanyue, Chan Master Chaozong Huifang of He Mountain in Jizhou, ascended the hall and, raising his whisk, said: "Look! Look! It is just this."
This "One" (ge): in Linji, it is the simultaneous operation of illumination and function; in Yunmen, it is the complete presence of principle and phenomenon;
in Caodong, it is the mutual penetration of the partial and the correct; in Guishan, it is the dark mechanism’s perfect union; and in Fayan, how could it be merely "mind-only"?
Nevertheless, while each of these five houses has its own distinct pedagogical arrangements and institutional methods, even if one were able to discern them with such extraordinary clarity—
"Clarifying departure" is still merely a matter of shadows and light. If you wish to resist and overcome birth and death, there is a vast difference between them, as wide as heaven and earth.
Furthermore, how would you express the single phrase "transcending birth and death"? After a long silence, he said: "I have nearly provided a mistaken footnote."
Chan Master Chongjue Kong of Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Gushu. He ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates.
Pure and naked, bright and clear—there is nothing to grasp. He then raised his whisk and said:
"The old fellow Guǎngxī, at the crossroads of the street, flaunted his elegance and peddled his cleverness, saying, 'I know how to string pearls; I know how to string pearls...'"
Jade tablets, tangled silk from the Huai River, rolls of fine silk—prostitutes’ dens and wine shops, commoners and servants gathered like broken tiles.

In tiger dens and demon palaces, Nanda and Kumbhakarṇa display their fury; yet when they encounter King Wen, they promote ritual and music, while meeting Jie and Zhou, they brandish spears and shields.
Today, having been spotted by Chongjue, they are left utterly humiliated. The Master composed a verse on the "Wild Fox" story, saying: "Spitting blood at others first soils one’s own mouth."
Mouth. Baizhang’s Wild Fox lost his head and ran madly; suddenly called back, he performed a somersault.
Chan Master Zu Xiū of Shàngfēng in Tánzhōu, a native of the Hé family of Chángdè Prefecture, ascended the hall and said:
"Before the cliff of the withered tree, the night-blooming flower opens; the iron ox still lies in the misty sands. I bring forth once more the shadow of the whip. He struck the whisk.
He said, "A single thought of turning back the mind brings one home. He then gave a shout and descended from his seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Jixing Huiquan of Jiuding in Jiading Prefecture, "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sutra;

when the mind awakens, it turns the Lotus Sutra. I do not know what the meaning of this is. The Master said, "The wind is warm and the birds' songs shatter; the sun is high and the flower shadows dance."
[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "In the past, Yunmen had three phrases:
the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth, the phrase that cuts off all streams, and the phrase that follows the waves. Today, Jiuding also has three phrases: the phrase 'when hungry, eat';
the phrase 'when cold, turn toward the fire'; and the phrase 'when weary, sleep. If we discuss this from the perspective of the Buddha-dharma, then Jiuding—"

"Facing Yunmen, standing directly downwind. If one discusses this according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then "facing Yunmen" and "standing directly downwind" are two contradictory statements.
Furthermore, what is the point of Nine Summits’ way of teaching people?

The Chan Master Xingkong Miaopu of Huating, Jiaxing Prefecture, was a native of Hanzhou. Having long relied upon Sīxīn (Sīxìn) and attained realization, he traveled to Xiushui, where he followed the legacy of Chuánzǐ (Fànzhōu).
He built a thatched hut in the wilds of Qīnglóng and amused himself by blowing an iron flute.
He composed many verses, which those who obtained them invariably treasured. One of his mountain retreat poems says: "When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, one is still separated..."
"Delusion! When the single dust of form is not two, what remains of other dusts? A hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more; who knows who is the person dwelling in the hermitage?
He further warned the assembly, saying: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city: by day one wards off the six thieves, and by night one remains wide awake."
The Commander-in-Chief of the Central Army can carry out his orders; without moving a blade of grass or a grain of dust, he brings about Great Peace. It is also said:

"Eating without plowing and wearing clothes without sericulture—tranquil and at leisure beyond the mundane world, one finds fulfillment in this sagely age. Yet, if you have not yet passed through the Master’s pivotal gate, you must still maintain your intent and act with practicality.
It is further said: "In the twelve hours of the day, do not let your work cease; pursue it to its depths until you reach the infinite."
"One must penetrate thoroughly to the bottomless depths; one must trample down the first peak of Mount Sumeru.
At the beginning of the Jianyan era, Xu Ming rebelled and passed through Wuzhen, carrying out a massacre. Many of the local people fled, but the Master alone went forth carrying his staff.

When the rebels saw his imposing and extraordinary appearance, they suspected he was a hidden spy and questioned him as to why he had come. The Master replied, "I am a Chan practitioner; I wish to go to Miyin Temple."
The bandits were enraged and intended to behead him. The Master said, "If a great man requires his head, cut it off at once;
why be angry? My death is certain. I only wish to have one meal as a parting offering. The bandits brought him meat and rice.
After the Master had finished his usual midday meal, he said, "Who shall compose a literary inscription for my sacrifice? The bandits laughed and did not answer. The Master then asked for a brush.
It is written in large characters: "Alas! That the spirit is made to toil through life is the fault of the Great Mass (the Earth).
That the spirit is extinguished by longevity is the error of Yin and Yang. That the spirit is deprived of wealth is due to the lack of rectitude in the Five Elements.

That the spirit is constrained by fate is due to the inauspiciousness of the time and day. Oh, how profound! How ultimate! Fortunately, there is the Way that transcends the mundane, which awakens my nature and its wondrous subtlety."
The mind—this wondrous mind—is what it neighbors with? Above, it accords with the true transformation of all Buddhas; below, it merges with the ignorance of ordinary beings.
Not a speck of dust moves; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. How wondrous! How wondrous! The sun and moon are not sufficient to be called luminous;
heaven and earth are not sufficient to be called great. It is vast and expansive, without obstruction or hindrance. Six.
For over ten years, he blended his light with the mundane world. At forty-two *lǎ*, he wandered at ease and in freedom.
He rejoiced upon meeting people, yet did not bow even before a Buddha. "How joyful! How joyful! Alas for this young man; his refined elegance was so radiant.
He returns home with composure, entrusting himself to the spring breeze; his body is like empty space, ultimately indestructible. *Shàngxiǎng*. Thereupon, he raised his chopsticks and ate heartily.
The bandits laughed aloud. After they had finished eating, he spoke again, saying, "Since we have encountered this era of calamity and chaos, I am a man of joyous spirit.
Now is precisely the time to act; let me cut you into two pieces with a single stroke! He then shouted, "Strike! Strike!

Just as the bandits were struck with awe and wonder, they bowed their heads in apology for their transgression and escorted him out under guard. Thus, the houses of Wuzhen were spared from burning; this was truly the Master’s kindness.

When both the clergy and the laity heard of this, their reverence for him increased all the more. A monk saw the Master seeing the Buddha but not bowing; he approached and asked, "Since you have seen the Buddha, why do you not bow?
The Master struck him with his palm and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master struck him again and said: [The text ends here].
"A household has no two masters. In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Xiangshi era, he constructed a large basin, pierced it with holes, and then plugged them.
He wrote a letter to Chan Master Chi of Xuedou, saying: "I shall undergo water burial. In the Renxu year, Chi arrived and saw that [Xingkong] was still alive.
He composed a verse to mock him, saying: "Alas, old Xingkong! You stubbornly wish to feed the fish and turtles. If you were to go, you would not have gone properly; you merely—"

[The Master] told Guan to tell others. The Master read the verse and said with a smile, "I shall wait for my elder brother to come and provide testimony. He ordered that this be announced throughout the fourfold assembly.
When the assembly had gathered, the Master expounded the essentials of the Dharma and further spoke a verse:

"To die while sitting or standing is not as good as water burial; First, it saves the need for firewood; second, it saves the digging of a grave. To cast off the hands and go forth—how unimpeded and refreshing! Who is the one who knows this sound? A boat."
Master Zi’s lofty style was difficult to emulate for a thousand years. Few could sing the single verse of the fisherman’s song.
He then sat cross-legged in a basin and drifted downstream with the tide. The assembly followed him all the way to the seashore, gazing until their eyes nearly failed them.

The Master took out the plug, bailed out the water, and returned; the crowd crowded around to watch, but the water had no place to enter. He then rode the current away once more, singing: "The boatman..."
He returned to his hometown in his later years; his traces vanished, and his wondrousness was immeasurable. His true spirit was universally entrusted to those who could appreciate it;

he played his iron flute crosswise as the finale of his performance. The sound of that flute was mournful. Shortly thereafter, amidst the vast expanse, he was seen throwing his flute into the air and vanishing.
The multitude mourned him with longing and worshipped his image. Three days later, he appeared on the sand, sitting in the lotus posture as if alive. Thus it was said.

The common people vied with one another to go and welcome him back. He remained for five days. When his body was cremated, the *śarīra* relics were as numerous as they could not be counted, each as large as a soybean.
Two cranes circled and hovered in the air; only when the fire was extinguished did they depart. The multitude took the *śarīra* relics and the sacred bones and erected a stupa at Qinglong.
Chan Master Daolong of Zhongshan in Yanzhou was the son of the Dong family of Tonglu. He received full ordination at Zhongshan Temple.

Wherever he traveled during his peregrinations, veteran monks alike held him in high esteem. In his later years, he arrived at Huanglong, where Sishi invited him to serve as the head of the assembly (*zuoyuan*).
Upon Sishi’s passing, he returned to seclusion at Zhongshan. Admiring the world-transcending character of the venerable elder Chen, he closed his quarters and withdrew from worldly affairs.
He would sell several skeins of thread each day for his own amusement, yet no one recognized him. He always wore a single sock on one hand.
Whenever a Zen practitioner arrived, he would hold it up and show it to them, saying, "I have worn this sock of mine for thirty years. A monk from a local temple asked him jokingly:
"What is the samādhi of non-contention? The Master then struck him with his palm.
The head seat Qi Mi of Yangzhou was a native of that very prefecture; Si Xin called him a "thorough practitioner.
Although various scholars repeatedly invited him to famous mountains, he would not go. Later, he manifested his passing at Gushan in Tan. His miraculous traces were numerous. His disciples...
I once had his portrait painted and requested a eulogy. I wrote for it: "This fellow has a head of ash and a face of dust; ordinarily he does not wish to reveal himself.
Now that he has been brought before people in this painting, it is much like piercing empty space with an arrow—how vexing! What a pity to have wasted three feet of human silk."
The Chan practitioner Zhītōng of the Empty Chamber was the daughter of Fàn Xūn, a Grand Marshal of the Imperial Secretariat.

From childhood she was intelligent and wise; as she grew up, she married Tí, the grandson of Chancellor Sū Sòng. Not long after, she grew weary of worldly phenomena and returned home to request ordination. Her father opposed this, so she instead practiced pure cultivation.

Upon studying the *Fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm), she suddenly attained realization and composed two successive verses to express her insight. The first says: Vast and boundless is the dust of the world...

The central essence is one suchness; vertically and horizontally, they interpenetrate and seal Vairocana. The entire wave is water, yet the wave is not the water; the entire water becomes waves, yet the water remains distinct.
It is further said: "Things and self are fundamentally non-different; the myriad phenomena are like reflections in a mirror. Clearly and brightly, they transcend the roles of principal and attendant;
perfectly and thoroughly, they penetrate the true void. A single body contains many dharmas, interlacing within the Indra’s Net; layer upon layer, there is no end."

At the point of exhaustion, both movement and stillness are entirely pervasive and unobstructed. Later, when his parents had both passed away, his elder brother Jian took up the post of magistrate of Fening, and Tong accompanied him.
Hearing that the reputation of Sijian (Sixin) was great, he went to visit him. Upon seeing him, Sijian recognized what Tong had attained and immediately asked:
"When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sold his heart and liver, whom did he teach to study Prajñā? Tong replied: "If you have no mind, I shall also cease. Furthermore—
Question: "When nourished by the same rain, why do roots and sprouts differ? Upon a ground where there is neither yin nor yang, what can possibly grow?

Tong said: "A single flower with five petals. He asked again: "Throughout the twelve hours of the day, where do you establish yourself and find your livelihood? Tong said: [A single flower with five petals.]
"Preceptor, you had better save your eyebrows," Xuefeng said. Yunmen struck him, saying, "This woman is creating disorder out of sequence.
He then bowed in greeting, and Xuefeng approved. Thereupon, his reputation for the Way became widespread. During the Zhenghe era, he resided in Jinling.

Once, while providing a communal bath at Baoning Monastery, he posted a notice on the gate that read: "If there is not a single thing, what is there to wash? If even a speck of dust exists, from where does it arise?"

"Where do you come from? You must first grasp a single phrase of the profound mystery before we can all enter the bath together. Guling only knew how to rub backs; the Bodhisattva had never yet clarified his mind.
When one wishes to realize the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, it is necessary for the entire body to break into a sweat.
Everyone says that water can wash away grime, but who knows that water itself is also dust? Even if the water and grime were suddenly removed, upon reaching this point, one must still—
After washing away [her defilements], she later became a nun named Weijiu. She hung up her staff at Xizhu in Gusu. Among the monastics and laypeople, many attained the Way through her teachings.
Suddenly, manifesting illness, she wrote a verse and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Her *Mingxin lu* (Record of Illuminating the Mind) circulated in the world.
Chan Master Focin Cai of Shangfeng on Mount Tan, a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Qing, was the son of the Yao family of Fuzhou.

Having received the tonsure and full ordination at a young age, he traveled to study under various masters until he reached Dazhong, where he relied upon Chan Master Haiyin Long. There he saw an elderly master named Dadao reading a scripture, which reached the following passage:

A single hair-tip lion appeared, and simultaneously, ten billion hair-tip lions manifested. The Master pointed at them and asked, "How does one hair-tip lion come to manifest ten billion hair-tip lions all at once?
Da replied, "You have only recently entered the forest; how could you possibly comprehend such a matter yet?
The Master was thus struck with doubt and subsequently resolved to take on the position of *jingtou* (sanitation officer). One night, he performed the sweeping and cleaning duties.

Next, when Yin arrived for the evening session, he encountered the closing of the assembly. Throwing down his staff, [the Master] said: "To realize it, one swallows the vast ocean at the tip of a hair;
only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust. At these words, Yin attained a sudden awakening.

Upon leaving Fuzhou, he traveled to Mount Huanglong in Yuzhang, but his mental resonance did not accord with Siji. He then went to study under Lingyuan; every time he entered the inner room for instruction, he would emerge weeping. From himself...
Song said, "I see this matter very clearly; it is simply that when the moment arrives, I cannot bring myself to speak it out. What can be done?
Lingyuan, knowing the Master’s diligent devotion, told him, "You must achieve a great penetration before you will attain mastery. Not long after, [the Master attained realization].

I observed that the monk at the neighboring station was reading the *Extensive Record of Caodong*. When he reached the passage where Yaoshan returns from gathering firewood and a monk asks, "Where have you come from?
Yaoshan replies, "I have come to gather firewood. The monk points to the knife at Yaoshan’s waist and says, "That clanging sound—what is it?
Yaoshan draws the knife and makes a gesture of striking. The Master suddenly felt great joy; he slapped the monk at the neighboring station once, pulled back the curtain, and hurried away.
He emerged and, with a piercing voice, spoke this verse: "Penetrating! Penetrating! The great ocean dries up; empty space splits asunder.

In the four directions and eight points there is no obstruction; the myriad phenomena all reveal themselves together. Later, he shared the seat at Zhencheng in response to the command of the Imperial Envoy.
He moved through several renowned monasteries, and while residing at Qianyuan, he ascended the hall to address the assembly, saying: "The hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi..."

Measuring the treasury of merit: this is letting go, like opening a military armory where weapons flash in chaotic brilliance. Holding fast: this is like snow covering reeds, such that one’s entire being cannot be discerned.
It causes those who see it to spring up and act immediately; it causes those who hear it to enter directly with a single blade.
Each individual possesses the true eye atop the head; every person hangs the efficacious talisman behind the elbow. This sweeps away the views of Buddhas and patriarchs.

I understand. This has brought calamity upon the monastic community. I recall that on the day Bao-shou opened the hall for his first sermon, San-sheng pushed forward a monk, whereupon Bao-shou struck him.
San-sheng then said, "If you act as a teacher in this manner, you will blind the people of the entire city of Zhenzhou."
For instance, today as I open the hall at Qiyuan, if there is a monk who steps forward, I shall strike him as well.
Not only will this story spread far and wide, but I also wish to open the eyes of the people of the entire city of Fuzhou. Why?
Because "The sword leaves its precious sheath because of injustice; the medicine comes from the golden jar to save the sick. [Ascending the hall: Before Bodhidharma came to this eastern land...
Everyone cherishes the pearl from the water of Maitreya; every single person embraces the raw jade of Mount Jing. This may be called standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
Yet, after the Second Patriarch performed his three prostrations, each one traveled south to seek out their companions and went north to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
"What a fine, great man! Perhaps there is one or half a person who seeks not after the sages and values not their own spiritual brilliance;

with a single horse and a solitary spear, they cast their blade into the void. This is truly a life lived with joy and fulfillment. Is there anyone like this today? 'Since now there is no returning, once one returns it is attained;
who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? [He] ascended the hall and said: "The proclamation of the Dharma-lineage is wondrous beyond words."
A single phrase is all-pervasive; heaven and earth are contained within its cover. It is like the central eye of Śiva, projecting vertically from his face;

it is also like three dots arranged in a circle, encompassing the Dharma-realm horizontally. Then, striking the meditation staff upright, he said: "If you can understand clearly beneath this very dot..."
"One's origins may still be changed; to cast off one’s entire being and accord with the Way should be difficult. Again, he struck the meditation staff and said:

"If you can realize it beneath the second dot, you will traverse back and forth beyond the three realms, with your body manifesting or concealing throughout the ten directions. Again, he struck the meditation staff and said:

"If you can realize it beneath the third dot, the fish and dragons will lock their doors and the Buddhas and Patriarchs will hide their traces. Otherwise, let this one move pass by, and act according to your lot."
There is the color of spring; on a single branch, three or four blossoms bloom. Entering the hall [the Master said]: "One Dharma has form that encompasses all moving and stationary things;
the hundred rivers rush and surge, competing to flow toward the sea. The Zhao-zither is not struck, and the clouds and sky are serene;

I imagine the old, sickly monk of Vaiśālī. When Vimalakīrti was ill, it was Shangfeng who was ill; when Shangfeng was ill, it was the staff that was ill; when the staff was ill, it was the myriad phenomena."
The myriad phenomena are ill; the entire array of the ten thousand phenomena is ill. Thus, both the ordinary and the sage are ill. Do you all perceive where the root of this illness arises?
If you do perceive it, then the sentient and the insentient are of one and the same substance, and every place is identical to the true Dharma-realm.
Should this not yet be so for you, then the sweet melon is sweet all the way to its stem, and the bitter gourd is bitter down to its roots.
Chan Master Tongzhao Hedefeng of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Hu family of Jing’an in the prefecture. At birth, he possessed thick eyebrows.
At the age of seventeen, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Jin of Shanglan and subsequently relied upon Linyuan, whereupon he immediately realized the profound meaning [of the teachings].
Once, while ascending the hall, he cited the story of Jia Shan’s "Realm" and said: "Fayan merely had these words; he did not realize that Jia..."
The old man of the mountains was so subtly pressed by this monk that he was left with no place to stand, neither before nor behind.
Even if one does not interpret this as a "boundary-phrase," one still remains halfway there.
Chan Master Yingduan of Falun Monastery in Tanzhou was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. In his youth, he relied upon Huayu’s Shanyue;

having shaved his head, he received full ordination. He visited Chan Master Zhenjing Wenyi, but their karmic affinity did not harmonize. Upon arriving at Yunju, he encountered Lingyuan, who shared the teaching seat with him.

He became highly agitated for the sake of the assembly and pressed the Master on the essential meaning. However, he prided himself on having entered the various sutras with subtlety; Yuan once severely rebuked him.
The Master then cited the pivotal dialogues of Mazu and Baizhang, as well as the fundamental tenets of the Avatamsaka Sutra, as evidence. Yuan laughed and said:

"Though Mazu and Baizhang were certainly mistaken, the fundamental tenets of the Avataṃsaka and this matter have no affinity at all," the Master said, filled with indignation and desiring to depart elsewhere.
He then requested leave to go. As he lifted the curtain, he suddenly attained great enlightenment; sweat poured down his back.
When Huayan saw this, he said, "This man now knows good from evil! Mazu, Baizhang, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra were nearly led astray by you!"
Consequently, his reputation spread in all directions, and eminent men vied with one another to entreat him to appear in the world, yet he declined them all.
Toward the end of the Zhenghe era, the Grand Preceptor Zhang Gongsheng urged Baizhang to insist that he establish the Dharma; having no choice, the Master finally complied.

Upon ascending the hall, he cited the story of the great kalpa-fire of the Sui dynasty and said: "The six realms of existence overturn and come crashing against my face; for a moment, I strip away..."
Hemp fibers mixed with dust; driven by the wind, the fire is but a trivial matter. It draws in travelers who refuse to turn back.

Whether ruined or not, whether following or not—this is merely using what one hears and sees to force a needle through a cone. The Three Hundred and Sixty Thousand Ponds of Lake Tai—the moon speaks from the heart of the waves;
to whom does it speak? A monk asked, "What is a guest among guests? The Master said, "Straw sandals and bamboo staff."

[The monk] went into the red dust [of the world]. He asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "Meeting the Patriarch at the crossroads. He asked, "What is the guest within the host?
The Master said, "The golden whip for the imperial horse mingles with the four classes of people. He asked, "What is the host within the host?
The Master said, "Who would dare to lift their eyes and look at the Golden Gate? He said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding guest and host; toward..."
"What further is the ultimate vehicle? The Master said: "Last night the frosty wind scraped the earth with its cold; an old ape cries atop the ridge under the waning moon.
Chan Master Shouzhuo Changling of Tianting in Dongjing, a native of the Zhuang family of Quanzhou, ascended the hall and said: "Three thousand..."
As for the swordsman, Zhuang Zhou alone was granted permission; why was he unable to leap out? At the gate of a skilled physician, there are many patients;

why does it not take but a single prescription to cure them? Those who have already penetrated the barrier, please examine this further with discernment. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "It is like the faculty of the eye."
Not seeing the eye for oneself, its nature is inherently equal; where there is no one to attain equality, one simply proceeds thus. A holeless iron hammer—let it rest for now.
It reaches the point where entering the forest does not stir the grass, and entering the water does not stir the waves;

this too is a provisional skillful means. If, however, the bamboo shoots within the fence emerge as bamboo sprouts outside the fence, and the flowers on the east side of the stream bloom red on the west side, then wait further still.
[The Master] examined him and struck him. A monk asked, "When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward's eyebrows and beard fall out?
The Master said, "A cat trying to climb a tree. [The monk] said, "Had I known it would be thus from the start, it would have been better not to be thus.
The Master said, "Save your eyebrows. A monk asked, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? The Master said, "Drought makes one worry for the people. A monk asked, "Before the Buddha..."
"How is it when he emerges from the world? The Master said, "Not a hair's breadth, not a speck of dust. "How is it after he has emerged?
The Master said, "Filling the ditches and blocking the ravines. "What is the difference between his emerging and his not emerging? The Master said, "When a person is level, they do not speak;

when water is level, it does not flow. He ascended the hall and said: "Leveling the high and conforming to the low invites thieves to ruin the house. Cutting through iron and severing nails—the fox still lingers in its den."
It is not like that at all. How should it be? Therefore it is said: "To let go completely at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff requires a man of such caliber.
As for the phrase regarding holding the alms bowl in the Land of Fragrant Accumulation—how do you speak of it? After a long silence, he said:

"One must strictly avoid letting the wind blow [it] into another tune. Ascending the hall, he said: "Śākyamuni’s closing his room in silence was an offense as vast as the heavens; Vimalakīrti’s refusal to speak..."
He was unable to save himself. How tragic, how tragic! His mouth was too small for his wisdom.

On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Xuanhua era, he suddenly manifested parinirvāṇa. On the day of his cremation, the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense.

Holding a golden platter, the messenger sought śarīra relics. Once the incense had been burned, something resonated sharply within the platter. Upon inspection, there were several five-colored grains, each as large as a bean.
The messenger returned with it, and when the Emperor saw it, he was greatly pleased.
On New Year’s Day, Chan Master Jing of Boshan Wuyin in Xinzhou ascended the hall and said: "Harmonious breath arises from withered stumps;

cold clouds disperse across the distant outskirts. The wooden man divines auspicious signs; at midnight, the hexagrams of the tortoise shell are revealed. All you venerable Chan practitioners, the hexagrams of the tortoise shell have been revealed."
The patterns are already manifest; one sees the twelve months of the year, each month being thus;
the twelve hours of the day, each hour being the same. Reaching this point, it is truly like the yellow of gold and the white of jade;
from the beginning of vast kalpas, it has never been a different color. Do you see it? If not yet, then for now follow Zhang San’s three passages.
Regarding the sequence of seasons, let us follow the teaching that Li Si’s hair has turned white and gray.
Baizhang of Lixing Prefecture was originally from Xinghua; he was a disciple of Master Qiseng. He ascended the hall and said:

"When Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the Han and Bodhidharma came to the Liang, the tracks were already established. Yet the descendants of later generations open their eyes and lose their way. If one is truly alert..."
In the end, one never picks flowers from the sky or grasps the moon in the waves; such efforts are merely a waste of physical and mental energy—what is the ultimate point?
Today, this mountain monk has already raised a pile of bones upon level ground. As you all walk along, each of you must look with full alertness.
Chan Master Tanqing of Guangxiao Monastery in Shaoyang State ascended the hall and said: "To kill one's father and mother, one repents before the Buddha;
to kill the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, repentance does not suffice. Why does it not suffice? Because it allows the karmic debtors to attain liberation."
Chan Master Guangxiao Dezhou was the son of the Qu family of Xinzhou. He received the tonsure at Zunseng Monastery in Jingde.

Having pursued the Way for many years, he later went to Huanglong, where upon hearing the teaching regarding the wall-gazing of Shaolin, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed two verses to present to him, which Huanglong approved.
From then on, his reputation spread throughout Jiangzhe. He ascended the hall and said: "The entire body is manifest and majestic; ten..."
Just as it is, there is no obstruction; a thousand sages cannot transmit it, and ten thousand spirits wear it upon their crowns.
If you wish to deliberate upon it together, the moment you open your mouth, it shatters into a hundred pieces. But how is it before the mouth has even opened? *Pah!* [He] ascends the hall and says:
"Mutual accommodation or non-accommodation—look and there is nothing to be seen. Having penetrated the barrier of the Patriarchs, one tramples the path of humans and devas. A-he-he!"
Whether one awakens or does not awaken—where do the falling flowers and flowing waters go?
The Layman Dai Daochun, whose courtesy name was Fuzhong and who served as a Temple Administrator, sought instruction from Lingyuan. One day he attained realization and presented this verse:
"At the bottom of the profound and dark source, where the total function resides, A single petal of the mind-flower reveals its imprinted patterns. I know how many lifetimes it has taken..."
He had previously made offerings [to past Buddhas]. From time to time, he would smile, causing clouds of fragrance to stir.
Chan Master Tang Daozhen of Huanglong Mountain in Longxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Letan Qing; he was the son of Zhao of Jinling. In his youth, he relied upon Jueyin.
Master Ying was a youth. When Ying moved to Puzhao Temple in Si, it happened that the Imperial Consort was selecting youths for ordination;

the Master thus received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). After some time, he took his leave to visit Chan Master Danxia Chun. One day, while discussing the fundamental tenets of the Dongshan school, the Master presented this verse:
"White clouds deeply shroud the ancient, cold crags; Strange herbs and numinous flowers are carried by the resplendent phoenix. At night..."

Half a day later, when it was noon the following day, he was riding a cow with his back turned and wearing boots and robes. Ch’un (Dongshan Liangjie) esteemed him; the Master himself felt this was an obstacle and abandoned him to rely on Cao Tang (Yaoshan).
Upon seeing him once, they reached a mutual accord. Every day he would take out the Tripitaka to read it. One night, hearing the drum for the evening sermon, he stepped out from the sutra hall;
looking up, he saw the moon and attained great enlightenment. He hurried to the abbot’s quarters, where Cao Tang saw him from afar and immediately—
To certify this, he first resided at Caoshan, and subsequently moved to Guangshou and Huanglong. He ascended the hall and said: "I cite an ancient precedent to ask you, *ācārya*.
You must not interpret it as something of the past; if you interpret it as something of the past, you lose the eye right before your face.
I cite a present-day precedent to ask you, *ācārya*. You must not interpret it as something of the present; if you interpret it as something of the present..."

"Meeting [the situation], it obstructs the *ācārya*’s original eye. Even if one does not lose it and does not obstruct it—being neither ancient nor modern—it is still merely a teaching of medicine and disease treating one another, a story told to stop a child’s crying. As for that single phrase of transcendent liberation, can you say it, *ācārya*, or not?
If you cannot say it, wait until I am at the depths of Luohan Peak discussing the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and then I will tell you. He ascended the hall.
At Shaolin, he sat in cold seclusion, yet his disciples each propounded divergent views, much like a group of blind men feeling an elephant.
When Shen Guang performed three prostrations and stood in his place, Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow. Yet this dark-faced Brahmin had not even touched the ground with his heels.
Entering the hall, a stone man asked a withered stump, "When will you bloom? The withered stump grew angry.
The stone man—how could he fail to speak? The stone man laughs aloud; from a withered stump, wondrous blossoms emerge.
Crimson clouds illuminate the jade elephant; white jade grinds against golden sand. I ask the master who has penetrated the profound: who is there that has not returned home?
Chan Master Fayi Xuechao of Wanyan in Taizhou was the great-great-grandson of Li Gong Zunmian, the Grand Preceptor and Prince of Xiangyang.

His family had resided for generations in Xiangfu County, Kaifeng. When his mother dreamed that an elderly monk arrived and she subsequently gave birth to him, he was seventeen years old when he sat for the examinations at the Imperial Academy.
His paternal great-uncle held office in Huainan and wished to appoint him to an official post, but he did not accept; instead, he intended to renounce worldly affairs and pursue the path of a monk.
Cijue Ze, the Zen Master, was not permitted by his grandfather. His mother said, "This child must have been a śramaṇa in a previous life;

I pray you do not thwart his resolve. Not long after, Cijue passed away. At the beginning of the Daguan era, he paid respects to Chan Master Lingyan Tongzhao Yuan, shaved his head, and received full ordination.
He relied upon Yuan for ten years, yet remained confused and unable to penetrate the teaching. He then visited Yuanwu at Jiangshan, where Yuanwu said:

This man was a vessel of the Dharma. Upon receiving an imperial decree, he was transferred to Tianning Monastery in the capital, where the Master attended him during his travels. At the end of the Jingkang era, he visited Caotang at Shushan;

upon a single word being spoken, the Great Dharma was suddenly clarified. In the seventh year of the Shaosheng era, Liu Gong Yanxiu, the Director of the Department of Scholarly Culture and Governor of Quan, invited him to reside at Yanfu Monastery.
Later, he moved through four great monasteries. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "The staff..."
At times this staff becomes a water-dwelling dragon; then for ten thousand *li* the clouds and mist never cease.
At times it becomes a crouching lion; then for a hundred years the tracks of monsters vanish. At times, mind and phenomena are both forgotten, and it stands alone as the illuminating essence.
At times, illumination and function are simultaneous, and host and guest are used interchangeably. Drawing with the staff, he said: "Under the Gate of Yanfu, all is employed."
[He] struck [the seat]. "Tell me, what does Yanfu usually use? He planted his staff upright, gave a shout, and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Looking up, one does not see the sky; looking down, one does not see the earth. Before the ancient sword and the skull, the great ocean’s waves boil.
He retired to the Wannian Guanyin Temple on Mount Tiantai. Suddenly, he manifested a slight illness and wrote a verse, saying: "Now..."
At the age of seventy-five, he returned to serve as the abbot of the hermitage. "Precious and weighty is Avalokiteśvara! A clay snake swallows a stone tiger.
He entered his coffin, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.

Chan Master Huikong of Dongshan at Xuefeng in Fuzhou was a native of the Chen clan of that same prefecture. At fourteen, he received the tonsure and immediately traveled to various regions to visit many veteran masters.
In his later years, he attained realization under Caotang. In the *Guiyou* year (1133) of the Shaoxing era, he opened the Dharma at Xuefeng.

On the day he accepted the invitation, he ascended the hall and said: "Those who are quick-witted and sharp will set off as soon as they are pointed toward the truth; those who are dull and obtuse cannot be pushed or pulled forward."
If he moves, everyone rejoices; if he does not move, everyone feels resentment. I, this mountain monk, shall now transform this dull stupidity into a state of swift agility.
(He snaps his fingers once. He says: "That which previously could not be pushed or pulled out, is now out.
That which previously would not dwell in a monastery, now dwells there. That which previously was loathed for not acting as a Buddha, now acts as one."

Formerly, out of disdain for the Dharma, he did not speak; now he speaks. Let us set aside for a moment whether he emerges or does not emerge, whether he abides or does not abide. I venture to ask you all:
what kind of Buddha is it that you have realized? Is it Vairocana Buddha? Is it Dīpaṃkara Buddha? Or is it Śākyamuni Buddha?
"Maitreya Buddha? What dharma is that which you speak? Is it the fundamental dharma? Is it the dharma of non-arising?
Is it a worldly dharma? Or is it a supramundane dharma? Is there anyone in this assembly who can speak of it?
If you can speak of it, this mountain monk’s work in appearing in the world will be finished. If not, do not misrepresent it when meeting people. He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Yunmen addressing the assembly, who said: "This very thing brings misery upon people. The Master said:
"Yunmen’s usual bearing was like that of a king; yet to speak in such a way is much like a poor man lamenting that he has too many people to support.
I, this mountain monk, am not so: this very thing brings joy to people. Why? Because only when the heavy rain has passed does one sit inside the house. The karmic winds—"
The wind blows and again circles the mountains. Even so, this is merely a beggar seeing small profit.
But how do you speak that single phrase which does not harm the meaning of things? Ascending the hall, he said: "A single punch knocks down Yellow Crane Tower;
A single kick overturns Parrot Isle. When there is spirit, add more spirit; Where there is no elegance, there too is elegance. How magnificent! How magnificent!"
Ah! How joyful, how joyful! He is just like a seventeen or eighteen-year-old crown prince. Who cares for heaven? Who cares for earth?
When the sovereign mind does not stir falsely, the six realms are simultaneously penetrated. Lay aside the three-foot sword; cease playing with the bow.
Free and easy, free and easy! How joyful, how joyful! It is just like an eighty- or ninety-year-old man acting as a ruler.
The signs are concordant; the winds blow in their proper season, and the rains fall in their proper season. The five grains flourish, and the myriad people are at peace.
Raising his staff, he said: "O Great Assembly! These two things, together with this mountain monk’s staff, make one whole.
When a patch-robed monk arrives at the gate of Xuefeng, he merely knows how to follow the custom and eat his fill; he can also get three coins to buy straw sandals. He gave a shout.
[The Master] leaned on his staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "How was it before the Master had seen Caotang? The Master said, "There is [it] in Jiangnan.
The monk asked, "How is it after having seen him? The Master said, "There is none in Jiangbei."
Chan Master Yetao Puchong of Yewang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture was a native of that very province. He addressed the assembly, citing:
"The Abbot of Baling said, 'It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. If it is neither the wind nor the banner, then where does it rest?
If there is anyone who can speak up for the Patriarch and come forth to meet Baling, let them step forward. Then, Chan Master Xuedou said:
"The wind moves, the banner moves. Since it is both wind and banner, where else could they be placed? Someone came forward to speak on behalf of Ba Ling, saying, "I will come out to meet Xuedou.
The Master said: "Neither wind nor banner—nowhere to place them; it is the banner and it is the wind—there is no place for attachment.
The swift falcon soaring through the vast heavens loses its tracks; the golden-haired lion crouching on the ground likewise falls into confusion. A-ha!"
Ha! Whether one awakens or not, it makes one longingly recall Master Xie Sanlang: "A single thread of line, fishing alone in the cold river rain.

A monk asked Chan Master Liangshan Huan of Tanzhou, successor to Chan Master Xing of Qingyuan: "The great assembly has gathered like clouds; we pray for the Master’s instruction. The Master said: "Heaven..."
"In stillness, one does not know where the clouds have gone; because the ground is cold, the snow remains for a long time. The monk said, "I, your student, do not yet understand these profound words.
I beg the Master to grant me further expedient means. The Master said, "Behind each mountain range, there is another person."
Chan Master Zhengfa Ximing of Chengdu Prefecture was a native of Hanzhou. Upon the conclusion of the retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "Leaves fall in profusion from the forest;
heaven and earth announce the early autumn. This is clearly the meaning of the Western Patriarch; why need one seek it further?

If you can understand it in this way, you will finally believe that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is fundamentally level and even, and that the Great Gate of Liberation has never had a lock or key."
It encompasses the universe and fills the void; its measure is inexhaustible and its wisdom unfathomable.

If one has not yet clarified this essential meaning and attained understanding of its source, then even if one undergoes the cultivation of merit for a hundred kalpas and refines one's conduct through a thousand lifetimes, it will be nothing more than a fruitless exhaustion of self.

There is no mutual interaction whatsoever. If one deeply clarifies this principle and thoroughly penetrates its source, one will know that every movement and stillness, every action and undertaking, every walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, accords with the Way at every point and flows toward the ultimate source in every thought-moment. As the Patriarch said: "Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation;
awakening is free from likes and dislikes. Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. If this is so, then who is deluded and who is awakened? Who is right?
Who is not at fault? It is these people alone who give rise to divergent views; they perceive the great as small, and cling to existence and non-existence.

The numinous spirit shines uniquely, yet they refuse to accept it; the moon of the mind is solitary and full, yet they naturally turn away from it. How is this different from abandoning one’s father within one's own home?
A pearl was forgotten within one’s robes, causing thorns to form a forest upon the path to Bodhi and clouds of delusion to obscure the sun in the sky of liberation.
Today, I, this mountain monk, am fortunate to encounter the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the assembly, the return of the patron to the mountain, and the intentional visit of all you virtuous ones.
I cannot remain silent; thus, following my humble capacity, I shall offer some tangled words to address the present age, briefly opening a skillful means.
"You must all fix your eyes upon this; each of you should observe it with clear attention. If you further hesitate or engage in discursive thought, there will be ten thousand miles of white clouds.
He then took up his staff and said, "If you can understand this clearly, the assembly on Vulture Peak is solemnly present before your eyes.
If this is not yet so, wait for me to deliver it tomorrow morning."
After seeing Qingyuan, the Venerable Ancestor Zuan built a hut among the peaks of Mount Heng and remained there for over thirty years, unknown to anyone.
One day, moved by inspiration, he composed a verse: "A small cauldron boils vegetables while rice steams above; The vegetables are cooked and the rice fragrant, yet people are still hungry.
Once the hunger-wound is mended, there is nothing more to do; Tomorrow morning, I shall paint a cat exactly as it was. From this, the monastics [took up his practice].
He knocked on the door with a hazel stick. Master Zhang Wujin exerted great effort to persuade him to open the Dharma gate, but he did not comply; he ultimately passed away on this mountain.
Chan Master Qinshan Qianming Puchu, a successor of Chan Master Jia Shan Chun, ascended the hall and after a long silence said: "To proclaim and uphold the fundamental tenets..."

I offer my felicitations for the imperial foundation. I humbly pray that auspicious clouds and the celestial star shall appear together, and that the sweet spring water and the nectar of immortality shall manifest as a pair.

May the sovereign be a ruler like Yao and Shun, and may the customs of the people be those of Cheng and Kang. Let this rustic hermit beneath the forest trees unconsciously compose a song of Great Peace.
But what, then, is this song of Great Peace? To act through non-action; to transform through the divine; to bestow virtue.
The rain falls in torrents; the wind of benevolence blows, bringing harmony and prosperity. The people are like wild deer; the sovereign is like the branches of a tree.
O eighteen sons, do you know or not? *Liri la*, *lari li*. (A single clap of the hands. Descend from your seats.
Chan Master Xiyu Xianjing of Shengyin Monastery in Chu Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Letan Qian, was the son of the Gao family of that same prefecture. He ascended the hall and said:

"Having traveled throughout the world, you should know that not a single step has ever been moved. Having passed through every gate and courtyard, you must find that in every household there is at least some smoke rising from the hearth."

Therefore, with a staff over the shoulder and steep-soled sandals upon the feet, he walks as his inspiration moves him; casting the hook and letting the line sink, he dwells according to his natural disposition.

It is not because the lands of his native village are fine; wherever the conditions are ripe, there he makes his home. Today, he takes whatever comes to hand; how often has he deliberated on this in the past?

He does not depart from the established patterns of old, yet each time it is raised, it is new again. For those with clear eyes: *Note: This passage is a Zen-style commentary on the life and practice of a monk, emphasizing spontaneity, non-attachment to worldly concerns, and the ever-fresh realization of the Dharma within familiar routines.*
Upon a mere glance, he turned back. For those who have not yet awakened, recognize this very face. Now tell me, what is this original face? After a long silence, he said:
"The flowers bloom on the front stage, yet they are seen from behind; the bell tolls in the upper realm, yet it is heard below.

He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: "When the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha, he preached the Dharma for the assembly."

As the summer retreat was about to begin, he said to Ānanda, "My great disciples and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans have never shown reverence or respect as I constantly preached the Dharma.
Now I shall enter the Piṇḍoddhāra Cave and observe the ninety-day summer retreat.
Should anyone come to inquire about the Dharma at that time, you must speak on my behalf: 'All dharmas are unarisen; all dharmas are unceasing.'"

"Extinction. Having said this, he closed his room and sat down. The Master called to the assembly, saying, "When Śākyamuni first attained the Way of the Buddha, for the most part he had no choice in the matter.
As soon as he had established this community, he already gave rise to thoughts of weariness and retreat.
If Shengyin had seen him at that time, he would have driven a nail through the door of the room, leaving him with no way out for the rest of his life."

This is to prevent future generations from imitating one another. Have you not heard it said: "If one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, one cannot be called a repayer of gratitude"?
[The Master] strikes the whisk and descends from the seat. Later, he dwelt in seclusion at Tianning in Lianyi.
Manifesting a slight illness, he wrote a verse, saying: "The shadow-play performance is finished; seventy-one years have passed. If you ask further how it is, come back for another match.
Having set down his pen, he passed away.
Chan Master Longya Zongmi of Tanzhou was a native of Yuzhang. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Do not speak in your sleep.
The monk asked, "What are all dharmas? The Master said, "Already fallen into the secondary. He ascended the hall; when the assembly had gathered, [he spoke].
The Master said: "It is already a perfect sphere; there is no need for carving or polishing. Return to the hall and drink tea. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Do not take the courtyard flowers to be like this body; When the courtyard flowers fall, spring comes again. But once this body has departed, who knows where it will go? The vast expanse of the three realms is enough to make one weep with grief."
Chan Master Zu Jian Congmi of Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou was a native of Tingzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "Opening one's mouth is not Chan;
closing one's mouth is not the Way. If you step forward with the intent to advance, your entire body will fall into the wild weeds."

Chan Master Putong Jiao of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture was the son of the Bi family from Wanling in the same commandery. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent; before reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
He went to Nanping to study the teachings of the Tiantai school and subsequently served as a patron for performing *chánmó* (confessional repentance) rites. Someone asked him:
"Regarding the transgressions you repent for, do you repent for your own sins or for those of others? If you repent for your own sins, from where does the nature of sin arise?"

When he attempted to repent for another’s transgression, the master said, "That person's offense is not yours; how can you repent for it? The master was unable to respond and subsequently changed his robes to travel as a wandering monk.
He went to Lestam (Lengyan). As soon as his foot touched the threshold, Lestan scolded him. When the master prepared to ask a question, Lestan immediately brandished his staff and drove him away.
One day, Lestan suddenly called the master to his quarters and said, "I have an ancient public case that I wish to discuss with you."
As the Master was about to offer a word in response, Xuedou Tan suddenly shouted. The Master attained sudden enlightenment and laughed heartily.
Tan descended from his rope seat, took the Master’s hand, and asked, "Do you understand the Buddha-dharma? The Master then shouted and pushed him away. Tan laughed loudly.

Thereupon, the Master's fame spread in all directions, and students revered him as their master. Later, he returned to his hometown and stayed at Tiantong, where he remained in seclusion behind closed doors for many years.

In the eighth year, the monastery happened to have a vacancy. The local officials ordered the Master to expound the Dharma; fearing he might flee, they had previously dispatched an official to wait for him on the road.
Thus, he could not decline. On the day he accepted the invitation, he ascended the hall and said: "Alas! Old Man of the Yellow Face, you have entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers.
You, a dispassionate guest beneath the forest trees, are being driven to death by an official summons. Is there no one who knows the bottom of the heart? Pray, save me from this."
"Ma! If there were none, one could not help but take the wrong for the right. Thereupon he descended from his seat. Whenever a monk approached, the Master would invariably scold him, saying:
"When you had not yet taken up the *zhulu* staff, I already explained it for you. Now tell me, what did I explain? He would then beckon with his hand or wash his bowl.
"Holding up a fan, drawing a bow; Zhaozhou’s ‘cypress tree’; Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms—let these be cast aside for now.
This mountain monk has no such idle lips with which to engage you in verbal entanglements. Why not simply rest? With these words, he took up his staff and drove them out.
On the twentieth day of the third month in the sixth year of the Xuanhe era, he bathed, ascended the hall, and spoke a verse. He passed away with utter ease.
Ji. A verse says: The jeweled staff knocks upon the void; where it touches, spring arrives. Within this, the message is uniquely pervasive. Last night the wind stirred, the cold crags grew chill;
A clay ox was startled awake to plow the white clouds. He was seventy-seven years old; his dharma age was fifty-eight.
Chan Master Yuantong Daomin Yuanji of Jiangzhou was popularly known as an ancient Buddha. He was the son of Cai of Xinghua. His mother dreamed of swallowing a maṇi jewel before she conceived him.
When he was five years old, his feet would not touch the ground and his mouth would not speak. His mother carried him to visit Ximing Temple;
upon seeing a Buddhist statue, he suddenly stepped onto the floor, pressed his palms together, and recited "Namo Buddha," thereafter performing a prostration. This amazed the people.

He found this strange. Later, while pursuing his official studies in Daliang, he took refuge with Master Dexiang at Jingde Temple and left the household life. He passed the scriptural examination to receive ordination and traveled everywhere to seek instruction, gaining a taste of the teachings from all.
He stayed with Chan Master Zhe of Mt. Wei for the longest time, but later he admired Letan and went there to pay his respects.
Zhantang observed his silent composure. The Master recounted the realizations he had gained from his successive visits to various teachers, but he did not receive their seal of approval.

Zhantang raised the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling, asking him about it; again, they did not reach accord. Later, while attending Zhantang as they were walking, Zhantang rested his staff on his shoulder and sighed deeply, saying, "Do you understand?
The Master was about to respond when Zhantang struck him. After a short while, he again held up a blade of grass and showed it to him.
[The Master] asked, "What is this? The Master was about to respond when Tanzhu gave a shout. Thereupon, [the Master] suddenly realized the Great Dharma.

He made the gesture of holding up a flower and said, "This time I cannot deceive Upādhyāya Min. Tanzhu pulled him back and said, "Say more! Say more! The Master replied, "Clouds rise on the southern mountain;
rain falls on the northern mountain. He then prostrated himself. Tanzhu nodded in approval. Later, the Master propagated the Dharma at Guankxi.
Next he resided at Yuantong, following the prophecy of Chan Master Daoji. Students flocked there in great numbers.
When the imperial court heard of his realization of the Way, the ministers petitioned once more on his behalf, and he was granted ceremonial robes and the title "Complete Mechanism" (Yuanji).

He ascended the hall and said: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, they have no dharma to give to others; they merely extract nails and pull out wedges, removing doubts and severing delusions. For those who study the Way..."
Do not deceive yourself. If you have even a single doubt the size of a mustard seed, this person is your true spiritual friend.
[He] lets out a shout and says: "What is it? Do not, by any means, thrust your head into a vat of glue!"

The Abbot Zhihe of Niliang Hermitage in Qingyuan Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of Yufeng on Mount Sui. When he was a child, he once practiced seated meditation while hanging from the eaves of a hall.

When the hall collapsed, his parents thought he must have perished; however, the Master remained with his eyes closed as if nothing had happened. Consequently, they allowed him to enter the monastic order.
Having reached the age for full ordination, he went to visit Letan. Upon seeing him, Letan asked, "What are you doing?

As the Master was about to respond, Letan struck him and shouted, "What do you call 'Chan'? The Master suddenly grasped the essential meaning and immediately said, "Chan! It has no beginning and no end;
the waves settle in the great ocean, and the moon is reflected in the blue sky. Letan asked again, "What is the Way? The Master replied, "The Way! The red dust of the mundane world."
Vast and expansive, it requires no contrivance; fundamentally, there is nothing lacking. It is profoundly still. Next, he visited Chan Master Bian of Mount Heng, who held him in even greater esteem.
During the Yuánfú era, he stayed at Zhōngfēng and Xīyún, two hermitages on Mount Xuědòu, for more than twenty years.
He once composed a verse that says: "Two or three sheng of wild water from the bamboo pipes; Seven or five fragments of idle clouds at the pine-window. The Way..."
The livelihood of a person is merely like this; it is left for those in the human world to see and hear. Many who are resolved upon the Way go to visit him.
When a monk arrived to pay his respects, the Master asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The monk replied, "Tiantong. The Master asked, "How high is Mount Taibai?
The monk struck his forehead with his hand and made a gesture of looking upward. The Master said, "There is still this one remaining. The monk said, "However..."
"Please, Abbot, speak. The Master instead made the gesture of tilting his head back as if looking up. The monk hesitated; the Master struck him immediately.

Initially, the Master had traveled with Zen Master Jiao of Tiantong to inquire about the Way. They made a vow, saying: "In days to come, the two of us should occupy the solitary peaks and highest summits, gazing at the heavens and the Milky Way, becoming men beyond the world.
We must not register our names in government offices of this age, nor should we bow our heads in subjection."

Regarding his relationship with people: later, when the covenant was broken, the Master ultimately refused to receive them. Zhengyan stated that Lord Gong used stratagems to entice the Master out of the mountains to reside at Er-ling.
For thirty years, he possessed no possessions beyond what was necessary; only two tigers attended to his right side.

One day, they became more formidable than humans, so he dismissed them with a verse. On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Xuande era (1125), he passed away while seated in the lotus posture.
He passed away while seated. Zhengyan composed a formal biography detailing Master Xing’s life, including a very detailed account of his final illness and extraordinary manifestations.
Furthermore, he had an image of him sculpted, attended by two tigers, which remains extant to this day.

Chan Master Cishi Ruixian of Shaoxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Kaixian Ying. A native of the same prefecture, he left home at the age of twenty and received ordination through the examination of the scriptures.
He studied the *vinaya*, yet upon realizing that the nature of the precepts is like empty space and that those who cling to them are deluded, he said: "The precepts..."
This is the method for binding the body. Why bind oneself? Thereupon, he delved into the teachings of the Platform and further read:

"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without cause. Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. He then had a doubt, asking:

"If they do not arise from self, from another, from both together, or without cause, then ultimately from where do they arise? Immediately, he reflected and said: "They are produced by causes and conditions..."
The three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle give rise to and stir the ocean of nature. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings differ in name but are identical in essence.
Through the ten objects and ten vehicles, consciousness is transformed into wisdom. The inconceivable realm is clarified only by the illumination of wisdom;

it is beyond the reach of verbal explanation. He traveled to various regions and eventually arrived at Touzi. When Guangjian asked, "Where is your hometown? the Master replied, "Dongyue in the two provinces of Zhejiang. Guangjian—
[Daoyuan] asked, "What about the matter of Dongyue? The Master said, "The Qinwang Peak is high; the Jiangu Lake is vast.
[Daoyuan] asked, "Is the Qinwang Peak the same as yourself, or is it different? The Master said, "Sanskrit in the Western Heaven; Chinese in this land."
Jian said, "This is still just a formal response within the monastic community. Ultimately, are they the same or different? The Master then shouted; Jian then struck him.
The Master said, "The kindness is too great to repay," and then prostrated himself. Later, he returned to his hometown and established the Dharma at Cishi. In his quarters, he once asked a monk:
"Three camels with two legs travel ten thousand miles a day, yet you cannot catch up. Now, where do you keep them?"
Mount Yùquán (Jade Spring Mountain): Do not allow people of this age to make arbitrary interpretations. Where, then, do you all meet the Venerable Xian?
Chan Master Hǎipíng of Dàméi in Tánzhōu ascended the hall and said: "The lantern performs a dance; the pillar hides within."

The Shen of the Sands manifested his malevolence, and the Kunlun slave gave rise to anger. He let out a roar and said: "A single phrase that fits the head [of the teaching] leads to ten thousand kalpas of falling into the ford of delusion."
Chan Master Jingguang Liaowei Furi of Wenzhou, successor to Chan Master Yuantong Xian, was asked by a monk: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said: "A journey of one night or two nights; the moon over a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks. The monk asked: "What is the underlying intent? The Master said: "The morning..."
[The Master] looked toward the southeast; at dusk, he looked toward the northwest and asked, "Is there anything further above this?
The Master said, "A person's heart is difficult to satisfy; a ravine is easy to fill. [The student] asked, "I do not ask about the seasonal causes and conditions; how is the story of Huichao?"
The Master said, "The Persian draws his bow; his face turns black. [The student] asked, "What is the meaning? The Master said, "It pierces through the skull; the laughter does not cease.
[The student] said, "I ask this question in all sincerity. The Master said, "In the Yellow Springs there are no inns; tonight, in whose house shall one lodge?"

Chan Master Xuedou Chi of Qingyuan Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xiangtian Qing. He was a native of the Lu clan of that prefecture. A monk asked, "What is it like when the moon is not seen on the Mid-Autumn Festival? The Master said, "Wait until the night is deep and you shall see. The monk said, "What if dark clouds have not yet dispersed? The Master replied, "Then look at the sky. The monk said, "If the clouds do not disperse, what then? The Master said, "The moon is right there. The monk said, "How about when the clouds suddenly part? The Master said, "It is like a bright pearl emerging from the depths of the sea. The monk said, "What if the pearl is swallowed by a dragon? The Master said, "The heavens and earth are both illuminated. The monk said, "What if the pearl is lost? The Master said, "The ten directions are all empty. The monk said, "What if the pearl is found? The Master said, "The whole world is filled with light. The monk said, "What if the pearl is broken? The Master said, "A single ray of light pierces the void. The monk said, "What if the pearl is restored? The Master said, "The three realms are all within it. The monk said, "What if the pearl is stolen? The Master said, "The thief is right here. The monk said, "What if the thief is caught? The Master said, "The thief is revealed. The monk said, "What if the thief is released? The Master said, "The thief is gone. The monk said, "What if the thief returns? The Master said, "The thief is gone. "Ten thousand streams flow crosswise, yet all head toward the east; transcending in every direction, it is naturally clear and resonant. The courage of ten thousand men is shattered like sand."

When Yangshan was sitting with Guishan, he asked, "After the Master has passed away, if someone asks about the Dharma-way of the late teacher, how will you respond? Guishan said, "One bowl of gruel, one bowl of rice.

This is known to all; do not distinguish between "self" and "other. There is no difference between self and other. A weary fish stays in the shallow pool; a sick bird perches on the reeds.

The Dharma Master Luán of Xichū was well-versed in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. When Fózhuò retired from his duties, he resided at Jìngdé Temple.

The Master asked Fózhuò, "Why is it that much of what is said in the Chan school lacks a firm foundation? Fózhuò replied, "What sutras and śāstras have you studied? The Master said, "I have a rough knowledge of various sutras."
Fotu was somewhat versed in the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*. Zhao said, "Just like yesterday’s rain and today’s sun—within which dharma are these contained?
Fotu was bewildered. Zhao raised his *yǎnghézi* (itching-comforter) and struck him, saying, "Do not say that what the Chan school speaks is without foundation.
Fotu said indignantly, "Yesterday’s rain and today’s sun—after all, within which dharma are they contained? Zhao said, "The second [dharma]."
At the fourteenth watch, [the Master] was included among the non-associated dharmas (*viprayukta-dharma*). The Teacher was suddenly enlightened and immediately prostrated in gratitude.

Later, he returned to Shu and resided at a lecture hall, instructing his disciples through the direct path without adhering to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, many withdrew. He then recited a verse and concluded his lectures, saying:
"The multitude sell flowers, while I alone sell pines; Though their green color is not as red as theirs, When calculated, it will ultimately..."
In harmony with the times, he returned to the midst of the verdant mists. Thus, he lived in seclusion for twenty years.

As both monastics and laypeople pursued him with longing, he was summoned once more to expound the Dharma. He responded with a verse, saying: "Withdrawing my traces, I hid upon a high peak; Yet even that high peak could not contain me.

It is better to return to Jinli Village, And as before, sell my green pines. The assembly prostrated themselves in repentance, and lecturers from the two provinces vied with one another to rely upon his guidance.

...[he] followed [him]. Chan Master Tianyou Dianyuan of Yuyan Monastery in Longxing Prefecture was a descendant of Chan Master Litan Zhun; he was the son of Zheng of Chengdu. Initially, he sat for the examinations at the local prefectural school.
He went again to take the examination in Zizhou; he was placed on the list of candidates for both locations, yet the Master did not dare accept it and fled through the frontier pass.
It happened that a mountain-dweller was returning westward, and upon seeing his extraordinary bearing and transcendent discourse, [the Master] traveled downriver with him in the same boat.
They eventually went to Mount Lu, where he shaved his hair under the Master, retaining his original name, and first attended upon Sīxin.
Qie subsequently relied upon Zhantang at Letan. One day, Letan was giving a general discourse (pushe), saying, "Everyone is so painfully seeking the Buddha-dharma from Elder Zhuan.

Because he stayed at a hermitage in Wuning, he named it "Tianniu" (The Cow Keeper) and never left for the rest of his life. Tudu saw him when he was already ninety-three years old.
Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation staff and said, "Long rains have not cleared. *Zha*! The golden crow flies upon the corner of the bell tower.
He struck once more and said, "It is still within the eggshell. Striking again, he said, "Let the monks do as they please with their names and reputations.
Ascending the hall, [he said: "Mazu’s single shout caused Baizhang to miss the mark. Linji, that little fellow, picked up a broken piece of pottery from a heap of refuse."

He ascended the hall and said: "Baofeng has a secret formula; I shall explain it clearly before the assembly. Last night before the third watch, a tortoise swallowed a turtle. At the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall and said:

In place of [the previous statement], both the Great and Small Yuquan [temples] stirred waves where there was no wind. Yunyan, seeing injustice on the road, brought down a single blow that smashed everything to pieces.

[He] was able to relax. Under Yunyan’s gate, let those coming from the south or the north do as they please; just pass the time like this.
