A monk asked, “Because of the mountains one sees the water; seeing the water, one forgets the mountains. When both mountain and water are forgotten, where does the principle return?”
"What is it? the Master asked. "This mountain monk has sat his tongue down; heaven and earth are pitch black. An old master once offered this turning phrase:
"A thatched hut is built in the middle of the crossroads, yet people are not permitted to defecate there. A monk brought this up to question the Master.
The Master said, "You have already defecated yourself; what more do you want anyone else to do? When the old master heard this, he burned incense and gazed toward him from afar.
Da Su bowed twice in gratitude. In the seventh month of the autumn of the Yimao year of the Xiangsheng era, there was a great fall of rain and snow, and strange omens appeared in the mountains.
The Master said, "My time has come. On the seventeenth day, he took his leave of the Prefectural Governor and his subordinates. Three days later, at Tianpeng, he manifested a slight ailment.
On the night of the twenty-fourth, he asked a monk in attendance, "When it is dawn and there is no moon, what then? The monk—

Wu-dui said, "It would only be right if you were to instruct me to perform the cremation for you. The following day, he returned to the Xiangkou Monastery, where he left behind his final instructions.
He then passed away peacefully. His disciples escorted his entire remains back home; smoke and mist gathered from all sides, and monkeys and birds wailed in grief.
During the cremation, a rare fragrance filled the wilds. His tongue remained intact as before, and five-colored śarīras were found in incalculable numbers.

He was interred to the west of the Dingguang Pagoda. Later, while residing at Tiantong, Tianmu, and Wenli, he composed a eulogy for his portrait, which may serve to supplement the deficiencies in his *xing-shi* (biography).
Therefore, I have recorded this eulogy here as well: "Among those of the Dongshan assembly, only he was not petty;
dwelling in a quiet room elsewhere, he was difficult for the monastic community to fathom. From the waters of Fang, a serpent emerged to startle the world—how dull!"

An iron cauldron, a rooster crowing in broad daylight; a mixed theater performance comes rushing in. Full fire is on standby. In his later years, he grew lax and indolent, yet remained in harmony with the mundane world.
When Qin Bazi sent someone to investigate him, he simply tossed down an incense tablet to reveal his true style.
There is no Buddha in Dīpaṃkara; it is a waste of effort to set up a cage. As he departs, he shakes his bell toward the void—who knows that the White Cloud School has been utterly extinguished?
Chan Master Wúwéi Zōngtài of Hànzhōu was a native of Fúchén. After leaving the Guān Pass, he traveled extensively among various monastic communities.
Upon arriving at the Fifth Patriarch’s assembly on the day of the incense offering, the Patriarch presented him with the story of Zhàozhōu washing the alms bowl and instructed him to investigate it.

When the time came for the private interview, the Patriarch brought up this same story and asked the Master, "Tell me, what did Zhàozhōu say to that monk? That monk attained enlightenment immediately. The Master replied, "Washing the bowl."
Yunqu went away. Nanquan said, "You know only the matters of the road; you do not know the flavor of the road.
The Master said, "Since I know the matters of the road, what flavor could there be on the road? Nanquan said, "Do you not know? He asked again, "Have you ever traveled to Zhejiang?
The Master said, "No. Nanquan said, "You have not yet awakened. From that time on, for five years, the Master... [did not speak].
Nengdui was present. One day, the Patriarch ascended the hall, looked at the assembly, and said, "An eighty-year-old old man rolls a brocade ball," and then descended from his seat.
Master Nengdui joyfully stepped forward from the crowd and said, "Let the Abbot try rolling one for us.

The Patriarch made a gesture with his hands as if beating a war drum and sang a folk song from Mianzhou in the Shu dialect: "On Mount Douzi, they beat the earthen drums; On Mount Yangping, they scatter..."

"White rain! White rain falls! Take the dragon girl; she has woven five zhang and five chi of silk. Half belongs to Luo Jiang, and half belongs to Wu Xu. Upon hearing this, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He covered the Patriarch’s mouth, saying, "It need only be sung as far as this point. The Patriarch laughed heartily and returned home.
Later, when the Master returned to Shu, the fourfold assembly requested that he open the Dharma for them at Wúwéi. He moved to Zhèngfǎ, where he ascended the hall and said: "This..."
This is the causal condition for the one great matter. Since the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kāśyapa smiled, the World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. Thereafter, it was passed down from lamp to lamp and transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, continuing until the present day without interruption.
It has truly reached the point where flowers bloom everywhere on the ground; thus it is called the Wondrous Nirvāṇa.

The mind. It is also called the original mind, the original nature, the original face, the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), the śakara-eye, and the Mahā-prajñāpāramitā. In a man it is a man; in a woman it is a woman.
You all, simply awaken to this yourselves! All such things are merely idle words. [He] then picked up [the whisk].
The Whisker Master said: "To understand it is called Zen; for one who has not yet awakened, it is truly difficult—difficult, indeed!
Before one's eyes stands Mount Sumeru. To awaken is easy—easy, indeed! To speak as one pleases, there is nothing that is not so. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said, "Who taught you to ask such a question? The monk hesitated, and the Master said, "Finished.
Chan Master Wuzu Biaozhi of Qizhou was a native of Huai’an. He initially relied upon the Patriarch for the longest period of time, yet he had not yet attained realization.
At that time, Yuanwu was the head of the assembly (zuo-yuan). The Master went to seek his instruction. Yuanwu said, "Brother, try telling me where you have doubts.
The Master then cited the passage from Deshan’s informal sermon: "I do not answer questions; those who ask questions receive thirty blows of the staff. Yuanwu said, "Prostrate yourself!"
"I have become your teacher, yet you still do not understand this story. After the master had finished bowing, Wuzu told him to bring up the previous story again.
The master said, "At Deshan’s informal lecture, he would not answer questions. Wuzu covered his mouth and said, "Just look at it like this. The master then departed.
He raised his voice and said, "How can there be a public case that merely teaches one to look at the principle of a single phrase?
A monk said to him, "Brother, you should not speak thus; the Head Seat must have some skillful means. Thereupon, he sat in stillness to investigate.
At the end of the ten-day period, [Dao]jun suddenly resolved his doubts and went to pay his respects to Huineng, who said, "Brother, you have finally realized that I did not deceive you.

He then went to the abbot’s quarters; Master Nanyue welcomed him with a smile. From that day on, [Dao]jun’s understanding of the profound and mysterious became deep. When Master Nanyue was about to pass away, he left a message for the regional governor.
Shouming succeeded him on the seat. Monks arrived from all directions in such numbers they could not be stopped. The Master posted a notice at the gate of his attendants' quarters, saying:
"Dongshan has three phrases. If anyone can speak them, they shall be admitted to the community. The monks were all disheartened.
One day, a monk carrying his sitting mat went straight to the master’s chamber and said to him, "I cannot speak them; I simply wish to be admitted. The Master—[was greatly moved].
Xì called for the *vinaya-dhara* to prepare the seating beneath a bright window. He ascended the hall and said:
"When the World-Honored One held up the flower and Kāśyapa smiled, people knew only of the holding of the flower and the smile; yet they did not recognize the World-Honored One.

A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Dancing the *zhèzhī* within a thicket of brambles. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said: [He held up his whisk.]
The Newborn Child Throws the Gold Basin.
Chan Master Daochu of Longhua in Qizhou was the son of the Ma family. He served as the attendant to Master Zu for many years.

On the day he took up residence at Longhua, he ascended the hall and said: "When a rooster sees [another], it fights; when a dog sees [another], it bites. The *chīwén* (ceramic ridge-end ornament) atop the hall remains so all day long."
[The guest] asked, "In contrast [to this], why did you not become angry? He then descended from his seat. The Master’s wit and eloquence were sharp and swift;
his disciples were unable to fathom the depth of his realization. One day he said to the assembly, "Yesterday I left the city; white clouds came and went through the void.

The wind through the pines cleared my ears and eyes; it was truly superior to the human world. He called to the assembly and said, "This is the final word of my late master. After a short while, he passed away.
Yet he passed away.

Chan Master Qing-su of Jiuding Peak in Jiazhou was the son of the Guo family of that prefecture. He received the tonsure and the precepts at Qianming Temple and traveled widely to knock at the gates of various Chan masters.
Later, he visited the Fifth Patriarch and, upon hearing the words of Shoushan regarding the meaning of the Westward Journey, he attained sudden enlightenment.
He spoke a verse, saying: "Upside down, upside down! Upside down, upside down! The new bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it. To act thus is quite groundless;
Turning one's head, one does not realize one’s robe has been torn. When Mazu saw this, he asked, "As for Baizhang’s story of the wild fox, what do you say?
The Master said, "Those who come to speak of right and wrong are themselves the people of right and wrong. Mazu was greatly pleased. After some time, the Master took his leave.

He returned and stayed at Qingxi. Later, he moved to Jiuding. When Governor Lü came to behold the Great Image, he asked, "Since this is the Great Image, why does it carry two pillars upon its shoulders?
The Master replied, "There are no idle workers on a boat. Upon reaching the pavilion below, seeing the Avalokiteśvara image, he asked again, "This is the realm of Maitreya;
from where has Avalokiteśvara come? The Master replied, "In a wealthy household, the young children are spoiled."
Shou then paid his respects. When Qin Laosu arrived, the Master asked, "When the sword is at the throat during a dance, what then?

Qin replied, "I humbly pray that you will partake. The Master scolded him, saying, "Old thief, go die! You ask me! Qin repeated his previous words and asked again. The Master folded his hands, bowed, and said, "Drag it apart!
On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month in the year of Yimao (1135) of the Xiangxing era, he contracted a slight illness and wrote a verse:
He addressed his followers, saying: "The wooden man prepares the boat; the iron man prepares the horse. The child of the Bing and Ding stems mounts steadily;
with a shout, he scatters the white clouds and returns. Thereupon, he finally passed into stillness.
The head seat Yuanli was a native of Min. He had studied under Jiaoshan and initially attended upon Master Yan at Baiyun.

Whenever he entered the room for instruction, Yan would invariably say to him, "Monks of our lineage, you must clearly distinguish between the black and the white. The master harbored this doubt without ceasing.
One day, as Yan ascended the hall, he cited the saying of Shoushan: "The bride riding the donkey, led by her mother-in-law," and said, "If you all wish to understand..."
"Do not ask about the daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law; avoid troubling yourself with idle chatter on the road. When you meet rice, eat rice; when you meet tea, drink tea.
To enter and exit the same gate is to be an enemy from a past life. At these words, the Master was suddenly enlightened and said, "Today, the distinction between the monastic and the lay is clear.

Two years later, when Fayan moved his seat to the ancestral mountain (Mount Guishan), he invited [Zhaozhou] to share the teaching seat, but he did not accept. After Fayan passed away, he immediately...
In the Chongning era, he went again to Wuzu. A monk asked, "Where has Wuzu gone after his parinirvāṇa?
The Master said, "Having eyes but no ears; sitting by the fire in the sixth month. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this?

The Master said, "A poor home is still tolerable; a poor road brings one to despair. Or, when asked, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, 'All wholesome dharmas'—how [should these be understood]?"
"This is the Dharma," the Master said. "Above is heaven; below is earth. As for that which sits in the middle—if it is sitting, let it sit;
if it is standing, let it stand. What do you call this 'wholesome dharma'? The monk had no reply. The Master then struck him. Later, he passed away at Ruiyan in Siming.

Puyong Zhizang was a native of Fuzhou. Upon reaching the Fifth Patriarch’s quarters for his formal interview, the Patriarch brought up the story of the "Two Women and the Separated Souls" to question him.
Puyong attained a realization and presented this verse: "The two women merge into one daughter-in-law; The turning wheel is severed, impossible to reverse.
From of old, coming and going leave no trace; Travelers need not ask the path by which they came. Whenever there were monks from his hometown...
The visitor came to pay his respects and, speaking in the Min dialect, recited in the vernacular: "At the beginning of the letter, she teaches her mother-in-law to be diligent in rising and resting;
at the end of the letter, she teaches her mother-in-law not to doze off. But tell me, what does she say in between? As the monk prepared to respond, the Master pushed him out.

The Elder Fahsu had long relied upon the Fifth Patriarch, yet he had not yet attained realization. One day he went to the Patriarch’s quarters, and the Patriarch asked him, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Fahsu replied, "Fahsu is not like that. The Patriarch pointed at him with his finger and said:
"Abiding! Abiding! "The Dharma-multitude is not so. How is it? At this, the Master attained enlightenment. Later, he went to the seat of Chan Master Xianming Du at Donglin.

Seeing that Du had attained the essence of the "plain and real," one day [the Master] held up a flower, walked once around Master Du’s meditation seat, turned his back, and inserted it into the incense burner, saying, "Venerable Sir, tell me: what is the meaning of this? Du repeatedly...
He offered several responses, none of which were accepted. After two months had passed, he finally asked the Master to try explaining it for him.
The Master said, "I have merely taken some flowers and placed them in the incense burner; why does the Master suspect that there is anything else going on?"
A monk asked Master Chengtian Zixian of Nanyue in Tanzhou, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Yungeben: "The great assembly has already gathered and awaits your thunderous voice;
now that you have ascended the lion throne, we pray that you will reveal the truth. The Master said, "Performing somersaults atop the top of the *kṣa* pole. The monk said, "In that case..."
"In that case, auspicious mists rise before Mount Yue-lu, and auspicious clouds emerge beneath Mount Zhurong. The Master said, "Glistening pearls within a purple silk curtain.
He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing."
He struck the meditation seat once and said, "I have shattered the cave of your spirit for you; though dust is stirred and earth is scattered, there is nowhere to seek it.
Ten thousand mountains stand empty and towering. He struck once more and said, "Return to the hall and practice. Ascending the hall, he said: "The solitary, high hermitage belongs only to Nanyue.
I laugh at myself, thinking my own solitary cloud is not yet truly at ease. As for those who sit upright by the pines and beside the water—"
"One should speak according to precedent regarding dwelling in the mountains. *Tut!* He ascended the hall. "The waning moon falls at the end of the fifth watch; the white clouds fly as day breaks.
This is a matter clearly before one's eyes, yet it is not the mechanism of the present moment. Since it is a matter before one's eyes, why is it not the mechanism of the present moment?
After a long silence, he said: "Wishing to speak, words fail; beneath the trees, they deliberate instead."
The nun Yudo, a successor of Chan Master Langye Huiqiu, was a native of Jinling.
She made her living by selling oil cakes and regularly joined the assembly to seek instruction from Langye.
Langye showed her the koan of Linji’s “True Person of No Rank. One day, she heard a beggar singing a Lotus Song that said: [...text continues...]
If it were not for Liuyi’s delivery of the letter, by what means could one have reached Lake Dongting? Suddenly she attained great enlightenment; she threw the rice-cake tray to the ground.
Her husband looked on askance and said, "You are mad. His wife slapped him and said, "This is not your sphere of experience. Go see Langya."
Xielang observed him and recognized his profound realization. He asked, "Who is that person of no rank?
Ba replied at once, "There is a person of no rank who has six arms and three heads; with great effort he rages in anger. With one blow he splits Mount Huashan into two paths;

the flowing waters of ten thousand years know nothing of spring. From this point on, his reputation spread far and wide. Whenever a monk arrived, he would say, "Child! Child! The monk would then [respond].
As he was about to deliberate on this, the woman immediately closed the door. Chan Master Fodeng Xun went there to investigate her.
When the woman saw him, she asked the same questions as before. Xun said, "Where is your father? The woman turned around and bowed toward a pillar.

Xun then kicked it over and said, "I thought there was something truly extraordinary here," and he departed. The woman scrambled up and called out, "Son! Son! Come back! I cherish you! But Xun did not return.
The head seat An arrived. The old woman asked, "Where have you come from? An replied, "From De Shan. The old woman said, "De Shan Tai was the son of an old woman.
An asked, "And whose son are you, old woman? The old woman said, "Upon being questioned by you, Senior, I was driven to stand right there and urinate.
The old woman once composed a verse on the occasion of Mazu’s illness, which begins: "The face of the sun, the face of the moon; empty..."
A flash of lightning in the void. Although it cuts off the tongues of all the monks under heaven, it clearly says only half the truth.
A successor in the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage, Chan Master Daowei Qin of Zhaojue.
Chan Master Dahui Pujue Zonggao of Mount Jing in Lin’an was the son of the Xi family of Xuancheng. From his youth, he possessed a brilliant spirit.
At the age of twelve, he entered the local school. One day, while playing with his classmates, he threw a inkstone at one of them by mistake and struck the teacher’s hat.
He returned home after paying restitution in gold and said: "If a great man reads worldly books, how can that compare to investigating the Way?"
Regarding worldly affairs, he went directly to Huìyún Yúan on Mount Dōng to attend upon Huìqí. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and received full ordination in the *vinaya*.

While casually reading the records of the ancient Yúnmén, he felt as though they were like old acquaintances. He then went to rely upon Chán Master Chéng of Guǎngjiào, after which he abandoned that place to travel in all directions.
Following various elder masters of the Cáo-dòng lineage, once he had mastered their teachings, he departed for Bǎofēng to pay his respects to Chán Master Zhàntáng Zhǔn.

When the Master [Yunmen] first saw him in the hall, he found him extraordinary and had him attend to his handkerchief and sash, pointing him toward the shortcut for entering the Way. The Master’s responses were swift and unyielding;
Yunmen reprimanded him, saying, "You have not yet attained awakening. Your illness lies in your reliance on conscious understanding, which constitutes the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)."
When Master Tang was on his deathbed, he instructed the Master, saying: "After I am gone, you must see Chuan Qin; he will surely be able to fully employ your spiritual faculties" (Qin was Yuanwu).
After Master Tang passed away, the Master hurried to pay his respects to the Layman Wujin to request an inscription for Tang’s stupa. The Layman’s standards were high and he rarely gave approval;
however, upon a single word of mutual accord with the Master, he offered him lodging and invited him to stay. He named the Master’s hermitage Miaoxi. Subsequently...
He visited him again and was further instructed to see Yuanwu. When the Master arrived at Tianning Monastery, one day he heard Yuanwu ascend the hall and cite a case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said, "On the water above the Eastern Mountain.
"If it were Tianning," [Yuanwu] continued, "it would not be so. Suppose someone were to ask me, 'What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? I would simply point to him..."
The Way: "A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. Upon these words, the Master’s past and future suddenly severed.
Although the appearance of movement did not arise, he remained seated in a state of pure nakedness. Wuzhuo said to him, "This was no easy matter."
"You have obtained this field; it is a pity that you have died and cannot live again. Not doubting the words and phrases is itself a great illness. Have you not heard it said:
'Letting go at the precipice, one spontaneously accepts the responsibility; after death, one revives again—this cannot deceive the Master.
You must believe that such a principle exists. He then assigned him to reside in the Jue-mu Hall as an attendant who does not manage administrative affairs.

One day, when the Great Officer entered the room (the place where court officials rest after choosing their trees), Wuzu would frequently raise the "having-phrase" and "no-phrase" kōan, asking, "It is like a vine leaning against a tree.

As soon as the Master opened his mouth, Wuzu would say, "Not so! Not so! This continued for half a year, until the Master finally asked Wuzu, "I heard that you once raised this very question while at Wuzu; I wonder what Wuzu said to you."
Damo laughed but did not answer. The Master said, "The Venerable One ought to have asked this before the assembly at that time;
what harm is there in saying it now? Being left with no choice, Huineng said, "I asked: 'There is a phrase, yet there is no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree.
What was the meaning of this? The Patriarch replied, "'It cannot be sketched, nor can it be painted. He asked again, "When the tree falls and the vine withers..."
"How is it now? the Patriarch asked. Yunju replied, "I have come along with you. At these words, the Master was immediately relieved and said, "I understand.
Yunwu then cited several karmic conditions (*nidāna*) to cross-examine him; Yunju responded without hesitation.

Yunwu said, "Now I know that I did not deceive you," and he subsequently composed the *Record of the True Lineage of Linji* and entrusted it to him, appointing him as the head of the record office (*jishi*). Before long, he ordered him to share the seat in the meditation hall. In the room, he held...
He used the bamboo whisk to test his disciples, and the monastic communities universally accorded him great respect. His fame resounded throughout the capital.
Prime Minister Lü Shuntú memorialized the throne to grant him purple robes and the title "Buddha-Sun" (Fó rì). During the Jurchen upheaval, the chieftain intended to take several dozen Chan monks;
the Master was among those selected but managed to escape. He went to Tiger Hill in Wú to spend the summer retreat, whereupon he studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

When the Bodhisattva ascended to the seventh stage and realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he thoroughly understood the circumstances of the previously inquired-about incident concerning how Caṅkramāra (Yanguè móluó), while holding his almsbowl, went to the house of a woman in childbirth at the request of Zhandang. At that time, Yuánwù was summoned to reside at Yúnjū;

the Master went there to pay his respects. On the second day of his arrival at the mountain, Yuánwù immediately invited him to serve as the First Seat (*prathama-āsana*). At that time, there were many "dragons and elephants" among the assembly.
Yuanwu had long held the position of Seat-Holder (Zuoyuan) and had been waiting for the Master’s arrival; he harbored a sense of resentment.
When the winter solstice arrived, Chan Master Zhaoguo Yuan took up the whisk, and a monk from the assembly stepped forward and asked, "What is it like when a sword hangs between the eyebrows?
The Master replied, "Blood splatters against the Brahma Heaven. Yuanwu, from beneath his seat, gestured with his hand and said, "Stop! Stop! That was an excellent question, and the answer was..."
Even more extraordinary was that Yuan eventually returned to the assembly, and from this point on, the monastic communities underwent a transformation.
When Yuanwu returned to Sichuan, the Master established a hermitage at the ancient site of Yunmen behind Mount Yungju to reside there.

Students gathered like clouds, and after some time, he traveled to Min Province, where he built a thatched hut at Yangyu in Changle. Thirteen people who followed him attained the Dharma. He later moved to Yunchu in Xiaoxi.
Mennan. Later, he accepted the invitation of Chancellor Zhang Wei-gong Xu to Mount Jing. On the day he ascended the hall, a monk asked:
"The assembly of humans and devas has gathered; the field for selecting Buddhas is opened. The Patriarchal Command is being enacted—how do you proclaim it?

The Master said: "A dull bird flies against the wind. The monk said: "Throughout the entire world there is no place to seek; clearly, a single point is perfect within the seat. The Master said: "People..."
There is no water that does not flow toward the east. Furthermore, as monks vied with one another to emerge, the Master restrained them, saying:
"Suppose the entire great earth were ground into dust, and each grain of dust possessed a single mouth; suppose each mouth were endowed with the mark of a broad and long tongue free from obstruction;
suppose each tongue produced immeasurable varieties of sound; and suppose each sound uttered immeasurable varieties of speech."
Regarding these words: each and every word possesses immeasurable distinctions of wondrous meaning, as numerous as the atoms of the aforementioned dust.

Suppose every patch-robed monk were to possess such a mouth, such a tongue, such a voice, such words, and such wondrous meanings, and simultaneously posed hundreds of thousands of difficult questions—each question distinct from the others—and yet, they would all be resolved at once by the Elder’s single cough.
The answer is finished. Taking advantage of that moment, within that interval, he performs immeasurable, boundless, and vast Buddha-works;

each and every Buddha-work pervades the entire Dharma-realm. That is to say, manifesting spiritual transformations from a single hair, all Buddhas together preach the sutras for immeasurable eons without reaching their limit.
If you simply proceed in this manner, you will attain entry into the bustling gate and courtyard; yet, you must observe this with the True Eye.
"Come! This is precisely the state where karmic consciousness is vast and desolate, with no foundation to rely upon. Under the gate of the Patriarchs, not even a single point is of use;
how much less so are these pedantic phrases and the flaunting of verbal acuity? Not only do they bury the ancestral vehicle of the past, but they also break open the nostrils of the monks.
Therefore it is said: 'A thought tied to a hair’s breadth is the cause for the three realms of suffering. In a mere flash..."
Sentiments arise; ten thousand kalpas of bondage ensue. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? When you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction.
Observe how the former sages issued such warnings: they were like the weapons of a state, used only when there was no other choice. This is the fundamental matter.
Above, there is likewise no such news. Today, this mountain monk’s raising of this theme is much like speaking of a dream while dreaming, or gouging a sore on healthy flesh.
If one were to examine this closely, he deserves a blow from the staff. Is there anyone present now who can bring down that lethal hand?
If there is, you will be worthy of repaying unrequited kindness and assisting in the transformation of non-action. If not, [it is] overturned.
"By practicing this, one causes [delusion] to depart. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Holding the Mohe sword crosswise, I issue the full decree;

throughout the realm of Great Peace, I slay the foolish and obstinate. He struck the ground with the staff, gave a shout, and immediately descended from the seat. The prosperity of his Dharma teachings was unsurpassed in that era;
his assembly numbered over two thousand, all of whom were eminent talents from every quarter. Zhang Gong Jiucheng, the Minister of the Board of Rites, also followed him as a disciple.
He attained a clear and sudden realization. One day, as a result of discussing state affairs, he incurred trouble along with the Master.
In the fifth month of the *xinyou* year of the Shaoxing era, he surrendered his monastic certificates and lived in seclusion in Hengyang.

There, he compiled the recorded sayings of former virtuous masters, interspersing them with his own critical comments (*nianti*), dividing them into three fascicles and titling them *Zhengfayan zang* (The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye). After ten years, he moved to Mei Yang; five years later, Emperor Gaozong...

By the Emperor’s special grace, he was released and returned home. In the spring of the following year, he donned the *saṃghāṭī* robe once more; though invitations were extended from all quarters with vacant seats prepared for him, he generally did not accept them.

Later, he received an imperial decree to reside at Yuyang Monastery. More than a year later, by imperial edict, he was transferred to Mount Jing. Monastics and laypeople admired him as they had before.
When Emperor Xiaozong was still the Prince of Puan, he dispatched an Inner Palace Supervisor into the mountains to pay his respects to the Master.

The Master composed a verse as an offering. While [the Emperor] was residing at the imperial residence, he again dispatched an inner attendant to the mountain to provide offerings for five hundred arhats and requested the Master to preach the Dharma to extend the Emperor’s holy longevity.
The Emperor personally inscribed the three characters "Miaoxi An" (Wondrous Joy Hermitage) and composed a eulogy to honor and send it to him.
