Chan Master Xing of Daopei in Tanzhou ascended the hall, held his staff horizontally, and said:
"All of you, if you understand it here, it is like Ji Xin mounting the nine-dragon carriage; if you do not understand it here, it is like Xiang Yu losing his thousand-li black steed.
Even if you manage to avoid both of these, you still fall into the armor of non-action. If you turn toward this..."
Having cleared away all obstructions along the way, turned his body, and exhaled his breath, the mountain monk handed him the staff and leaned upon it.
He descended from the seat and ascended the hall, saying: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not an object. Tell me, what is it?
It is not within, it is not without, it is not in between. Ultimately, where does it reside? Suffering! Suffering! There is."
It cannot be expressed in words. Having no home, where can one return?
A monk asked Chan Master Yuan of Daolin in Tanzhou, "Before the bell has tolled and before the drum has sounded, toward what destination does one go when striking the alms bowl?
Deshan simply lowered his head and returned to his quarters. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A rushing lightning bolt; a bursting fire."
[The student] asked: "Yantou said, 'This old fellow has not yet realized the final word.
What about that? The Master said: "He followed along. [The student] asked: "Yantou secretly revealed his meaning. I do not know where it was that he secretly revealed it.
The Master said: "The Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands on Mount Zhurong. [The student] said: "Even so, he could only live for three years. After three years..."

When the Master was about to pass away, he ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, addressed the assembly, saying: "Setting aside form, sound, and speech, bring me a single phrase. The assembly remained silent. The Master said: "Beyond movement and stillness, beyond sound and form—people of this age refuse to respond. This applies to both the mundane and the supramundane. He then passed away. At the time of his final departure, he returned to the fundamental point; was there not indeed an end? The Master said: *Mānida huṃ phaṭ*.

When he was about to manifest his nirvana, he ascended the hall, took up his staff, and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Apart from form and sound, apart from words and language, speak a single phrase! The assembly had no response. The Master said:

"Outside of movement and stillness, outside of sound and form, people of this age are unwilling to respond. [This holds true for] the mundane world and the world-transcending realm. He finished speaking.
"Ultimately, who can understand this? Having finished speaking, he leaned on his staff and passed away.
Chan Master Zu Zheng, an elder monk from Dahuang in Suizhou and a native of the Pan family of Tanzhou, ascended the hall and said:
"Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. How can one explain the principle of this 'alone being revealed'? Raising his whisk, he said: "Reaching the river..."
The territory of Wu has come to an end; across the river, the mountains of Yue are many. A monk asked:

"Yunmen asked a monk, 'Luminous and silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges—this is surely the speech of the scholar Zhang Zhuo, is it not? The monk said, 'It is. Yunmen said, 'Your words have fallen.
I do not know where this monk’s words fell. The Master said: "A catfish climbing a bamboo pole. [The monk] asked: "Setting aside words and phrases, please..."
The Master pointed directly. The Master held up his whisk. The monk asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "There is.
The monk asked, "What is that which is further beyond? The Master said, "Quickly prostrate three times."
Chan Master Shantang Dechun of Letan in Longxing Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Juzhi’s single finger-tip; a single hair plucks out nine oxen.
The Flower Peak mountains reach to the azure heavens; the Yellow River flows from its very depths. Cut off the finger and quickly look back!
Before the green bamboo hat, there are boundless matters; beneath the green straw raincoat, everything ceases at once."
Chan Master Fukan of Buan Monastery in Yixing, Changzhou, a native of the Lin family of Fuzhou, ascended the hall and said:
"The heavens are vast and the earth is wide; the wind is clear and the moon is bright. This is the season when the world is at peace.
When a patch-robed monk is casually questioned about it, ten out of ten have five or six who know it exists. But as for the night when the pond of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra swallows up Yang..."
"Disciples, when Kaibiao Bridge struck down Pingshan Pagoda, did you all know it?
If you do know, try bringing forth a single phrase from the realm of the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought. If you do not yet know, [the Master] threw down his whisk and said:
'It must be this mountain monk’s whisk that can do so.'"
Zen Master Zu Xuan of Shiting Wild Hermitage in Longxing Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Have you finished eating your congee? Zhaozhou had no taboos;
yet he further ordered the bowl to be washed—this is truly beyond reproach. To claim one has attained awakening is not yet being a true man.
This monk could not avoid being smeared with such nonsense. Whether there is an instruction or no instruction, the four corners of Mount Shao have completely collapsed."
The ground; entering hell like an arrow shot. From the cloud-capped peaks, a pure breeze arises in the great hall. Meeting, they take each other’s hands and ascend the high mountain.
The author must distinguish between the true and the false. How can one discuss the distinction between the true and the false? At midnight, the cold moon emerges from the sea gate.
Master Shishuang Zuigan of Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "Sending off the old year and welcoming the new year—every movement and function does not depart from within the light and shadow.
The clear radiance is profound and deep; the night hall is cold. I ask you all: do you understand?
If you do understand, you add flaws and blemishes. If you do not understand, you remain as before in ignorance. I shall point out for you the mechanism that cuts off the flow. White clouds..."
Outside the Green Mountains:

Chan Master Nankang Jun Yunju Peng’an Dehui, a successor of National Teacher Shitou Hui, was a native of the He family in Chongqing Prefecture. Once, he ascended the hall and said: [He] raised the following case:
The teaching is the Middle Way. If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. What is the principle of these "non-marks"?
Feigning flight, feigning shame, casting a sidelong glance: the bamboo gate is half-closed, a single branch of blossoms.
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Monastery in Quanzhou,

a descendant of the seventeenth generation under Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Jiaozhong Guang, was born to the Cai family in Ganzhou. On a spring day, he ascended the hall and held up [the whisk].
He struck the ground once with his staff and said, "First, strike the head of the spring ox. He struck it again and said, "Afterward, strike the tail of the spring ox.
Startled, he leaps from the void into the interior of a lotus fiber; Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks, and Maitreya flees in haste for a thousand li.
Mañjuśrī, however, knows where it lands; he claps his hands and laughs with joy. But tell me, what is it that he rejoices in?

"The spring breeze entered the gate last night; behold, a thousand blossoms have sprouted from the tip of the pestle. Entering the hall, he said: "The pavilions and towers of a thousand households, all in a single gust of autumn wind.
One knows only that a coolness arises in one's sleeves, unaware that the leaves are falling from the gardens. If you can realize this point, [you will understand].
The entire realm of touch is the absolute reality. Should this not yet be so, let us meet for a moment with formal greetings regarding the weather.

Entering the hall, [the Master] cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying: "The Buddha told Subhūti: 'In all those lands, whatever various kinds of minds sentient beings possess, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all these minds are non-minds; it is precisely because they are thus called mind. He continued: "Essentially..."
"Do you understand? When one’s ambition is fulfilled by the spring breeze, the horse’s hooves race swiftly; in a single day, one beholds all the splendors of Chang’an.

A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the past established the precepts for the summer retreat to guard the feet and dwell in seclusion. What is the underlying principle of this? The Master said, "Mount Sumeru is placed within a lapis lazuli bowl."
The monk shouted; the Master struck him.
Chan Master Tanyu of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an, whose secular surname was Lu of Tiantai, left home under Dao-rong of Zifu Monastery.
At sixteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. Later, he abandoned that path to visit Dahui at Mount Jing and call upon Xuechao.
At first, Ciyuan entered Min Province and stayed at Dongshan and Xishan Chan monasteries, but he had no realization. He went to Quannan, where Jiaozhong appointed him as the attendant (*yuèzhòng*).
Upon resigning from his post, he returned to his former quarters. One day, while casually discussing the karmic conditions of Xiangyan striking the bamboo, he attained sudden and clear awakening.

He composed a verse and presented it to Zong. Zong cited Xuefeng’s words, "Xiansha has not yet reached the ultimate," to interrogate him; Ciyuan responded without obstruction. Zong said, "Only then may you see the wondrous."
Xiji immediately took his leave and went to Mei Yang, where he served with diligence for four years. After taking up residence there, he ascended the hall and said:

"The Buddhas appearing in the world rob and kill; the Patriarchs coming from the West blow wind and set fires. The spiritual friends of past and present have the mouths of Buddhas but the hearts of snakes.
The monks of the world throw themselves into cages and traps; is there not one man of natural magnanimity and exceptional integrity to serve as a pillar for the School?"
He extended one hand and asked, "Is this one who upholds the Buddha-dharma? After a long silence, he said, "Even if there were such a person, they would still have to be cut into three pieces.
He ascended the hall and said, "Deshan’s informal teaching (xiaocan) was 'no speaking in response. For a thousand ages, the monastic communities have made this a famous saying.

To those who ask questions, he gave thirty blows; he was well-versed in scolding and rebuking. At that time, a monk stepped forward—one truly capable of breaking through—and Deshan immediately [struck him].
Beating the elegant and refined scholar. Before you have even asked a question, he has a cangue upon his head and shackles upon his feet.
"Where are you from?"—at this first meeting, one's spirit is wounded. A man from Silla smiles joyfully as he takes my hand;
before he has even stepped onto the ship's railing, thirty blows are well-deserved. Still following along, deceiving one another—today, Huinuan issues such a verdict.

Later, he passed away, and his stupa was erected at his home mountain.

Jade dew hangs from the green grass; the golden wind stirs the white duckweed. A single cry from a cold wild goose calls forth those who have not yet awakened.
The Monk Fayan of Ba’en in Tingzhou was a native of Guozhou. He ascended the hall and, citing the karmic occasion of Juzhi pointing his finger, the Master said:
"A beautiful woman, having risen from sleep, is too lazy to comb her hair; she takes up a golden hairpin and, having inserted it, leaves it at that. In the end, one must return it to him."
His physique and bones were excellent; he possessed a refined elegance that required no rouge or powder.
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Sheng family of Yuanquian.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Yikan of Mingkong Monastery as his teacher. He first studied under Dayu Hongzhi and Zhengtang Daoyuan. Later, he heard Donglin say:
The assembly said, "In our place there is nothing else mysterious or subtle; we have only gruel made of wood shavings and rice with iron nails for you to chew.

The Master secretly rejoiced at these words and went directly to pay his respects. He set forth his insights and understanding, to which Lin replied, "According to your way of seeing, you are sitting right within the realm of reflective awareness.
The Master’s doubts did not cease, so he cast away everything he had previously acquired all at once. One day—
He heard the assembly cite Nanquan’s saying: "When people of this age see this single stalk of blossoms, it is as if they were in a dream.
He silently attained an awakening and said, "Beating the grass is only intended to startle the snake. The next day, he entered the room. Lin asked, "Where did Yantou secretly reveal his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief red-handed. Lin said, "The nature of the Great Master Bodhidharma..."
"Your life is in your own hands. As the Master was about to open his mouth, [Linji] suddenly struck him across the chest with a fist.

He was instantly awakened to the Great Enlightenment, to the point that sweat poured down his back. Nodding his head, he said to himself: "When Linji said, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this,' how could it have been empty words?
He then presented a verse, saying: "To act for others, one must act thoroughly; to kill a person, one must see blood. Deshan and...
Yantou said, "Ten thousand miles, a single line of iron. Later, after Linran had taken up residence, he ascended the hall and said:

"The World-Honored One spoke what was not spoken; Kāśyapa heard what was not heard. He struck his staff and said: "Where do the flowing waters and yellow leaves come from? An ox, trailing crows of winter, passes through a distant village.
Ascending the hall again, he cited Xuefeng’s instruction to the assembly: "The entire earth is this gate of liberation. Why..."
He tried to pull him in, but could not; the Master said, "Great Xuefeng has split the conversation into two parts.
Since the entire earth is this gate of liberation, why use force to pull? Ascending the hall, he said: "If you go on in this way exclusively, the weeds before the Dharma Hall will be a fathom deep.
If you come back in this way exclusively, the mud underfoot will be three feet deep. Tell me, what is it then? Three.
A year has encountered an intercalary month; the rooster cries toward the fifth watch. Ascending the hall, the Master raised the example of the late teacher Wan’an, who said:
"Sitting on the Buddha’s seat, he hacks at the Buddha’s feet; he does not revere Confucius of the eastern house, yet goes abroad to practice ritual and music.

The Master said: "There is no doubt that he enters the mud and the water, but what can the late teacher do? A cicada clings to a withered tree; its weeping is exhausted, yet it does not turn its head back."
Holding up his staff, he said, "It is evident that there are those who do not turn their heads back. At Jingci, I would prostrate three times to you from within a grain measure.

Entering the hall, [he said]: "The Buddhas of the three periods speak of existence within non-existence, like picking out a flower-needle from a heap of chaff. The Patriarchs of the six generations..."
Seeking existence within non-existence is like a monkey reaching for the moon reflected in water. How can one speak of the Dharma by departing from these two paths?

I, this fellow, care not for matters of rise and fall; all day long I dwell amidst the clouds, occupying the Lake Dongting. When Yuan’an received an invitation from Zhìzhě, he led the assembly, saying:
On the Southern Mountain dwells an old Demon King. His piercing eyes emit flashes of lightning; his mouth is like a blood-basin as he scolds the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
his teeth are like sword-trees as he reviles all quarters. Several times the winds of karma have blown upon him, yet he remains unmoved.

But when they can move him—by the Yellow Clouds and Mount Huang, alongside Sengtou Tuo and Fu Dashi, with one great conflagration that razes his dwelling—he returns once more to his old self, Meng Bala. What a rascal!
He deluded countless men and women; with eyes wide open, he entered the boiling cauldron in full view.
Suddenly, a monk came forth and said, "Since you are a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend), why do you lead people into the boiling cauldron? He replied to him, "This is not within your sphere.
Later, he passed away and was interred in a small hermitage to the south of the temple.
Chan Master Zhizhe Yu’nan Zhenci of Wuzhou was a native of Tongchuan. His secular surname was Li. Initially, he took refuge with Chengdu Zhengfa Monastery to enter the monastic order.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled among the lecture halls to study the teachings. While listening to a discourse on the *Awakening of Faith*, he reached the passage:

"When the four great elements are each separated, where will this deluded body now abide? Ultimately it has no substance; it is truly identical to a magical illusion. Thereupon, he attained a realization and composed [this verse]: [Verse follows]
The verse says: A single bright pearl is here with me; touch it or move it, and it emits light that shakes the earth.
When presented to various lecturers, none were able to understand it. Returning home, he presented it to his own teacher, who then questioned him using the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan.
The teacher said: "Though there be hundreds, thousands, ten millions, or billions of koans, they do not go beyond this verse. His teacher, [having realized this...]
[The Master] considered this disrespectful and shouted at him to leave. Thereupon, the Master traveled south and stayed at the Yuan Tong Monastery on Mount Lu to have his portrait enshrined.

At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Preceptor. When he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following koan: "A monk asked Yunmen, 'When one sweeps away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, 'The Buddha is also dust.
As soon as Wan’an uttered these words, the Master let out a shout and pointed to his chest, saying, "The Buddha is also dust! The Master [then departed].
Again, he spoke in verse: "Shaking off the dust, one sees the Buddha; the Buddha, too, is but dust. Question resolved, answer resolved—turning over directly beneath one's feet.
I urge you to drink yet another cup of wine: once you have passed the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friend remaining. He further spoke a verse on the Samādhi of Dust-to-Dust:
Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket; a rare *kūṇapa* (Kunlun man) sits at the bottom of the abyss. One speck of dust climbs up Mount Sumeru.
A clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers. He laughs and snaps his fingers: a pure breeze rises upon the coral branches. Wanzan deeply approved of this.
Chan Master Mukan An’ō of Gushan, Fuzhou, successor of Chan Master Xū of Xichán: He was the son of the Wu family of Min County. At the age of twenty, he became a monk.
Not long after, he visited Lǎn’ān at Yúnmén. One day, while entering the inner chamber for instruction, Lǎn’ān said: “I do not ask about words; I do not ask about no-words.”

He said, "World-Honored One," and after a long pause, he could not find the World-Honored One in the place where he had been standing for so long. He then gave a shout and suddenly attained realization.

He prostrated and said, "Had it not been for today's question, how could I have lost the opportunity right before my eyes? Yunmen granted him permission. After he took up residence there, [he continued his teaching].
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "If you wish to clarify this matter, you must possess the skillful means of the 'flashing lightning' and the 'striking spark.
Only then can you cast off your entire body at the precipitous crag and find great peace in the depths of the white clouds.

If you instead peer about the ground searching for a golden needle, your skull will surely burst asunder right now. Even if you were to adapt yourself according to the situation upon reaching this point," [he continued].

To encounter the sharp edge [of the sword] and emerge with one's whole body alone and liberated is like wading through mud and water. But as for this single phrase of the fundamental division being fully raised—how would you speak of it?
He struck the whisk and said: "The seven stars are drawn forth, their light brilliant; having mastered the art of wielding them, one may roam freely throughout the world.
He ascended the hall and cited Master Muzhou’s address to the assembly, saying: "If you people have not yet attained an entrance, you must first attain one..."
"Regarding the point of entry: once you have attained this point of entry, you must not forget this old monk.
The Master said, "Speaking in such a manner—how thick is your face? Muduan said, "It is not so. As long as you people have not attained a point of entry, you must attain a point of entry.
Once you have attained a point of entry, you must cast that very point of entry away before you can succeed. He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said:
Linji’s little servant boy has never spoken directly to the point; today he puts on a display of total feigned innocence, wishing for everyone to know that there is something more.
He throws down his staff and descends from the seat. A monk asked, "What is it like when one turns over and stands upside down atop Mount Sumeru?
The Master said, "I have never seen the Morning Star appear. The monk said, "In that case, the oceans will overflow and the mountains will topple."
The Master said, "Do not act recklessly. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "The sound of thunder is vast, yet there are no drops of rain.
Zen Master Nanya of Longxiang Baitang in Wenzhou ascended the hall and said: "Upon the summit of Rui Peak, by the Phoenix Pavilion, we rely on each other with a bowl of plain congee;
with our hundred-seam robes covering our heads, we sit in meditation. The Second Patriarch prostrated three times and remained in his place."
To stand up [and speak] like this is already a complete and exhaustive explanation. Old Dharma, that barbarian from the north, has stripped away both marrow and skin;
it is a scene of total disorder. As for the rest of his followers, what is there worth mentioning? When Potaung speaks thus, will he escape the censure of the various quarters? Or not?

Tapping the rope bed, he said: "It would have been better to let the prisoner remain so that his wisdom might grow. He ascended the hall and said: "The great capacity values directness; the great function values sudden manifestation.

Even if there were a 'biting-the-lead' mechanism, it must be struck down with a single hammer-blow. Why? Because within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade. He ascended the hall and said:
"The purple ferns stretch out their fists as the bamboo shoots break through the tips; the willow blossoms have flown away, and the green shadows interlace."
This is clearly the single-line transmission of the Western Patriarch: the oriole calls and the swallow speaks in its nest.

If you can see the truth here and believe it thoroughly, then according to the standards of other quarters, you would be settled beneath a bright window. But under the gate of Longxiang, one is simply struck dead by a single blow of the mallet.
Why? It is not that I find it difficult to dwell with others; rather, for the most part, the distinction between the ordained and the laity must be clear.
Chan Master Tianwang Zhiqing of Fuzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he said:
"This very thing cannot be covered by heaven, nor can it be supported by earth. It pervades the world and pervades space; it forms a mass and forms a lump.
Reaching this point, where can the Buddhas of the three periods find it to grasp? Where can the Patriarchs of the six generations find it to uphold? All you patch-robed monks under heaven..."
Monk, where is "miao" (to reach/attain) to be found? Unless one attains it for oneself and realizes it for oneself, one merely practices the dual movement of striking and singing.
Even so, this is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk walks. What, then, is the place where a patch-robed monk walks?
He plunges his body across the sea of right and wrong; he strides freely through the thicket of jackals and tigers.
The Master of the Anfen Hermitage at Jianmen in Nanjian Prefecture had studied under Mukan in the Ankuo Monastery during his youth.
Later, he relied upon Lan’an, yet he had not yet attained profound realization. He took leave to visit Daie of Jing Mountain; while traveling along the riverbank, he gazed up at the imperial palace.
Hearing the Street Official shout, "The Minister is coming," he was suddenly and greatly enlightened. He composed a verse, saying: "For many years this matter has hung upon my breast;
I have questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened. Now, at this moment, liver and gall are both rent asunder— A single cry:
'The Minister comes upon the river! He then went straight back to Xichan. Lan’an welcomed him and bestowed upon him the *kāṣāya*. From that time on, he no longer followed formal regulations.
Yuyu later lived as a hermit at Jianmen, where his transformative influence spread throughout the regions south of the Ling Mountains. Students followed him;
the gāthās and verses he composed were produced with the speed of a swift hand, totaling over a thousand pieces that became widely circulated in the world. He addressed the assembly:

"Regarding this very field of land, you people—tell me, before heaven and earth were yet divided, where did it abide? Penetrate directly to the bottom right now; otherwise, you will already be dull-witted."
"Setting aside the matter of the *śrāmaṇera* and the *sthavira*, it is not yet finished. If you further attempt to deliberate or reflect, it will be more than ten thousand miles of white clouds.
He suddenly seized his staff, dispersed the assembly, and addressed them: "From the Buddhas above down to all sentient beings below, their very lives are entirely in the hands of this mountain monk.
When examined, there is immeasurable transgression; is there anyone who can examine it?"
"Is this it? He struck his staff once and said, "The wrongdoer has a head; the debt has a master.
Then, looking left and right, he said, "Since coming out of the cave, there has been no rival hand; where one can show leniency, one should show leniency. He addressed the assembly:
"Before the fifteenth day, all the stars in heaven face north; after the fifteenth day, among men, there is no water that does not flow toward the sea."
"East! Both what has come before and what follows after are cast aside. In every place, local dialects differ. He then snapped his fingers and said:
"One, two, three, four, five; six, seven, eight, nine, ten; eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen.
Brothers, today is the [what]th? After a long pause, he said: "In our shop, we do not sell on credit for even a single coin."
Chan Master Zongdai of Gushan, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Dongchan Yue, ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One said: 'One should know thus; one should see thus.'"
Understanding it thus, he did not give rise to the notion of dharmas. He then shouted, saying: "Jade is originally without flaw, yet it has flaws.

Chan Master Zongying of Qianyuan in Fuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Jing of Xichan, ascended the hall. Striking his staff on the ground, he said: "A hot-tempered fellow is found in but one [place]."
[He] struck [the ground]. Leaning on his staff, he said, "A person of keen intelligence does not need to be prompted again. Is there anyone here now who is so keen?
After a long silence, he said, "When one attempts to capture a qilin, even a rabbit does not appear."
The Daoist Wu Shisan of Mount Xianzhou in Jianning Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Kai Shan Qian. He frequently used his own spiritual matters to question various Chan masters.

When Kai Shan returned, he built a thatched hut to the left [of the mountain] and Wu Shisan went there to serve him. On the eighth day of the third month in the Gengshen year of the Xiaoshing era (1140), at night—
Suddenly, he attained awakening and presented a verse to Shōan, saying: "Originally there was no seam or crack; Upon being touched, it immediately shines forth.
Since this is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, Why need one use it to shoot at sparrows? Shōan replied: "When it snaps with a *tsū* sound, true joy and liberation arise;
Birth-and-death, ordinary and sage, all sink into stillness. Laughing "ha ha" beneath the mountain of Senjū, I do not fail the heart we pledged to each other long ago."

Chan Master Mian Xianjie of Tiantong in Qingyuan Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tiandong Huihua. He was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou. His mother dreamed that an old monk from Mount Lu entered her quarters before she gave birth to him.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and awakened; he left home to become a monk and, undaunted by the hardships of travel, went everywhere to seek instruction.
Zhishi later visited Ying’an at Mingguo Monastery in Quzhou. Ying’an was solitary and rigid, difficult to approach, and Zhishi was frequently rebuked by him.
One day, Ying’an asked, “What is the True Dharma Eye? The Master immediately replied, “A broken sandpot. Ying’an nodded his approval.

Not long after, Zhishi took his leave to return home to visit his parents. As he departed, Ying’an sent him off with this verse: “The Great Penetration of the Opportune Phrase, Revealing the Summit of the Head in the Open Presence.”

We have followed one another for four years now; though you interrogated me exhaustively, not a trace remains. Although I have not yet handed over the bowl and robe, my spirit and bearing swallow the heavens and earth.
Yet you take the Eye of the True Dharma and call it a broken sand-pot. On this journey to pay your respects, take care not to simply kick up your heels.
"I have my final word; wait until you return, and I shall require you to follow it. He was the founder of the Quyu Monastery in Chushi. Subsequently, he moved to Xiangfu, Jiangshan, and Huazang.
Before long, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Jingshan and Lingyin. In his later years, he lived at Taibai. A monk asked, "What is it like when empty space itself dissolves?
The Master said, "The punishment shall not be doubled for the crime. He ascended the hall and said: "Niutou expounded horizontally and vertically, yet..."
To know that there is a "transcendental pivot" (shangxiang guanzili) is something entirely different from those lacquer-jar types who cannot distinguish east from west or north from south;
for them to ask, "What is the transcendental pivot? is no different from wetting one's bed while wide awake. Huazang has a turning phrase that lies neither above nor below;
even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot find it by groping about, for it is like a cold rain with nowhere to fall.
Dried in the sun. Today there was a communal labor (fussing) for the sake of making offerings to the great assembly. After a long while, he said: "Master Bodhidharma had no front teeth.
He ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One spoke what is not spoken; he twisted the crooked to make it straight. Kāśyapa heard what is not heard; he called out to the empty sky.
Mazu’s 'This very mind is Buddha' is like hanging a goat's head to sell dog meat. Zhaozhou’s examination of the hermitage master is buying at a high price."
Selling it cheaply, it is not worth a single coin. Take for instance Mañjuśrī, the teacher of the seven Buddhas—why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
When the river sky reflects the moon’s halo, the fish spawn; when the wind stirs the oak leaves, the deer grow their antlers.
Entering the hall, he struck the meditation staff and said, "When deluded, one is deluded by this very thing. Striking it once more, he said, "When awakened, one awakens to this very thing."
When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, one adds another scoop of dung to the refuse heap.
Can anyone say a single word from the place where the total function is uniquely liberated—where one emerges in the east and sinks in the west? If you cannot say it, Huazang shall speak for himself.
He threw down his staff and said, "Thirty years hence. He then ascended the hall and cited Master Jinfeng’s address to the assembly, which said:
"Twenty years ago, this old monk possessed a 'motherly heart'; twenty years hence, I shall have no 'motherly heart. At that time, a monk asked:

"What is it like for the Master to have had a 'motherly heart' twenty years ago? Feng said, "If asked about the ordinary, I answer with the ordinary; if asked about the sacred, I answer with the sacred.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like for the Master to have no 'motherly heart' twenty years later? Feng said, "If asked about the ordinary, I do not answer with the ordinary;
if asked about the sacred, I do not answer with the sacred. The Master said, "Had Wugu seen this at the time, he would simply have let out two cold laughs."
If this old fellow were suddenly to have a glimpse of reality, he would naturally not fall into the conceptual traps of the holy or the ordinary.
Entering the hall, the Master raised the case of the old woman burning the hermitage. He said, "Regarding this koan, there are few in the monastic communities who can properly address it.
I, Zen Master Jie, have torn my own face open; I cannot avoid suffering a defeat here, yet I wish for those from all quarters to examine it. Thereupon, he called to the assembly.
It is said: This old woman’s inner chamber is deep and secure, impenetrable as a sealed vessel. Yet she uniquely gathers blossoms upon withered trees and ignites flames within cold crags.

This monk stands solitary and remote, accustomed to entering surging waves; he casually cuts off the tide that rises to the heavens, yet in the end his body remains without so much as a drop of water.
If one examines this closely, it is not a matter of striking shackles or beating chains.
"There are not two people. If this is so, you have not even dreamed of the Buddha-dharma. Wugu, in maintaining such a stance, where does his ultimate intent lie?
After a long silence, he said: "A handful of willow threads cannot be gathered; they are draped with mist upon the jade balustrade."

Ascending the hall, he said: "A single movement of the strings reveals a different melody; a fallen leaf makes known the autumn. To raise one and clarify the three is to discern the weight of every grain with the eye.
Like a king wielding a sword, killing or giving life is decided in the moment—yet this is still like ripples upon a windless lake.
As for the one path beyond, where the thousand sages walk hand-in-hand, it would be fitting to enter the hells. At such a time as this, what should be done? The River."

In the two provinces of Zhejiang, spring is cold and autumn is hot. Entering the hall for instruction: To call the entire universe and all the great earth "one phrase" is to carry a cangue and wear shackles;
not to call it "one phrase" is to have one's karmic consciousness wandering in a blur. To be completely liberated from both extremes is to be pure and naked.
"Naked and bare, there is nothing to grasp. The single school of Bodhidharma has been swept away to its very foundations. Thus did Master Yunmen say:
"Even if the entire universe were free of even the slightest affliction, it would still be a 'turning phrase. To not see a single dharma—"

This was merely a partial presentation; one must further know that there is also a time for the complete presentation. Master Yunmen, great as he was, has long since had his sword taken away, yet here we are marking the boat.
Later, he passed into nirvana and was interred in a stupa on the central peak of the monastery.
Nanshujia was a native of Fuzhou. Having long relied upon Ying’an, he attained a sudden and profound realization through the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature.
He composed a verse which said: “The dog has no Buddha-nature; Rāhu enters its destiny.
It is not that it kills people; Rather, it is surely killed by others. When Ying’an saw this, he rejoiced in his carefree liberation. At the end of the Shaoxing era, he passed away at Guizong.
The layman Li Hao, a Minister of the Court (Shilang), whose courtesy name was De-yuan and sobriquet Zheng-xin, had read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as a youth;

it was as if he were wandering through a familiar old country, and he held it in his mind without forgetting. Later, while serving in office, he visited Mingguo Temple and entered the room to seek instruction from Ying’an.

Ying’an thrust his hand toward the layman’s chest and asked, “After you die, Minister, where will you go? The layman was struck with terror and broke into a cold sweat. Ying’an shouted at him and sent him out. The layman—
He withdrew from formal study, yet within less than ten days he had ascended to the inner sanctum of the Dharma hall. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kangchao, saying:

"The gate has the shop of Sun Bin; The home preserves the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early in the morning— Who awakens, and who is deluded? Yuan'an was praised as virtuous by the hermitage.
There was also a seller of rouge who had likewise long studied under Ying’an and considered himself quite accomplished. Yuan’an presented him with this verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Without applying rouge or powder, he is naturally elegant and refined. Often, practitioners of Chan stop here.
Having passed through the snares of past and present, they come back here to receive a blow of the fist.
Chan Master Youquan Yian of Huazang in Changzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Quan of Daochang. He was the son of the Qi family of Qihua in Lin’an.
At the age of fourteen, he received full ordination; at eighteen, he paid his respects to Chan Master Fozhi Yu at Lingyin Monastery, where Wuan was then the first seat.
While seated in his room, he questioned [his teacher] about how all phenomena are established from the root of non-abiding.
After a long time, the Master attained realization and replied: "Sewing a needle in the dark; drawing breath through the ears. The Hermit approved and secretly transmitted the seal of mind to him.

Once, while sitting in meditation through the night until dawn, the one who distributed rice gruel arrived; the Master forgot to spread out his alms bowl. A neighboring monk touched it with his hand, whereupon the Master was awakened and composed a verse.
He said: "A black-lacquered Kunlun man holds a fishing rod; the ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the surging rapids.

Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, drawing the blind turtle onto the fishing boat. Fozhi once asked: "When the mind encompasses the great void and its capacity spans the vast realms of the sands, what then?
The Master replied: "The great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Fozhi stroked his seat and said: "This boy..."
"One day you shall occupy this seat; then you will go about scolding the Buddhas and reviling the Patriarchs. From that time on, the Master concealed his talents and remained increasingly humble.
He traveled through the regions of Lake Dongting, the Xiang, the Yangtze, and Zhejiang for nearly ten years. He stayed with Ying’an at Guizong and studied under Dahui at Mount Jing.
When Wuan resided at Daochang, he invited the Master to share the teaching seat. Thereupon, his reputation became widely known.
After residing [in the monastery], he ascended the hall and said: "Today, the mouth of the sack is tied shut. You clear-eyed monks, do not run about in confusion.
When mental activity ceases, one turns the body around; even a sneeze becomes a lion’s roar. In a sandalwood forest, let them gallop at will.

Raising the eyebrows, they grow upon the crown of the head; carving flesh to form a sore reveals the family’s disgrace. He ascended the hall again and said: "Zen! Zen! Without faction, without partiality."
When deluded, one is separated by a thousand li; when awakened, it lies right at the edge of the lips. Thus, a monk asked Shishuang, "What is Chan?
Shishuang replied, "A glazed brick. Again, a monk asked Muzhou, "What is Chan? Muzhou said, "A fierce fire frying oil."
Furthermore, a monk asked Shoushan, "What is Chan? Shoushan replied, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind its head.

"Great assembly, the Way has no crossroads; where one stands is solitary and precarious. These three great elders traveled upon the living path before sound and employed the spiritual mechanism beyond kalpas.
Yet, if one were to examine them with the true eye of a patch-robed monk, there would be no lack of distinctions in their excellence. One was like Zhang..."
Excellent entry into the fray! One man employs his troops like Xiang Yu; another gauges the enemy like Kongming.
If one can discern between them clearly, they may stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Even so, suddenly a monk might come forth and say:
The Elder has split his words into two parts. Just now you said, "The Way has no cross-paths; it is without factionalism and without partiality.

Yet now you have again divided it into so many degrees of superiority and inferiority. How will you respond to this? Do you understand thoroughly? "Holding hands while climbing the mountain, we exert our strength together;
the breath passing through the throat is known only by oneself. In the autumn of the Gengzi year of the Chunxi era, he manifested a slight illness and left behind [these words].
Verse: He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Upon cremation, his teeth and tongue remained unburnt, and countless śarīras of five colors were obtained.
His remains were interred in a stupa on Mount Heng, and a portion of his bones was divided and returned for burial at Wannian Mountain Temple.

Shuanglin Yong Chanshi’s Dharma Successor, Master Sanfeng Yin of Wuzhou, ascended the hall and cited the story of the Wild Fox, saying: "Not falling and not being obscured—this is the crime of slandering others.
Not being obscured and not falling—this is binding oneself without a rope. Piteous indeed are the willow catkins following the spring breeze; sometimes they drift on their own."
Returning from the West to the East:
Chan Master Ziju Yuan of Deshan, a successor of Chan Master Xing of Dayue, was a native of Tongchuan. He ascended the hall and said: "When seeing the seeing..."
"It is not seeing. Even seeing is already apart from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. He then shouted, "The whale swallows the ocean until it is empty, revealing the coral branches!
Among the assembly, if a monk were suddenly to come forward and say, "Elder, stop your drowsy talk," he would grant that such a person possesses the "one eye.
Ascending the hall, he held his staff crosswise and said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven."
"7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Count them backward and forward in rotation until you reach the inexhaustible days of the future.
Because of seven, you see one; because of one, the seven vanish. You tread through the vast void; even the iron ox breaks into a sweat. Breath ceases; no trace remains.
He threw down his staff and said, "You must let go of this as well before it can truly be called the business of study."
[The discourse] concluded. He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not;
the staff wanders freely in all directions. Sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not; this mountain monk is topsy-turvy. Sometimes both person and environment are taken away;
the staff and I both erase our traces and swallow our voices. Sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away. [He struck the ground with the staff.]
The staff said: "Accompanying me for a thousand li, you have carried me across ten thousand mountains. Now that we have suddenly encountered Great Master Linji, what then?
He shouted: "Without clarifying the seal of the mind-ground, it is difficult to pass through the barrier of the Patriarchs."
The Five Lamps Compiled (Wǔdēng Huìyuán), Fascicle Twenty (End)
